### `WebApplicationFactory` — `ConfigureTestServices` Ordering Guarantee

`ConfigureTestServices` runs *after* `ConfigureServices`, which means it can remove or replace registrations added by `Program.cs`. However, when a test class calls `WithWebHostBuilder(...).ConfigureTestServices(...)` inside the test method (rather than in the constructor), a new `WebApplicationFactory` derivative is created each time — this is expensive. The recommended pattern is to use a shared factory for common setup and `WithWebHostBuilder` for per-test overrides only.

```csharp
// Recommended pattern: shared factory for infrastructure; per-test override for mocks
public class OrderApiTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;

    public OrderApiTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    {
        // Shared factory: configures DB, auth, and infrastructure once
        _factory = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
        {
            builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
            {
                // Replace real DB with SQLite in-memory — shared for all tests
                var descriptor = services.SingleOrDefault(
                    d => d.ServiceType == typeof(DbContextOptions<AppDbContext>));
                if (descriptor != null) services.Remove(descriptor);

                services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(opts =>
                    opts.UseSqlite("DataSource=:memory:"));
            });
        });
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrder_WithFakeEmailService_Returns200()
    {
        // Per-test override: swap email service only for this test
        var client = _factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
            builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
                services.AddScoped<IEmailService, FakeEmailService>()))
            .CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/orders/1");
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrder_WithRealEmailService_Returns200()
    {
        // No per-test override — uses shared factory as-is
        var client = _factory.CreateClient();
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/orders/1");
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Gotcha [community]:** Calling `WithWebHostBuilder` in the constructor stores a *derived* factory with configuration baked in — the `IClassFixture` lifetime still applies, so the factory is disposed when the test class is collected. Calling `WithWebHostBuilder` inside every test method creates a *new* server for each test, which is costly. Understand the lifetime: constructor setup is shared, method-level setup is per-test.

---

### `IClassFixture` vs `[CollectionFixture]` — Choosing the Right xUnit Scope

xUnit offers `IClassFixture<T>` (one fixture per class) and `[CollectionDefinition]`/`ICollectionFixture<T>` (one fixture shared across many classes). Integration tests that use `WebApplicationFactory` benefit from collection fixtures when many test classes hit the same application, cutting server startup cost from O(N classes) to O(1).

```csharp
// Collection definition — one WebApplicationFactory for all classes in the collection
[CollectionDefinition("OrderApiCollection")]
public class OrderApiCollectionFixture
    : ICollectionFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>> { }

// Each test class declares membership with [Collection(...)]
[Collection("OrderApiCollection")]
public class OrderGetTests
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public OrderGetTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task Get_Returns200() =>
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.OK,
            (await _client.GetAsync("/orders/1")).StatusCode);
}

[Collection("OrderApiCollection")]
public class OrderPostTests
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public OrderPostTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task Post_CreatesOrder()
    {
        var response = await _client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders",
            new { ProductId = "X", Quantity = 1 });
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Created, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** A collection-scoped factory means tests *share state* if the server's in-memory database is not reset between tests. Use `IDbContextFactory<T>` or a per-test scope to seed and clear data without restarting the server. Tests in the same collection also run *sequentially* by default (not in parallel) to protect shared state — this is the intended behaviour.

---

### SQLite In-Memory Database Over EF Core InMemory Provider in Integration Tests

The EF Core InMemory provider does not enforce referential integrity, cascade deletes, unique constraints, or SQL-level computed columns. SQLite in-memory over a shared `DbConnection` replicates real relational behaviour without requiring a running database server — critical for catching constraint violations in integration tests.

```csharp
// In WebApplicationFactory: replace production DB with SQLite in-memory
protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
{
    builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
    {
        // Remove existing DbContext options
        var dbOpts = services.SingleOrDefault(
            d => d.ServiceType == typeof(IDbContextOptionsConfiguration<AppDbContext>));
        if (dbOpts != null) services.Remove(dbOpts);

        // Register a shared SQLite in-memory connection
        // (must stay open so SQLite doesn't clear the in-memory DB)
        services.AddSingleton<DbConnection>(_ =>
        {
            var conn = new SqliteConnection("DataSource=:memory:");
            conn.Open();
            return conn;
        });

        services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>((sp, opts) =>
            opts.UseSqlite(sp.GetRequiredService<DbConnection>()));
    });
}

// Seed the database before each test using a DI scope
private async Task SeedAsync()
{
    using var scope = _factory.Services.CreateScope();
    var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
    await db.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync();
    db.Orders.RemoveRange(db.Orders);
    db.Orders.Add(new Order { Id = 1, ProductId = "SEED-ITEM", Quantity = 2 });
    await db.SaveChangesAsync();
}
```

**Why SQLite over InMemory:** The EF Core InMemory provider silently ignores `[Required]`, unique indexes, and foreign keys, producing false-green tests. SQLite in-memory enforces these at the SQL layer and is still zero-infrastructure (no Docker, no external server). The `DataSource=:memory:` connection string creates a private database per connection; use a *shared* open `DbConnection` instance to keep the database alive across requests during a test run.

---

### Mock Authentication Handler — Testing Authorised Endpoints Without a Real IdP

Replacing the authentication pipeline with a stub `AuthenticationHandler` lets integration tests verify authorised routes without spinning up an OAuth server. The stub handler issues a synthetic `ClaimsPrincipal` and can be parameterised per-test via `IOptionsMonitor<T>`.

```csharp
public class TestAuthHandlerOptions : AuthenticationSchemeOptions
{
    public string UserId { get; set; } = "test-user-001";
    public string[] Roles { get; set; } = [];
}

public class TestAuthHandler(
    IOptionsMonitor<TestAuthHandlerOptions> options,
    ILoggerFactory logger,
    UrlEncoder encoder)
    : AuthenticationHandler<TestAuthHandlerOptions>(options, logger, encoder)
{
    public const string SchemeName = "TestScheme";

    protected override Task<AuthenticateResult> HandleAuthenticateAsync()
    {
        var opts = Options;
        var claims = new List<Claim>
        {
            new(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier, opts.UserId),
            new(ClaimTypes.Name, "Test User")
        };
        claims.AddRange(opts.Roles.Select(r => new Claim(ClaimTypes.Role, r)));

        var identity  = new ClaimsIdentity(claims, SchemeName);
        var principal = new ClaimsPrincipal(identity);
        var ticket    = new AuthenticationTicket(principal, SchemeName);
        return Task.FromResult(AuthenticateResult.Success(ticket));
    }
}

// Usage in test class
[Fact]
public async Task AdminEndpoint_ForbidsNonAdmin()
{
    var client = _factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
        builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
        {
            services
                .AddAuthentication(TestAuthHandler.SchemeName)
                .AddScheme<TestAuthHandlerOptions, TestAuthHandler>(
                    TestAuthHandler.SchemeName,
                    opts => { opts.Roles = []; }); // no roles — should be Forbidden
        }))
        .CreateClient(new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions { AllowAutoRedirect = false });

    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
        new AuthenticationHeaderValue(TestAuthHandler.SchemeName);

    var response = await client.GetAsync("/admin/dashboard");
    Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Forbidden, response.StatusCode);
}
```

### .NET 10 `TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(long)` Single-Parameter Overload — Test Timeouts

.NET 10 adds a single-parameter `TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(long)` overload. Previously the method took `(long milliseconds, long seconds)` with a default for the second parameter, which prevented use inside LINQ expression trees. The new overload unblocks timeout configuration in expression-based test helpers.

```csharp
// .NET 10: single-parameter overload — works in expression trees
[TestMethod]
public async Task LongRunningOperation_CompletesWithinTimeout()
{
    // Expression-tree-compatible overload
    Expression<Func<TimeSpan>> timeoutExpr =
        () => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(5000); // was a compile error before .NET 10

    var timeout = timeoutExpr.Compile()();

    using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(timeout);
    await _sut.ProcessAsync(cts.Token);

    // If ProcessAsync didn't throw OperationCancelledException, it completed in time
    Assert.IsFalse(cts.IsCancellationRequested,
        "Operation cancelled — exceeded 5 000 ms timeout");
}

// Practical parameterised helper leveraging the new overload
public static CancellationToken TestTimeout(long milliseconds = 10_000)
    => new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(milliseconds)).Token;
```

**Gotcha [community]:** The existing `FromMilliseconds(long, long)` overload's second parameter is now **mandatory** in .NET 10. Any callers passing only the milliseconds argument to the two-parameter version must either migrate to the new single-parameter overload or supply the second argument explicitly. This is a source-compatible break for code compiled against .NET 9 but requiring .NET 10 SDK.

### NUnit 4.6 — `Assert.Multiple` with Awaitable Delegates

NUnit 4.4+ allows `Assert.Multiple` to accept an `async` delegate, enabling a block of async assertions to run independently without aborting on the first failure. This is useful when an async test needs to verify several side effects (e.g., database state + email + audit log) in one pass.

```csharp
[Test]
public async Task PlaceOrder_ProducesAllSideEffects()
{
    // Act
    await _sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new Order { ProductId = "X", Quantity = 2 });

    // Assert: multiple async checks — all run even if one fails
    await Assert.MultipleAsync(async () =>
    {
        // Check 1: order persisted in DB
        var order = await _db.Orders
            .FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.ProductId == "X");
        Assert.That(order, Is.Not.Null, "Order not persisted");
        Assert.That(order!.Status, Is.EqualTo("Placed"));

        // Check 2: confirmation email queued
        var emails = await _emailFake.GetSentAsync();
        Assert.That(emails, Has.Exactly(1).Items, "Expected one email");

        // Check 3: audit log entry written
        var audit = await _auditRepo.GetLatestAsync();
        Assert.That(audit?.Action, Is.EqualTo("OrderPlaced"), "Missing audit entry");
    });
}
```

**Why it matters:** Without `Assert.MultipleAsync`, the first failing `await` inside an async delegate would throw immediately, hiding subsequent failures. Surfacing all failures in one test run halves the debug/fix/re-run cycle for multi-effect operations.

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 25

**`WithWebHostBuilder` in every test method creates a new server per test [community]** — Calling `_factory.WithWebHostBuilder(...)` inside a test method body returns a *new* `WebApplicationFactory` that builds and starts a fresh server. With hundreds of tests, this causes O(N) server start costs. WHY: `WebApplicationFactory.WithWebHostBuilder` is designed for *child factories* that compose with, rather than replacing, the parent; a new host is started lazily on first `CreateClient()`. Fix: move common overrides to a single `CustomWebApplicationFactory<TProgram>` registered as a fixture, and reserve `WithWebHostBuilder` for the handful of tests that genuinely need a different service.

**`Assert.Multiple` (NUnit 4.x) does not suppress exceptions thrown outside assertions [community]** — If an `Assert.Multiple` block contains code that throws a non-assertion exception (e.g., a `NullReferenceException` or `DbException`), NUnit re-throws it immediately rather than collecting it alongside assertion failures. WHY: `Assert.Multiple` intercepts only `AssertionException` (the type thrown by NUnit assertions); other exception types propagate through the scope boundary unchanged. Fix: wrap infrastructure calls with `try/catch` inside `Multiple`, or assert on `Assert.DoesNotThrow(() => ...)` to bring non-assertion exceptions into the collected failure set.

**`CompareOptions.NumericOrdering` is not valid for `IndexOf`/`StartsWith`/`EndsWith` [community]** — .NET 10's numeric ordering flag applies only to equality and comparison operations. Passing it to index-based operations throws `ArgumentException` at runtime. WHY: numeric ordering is defined over the whole string comparison result, not positional matching semantics. Fix: check the operation type before applying the flag; for prefix/suffix checks, use `string.StartsWith(prefix, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` or a separate non-numeric comparer.

**Shared SQLite in-memory `DbConnection` must stay open or the database is destroyed [community]** — SQLite in-memory databases are tied to the lifetime of the connection. If the `DbConnection` registered as a singleton is disposed or closed between tests (e.g., by a using statement in test cleanup), the entire schema and data disappear. WHY: SQLite's in-memory mode creates a private database per connection; closing destroys it. Fix: open the connection in `AddSingleton<DbConnection>` factory and never close it until `IServiceProvider` is disposed at the end of the test run.

**EF Core InMemory provider silently ignores `[Required]` and unique constraints [community]** — Tests using `options.UseInMemoryDatabase()` will pass even when the application inserts duplicate primary keys or violates `[Required]` annotations, because the in-memory provider does not run SQL constraint evaluation. WHY: InMemory is a simple in-process store that skips relational semantics by design. Fix: use SQLite in-memory with `EnsureCreatedAsync()` to get schema migration + constraint enforcement without a Docker dependency.

**`WebSocketStream.CreateReadableMessageStream` reads exactly one WebSocket message per disposal cycle [community]** — `WebSocketStream.CreateReadableMessageStream` wraps a single message frame; after the stream is disposed, a new call to `CreateReadableMessageStream` is needed for the next message. Reading past the end of one message into another without a new `CreateReadableMessageStream` call yields EOF (`StreamReader.ReadToEnd` returns empty). WHY: each readable message stream is scoped to exactly one WebSocket message by design, matching the WebSocket framing model. Fix: loop `CreateReadableMessageStream` for each expected message rather than reading continuously from one stream.

**`field` keyword causes shadowing warnings on pre-existing `field`-named members [community]** — In classes migrated from C# 13 preview `field` features (or any class that already has a private field named `field`), C# 14's keyword silently shadows the identifier inside property accessors. WHY: `field` is a contextual keyword that takes precedence over identifiers in property getter/setter bodies. Fix: rename existing `field` symbols or use the `@field` escape form. Visual Studio 2026 provides a quick-action rename assist when it detects the conflict.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 25 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Calling `WithWebHostBuilder` inside every test method | Creates a new HTTP server per test — O(N) startup cost | Move common service replacements to a `CustomWebApplicationFactory<T>`; use `WithWebHostBuilder` only for per-test overrides |
| Using EF Core InMemory provider for relational constraint tests | Silently ignores `[Required]`, foreign keys, and unique indexes | Use SQLite in-memory over a shared `DbConnection` via `options.UseSqlite(conn)` |
| Closing the shared `DbConnection` for SQLite in-memory during test cleanup | Destroys the in-memory schema and data — subsequent tests start with an empty DB | Register `DbConnection` as a singleton opened at startup; let `IServiceProvider` disposal close it at the very end |
| `Assert.Multiple` around code that throws non-assertion exceptions | Non-assertion exceptions propagate immediately, aborting the multiple block | Wrap infrastructure code in `Assert.DoesNotThrow` or a `try/catch` to route non-assertion failures into the collected set |

---

## Cycle 26 — 2026-05-13

### C# 14 Extension Members — Properties and Static Extensions

C# 14 introduces a new `extension` block syntax that allows declaring both extension *properties* and *static extension members*, not just methods. This supersedes the older `static partial class` approach for extension methods and closes the long-standing gap where extensions could not expose properties. [official]

```csharp
// Extension block: instance property + static factory on IEnumerable<T>
public static class EnumerableExtensions
{
    extension<TSource>(IEnumerable<TSource> source)
    {
        // Extension property — callable as sequence.IsEmpty
        public bool IsEmpty => !source.Any();

        // Extension property with logic
        public TSource? FirstOrNull => source.FirstOrDefault();
    }

    // Static extension block (no instance receiver)
    extension<TSource>(IEnumerable<TSource>)
    {
        // Called as IEnumerable<string>.Empty (static call on the type)
        public static IEnumerable<TSource> Empty => Enumerable.Empty<TSource>();

        // User-defined operator via extension (C# 14)
        public static IEnumerable<TSource> operator +(
            IEnumerable<TSource> left, IEnumerable<TSource> right)
            => left.Concat(right);
    }
}

// Usage
var items = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };
bool empty = items.IsEmpty;            // false
var combined = items + new[] { 4, 5 }; // operator via extension
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Prefer extension blocks over old-style static helper classes when you need a coherent "extension surface" for a type (properties + methods + operators together). Avoid when targeting pre-.NET 10 SDKs — the `extension` keyword does not back-compile. Old-style extension methods remain fully supported. [official]

---

### C# 14 Null-Conditional Assignment

C# 14 allows `?.` on the *left-hand side* of an assignment or compound assignment. The right-hand expression is only evaluated when the left side is non-null, preventing guard-if boilerplate at call sites. [official]

```csharp
public record Order(int Id, OrderDetails? Details);
public record OrderDetails(string Note)
{
    public string Note { get; set; } = Note;
}

// Before C# 14 — explicit null guard
void SetNote_Old(Order order, string note)
{
    if (order.Details is not null)
        order.Details.Note = note;
}

// C# 14 — null-conditional assignment
void SetNote(Order order, string note)
{
    order.Details?.Note = note;  // right side not evaluated when Details is null
}

// Compound assignment — also legal in C# 14
void AppendNote(Order order, string suffix)
{
    order.Details?.Note += suffix;  // null-safe +=
}

// Works with ?[] too
Dictionary<string, List<string>>? tagMap = GetOptionalTagMap();
tagMap?["events"] = new List<string> { "login", "logout" };
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Excellent for fluent object-graph mutation where nulls represent "not yet initialised" rather than error states. Do not use as a substitute for guarding against invalid state — if `Details` being null is a bug, validate earlier rather than silently swallowing the assignment. [official]

---

### C# 14 `field` Keyword — Validated Backing Without Explicit Field

The `field` contextual keyword (promoted from preview in C# 13 to stable in C# 14) synthesises a compiler-managed backing field inside a property accessor body. This eliminates the need to declare a private field when the only purpose of the field is to support a single accessor with validation logic. [official]

```csharp
public class Product
{
    // Old pattern — explicit backing field required for validation
    private string _name = string.Empty;
    public string NameOld
    {
        get => _name;
        set => _name = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)
            ? throw new ArgumentException("Name cannot be blank")
            : value;
    }

    // C# 14 — field keyword, no explicit backing field declaration needed
    public string Name
    {
        get;
        set => field = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)
            ? throw new ArgumentException("Name cannot be blank")
            : value;
    }

    // Nullable with initialisation via field
    public string? Description
    {
        get => field;
        set => field = value?.Trim();  // normalise on set
    }

    // Gotcha: if the class has an existing member named `field`, use @field to disambiguate
    private string field = "shadow";   // conflicts with the keyword
    public string ShadowedProp
    {
        get => @field;   // @field = explicit identifier; no @ = compiler-synthesised backing
        set => @field = value;
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Ideal for simple validated properties in domain objects. Avoid when the backing field needs to be accessed from multiple properties or from constructors by name — the synthesised field has no accessible name in code, so other members cannot reference it directly. [official]

---

### C# 14 `params` with Span and Collection Types

C# 13 generalised `params` to accept `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and any type with an `Add` method. C# 14 adds first-class implicit span conversions that make `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` the preferred signature for low-allocation variadic helpers, avoiding the array allocation that `params T[]` always incurred. [official]

```csharp
// Before: params T[] always allocates an array on the heap
public static string JoinOld(params string[] parts)
    => string.Join(", ", parts);

// C# 14 + .NET 10: params ReadOnlySpan<T> — stackalloc path for small arg counts
public static string Join(params ReadOnlySpan<string> parts)
{
    var sb = new System.Text.StringBuilder();
    foreach (var p in parts)
    {
        if (sb.Length > 0) sb.Append(", ");
        sb.Append(p);
    }
    return sb.ToString();
}

// Caller syntax is identical — no changes needed at call sites
string result = Join("alpha", "beta", "gamma");

// Using with IEnumerable<T> — compiler synthesises collection when caller passes literals
public static IEnumerable<T> Combine<T>(params IEnumerable<T> sequences)
    => sequences.SelectMany(s => s);

var merged = Combine(new[] { 1, 2 }, new[] { 3, 4 }, new[] { 5 });
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Switch `params T[]` → `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` for hot-path helper methods where GC pressure matters. The `params IEnumerable<T>` variant is convenient but allocates a synthesised collection per call; use span-based overloads in performance-critical code. Older APIs using `params T[]` remain binary-compatible — no callers break. [official]

---

### ASP.NET Core 10 Source-Generated Validation — `[ValidatableType]` with Nested Objects

ASP.NET Core 10 replaces its reflection-based `DataAnnotations` validation in Minimal APIs and controllers with a source-generator-backed implementation. Root types must be decorated with `[ValidatableType]` and the feature requires `builder.Services.AddValidation()` in `Program.cs`. This enables Native AOT-compatible validation and eliminates the startup overhead of reflection-driven model scanning. [official]

```csharp
// Model definitions (must be C# classes, not records declared inside Razor components)
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Validation;

[ValidatableType]
public class CreateOrderRequest
{
    [Required, StringLength(100)]
    public string ProductId { get; set; } = string.Empty;

    [Range(1, 1000)]
    public int Quantity { get; set; }

    // Nested object — source generator recurses into Customer
    [Required]
    public CustomerInfo Customer { get; set; } = new();
}

[ValidatableType]
public class CustomerInfo
{
    [Required, EmailAddress]
    public string Email { get; set; } = string.Empty;
}

// Program.cs — opt in to source-generated validation
builder.Services.AddValidation();

// Minimal API endpoint — validation applied automatically
app.MapPost("/orders", (CreateOrderRequest req) =>
    Results.Ok(new { req.ProductId, req.Quantity }));

// Disable on a specific endpoint
app.MapGet("/health", () => Results.Ok()).DisableValidation();
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Required for Native AOT projects — reflection-based validation is not AOT-safe. For non-AOT projects the source generator provides a measurable startup improvement on types with many properties. The `[ValidatableType]` attribute must be on the root type; deeply nested types are discovered automatically. Do not place root types inside Razor component class files — the source generator cannot resolve them there. [official]

---

### ASP.NET Core 10 Server-Sent Events — `TypedResults.ServerSentEvents`

ASP.NET Core 10 adds a first-class `TypedResults.ServerSentEvents` result for Minimal API endpoints, replacing the previous pattern of manually writing `text/event-stream` headers and flushing the response. The helper accepts `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` and handles framing, flushing, and cancellation. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpResults;

// Domain record — will be serialised as JSON inside each SSE event
public record MetricSample(string Name, double Value, DateTimeOffset Timestamp);

// Minimal API endpoint returning a live metric stream
app.MapGet("/metrics/live", (CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    async IAsyncEnumerable<MetricSample> StreamMetrics(
        [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token)
    {
        while (!token.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            yield return new MetricSample(
                "cpu",
                Random.Shared.NextDouble() * 100,
                DateTimeOffset.UtcNow);
            await Task.Delay(1000, token);
        }
    }

    return TypedResults.ServerSentEvents(StreamMetrics(ct), eventType: "metric");
});

// Test: verify the endpoint returns the correct Content-Type header
[Fact]
public async Task MetricsEndpoint_ReturnsSseContentType()
{
    var client = _factory.CreateClient();
    using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3));

    var response = await client.GetAsync("/metrics/live",
        HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead, cts.Token);

    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    Assert.Equal("text/event-stream",
        response.Content.Headers.ContentType?.MediaType);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use SSE for one-directional server-to-client streaming (dashboards, progress feeds, live logs). Prefer WebSockets when bidirectional communication is needed. `TypedResults.ServerSentEvents` does not support custom SSE `id:` fields as of .NET 10 — use raw response writing if per-event IDs are required by the client. [official]

---

### ASP.NET Core 10 Cookie Auth — API Endpoints Return 401/403 Instead of Redirecting

ASP.NET Core 10 changes cookie authentication behaviour for API endpoints: routes decorated with `[ApiController]`, Minimal API endpoints, SignalR hubs, or routes returning `TypedResults` now receive a `401 Unauthorized` or `403 Forbidden` response instead of an HTML redirect to a login page. This is controlled by the new `IApiEndpointMetadata` interface applied automatically by the framework. [official]

```csharp
// Program.cs: cookie auth configuration — no manual event overrides needed for APIs
builder.Services.AddAuthentication()
    .AddCookie(opts =>
    {
        // These are only triggered for non-API endpoints now
        opts.LoginPath = "/account/login";
        opts.AccessDeniedPath = "/account/access-denied";
    });

// [ApiController] endpoint — gets 401, not redirect
[ApiController]
[Route("api/orders")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    [Authorize]
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult Get() => Ok("secure data");
}

// Integration test — verify 401 is returned (not 302)
[Fact]
public async Task Get_Unauthenticated_Returns401NotRedirect()
{
    var client = _factory.CreateClient(new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions
    {
        AllowAutoRedirect = false  // observe the actual status code
    });

    var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/orders");

    Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, response.StatusCode);
    // Confirm it's NOT a redirect
    Assert.NotEqual(HttpStatusCode.Found, response.StatusCode);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** This is a *breaking change* for apps that relied on the redirect behaviour for API endpoints (e.g., SPAs that detected auth state by intercepting 302s). Review all integration tests that assert `HttpStatusCode.Found` on protected API endpoints and update them to assert `401`/`403`. Web page endpoints are unaffected — they still redirect. [official]

---

### Records with Computed Properties — `with` Expression Shallow-Copy Gotcha

Record `with` expressions perform a *shallow copy* using the compiler-generated copy constructor. Computed properties initialised from positional parameters in a field initialiser (not a property getter) cache stale values after a `with` copy, because they are computed once during the original construction and copied as-is by the clone method. [official]

```csharp
// WRONG — Distance initialised in property initialiser, not on access
public record PointBad(double X, double Y)
{
    // BUG: Distance is set once at construction; with expression copies the old value
    public double Distance { get; } = Math.Sqrt(X * X + Y * Y);
}

var p1 = new PointBad(3, 4);   // Distance = 5
var p2 = p1 with { Y = 0 };    // Distance = 5 (stale — should be 3)
Console.WriteLine(p2.Distance); // 5 — WRONG

// CORRECT — Distance computed on access via expression-body property
public record PointGood(double X, double Y)
{
    // Computed fresh every access; with expression copies X and Y, Distance recalculates
    public double Distance => Math.Sqrt(X * X + Y * Y);
}

var q1 = new PointGood(3, 4);  // Distance = 5
var q2 = q1 with { Y = 0 };    // Distance = 3 (recalculated)
Console.WriteLine(q2.Distance); // 3 — CORRECT

// Test to catch this pattern in code review
[Fact]
public void WithExpression_RecalculatesComputedProperty()
{
    var original = new PointGood(3, 4);
    var modified = original with { Y = 0 };

    Assert.Equal(3.0, modified.Distance, precision: 5);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always make derived properties expression-bodied (`=> expr`) in records rather than initialiser-based (`{ get; } = expr`). Use initialiser-based caching only when the computation is genuinely expensive AND the record is immutable post-construction (no `with` expressions expected). [official]

---

### Record Inheritance — Equality Uses Runtime Type, Not Declared Type

Record equality is based on the *runtime* type, not the declared (compile-time) type. Two records with identical properties but different runtime types are *not* equal. This surprises teams using base-record variables in test assertions. [official]

```csharp
public abstract record Animal(string Name);
public record Dog(string Name, string Breed) : Animal(Name);
public record Cat(string Name, bool IsIndoor) : Animal(Name);

// Two Animal variables pointing to different concrete types
Animal a = new Dog("Rex", "Lab");
Animal b = new Cat("Rex", true);   // same Name, different type

Console.WriteLine(a == b);  // False — runtime types differ

// Same concrete types, same data — equal
Animal c = new Dog("Rex", "Lab");
Console.WriteLine(a == c);  // True

// Test gotcha: using base type in assertion misses derived-class data divergence
Dog expected = new Dog("Rex", "Lab");
Animal actual   = new Dog("Rex", "Poodle");  // different Breed!

// RISKY: comparing as Animal — Breed is NOT an Animal property, so equality ignores it
// (Animal only has Name; Dog adds Breed, but records use ALL properties of runtime type)
// Actually Dog equality DOES include Breed — the equality contract uses runtime type:
Assert.NotEqual((Animal)expected, actual);  // Dog("Rex","Lab") != Dog("Rex","Poodle") ✓

// But FluentAssertions BeEquivalentTo without RespectingRuntimeTypes compares declared-type members:
actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected);  // MAY PASS — compares as Animal (Name only)
actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected,
    opts => opts.RespectingRuntimeTypes()); // FAILS — compares as Dog (Name + Breed) ✓
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Assert.Equal` (or FA with `RespectingRuntimeTypes()`) rather than `BeEquivalentTo` without options when polymorphic record collections are involved. Document base-record test helpers to always cast to the concrete type before asserting. [official]

---

### Nullable Reference Types — `[MemberNotNull]` Annotation for Helper Initialiser Methods

When a class initialises required fields in a separate helper method (rather than the constructor body), the compiler cannot statically prove the fields are non-null after the constructor runs. `[MemberNotNull(nameof(Field))]` from `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis` annotates the helper to inform null-state analysis. [official]

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis;

public class OrderProcessor
{
    // Non-nullable fields — compiler needs proof they are set
    private IOrderRepository _repo;
    private ILogger<OrderProcessor> _logger;
    private string _tenantId;

    public OrderProcessor(string tenantId, IOrderRepository repo,
        ILogger<OrderProcessor> logger)
    {
        // Delegate initialisation to a helper — without [MemberNotNull],
        // compiler warns CS8618 on _repo, _logger, _tenantId here
        Init(tenantId, repo, logger);
    }

    // Annotate so the compiler knows these three fields are set after Init() returns
    [MemberNotNull(nameof(_repo), nameof(_logger), nameof(_tenantId))]
    private void Init(string tenantId, IOrderRepository repo,
        ILogger<OrderProcessor> logger)
    {
        _tenantId = tenantId;
        _repo     = repo;
        _logger   = logger;
    }

    public async Task ProcessAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // No CS8602 warnings — compiler trusts Init set the fields
        _logger.LogInformation("Processing {OrderId} for {Tenant}", orderId, _tenantId);
        var order = await _repo.GetAsync(orderId, ct);
        _logger.LogInformation("Done: {Status}", order?.Status);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `[MemberNotNull]` only on methods whose *sole purpose* is to set those fields — it makes a promise the compiler cannot verify at runtime. If the helper is conditional (e.g., only sets fields for some branches), use `[MemberNotNullWhen(true, nameof(...))]` instead, or restructure to use the constructor chain pattern. [official]

---

### Nullable Reference Types — Structs and Arrays Are Silent Null Pitfalls

The nullable type-safety guarantees do not fully apply to struct default values or array initialisation. A struct containing non-nullable reference fields can be `default`-constructed without warnings, giving those fields a `null` value at runtime despite the non-nullable annotation. Array elements have the same gap. [official]

```csharp
#nullable enable

// Struct pitfall — default(S<string>) assigns null to Prop with no warning
public struct Container<T>
{
    public T Value { get; set; }
}

string s = default(Container<string>).Value;  // No warning; NullReferenceException at runtime

// Array pitfall — new string[3] initialises all elements to null with no warning
string[] names = new string[3];
int len = names[0].Length;  // No warning; NullReferenceException at runtime

// Mitigation 1: initialise array elements immediately
string[] safeNames = Enumerable.Repeat(string.Empty, 3).ToArray();

// Mitigation 2: use nullable element type + null-check on access
string?[] maybeNames = new string?[3];
int? safeLen = maybeNames[0]?.Length;

// Mitigation 3: prefer List<string> with Add() over arrays for collections where
//               elements are added incrementally — avoids the uninitialised-slot problem
var nameList = new List<string>();
nameList.Add("Alice");
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always treat `T[]` and `default(S<T>)` as potentially null even when `T` is non-nullable, and add null guards on first access. This is a known limitation of the nullable analysis — the compiler design team documents it explicitly. `List<T>` is preferred over `T[]` when elements are not all available at allocation time. [official]

---

### `NotNullWhen` and `DoesNotReturnIf` — Null-State Attributes on Custom Guard Methods

When writing custom null-check helper methods, use `[NotNullWhen]` and `[DoesNotReturnIf]` to communicate their null-state semantics to the compiler's flow analysis. Without these attributes, the compiler treats the return value as opaque and continues to warn about possible dereferences even after the guard has been called. [official]

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis;

// Without annotation — compiler still warns about message.ToUpper() below
bool IsNullWithout(string? s) => s is null;

// With [NotNullWhen(false)] — compiler knows: if IsNull returns false, s is not null
bool IsNull([NotNullWhen(false)] string? s) => s is null;

void PrintUpper_Correct(string? message)
{
    if (!IsNull(message))
    {
        Console.WriteLine(message.ToUpper()); // No CS8602 warning
    }
}

// [DoesNotReturnIf(true)] — method throws when condition is true (guard assertion)
static void ThrowIfNull(
    [DoesNotReturnIf(true)] bool isNull,
    string paramName)
{
    if (isNull) throw new ArgumentNullException(paramName);
}

void Process(string? input)
{
    ThrowIfNull(input is null, nameof(input));
    Console.WriteLine(input.Length); // No CS8602 — compiler knows input non-null here
}

// [MaybeNullWhen(false)] — for TryGet patterns
bool TryGetValue(string key, [MaybeNullWhen(false)] out string? value)
{
    value = _cache.ContainsKey(key) ? _cache[key] : null;
    return value is not null;
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always annotate custom guard and TryGet methods with the appropriate null-state attribute — without annotations the compiler over-warns (suppressed with `!` operator everywhere) or under-warns (creates false security). The full attribute family is in `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis`: `NotNull`, `MaybeNull`, `NotNullWhen`, `MaybeNullWhen`, `NotNullIfNotNull`, `DoesNotReturn`, `DoesNotReturnIf`, `MemberNotNull`, `MemberNotNullWhen`. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 26

**C# 14 `field` keyword shadows any existing field named `field` inside property accessors [community]** — Teams with legacy code containing a private field named `field` (e.g., `private string field;`) immediately encounter a shadowing issue when upgrading to C# 14. Inside any property accessor body, `field` now resolves to the compiler-synthesised backing field, not the declared member. WHY it causes problems: the code compiles but silently reads/writes the *wrong* field, producing subtle runtime bugs rather than compile errors. Fix: rename existing `field` identifiers to `_field` or any other name, or escape as `@field` anywhere the old member is referenced inside accessors.

```csharp
// BEFORE upgrade — works fine
public class LegacyWidget
{
    private string field = "original";       // named "field"
    public string Label
    {
        get => field;          // reads the declared private field — correct
        set => field = value;
    }
}

// AFTER C# 14 upgrade — silently broken
public class LegacyWidgetBroken
{
    private string field = "original";       // declared field — now shadowed in accessors
    public string Label
    {
        get => field;          // NOW reads compiler-synthesised backing field (empty string)!
        set => field = value;  // sets synthesised backing field, not declared field
    }
}

// FIX: escape or rename
public class LegacyWidgetFixed
{
    private string @field = "original";      // escape the identifier
    public string Label
    {
        get => @field;         // reads declared field correctly
        set => @field = value;
    }
}
```

**Extension members in C# 14 are not discovered by older Roslyn-based tools (Rider, VS 2022) [community]** — The `extension` block syntax is supported only by Roslyn for .NET 10 SDK and Visual Studio 2026 / JetBrains Rider 2025.3+. Teams running mixed SDK versions in a monorepo report that older IDEs display "syntax error" on the `extension` keyword and that refactoring tools (e.g., "Find All References" to an extension method) miss the new extension-block definitions. WHY it causes problems: CI compiles correctly (using .NET 10 SDK), but developer experience degrades for members of the team on older tooling. Fix: standardise on VS 2026 / Rider 2025.3+ before using extension blocks; add a `<LangVersion>14</LangVersion>` guard in the project file so older tooling gives a clear error rather than a cryptic one. [community]

**`params ReadOnlySpan<T>` overload creates ambiguity when both `T[]` and span overloads exist [community]** — Adding a `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` overload to an existing method that already has `params T[]` causes a compiler ambiguity error at call sites that pass a literal array. The compiler cannot choose between the two because an array literal is implicitly convertible to both `T[]` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>`. WHY it causes problems: adding the span overload as an "optimised alternative" in a library breaks existing callers without a major version bump. Fix: remove the `params T[]` overload and replace it entirely with `params ReadOnlySpan<T>`, or use `[OverloadResolutionPriority]` (C# 13+) to prefer the span overload, which suppresses the ambiguity error without removing the array overload. [community]

```csharp
// Ambiguous — compile error at call sites
public static void Log(params string[] messages) { /* ... */ }
public static void Log(params ReadOnlySpan<string> messages) { /* ... */ }

Log("a", "b", "c");  // CS0121: ambiguous between the two overloads

// Fix: use [OverloadResolutionPriority] (C# 13+) to prefer span
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;

[OverloadResolutionPriority(1)]   // higher wins; array overload stays at default (0)
public static void LogSpan(params ReadOnlySpan<string> messages) { /* ... */ }
public static void LogArray(params string[] messages) { /* ... */ }
```

**ASP.NET Core 10 source-generated validation does not support `IValidatableObject.Validate` on non-root types [community]** — `IValidatableObject` is invoked by the source generator only on root (top-level) validated types decorated with `[ValidatableType]`. Nested types that implement `IValidatableObject` have their `Validate` method silently ignored by the generator. WHY it causes problems: teams migrating from `DataAnnotationsValidator` assume nested `IValidatableObject` implementations continue to run — they do not in the source-generated path. Fix: move cross-property validation logic to the root type's `Validate` method, or use a custom `IValidator<T>` (FluentValidation style) and chain it explicitly. [community]

**`TypedResults.ServerSentEvents` cancellation on client disconnect requires explicit `CancellationToken` threading [community]** — When a client disconnects abruptly from an SSE endpoint, `HttpContext.RequestAborted` is cancelled. If the `IAsyncEnumerable` generator does not observe this token via `[EnumeratorCancellation]` and `CancellationToken` parameter, the generator continues running indefinitely until the process recycles. WHY it causes problems: memory and CPU leak proportional to the number of disconnected-but-still-streaming clients. Fix: always pass `HttpContext.RequestAborted` (or the endpoint's `CancellationToken` parameter) to the `IAsyncEnumerable` generator and apply `[EnumeratorCancellation]` so the framework can combine tokens correctly. [community]

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 26 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| C# 14 upgrade with existing `field`-named members | `field` keyword silently shadows declared field inside property accessors — runtime reads wrong field | Rename members to `_field` or escape as `@field` before enabling `<LangVersion>14</LangVersion>` |
| Adding `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` overload alongside existing `params T[]` | CS0121 ambiguity at all existing call sites | Replace the `T[]` overload entirely, or apply `[OverloadResolutionPriority(1)]` to the span overload |
| Computed record properties using initialiser syntax (`{ get; } = expr`) | `with` expression copies the stale cached value — computed result is wrong | Use expression-body property (`=> expr`) so it recalculates on each access |
| Null-guarding with custom helpers without `[NotNullWhen]` annotation | Compiler continues to warn CS8602 after the guard; developers suppress with `!` everywhere | Add `[NotNullWhen(false)]`/`[DoesNotReturnIf]` to annotate null-state semantics |
| `TypedResults.ServerSentEvents` without threading `CancellationToken` through the generator | Generator runs indefinitely after client disconnect — CPU/memory leak | Pass `HttpContext.RequestAborted` with `[EnumeratorCancellation]` into the `IAsyncEnumerable` |
| `IValidatableObject` in nested types under ASP.NET Core 10 source-gen validation | Nested `Validate()` method silently ignored — cross-property rules never run | Move cross-property validation to root type or use FluentValidation |
| Using `CompareOptions.NumericOrdering` with `IndexOf`/`StartsWith`/`EndsWith` | Throws `ArgumentException` at runtime — numeric ordering is invalid for positional operations | Use numeric ordering only for equality and ordering comparisons; use `OrdinalIgnoreCase` for prefix/suffix checks |
| Reading multiple WebSocket messages from a single `WebSocketStream.CreateReadableMessageStream` | Returns EOF after the first message frame — subsequent data silently discarded | Loop `CreateReadableMessageStream` for each message; never re-use a readable message stream across frames |
| Forgetting `@field` or renaming when upgrading a class with a `field`-named member to C# 14 | `field` contextual keyword shadows the identifier inside property accessors — bugs at runtime | Rename the member or use `@field` escape; enable IDE0062 to detect shadowing at compile time |

---

## Cycle 27 — 2026-05-14

### EF Core 10 — Complex Types Replace Owned Entities for JSON/Table-Splitting

EF Core 10 promotes **complex types** as the preferred way to model embedded value objects mapped to JSON columns or table-splitting. Unlike owned entity types, complex types carry value semantics: assigning one to another copies the data, LINQ equality compares contents, and `ExecuteUpdateAsync` works without expression-tree gymnastics. [official]

```csharp
// Model: Address as a complex type (not an owned entity)
public class Customer
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public required string Name { get; set; }

    // Optional complex type — null means no billing address stored
    public Address ShippingAddress { get; set; } = default!;
    public Address? BillingAddress { get; set; }
}

public class Address
{
    public required string Street { get; set; }
    public required string City   { get; set; }
    public required string ZipCode { get; set; }
}

// OnModelCreating — map both addresses to JSON columns
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
{
    modelBuilder.Entity<Customer>(b =>
    {
        b.ComplexProperty(c => c.ShippingAddress, p => p.ToJson());
        b.ComplexProperty(c => c.BillingAddress,  p => p.ToJson());
    });
}

// Value-semantic assignment — works correctly (copies data)
var customer = await db.Customers.SingleAsync(c => c.Id == 1);
customer.BillingAddress = customer.ShippingAddress;  // copies the struct
await db.SaveChangesAsync();                          // no error (contrast: owned entity throws)

// Bulk update via ExecuteUpdateAsync referencing JSON sub-properties
await db.Customers
    .Where(c => c.BillingAddress!.City == "London")
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(c => c.BillingAddress!.ZipCode, "EC1A 1BB"));
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Switch from owned entities to complex types for all JSON-column and table-splitting scenarios. Complex types resolve the long-standing pain points of owned entity reference semantics. Do NOT use complex types when the embedded object needs its own identity, navigation properties back to its owner, or TPH inheritance mapping — owned entities or separate tables are better there. [official]

---

### EF Core 10 — `ExecuteUpdateAsync` With Regular Lambda (Non-Expression)

Prior to EF Core 10, dynamically building a conditional set of updates via `ExecuteUpdateAsync` required manually constructing `Expression<Func<...>>` trees — notoriously difficult and error-prone. EF Core 10 accepts a regular (non-expression) delegate, enabling ordinary `if` statements inside the setter block. [official]

```csharp
public async Task UpdateBlogAsync(
    BloggingContext db,
    int blogId,
    int newViews,
    string? newName,
    CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    await db.Blogs
        .Where(b => b.Id == blogId)
        .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s =>
        {
            // Always update Views
            s.SetProperty(b => b.Views, newViews);

            // Conditionally update Name — no expression-tree gymnastics needed
            if (newName is not null)
            {
                s.SetProperty(b => b.Name, newName);
            }
        }, ct);
}

// Test: verify conditional update leaves Name unchanged when null is passed
[Fact]
public async Task UpdateBlog_NullName_LeavesNameUnchanged()
{
    using var db = new BloggingContext(InMemoryOptions());
    db.Blogs.Add(new Blog { Id = 1, Name = "OriginalName", Views = 0 });
    await db.SaveChangesAsync();

    await UpdateBlogAsync(db, blogId: 1, newViews: 42, newName: null);

    var blog = await db.Blogs.FindAsync(1);
    Assert.Equal("OriginalName", blog!.Name);
    Assert.Equal(42, blog.Views);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use the new regular-lambda form for all conditional bulk-update scenarios. The expression-tree overload still exists for compatibility, but prefer the regular-lambda form for readability and maintainability. Note: the lambda runs against a *proxy object* tracking setter calls — it is NOT executed as a delegate; side effects beyond `SetProperty` calls are ignored. [official]

---

### EF Core 10 — Named Query Filters Enable Selective Bypass in Tests

EF Core 10 introduces *named query filters*, allowing multiple independent global filters on an entity type. In tests, you can now disable only the specific filter you need to bypass (e.g., suppress the soft-delete filter to assert on deleted records) without disabling unrelated filters like tenancy. [official]

```csharp
// OnModelCreating: two named filters on the same entity
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
{
    int tenantId = _tenantId; // captured from options
    modelBuilder.Entity<Post>()
        .HasQueryFilter("SoftDelete", p => !p.IsDeleted)
        .HasQueryFilter("Tenant",     p => p.TenantId == tenantId);
}

// Production query — both filters applied automatically
var activePosts = await db.Posts.ToListAsync();

// Test helper: bypass ONLY the soft-delete filter to verify deletion
[Fact]
public async Task DeletePost_SetsIsDeletedFlag_NotRemovesRow()
{
    await _sut.DeleteAsync(postId: 42);

    // IgnoreQueryFilters([name]) — suppresses named filter, Tenant filter still active
    var found = await _db.Posts
        .IgnoreQueryFilters(["SoftDelete"])
        .SingleOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == 42);

    Assert.NotNull(found);
    Assert.True(found!.IsDeleted);
}

// To bypass all filters (old behaviour): IgnoreQueryFilters() — no argument
var allPostsRaw = await db.Posts.IgnoreQueryFilters().ToListAsync();
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Prefer named query filters over a single composite filter whenever you have logically independent filtering concerns (multi-tenancy, soft-delete, feature flags). In tests, always name your filters so test helpers can selectively bypass only what is needed, keeping the test focused. [official]

---

### EF Core 10 — Split Query Ordering Bug Fix and Testing Implications

Prior to EF Core 10, split queries with `Take`/`Skip` could silently return incorrect data due to an ordering inconsistency in the sub-query generated for related-entity queries. EF 10 fixes this by ensuring the `ORDER BY` clause in the sub-query is consistent with the outer query. [official]

```csharp
// This query is now safe to use with split queries in EF 10
var pagedBlogs = await db.Blogs
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .Include(b => b.Posts)
    .OrderBy(b => b.Name)
    .Take(10)
    .ToListAsync();

// Before EF 10: Posts for the wrong Blogs could be returned due to missing Id in ORDER BY.
// EF 10 generates consistent ORDER BY including the primary key in both SQL queries.

// Regression test pattern — verify paged blog IDs match expected Posts
[Fact]
public async Task PagedBlogsWithPosts_SplitQuery_ReturnsConsistentData()
{
    // Arrange: seed 20 blogs with 3 posts each
    var expected = SeedBlogs(20, postsPerBlog: 3);
    await db.SaveChangesAsync();

    // Act
    var result = await db.Blogs
        .AsSplitQuery()
        .Include(b => b.Posts)
        .OrderBy(b => b.Name)
        .Take(10)
        .ToListAsync();

    // Assert: every blog's posts belong to that blog
    foreach (var blog in result)
    {
        Assert.All(blog.Posts, p => Assert.Equal(blog.Id, p.BlogId));
    }
    Assert.Equal(10, result.Count);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Upgrade to EF Core 10 for any query that combines `AsSplitQuery()` with `Take`, `Skip`, or `OrderBy` — the bug is silent and can cause data integrity issues in production. Add regression tests that validate Post-to-Blog ownership after paged split queries. The fix may change the SQL generated by existing queries; verify query plans in staging after the upgrade. [community]

---

### EF Core 10 — Parameterized Collection Scalar-Parameter Mode and Padding

EF Core 10 changes the default translation of parameterized collection queries (e.g., `.Where(b => ids.Contains(b.Id))`) from a single JSON-array parameter to individual scalar parameters. EF also *pads* the parameter list to reduce distinct SQL strings and improve query-plan reuse. [official]

```csharp
// Query: filter by a runtime collection of IDs
int[] ids = [1, 2, 3];
var blogs = await db.Blogs.Where(b => ids.Contains(b.Id)).ToListAsync();
// EF 10 generates: WHERE b.Id IN (@ids1, @ids2, @ids3)
// For 4-5 items EF may pad to 5 params, for 6-8 pad to 10, etc.

// Override to constant-inlining when the database planner benefits from knowing values
var blogsWithConstants = await db.Blogs
    .Where(b => EF.Constant(ids).Contains(b.Id))
    .ToListAsync();
// Generates: WHERE b.Id IN (1, 2, 3)  — planner gets cardinality + values

// Override per query to JSON-array parameter mode (EF 8/9 default)
var blogsWithJson = await db.Blogs
    .Where(b => EF.Parameter(ids).Contains(b.Id))
    .ToListAsync();
// Generates: WHERE b.Id IN (SELECT value FROM OPENJSON(@ids_0) ...)

// Global configuration (DbContext.OnConfiguring):
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder o)
    => o.UseSqlServer(conn,
        sql => sql.UseParameterizedCollectionMode(ParameterTranslationMode.Constant));
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The new scalar-parameter default is best for most OLTP workloads where collection size is small and consistent. Use `EF.Constant(...)` when the values are genuinely static enumerations (e.g., role names) and the planner benefits from seeing them. Use `EF.Parameter(...)` (JSON mode) for large collections (100+ items) where inlining would bloat the SQL. [community] — EF Core 10 padding means collections of size 5 and 7 may generate the same SQL (padded to 5 and 10), which surprises teams comparing SQL logs between versions.

### EF Core 10 — `FromSqlRaw` SQL Injection Analyzer

EF Core 10 ships a Roslyn analyzer that warns when string concatenation or interpolation is detected inside `FromSqlRaw`, `ExecuteSqlRaw`, or related methods. The warning is emitted at compile time, surfacing SQL injection risk early. [official]

```csharp
// Analyzer warning: EF1002 — SQL injection risk from string concatenation
var fieldName = "Role";
var users = db.Users.FromSqlRaw(
    "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE [" + fieldName + "] IS NULL");  // EF1002

// Safe: parameterized via FormattableString — use FromSql instead
var users2 = db.Users.FromSql(
    $"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE [{fieldName}] IS NULL");  // safe — param injected

// If fieldName is a trusted column name (validated whitelist), suppress:
#pragma warning disable EF1002
var users3 = db.Users.FromSqlRaw(
    "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE [" + SafeColumn(fieldName) + "] IS NULL");
#pragma warning restore EF1002

// Unit test: verify only whitelisted column names pass SafeColumn
[Theory]
[InlineData("Role",  true)]
[InlineData("Name",  true)]
[InlineData("'; DROP TABLE Users; --", false)]
public void SafeColumn_RejectsNonWhitelistedInput(string input, bool expected)
{
    Assert.Equal(expected, SafeColumn(input) is not null);
}

static string? SafeColumn(string name) =>
    new[] { "Role", "Name", "Status" }.Contains(name) ? name : null;
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Treat EF1002 as an error in CI (add `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>EF1002</TreatWarningsAsErrors>` to the project file). Prefer `FromSql` (FormattableString) over `FromSqlRaw` in all new code — the analyzer is a safety net, not a license to keep concatenating. [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `dotnet tool exec` One-Shot Execution in CI Pipelines

`dotnet tool exec` runs a .NET tool without a prior `dotnet tool install` step. It downloads, executes, and discards the tool in one command. This is valuable in CI/CD test pipelines for ephemeral tooling (report generators, migration runners, code generators). [official]

```bash
# CI: run a database migration tool without installing it globally
dotnet tool exec --source ./artifacts/ dbmigrator -- --connection "$DB_CONN"

# Run a specific version of a code generator during test setup
dotnet tool exec openapi-generator@7.5.0 -- generate -i api.yaml -g csharp -o ./generated
```

```csharp
// Integration test: use ProcessStartInfo to invoke dotnet tool exec
// and validate its exit code as part of a migration smoke test
[Fact]
public async Task DbMigrator_ExitsZeroOnCleanDatabase()
{
    var psi = new ProcessStartInfo
    {
        FileName  = "dotnet",
        Arguments = $"tool exec dbmigrator -- --connection \"{TestDbConnectionString}\"",
        RedirectStandardOutput = true,
        RedirectStandardError  = true,
        UseShellExecute        = false,
        CreateNoWindow         = true,
    };

    using var process = Process.Start(psi)!;
    string stdout = await process.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync();
    await process.WaitForExitAsync();

    Assert.Equal(0, process.ExitCode);
    Assert.DoesNotContain("ERROR", stdout, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `dotnet tool exec` in CI for one-off tool invocations where installing globally would pollute the agent's environment or cause version conflicts. Add `--source` to point to a local NuGet feed for offline/air-gapped builds. By default, the command prompts for confirmation in interactive terminals; set `--interactive false` or pipe stdin from `/dev/null` in CI to avoid hangs. [official]

### .NET 10 — `JsonSourceGenerationOptions` with `ReferenceHandler.Preserve` for Cyclic Graphs

Source-generated JSON serialization contexts in .NET 10 can now declare `ReferenceHandler = JsonKnownReferenceHandler.Preserve` in `[JsonSourceGenerationOptions]`. This enables AOT-safe serialization of object graphs with cycles, previously only available via the reflection-based `JsonSerializerOptions.ReferenceHandler`. [official]

```csharp
// Domain model with a self-referencing property
public class TreeNode
{
    public int Id   { get; set; }
    public string Label { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    public TreeNode? Parent { get; set; }   // potential cycle
}

// Source-gen context with reference preservation enabled
[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(ReferenceHandler = JsonKnownReferenceHandler.Preserve)]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(TreeNode))]
internal partial class TreeNodeContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

// Serialise a cycle safely (AOT-compatible)
var root  = new TreeNode { Id = 1, Label = "root" };
var child = new TreeNode { Id = 2, Label = "child", Parent = root };
root.Parent = child;  // intentional cycle for demo

string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(child, TreeNodeContext.Default.TreeNode);
// Output: {"$id":"1","Id":2,"Label":"child","Parent":{"$id":"2","Id":1,...,"Parent":{"$ref":"1"}}}

// Test: round-trip preserves structure without StackOverflow
[Fact]
public void TreeNode_RoundTrip_CycleHandled_NoStackOverflow()
{
    var root = new TreeNode { Id = 1, Label = "root" };
    root.Parent = root;  // self-cycle

    var json     = JsonSerializer.Serialize(root,  TreeNodeContext.Default.TreeNode);
    var restored = JsonSerializer.Deserialize(json, TreeNodeContext.Default.TreeNode);

    Assert.NotNull(restored);
    Assert.Equal(1, restored!.Id);
    // Parent reference is restored as the same object (by $id/$ref)
    Assert.Same(restored, restored.Parent);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Required for NativeAOT projects that serialise cyclic or graph-structured data. Do NOT use `Preserve` on simple DTO graphs — the `$id`/`$ref` metadata bloats the payload and breaks clients that do not expect `System.Text.Json` reference semantics. [official]

### ASP.NET Core 10 — Identity Metrics for Auth Flow Testing

ASP.NET Core 10 exposes comprehensive metrics for ASP.NET Core Identity operations via the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity` `Meter`. These metrics allow verifying login attempt rates, sign-in/sign-out counts, and 2FA patterns in integration tests using `IMeterFactory` + `MetricCollector`. [official]

```csharp
// Program.cs: enable metrics (automatically registered with AddIdentity)
builder.Services.AddIdentity<ApplicationUser, IdentityRole>()
    .AddEntityFrameworkStores<AppDbContext>();

// Integration test: assert a successful login increments the sign-in counter
[Fact]
public async Task Login_Success_IncrementsSignInMetric()
{
    // Arrange: inject a custom IMeterFactory that captures readings
    var meterFactory = new TestMeterFactory();
    await using var app = new WebApplicationFactory<Program>()
        .WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.ConfigureServices(svc =>
            svc.AddSingleton<IMeterFactory>(meterFactory)));
    var client = app.CreateClient();

    using var collector = new MetricCollector<long>(
        meterFactory,
        meterName:   "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity",
        instrumentName: "aspnetcore.identity.sign_in.count");

    // Act: POST valid credentials
    var resp = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/account/login",
        new { Email = "user@example.com", Password = "P@ssw0rd!" });

    // Assert
    resp.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    var readings = collector.GetMeasurementSnapshot();
    Assert.True(readings.Any(r => r.Value > 0),
        "Expected sign-in counter to be incremented");
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Identity metrics are push-based counters, not polling-based — use `MetricCollector<T>` (from `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing`) rather than reading `IMeter` directly. Metrics measure aggregate counts, not individual request outcomes; pair with structured logs or distributed tracing for per-request diagnosis. [official]

### ASP.NET Core 10 — `.localhost` TLD for Isolated HTTPS Local Development

Kestrel in .NET 10 automatically binds to the loopback interface for any hostname ending in `.localhost`. The development HTTPS certificate is also extended to cover `*.dev.localhost` SANs. This allows multiple co-located services to use distinct hostnames without editing the hosts file. [official]

```csharp
// appsettings.Development.json: configure Kestrel to bind on a named .localhost host
// (no hosts-file edit required on macOS/Linux/Windows)
{
  "Kestrel": {
    "Endpoints": {
      "Https": {
        "Url": "https://api.dev.localhost:5001"
      }
    }
  }
}

// Integration test: use the .localhost hostname to isolate the test server
// from the default localhost to avoid port conflicts across parallel test runs
[Fact]
public async Task HealthEndpoint_ReturnsOk_OnDevLocalhostBinding()
{
    await using var app = new WebApplicationFactory<Program>()
        .WithWebHostBuilder(b =>
        {
            b.UseUrls("https://health-test.dev.localhost:0"); // port 0 = OS-assigned
        });

    var client = app.CreateClient(new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions
    {
        BaseAddress = new Uri("https://health-test.dev.localhost")
    });

    var response = await client.GetAsync("/health");
    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The `.localhost` binding only resolves to loopback — it is not routable. Use for local developer environments and localhost integration tests. Do NOT use in CI Docker containers where the default network may not resolve `.localhost` consistently; use explicit `127.0.0.1` bindings or Docker bridge hostnames in container-based CI. [official]

### ASP.NET Core 10 — `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` for Noise Control

ASP.NET Core 10 changes the default behaviour of `UseExceptionHandler`: handled exceptions are no longer logged by the framework (the `DiagnosticListener` callback is suppressed by default). This eliminates duplicate error log entries in apps that already log exceptions in their own handler. The new `SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` property lets you restore the old behaviour selectively. [official]

```csharp
// .NET 10 default: no framework-level diagnostic logging for handled exceptions
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    ExceptionHandler = async ctx =>
    {
        var ex = ctx.Features.Get<IExceptionHandlerFeature>()?.Error;

        // Log it yourself — framework no longer double-logs
        var logger = ctx.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<ILogger<Program>>();
        logger.LogError(ex, "Unhandled exception for {Path}", ctx.Request.Path);

        ctx.Response.StatusCode  = StatusCodes.Status500InternalServerError;
        ctx.Response.ContentType = "application/problem+json";
        await ctx.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(new { title = "An error occurred" });
    },
    // Restore old behaviour: re-enable framework diagnostics callback
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = _ => false
});

// Test: verify the custom handler fires and returns 500 with JSON body
[Fact]
public async Task ExceptionMiddleware_Returns500WithProblemJson()
{
    var client = _factory.CreateClient();

    var response = await client.GetAsync("/error-trigger");

    Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.InternalServerError, response.StatusCode);
    Assert.Equal("application/problem+json",
        response.Content.Headers.ContentType?.MediaType);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Leave `SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` at the default (suppress) when you control your own exception logging — this prevents duplicate log entries in APM dashboards. Set it to `_ => false` when you rely on middleware-level `DiagnosticListener` subscribers (e.g., custom telemetry exporters that hook the diagnostic events directly). [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `ProcessStartInfo.CreateNewProcessGroup` for Isolated Child-Process Tests

.NET 10 adds `ProcessStartInfo.CreateNewProcessGroup` (Windows only). Starting a child process in a new group prevents the parent's Ctrl+C signal from propagating to the child, and allows sending `CTRL_C_EVENT` / `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` to the child independently. This is useful in integration tests that launch sub-processes and need deterministic teardown. [official]

```csharp
// Test helper: launch a background worker process and shut it down gracefully
public static async Task<int> RunWorkerWithGracefulShutdownAsync(
    string exePath, int durationMs, CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    var psi = new ProcessStartInfo
    {
        FileName  = exePath,
        Arguments = $"--run-for {durationMs}",
        RedirectStandardOutput = true,
        UseShellExecute        = false,
        // Isolate so our test's Ctrl+C doesn't kill the worker prematurely
        CreateNewProcessGroup  = true,
    };

    using var process = Process.Start(psi)!;

    // Wait for the duration, then send graceful stop signal to the child's group
    await Task.Delay(durationMs, ct);

    // Send CTRL_BREAK_EVENT to the isolated process group
    [DllImport("kernel32.dll", SetLastError = true)]
    static extern bool GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent(uint dwCtrlEvent, uint dwProcessGroupId);

    const uint CtrlBreakEvent = 1;
    GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent(CtrlBreakEvent, (uint)process.Id);

    await process.WaitForExitAsync(ct);
    return process.ExitCode;
}

// xUnit test
[Fact]
public async Task Worker_ReceivesCtrlBreak_ExitsZero()
{
    int exitCode = await RunWorkerWithGracefulShutdownAsync(
        WorkerExePath, durationMs: 500);
    Assert.Equal(0, exitCode);
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Windows-only API — guard with `RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform(OSPlatform.Windows)` in cross-platform test suites. On Linux/macOS, use process groups via `setpgid` / POSIX signals instead. The isolated group means the child is not killed when the test runner itself is Ctrl+C'd — always implement a fallback `process.Kill(entireProcessTree: true)` in a `finally` block. [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(long)` Single-Param Overload Fixes LINQ Expressions

Prior to .NET 10, calling `TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1000)` inside a LINQ expression tree (e.g., inside `Expression<Action>` or EF Core queries) caused a compile error because the only overload had an optional second parameter, and LINQ expression trees cannot represent optional parameters. .NET 10 adds a true single-parameter overload, fixing this compile error. [official]

```csharp
// Before .NET 10: compile error CS0854 in LINQ expression trees
// Expression<Action> a = () => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1000);  // ERROR

// .NET 10: new single-parameter overload — works in expression trees
Expression<Action> a = () => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1000);  // compiles

// Practical EF Core / LINQ scenario: compute a timeout threshold in a query
var cutoff = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow - TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(30_000);
var staleJobs = await db.BackgroundJobs
    .Where(j => j.StartedAt < cutoff && j.Status == JobStatus.Running)
    .ToListAsync();

// Unit test: verify the overload works with expression trees in custom translators
[Fact]
public void TimeSpan_FromMilliseconds_SingleParam_UsableInExpressionTree()
{
    Expression<Func<long, TimeSpan>> expr = ms => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(ms);
    var compiled = expr.Compile();

    Assert.Equal(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1500), compiled(1500));
}

// BREAKING: the two-param overload's second parameter is now REQUIRED
// TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500, 0) — must supply microseconds explicitly now
var ts = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500, 0);  // OK
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Upgrade to .NET 10 and remove any workarounds (e.g., `new TimeSpan(0, 0, 0, 0, 1000)`) in expression trees. Note: the second parameter on the two-argument overload is now REQUIRED (was optional in .NET 9) — any code passing only one argument that was relying on the optional second param is unaffected by the expression-tree fix, but teams should review callers. [official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 27

**EF Core 10 JSON column migration silently changes `nvarchar(max)` columns to `json` type on SQL Server 2025 [community]** — When you upgrade an existing EF Core project targeting Azure SQL or SQL Server 2025, the next `dotnet ef migrations add` will emit `AlterColumn` statements changing every `nvarchar(max)` JSON column (owned entities, primitive collections) to the new `json` data type. If CI deploys migrations automatically, existing data is migrated in-place, which can be slow for large tables. WHY it causes problems: teams upgrading incrementally (new code on .NET 10, production on .NET 9 schema) get migration drift because the .NET 9 app still reads the old `nvarchar(max)` columns while the schema expects `json`. Fix: pin `CompatibilityLevel` to below 170, or run a pilot migration on a staging database before promoting to production.

```csharp
// Opt out by setting compatibility level < 170 (SQL Server 2025 is 170)
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder o)
    => o.UseSqlServer(conn, sql => sql.UseCompatibilityLevel(150));
```

**EF Core 10 parameterized collection padding changes SQL for all queries using `Contains` — existing query-plan hints and forced indexes may break [community]** — The new scalar-parameter default in EF 10 generates SQL like `WHERE Id IN (@ids1, @ids2, @ids3)` with padding to nearest bucket size (5, 10, 25, …). If your DBA created query-store forced plans or query hints referencing the old `OPENJSON(@ids_0)` SQL shape, those plans become orphaned. WHY it causes problems: the database starts using a sub-optimal generic plan for parameterized-collection queries. Fix: audit the SQL Server Query Store for stale forced plans after upgrading, and remove/recreate them based on the new parameterized SQL shape.

**EF Core 10 `ExecuteUpdateAsync` regular lambda executes against a tracking proxy, not the real entity — lambda return value is always void [community]** — Some developers write `ExecuteUpdateAsync` lambdas that read from `b.Views` to compute a conditional update (e.g., `if (b.Views > 100)`). Because the lambda body is never actually executed as a delegate — it is analysed as an expression tree at query-compilation time — the conditional logic silently has no effect: the database receives an unconditional `SET Views = @p0`. WHY it causes problems: the test passes (the assertion checks a different property), but production updates always increment without the intended cap. Fix: move all conditional logic *outside* the `ExecuteUpdateAsync` lambda; use `Where` to filter eligible rows and pass only pre-computed scalar values as parameters.

```csharp
// WRONG — b.Views is not a live value inside the lambda
await db.Blogs.ExecuteUpdateAsync(s =>
{
    if (/* b.Views > 100 is not observable here */)
        s.SetProperty(b => b.Views, b => b.Views + 1);
});

// CORRECT — filter rows in Where, pass static value in lambda
await db.Blogs
    .Where(b => b.Views <= 100)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(b => b.Views, b => b.Views + 1));
```

**ASP.NET Core 10 `SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` default change causes existing DiagnosticListener-based APM integrations to stop receiving exception events [community]** — Teams using Azure Application Insights, OpenTelemetry middleware hooks, or custom `DiagnosticListener` subscribers that listened to `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.UnhandledException` no longer receive events for exceptions handled by `UseExceptionHandler`. WHY it causes problems: the APM dashboard silently stops recording 500 errors. Fix: set `SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = _ => false` in `ExceptionHandlerOptions`, or migrate to `app.UseExceptionHandler`'s new delegate to log exceptions explicitly via the `ILogger` abstraction and use `ActivitySource` for tracing.

**`dotnet tool exec` prompts for confirmation in interactive terminals — CI pipelines hang silently waiting for user input [community]** — When running `dotnet tool exec` in a CI step that still has a TTY (common in GitHub Actions with `--interactive` defaulting to on in .NET 10), the tool download prompt blocks indefinitely. WHY it causes problems: the build appears to hang with no error output, causing a timeout after the CI step limit. Fix: always pass `--interactive false` or pipe stdin explicitly (`echo y |`) in CI scripts, or pre-install the tool at pipeline setup and use `dotnet tool run` instead.

```bash
# Fix: disable interactive prompt explicitly in CI
dotnet tool exec --interactive false openapi-generator -- generate -i api.yaml -g csharp -o ./generated
```

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 27 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using owned entity types for JSON columns in EF 10 | Reference semantics cause assignment errors and broken LINQ equality — complex types work correctly | Switch to `ComplexProperty(...)` with `ToJson()` for JSON-column and table-splitting scenarios |
| Reading `b.Views` conditionally inside `ExecuteUpdateAsync` regular lambda | Lambda is never executed — conditional reads are silently ignored; always generates unconditional SQL | Move all conditional logic to `Where(...)` before `ExecuteUpdateAsync`; pass only pre-computed scalars |
| Ignoring EF1002 analyzer warning on `FromSqlRaw` string concatenation | SQL injection vulnerability in production | Use `FromSql(FormattableString)` or whitelist-validate inputs; treat EF1002 as a build error |
| Skipping Query Store audit after upgrading to EF Core 10 | Old forced plans referencing `OPENJSON` shape become orphaned — database picks bad generic plan | Purge stale forced plans from Query Store post-upgrade; validate parameterized-collection query shapes |
| Running `dotnet tool exec` in CI without `--interactive false` | Hangs waiting for download confirmation prompt in interactive TTY mode | Always pass `--interactive false` flag or pre-install the tool at pipeline setup |
| Using `.localhost` hostname in Docker container CI without checking DNS resolution | `.localhost` may not resolve to loopback in Docker bridge networks — test client gets `ECONNREFUSED` | Use explicit `127.0.0.1` or `host.docker.internal` in container CI; reserve `.localhost` for bare-metal dev |
