## Cycle 28 — 2026-05-14

### xUnit v3 — `TheoryData<T1, T2>` Strongly-Typed Theory Data With Compile-Time Safety

xUnit v3 ships `TheoryData<T>` through `TheoryData<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5>` generics. Unlike `IEnumerable<object[]>`, each row is type-checked at compile time, IDE autocomplete works on the constructor arguments, and mismatched argument counts are caught before the test runs. The data class can be declared inline as an anonymous expression or as a standalone named class for reuse. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class PriceCalculatorTheoryData : TheoryData<decimal, int, decimal>
{
    public PriceCalculatorTheoryData()
    {
        Add(10.00m, 1,  10.00m);
        Add(10.00m, 3,  30.00m);
        Add(9.99m,  10, 99.90m);
        Add(0.00m,  5,  0.00m);
    }
}

public class PriceCalculatorTests
{
    [Theory]
    [ClassData(typeof(PriceCalculatorTheoryData))]
    public void Calculate_Total_ReturnsExpectedResult(decimal unitPrice, int quantity, decimal expected)
    {
        var calculator = new PriceCalculator();
        var result = calculator.Total(unitPrice, quantity);
        Assert.Equal(expected, result);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `TheoryData<T...>` for all new theory tests in xUnit v3 — it eliminates the casting noise of `object[]` rows and makes refactoring safe. Use `IEnumerable<object[]>` only when row data is generated dynamically from external sources (databases, files) where type inference is impractical. Alternative: MSTest `[DynamicData]` with a static property, NUnit `[TestCaseSource]`. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[DynamicData]` With `DynamicDataDisplayName` for Human-Readable Test Names

MSTest's `[DynamicData]` attribute now accepts a `DynamicDataDisplayName` parameter pointing to a static method that generates a descriptive string per row. Without it, the test runner renders rows as `TestMethod (System.Object[])`, which is useless for failure diagnosis. The display-name method receives the `MethodInfo` and the current row's `object[]`. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Reflection;

[TestClass]
public class OrderValidatorTests
{
    public static IEnumerable<object[]> InvalidOrderCases()
    {
        yield return new object[] { null,  "null order" };
        yield return new object[] { new Order { Quantity = -1 }, "negative quantity" };
        yield return new object[] { new Order { Price = 0 }, "zero price" };
    }

    public static string GetDisplayName(MethodInfo method, object[] row)
        => $"{method.Name}: {row[1]}";

    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(nameof(InvalidOrderCases),
                 DynamicDataSourceType.Method,
                 DynamicDataDisplayName = nameof(GetDisplayName))]
    public void Validate_InvalidOrder_ThrowsValidationException(Order order, string _)
    {
        Assert.ThrowsException<ValidationException>(() => OrderValidator.Validate(order));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always provide `DynamicDataDisplayName` in CI-heavy teams — readable test names speed up triage dramatically when a specific data scenario regresses. The display-name method must be `public static string MethodName(MethodInfo, object[])` — any other signature silently falls back to the default name without warning. Alternative: xUnit `TheoryData<T>` with `[ClassData]` (type-safe, no separate method needed), NUnit `[TestCaseSource]` with named test cases. [official]

### `FakeLogger<T>` — Unit Testing Structured Log Output Without a Real Log Sink

`Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing` (NuGet: `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing`) ships `FakeLogger<T>` and `FakeLogCollector`, allowing tests to assert on log messages, log levels, and structured properties without wiring up a real logging provider. This is far more targeted than capturing `ILogger` output via `ITestOutputHelper`. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;
using NSubstitute;
using Xunit;

public class OrderProcessorLogTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrder_WhenPaymentFails_LogsWarning()
    {
        var collector = new FakeLogCollector();
        var logger = new FakeLogger<OrderProcessor>(collector);
        var payment = Substitute.For<IPaymentGateway>();
        payment.ChargeAsync(Arg.Any<Order>())
               .Returns(Task.FromResult(PaymentResult.Declined));
        var processor = new OrderProcessor(logger, payment);

        await processor.ProcessAsync(new Order { Id = 42, Total = 99.99m });

        var entry = Assert.Single(
            collector.GetSnapshot().Where(e => e.Level == LogLevel.Warning));
        Assert.Contains("payment declined", entry.Message,
                        StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        Assert.Equal(42, entry.StructuredState
                              .First(kv => kv.Key == "OrderId").Value);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `FakeLogger<T>` when the class under test produces meaningful log output that consumers (dashboards, alerts) depend on. Do NOT test log output for every method — focus on warning/error boundary paths. When using Serilog or NLog, `FakeLogger<T>` won't capture sink-specific enrichment (correlation IDs from Serilog enrichers won't appear); test the enricher separately. Alternative: `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions.NullLogger<T>` (ignores output), custom `ILogger` spy. [official]

---

### `AutoFixture` With `AutoMoqCustomization` — Removing Boilerplate From Mock-Heavy Tests

AutoFixture's `AutoMoqCustomization` automatically creates `Mock<T>` instances for constructor parameters that are interfaces or abstract classes. Combined with `[AutoMoqData]` via `AutoFixture.Xunit2`, this eliminates `new Mock<IRepo>()` setup noise for the 80% of tests that only need mocks to *exist* (not be configured). [community]

```csharp
using AutoFixture;
using AutoFixture.AutoMoq;
using AutoFixture.Xunit2;
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public class AutoMoqDataAttribute : AutoDataAttribute
{
    public AutoMoqDataAttribute()
        : base(() => new Fixture().Customize(new AutoMoqCustomization())) { }
}

public class ProductServiceTests
{
    [Theory, AutoMoqData]
    public void GetProduct_WhenFound_ReturnsMappedDto(
        [Frozen] Mock<IProductRepository> repoMock,
        ProductService sut)
    {
        // Arrange — AutoFixture wired repoMock into sut automatically
        var expected = new Product { Id = 7, Name = "Widget" };
        repoMock.Setup(r => r.FindById(expected.Id))
                .Returns(expected);

        // Act
        var dto = sut.GetProduct(expected.Id);

        // Assert
        Assert.Equal(expected.Name, dto.Name);
        Assert.Equal(expected.Id, dto.Id);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Extremely effective for service-layer unit tests with three or more dependencies. Use `[Frozen]` to ensure the same `Mock<T>` instance is injected into the SUT and returned to the test body. Always place `[Frozen]` parameters *before* the SUT parameter — AutoFixture resolves parameters left-to-right and the SUT is constructed with whatever mocks are already frozen at resolution time. Avoid AutoMoq for tests that need strict mock configuration across many methods — the implicit auto-creation makes it harder to see what the SUT's dependencies are. Alternative: explicit `Mock<T>` setup (verbose but explicit), NSubstitute with manual constructor injection. [community]

---

### FluentAssertions — `SatisfyRespectively` for Ordered Per-Element Assertions

`SatisfyRespectively` asserts a collection element-by-element against a list of inspectors, in order. Unlike `Satisfy` (which checks that some element satisfies each inspector in any order), `SatisfyRespectively` is fully positional — inspector[0] applies to element[0]. This is ideal for ordered result sets where both position and value matter. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class LeaderboardServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GetTopThree_ReturnsSortedByScoreDescending()
    {
        var service = new LeaderboardService();
        var results = service.GetTopThree();

        results.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
            first  => first.Score.Should().Be(980),
            second => second.Score.Should().Be(870),
            third  => third.Score.Should().BeInRange(100, 869));

        results.Should().HaveCount(3);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `SatisfyRespectively` whenever element order matters and you need rich per-element assertions that go beyond equality (e.g., checking a subset of properties or applying different conditions per position). Do NOT use it when only collection membership matters — `BeEquivalentTo` with `Using(options => options.WithStrictOrdering())` is more declarative. Alternative: manual indexed access with `results[0].Score.Should().Be(...)`, `BeEquivalentTo` with strict ordering. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions — `BeAssignableTo<T>` and `BeOfType<T>` in Polymorphic Assertions

`BeOfType<T>()` asserts the *exact* runtime type (fails if the object is a subclass). `BeAssignableTo<T>()` asserts that the object is assignable to `T` — passes for the exact type and derived types. The `.Subject` property on either returns the strongly-typed instance for chained property assertions. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class ShapeFactoryTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Create_Circle_ReturnsExactCircleType()
    {
        var shape = ShapeFactory.Create(ShapeType.Circle);

        // Exact type check — fails if Create() returns a proxy or subclass
        shape.Should().BeOfType<Circle>();
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Create_AnyShape_ImplementsIShape()
    {
        var shape = ShapeFactory.Create(ShapeType.Triangle);

        // Contract check — passes for Triangle, derived MockTriangle, or any subclass
        shape.Should().BeAssignableTo<IShape>();
        shape.Should().BeAssignableTo<Shape>(); // abstract base
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Create_Circle_SubjectEnablesChainedPropertyAssertions()
    {
        var shape = ShapeFactory.Create(ShapeType.Circle);

        // .Subject returns strongly-typed Circle — no cast needed
        var circle = shape.Should().BeOfType<Circle>().Subject;
        circle.Radius.Should().BePositive();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Prefer `BeOfType<T>()` for factory/builder tests where the exact concrete type is the contract. Prefer `BeAssignableTo<T>()` for interface and abstract-base compliance tests. Use `.Subject` to access the typed value after the type assertion — it avoids a redundant explicit cast. [official]

### NUnit — `[Values]` Combinatorial Parameter Generation and `[Sequential]`

NUnit generates the full Cartesian product of all parameter value sets when multiple `[Values]` parameters are present (default combinatorial behavior). `[Sequential]` zips parameter lists instead. Both approaches eliminate manual row enumeration for permission matrices and boundary conditions. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
public class PermissionMatrixTests
{
    // Sequential: (Admin,Read), (Editor,Write), (Viewer,Delete) — zip, NOT cartesian
    [Test, Sequential]
    public void Permission_ZippedRoleAction_VerifiesNoException(
        [Values(Role.Admin, Role.Editor, Role.Viewer)] Role role,
        [Values(Action.Read, Action.Write, Action.Delete)] Action action)
    {
        var policy = new PermissionPolicy();
        Assert.DoesNotThrow(() => policy.IsAllowed(role, action));
    }

    // Default combinatorial — generates 3x3 = 9 test cases automatically
    [Test]
    public void Permission_AllRoleActionCombinations_DoNotThrow(
        [Values(Role.Admin, Role.Editor, Role.Viewer)] Role role,
        [Values(Action.Read, Action.Write, Action.Delete)] Action action)
    {
        var policy = new PermissionPolicy();
        bool allowed = policy.IsAllowed(role, action);
        Assert.That(allowed, Is.TypeOf<bool>());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use NUnit combinatorial generation for exhaustive boundary / permission matrix tests with small value sets (≤5 values per parameter). For large value sets (5+ × 5+ = 25+ cases), combinatorial explosion slows the suite — consider property-based testing with FsCheck or CsCheck instead. Alternative: xUnit `TheoryData<T1,T2>` with explicit rows, MSTest `[DataRow]` or `[DynamicData]`. [official]

### `BenchmarkDotNet` — Micro-Benchmarks With `[MemoryDiagnoser]` and Multi-Runtime `[SimpleJob]`

BenchmarkDotNet is the standard tool for .NET micro-benchmarking. `[MemoryDiagnoser]` adds Gen0/Gen1/Gen2 GC counts and allocated bytes columns. `[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net100)]` targets .NET 10 alongside a .NET 9 baseline for multi-runtime throughput and allocation comparison. [official]

```csharp
using BenchmarkDotNet.Attributes;
using BenchmarkDotNet.Jobs;
using BenchmarkDotNet.Running;
using System.Text.Json;

[MemoryDiagnoser]
[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net90,  baseline: true)]
[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net100)]
public class SerializationBenchmarks
{
    private readonly Order _order = new() { Id = 1, Total = 99.99m, Lines = 10 };
    private readonly JsonSerializerOptions _opts = new() { WriteIndented = false };

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public string SerializeWithOptions() =>
        JsonSerializer.Serialize(_order, _opts);

    [Benchmark]
    public string SerializeNoOptions() =>
        JsonSerializer.Serialize(_order);

    [Benchmark]
    public Order? RoundTrip()
    {
        var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(_order, _opts);
        return JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Order>(json, _opts);
    }
}

// Entry point — must live in a SEPARATE console project (not test project)
// BenchmarkRunner.Run<SerializationBenchmarks>();
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always run BenchmarkDotNet in a *separate console project* built in `Release` configuration (`dotnet run -c Release`) — running under a test runner or debugger invalidates results because the JIT does not apply the same optimisations. Set `[MemoryDiagnoser]` on every benchmark class — allocation regressions are the most common performance bug in .NET. Alternative: `System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch` for rough timings (inaccurate for sub-millisecond work), `dotnet-trace` + `dotnet-counters` for production profiling. [official]

### Polly v8 + `Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience` — Unit Testing Retry Pipelines With `FakeTimeProvider`

Polly v8 ships a redesigned API built on `ResiliencePipeline<T>`. Testing retry pipelines with real delays is too slow for unit tests — a 3-retry pipeline with 1-second delays takes 3+ seconds per test. Inject `FakeTimeProvider` via `DelayGenerator` to collapse delays to zero while still exercising the retry count and backoff logic. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using Polly;
using Polly.Retry;
using Xunit;

public class RetryPipelineTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task RetryPipeline_OnTransientHttpError_RetriesThreeTimes()
    {
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider();
        int callCount = 0;

        var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>()
            .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions<HttpResponseMessage>
            {
                MaxRetryAttempts = 3,
                Delay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1),
                UseJitter = false,
                ShouldHandle = new PredicateBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>()
                    .HandleResult(r => (int)r.StatusCode >= 500),
                DelayGenerator = _ =>
                {
                    fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
                    return ValueTask.FromResult<TimeSpan?>(TimeSpan.Zero);
                }
            })
            .Build();

        var result = await pipeline.ExecuteAsync(async _ =>
        {
            callCount++;
            return callCount < 4
                ? new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable)
                : new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK);
        });

        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, result.StatusCode);
        Assert.Equal(4, callCount); // 3 transient failures + 1 success
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `FakeTimeProvider` with a custom `DelayGenerator` to eliminate real waits in retry tests. Do NOT use `Thread.Sleep` or `Task.Delay(ms)` in retry pipeline tests. For `AddStandardHedgingHandler` / `AddStandardResilienceHandler`, test via `IHttpClientFactory` with a fake `HttpMessageHandler` injected through `WithWebHostBuilder`. Alternative: Polly v7's `Policy.Handle<>().Retry()` API (simpler but not DI-integrated). [official]

---

### ASP.NET Core 10 — `MapStaticAssets` Fingerprinted URLs in Integration Tests

`MapStaticAssets` (introduced in .NET 9, refined in .NET 10) replaces `UseStaticFiles` for most scenarios. It generates content-hash fingerprinted URLs for static assets and sets far-future `Cache-Control` headers automatically. Integration tests must match fingerprinted URL *patterns* (regex) rather than hardcoded hash strings. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using Xunit;

public class StaticAssetsIntegrationTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public StaticAssetsIntegrationTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetPage_Html_ReferencesFingerPrintedCssUrl()
    {
        var html = await _client.GetStringAsync("/");

        // Fingerprinted URL contains a hash segment — not a static string
        Assert.Matches(@"/app\.[a-z0-9]{8,}\.css", html);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetStaticAsset_WithFingerprintedUrl_ReturnsFarFutureCacheControl()
    {
        var pageHtml = await _client.GetStringAsync("/");
        var match = Regex.Match(pageHtml, @"(/app\.[a-z0-9]{8,}\.css)");
        Assert.True(match.Success, "No fingerprinted CSS URL found in page HTML");

        var cssResponse = await _client.GetAsync(match.Value);
        var cacheHeader = cssResponse.Headers.CacheControl;

        Assert.NotNull(cacheHeader);
        Assert.True(cacheHeader!.MaxAge >= TimeSpan.FromDays(365));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Test the fingerprinted URL *pattern* (regex) rather than a hardcoded hash — hashes change every build. `MapStaticAssets` requires the static web assets build infrastructure (Razor Pages or Blazor projects). Do NOT call it in minimal-API projects that serve static files directly via `app.UseStaticFiles()`. Alternative: `UseStaticFiles()` with explicit `ETagHeaderValue` assertions. [official]

---

### .NET 9+ — `Task.WhenEach` for Streaming Task Completions in Completion Order

`Task.WhenEach(IEnumerable<Task<T>>)` returns an `IAsyncEnumerable<Task<T>>` that yields each task as it completes, in completion order (not submission order). This eliminates the `Task.WhenAny` + remove-from-list polling pattern and works naturally with `await foreach`. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class WhenEachTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task WhenEach_YieldsCompletedTasksInCompletionOrder()
    {
        var results = new List<int>();

        var tasks = new[]
        {
            Task.Delay(300).ContinueWith(_ => 3),
            Task.Delay(100).ContinueWith(_ => 1),
            Task.Delay(200).ContinueWith(_ => 2),
        };

        await foreach (var completed in Task.WhenEach(tasks))
        {
            results.Add(await completed);
        }

        // Arrives in completion order (fastest first): 1, 2, 3
        Assert.Equal(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, results);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task WhenEach_WithCancellation_StopsProcessingMidway()
    {
        using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(150));
        var processed = new List<int>();

        var tasks = Enumerable.Range(1, 5)
            .Select(i => Task.Delay(i * 100).ContinueWith(_ => i))
            .ToArray();

        await foreach (var t in Task.WhenEach(tasks)
                                    .WithCancellation(cts.Token))
        {
            processed.Add(await t);
        }

        Assert.Equal(new[] { 1 }, processed); // only first completed within 150ms budget
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Task.WhenEach` when you need to process results as they arrive (streaming progress, partial result display, first-N-wins semantics). Do NOT use when you need all results and order matters — use `Task.WhenAll` + sort by a key. `Task.WhenEach` requires .NET 9+ — gate with `#if NET9_0_OR_GREATER` in multi-target libraries. Alternative: `Task.WhenAny` loop (more allocation, O(n²) removal), `Channel<T>` producer/consumer (more control, more boilerplate). [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `Guid.CreateVersion7()` for Time-Ordered ID Generation and Testing

`Guid.CreateVersion7()` generates a UUIDv7 — a 128-bit ID with a time-ordered prefix derived from the current Unix timestamp (millisecond resolution). UUIDv7 IDs sort lexicographically by creation time, making them ideal as database primary keys to avoid B-tree page fragmentation caused by random v4 GUIDs. The overload `Guid.CreateVersion7(DateTimeOffset)` accepts an explicit timestamp for deterministic test data. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class GuidVersion7Tests
{
    [Fact]
    public void CreateVersion7_MultipleIds_SortInCreationOrder()
    {
        var ids = new List<Guid>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
        {
            // Insert small delay so each ID has a distinct millisecond timestamp
            System.Threading.Thread.Sleep(2);
            ids.Add(Guid.CreateVersion7());
        }

        var sorted = ids.Order().ToList();
        Assert.Equal(ids, sorted);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void CreateVersion7_WithExplicitTimestamp_IsLessThanCurrentId()
    {
        var pastTimestamp = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddDays(-1);
        var pastId  = Guid.CreateVersion7(pastTimestamp);
        var nowId   = Guid.CreateVersion7();

        Assert.True(pastId.CompareTo(nowId) < 0);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void CreateVersion7_VersionNibble_IsSeven()
    {
        var id = Guid.CreateVersion7();
        int version = (id.ToByteArray()[7] >> 4) & 0xF;
        Assert.Equal(7, version);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Guid.CreateVersion7()` as the default ID generator for new entity tables — it eliminates B-tree page splits caused by random v4 GUIDs without requiring `NEWSEQUENTIALID()` SQL function. Use `Guid.CreateVersion7(DateTimeOffset)` in tests to inject a known timestamp for deterministic ordering assertions. Do NOT use when global uniqueness across multiple data centers with strictly synchronized millisecond clocks is required — two IDs created within the same millisecond differ only in random sub-ms bits. Alternative: `Ulid.NewUlid()` (third-party NuGet), `Guid.NewGuid()` (v4, random, no ordering). [official]

---

### `ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler` — Stubbing Named `IHttpClientFactory` Clients in Integration Tests

When integration-testing code that uses named or typed `IHttpClientFactory` clients, injecting a custom `PrimaryHttpMessageHandler` via `WithWebHostBuilder` replaces the lowest-level handler while preserving all delegating handlers (logging, retry, auth token injection). This ensures the full pipeline runs against a fake transport. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using System.Net.Http;
using Xunit;

public class WeatherClientIntegrationTests
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;

    public WeatherClientIntegrationTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _factory = factory;

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetForecast_StubsDownstreamApi_Returns200WithPayload()
    {
        var stub = new FakeMessageHandler(
            new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK)
            {
                Content = new StringContent(
                    """[{"date":"2026-05-14","tempC":22}]""",
                    System.Text.Encoding.UTF8,
                    "application/json")
            });

        using var client = _factory
            .WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.ConfigureServices(services =>
                services.AddHttpClient("WeatherApi")
                        .ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler(() => stub)))
            .CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/forecast");

        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
        Assert.Equal(1, stub.CallCount);
    }

    private sealed class FakeMessageHandler(HttpResponseMessage response)
        : HttpMessageHandler
    {
        public int CallCount { get; private set; }
        protected override Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(
            HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
        {
            CallCount++;
            return Task.FromResult(response);
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler` is the correct integration-test hook — it replaces only the transport layer, so delegating handlers (auth, retry, logging) still run. Do NOT replace the entire pipeline via `AddHttpMessageHandler` in tests unless you explicitly want to bypass delegating handlers. For isolated unit tests of an HTTP consumer class, prefer `RichardSzalay.MockHttp` or `WireMock.Net` for richer request matching. [official]

---

### `Respawn` — Fast Database Row Reset Between Integration Tests

`Respawn` (NuGet: `Respawn`) deletes all rows from non-system tables between test runs by generating a `DELETE` statement that respects FK constraint order — significantly faster than dropping and recreating the database schema. Supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite. [community]

```csharp
using Npgsql;
using Respawn;
using Xunit;

public class DatabaseFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public NpgsqlConnection Connection { get; private set; } = null!;
    private Respawner _respawner = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        Connection = new NpgsqlConnection(
            "Host=localhost;Database=integration_tests;Username=sa;Password=pass");
        await Connection.OpenAsync();
        _respawner = await Respawner.CreateAsync(Connection, new RespawnerOptions
        {
            DbAdapter       = DbAdapter.Postgres,
            TablesToIgnore  = ["__EFMigrationsHistory", "seed_data"]
        });
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await Connection.DisposeAsync();

    public async Task ResetAsync() => await _respawner.ResetAsync(Connection);
}

[Collection("Database")]
public class OrderRepositoryTests(DatabaseFixture db) : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public Task InitializeAsync() => db.ResetAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()    => Task.CompletedTask;

    [Fact]
    public async Task SaveOrder_Persists_RetrievableById()
    {
        var repo   = new OrderRepository(db.Connection);
        var order  = new Order { Total = 42.00m };
        var id     = await repo.SaveAsync(order);
        var loaded = await repo.FindByIdAsync(id);
        Assert.Equal(order.Total, loaded!.Total);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Respawn` is significantly faster than `DROP`/`CREATE` for large schemas — a 50-table schema resets in ~10ms vs ~2s for schema recreation. Requires an open `DbConnection` (not a `DbContext`) — call `db.Database.GetDbConnection()` if using EF Core. Do NOT list tables in `TablesToIgnore` that have inbound FKs from non-ignored tables — FK ordering in the delete traversal can fail or leave orphaned rows. Use `TablesToInclude` (allowlist) mode instead for tighter control. Alternative: EF Core In-Memory provider (no real SQL, catches fewer real-world bugs), Testcontainers with new container per class (total isolation, slower). [community]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 28

**`AutoFixture.AutoMoqCustomization` requires `[Frozen]` to appear *before* the SUT parameter — wrong parameter order means the SUT gets a different mock instance than the test body [community]** — When you write `[Theory, AutoMoqData] public void Test(ProductService sut, [Frozen] Mock<IRepo> repo)`, AutoFixture resolves `sut` first (constructing it with an *unfrozen* auto-created mock), then freezes `repo` — the SUT holds a mock the test body never configured. WHY it causes problems: `repo.Verify(...)` always passes because the SUT's injected mock is a separate, unverified instance; `repoMock.Setup(...)` in the test body silently has no effect on the SUT's behaviour. Fix: always put all `[Frozen]` parameters *before* the SUT parameter in the method signature.

**`FakeLogger<T>` only captures logs for category `typeof(T).FullName` — private nested types and sub-class loggers emit to different categories and are invisible to `GetSnapshot()` [community]** — If `OrderProcessor` internally creates an `ILogger<InternalHelper>`, those log entries use the `InternalHelper` category and do not appear in `FakeLogger<OrderProcessor>`'s snapshot. WHY it causes problems: the test passes (the assertion against the snapshot finds nothing unexpected), but real production log routes may be misconfigured. Fix: use `services.AddFakeLogging()` to register a `FakeLogCollector` on the shared `ILoggerFactory` — all categories within the DI scope write to the same collector.

```csharp
// Correct registration capturing all categories
services.AddFakeLogging(); // ILoggerFactory uses FakeLogCollector globally
var collector = services.BuildServiceProvider()
                        .GetRequiredService<FakeLogCollector>();
```

**`Task.WhenEach` is .NET 9+ only — referencing it in a `netstandard2.0` or `net8.0` multi-target library compiles successfully (reference assembly present) but throws `PlatformNotSupportedException` at runtime on older TFMs [community]** — Teams shipping multi-TFM NuGet packages discover this only when a consumer on .NET 8 reports a runtime exception. WHY it causes problems: there is no compile-time error to catch this; the method exists in the reference assembly surface for all TFMs but the implementation is only present in .NET 9+. Fix: guard with `#if NET9_0_OR_GREATER` preprocessor directives and provide a `Task.WhenAny`-based fallback for older targets.

**`Guid.CreateVersion7()` IDs created within the same millisecond are NOT guaranteed to sort in creation order — .NET's sub-ms bits are random, not monotonic [community]** — Tests that call `Guid.CreateVersion7()` multiple times in a tight loop and assert lexicographic ordering are non-deterministically flaky: the 12 random sub-ms bits can produce any ordering for IDs sharing the same millisecond timestamp. WHY it causes problems: the test passes most of the time (different milliseconds by chance) but fails under load or on fast hardware. Fix: insert `Thread.Sleep(2)` between creates in ordering-assertion tests, or use `Guid.CreateVersion7(explicitTimestamp)` with incrementing timestamps.

**`Respawn`'s `TablesToIgnore` list silently causes FK-violation failures when ignored tables have inbound foreign keys from non-ignored tables [community]** — If `orders` has a FK to `seed_data` (ignored), `Respawn`'s FK traversal skips `seed_data` but still attempts to delete `orders` rows — and in some adapters the FK check during `DELETE` succeeds, leaving the table in an unexpected state, while in others it throws a constraint violation. WHY it causes problems: the first test in a suite passes; the second test fails with a unique-constraint or FK-violation error that looks unrelated to Respawn. Fix: switch to `TablesToInclude` (allowlist) mode for any schema where ignored tables have inbound references, or structure seed data in a separate schema that `Respawn` can be configured to skip entirely.

**`BenchmarkDotNet` inside an xUnit `[Fact]` produces meaningless results — the test runner loads the assembly without JIT optimisations and the benchmark "warm-up" is performed inside the same test process [community]** — `BenchmarkRunner.Run<T>()` spawns child processes in production but when called under a test runner those child processes inherit the test runner's launch conditions, including debug-mode JIT. WHY it causes problems: allocation counts are 2–10× higher, throughput is 3–8× lower, and the confidence intervals are enormous, giving a false sense that performance is worse than in real usage. Fix: always isolate benchmarks in a `*.Benchmarks` console project run with `dotnet run -c Release`.

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 28 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Placing `[Frozen]` mock *after* the SUT parameter in `[AutoMoqData]` tests | SUT is constructed with an unfrozen mock instance; test body configures a different mock that never gets called | Always put all `[Frozen]` parameters before the SUT parameter |
| Calling `BenchmarkRunner.Run<T>()` inside a `[Fact]` or `[Test]` | Test runner loads assembly without JIT optimisations; allocation/throughput results are invalid by 2–10× | Use a separate `*.Benchmarks` console project with `dotnet run -c Release` |
| Asserting a hard-coded fingerprinted CSS/JS URL hash in integration tests | Hash changes on every asset rebuild; tests fail on every content change | Assert the URL *pattern* (regex) rather than the exact hash string |
| Creating multiple `Guid.CreateVersion7()` IDs in a tight loop and asserting lexicographic order | Sub-ms random bits are non-monotonic; same-millisecond IDs sort non-deterministically | Insert `Thread.Sleep(2)` between creates, or use `CreateVersion7(explicitTimestamp)` with distinct times |
| Using `Task.WhenEach` in a `netstandard2.0` or `net8.0` multi-target library without a TFM guard | Compiles without error but throws `PlatformNotSupportedException` on older runtimes | Gate with `#if NET9_0_OR_GREATER` and provide a `Task.WhenAny`-based fallback |
| Using `Respawn` `TablesToIgnore` for tables that have inbound FKs from non-ignored tables | FK traversal leaves orphaned rows or throws constraint violations; next test run gets unexpected failures | Use `TablesToInclude` allowlist mode, or ensure ignored tables have no inbound FKs from kept tables |

## Cycle 29 — 2026-05-14

### xUnit v3 — `IAssemblyFixture<T>` for Assembly-Scoped Shared Resources

xUnit v3 introduces `IAssemblyFixture<T>` — an interface that any test class can implement to receive a fixture instance shared for the *entire assembly* (not just a `[Collection]`). This eliminates the need to declare a named collection solely to share a heavy resource like a database container or a licensed service client. The fixture lifetime begins before the first test in the assembly and is disposed after the last. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

// Fixture: starts one SQL Server container for the whole test assembly
public class SqlServerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public string ConnectionString { get; private set; } = string.Empty;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        // In real code: use Testcontainers.MsSql
        ConnectionString = "Server=localhost;Database=AssemblyDB;...";
        await Task.CompletedTask; // container startup would go here
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await Task.CompletedTask; // container teardown here
    }
}

// Two unrelated test classes sharing the same fixture without a [Collection]
public class OrderRepositoryTests(SqlServerFixture db)
    : IAssemblyFixture<SqlServerFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FindById_ReturnsOrder()
    {
        using var conn = new SqlConnection(db.ConnectionString);
        // ... test logic
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

public class CustomerRepositoryTests(SqlServerFixture db)
    : IAssemblyFixture<SqlServerFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FindByEmail_ReturnsCustomer()
    {
        using var conn = new SqlConnection(db.ConnectionString);
        // ... test logic
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `IAssemblyFixture<T>` for expensive shared resources (containers, licensed services, compiled Roslyn workspaces) where you want assembly-wide sharing without coupling classes into a named collection. Do NOT use it when different test classes need independent fixture state — the single shared instance means any mutation in one test class leaks into others; prefer `IClassFixture<T>` in that case. Alternative: xUnit v2 `[Collection]` + `ICollectionFixture<T>` (still works in v3 for group-level sharing). [official]

---

### NUnit — `[TestFixtureSource]` for Parameterized Fixture Classes

NUnit's `[TestFixtureSource]` applies parameterization at the *class* level: the same test class is instantiated multiple times, once per parameter set. This is more expressive than data-driven tests when *all tests in the fixture* should run against multiple configurations (e.g., different database providers, serialization formats, or feature-flag combinations). [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

// Parameters are provided at the fixture level
[TestFixtureSource(typeof(DatabaseProviderSource))]
public class ProductRepositoryTests
{
    private readonly string _connectionString;
    private readonly string _providerName;

    public ProductRepositoryTests(string connectionString, string providerName)
    {
        _connectionString = connectionString;
        _providerName = providerName;
    }

    [Test]
    public async Task Save_ThenFindById_ReturnsSameProduct()
    {
        var repo = RepositoryFactory.Create(_connectionString, _providerName);
        var product = new Product { Name = "Widget", Price = 9.99m };
        var id = await repo.SaveAsync(product);
        var found = await repo.FindByIdAsync(id);
        Assert.That(found!.Name, Is.EqualTo(product.Name));
    }

    [Test]
    public async Task FindByName_CaseSensitive_ReturnsCorrectCount()
    {
        var repo = RepositoryFactory.Create(_connectionString, _providerName);
        var count = await repo.CountByNameAsync("widget");
        Assert.That(count, Is.GreaterThanOrEqualTo(0));
    }
}

public class DatabaseProviderSource : IEnumerable<TestFixtureData>
{
    public IEnumerator<TestFixtureData> GetEnumerator()
    {
        yield return new TestFixtureData("Server=sqlserver;...", "SqlServer")
            .SetArgDisplayNames("SqlServer");
        yield return new TestFixtureData("Host=postgres;...", "Postgres")
            .SetArgDisplayNames("Postgres");
    }

    IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() => GetEnumerator();
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Ideal when a repository, service, or adapter has multiple backend implementations and you want identical behavioral tests for each. Do NOT use when only a handful of tests differ between configurations — data-driven `[TestCase]` within those specific test methods is simpler. Overusing `[TestFixtureSource]` multiplies test count rapidly; large suites add minutes to CI. Alternative: `[Theory]` + xUnit `ClassData` (data at method level), abstract base test class pattern (same logic, different subclass setup). [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[DataRow]` With `DisplayName` Property for Readable Parameterized Tests

MSTest v3 adds a `DisplayName` property to `[DataRow]`, eliminating the need for a separate `DynamicDataDisplayName` method for simple parameterized tests. The display name appears directly in Test Explorer and CI reports, making failure triage immediate without navigating to the data source. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class PasswordStrengthTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow("",          false, DisplayName = "empty password is weak")]
    [DataRow("abc",       false, DisplayName = "three-char password is weak")]
    [DataRow("Abc1!",     false, DisplayName = "five-char mixed is still weak")]
    [DataRow("Abc1!xyz",  true,  DisplayName = "eight-char complex is strong")]
    [DataRow("P@ssw0rd!", true,  DisplayName = "classic strong password passes")]
    public void IsStrong_ReturnsExpected(string password, bool expected)
    {
        var result = PasswordStrengthChecker.IsStrong(password);
        Assert.AreEqual(expected, result,
            $"Password '{password}' strength check failed");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always add `DisplayName` to `[DataRow]` for any non-trivial test — the 30-second investment in writing a clear label saves hours in CI failure triage. Do NOT rely on the default auto-generated name (e.g., `IsStrong_ReturnsExpected ("",False,...)`) — it is hard to read and leaks implementation detail. For large parameterized sets (>10 rows), prefer `[DynamicData]` with a display-name method. Alternative: xUnit `[Theory]` with `TheoryData<T>` (type-safe, compile-time checked), NUnit `[TestCase]` with `TestName` property. [official]

---

### Moq — `Capture.In<T>()` Argument Capture for Multi-Call Verification

Moq's `Capture.In<T>(list)` callback captures every argument passed to a mocked method across multiple calls into a `List<T>`. This lets you assert on the *full sequence* of calls — order, count, and values — without complex `Callback` lambda state machines. [community]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class NotificationServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrders_SendsOneEmailPerOrder_WithCorrectSubjects()
    {
        // Arrange
        var capturedSubjects = new List<string>();
        var emailSender = new Mock<IEmailSender>();
        emailSender
            .Setup(s => s.SendAsync(
                Capture.In(capturedSubjects),   // captures subject arg
                It.IsAny<string>()))            // body arg — not captured
            .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

        var service = new OrderService(emailSender.Object);
        var orders = new[]
        {
            new Order { Id = 1, CustomerEmail = "a@example.com" },
            new Order { Id = 2, CustomerEmail = "b@example.com" },
        };

        // Act
        foreach (var order in orders)
            await service.PlaceOrderAsync(order);

        // Assert — verify call count and captured arg values
        emailSender.Verify(s => s.SendAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<string>()),
            Times.Exactly(2));
        Assert.Equal(new[] { "Order #1 Confirmed", "Order #2 Confirmed" },
            capturedSubjects);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Capture.In` when you need to inspect argument values across multiple calls to the same method without setting up individual `Callback` closures for each call. Do NOT use it when only a single call is expected — `Verify(m => m.Method(It.Is<T>(x => x == expected)), Times.Once())` is more readable. Be aware that `Capture.In` captures by reference: the list is populated during test execution, so read it *after* the act phase. Alternative: `It.Is<T>()` inline predicates (single-call), `mock.Invocations` property (full invocation history). [community]

---

### FluentAssertions — `BeJsonEquivalentTo` for JSON String Comparison

FluentAssertions (v7+) ships `BeJsonEquivalentTo` for asserting that two JSON strings represent the same semantic document, ignoring property order and whitespace differences. This avoids fragile string equality that breaks when serialization changes key ordering. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;
using System.Net.Http.Json;

public class ProductApiJsonTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProduct_ReturnsExpectedJson()
    {
        using var factory = new WebApplicationFactory<Program>();
        using var client  = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/products/1");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        var actualJson = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        // Order of JSON keys does not matter; whitespace is ignored
        actualJson.Should().BeJsonEquivalentTo("""
            {
                "id": 1,
                "name": "Widget",
                "price": 9.99,
                "available": true
            }
            """);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void SerializedOrder_HasRequiredFields()
    {
        var order = new Order { Id = 42, Total = 199.99m };
        var json = System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer.Serialize(order);

        json.Should().BeJsonEquivalentTo(
            """{"id":42,"total":199.99}""",
            because: "serialized order must expose id and total");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `BeJsonEquivalentTo` instead of `Be(expectedJsonString)` for all JSON string assertions — it is immune to property ordering and whitespace differences that arise from serializer upgrades. Do NOT use it when you need to assert only a *subset* of JSON fields; parse the JSON with `System.Text.Json.JsonDocument` and assert specific properties individually instead. Alternative: `Newtonsoft.Json.Linq.JToken.DeepEquals` (manual, no FluentAssertions integration), `System.Text.Json.JsonElement` comparison (verbose). [official]

---

### NSubstitute — `Arg.Is<T>` With Predicate for Complex Argument Matching

NSubstitute's `Arg.Is<T>(predicate)` overload accepts a `Func<T, bool>` for matching arguments against any condition, not just equality. This enables expressive, readable assertions on complex objects passed to mocked dependencies without creating custom equality comparers. [official]

```csharp
using NSubstitute;
using NSubstitute.ExceptionExtensions;
using Xunit;

public class InvoiceServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task CreateInvoice_PassesCorrectLineItemsToRepository()
    {
        // Arrange
        var repo    = Substitute.For<IInvoiceRepository>();
        var service = new InvoiceService(repo);
        var items   = new[] { new LineItem("Widget", 2, 9.99m) };

        repo.SaveAsync(Arg.Any<Invoice>()).Returns(Task.FromResult(1));

        // Act
        await service.CreateAsync(customerId: 5, items);

        // Assert — verify repo received an invoice with the right total
        await repo.Received(1).SaveAsync(
            Arg.Is<Invoice>(inv =>
                inv.CustomerId == 5 &&
                inv.Total == 19.98m &&
                inv.Lines.Count == 1 &&
                inv.Lines[0].ProductName == "Widget"));
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task CreateInvoice_WhenRepoThrows_PropagatesException()
    {
        var repo    = Substitute.For<IInvoiceRepository>();
        var service = new InvoiceService(repo);

        repo.SaveAsync(Arg.Any<Invoice>())
            .ThrowsAsync(new InvalidOperationException("DB error"));

        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<InvalidOperationException>(
            () => service.CreateAsync(customerId: 1, Array.Empty<LineItem>()));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Arg.Is<T>(predicate)` when asserting on a complex domain object — it reads like a specification and requires no `IEqualityComparer<T>` implementation. Do NOT use for trivial equality checks — `Arg.Is(expectedValue)` or direct `Arg.Is<int>(x => x == 5)` is cleaner. Long predicate lambdas become hard to read; extract them into named `bool Is<T>(T x)` helper methods for reuse. Alternative: Moq `It.Is<T>(predicate)` (same pattern), custom `IArgumentMatcher<T>` for NSubstitute (registerable reusable matcher). [official]

---

### `WebApplicationFactory<T>` — Scoped Service Resolution in Tests

`WebApplicationFactory<T>` exposes `Services` (the root `IServiceProvider`), but resolving scoped services from the root throws or returns wrong instances. The correct pattern is to create an explicit scope with `Services.CreateScope()` inside the test, mirror how ASP.NET Core creates a request scope, and assert on the scope's resolved service state. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Xunit;

public class ScopedServiceIntegrationTests
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;

    public ScopedServiceIntegrationTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _factory = factory;

    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_CommitsToDatabase()
    {
        // Trigger the operation via HTTP
        using var client = _factory.CreateClient();
        var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/payments",
            new { Amount = 100m, Currency = "USD" });
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        // Verify side-effects by resolving the scoped DbContext
        using var scope = _factory.Services.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
        var payment = await db.Payments
            .OrderByDescending(p => p.CreatedAt)
            .FirstOrDefaultAsync();

        Assert.NotNull(payment);
        Assert.Equal(100m, payment.Amount);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void ScopedService_IsolatedPerScope_DoesNotLeakState()
    {
        using var scope1 = _factory.Services.CreateScope();
        using var scope2 = _factory.Services.CreateScope();
        var svc1 = scope1.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IUserContext>();
        var svc2 = scope2.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IUserContext>();
        Assert.NotSame(svc1, svc2);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always use `Services.CreateScope()` to resolve scoped services in integration tests — calling `Services.GetRequiredService<IScopedService>()` directly on the root provider either throws (`InvalidOperationException: Cannot resolve scoped service from root provider`) or returns the wrong singleton if the service was registered incorrectly. Do NOT keep a scope open across multiple tests — dispose it in the same `using` block. Alternative: override `ConfigureTestServices` to register singleton spies, `IServiceScopeFactory` for programmatic scope management. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `Assert.Multiple` Soft Assertions

xUnit v3's `Assert.Multiple` runs all assertion lambdas inside the block and collects *all* failures before reporting — instead of stopping at the first failure. This is the "soft assertion" pattern: useful when you want to see all assertion failures in a single test run rather than fix one failure per CI cycle. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class CustomerDtoMappingTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void MapToDto_AllFieldsMappedCorrectly()
    {
        var entity = new Customer
        {
            Id        = 99,
            FirstName = "Jane",
            LastName  = "Doe",
            Email     = "jane.doe@example.com",
            IsActive  = true,
            CreatedAt = new DateTime(2025, 1, 15)
        };

        var dto = CustomerMapper.MapToDto(entity);

        Assert.Multiple(
            () => Assert.Equal(entity.Id,        dto.Id),
            () => Assert.Equal("Jane Doe",        dto.FullName),
            () => Assert.Equal(entity.Email,      dto.Email),
            () => Assert.True(dto.IsActive),
            () => Assert.Equal("2025-01-15",      dto.CreatedDate),
            () => Assert.False(dto.IsDeleted),
            () => Assert.Null(dto.DeletedAt)
        );
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Assert.Multiple` for *mapping* and *serialization* tests where many properties are being verified simultaneously — you want to see all field mismatches in one shot. Do NOT use it for test flows with sequential dependencies (e.g., asserting that step 2 ran before step 3) — failure in an early assertion may make later assertions meaningless. Also avoid nesting `Assert.Multiple` blocks — the failure messages become harder to read. Alternative: FluentAssertions `AssertionScope` (similar concept, richer messages), NUnit `Assert.Multiple` (same pattern). [official]

---

### Polly v8 — Unit Testing a `ResiliencePipeline` With `ResiliencePipelineBuilder`

Polly v8 separates *building* a pipeline from *executing* it. For unit tests, build the same pipeline using `ResiliencePipelineBuilder<T>` in the test (or inject the builder), then verify that retry, circuit-breaker, and fallback strategies fire correctly by supplying a handler that throws or returns errors on a predictable schedule. [official]

```csharp
using Polly;
using Polly.Retry;
using Xunit;

public class PollyRetryPipelineTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Pipeline_OnTransientFailure_RetriesThreeTimes()
    {
        int callCount = 0;

        var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>()
            .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions<HttpResponseMessage>
            {
                MaxRetryAttempts = 3,
                Delay             = TimeSpan.Zero,   // no delay in unit tests
                ShouldHandle      = new PredicateBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>()
                    .Handle<HttpRequestException>()
            })
            .Build();

        // Act — handler throws twice, succeeds on third attempt
        var response = await pipeline.ExecuteAsync(async ct =>
        {
            callCount++;
            if (callCount < 3)
                throw new HttpRequestException("transient");
            return new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK);
        });

        // Assert
        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
        Assert.Equal(3, callCount);   // 2 failures + 1 success
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Pipeline_AfterMaxRetries_ThrowsLastException()
    {
        var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder()
            .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions
            {
                MaxRetryAttempts = 2,
                Delay             = TimeSpan.Zero,
                ShouldHandle      = new PredicateBuilder().Handle<InvalidOperationException>()
            })
            .Build();

        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<InvalidOperationException>(() =>
            pipeline.ExecuteAsync(_ =>
                ValueTask.FromException(new InvalidOperationException("always fails"))));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always set `Delay = TimeSpan.Zero` in unit test pipeline configurations — using real delays makes tests slow and unreliable. For testing delay *durations* (backoff algorithms), inject `FakeTimeProvider` and advance it via `Advance()` after the failing execution. Do NOT test Polly's retry count logic — test that *your application code* handles the recoverable scenario correctly; assume Polly's logic is correct. Alternative: `ResiliencePipelineProvider<TKey>` (named pipeline via DI, inject into app), `HttpStandardResilienceOptions` for `AddStandardResilienceHandler`. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions — `ExecutionTimeOf` for Performance Regression Assertions

`FluentAssertions.ExecutionTimeOf` measures wall-clock time of a synchronous or asynchronous action and asserts an upper bound. It provides a low-ceremony way to add performance regression guards to integration tests without standing up a full BenchmarkDotNet suite. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using FluentAssertions.Extensions;
using Xunit;

public class SearchPerformanceTests
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;

    public SearchPerformanceTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _factory = factory;

    [Fact]
    public void ProductSearch_Returns100Results_Under500ms()
    {
        using var client = _factory.CreateClient();

        // Act + Assert performance bound
        Func<Task> act = () => client.GetAsync("/products?q=widget&limit=100");

        act.ExecutionTime().Should().BeLessThan(500.Milliseconds());
    }

    [Fact]
    public void FrozenDictionaryLookup_Under1Microsecond()
    {
        var dict = Enumerable.Range(0, 10_000)
            .ToFrozenDictionary(i => i, i => i.ToString());

        Action lookup = () => _ = dict[5_000];

        // Coarse guard: any JIT-warmed lookup must be << 1 ms
        lookup.ExecutionTime().Should().BeLessThan(1.Milliseconds());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `ExecutionTimeOf` as a *regression guard* — catch catastrophic slowdowns (accidental O(n²) query, missing index) without the overhead of BenchmarkDotNet. Set generous thresholds (2–5× expected time) to avoid flaky failures on loaded CI agents. Do NOT use it as a benchmark — results are affected by JIT warmup, GC pauses, and CI machine load; use BenchmarkDotNet for precision. Alternative: `Stopwatch`-based manual assertions (more code, no FA integration), Crank / k6 for load testing. [official]

---

### Moq — `SetupProperty` and `VerifyGet`/`VerifySet` for Property Mocking

Moq provides first-class property mocking: `SetupGet`/`SetupSet` for configuring getters and setters independently, `SetupProperty` to make a property fully trackable (reads return the last written value), and `VerifyGet`/`VerifySet` to assert that a property was read or written. [community]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public interface IUserSession
{
    string UserId   { get; set; }
    bool   IsExpired { get; }
}

public class SessionAwareServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Execute_SetsUserIdOnSession()
    {
        var session = new Mock<IUserSession>();

        // SetupProperty makes UserId trackable (get returns last set value)
        session.SetupProperty(s => s.UserId, initialValue: string.Empty);

        // IsExpired is read-only — just configure the getter
        session.SetupGet(s => s.IsExpired).Returns(false);

        var service = new SessionAwareService(session.Object);
        service.Execute(userId: "user-42");

        // Assert the property was written with the correct value
        session.VerifySet(s => s.UserId = "user-42", Times.Once());
        Assert.Equal("user-42", session.Object.UserId);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Execute_WhenSessionExpired_DoesNotReadUserId()
    {
        var session = new Mock<IUserSession>(MockBehavior.Strict);
        session.SetupGet(s => s.IsExpired).Returns(true);

        var service = new SessionAwareService(session.Object);
        service.Execute(userId: "user-42");

        // Verify UserId getter was never accessed
        session.VerifyGet(s => s.UserId, Times.Never());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `SetupProperty` when the property must behave like a real backing field (subsequent reads return what was last written). Use `SetupGet`/`SetupSet` when getter and setter need independent behaviour. Do NOT combine `SetupProperty` and `SetupGet` on the same property — `SetupGet` overrides the tracking behaviour installed by `SetupProperty`, silently breaking the round-trip. Alternative: NSubstitute — properties automatically track the last-set value without any setup (simpler default). [community]

---

### ASP.NET Core — SignalR Hub Unit Testing With `HubCallerClients` and `Mock<T>`

ASP.NET Core SignalR hubs can be unit-tested by mocking `IHubCallerClients`, `IClientProxy`, and `HubCallerContext`. Inject the mocks into the hub constructor and assert that the correct group or client methods were called with the expected arguments — no real WebSocket connection needed. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR;
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public class ChatHub : Hub
{
    public async Task SendMessage(string user, string message)
    {
        await Clients.All.SendCoreAsync("ReceiveMessage",
            new object[] { user, message });
    }

    public async Task JoinGroup(string groupName)
    {
        await Groups.AddToGroupAsync(Context.ConnectionId, groupName);
        await Clients.Group(groupName).SendCoreAsync("UserJoined",
            new object[] { Context.ConnectionId });
    }
}

public class ChatHubTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task SendMessage_BroadcastsToAllClients()
    {
        // Arrange
        var mockClients = new Mock<IHubCallerClients>();
        var mockProxy   = new Mock<IClientProxy>();
        mockClients.Setup(c => c.All).Returns(mockProxy.Object);

        var hub = new ChatHub { Clients = mockClients.Object };

        // Act
        await hub.SendMessage("Alice", "Hello, world!");

        // Assert
        mockProxy.Verify(p => p.SendCoreAsync(
            "ReceiveMessage",
            It.Is<object[]>(args =>
                (string)args[0] == "Alice" &&
                (string)args[1] == "Hello, world!"),
            default), Times.Once());
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task JoinGroup_AddsConnectionAndNotifiesGroup()
    {
        var mockClients = new Mock<IHubCallerClients>();
        var mockProxy   = new Mock<IClientProxy>();
        var mockGroups  = new Mock<IGroupManager>();
        var mockContext = new Mock<HubCallerContext>();

        mockContext.Setup(c => c.ConnectionId).Returns("conn-1");
        mockClients.Setup(c => c.Group("room-A")).Returns(mockProxy.Object);

        var hub = new ChatHub
        {
            Clients = mockClients.Object,
            Groups  = mockGroups.Object,
            Context = mockContext.Object
        };

        await hub.JoinGroup("room-A");

        mockGroups.Verify(g =>
            g.AddToGroupAsync("conn-1", "room-A", default), Times.Once());
        mockProxy.Verify(p =>
            p.SendCoreAsync("UserJoined", It.IsAny<object[]>(), default), Times.Once());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Hub unit tests with mocks are fast and isolate business logic (authorization checks, message routing, group membership decisions). Do NOT rely on them alone for SignalR work — use `WebApplicationFactory` + a real SignalR test client (Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client) for end-to-end connection lifecycle tests. Setting `Context`, `Clients`, and `Groups` directly on the hub instance is intentional — they are settable in tests because ASP.NET Core sets them via the framework lifecycle. Alternative: `HubConnectionBuilder` with `UseStatefulReconnect` (true e2e), WireMock.Net for WebSocket-level mocking. [official]

---

### `IHostedService` / `BackgroundService` Testing With `IServiceScopeFactory`

Background services are hard to test because they run on a `Task` started by the host. The correct pattern is to test the *core work method* directly (extract it from `ExecuteAsync`), and for integration tests, start the service via `IHost` and use synchronization primitives to wait for completion. [community]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using System.Threading.Channels;
using Xunit;

// Background service that processes orders from a Channel
public class OrderProcessingService(
    ChannelReader<Order> queue,
    IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        await foreach (var order in queue.ReadAllAsync(stoppingToken))
            await ProcessOrderAsync(order, stoppingToken);
    }

    // Extracted: testable without the IHostedService machinery
    public async Task ProcessOrderAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var scope  = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
        var repo         = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>();
        order.ProcessedAt = DateTime.UtcNow;
        await repo.SaveAsync(order, ct);
    }
}

public class OrderProcessingServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrderAsync_SetsProcessedAt_AndSavesToRepo()
    {
        // Arrange
        var savedOrders = new List<Order>();
        var repo        = new Mock<IOrderRepository>();
        repo.Setup(r => r.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
            .Callback<Order, CancellationToken>((o, _) => savedOrders.Add(o))
            .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

        var services = new ServiceCollection();
        services.AddScoped(_ => repo.Object);
        var scope = new Mock<IServiceScope>();
        scope.Setup(s => s.ServiceProvider)
             .Returns(services.BuildServiceProvider());
        var scopeFactory = new Mock<IServiceScopeFactory>();
        scopeFactory.Setup(f => f.CreateScope()).Returns(scope.Object);

        var channel = Channel.CreateUnbounded<Order>();
        var svc     = new OrderProcessingService(channel.Reader, scopeFactory.Object);
        var order   = new Order { Id = 1 };

        // Act
        await svc.ProcessOrderAsync(order, CancellationToken.None);

        // Assert
        Assert.Single(savedOrders);
        Assert.NotEqual(default, savedOrders[0].ProcessedAt);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Extract the core logic from `ExecuteAsync` into a dedicated method (`ProcessOrderAsync`, `DoWorkAsync`) and unit-test that method directly — it removes the need to start the host and use `Task.Delay`/manual `CancellationToken` manipulation. For full lifecycle tests (start/stop, graceful shutdown), use `IHostBuilder.Build().StartAsync()` in a `[Collection]`-scoped fixture with a `CancellationTokenSource`. Do NOT call `ExecuteAsync` directly in tests — it is `protected` by design and bypassing it via casting breaks encapsulation. Alternative: `TestServer` with a hosted service registered, `Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Testing` (xUnit integration for hosted services). [community]

---

### xUnit v3 — `TestContext` Static API for Diagnostic Logging and Cancellation

xUnit v3 ships `TestContext.Current` — a static ambient property available during test execution providing: the test's display name, the current `CancellationToken` (automatically cancelled on test timeout), `SendDiagnosticMessage` for logging to the test output, and `TestState` for reading pass/fail/cancelled state *inside* the test. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Sdk;

public class DiagnosticAwareTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task LongRunningOperation_CompletesBeforeTimeout()
    {
        // Use the test's own CancellationToken — xUnit cancels it on timeout
        var ct = TestContext.Current.CancellationToken;

        TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage(
            "Starting long-running operation at {0}", DateTime.UtcNow);

        try
        {
            await Task.Delay(50, ct); // simulated work
            TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage("Operation completed");
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
        {
            TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage(
                "Operation was cancelled (timeout or explicit cancel)");
            throw;
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void TestName_IsAvailableAtRuntime()
    {
        // Useful for conditional logic or diagnostic labels
        var displayName = TestContext.Current.Test.TestDisplayName;
        Assert.Contains("TestName_IsAvailableAtRuntime", displayName);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void TestState_IsRunningDuringExecution()
    {
        // TestState == Running during the test body; Passed/Failed after
        var state = TestContext.Current.TestState;
        Assert.Equal(TestEngineStatus.Running, state);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` everywhere you previously passed `CancellationToken.None` to async operations in tests — it gives xUnit timeout enforcement for free without manual `CancellationTokenSource` setup. Use `SendDiagnosticMessage` instead of `ITestOutputHelper.WriteLine` for infrastructure-level messages (the output channel is the same, but it's accessible without constructor injection). Do NOT read `TestContext.Current` from a thread-continuation that outlives the test body — the context is only valid on the thread that entered the test method (or awaited continuations scheduled on the same logical context). Alternative: `ITestOutputHelper` constructor injection (xUnit v2 pattern, still works in v3). [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 29

**`WebApplicationFactory<T>.Services` resolves singletons correctly but silently returns a new scoped instance on each call instead of throwing — the behavior changed between ASP.NET Core 6 and 8 [community]** — In ASP.NET Core 6, calling `factory.Services.GetRequiredService<IScopedService>()` throws `InvalidOperationException`. In ASP.NET Core 8 with scope validation disabled (the default in `Development` only), the same call may succeed and return a new instance that is NOT the one used by your HTTP handler. WHY it causes problems: assertion tests appear to pass (the service resolves without error) but they assert against a *different* instance than the one that actually handled the request, producing false-green tests. Fix: always use `factory.Services.CreateScope()` and resolve services from `scope.ServiceProvider`.

**NSubstitute `Arg.Is<T>(predicate)` predicates that throw exceptions are silently swallowed — the argument is treated as not-matched and no error is reported [community]** — If the predicate lambda throws (e.g., `NullReferenceException` when accessing a property on a null argument), NSubstitute catches the exception internally and treats the match as `false`. WHY it causes problems: the `Received()` call says "method was never called with those args" — which is technically correct for the failing match — but the real problem is the null argument passed to the predicate; the root cause is hidden. Fix: add null-guards at the top of `Arg.Is<T>` predicate lambdas, and enable `MockBehavior.Strict` equivalent (`Substitute.ForPartsOf` with `Returns(x => throw ...)`) to catch unexpected calls early.

**xUnit v3 `Assert.Multiple` does not catch `OperationCanceledException` — a cancelled assertion inside the block aborts the entire `Multiple` block and discards uncollected failures [community]** — If an assertion inside `Assert.Multiple` internally awaits a `Task` that is cancelled (e.g., an async assertion against a timed-out `HttpClient`), the `OperationCanceledException` escapes the `Multiple` block. WHY it causes problems: developers see "Task cancelled" instead of the expected assertion failure, and the other assertions in the block never run. Fix: wrap timeout-sensitive async work in `try/catch(OperationCanceledException)` before passing the assertion lambda into `Assert.Multiple`, or use `Assert.Multiple` only for synchronous assertions.

**Moq's `SetupProperty` and `SetupGet` conflict on the same property — `SetupGet` wins, breaking the round-trip tracking installed by `SetupProperty` [community]** — When you call `mock.SetupProperty(m => m.Foo)` (which makes the property trackable) and then call `mock.SetupGet(m => m.Foo).Returns("bar")`, the `SetupGet` replaces the dynamic getter that `SetupProperty` installed. WHY it causes problems: `mock.Object.Foo = "baz"` sets the value, but `mock.Object.Foo` returns `"bar"` (the `SetupGet` return value), so assertions like `Assert.Equal("baz", mock.Object.Foo)` silently fail. Fix: choose one — use `SetupProperty` for round-trip tracking, or use `SetupGet`/`SetupSet` independently if getter and setter need distinct behavior.

**`IAssemblyFixture<T>` in xUnit v3 is NOT automatically discovered when the fixture class is in a *different assembly* from the test classes that implement it [community]** — If `SqlServerFixture` lives in a shared `*.TestInfrastructure` assembly and `OrderRepositoryTests` lives in `*.Tests`, the xUnit v3 assembly fixture discovery only scans the *test assembly* for `IAssemblyFixture<T>` registrations. WHY it causes problems: the fixture is never instantiated, its constructor never runs, and the `SqlServerFixture` parameter in the test class constructor resolves to `null` (or throws), causing every test in the class to fail with a cryptic constructor-injection error. Fix: place the `IAssemblyFixture<T>` registration in a test class within the test assembly itself, even if it's just an empty marker class.

**FluentAssertions `ExecutionTimeOf` measures wall-clock time including thread scheduling latency — CI agents with high load produce intermittent failures on tight thresholds [community]** — A 200ms threshold for a normally 50ms operation sounds safe, but CI agents under peak load can add 200–400ms of scheduling jitter. WHY it causes problems: the assertion fails only on loaded CI, never locally, and the failure message shows a time of 210ms vs 200ms limit — making the test look flaky. Fix: set thresholds at least 5–10× the expected operation time for CI-safe bounds, or move performance assertions to a separate job that runs on a dedicated performance agent.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 29 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Calling `factory.Services.GetRequiredService<IScopedService>()` directly in integration tests | Returns a new instance not used by HTTP handlers; assertions are against a ghost object | Always use `factory.Services.CreateScope()` and resolve from `scope.ServiceProvider` |
| Using `Assert.Multiple` with async lambdas that can be cancelled | `OperationCanceledException` escapes the block, discarding all pending assertions | Use `Assert.Multiple` only for synchronous assertions; handle async timeouts explicitly |
| Combining `SetupProperty` and `SetupGet` on the same Moq mock property | `SetupGet` overrides the round-trip tracking installed by `SetupProperty`; getter returns wrong value | Use one or the other: `SetupProperty` for tracking, `SetupGet`/`SetupSet` for independent control |
| Placing `IAssemblyFixture<T>` implementation in a shared infrastructure assembly | xUnit v3 only scans the test assembly; fixture is never instantiated, all tests fail at constructor injection | Register `IAssemblyFixture<T>` via a class in the test assembly |
| Using `FluentAssertions.ExecutionTimeOf` with tight thresholds in CI | CI scheduling jitter causes intermittent failures; threshold appears met locally but breached under load | Set threshold at 5–10× expected time; run perf-sensitive tests on dedicated performance agents |

## Cycle 30 — 2026-05-14

### Testcontainers.NET — `WithReuse()` for Faster Integration Test Warm-Up

Testcontainers.NET v4 introduced `WithReuse(true)` on any container builder. When enabled, the library checks whether a container with an identical configuration hash is already running and reuses it instead of creating a new one. This dramatically cuts integration test warm-up on developer machines from ~20 seconds per run to near-zero on subsequent runs. [official]

```csharp
using Testcontainers.PostgreSql;
using Xunit;

public class PostgreSqlReusableFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    // WithReuse(true) keeps the container alive across test runs on the same machine.
    // The container is identified by a hash of its builder configuration.
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _db = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
        .WithDatabase("integrationdb")
        .WithUsername("tester")
        .WithPassword("s3cr3t")
        .WithReuse(true)              // v4+ — reuses if hash matches
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _db.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _db.StartAsync();       // no-op if already running and reuse=true
        // Run migrations here — use idempotent SQL or a migration tool
        await ApplyMigrationsAsync(ConnectionString);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        // With WithReuse, DisposeAsync does NOT stop the container —
        // it persists for the next test run. Testcontainers manages cleanup
        // via a Ryuk cleanup container on Docker shutdown.
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    private static Task ApplyMigrationsAsync(string cs) => Task.CompletedTask;
}

[Collection("PostgreSql")]
public class ProductRepositoryTests(PostgreSqlReusableFixture fixture)
    : IClassFixture<PostgreSqlReusableFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Insert_ThenQuery_ReturnsSameRow()
    {
        await using var conn = new Npgsql.NpgsqlConnection(fixture.ConnectionString);
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        // ... real DB assertion
        Assert.True(conn.State == System.Data.ConnectionState.Open);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `WithReuse(true)` during local development to skip container startup overhead on every `dotnet test` invocation. Do NOT enable it in CI without also setting `TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true` and managing container lifecycles explicitly — reuse in ephemeral CI agents means the "running" container may be gone, causing a confusing start failure. On CI, omit `WithReuse` to always get a clean container. Alternative: `IClassFixture<T>` with `[Collection]` for assembly-level sharing (already covered), `docker compose up -d` pre-seeded DB in CI (external lifecycle). [official]

---

### NetArchTest — Architecture Rule Enforcement Tests

NetArchTest is a .NET library for writing executable architecture assertions: "domain classes must not reference infrastructure", "all controllers must have `Controller` suffix", etc. Architecture drift is caught at `dotnet test` time rather than in PR review. [community]

```csharp
using NetArchTest.Rules;
using Xunit;

public class ArchitectureTests
{
    private const string DomainAssembly        = "MyApp.Domain";
    private const string InfraAssembly         = "MyApp.Infrastructure";
    private const string ApplicationAssembly   = "MyApp.Application";

    [Fact]
    public void Domain_ShouldNot_ReferenceInfrastructure()
    {
        var result = Types.InAssembly(typeof(MyApp.Domain.Order).Assembly)
            .ShouldNot()
            .HaveDependencyOn(InfraAssembly)
            .GetResult();

        Assert.True(result.IsSuccessful,
            $"Domain leaked into Infrastructure:\n" +
            string.Join("\n", result.FailingTypes?.Select(t => t.FullName) ?? []));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Controllers_Should_LiveInWebLayer_And_Have_ControllerSuffix()
    {
        var result = Types.InAssembly(typeof(MyApp.Web.HomeController).Assembly)
            .That()
            .Inherit(typeof(Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ControllerBase))
            .Should()
            .HaveNameEndingWith("Controller")
            .GetResult();

        Assert.True(result.IsSuccessful,
            string.Join("\n", result.FailingTypes?.Select(t => t.FullName) ?? []));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Application_Services_Should_Be_Sealed_Or_Abstract()
    {
        // Application services should not be accidentally subclassed
        var result = Types.InAssembly(typeof(MyApp.Application.OrderService).Assembly)
            .That()
            .HaveNameEndingWith("Service")
            .Should()
            .BeSealed()
            .Or()
            .BeAbstract()
            .GetResult();

        Assert.True(result.IsSuccessful,
            string.Join("\n", result.FailingTypes?.Select(t => t.FullName) ?? []));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Add one architecture test file per solution to encode the project's layer rules — they act as a living constraint document. Do NOT overspecify (e.g., every class must be sealed) — overly rigid rules create friction when the design legitimately needs to evolve. Run architecture tests in the same test project as unit tests so violations surface in `dotnet test`. Alternative: Roslyn Analyzers with custom rules (more power, much more code), `Packer` / `Depend` (paid tools), manual code review checklists. [community]

---

### `Shouldly` — Human-Readable Assertions as an Alternative to FluentAssertions

Shouldly is a lightweight assertion library focused on producing exceptionally clear failure messages without verbose assertion chains.
