**ASP.NET Core Output Cache `Age` header is absent on the first request to a fresh `WebApplicationFactory` instance even when the route is decorated with a cache policy [community]** — The in-memory `IOutputCacheStore` is empty when the factory is first created. The first HTTP request always results in a cache miss; the `Age` header only appears on the second and subsequent requests within the same factory lifetime. WHY it causes problems: test assertions that check for the `Age` header on the first response always fail, even though the caching policy is correctly configured. Fix: always send a warm-up (cache-populating) request before asserting on cache-hit headers; use `[Collection]` to share the factory across test classes so the warm-up cost is paid only once.

**`DelegatingHandler` test doubles that store `HttpRequestMessage` objects for later assertion read from a disposed content stream [community]** — `HttpRequestMessage` is `IDisposable`. The `HttpClient` framework disposes the request after `SendAsync` returns. If the recording handler stores the live `HttpRequestMessage` and the test calls `request.Content.ReadAsStringAsync()` after `SendAsync` completes, the content stream has already been disposed. WHY it causes problems: `ReadAsStringAsync()` throws `ObjectDisposedException` in the assertion phase, and the failure appears to be an assertion error rather than a lifecycle issue. Fix: always read and copy the request body content inside the overriding `SendAsync` method before returning the stub response; store the copied string, not a reference to `HttpRequestMessage.Content`.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 31 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Calling `Monitor()` after the act-step in FluentAssertions event tests | Events fired before `Monitor()` are not recorded; assertion always reports "event not raised" | Call `Monitor()` before the state-mutating act-step |
| `[CancelAfter]` on NUnit async test without a `CancellationToken ct` parameter | Timeout fires internal source but code runs with `None`; hangs until I/O completes | Declare `CancellationToken ct` in every `[CancelAfter]` test; propagate it everywhere |
| Placing `AddChaosFault` without understanding Polly strategy ordering | Chaos exhausts retries silently or bypasses them — test verifies wrong behavior | Draw the pipeline diagram (first declared = outermost); comment the intended position |
| Asserting `Age` header on first `WebApplicationFactory` request for output cache | First request is always a cache miss; test is a permanent false failure | Send a warm-up request first; share factory across tests with `[Collection]` |

## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### xUnit v3 — `ITestContextAccessor` for Per-Test Diagnostics and Structured Logging

xUnit v3 exposes `ITestContextAccessor` (injected via DI or accessed via `TestContext.Current`) so tests can write structured diagnostic messages that appear only in the output of failing tests. Unlike `ITestOutputHelper`, which must be constructor-injected into every test class, `ITestContextAccessor` is resolvable from the test DI container and usable in helper libraries without threading the output interface through every call. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;
using Xunit.v3;

public class PaymentProcessorTests(ITestContextAccessor contextAccessor)
{
    // xUnit v3 injects ITestContextAccessor automatically — no [ClassFixture] needed
    private readonly ITestContextAccessor _ctx = contextAccessor;

    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_ValidCard_ReturnsApproved()
    {
        _ctx.Current?.TestOutputHelper?.WriteLine("[Arrange] Building payment request");
        var request = new PaymentRequest
        {
            CardNumber = "4111111111111111",
            Amount     = 150.00m,
            Currency   = "USD"
        };

        _ctx.Current?.TestOutputHelper?.WriteLine($"[Act] Submitting {request.Amount} {request.Currency}");
        var sut    = new PaymentProcessor(new FakeGateway());
        var result = await sut.ProcessAsync(request);

        _ctx.Current?.TestOutputHelper?.WriteLine($"[Assert] Status={result.Status}");
        Assert.Equal(PaymentStatus.Approved, result.Status);
        Assert.NotEmpty(result.TransactionId);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `ITestContextAccessor` when diagnostic output helpers must live inside shared infrastructure (builders, fakes, test utilities) rather than in the test class itself. Do NOT inject `ITestContextAccessor` into production code — it is a test-only seam and should remain in test assemblies or behind a compile-time conditional. Alternative: `ITestOutputHelper` for simple per-class injection, `Serilog.Sinks.XUnit` when you want structured log output routed through the existing logging pipeline. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — Assembly-Level Parallelism Configuration via `[assembly: ParallelizeTestCollections]`

xUnit v3 ships a new `[assembly: ParallelizeTestCollections(maxParallelThreads: N)]` attribute that replaces the `xunit.runner.json` `parallelizeTestCollections` / `maxParallelThreads` settings. The attribute lives in code, is version-controlled alongside the tests, and takes precedence over runner JSON configuration. Tests within a `[Collection]` still run serially; the attribute controls how many collections execute concurrently. [official]

```csharp
// AssemblyInfo.cs — applies to every test collection in the assembly
using Xunit;

[assembly: ParallelizeTestCollections(maxParallelThreads: 4)]
// Four test collections can now run concurrently; tests within a [Collection] remain serial.

// --- Test collections that share state use [Collection] to serialize ---
[Collection("Database")]
public class CustomerRepositoryTests(DatabaseFixture db) : IClassFixture<DatabaseFixture>
{
    private readonly DatabaseFixture _db = db;

    [Fact]
    public async Task Insert_NewCustomer_PersistsToDatabase()
    {
        var customer = new Customer { Name = "Acme Corp", Email = "acme@example.com" };
        var id = await _db.Repository.InsertAsync(customer);
        var retrieved = await _db.Repository.FindAsync(id);

        Assert.NotNull(retrieved);
        Assert.Equal("Acme Corp", retrieved.Name);
    }
}

[Collection("Database")]
public class OrderRepositoryTests(DatabaseFixture db) : IClassFixture<DatabaseFixture>
{
    // This collection is serialized with CustomerRepositoryTests — same "Database" key
    private readonly DatabaseFixture _db = db;

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_ValidCustomer_CreatesOrderRecord()
    {
        var orderId = await _db.Orders.PlaceAsync(customerId: 1, total: 299.99m);
        Assert.True(orderId > 0);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use the assembly attribute when you need all developers and CI runners to agree on parallelism without maintaining a separate `xunit.runner.json` file. Set `maxParallelThreads` to `Environment.ProcessorCount` or a fixed low value for I/O-heavy integration tests. Do NOT set a value higher than the number of independent database/container instances your fixture layer can provision simultaneously — you will get port conflicts and deadlocks. Alternative: `xunit.runner.json` for runner-specific overrides that should not be committed (e.g., to halve parallelism on a slow CI agent). [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `Assert.Multiple` With `async` Lambdas via `Assert.MultipleAsync`

NUnit 4.2 added `Assert.MultipleAsync` — an `async`-native counterpart to `Assert.Multiple`. The synchronous overload cannot await lambdas; calling `await` inside `Assert.Multiple(async () => { ... })` silently drops the continuation. `Assert.MultipleAsync` awaits each assertion lambda and correctly collects failures from all awaited paths before reporting. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestFixture]
public class UserApiTests
{
    private HttpClient _client = null!;

    [SetUp]
    public void SetUp() => _client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com") };

    [TearDown]
    public void TearDown() => _client.Dispose();

    [Test]
    public async Task GetUser_ExistingId_ReturnsCompleteProfile()
    {
        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/users/42");
        var user     = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<UserDto>();

        // Assert.MultipleAsync awaits each delegate before recording failures
        await Assert.MultipleAsync(async () =>
        {
            Assert.That(response.StatusCode, Is.EqualTo(HttpStatusCode.OK));
            Assert.That(user, Is.Not.Null);
            Assert.That(user!.Id,    Is.EqualTo(42));
            Assert.That(user.Email,  Does.Contain("@"));
            Assert.That(user.Roles,  Is.Not.Empty);

            // Nested async assertion — correctly awaited
            var avatar = await _client.GetAsync(user.AvatarUrl);
            Assert.That(avatar.IsSuccessStatusCode, Is.True, "Avatar URL must be reachable");
        });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Assert.MultipleAsync` any time your assertion block needs to await anything — HTTP calls, database reads, file I/O. Do NOT use `Assert.Multiple` (synchronous) for async lambdas because the framework cannot observe whether the awaited task completed before the block exits; failures are swallowed silently. Alternative: xUnit's `Assert.Multiple` (xUnit v3) also supports async delegates; FluentAssertions does not have a built-in multi-assert block — use `using (new AssertionScope())` instead. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[DynamicData]` With `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` and Custom Display Names

MSTest v3 extends `[DynamicData]` to support a `DynamicDataDisplayNameProvider` method. Previously every data-driven row showed an auto-generated name like `TestMethod (System.Object[])`, making failures hard to identify in CI logs. With a named display provider the explorer shows the actual input values. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Collections.Generic;

[TestClass]
public class DiscountCalculatorTests
{
    // Data source returns IEnumerable<object[]>
    public static IEnumerable<object[]> DiscountScenarios()
    {
        yield return new object[] { "EMPLOYEE",  500m,  0.20m,  400m  };
        yield return new object[] { "VIP",       200m,  0.15m,  170m  };
        yield return new object[] { "NONE",      100m,  0.00m,  100m  };
        yield return new object[] { "STUDENT",   80m,   0.10m,  72m   };
    }

    // Display name provider — receives the test method + data row
    public static string DiscountDisplayName(MethodInfo method, object[] data)
        => $"Code={data[0]}, Gross={data[1]:C}, ExpectedNet={data[3]:C}";

    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(
        nameof(DiscountScenarios),
        DynamicDataSourceType.Method,
        DynamicDataDisplayName = nameof(DiscountDisplayName))]
    public void ApplyDiscount_ProducesExpectedNetPrice(
        string code, decimal gross, decimal rate, decimal expectedNet)
    {
        var calculator = new DiscountCalculator();
        var net        = calculator.Apply(code, gross);

        Assert.AreEqual(expectedNet, net, $"Discount code '{code}' produced wrong net price");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `DynamicDataDisplayName` whenever test data rows have business-meaningful names that must be readable in CI failure reports. Do NOT use overly-verbose display names that truncate in test explorers (keep under ~100 characters). Alternative: `[DataRow]` for small fixed datasets that can be hardcoded inline; NUnit `[TestCase("EMPLOYEE", ...)]` has inline display names by default. [official]

---

### Moq — `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` vs `default` in Async Setups

A persistent source of flaky Moq tests is setting up an async method with `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` but calling it in production code with `CancellationToken.None` (or vice versa). Moq's argument matching treats `CancellationToken.None` and `default(CancellationToken)` as identical, but a cancelled token does not match `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` unless the matcher is specified as such. The correct robust pattern is to always use `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` for stubs that should respond regardless of the token state. [community]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class OrderServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FulfillOrder_WhenRepositorySaves_ReturnsSuccess()
    {
        var mockRepo = new Mock<IOrderRepository>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        // CORRECT: match any CancellationToken so the stub fires even when
        // the production code passes a real CancellationToken from a controller
        mockRepo
            .Setup(r => r.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(1);

        var svc    = new OrderService(mockRepo.Object);
        using var cts    = new CancellationTokenSource();
        var result = await svc.FulfillAsync(new Order { Id = 99 }, cts.Token);

        Assert.Equal(FulfillmentStatus.Success, result.Status);
        mockRepo.Verify(r => r.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()), Times.Once);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task FulfillOrder_WhenCancelled_PropagatesCancellation()
    {
        var mockRepo = new Mock<IOrderRepository>();
        using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();

        // Simulate a slow save that respects cancellation
        mockRepo
            .Setup(r => r.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
            .Returns<Order, CancellationToken>(async (_, ct) =>
            {
                await Task.Delay(5_000, ct);   // will throw OperationCanceledException
                return 1;
            });

        var svc = new OrderService(mockRepo.Object);
        await cts.CancelAsync();

        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            () => svc.FulfillAsync(new Order { Id = 1 }, cts.Token));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always use `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` in Moq setups for any method that accepts a `CancellationToken` unless you are specifically testing cancellation propagation. Do NOT match on `CancellationToken.None` as a literal value because production callers may pass a real token from a parent scope, causing the stub not to match and the mock to throw `MockException`. Alternative: NSubstitute uses `Arg.Any<CancellationToken>()` with the same semantics; FakeItEasy uses `A<CancellationToken>._`. [community]

---

### FluentAssertions — `AssertionScope` With Named Context for Batch Property Assertions

`AssertionScope` collects all assertion failures in its block and throws a single aggregated exception, avoiding the need to re-run a test to discover each subsequent failure. Naming the scope adds the context string to every failure message in the batch, making CI logs point immediately to which object's property failed. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using FluentAssertions.Execution;
using Xunit;

public class InvoiceResponseAssertions
{
    [Fact]
    public void CreateInvoice_ValidRequest_ResponseHasAllRequiredFields()
    {
        var invoice = InvoiceFactory.Create(new InvoiceRequest
        {
            CustomerId  = "CUST-001",
            LineItems   = [new LineItem("SKU-A", qty: 2, unit: 49.99m)],
            DueDaysFromNow = 30
        });

        using (new AssertionScope("Invoice response"))
        {
            invoice.Should().NotBeNull();
            invoice.Id.Should().MatchRegex(@"^INV-\d{8}$",
                "invoice ID must match the company numbering format");
            invoice.CustomerId.Should().Be("CUST-001");
            invoice.TotalAmount.Should().BeGreaterThan(0);
            invoice.LineItems.Should().HaveCount(1);
            invoice.LineItems[0].UnitPrice.Should().Be(49.99m);
            invoice.DueDate.Should().BeAfter(DateTime.UtcNow);
            invoice.Status.Should().Be(InvoiceStatus.Draft,
                "newly created invoices are always in Draft state");
        }
        // All failures reported together — no re-run needed to find the next broken property
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use named `AssertionScope` for multi-property object validation where any single property failure should not hide sibling failures. Do NOT create deeply nested `AssertionScope` blocks — failures from the inner scope propagate to the outer scope and produce duplicate messages. Alternative: xUnit `Assert.Multiple` (v3) and NUnit `Assert.MultipleAsync` for framework-native batch assertion; MSTest does not have a built-in equivalent — use FluentAssertions `AssertionScope` instead. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET — `IContainer.CopyAsync` for Seeding Files Into Running Containers

Testcontainers.NET exposes `CopyAsync(byte[] content, string containerPath)` and `CopyAsync(DirectoryInfo source, string containerPath)` on the `IContainer` abstraction. These methods transfer files into an already-running container without rebuilding the image or mounting a host volume, which is not possible on all Docker hosts. This is useful for seeding SQL scripts, certificate files, or configuration into a container after startup. [official]

```csharp
using System.IO;
using System.Text;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Testcontainers.PostgreSql;
using Xunit;

public class PostgresSeedFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _db = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _db.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _db.StartAsync();

        // Copy a seed SQL script into the running container, then execute it
        var seedSql = await File.ReadAllBytesAsync("TestData/seed.sql");
        await _db.CopyAsync(seedSql, "/tmp/seed.sql");

        var execResult = await _db.ExecAsync(
            ["psql", "-U", "postgres", "-d", "postgres", "-f", "/tmp/seed.sql"]);

        if (execResult.ExitCode != 0)
            throw new InvalidOperationException(
                $"Seed failed:\n{execResult.Stderr}");
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _db.DisposeAsync();
}

[Collection("Postgres")]
public class ProductRepositoryTests(PostgresSeedFixture fixture) : IClassFixture<PostgresSeedFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FindBySku_SeededProduct_ReturnsCorrectRecord()
    {
        var repo    = new ProductRepository(fixture.ConnectionString);
        var product = await repo.FindBySkuAsync("SKU-SEED-001");

        product.Should().NotBeNull();
        product!.Name.Should().Be("Seeded Product");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `CopyAsync` when test data cannot be baked into the container image (e.g., generated data, environment-specific config) or when you want to avoid maintaining a custom Docker image per test scenario. Do NOT use `CopyAsync` for large binary assets — the bytes are transferred over the Docker daemon socket and can significantly slow test startup. Alternative: Docker volume mounts via `.WithBindMount(host, container)` for large or frequently-changing files; baking seed data into a custom image for maximum startup speed. [official]

---

### ASP.NET Core — `WebApplicationFactory` Custom `IServiceCollection` Replacement for Isolation

When integration tests need to replace a registered service with a test double, the common pattern is `WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.ConfigureTestServices(...))`. However `ConfigureTestServices` runs after `ConfigureServices`, meaning transient decorators or hosted services registered by the app may have already captured the real dependency. A more robust pattern is to use `services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<T, TFake>())` which properly replaces the registration regardless of decoration order. [community]

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;

public class CustomWebAppFactory : WebApplicationFactory<Program>
{
    // Expose for assertion in tests
    public FakeEmailSender EmailSender { get; } = new FakeEmailSender();

    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
        {
            // ServiceDescriptor.Singleton ensures the SAME instance is used everywhere
            services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IEmailSender>(EmailSender));

            // Also replace scoped services using the appropriate lifetime
            services.Replace(
                ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IPaymentGateway, FakePaymentGateway>());
        });
    }
}

public class CheckoutTests(CustomWebAppFactory factory)
    : IClassFixture<CustomWebAppFactory>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_SendsConfirmationEmail()
    {
        var client   = factory.CreateClient();
        var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/api/orders",
            new { ProductId = 1, Quantity = 2 });

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        factory.EmailSender.SentMessages
            .Should().ContainSingle()
            .Which.Subject.Should().Contain("Order Confirmation");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `services.Replace` instead of `services.AddSingleton` / `services.AddScoped` for service substitution in integration tests — `Add` registers a second implementation and the DI container resolves the last-registered one, but keyed services or decorated registrations may still resolve the original. Do NOT replace the entire `ILoggerFactory` — doing so silences all structured logging that integration test diagnostics rely on. Alternative: `services.RemoveAll<T>()` followed by `services.AddSingleton<T>(fake)` for complete removal of a registration before adding the fake. [community]

---

### Moq — `MockSequence` for Ordered Call Verification

When a unit under test must call collaborators in a specific order (e.g., validate then persist then notify), `MockSequence` enforces that ordering at the mock level. Unlike `Verify()` call-count checks, `MockSequence` throws immediately when an out-of-order call is made, pinpointing the exact method that violated the contract. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public class OrderProcessingPipelineTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void ProcessOrder_ExecutesStagesInCorrectOrder()
    {
        var seq       = new MockSequence();
        var validator = new Mock<IOrderValidator>(MockBehavior.Strict);
        var repo      = new Mock<IOrderRepository>(MockBehavior.Strict);
        var notifier  = new Mock<IOrderNotifier>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        // Setup in expected call order — sequence enforces this ordering
        validator.InSequence(seq).Setup(v => v.Validate(It.IsAny<Order>()))
                 .Returns(ValidationResult.Valid);

        repo.InSequence(seq).Setup(r => r.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()))
            .Returns(101);

        notifier.InSequence(seq).Setup(n => n.Notify(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<string>()));

        var pipeline = new OrderProcessingPipeline(validator.Object, repo.Object, notifier.Object);
        pipeline.Process(new Order { CustomerId = 7, Total = 99.50m });

        // Explicit verify confirms each stage was called exactly once
        validator.Verify(v => v.Validate(It.IsAny<Order>()), Times.Once);
        repo.Verify(r => r.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()), Times.Once);
        notifier.Verify(n => n.Notify(101, It.IsAny<string>()), Times.Once);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `MockSequence` when the order of side effects is part of the observable contract (e.g., a payment must be authorized before an inventory reservation is made). Do NOT use `MockSequence` for pure query methods (no side effects) — order does not matter for queries and enforcing it makes tests brittle. Alternative: NSubstitute does not have a native sequence mechanism; use `Received.InOrder(...)` from the `NSubstitute.Extensions` package. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions — `SatisfyRespectively` for Per-Element Collection Assertions

`SatisfyRespectively` asserts a heterogeneous set of per-element predicates in a single readable block. Unlike `.ElementAt(n).Should()...` repeated for each index, `SatisfyRespectively` fails with all element-level failures collected, and the failure message identifies the offending position by index. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class ReportLineAssertionTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GenerateReport_ProducesCorrectLineItems()
    {
        var report = new ReportGenerator().Generate(new ReportRequest
        {
            PeriodStart = new DateTime(2026, 1, 1),
            PeriodEnd   = new DateTime(2026, 3, 31)
        });

        report.Lines.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
            first =>
            {
                first.Month.Should().Be("January 2026");
                first.Revenue.Should().BeApproximately(12_500m, precision: 1m);
                first.IsFinalised.Should().BeTrue();
            },
            second =>
            {
                second.Month.Should().Be("February 2026");
                second.Revenue.Should().BePositive();
                second.IsFinalised.Should().BeTrue();
            },
            third =>
            {
                third.Month.Should().Be("March 2026");
                third.Revenue.Should().BePositive();
                third.IsFinalised.Should().BeFalse("Q1 is still open");
            });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `SatisfyRespectively` for small fixed-length collections where each position has distinct meaning (e.g., monthly report lines, a known-count API result). Do NOT use it for large or variable-length collections — when the collection length differs from the predicate count, the entire assertion fails with a confusing count mismatch rather than element-level feedback. Alternative: `Should().AllSatisfy(item => ...)` for homogeneous element assertions; `Should().ContainSingle(x => x.Id == id)` for single-element search. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[Timeout]` on `[TestMethod]` With Cooperative Cancellation

MSTest v3.3 revised `[Timeout(int ms)]` behavior: when a test method declares a `CancellationToken ct` parameter, MSTest now injects a token linked to the timeout deadline, enabling cooperative cancellation instead of the legacy behavior of aborting the thread. Tests that receive the token and propagate it to `await` calls are interrupted cleanly at the deadline. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestClass]
public class CacheWarmUpTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(2_000)]   // 2-second deadline
    public async Task WarmUp_CompletesWithinDeadline(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // ct is linked to the 2-second timeout — propagate it everywhere
        var cache = new DistributedCache(new CacheOptions { MaxEntries = 500 });

        await cache.WarmUpAsync(ct);

        Assert.IsTrue(cache.IsWarmed, "Cache must be warm before the deadline");
        Assert.IsTrue(cache.EntryCount > 0, "Warm-up must load at least one entry");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(500)]
    public async Task SlowOperation_TimeoutToken_IsPassedToChildCalls(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Verifies that cancellation propagates — expects OperationCanceledException
        await Assert.ThrowsExceptionAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            () => Task.Delay(10_000, ct));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `[Timeout]` with `CancellationToken ct` parameter for all async integration tests that perform I/O. Cooperative cancellation is always safer than thread abort; it allows finally-blocks and `IAsyncDisposable` cleanup to run. Do NOT set the timeout value below ~3× the observed P99 execution time on the slowest CI agent — scheduling jitter causes intermittent failures. Alternative: NUnit `[CancelAfter]` with the same cooperative model; xUnit v3 uses `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` bound to a configurable timeout. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET — `NetworkBuilder` for Multi-Container Integration Tests

When testing services that communicate with each other (e.g., an API calling a Redis sidecar or a RabbitMQ broker), Testcontainers.NET's `NetworkBuilder` creates an isolated Docker network for the test session. Containers on the same network can resolve each other by the alias set with `WithNetworkAliases`, enabling realistic inter-service calls without hardcoded ports. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Networks;
using Testcontainers.RabbitMq;
using Testcontainers.Redis;
using Xunit;

public class MessagingStackFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly INetwork _network = new NetworkBuilder()
        .WithName("messaging-test-net")
        .Build();

    private readonly RabbitMqContainer _rabbit;
    private readonly RedisContainer    _redis;

    public string RabbitMqConnectionString => _rabbit.GetConnectionString();
    public string RedisConnectionString    => _redis.GetConnectionString();

    public MessagingStackFixture()
    {
        _rabbit = new RabbitMqBuilder()
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithNetworkAliases("rabbitmq")          // resolvable by alias inside the network
            .Build();

        _redis = new RedisBuilder()
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithNetworkAliases("redis")
            .Build();
    }

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _network.CreateAsync();
        await Task.WhenAll(_rabbit.StartAsync(), _redis.StartAsync());
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await Task.WhenAll(_rabbit.DisposeAsync().AsTask(), _redis.DisposeAsync().AsTask());
        await _network.DeleteAsync();
    }
}

[Collection("MessagingStack")]
public class OrderEventPublisherTests(MessagingStackFixture stack)
    : IClassFixture<MessagingStackFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task PublishOrderCreated_MessageArrivesOnQueue()
    {
        var publisher = new OrderEventPublisher(stack.RabbitMqConnectionString);
        await publisher.PublishAsync(new OrderCreatedEvent { OrderId = 55 });

        var consumer = new TestQueueConsumer(stack.RabbitMqConnectionString, "order.created");
        var message  = await consumer.WaitForMessageAsync(timeout: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));

        message.Should().NotBeNull();
        message!.OrderId.Should().Be(55);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `NetworkBuilder` any time two or more containers must communicate directly — without it, inter-container calls must go through the host-mapped port, which varies between runs and fails in nested Docker (CI) environments. Do NOT create a new network per test method — network creation is slow (~500 ms); share the network via a class or collection fixture. Alternative: Docker Compose via `.WithDockerfileDirectory()` for teams that already maintain a `docker-compose.yml`; the Testcontainers.NET approach is preferable for programmatic, code-first environments. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `TheoryData<T1, T2>` Strongly-Typed Theory Data for Compile-Time Safety

xUnit v3 ships `TheoryData<T1>` through `TheoryData<T1,...,T10>` — generic theory data classes that eliminate the `object[]` boxing and provide compile-time type checking for `[Theory]` data. Passing the wrong type to a data row is a compile error rather than a runtime `InvalidCastException`. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class CurrencyConverterTests
{
    // TheoryData<T1, T2, T3> — fully typed; compiler rejects wrong argument types
    public static TheoryData<string, string, decimal> ConversionScenarios => new()
    {
        { "USD", "EUR", 0.92m   },
        { "USD", "GBP", 0.79m   },
        { "EUR", "USD", 1.09m   },
        { "GBP", "JPY", 193.40m },
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(ConversionScenarios))]
    public void Convert_KnownPair_ReturnsExpectedRate(
        string fromCurrency,
        string toCurrency,
        decimal expectedRate)
    {
        var converter = new CurrencyConverter(new StubRateProvider());
        var rate = converter.GetRate(fromCurrency, toCurrency);

        rate.Should().BeApproximately(expectedRate, precision: 0.01m,
            because: $"{fromCurrency}→{toCurrency} rate must match the stub");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always prefer `TheoryData<T>` over `IEnumerable<object[]>` in new xUnit v3 code — it is less error-prone and produces cleaner IDE tooltips. Do NOT use `TheoryData` when the data source is external (CSV, database) and the types are only known at runtime — `IEnumerable<object[]>` or `[MemberData]` returning `IAsyncEnumerable<ITheoryDataRow>` is the correct extension point for dynamic data. Alternative: NUnit `[TestCaseSource]` returning `TestCaseData` achieves the same result with named arguments and custom display names. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` for True Test Isolation

By default NUnit creates a single `[TestFixture]` instance and runs all its test methods on it, meaning shared mutable fields persist between tests. `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` instructs NUnit to construct a fresh instance for every test method — matching xUnit's default per-test construction model and eliminating state leakage between tests without requiring manual cleanup. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Collections.Generic;

[TestFixture]
[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]
public class ShoppingCartTests
{
    // Safe to use instance fields — a fresh instance is created for every test
    private readonly ShoppingCart _cart = new ShoppingCart();

    [Test]
    public void AddItem_SingleItem_CartHasOneEntry()
    {
        _cart.Add(new CartItem("SKU-001", quantity: 1, price: 9.99m));

        Assert.That(_cart.Items, Has.Count.EqualTo(1));
        Assert.That(_cart.TotalAmount, Is.EqualTo(9.99m));
    }

    [Test]
    public void AddItem_DuplicateSku_IncreasesQuantity()
    {
        _cart.Add(new CartItem("SKU-001", quantity: 1, price: 9.99m));
        _cart.Add(new CartItem("SKU-001", quantity: 2, price: 9.99m));

        // No bleed from AddItem_SingleItem_CartHasOneEntry because this is a fresh instance
        Assert.That(_cart.Items, Has.Count.EqualTo(1));
        Assert.That(_cart.Items[0].Quantity, Is.EqualTo(3));
    }

    [Test]
    public void RemoveItem_NonExistentSku_DoesNotThrow()
    {
        // _cart is empty — no bleed from previous tests
        Assert.DoesNotThrow(() => _cart.Remove("SKU-NONEXISTENT"));
        Assert.That(_cart.Items, Is.Empty);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` for any NUnit fixture whose tests involve mutable state — it is the safest default for new fixtures. Do NOT use this lifecycle for fixtures that hold expensive resources (database connections, containers) in instance fields — each test would start and stop the resource; use `[OneTimeSetUp]` / static fields for those. Alternative: xUnit does per-test instantiation by default (no attribute needed); MSTest uses `[TestInitialize]` to reset state but shares the instance by default. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 32

**xUnit `IClassFixture<T>` and `IAsyncLifetime` share the same instance across all tests in the class, so mutations to fixture state in one test corrupt subsequent tests — the fixture is not reset between tests [community]** — `IClassFixture<T>` creates one fixture instance for the entire test class, shared across all parallel and sequential test methods. Mutations to properties or collections on the fixture in test A are visible to test B. WHY it causes problems: tests that write to a `List<T>` on the fixture, set a property, or call a method that changes internal state produce order-dependent failures that appear intermittently in parallel runs but pass locally when run in IDE order. Fix: make fixture state readonly after initialization; expose reset methods via `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync`-equivalent per-test setup, or use `IClassFixture<T>` only for truly immutable, lazily-initialized resources.

**Moq `SetupSequence` is order-sensitive and does not wrap around — once all configured returns are consumed it throws `MockException` on subsequent calls unless a final `.Returns()` fallback is configured [community]** — `SetupSequence` returns values in declaration order and has no looping behavior. If production code calls the method more times than you configured values, Moq throws a `MockException` ("invocation failed with mock behavior Strict") or returns the default value (Loose), not the first value again. WHY it causes problems: retry or polling loops that call the same method N+1 times (e.g., a health check polled until healthy) exhaust the sequence and throw unexpectedly, making the failure look like a production bug rather than a test setup error. Fix: append a final `.Returns(lastValue)` (or `.ReturnsAsync(lastValue)`) to the sequence as a "steady state" fallback.

**FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` performs deep structural comparison by default — value-type properties that differ by even one decimal digit cause the assertion to fail without identifying which property differs [community]** — `BeEquivalentTo` compares every public property recursively. For `decimal` and `double` properties, it uses exact equality unless you configure `options.Using<decimal>(ctx => ctx.Subject.Should().BeApproximately(ctx.Expectation, precision: 0.01m)).WhenTypeIs<decimal>()`. WHY it causes problems: tests comparing API response models that include floating-point amounts produce assertion failures whose error messages say "Expected X but found Y" without specifying the field path unless `options.WithTracing()` is enabled, leading to minutes of confusion for every precision mismatch. Fix: always configure `BeEquivalentTo(options => options.Using<decimal>(...).WhenTypeIs<decimal>())` for domain models with monetary or measurement values; enable `options.WithTracing()` during debugging.

**Testcontainers.NET `WithReuse(true)` silently ignores configuration changes — if you update the container builder (image tag, env vars, ports) the hash may collide with the old running container and the stale container is reused [community]** — `WithReuse(true)` identifies containers by a hash of the builder configuration. In practice the hash does not cover every builder field (custom labels, some network settings) so a partially-matching stale container can be reused when a fresh one is needed. WHY it causes problems: developers changing a Postgres image from `postgres:15-alpine` to `postgres:16-alpine` may continue to get the old container, causing migration compatibility failures that appear unrelated to the version bump. Fix: always verify the container image version with `_db.Image.Tag` in the fixture `InitializeAsync` and throw if it does not match the expected tag; or call `docker rm -f` in a teardown hook when changing image versions during development.

**`WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>` does not automatically reset `IMemoryCache` between test cases — stale cached values from one test affect subsequent tests in the same factory lifetime [community]** — The in-process server shares a single `IMemoryCache` instance for the factory's lifetime. Cache entries written during test A (e.g., a cached product catalogue) survive into test B if the TTL has not expired, causing test B to read stale data that was written by test A. WHY it causes problems: the failure only reproduces when tests run in a specific order; running test B in isolation passes because the cache is empty. Fix: either clear the cache between tests by resolving `IMemoryCache` from the factory's service provider and calling `((MemoryCache)cache).Compact(1.0)`, or replace `IMemoryCache` with a `NoOpMemoryCache` in `ConfigureTestServices` for tests that require a clean state.

**NUnit `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.All)]` at the fixture level causes `[SetUp]` and `[TearDown]` methods to race when they access shared static state — e.g., a static `TestContext` or ambient thread-local that is not indexed by test ID [community]** — `ParallelScope.All` allows test methods within the fixture to run concurrently. `[SetUp]` methods run on the same thread as the test but share static/ambient state with sibling tests that are running simultaneously on other threads. WHY it causes problems: ambient state written in `[SetUp]` (e.g., `HttpContext.Current`, a static logger instance, a shared counter) is overwritten by a concurrent `[SetUp]` invocation before the test method reads it, causing test A to observe test B's setup context and assert against the wrong data. Fix: move all mutable ambient state to instance fields (safe with `LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase`) or `AsyncLocal<T>` / `ThreadLocal<T>` keyed to the test ID; add `[NonParallelizable]` to any test that cannot be safely isolated.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 32 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Setting up Moq async methods without `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` | Production code passes a real token; stub does not match; `MockException` thrown | Always use `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` unless specifically testing cancellation |
| Using `Assert.Multiple` (sync) with `async` lambdas in NUnit | Async continuations are dropped; failures are silently swallowed | Use `Assert.MultipleAsync` for any block containing `await` |
| Mutating `IClassFixture<T>` state inside test methods | State persists across tests; order-dependent failures appear in parallel runs | Keep fixture state immutable after `InitializeAsync`; use per-test setup for mutable state |
| Relying on `WithReuse(true)` after changing container image tags | Hash may match stale container; wrong image version silently reused | Verify `container.Image.Tag` in `InitializeAsync` or clear stale containers manually |
| Not scoping `AssertionScope` with a meaningful name | Failure messages lack context; developer cannot identify which object failed | Always pass a descriptive label to `new AssertionScope("entity type or scenario")` |
| Storing live `HttpRequestMessage` in recording handler and reading content after `SendAsync` | Content stream is disposed; `ObjectDisposedException` in assertion phase | Read and copy body content inside `SendAsync` before returning stub response |

## Cycle 33 — 2026-05-14

### C# 13 `params` Collections With `ReadOnlySpan<T>` for Zero-Allocation Test Helpers

C# 13 expands the `params` modifier beyond arrays to include `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `Span<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`, and other collection types. In test code this allows writing compact assertion helpers that accept a variable number of items without forcing a heap allocation for each call — useful in tight loops that assert over large generated datasets. The compiler synthesizes stack-allocated storage for the span when calling sites pass inline arguments. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public static class AssertExtensions
{
    // C# 13: params ReadOnlySpan<T> — stack-allocated; no heap array per call
    public static void AllShouldBePositive(params ReadOnlySpan<decimal> values)
    {
        foreach (var v in values)
            v.Should().BePositive(because: $"value {v} was expected to be positive");
    }
}

public class PricingEngineTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void CalculateMargins_AllItems_ArePositive()
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();
        decimal margin1 = engine.GetMargin("SKU-001");
        decimal margin2 = engine.GetMargin("SKU-002");
        decimal margin3 = engine.GetMargin("SKU-003");

        // No array allocation; compiler uses stack storage for the span
        AssertExtensions.AllShouldBePositive(margin1, margin2, margin3);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` for assertion helpers called thousands of times in data-driven tests where GC pressure from transient `object[]` allocations is measurable. Do NOT use it when the parameter count can exceed the stack limit (~1 MB per frame) — prefer `IEnumerable<T>` or a `List<T>` parameter instead. Alternative: Keep `params T[]` if the test project targets .NET 8 or earlier; `params Span<T>` requires .NET 9+ and C# 13. [official]

---

### C# 13 `partial` Properties in Source-Generated Test Fixture Builders

C# 13 allows `partial` properties (declaring and implementing declarations in separate files), enabling source generators to emit the backing implementation while the developer writes only the declaring declaration in the test project. This pattern is especially useful with `[AutoFixture]`-style generators that produce `partial` test fixture classes, letting generators fill in complex property logic without polluting the handwritten file. [official]

```csharp
// File: OrderFixture.Partial.cs  — developer-written declaring declaration
using Xunit;

public partial class OrderFixture
{
    // Declaring declaration only — implementation generated in OrderFixture.g.cs
    public partial Order BuildDefaultOrder();
    public partial Order BuildOverdueOrder();
}

// File: OrderFixture.g.cs  — source-generator output (implementation declarations)
public partial class OrderFixture
{
    public partial Order BuildDefaultOrder()
        => new Order
        {
            Id        = Guid.NewGuid(),
            Status    = OrderStatus.Pending,
            CreatedAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow,
            Lines     = [new OrderLine("SKU-001", qty: 1, price: 9.99m)],
        };

    public partial Order BuildOverdueOrder()
        => BuildDefaultOrder() with
        {
            DueDate = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddDays(-5),
            Status  = OrderStatus.Overdue,
        };
}

public class OrderServiceTests(OrderFixture fixture) : IClassFixture<OrderFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public void ProcessOrder_OverdueOrder_ThrowsDeadlineExceededException()
    {
        var order   = fixture.BuildOverdueOrder();
        var service = new OrderService();

        var act = () => service.Process(order);

        act.Should().Throw<DeadlineExceededException>();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use partial properties with source generators to keep handwritten test files lean and let generated code own boilerplate factory logic. Do NOT rely on partial properties in projects that do not use source generators — the split between declaring and implementing declarations adds complexity with no benefit. Alternative: Use the Builder pattern (`OrderBuilder.WithStatus(...).Build()`) or AutoFixture `ICustomization` when source generators are not in scope. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `ITestContextAccessor` for Structured Per-Test Logging and Diagnostics

xUnit v3 introduces `ITestContextAccessor`, a DI-injectable service that provides access to the current `ITestContext` — including a `TestOutputHelper` equivalent for writing per-test diagnostic lines, cancellation token, and test metadata. Injecting `ITestContextAccessor` into system-under-test logging adapters captures structured logs per test without relying on `ITestOutputHelper` constructor injection. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;
using Xunit;
using Xunit.v3;

// Adapter: forwards ILogger output to xUnit per-test output via ITestContextAccessor
public sealed class XunitLoggerProvider(ITestContextAccessor accessor) : ILoggerProvider
{
    public ILogger CreateLogger(string categoryName) =>
        new XunitLogger(categoryName, accessor);

    public void Dispose() { }
}

public sealed class XunitLogger(string category, ITestContextAccessor accessor) : ILogger
{
    public IDisposable? BeginScope<TState>(TState state) => null;
    public bool IsEnabled(LogLevel logLevel) => true;
    public void Log<TState>(LogLevel level, EventId id, TState state,
        Exception? exception, Func<TState, Exception?, string> formatter)
    {
        var message = formatter(state, exception);
        // TestContext.Current exposes the test's output sink
        accessor.TestContext?.TestOutputHelper?.WriteLine(
            $"[{level}] {category}: {message}");
    }
}

public class OrderProcessorTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrder_ValidOrder_LogsCompletionMessage()
    {
        var accessor = TestContextAccessor.Instance;
        var loggerFactory = LoggerFactory.Create(b =>
            b.AddProvider(new XunitLoggerProvider(accessor)));

        var processor = new OrderProcessor(loggerFactory.CreateLogger<OrderProcessor>());
        await processor.ProcessAsync(new Order { Id = 42 });

        // Diagnostic lines are visible in the test output window per test
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `ITestContextAccessor` when the system under test uses `ILogger<T>` and you want structured logs captured per test without cluttering constructor signatures with `ITestOutputHelper`. Do NOT inject `ITestContextAccessor` as a field on a shared `IClassFixture<T>` and call it during fixture construction — the context is only valid during a test method execution, not during fixture setup. Alternative: xUnit v2 uses `ITestOutputHelper` constructor injection directly; the v3 accessor is more flexible but requires the v3 NuGet packages. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `Assert.MultipleAsync` for Collecting All Async Assertion Failures

NUnit 4 adds `Assert.MultipleAsync` — the async-aware counterpart to the synchronous `Assert.Multiple`. It accepts a `Func<Task>` and ensures that all `await`-ed assertions inside the block are collected, even if earlier ones fail, producing a single consolidated failure report instead of stopping at the first exception. Using the synchronous `Assert.Multiple` with async lambdas silently drops failures because async continuations escape the synchronous exception capture mechanism. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
public class InvoiceApiTests
{
    private HttpClient _client = null!;

    [OneTimeSetUp]
    public void Setup()
    {
        // Assume WebApplicationFactory already configured
        _client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:5000") };
    }

    [Test]
    public async Task GetInvoice_ValidId_ReturnsCompleteInvoiceDocument()
    {
        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/api/invoices/1001");
        var body     = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<InvoiceDto>();

        // Collect ALL async assertion failures, not just the first one
        await Assert.MultipleAsync(async () =>
        {
            response.StatusCode.Should().Be(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK);
            body.Should().NotBeNull();
            body!.InvoiceNumber.Should().StartWith("INV-");
            body.TotalAmount.Should().BeGreaterThan(0m);

            // Nested async assertion: verify sub-resource is also reachable
            var lineResponse = await _client.GetAsync($"/api/invoices/1001/lines");
            lineResponse.IsSuccessStatusCode.Should().BeTrue(
                because: "line items endpoint must be reachable for a valid invoice");
        });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Assert.MultipleAsync` whenever a single test method performs multiple `await`-ed assertions against an HTTP endpoint or async service — it ensures all assertions are evaluated and all failures are reported together. Do NOT use `Assert.MultipleAsync` to accumulate assertions across multiple test methods (each test must stand alone); and do NOT use it as an excuse to write tests that assert more than one logical behavior. Alternative: FluentAssertions `AssertionScope` with `using var scope = new AssertionScope()` achieves the same collection for synchronous assertions; for async use `await scope.AssertAsync()` (FA 7+). [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `Assert.ThrowsExactly<T>` vs `Assert.ThrowsException<T>` for Strict Exception Type Checking

MSTest v3 adds `Assert.ThrowsExactly<T>` alongside the existing `Assert.ThrowsException<T>`. The existing method passes if the thrown exception is assignable to `T` (i.e., it accepts subclasses), while `ThrowsExactly<T>` requires the exact runtime type — a stricter assertion that prevents subtypes from silently satisfying the check. This is relevant when distinguishing between `HttpRequestException` and `TaskCanceledException` (which inherits from `OperationCanceledException`). [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class PaymentGatewayTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_ExpiredCard_ThrowsExactlyPaymentDeclinedException()
    {
        var gateway = new PaymentGateway(new StubDeclineProvider());
        var request = new PaymentRequest { CardNumber = "4111111111111111", Amount = 100m };

        // ThrowsExactly<T>: fails if a subclass of PaymentDeclinedException is thrown
        await Assert.ThrowsExactlyAsync<PaymentDeclinedException>(
            async () => await gateway.ProcessAsync(request));
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_NetworkTimeout_ThrowsExactlyTimeoutException()
    {
        var gateway = new PaymentGateway(new StubTimeoutProvider());
        var request = new PaymentRequest { CardNumber = "4111111111111111", Amount = 50m };

        // Without ThrowsExactly, a TaskCanceledException subclass would also pass
        // ThrowsExactly ensures only TimeoutException itself is accepted
        await Assert.ThrowsExactlyAsync<TimeoutException>(
            async () => await gateway.ProcessAsync(request));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Assert.ThrowsExactly<T>` when the exact exception type communicates important semantic information (e.g., distinguishing `AuthenticationException` from `AuthorizationException` in security tests). Do NOT use it for exception types that intentionally use inheritance as part of their public API design (e.g., `ArgumentException` hierarchy) — `ThrowsException<T>` is more appropriate there. Alternative: xUnit `Assert.Throws<TExact>` and FluentAssertions `.ThrowExactly<T>()` provide equivalent strict checking. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions 7 — `BeEquivalentTo` With `RespectingRuntimeTypes()` for Polymorphic Collections

FluentAssertions 7 introduces `RespectingRuntimeTypes()` as a named option on `BeEquivalentTo`, replacing the older `options.ComparingByValue<object>()` approach. When a collection contains polymorphic items (a `List<Animal>` holding `Dog` and `Cat` instances), the default behavior compares only the declared base type's properties. `RespectingRuntimeTypes()` ensures the comparison uses each item's actual runtime type, checking derived-type properties. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public abstract record Animal(string Name);
public record Dog(string Name, string Breed) : Animal(Name);
public record Cat(string Name, bool IsIndoor) : Animal(Name);

public class AnimalRegistryTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GetAnimals_MixedTypes_ReturnsCorrectDerivedProperties()
    {
        var registry = new AnimalRegistry();
        registry.Register(new Dog("Rex",   "Labrador"));
        registry.Register(new Cat("Whiskers", IsIndoor: true));

        var actual = registry.GetAll().ToList();

        var expected = new List<Animal>
        {
            new Dog("Rex",   "Labrador"),
            new Cat("Whiskers", IsIndoor: true),
        };

        // Without RespectingRuntimeTypes, only Animal.Name is compared
        // With it, Dog.Breed and Cat.IsIndoor are also verified
        actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, options =>
            options.RespectingRuntimeTypes()
                   .WithStrictOrdering());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `RespectingRuntimeTypes()` whenever a collection's declared type is a base or interface type but the actual items are derived — omitting it silently ignores derived properties and produces false-positive tests. Do NOT use `RespectingRuntimeTypes()` indiscriminately on all calls — it adds overhead for each item's type resolution and can produce confusing failures if derived types have additional required fields not set in the expected collection. Alternative: Use explicit casting to derived types with individual property assertions for smaller collections where the polymorphic structure is already known at test-write time. [official]

---

### Moq — `Capture.In<T>` Argument Capturing for Post-Call Assertion

Moq provides `Capture.In<T>(list)` as an argument matcher that records all values passed to a mocked method into a provided `List<T>`. This eliminates the need to manually wire up `Callback` with a closure just to capture parameters, and allows asserting on every argument passed across all invocations after the test's Act phase. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public interface IEmailService
{
    Task SendAsync(string toAddress, string subject, string body);
}

public class OrderConfirmationServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_MultipleItems_SendsOneConfirmationEmailPerItem()
    {
        var capturedAddresses = new List<string>();
        var capturedSubjects  = new List<string>();

        var emailMock = new Mock<IEmailService>();
        emailMock
            .Setup(e => e.SendAsync(
                Capture.In(capturedAddresses),
                Capture.In(capturedSubjects),
                It.IsAny<string>()))
            .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

        var service = new OrderConfirmationService(emailMock.Object);
        await service.ProcessOrderAsync(new Order
        {
            Lines = [new("SKU-A", "buyer-a@example.com"),
                     new("SKU-B", "buyer-b@example.com")]
        });

        capturedAddresses.Should().HaveCount(2);
        capturedAddresses.Should().Contain("buyer-a@example.com");
        capturedAddresses.Should().Contain("buyer-b@example.com");
        capturedSubjects.Should().OnlyContain(s => s.StartsWith("Order Confirmation"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Capture.In<T>` when you need to assert the actual argument values passed to a dependency across multiple calls without polluting the Arrange phase with verbose `Callback` closures. Do NOT use `Capture.In` when you only need to verify the call count or a single call argument — `Verify(...)` with `Times.Once()` is cleaner for those cases. Alternative: NSubstitute `ReceivedCalls().Select(c => c.GetArguments())` achieves the same result with a fluent style on the substitute object after the call. [official]

---

### NSubstitute — `Received.InOrder` for Strict Call-Order Verification

NSubstitute 5+ provides `Received.InOrder(() => { ... })` for verifying that multiple method calls on one or more substitutes happened in a specific sequence. This is the NSubstitute equivalent of Moq's `MockSequence` but uses a lambda that reads like a narrative script, making test intent explicit without requiring separate sequence objects. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using NSubstitute;
using NSubstitute.ReceivedExtensions;
using Xunit;

public interface IWorkflowStep
{
    Task ExecuteAsync(WorkflowContext context);
}

public class PipelineOrchestratorTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task RunPipeline_ThreeSteps_ExecutedInOrder()
    {
        var step1 = Substitute.For<IWorkflowStep>();
        var step2 = Substitute.For<IWorkflowStep>();
        var step3 = Substitute.For<IWorkflowStep>();

        var orchestrator = new PipelineOrchestrator([step1, step2, step3]);
        var context      = new WorkflowContext { CorrelationId = Guid.NewGuid() };

        await orchestrator.RunAsync(context);

        // Verify the steps executed in declaration order
        Received.InOrder(async () =>
        {
            await step1.Received().ExecuteAsync(context);
            await step2.Received().ExecuteAsync(context);
            await step3.Received().ExecuteAsync(context);
        });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `Received.InOrder` for pipeline, saga, or state-machine tests where call ordering is a critical correctness invariant. Do NOT use it for service-level tests where call order is an implementation detail — ordering constraints in tests make refactoring harder. Alternative: Moq `MockSequence` with `InSequence()` provides equivalent ordering; xUnit does not have a built-in mechanism, making NSubstitute or Moq preferred for ordering tests. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET 4 — `IWaitUntil` Custom Wait Strategy for Non-Standard Health Checks

Testcontainers.NET 4.x exposes `IWaitUntil` as an extension point for writing custom wait strategies when the built-in HTTP health-check and log-output strategies are insufficient. Implementing `IWaitUntil` with a single `UntilAsync(IContainer)` method allows polling any custom condition (gRPC ping, Redis PING command, custom TCP probe) before the container is considered ready. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Configurations;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Containers;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

// Custom wait: issue a Redis PING and expect "PONG"
public sealed class WaitUntilRedisPong : IWaitUntil
{
    public async Task<bool> UntilAsync(IContainer container)
    {
        try
        {
            var (stdout, _) = await container.ExecAsync(
                ["redis-cli", "PING"]);
            return stdout.Trim().Equals("PONG", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        }
        catch
        {
            return false;
        }
    }
}

public class CacheServiceIntegrationTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly IContainer _redis = new ContainerBuilder()
        .WithImage("redis:7.4-alpine")
        .WithPortBinding(6379, assignRandomHostPort: true)
        .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer()
            .UntilMessageIsLogged("Ready to accept connections")
            .AddCustomWaitStrategy(new WaitUntilRedisPong()))
        .Build();

    public Task InitializeAsync() => _redis.StartAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()    => _redis.StopAsync();

    [Fact]
    public async Task SetAndGet_Value_ReturnsStoredValue()
    {
        var cache = new RedisCache($"localhost:{_redis.GetMappedPublicPort(6379)}");
        await cache.SetAsync("key", "hello");
        var value = await cache.GetAsync("key");
        value.Should().Be("hello");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `IWaitUntil` for non-HTTP services or when the default log-message strategy is unreliable because the startup log format changes between image versions. Do NOT layer more than two custom wait strategies — each strategy adds polling overhead, and chaining many increases container startup time significantly in CI. Alternative: For HTTP services use `.WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPath("/health")))` which is built in and requires no custom code. [official]

---

### Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP) — `global.json` MTP Mode for `dotnet test` in .NET 10

.NET 10 introduces a new `Microsoft.Testing.Platform` mode for `dotnet test` that replaces the legacy VSTest runner. Opting in via `global.json` removes the requirement for `Microsoft.Testing.Platform.MSBuild`, the extra `--` separator for MTP arguments, and the `TestingPlatformDotnetTestSupport` property. This makes CI scripts cleaner and eliminates the "mixed VSTest and MTP" confusion in solutions containing both MSTest and xUnit projects. [official]

```json
// global.json — opt into MTP mode for dotnet test (.NET 10 SDK and MTP 1.7+)
{
    "sdk": {
        "version": "10.0.100",
        "rollForward": "latestMinor"
    },
    "test": {
        "runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform"
    }
}
```

```xml
<!-- Directory.Build.props — route framework-specific filter args per project -->
<!-- Avoids "unrecognized option" exit-code 5 in mixed MSTest + xUnit solutions -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments
      Condition="'$(UsingMSTestSdk)' == 'true'">
      $(TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments) $(MSTestArgs)
    </TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments>
    <TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments
      Condition="'$(UsingMSTestSdk)' != 'true'">
      $(TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments) $(XUnitArgs)
    </TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
<!-- Usage from CI:
  dotnet test --solution MySolution.sln
    -p:MSTestArgs="--filter FullyQualifiedName~Integration"
    -p:XUnitArgs="--filter-trait Category=Integration" -->
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use MTP mode in new .NET 10 projects and when migrating CI pipelines away from VSTest — it provides deterministic, reflection-free test execution and native AOT compatibility. Do NOT enable MTP mode in solutions that still contain VSTest-only test projects (projects without `EnableMSTestRunner` / `EnableNUnitRunner`) — MTP mode generates an error for VSTest-only projects. Alternative: Keep VSTest mode with `TestingPlatformDotnetTestSupport=true` when a gradual migration is required; full MTP mode can be adopted project by project. [official]

---

### C# 14 — `field` Keyword in Property Accessors for Testable Validated Properties

C# 14 (stable in .NET 10) promotes the `field` contextual keyword from preview to stable. `field` accesses the compiler-synthesized backing field inside a property accessor body, eliminating the need for an explicit private field declaration. In test-fixture builders and domain entities used in tests, this reduces boilerplate while preserving custom validation logic in the setter. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class Invoice
{
    // No explicit backing field needed — `field` refers to the synthesized field
    public string InvoiceNumber
    {
        get;
        set => field = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)
            ? throw new ArgumentException("Invoice number cannot be blank.", nameof(value))
            : value.ToUpperInvariant();
    }

    public decimal TotalAmount
    {
        get;
        set => field = value >= 0
            ? value
            : throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(value), "Amount must be non-negative.");
    }
}

public class InvoiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void InvoiceNumber_SetLowerCase_StoredAsUpperCase()
    {
        var invoice = new Invoice();
        invoice.InvoiceNumber = "inv-0042";

        invoice.InvoiceNumber.Should().Be("INV-0042");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void TotalAmount_SetNegative_ThrowsArgumentOutOfRangeException()
    {
        var invoice = new Invoice();
        Action act = () => invoice.TotalAmount = -1m;

        act.Should().ThrowExactly<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>()
           .WithParameterName("value");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use the `field` keyword for any property that needs a single-line accessor body with validation — it avoids declaring a redundant private field. Do NOT use `field` in classes that already have a member named `field` — the compiler will shadow the identifier and produce a confusing compile error; use `@field` or rename the conflicting member. Alternative: C# 13 `partial` properties with source generators achieve a similar reduction in boilerplate when the validation logic is generated; use `field` for hand-authored validation. [official]

---

### C# 14 — Null-Conditional Assignment in Test Assertion Helpers

C# 14's null-conditional assignment (`?.=`) allows assigning to a property only when the left-hand side is non-null. In test helpers that configure optional response fields, this removes the `if (x is not null)` guards and produces more readable assertion setup code, especially when building expected-response objects with many optional fields. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public record ApiResponse
{
    public string? CorrelationId { get; set; }
    public ErrorDetail? Error     { get; set; }
    public string? TraceId        { get; set; }
}

public record ErrorDetail
{
    public string Code    { get; set; } = "";
    public string Message { get; set; } = "";
}

public class ApiResponseBuilderTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void BuildErrorResponse_WithOptionalFields_OnlyPopulatesNonNullFields()
    {
        ApiResponse? response = new ApiResponse();
        ErrorDetail? errorDetail = new ErrorDetail { Code = "404", Message = "Not Found" };

        // C# 14: null-conditional assignment — no if-guard needed
        response?.CorrelationId = "abc-123";
        response?.Error         = errorDetail;

        // Verify optional field assignment semantics
        response.Should().NotBeNull();
        response!.CorrelationId.Should().Be("abc-123");
        response.Error.Should().NotBeNull();
        response.Error!.Code.Should().Be("404");

        // Demonstrates: null-conditional on the target itself
        ApiResponse? nullResponse = null;
        nullResponse?.CorrelationId = "should-be-ignored"; // no-op; no NullReferenceException
        nullResponse.Should().BeNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use null-conditional assignment in test setup helpers that build optional response/request objects where many fields are conditionally populated based on test parameters. Do NOT use `?.=` to silently swallow assignments on objects that should be initialized — if `response` being null represents a bug in the test setup, prefer `response!.Field = value` (null-forgiving) so the `NullReferenceException` surfaces immediately. Alternative: C# 8+ null-coalescing assignment `??=` fills a related but complementary role: assigning only when the field itself is null, not when the holder is null. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions — `HaveCount` With `And` Chaining on Collections for Single-Line Assertions

FluentAssertions allows chaining `And` after a collection constraint to add further assertions on the same collection in one expression. Combining `HaveCount(n).And.OnlyContain(pred)` or `HaveCount(n).And.AllSatisfy(a => { ... })` produces self-documenting single-expression tests that report the exact constraint that failed. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class ProductCatalogTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GetFeaturedProducts_Always_ReturnsFiveActiveProducts()
    {
        var catalog  = new ProductCatalog(new StubProductRepository());
        var products = catalog.GetFeatured();

        products.Should()
            .HaveCount(5,           because: "featured list must always have exactly 5 items")
            .And.OnlyContain(p => p.IsActive,
                             because: "only active products should be featured")
            .And.AllSatisfy(p =>
            {
                p.Price.Should().BeGreaterThan(0m);
                p.Name.Should().NotBeNullOrWhiteSpace();
                p.CategoryId.Should().BePositive();
            });
    }

    [Fact]
    public void GetFeaturedProducts_WhenNoneActive_ReturnsEmptyList()
    {
        var catalog = new ProductCatalog(new StubEmptyProductRepository());

        catalog.GetFeatured().Should()
            .BeEmpty(because: "no active products means the featured list must be empty");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `.And` chaining when multiple constraints on the same collection are logically related and belong in the same test scenario — it reduces visual noise compared to repeating `products.Should()` on every line. Do NOT chain more than 3-4 constraints — excessively long chains become hard to read and hard to diagnose when one link fails. Alternative: `Assert.Multiple` (NUnit) or `AssertionScope` (FluentAssertions) for cases where the constraints represent genuinely independent behaviors that should each be reported as separate failures. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 33

**xUnit v3 `IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync` swallows the root-cause exception when `InitializeAsync` throws — a fixture that throws during init still has `DisposeAsync` called, and if `DisposeAsync` also throws, the init exception is replaced by the dispose exception [community]** — When xUnit v3 calls `InitializeAsync` and that method throws, the framework calls `DisposeAsync` to clean up partially-constructed state. If `DisposeAsync` also throws (e.g., a `NullReferenceException` because a field was never assigned), the second exception propagates and the original `InitializeAsync` exception is lost. WHY it causes problems: the test runner reports the `NullReferenceException` from `DisposeAsync` as the failure; developers spend time debugging a phantom dispose error when the real bug is in the setup code. Fix: guard every disposable field in `DisposeAsync` with null-conditional disposal — use `await (_resource?.DisposeAsync() ?? ValueTask.CompletedTask)` to prevent `DisposeAsync` from throwing when initialization was incomplete.

**Moq `SetupProperty` is required to make a mocked property store assigned values — writing `mock.Object.Status = "Active"` without `SetupProperty` silently discards the assignment and the getter always returns the default value [community]** — By default, Moq properties are not backed by a field. Writing `mock.Object.Status = "Active"` has no effect unless `mock.SetupProperty(m => m.Status)` was called first to install a getter/setter pair that stores the value. WHY it causes problems: test code that assigns a property and asserts on the same mock object gets back null or 0, producing a mysterious failure with no indication that the assignment was silently discarded. Fix: call `mock.SetupProperty(m => m.PropertyName)` (or `mock.SetupAllProperties()` for all properties) before the assignment; or use `mock.Setup(m => m.PropertyName).Returns(value)` for read-only access.

**NSubstitute argument matchers (`Arg.Any<T>()`) used outside a substitute call silently return `default(T)` and produce no match — capturing a matcher in a variable and reusing it causes verification to fail as if the call was never made [community]** — NSubstitute's argument matchers work by recording a pending matcher in thread-local state. They are only valid in the context of the immediately following substitute call. If a matcher is captured in a variable (`var any = Arg.Any<string>(); sub.Received().Method(any)`), the thread-local state has already been consumed and the second call receives a plain `default(T)` comparison. WHY it causes problems: the failure message says the expected call was not received even though the call was made with a non-default value, leading to incorrect conclusions that the method was never invoked. Fix: always write the matcher inline in the substitute call expression; never assign it to a variable and reuse it.

**FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` with `ExcludingMissingMembers()` silently skips properties present on the expected object but absent on the actual — renamed or removed fields pass the assertion undetected [community]** — `ExcludingMissingMembers()` suppresses failures for properties present on the expected type but absent on the actual. This is intended for comparing anonymous types against named types, but when misapplied broadly (e.g., comparing two concrete DTOs), it hides legitimate mismatches where a property was removed or renamed. WHY it causes problems: the test passes even though the actual response is missing a field that the expected model specifies, producing a false sense of correctness. Fix: only use `ExcludingMissingMembers()` when comparing anonymous types to concrete types; for concrete-to-concrete comparisons remove the option so that missing members fail the assertion.

**Testcontainers.NET pinning image to "latest" causes non-deterministic CI failures when the upstream registry pushes a breaking update — the developer machine uses a cached older layer while CI fetches the current "latest" [community]** — Testcontainers.NET resolves the "latest" tag at container start time from the Docker registry. On a developer machine Docker may serve a cached older layer; on a fresh CI runner `docker pull` fetches the current "latest" which may have breaking changes (new default config, removed commands, changed health-check endpoint path). WHY it causes problems: CI goes red without any code change; the failure is often in the wait strategy or schema initialization, not in the test logic, making root-cause analysis time-consuming. Fix: always pin an explicit version tag (e.g., `postgres:16.4-alpine`, `redis:7.4.1-alpine`); treat container image tags as versioned dependencies with the same rigor as NuGet package pinning. Testcontainers.NET 4.10.0 release notes explicitly call this out as a required best practice.

**`WebApplicationFactory<T>` derived instances created via `WithWebHostBuilder` must be disposed per test — storing the derived factory in a class field causes its DI modifications to bleed into sibling tests via shared singleton registrations [community]** — `WebApplicationFactory<T>.WithWebHostBuilder()` creates a new derived factory with an isolated `IServiceCollection` configuration. However, if that derived factory is stored in a shared field (a common mistake when trying to avoid re-creation overhead), its modified singletons persist across tests because the in-process server is reused. WHY it causes problems: a test that injects a stub `IEmailService` leaves the stub active for subsequent tests, causing them to silently use the stub instead of the real service; the failure is order-dependent. Fix: always store the result of `.WithWebHostBuilder()` in a local `using var` variable inside the test method, never assign it to a shared field; use `IClassFixture<CustomWebApplicationFactory>` for test-class-wide DI customizations that are safe to share.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 33 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using `params T[]` in tight assertion helpers on .NET 9+ | Allocates a transient heap array per call; adds GC pressure in data-driven loops | Switch to `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` (C# 13) for zero-allocation callers |
| Accessing `ITestContextAccessor.TestContext` during fixture construction | Context is only valid during test method execution; returns null or stale context during setup | Inject `ITestContextAccessor` into test class constructor, access only inside test methods |
| Using `Assert.ThrowsException<T>` when strict subtype checking is required | Passes for any subclass of T; a regression that throws a subtype silently satisfies the check | Use `Assert.ThrowsExactly<T>` (MSTest v3) or `.ThrowExactly<T>()` (FluentAssertions) |
| Pinning container image to "latest" tag in Testcontainers.NET | Upstream registry update breaks CI non-deterministically without any code change | Always pin a specific version tag; treat container images as versioned dependencies |
| Not calling `SetupProperty` before assigning to a Moq property | Assignment is silently discarded; assertion sees default value with no error | Call `mock.SetupProperty(m => m.Prop)` or `mock.SetupAllProperties()` before the assignment |
| Using `ExcludingMissingMembers()` in concrete-to-concrete `BeEquivalentTo` | Renamed/removed fields silently pass the assertion; produces false-positive tests | Remove `ExcludingMissingMembers()` for concrete-to-concrete; use it only for anonymous-to-concrete |
