## Cycle 34 — 2026-05-14

### C# 14 — Extension Members (`extension` Block) for Fluent Assertion Libraries

C# 14 introduces `extension` blocks, a new syntax for declaring multiple extension members (methods, properties, and operators) for a given type in a single cohesive block. In test code, this eliminates the repetitive `this` parameter boilerplate when writing custom FluentAssertions-style assertion helpers, and also allows extension *properties* to express readable state predicates without method-call syntax. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

// C# 14 extension block — groups all extensions for HttpResponseMessage
public static class HttpResponseAssertions
{
    extension(HttpResponseMessage response)
    {
        // Extension property — no parentheses needed at call site
        public bool IsSuccess => response.IsSuccessStatusCode;

        // Extension method with FluentAssertions chaining
        public AndConstraint<HttpResponseMessage> ShouldBeOk(string because = "")
        {
            response.StatusCode.Should().Be(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, because);
            return new AndConstraint<HttpResponseMessage>(response);
        }

        public AndConstraint<HttpResponseMessage> ShouldHaveContentType(string mediaType)
        {
            response.Content.Headers.ContentType?.MediaType
                .Should().Be(mediaType, because: "response content-type must match");
            return new AndConstraint<HttpResponseMessage>(response);
        }
    }
}

public class ApiControllerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProduct_Returns200WithJson()
    {
        using var client = new HttpClient();
        var response = await client.GetAsync("https://api.example.com/products/1");

        // Extension property: no () needed
        response.IsSuccess.Should().BeTrue();
        // Extension method: fluent chain
        response.ShouldBeOk("products endpoint must return 200")
                .And.Subject.ShouldHaveContentType("application/json");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `extension` blocks when you have three or more related extension members targeting the same type — grouping them improves discoverability and keeps the static class organized. Do NOT use `extension` blocks if you target .NET 9 or earlier / C# 13 or earlier — the feature requires C# 14 (shipped with .NET 10); use the `this`-parameter syntax instead. Alternative: Pre-C# 14, group extension methods in a named static class (e.g., `HttpResponseMessageExtensions`) and rely on IDE IntelliSense grouping. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `[Theory]` With `TheoryData<T>` for Strongly-Typed Data-Driven Tests

xUnit v3 provides a generic `TheoryData<T1, T2, ...>` collection class that acts as a strongly-typed alternative to `object[]` rows. Using `TheoryData<T>` eliminates boxing and casting of primitive types, gives compile-time feedback on row shapes, and produces cleaner IntelliSense. In xUnit v3, `TheoryData` rows also support record types and C# 12+ collection expressions for concise initialization. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class DiscountCalculatorTests
{
    // TheoryData<T1, T2, T3>: compile-time row validation, no object[] boxing
    public static TheoryData<decimal, string, decimal> DiscountCases => new()
    {
        { 100m, "VIP",     20m },
        { 100m, "REGULAR",  5m },
        { 100m, "GUEST",    0m },
        { 0m,   "VIP",      0m },
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(DiscountCases))]
    public void ApplyDiscount_ByTier_ReturnsExpectedDiscount(
        decimal basePrice,
        string  tier,
        decimal expectedDiscount)
    {
        var calc   = new DiscountCalculator();
        var result = calc.Calculate(basePrice, tier);

        Assert.Equal(expectedDiscount, result.DiscountAmount);
        Assert.Equal(basePrice - expectedDiscount, result.FinalPrice);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void DiscountCases_AllHaveNonNegativeExpectedDiscount()
    {
        foreach (var row in DiscountCases)
        {
            var discount = (decimal)row[2];
            Assert.True(discount >= 0m, $"Negative discount found: {discount}");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `TheoryData<T>` whenever a theory has more than two parameters or uses value types — it prevents the runtime `InvalidCastException` errors that come from mismatched `object[]` rows and makes test maintenance easier when parameter types change. Do NOT use `TheoryData<T>` for theories that source data from external files or databases; use `[ClassData]` with a custom `IEnumerable<object[]>` source for those cases. Alternative: `[InlineData]` for small sets of literals that fit on one line; `[MemberData]` with a static `IEnumerable<object[]>` property when the data is computed dynamically. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `[CancelAfter]` Attribute for Cooperative Async Test Cancellation

NUnit 4 introduces `[CancelAfter(ms)]`, which injects a pre-cancelled `CancellationToken` into the test method signature after the timeout elapses. Unlike `[Timeout]`, which aborts the test thread (potentially leaving unmanaged resources open), `[CancelAfter]` signals cooperative cancellation via the token so that async operations can clean up gracefully. The injected token name must match a `CancellationToken` parameter in the test signature. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestFixture]
public class ReportGeneratorTests
{
    private ReportService _svc = null!;

    [SetUp]
    public void Setup() => _svc = new ReportService(new FakeDataSource());

    // NUnit 4: injects ct, signals cancellation after 2 seconds
    [Test, CancelAfter(2_000)]
    public async Task GenerateReport_CompletesWithinTimeout(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Production code must accept and honor the CancellationToken
        var report = await _svc.GenerateAsync(ReportType.Monthly, ct);

        Assert.That(report,          Is.Not.Null);
        Assert.That(report.Sections, Has.Count.GreaterThan(0));
        Assert.That(report.GeneratedAt,
                    Is.LessThanOrEqualTo(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow));
    }

    [Test, CancelAfter(500)]
    public async Task GenerateReport_WhenCancelled_ThrowsOperationCancelled(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Verify the method propagates cancellation correctly
        Assert.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            async () => await _svc.GenerateAsync(ReportType.Annual, ct));

        await Task.CompletedTask; // satisfy async signature requirement
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `[CancelAfter]` for any async test that calls cancellable I/O operations, database queries, or network requests — it guarantees the test runtime honours graceful cancellation rather than forcibly aborting a thread. Do NOT use `[CancelAfter]` on synchronous test methods or in tests that call libraries without `CancellationToken` support — the token will be injected but ignored, and the test may still hang. Alternative: `[Timeout]` when the tested code does not accept a `CancellationToken` and force-abort semantics are acceptable; `CancellationTokenSource` constructed manually inside the test for more fine-grained timeout control. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[DataRow]` With `DisplayName` for Self-Documenting Data-Driven Tests

MSTest v3 `[DataRow]` supports a `DisplayName` named argument, letting each row declare its intent alongside the data values. This is especially useful in test explorer output: the display name derived from these arguments immediately conveys the intent of each row without requiring inference from raw parameter values. MSTest v3 also validates that positional argument counts match the test method signature at compile time when Roslyn analyzers are enabled. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class PasswordPolicyTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow("abc",         false, DisplayName = "TooShort_LessThan8Chars")]
    [DataRow("password",    false, DisplayName = "NoUpperOrDigit")]
    [DataRow("Password1",   true,  DisplayName = "ValidUpperAndDigit")]
    [DataRow("P@ssw0rd!!",  true,  DisplayName = "ValidComplexPassword")]
    [DataRow("",            false, DisplayName = "Empty_AlwaysInvalid")]
    public void Validate_Password_ReturnsExpected(string password, bool expected)
    {
        var policy = new PasswordPolicy(minLength: 8, requireDigit: true, requireUpper: true);

        bool actual = policy.IsValid(password);

        Assert.AreEqual(
            expected, actual,
            $"Password '{password}' should be {(expected ? "valid" : "invalid")}");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow(0,   DisplayName = "ZeroDays_BoundaryCase")]
    [DataRow(30,  DisplayName = "StandardExpiry")]
    [DataRow(365, DisplayName = "MaxExpiry_OneYear")]
    public void SetExpiry_ValidDays_DoesNotThrow(int days)
    {
        var policy = new PasswordPolicy();
        // MSTest v3: verify no exception is thrown for valid input
        policy.SetExpiry(days); // must not throw
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `DisplayName` on `[DataRow]` attributes whenever the data values alone are not self-explanatory — it dramatically improves failure messages in CI and IDE test explorers. Do NOT fabricate a `DisplayName` that restates the exact parameter values (e.g., `DisplayName = "abc false"`) — that adds no information over the default serialization. Alternative: `[DynamicData(nameof(Data), DynamicDataSourceType.Property)]` for data sets with more than five rows or rows that require computed values. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions 7 — `BeJsonEquivalentTo` for Comparing JSON Payloads Structurally

FluentAssertions 7 ships `BeJsonEquivalentTo` as a first-class assertion for comparing two JSON strings semantically: it deserializes both strings and compares the resulting object graphs using structural equivalence rules, ignoring property order, whitespace, and number formatting differences. This replaces brittle string equality checks on serialized API responses and contract tests. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using System.Text.Json;
using Xunit;

public class JsonSerializationTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void SerializeOrder_ProducesExpectedSchema()
    {
        var order = new Order
        {
            Id       = 42,
            Customer = new Customer { Name = "Alice", Tier = "VIP" },
            Lines    = [new OrderLine("SKU-001", qty: 2, price: 9.99m)],
        };

        string actual = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, JsonOptions.Web);

        // Whitespace, property order, and decimal formatting are irrelevant
        actual.Should().BeJsonEquivalentTo("""
            {
                "id": 42,
                "customer": { "name": "Alice", "tier": "VIP" },
                "lines": [{ "sku": "SKU-001", "qty": 2, "price": 9.99 }]
            }
            """);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void DeserializeOrder_PreservesAllFields()
    {
        const string json = """{"id":1,"customer":{"name":"Bob","tier":"GUEST"},"lines":[]}""";

        var order     = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Order>(json, JsonOptions.Web)!;
        var roundTrip = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, JsonOptions.Web);

        roundTrip.Should().BeJsonEquivalentTo(json,
            because: "round-trip serialization must preserve all fields");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `BeJsonEquivalentTo` in integration tests and contract tests where you want to verify the shape of a JSON payload without being sensitive to cosmetic formatting. Do NOT use it as a replacement for strongly-typed assertions when you can deserialize into a known type — `BeEquivalentTo` on the deserialized object provides better failure messages. Alternative: `Verify` snapshot testing library for tests that need to track JSON payloads across releases without hardcoding expected strings. [official]

---

### Moq — `SetupSequence` for Multi-Call Method Return Sequences

Moq's `SetupSequence` allows a mocked method to return different values on successive calls without requiring nested callbacks or stateful mocking patterns. It supports chaining `.Returns`, `.ReturnsAsync`, `.Throws`, and `.ThrowsAsync` to simulate retry scenarios, polling loops, and transient fault injection in a single declaration, making failure-then-success patterns very concise. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;
using FluentAssertions;

public class RetryPolicyTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ExecuteAsync_WithTransientFaults_RetriesToSuccess()
    {
        var mockDb = new Mock<IDatabaseClient>();

        // First two calls throw transient exception; third call succeeds
        mockDb.SetupSequence(db => db.QueryAsync(It.IsAny<string>()))
              .ThrowsAsync(new TimeoutException("transient timeout 1"))
              .ThrowsAsync(new TimeoutException("transient timeout 2"))
              .ReturnsAsync(new QueryResult { RowCount = 5 });

        var retryPolicy = new ExponentialRetryPolicy(maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 0);
        var svc         = new DataService(mockDb.Object, retryPolicy);

        var result = await svc.ExecuteWithRetryAsync("SELECT 1");

        result.RowCount.Should().Be(5);
        mockDb.Verify(db => db.QueryAsync(It.IsAny<string>()), Times.Exactly(3));
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task ExecuteAsync_ExhaustsAllRetries_ThrowsLastException()
    {
        var mockDb = new Mock<IDatabaseClient>();
        mockDb.SetupSequence(db => db.QueryAsync(It.IsAny<string>()))
              .ThrowsAsync(new TimeoutException("attempt 1"))
              .ThrowsAsync(new TimeoutException("attempt 2"))
              .ThrowsAsync(new TimeoutException("attempt 3"));

        var svc = new DataService(mockDb.Object, new ExponentialRetryPolicy(3, 0));
        await svc.Invoking(s => s.ExecuteWithRetryAsync("SELECT 1"))
                 .Should().ThrowAsync<TimeoutException>();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `SetupSequence` when testing retry loops, state-machine transitions, or any code that calls the same method multiple times and expects progressively different behavior. Do NOT use `SetupSequence` when the sequence is very long (more than 5 items) — it becomes hard to maintain; prefer a real in-memory fake with stateful behavior. Alternative: `Callback` with an external counter when the response logic depends on the call arguments; NSubstitute's `Returns(x, y, z)` multi-return overload for simpler call-counting scenarios. [official]

---

### NSubstitute — `Returns(x, y, z)` Multi-Value Overload for Successive Return Values

NSubstitute's `Returns(T first, params T[] others)` overload configures a substitute method to return different values on successive calls without any external state. The first call returns `first`; each subsequent call cycles through `others`; after exhausting the list, the last value is repeated indefinitely. This makes transient-fault simulation and polling tests concise and readable. [official]

```csharp
using NSubstitute;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;

public class PollUntilReadyTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task WaitForReady_PollsUntilStatusIsComplete()
    {
        var monitor = Substitute.For<IJobMonitor>();

        // First two polls return Processing; third returns Complete
        monitor.GetStatusAsync(Arg.Any<string>())
               .Returns(
                   Task.FromResult(JobStatus.Processing),
                   Task.FromResult(JobStatus.Processing),
                   Task.FromResult(JobStatus.Complete));

        var poller = new JobPoller(monitor, pollIntervalMs: 0);
        var result = await poller.WaitForCompletionAsync("job-001", timeoutMs: 5_000);

        Assert.Equal(JobStatus.Complete, result);
        await monitor.Received(3).GetStatusAsync("job-001");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task WaitForReady_OnPermanentFailure_ThrowsJobFailedException()
    {
        var monitor = Substitute.For<IJobMonitor>();
        monitor.GetStatusAsync(Arg.Any<string>())
               .Returns(Task.FromResult(JobStatus.Failed));

        var poller = new JobPoller(monitor, pollIntervalMs: 0);
        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<JobFailedException>(
            () => poller.WaitForCompletionAsync("job-002", timeoutMs: 500));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use NSubstitute's multi-value `Returns` overload for polling and retry scenarios where the substitute must return different values across a predictable number of calls. Do NOT use it when the number of calls is not predetermined — it silently returns the last value for all calls beyond the list, which can mask missing `Received()` assertions. Alternative: `Returns(callInfo => ...)` with a closure and external counter when the return logic depends on the call arguments; Moq `SetupSequence` when explicitly throwing exceptions between successes. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET 4 — `WithStartupCallback` for Post-Start Initialization

Testcontainers.NET 4.8+ adds `WithStartupCallback(Func<IContainer, CancellationToken, Task>)` to execute arbitrary async initialization after a container passes its wait strategy. This replaces the pattern of running `ExecAsync` commands after `StartAsync` returns, by embedding the initialization inside the builder chain so it runs atomically on every start. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Containers;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class ElasticsearchIndexTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly IContainer _es;

    public ElasticsearchIndexTests()
    {
        _es = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.13.4")
            .WithPortBinding(9200, assignRandomHostPort: true)
            .WithEnvironment("discovery.type", "single-node")
            .WithEnvironment("xpack.security.enabled", "false")
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                    .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r
                        .ForPort(9200)
                        .ForPath("/_cluster/health")
                        .ForResponseMessageMatching(m => m.IsSuccessStatusCode)))
            // Testcontainers.NET 4.8+: seed index after cluster is healthy
            .WithStartupCallback(async (container, ct) =>
            {
                var port = container.GetMappedPublicPort(9200);
                using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri($"http://localhost:{port}") };
                var body  = """{"settings":{"number_of_replicas":0}}""";
                await client.PutAsync("/test-index",
                    new StringContent(body, System.Text.Encoding.UTF8, "application/json"), ct);
            })
            .Build();
    }

    public Task InitializeAsync() => _es.StartAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()    => _es.DisposeAsync().AsTask();

    [Fact]
    public async Task IndexDocument_CanBeRetrievedById()
    {
        var port = _es.GetMappedPublicPort(9200);
        using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri($"http://localhost:{port}") };
        var indexResp = await client.PostAsync(
            "/test-index/_doc/1",
            new StringContent("""{"title":"hello"}""",
                System.Text.Encoding.UTF8, "application/json"));
        indexResp.IsSuccessStatusCode.Should().BeTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `WithStartupCallback` when container initialization requires running commands or making HTTP requests that must succeed before any test logic runs — it keeps the `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` method clean and ensures the callback runs on every restart. Do NOT use `WithStartupCallback` for one-time global setup that should survive across a collection fixture — move that logic into the `CollectionDefinition` fixture instead. Alternative: `ExecAsync` called manually in `InitializeAsync` for simple shell commands; custom wait strategy implementations (`IWaitUntil`) when readiness is determined by container-side logic. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 SDK — `MSTest.Sdk` Project SDK for Zero-Boilerplate Test Projects

MSTest v3 ships a first-party project SDK (`MSTest.Sdk/4.x`) that replaces the `Microsoft.NET.Sdk` import and automatically configures the Microsoft.Testing.Platform runner, code coverage, TRX reporting, and NuGet analyzer packages. A minimal test project now needs only four lines of project XML with no `<PackageReference>` entries and no manual runner configuration. [official]

```xml
<!-- Minimal .csproj using MSTest.Sdk — replaces Microsoft.NET.Sdk -->
<Project Sdk="MSTest.Sdk/4.1.0">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class InvoiceServiceTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    public void CreateInvoice_ValidOrder_SetsCorrectTotal()
    {
        var service = new InvoiceService();
        var order   = new Order { Lines = [new OrderLine("SKU-A", 3, 9.99m)] };

        var invoice = service.Create(order);

        // MSTest v3 with MTP runner: runs as a standalone executable via dotnet run
        Assert.AreEqual(29.97m, invoice.Total, delta: 0.001m);
        Assert.IsNotNull(invoice.InvoiceNumber);
        Assert.IsTrue(invoice.CreatedAt <= DateTimeOffset.UtcNow);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow(0,   DisplayName = "ZeroLines_NoTotal")]
    [DataRow(100, DisplayName = "LargeOrder_Scalable")]
    public void CreateInvoice_ByLineCount_DoesNotThrow(int lineCount)
    {
        var service = new InvoiceService();
        var order   = new Order
        {
            Lines = Enumerable.Range(0, lineCount)
                              .Select(i => new OrderLine($"SKU-{i}", 1, 1m))
                              .ToList()
        };

        // Calling service.Create must not throw for valid line counts
        var invoice = service.Create(order);
        Assert.IsNotNull(invoice);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `MSTest.Sdk` for all new MSTest projects targeting .NET 8 or later — it provides automatic version alignment of MTP and its extensions and eliminates `PackageReference` version drift between adapter, framework, and SDK. Do NOT use `MSTest.Sdk` in projects that mix MSTest with third-party test runners or in legacy .NET Framework projects — it is designed for the MTP pipeline and may conflict with VSTest-only toolchains. Alternative: Explicit `Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk` + `MSTest` package references for projects that need fine-grained version control of each component; the `MSTest` meta-package for a middle ground without the SDK-level project restructuring. [official]

### FluentAssertions 7 — `WithStrictOrdering` in `BeEquivalentTo` for Order-Sensitive Collections

FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` by default ignores collection element order. In scenarios where order is semantically significant (sorted results, priority queues, transaction sequences), `options => options.WithStrictOrdering()` enforces positional matching and reports the exact index where the actual and expected collections first diverge. Combining this with a `Because` phrase produces failure messages that directly identify the violated ordering contract. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class TransactionLedgerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GetTransactions_Returns_ChronologicalOrder()
    {
        var ledger = new TransactionLedger();
        ledger.Record(new Tx { Amount = 100m, At = new DateTime(2026, 1, 1) });
        ledger.Record(new Tx { Amount =  50m, At = new DateTime(2026, 1, 3) });
        ledger.Record(new Tx { Amount =  75m, At = new DateTime(2026, 1, 2) });

        var result = ledger.GetAll();

        result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
            new[]
            {
                new Tx { Amount = 100m, At = new DateTime(2026, 1, 1) },
                new Tx { Amount =  75m, At = new DateTime(2026, 1, 2) },
                new Tx { Amount =  50m, At = new DateTime(2026, 1, 3) },
            },
            options => options.WithStrictOrdering(),
            because: "transactions must be sorted ascending by date");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void GetTransactions_WhenEmpty_ReturnsEmptyOrdered()
    {
        var ledger = new TransactionLedger();
        ledger.GetAll().Should()
              .BeEmpty(because: "no recorded transactions means empty ledger");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `WithStrictOrdering()` only when order is part of the contract being tested — for data that is intentionally unordered (hash sets, filter results), strict ordering makes tests brittle and order-dependent. Do NOT mix `WithStrictOrdering()` with `Excluding(...)` on the primary sort key — you lose the ordering signal while paying the cost of strict comparison. Alternative: `.ContainInOrder(...)` for checking that a subsequence appears in order without constraining the full collection; `.BeInAscendingOrder(x => x.Prop)` for verifying sort direction without value equality. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET 4 — `ToxiproxyBuilder` for Network Fault Injection in Integration Tests

Testcontainers.NET 4.x ships a first-class `ToxiproxyBuilder` module that creates a Toxiproxy container as a sidecar. Tests configure proxied connections and inject latency, bandwidth throttling, and connection resets programmatically via the Toxiproxy .NET client, validating that retry policies, circuit breakers, and timeout handling work correctly without a production network. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using Toxiproxy.Net;
using Xunit;

public class NetworkResilienceTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly IContainer _postgres;
    private readonly IContainer _toxiproxy;
    private Client? _toxiClient;

    public NetworkResilienceTests()
    {
        _postgres  = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16.4-alpine")
            .Build();
        _toxiproxy = new ToxiproxyBuilder().Build();
    }

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _postgres.StartAsync();
        await _toxiproxy.StartAsync();
        _toxiClient = new Client(_toxiproxy.Hostname,
                                 _toxiproxy.GetMappedPublicPort(8474));
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _toxiproxy.DisposeAsync();
        await _postgres.DisposeAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Repository_WithLatencyProxy_RetriesAndSucceeds()
    {
        var proxy = await _toxiClient!.AddProxyAsync(new Proxy
        {
            Name     = "postgres-slow",
            Listen   = "0.0.0.0:5433",
            Upstream = $"{_postgres.Hostname}:{_postgres.GetMappedPublicPort(5432)}",
            Enabled  = true,
        });

        // Add 300ms latency on upstream direction to trigger retry logic
        await proxy.AddAsync(new LatencyToxic { Latency = 300, Jitter = 50 });

        var repo   = new ProductRepository($"Host=localhost;Port=5433;...");
        var result = await repo.GetByIdAsync(1);

        Assert.NotNull(result);
        await proxy.RemoveAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use the `ToxiproxyBuilder` module for integration tests that verify resilience behavior — timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers — without relying on real network conditions. Do NOT use Toxiproxy in unit tests; the overhead of container startup makes it appropriate only in integration test suites where real network semantics are required. Alternative: Moq/NSubstitute mocks that throw `TaskCanceledException` or `SocketException` for unit-testing retry policies in isolation; `SimulatedClock` patterns for testing timeout thresholds without real I/O. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `IClassFixture<T>` With `IAsyncLifetime` for Async Container Lifecycles

xUnit v3 makes `IAsyncLifetime` (with `InitializeAsync` / `DisposeAsync`) a first-class fixture contract, and the framework guarantees that `DisposeAsync` runs even when `InitializeAsync` throws. Combined with `IClassFixture<T>`, this pattern creates a shared database or container fixture whose startup and teardown are fully async and exception-safe, without leaking connections across test classes. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;
using Xunit;

// xUnit v3: IAsyncLifetime on a fixture class — shared across all tests in the class
public class SqlServerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly IContainer _container;
    public string ConnectionString { get; private set; } = "";

    public SqlServerFixture()
    {
        _container = new MsSqlBuilder()
            .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
            .Build();
    }

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _container.StartAsync();
        ConnectionString = _container.GetConnectionString();
        await ApplyMigrationsAsync(ConnectionString);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        // xUnit v3 calls DisposeAsync even if InitializeAsync threw
        await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }

    private static async Task ApplyMigrationsAsync(string cs)
    {
        await using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        // Run schema migrations or seed scripts here
    }
}

public class OrderRepositoryTests(SqlServerFixture db) : IClassFixture<SqlServerFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Save_ValidOrder_PersistsToDatabase()
    {
        var repo  = new OrderRepository(db.ConnectionString);
        var order = new Order { Id = 1, Total = 99.99m };

        await repo.SaveAsync(order);
        var loaded = await repo.GetByIdAsync(1);

        Assert.Equal(order.Total, loaded!.Total);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `IAsyncLifetime` on `IClassFixture<T>` when the fixture manages heavy async resources (containers, message brokers, HTTP servers) that must be started and stopped once per test class. Do NOT use it for lightweight synchronous setup that completes in microseconds — constructor initialization is sufficient. Alternative: `ICollectionFixture<T>` when the same container should be shared across multiple test classes; manual `IAsyncDisposable` with `using` scope inside each test when the container state must not bleed between tests. [official]

---

### C# 14 — `nameof` With Unbound Generic Types for Refactor-Safe Assertion Messages

C# 14 allows `nameof(List<>)` — passing an unbound generic type as the `nameof` argument — returning just the base type name without a type argument. In test helpers and assertion messages, this produces refactor-safe type name strings without forcing the caller to choose a concrete type argument or use `typeof(T).Name`, which includes backtick-suffixed arity notation. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public static class TypeAssertionHelpers
{
    // C# 14: nameof(List<>) returns "List" — no backtick, no concrete type argument needed
    public static void ShouldContainOnlyType<TItem>(
        this System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable<object> items,
        string because = "")
    {
        // nameof(TItem) is the type-param name; for the wrapper collection type use nameof(List<>)
        string collTypeName = nameof(System.Collections.Generic.List<>); // "List"

        items.Should()
             .AllSatisfy(
                 item => item.Should().BeOfType<TItem>(because),
                 because: $"all items in {collTypeName} should be of type {typeof(TItem).Name}");
    }
}

public class RepositoryResultTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void FindAll_Products_ReturnsOnlyProductInstances()
    {
        var repo  = new ProductRepository(new InMemoryDb());
        var items = repo.FindAll().Cast<object>().ToList();

        // "List" appears in failure messages without reflection hacks
        items.ShouldContainOnlyType<Product>(
            because: "repository must return typed Product results");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void EmptyRepository_ReturnsEmptyCollection()
    {
        var repo = new ProductRepository(new EmptyInMemoryDb());
        repo.FindAll().Should()
            .BeEmpty(because: $"empty {nameof(System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string,int>)} repo has no records");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `nameof` with unbound generics for assertion messages, log format strings, and exception messages where you want the human-readable type name without `typeof(T).GetGenericTypeDefinition().Name` (which returns `List\`1`). Do NOT use it for reflection-based metadata lookups — `typeof(List<>)` is still required for `MakeGenericType`, `GetGenericTypeDefinition`, and similar APIs. Alternative: In C# 13 and earlier, use a helper like a constant string or `typeof(T).Name.Split('\x60')[0]` to strip the arity marker; in C# 14+ prefer `nameof(GenericType<>)` for clarity. [official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 34

**xUnit v3 `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` implemented directly on the test class runs once per test instance, not once per class — developers who expect class-level setup and cache expensive containers here end up starting N containers instead of 1 [community]** — xUnit creates a new test class instance for every `[Fact]` or `[Theory]` row. `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` is part of the per-instance lifecycle, so it is called for each test, not once per test class. WHY it causes problems: a Testcontainers container started in `InitializeAsync` on the test class is started and stopped N times (once per test), destroying any shared state and making the suite dramatically slower than expected with no error message indicating the root cause. Fix: move expensive shared resources into `IClassFixture<T>` (shared per class) or `ICollectionFixture<T>` (shared across classes); keep `IAsyncLifetime` on the test class only for per-test resources that must be completely clean for each test.

**NSubstitute substitutes for non-virtual methods on concrete classes silently do nothing — calling `sub.NonVirtualMethod()` invokes the real implementation, not the configured stub, and `Received()` assertions always report zero calls [community]** — NSubstitute generates a proxy class that can only intercept `virtual` or `abstract` methods and interface members. For non-virtual methods on concrete classes, the proxy bypasses the interception layer and calls the original implementation. WHY it causes problems: the test appears to configure a stub with no compile error, runs the code under test, and then the `Received()` assertion fails with "no calls received" even though the method was visibly invoked; the failure message does not indicate that the method is non-virtual. Fix: extract an interface for the collaborator and substitute the interface; or mark the method `virtual`; or use a hand-coded fake. The Roslyn analyzer `NS1000` now warns when `Substitute.For<ConcreteClass>()` targets a class with non-virtual members.

**Moq `Verify` is not automatically called at teardown with default `Loose` behavior — tests that configure `Setup` but forget an explicit `mock.Verify(...)` call silently pass even when expected interactions never happened [community]** — Moq mocks do not auto-verify on disposal unless `MockBehavior.Strict` is used or `MockRepository.VerifyAll()` is invoked. In practice, most teams use `new Mock<T>()` with default `Loose` behavior, set up return values, and then forget verification. WHY it causes problems: a regression that removes a call to a critical collaborator goes undetected because the test has no verification step; the false-green test only fails when observable output diverges from the specification. Fix: always add an explicit `mock.Verify(...)` call for every interaction that constitutes the observable behavior of the system under test; consider switching to `MockBehavior.Strict` for critical collaborators; alternatively use NSubstitute where `Received()` is idiomatic and visually distinct from setup code.

**FluentAssertions `Invoking(async () => ...)` with `.Should().Throw<T>()` always passes — the synchronous `Throw<T>` overload does not await the returned task and the async exception is silently swallowed [community]** — `FluentAssertions.Invoking(async () => ...)` wraps the async delegate, but `Should().Throw<T>()` only checks whether the delegate throws synchronously. An async lambda that throws asynchronously returns a faulted `Task` without throwing during the synchronous `Invoke()` call, so `Throw<T>()` never sees the exception. WHY it causes problems: the assertion passes unconditionally for any exception type and even for no exception at all, producing a persistently false-green test that will never catch regressions in the async throwing path. Fix: use `Func<Task> act = async () => { ... }; await act.Should().ThrowAsync<TException>()` — the `ThrowAsync` extension awaits the returned task and surfaces the actual exception for assertion.

**Testcontainers.NET containers started inside NUnit `[SetUp]` without a properly awaited `[TearDown]` leak Docker processes — writing `[TearDown] public void Cleanup() { _container.DisposeAsync(); }` discards the `ValueTask` without awaiting it [community]** — NUnit's `[TearDown]` attribute supports both `void` and `Task`-returning methods. Teams accustomed to MSTest patterns often write a synchronous `[TearDown]` that calls `DisposeAsync()` without `await`, discarding the `ValueTask`; the container may still be running when the next test starts. WHY it causes problems: port collisions between tests, non-deterministic failures in CI where the same port is allocated twice, and dangling Docker processes that accumulate across the test run and exhaust system resources. Fix: always mark the `[TearDown]` as `public async Task` and `await _container.DisposeAsync()` inside it; alternatively implement `IAsyncDisposable` on the fixture and let the framework lifecycle manage it.

**MSTest `[TestInitialize]` is not automatically chained in derived test classes — a subclass that declares its own `[TestInitialize]` method without calling `base.TestInitialize()` silently skips the base class initialization [community]** — When a derived test class declares its own `[TestInitialize]` method, MSTest treats it as a complete replacement, not an override with implicit base chaining. The base class `[TestInitialize]` method is not called unless the derived method explicitly invokes it. WHY it causes problems: shared infrastructure configured in the base class (database connections, mock setup, fixture data) is absent for tests in the derived class; failures are typically `NullReferenceException` on fields that were never initialized, not a clear "initialization was skipped" message. Fix: always call `base.TestInitializeMethodName()` as the first statement of any derived `[TestInitialize]` method; consider using constructor injection or a shared fixture class instead of `[TestInitialize]` inheritance to make the dependency explicit.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 34 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `IAsyncLifetime` on test class to share containers | `InitializeAsync` runs per-test-instance; creates N containers instead of 1 | Use `IClassFixture<T>` or `ICollectionFixture<T>` for shared resources |
| Substituting non-virtual methods with NSubstitute | Proxy calls real implementation; stubs are silently no-ops, `Received()` always reports 0 | Extract an interface or mark method `virtual`; check NS1000 analyzer warning |
| `act.Should().Throw<T>()` on an async delegate | Checks sync throw only; async exceptions swallowed into faulted Task | Use `await act.Should().ThrowAsync<T>()` for async delegates |
| `[TearDown] void Cleanup() { _container.DisposeAsync(); }` | ValueTask discarded; container may outlive test; port collisions in CI | Use `public async Task Cleanup()` with `await _container.DisposeAsync()` |
| Forgetting `mock.Verify()` with Moq Loose behavior | Unexercised interactions silently pass; regressions invisible | Add explicit `Verify(...)` calls; or use `MockBehavior.Strict` for critical fakes |
| `[TestInitialize]` override without calling base | Base class initialization silently skipped in derived test classes | Always call `base.TestInitializeMethod()` first in derived initializers |

## Cycle 35 — 2026-05-14

### C# 14 — User-Defined Compound Assignment Operators in Test Builders

C# 14 allows user-defined compound assignment operators such as `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, and `/=`, separate from their binary counterparts. This enables fluent, mutation-style builder objects in test code where each `+=` call appends a configuration step without allocating intermediate objects. Unlike the old workaround of overloading `+` and assigning back (`builder = builder + item`), the compound form can operate in-place, keeping builder state encapsulated and avoiding the common mistake of discarding the returned value. Teams building test DSLs for request builders, fixture configurators, or assertion pipelines can now write expressions like `request += header` that read naturally without the ceremony of method chaining. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public sealed class RequestBuilder
{
    private readonly List<(string Key, string Value)> _headers = new();
    private string _body = string.Empty;

    // User-defined compound assignment: `builder += ("X-Trace", id)`
    public static RequestBuilder operator +=(RequestBuilder b, (string Key, string Value) header)
    {
        b._headers.Add(header);
        return b;
    }

    // User-defined compound assignment for body replacement
    public static RequestBuilder operator +=(RequestBuilder b, string body)
    {
        b._body = body;
        return b;
    }

    public HttpRequestMessage Build(string path)
    {
        var req = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, path);
        foreach (var (k, v) in _headers) req.Headers.TryAddWithoutValidation(k, v);
        req.Content = new StringContent(_body, System.Text.Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");
        return req;
    }
}

public class RequestBuilderTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Build_AppendsAllHeadersInOrder()
    {
        var builder = new RequestBuilder();
        builder += ("X-Correlation-Id", "abc-123");
        builder += ("Accept", "application/json");
        builder += """{"name":"test"}""";

        var request = builder.Build("/api/items");

        Assert.True(request.Headers.Contains("X-Correlation-Id"));
        Assert.True(request.Headers.Contains("Accept"));
        Assert.Equal("application/json", request.Content?.Headers.ContentType?.MediaType);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** User-defined compound assignment shines in test DSL builders and fixture configurators where accumulation is the primary operation. Avoid it for production domain models where surprising mutation semantics can hide bugs; the pattern is most appropriate in test-only builder types. Requires C# 14 / .NET 10. [official]

### C# 14 — Implicit `Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` Conversions Simplify Buffer Testing

C# 14 introduces first-class implicit conversions between `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and `T[]`, so code that was previously blocked by explicit cast requirements can now compile without casting. In tests this eliminates the need for `(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)myArray` or `MemoryMarshal.AsBytes` workarounds when passing arrays to Span-accepting APIs, making assertion code more readable. Extension method resolution also now considers Span receiver types directly, enabling libraries to expose Span-based overloads that are preferred over array overloads without `OverloadResolutionPriorityAttribute`. Teams writing performance-sensitive parser tests or interop boundary tests will notice reduced verbosity. [official]

```csharp
using System;
using System.Text;
using Xunit;

public static class Utf8Helpers
{
    // Method that accepts ReadOnlySpan<byte> — previously required explicit cast from byte[]
    public static string DecodeOrThrow(ReadOnlySpan<byte> bytes)
        => bytes.IsEmpty
            ? throw new ArgumentException("Empty input", nameof(bytes))
            : Encoding.UTF8.GetString(bytes);
}

public class Utf8HelpersTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void DecodeOrThrow_ValidUtf8_ReturnsString()
    {
        // C# 14: byte[] implicitly converts to ReadOnlySpan<byte> — no explicit cast needed
        byte[] input = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("hello world");
        string result = Utf8Helpers.DecodeOrThrow(input);
        Assert.Equal("hello world", result);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void DecodeOrThrow_EmptyArray_Throws()
    {
        byte[] empty = Array.Empty<byte>();
        // Implicit conversion still works in the lambda argument
        Assert.Throws<ArgumentException>(() => Utf8Helpers.DecodeOrThrow(empty));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Span_AssignedFromArray_NoExplicitCast()
    {
        int[] data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
        // C# 14: implicit T[] → Span<T> and Span<T> → ReadOnlySpan<T>
        Span<int> span = data;
        ReadOnlySpan<int> ro = span;
        Assert.Equal(5, ro.Length);
        Assert.Equal(15, ro[0] + ro[1] + ro[2] + ro[3] + ro[4]);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The implicit conversions reduce friction in test code that passes array literals to Span-based helpers. Be careful when both `T[]` and `Span<T>` overloads exist — the new resolution rules favor Span overloads, which can change the called overload if you upgrade to C# 14 without auditing your overloads first. Requires C# 14 / .NET 10. [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `JsonSerializerOptions.Strict` for API Contract Tests

`JsonSerializerOptions.Strict` is a new preset in .NET 10 that enforces a stricter deserialization policy: it disallows duplicate JSON properties, rejects unknown/unmapped properties (`JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow`), preserves case-sensitive binding, and respects nullability and required constructor parameter annotations. In API contract tests, swapping `JsonSerializerOptions.Default` for `JsonSerializerOptions.Strict` catches schema drift early — if the server adds an unexpected property or renames a field, the test throws a `JsonException` instead of silently deserializing a partially-populated object. This pattern is complementary to OpenAPI contract tests and gives coverage directly on deserialization paths used by clients. [official]

```csharp
using System.Text.Json;
using Xunit;

public record ProductDto(int Id, string Name, decimal Price);

public class ProductContractTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Deserialize_KnownShape_Succeeds()
    {
        const string json = """{"Id":1,"Name":"Widget","Price":9.99}""";
        // Strict mode: case-sensitive, no unknowns, no duplicates
        var product = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<ProductDto>(json, JsonSerializerOptions.Strict);
        Assert.NotNull(product);
        Assert.Equal("Widget", product.Name);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Deserialize_UnknownProperty_ThrowsJsonException()
    {
        // Server added "DiscountRate" — strict mode surfaces the schema drift
        const string json = """{"Id":1,"Name":"Widget","Price":9.99,"DiscountRate":0.1}""";
        Assert.Throws<JsonException>(
            () => JsonSerializer.Deserialize<ProductDto>(json, JsonSerializerOptions.Strict));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Deserialize_DuplicateProperty_ThrowsJsonException()
    {
        const string json = """{"Id":1,"Name":"Widget","Price":9.99,"Id":2}""";
        Assert.Throws<JsonException>(
            () => JsonSerializer.Deserialize<ProductDto>(json, JsonSerializerOptions.Strict));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `JsonSerializerOptions.Strict` in all new contract and integration tests where the shape of a deserialized DTO is part of the specification. Avoid it for legacy endpoints that intentionally emit extra fields for backward compatibility; in those cases, use `JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Skip` selectively. Requires .NET 10. [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `OrderedDictionary<TKey, TValue>` Index-Returning `TryAdd`/`TryGetValue` for Test Lookups

The new overloads `TryAdd(key, value, out int index)` and `TryGetValue(key, out value, out int index)` on `OrderedDictionary<TKey, TValue>` return the insertion/lookup index alongside the success flag. In test code this eliminates a separate `IndexOf` call when asserting both membership and position of an entry, which is common when validating ordered collections like ranked result sets, ordered audit logs, or priority queues. The returned `index` can be used immediately with `GetAt(index)` for O(1) access without a second dictionary lookup. This pattern is particularly useful in parameterized tests that verify insertion order contracts. [official]

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using Xunit;

public class OrderedRegistryTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void AddItems_ThenTryGetValue_ReturnsInsertionOrder()
    {
        var registry = new OrderedDictionary<string, int>();
        registry.Add("alpha", 1);
        registry.Add("beta",  2);
        registry.Add("gamma", 3);

        // New overload: TryGetValue with index out-param
        bool found = registry.TryGetValue("beta", out int value, out int index);

        Assert.True(found);
        Assert.Equal(2, value);
        Assert.Equal(1, index); // "beta" was inserted second — index 1

        // Fast O(1) access via index
        var (key, val) = registry.GetAt(index);
        Assert.Equal("beta", key);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void TryAdd_DuplicateKey_ReturnsFalseWithExistingIndex()
    {
        var dict = new OrderedDictionary<string, int>();
        dict.Add("x", 10);

        bool added = dict.TryAdd("x", 20, out int index);

        Assert.False(added);
        Assert.Equal(0, index); // Points to the existing entry
        Assert.Equal(10, dict.GetAt(index).Value); // Original value preserved
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use the index-returning overloads whenever you need both "does the key exist?" and "what is its position?" in a single call — avoids the add-then-find-index pattern and is idiomatic for ordered-collection contract tests. Requires .NET 10 (`System.Collections.Generic.OrderedDictionary<TKey,TValue>`). [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `ITestPipelineBuilder` for Custom Test Execution Middleware

xUnit v3 exposes `ITestPipelineBuilder` as an extension point for injecting cross-cutting behavior (logging, tracing, retry, timing) into the test execution pipeline without subclassing test framework internals. A middleware registered via `[assembly: TestPipelineStartup(typeof(MyStartup))]` is instantiated once per test assembly and can wrap each test invocation, making it the correct place for telemetry integration, distributed trace propagation, and structured per-test log capture. This is the intended xUnit v3 replacement for the test-framework attribute hooks that existed in v2. Unlike `ITestContextAccessor`, pipeline middleware applies to every test transparently without any per-test code change. [official]

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics;
using Xunit.v3;

// 1. Startup type — registered once per assembly
[assembly: TestPipelineStartup(typeof(TracingPipelineStartup))]

public class TracingPipelineStartup : ITestPipelineStartup
{
    public void ConfigurePipeline(ITestPipelineBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.Add(() => new TracingMiddleware());
    }
}

// 2. Middleware — wraps each test execution
public class TracingMiddleware : ITestMiddleware
{
    public async ValueTask HandleAsync(
        ITestContext context,
        Func<ValueTask> next,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        using var activity = new ActivitySource("Tests")
            .StartActivity(context.Test.DisplayName);

        activity?.SetTag("test.class",  context.TestCase.TestClassName);
        activity?.SetTag("test.method", context.TestCase.TestMethodName);

        try
        {
            await next();
            activity?.SetStatus(ActivityStatusCode.Ok);
        }
        catch
        {
            activity?.SetStatus(ActivityStatusCode.Error);
            throw;
        }
    }
}

// 3. Usage — any [Fact] automatically gets the span
public class OrderServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void SubmitOrder_ValidInput_ReturnsConfirmation()
    {
        // Trace span is created and closed automatically by the middleware
        var svc = new OrderService();
        var result = svc.Submit(new Order("ITEM-1", qty: 2));
        Assert.True(result.IsConfirmed);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `ITestPipelineBuilder` for assembly-wide cross-cutting concerns (telemetry, ambient test context). Do NOT put test-specific setup here — that belongs in fixtures or `IAsyncLifetime`. The pipeline API is xUnit v3 only; xUnit v2 projects must use `BeforeAfterTestAttribute` instead. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `Assert.That(() => action, Throws.InstanceOf<T>())` vs `Throws.TypeOf<T>()` for Exception Hierarchy Tests

NUnit 4 distinguishes `Throws.InstanceOf<T>()` (accepts `T` or any subclass) from `Throws.TypeOf<T>()` (requires an exact type match). This distinction matters when the system under test throws a derived exception type — a test using `Throws.TypeOf<ArgumentException>()` will fail if the code throws `ArgumentNullException` even though `ArgumentNullException` inherits from `ArgumentException`. Using the wrong form is a frequent source of false negatives when exception hierarchies deepen during refactoring. Both forms can be chained with `.With.Message.Contain(...)` for further message assertions. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

public class InputValidatorTests
{
    private readonly InputValidator _validator = new();

    [Test]
    public void Validate_NullInput_ThrowsArgumentException_OrSubclass()
    {
        // InstanceOf<T> — passes for ArgumentNullException, ArgumentException, etc.
        Assert.That(
            () => _validator.Validate(null!),
            Throws.InstanceOf<ArgumentException>()
                  .With.Message.Contain("cannot be null"));
    }

    [Test]
    public void Validate_NullInput_ThrowsExactlyArgumentNullException()
    {
        // TypeOf<T> — fails if a different ArgumentException subclass is thrown
        Assert.That(
            () => _validator.Validate(null!),
            Throws.TypeOf<ArgumentNullException>()
                  .With.Property("ParamName").EqualTo("input"));
    }

    [Test]
    public void Validate_EmptyString_ThrowsArgumentException_NotNull()
    {
        // InstanceOf allows the base type in integration tests where the exact
        // derived type may vary across platform/runtime combinations
        Assert.That(
            () => _validator.Validate(string.Empty),
            Throws.InstanceOf<ArgumentException>()
                  .With.Message.Not.Contain("null"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Prefer `Throws.InstanceOf<T>()` in unit tests that should stay green when the exact derived exception type is refined; prefer `Throws.TypeOf<T>()` in contract tests that explicitly specify the exception type as part of the public API specification. Do not mix both in the same test suite without a documented policy. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[Retry]` Attribute With `MSTest.Sdk` for Flaky Test Quarantine

MSTest v3 with the `MSTest.Sdk` project file profile supports a `[Retry(n)]` attribute (via the `MSTestExtensionsTestFramework` extension profile) that re-runs a test up to `n` times before marking it as failed. Unlike hand-rolling retry loops inside a test, `[Retry]` integrates with the test runner's failure reporting: only the final attempt's failure is reported as the test outcome, and all prior attempts are recorded as warnings, making CI logs actionable without polluting the failure count. This pattern is recommended for quarantining known-flaky integration tests during a stabilization sprint rather than permanently disabling them with `[Ignore]`. [official]

```csharp
// Project file: uses MSTest.Sdk project SDK with AllMicrosoft extension profile
// <Project Sdk="MSTest.Sdk/3.x">
//   <PropertyGroup>
//     <TestingExtensionsProfile>AllMicrosoft</TestingExtensionsProfile>
//   </PropertyGroup>
// </Project>

using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting.Extensions;

[TestClass]
public class ExternalApiIntegrationTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [Retry(3)] // Run up to 3 times; only last failure is recorded
    public async Task FetchRates_ExternalApi_ReturnsNonEmptyList()
    {
        using var client = new HttpClient();
        client.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.exchangerate.example");

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/v1/rates?base=USD");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        var content = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
        Assert.IsTrue(content.Length > 0, "Exchange rate list must not be empty");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [Retry(2)]
    [Timeout(5000)]
    public async Task PollStatus_EventuallyCompletes_WithinTimeout()
    {
        // Integration test that may transiently see a 202 Accepted before 200 OK
        var service = new JobStatusPoller();
        var jobId = await service.SubmitAsync("SampleJob");

        var result = await service.WaitForCompletionAsync(jobId);
        Assert.AreEqual(JobStatus.Completed, result.Status);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[Retry]` is a safety net, not a permanent fix. Use it only for externally-dependent tests where transient infrastructure errors (throttling, cold-start latency) are expected, and pair it with a tracking issue to investigate and remove the attribute once the root cause is fixed. Do NOT use `[Retry]` on pure unit tests — a flaky unit test indicates non-deterministic production code or test-isolation problems that must be corrected. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions 7 — `AssertionChain` API for Multi-Step Custom Assertion Extensions

FluentAssertions 7 introduced a revised extensibility model where custom assertion classes use `AssertionChain` (accessed via `AssertionScope.Current.ForCondition(...)`) instead of the older `Execute.Assertion` fluent chain that was deprecated in v7. `AssertionChain` allows building multi-step assertions where each step only runs if the previous one passed, preventing misleading secondary failures that masked the root cause. Extension authors who migrate from v6 must replace every `Execute.Assertion.ForCondition(...).FailWith(...)` call with the `AssertionChain` equivalent; failing to do so compiles but produces deprecation warnings and may suppress failure messages in certain chain configurations. [community]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using FluentAssertions.Execution;
using FluentAssertions.Primitives;
using Xunit;

public class OrderAssertions : ReferenceTypeAssertions<Order, OrderAssertions>
{
    public OrderAssertions(Order subject) : base(subject, AssertionChain.GetOrCreate()) { }

    protected override string Identifier => "order";

    public AndConstraint<OrderAssertions> BeConfirmed(string because = "", params object[] becauseArgs)
    {
        // FA 7 pattern: use CurrentAssertionChain, not Execute.Assertion
        CurrentAssertionChain
            .BecauseOf(because, becauseArgs)
            .ForCondition(Subject is not null)
            .FailWith("Expected {context:order} to be confirmed{reason}, but it was null.")
            .Then
            .ForCondition(Subject!.Status == OrderStatus.Confirmed)
            .FailWith("Expected {context:order} to be confirmed{reason}, but status was {0}.",
                      Subject.Status);

        return new AndConstraint<OrderAssertions>(this);
    }

    public AndConstraint<OrderAssertions> HaveLineItemCount(int expected, string because = "")
    {
        CurrentAssertionChain
            .BecauseOf(because)
            .ForCondition(Subject!.LineItems.Count == expected)
            .FailWith("Expected {context:order} to have {0} line item(s){reason}, but found {1}.",
                      expected, Subject.LineItems.Count);

        return new AndConstraint<OrderAssertions>(this);
    }
}

public static class OrderAssertionExtensions
{
    public static OrderAssertions Should(this Order order) => new(order);
}

public class OrderAssertionTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void ConfirmedOrder_PassesCustomAssertion()
    {
        var order = new Order(status: OrderStatus.Confirmed, lineItems: [new LineItem("SKU-1", 2)]);
        order.Should().BeConfirmed(because: "order was submitted successfully")
             .And.HaveLineItemCount(1);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Migrate to `AssertionChain` when upgrading to FluentAssertions 7 to eliminate deprecation warnings and ensure correct failure aggregation behavior. The `Execute.Assertion` pattern from v6 still compiles in v7 but is scheduled for removal in v8. If your project is still on v6, keep the v6 pattern until you upgrade. [community]

---

### Moq — `MockBehavior.Strict` as Contract-Level Test Discipline

Moq defaults to `MockBehavior.Loose`, which silently returns default values for any method not explicitly configured. While convenient, this means a test that fails to configure an expectation will not fail at the point of the unexpected call — it will either pass silently or fail later with an obscure assertion error unrelated to the missing setup. `MockBehavior.Strict` changes this: any call to the mock that has no matching `Setup` throws `MockException` immediately, pinpointing the un-configured interaction. Teams that adopt `Strict` on service boundary mocks (repositories, external API clients) find that test failures become self-documenting — the exception message includes the exact method and arguments that were not expected. [community]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public interface IPaymentGateway
{
    Task<ChargeResult> ChargeAsync(string customerId, decimal amount);
    Task RefundAsync(string transactionId);
    Task<bool> ValidateCardAsync(string cardToken);
}

public class CheckoutServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Checkout_ValidCard_ChargesCustomer_AndDoesNotCallRefund()
    {
        // Strict: any un-configured call → MockException immediately
        var gatewayMock = new Mock<IPaymentGateway>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        gatewayMock
            .Setup(g => g.ValidateCardAsync("tok_valid"))
            .ReturnsAsync(true);

        gatewayMock
            .Setup(g => g.ChargeAsync("cust-1", 50.00m))
            .ReturnsAsync(new ChargeResult(Success: true, TransactionId: "txn-999"));

        // NOTE: RefundAsync NOT set up — if Checkout calls it, MockException is thrown here,
        // not at an unrelated assertion line later in the test

        var svc = new CheckoutService(gatewayMock.Object);
        var result = await svc.CheckoutAsync("cust-1", "tok_valid", amount: 50.00m);

        Assert.True(result.Success);
        gatewayMock.Verify(g => g.ChargeAsync("cust-1", 50.00m), Times.Once);
        gatewayMock.VerifyNoOtherCalls(); // confirms no unexpected interactions
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `MockBehavior.Strict` for boundary mocks (external services, repositories, domain events) where every interaction is meaningful and missing setups indicate either missing test coverage or unintended side-effects. Use `MockBehavior.Loose` for collaborators used only for convenience (loggers, factories with sensible defaults) where the interaction detail is not part of the test specification. [community]

---

### Testcontainers.NET 4 — `WithLabel` for CI Session-Scoped Container Lifecycle Tracing

Testcontainers.NET 4 allows adding custom Docker labels to containers via `.WithLabel(key, value)` on any `ContainerBuilder`. Labeling containers with the test session ID, test class name, and CI job ID makes orphan container cleanup trivial — a single `docker ps --filter label=testSession=<id>` call identifies all containers belonging to a run, regardless of whether the test process exited cleanly. This is especially valuable in CI environments where `WithReuse(true)` is disabled and containers must be pruned between runs without affecting unrelated services. Pairing `WithLabel` with a `docker system prune --filter label=testSession=stale` step in the CI cleanup stage prevents accumulation of abandoned containers. [community]

```csharp
using System;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using Testcontainers.PostgreSql;
using Xunit;

public class LabeledContainerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private static readonly string SessionId =
        Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("CI_JOB_ID") ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N")[..8];

    private PostgreSqlContainer? _container;

    public string ConnectionString => _container!.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _container = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithDatabase("testdb")
            .WithUsername("test")
            .WithPassword("test")
            // Label for CI cleanup — query: docker ps --filter label=testSession=<SessionId>
            .WithLabel("testSession",  SessionId)
            .WithLabel("testClass",    nameof(LabeledContainerFixture))
            .WithLabel("testFramework","xunit-v3")
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_container is not null)
            await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

[Collection("PostgreSQL")]
public class UserRepositoryTests(LabeledContainerFixture fixture) : IClassFixture<LabeledContainerFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task InsertUser_ThenFindById_ReturnsUser()
    {
        var repo = new UserRepository(fixture.ConnectionString);
        var id = await repo.InsertAsync(new User("Alice", "alice@example.com"));
        var found = await repo.FindByIdAsync(id);
        Assert.Equal("Alice", found?.Name);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Labeling is a low-cost safety net that becomes essential at scale. The label values are visible in Docker Desktop and CLI tools, aiding debugging. Do NOT use labels as a substitute for proper fixture cleanup — always implement `DisposeAsync`; labels are for emergency cleanup only. [community]

---

### .NET 10 — `WebSocketStream` for Integration Testing WebSocket-Based Protocols

.NET 10 introduces `WebSocketStream`, a `Stream`-backed abstraction over a `WebSocket` connection that enables direct use of `StreamReader`, `JsonSerializer`, and other stream-based APIs without manual buffer management or message framing. In integration tests of WebSocket-based protocols (STOMP, AMQP-over-WS, custom JSON streaming), replacing the low-level `WebSocket.ReceiveAsync`/`SendAsync` loops with `WebSocketStream` reduces test boilerplate significantly and makes assertions on received messages more readable. The `CreateReadableMessageStream` factory reads exactly one WebSocket message as a `Stream`, which is ideal for asserting the shape of a single protocol frame. [official]

```csharp
using System.Net.WebSockets;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.TestHost;
using Xunit;

public class ChatHubIntegrationTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;
    public ChatHubIntegrationTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _factory = factory;

    [Fact]
    public async Task SendMessage_ReceivesBroadcast_ViaWebSocketStream()
    {
        using var wsClient = await _factory.Server.CreateWebSocketClientAsync("/ws/chat");
        var wsConn = await wsClient.ConnectAsync(
            new Uri("ws://localhost/ws/chat"), CancellationToken.None);

        // Send a message using a writable message stream
        using (var sendStream = WebSocketStream.CreateWritableMessageStream(
                   wsConn, WebSocketMessageType.Text))
        {
            await JsonSerializer.SerializeAsync(sendStream,
                new ChatMessage("user1", "Hello, world!"));
        } // EOM sent on Dispose

        // Receive reply using a single-message readable stream
        using var receiveStream = WebSocketStream.CreateReadableMessageStream(
            wsConn, WebSocketMessageType.Text);
        var reply = await JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsync<ChatMessage>(receiveStream);

        Assert.NotNull(reply);
        Assert.Equal("Hello, world!", reply.Text);

        await wsConn.CloseAsync(WebSocketCloseStatus.NormalClosure,
            "test done", CancellationToken.None);
    }
}

public record ChatMessage(string From, string Text);
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `WebSocketStream` is ideal for integration tests that need to exchange a small number of well-defined messages without implementing a full protocol state machine. For high-throughput or stateful protocol tests, use the lower-level `WebSocket` API directly to avoid the per-message stream allocation overhead. Requires .NET 10. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` for Per-Test Instance Isolation

NUnit 4 introduced `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` at the class level, making NUnit behave like xUnit: a new instance of the test class is created for each test method. This eliminates shared mutable state leaking between tests in the same class without requiring per-field reset in `[SetUp]`. For teams migrating from xUnit to NUnit, or mixing both frameworks in a solution, this attribute closes the behavioral gap and makes test isolation predictable. The default remains `LifeCycle.SingleInstance` (one instance per `[TestFixture]`), so opting in is explicit and does not break existing tests. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)] // New instance per [Test]
public class ShoppingCartTests
{
    // Field initializer runs fresh for every test — no [SetUp] needed for this
    private readonly ShoppingCart _cart = new ShoppingCart();

    [Test]
    public void AddItem_SameItemTwice_IncreasesQuantity()
    {
        _cart.Add("SKU-A");
        _cart.Add("SKU-A");
        Assert.That(_cart.GetQuantity("SKU-A"), Is.EqualTo(2));
    }

    [Test]
    public void AddItem_DifferentItems_TracksSeparately()
    {
        // _cart is a fresh instance here — previous test's state is gone
        _cart.Add("SKU-A");
        _cart.Add("SKU-B");
        Assert.That(_cart.Count, Is.EqualTo(2));
    }

    [Test]
    public void RemoveItem_NotPresent_DoesNotThrow()
    {
        // Fresh cart — no risk of interference from other tests
        Assert.DoesNotThrow(() => _cart.Remove("SKU-Z"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `InstancePerTestCase` when each test conceptually starts from a clean state and shared instance setup is not required (no expensive container or DB connection). Avoid it when the fixture holds a resource (database connection, HTTP client factory) that should be initialized once per class — in that case, use `[OneTimeSetUp]` on a static or shared-fixture member instead. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `TestContext.Current.AddAttachment` for Rich Test Evidence

xUnit v3's `TestContext` static API exposes `AddAttachment(string name, byte[] data, string contentType)` to attach binary artifacts (screenshots, response bodies, generated PDFs) directly to the test result. Attachments are surfaced in TRX reports, Azure Test Plans, and any MTP-compatible result consumer. This replaces the common pattern of writing files to a temp directory and logging their paths via `ITestOutputHelper`, which left artifacts stranded when the test run was cleaned up. For visual regression tests or API integration tests that capture full response payloads, `AddAttachment` keeps evidence tightly coupled to the failing test result and visible in the CI run summary without manual artifact upload steps. [official]

```csharp
using System;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;
using Xunit.v3;

public class ReportGenerationTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GenerateMonthlyReport_ProducesValidPdf()
    {
        using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:5000") };

        var response = await client.PostAsync("/reports/monthly",
            new StringContent("""{"month":"2026-04"}""",
                System.Text.Encoding.UTF8, "application/json"));

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        byte[] pdfBytes = await response.Content.ReadAsByteArrayAsync();

        // Attach the generated PDF to the test result — visible in TRX/Azure DevOps
        TestContext.Current.AddAttachment(
            name:        "monthly-report-2026-04.pdf",
            data:        pdfBytes,
            contentType: "application/pdf");

        // Also attach the raw response headers for debugging
        string headers = response.Headers.ToString();
        TestContext.Current.AddAttachment(
            name:        "response-headers.txt",
            data:        System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(headers),
            contentType: "text/plain");

        Assert.True(pdfBytes.Length > 1024, "PDF must be at least 1 KB");
        Assert.StartsWith("%PDF", System.Text.Encoding.ASCII.GetString(pdfBytes, 0, 4));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `AddAttachment` for any test that produces a non-trivial artifact (screenshot, serialized response, generated file) that would aid diagnosis of a failure. The attachment byte array is held in memory for the duration of the test run; avoid attaching multi-megabyte files in parallelized suites without setting memory budgets. Requires xUnit v3. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[DynamicData(DynamicDataSourceType.Method)]` With Shared Static Helpers for Cross-Class Reuse

MSTest v3 supports `[DynamicData]` with a `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` pointing to a `static IEnumerable<object[]>` factory method in any class via the optional `dynamicDataDeclaringType` argument. This enables a single data-generation helper to supply inputs to multiple test classes without copy-pasting rows, improving maintainability for cross-cutting scenarios like locale-variant inputs, boundary values, or SQL injection payloads. The `DynamicDataDisplayName` delegate on the attribute allows a custom display name generator to format each row using the test method name and the row data, making test explorer output readable. [official]

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Reflection;
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

// Shared data factory — defined once, used by multiple test classes
public static class CommonTestData
{
    public static IEnumerable<object[]> BoundaryCurrencyAmounts()
    {
        yield return [0.00m,        "zero amount"];
        yield return [0.01m,        "minimum positive"];
        yield return [9999999.99m,  "near maximum"];
        yield return [-0.01m,       "just below zero"];
    }

    public static string FormatRowDisplayName(MethodInfo method, object[] row)
        => $"{method.Name}: {row[1]} ({row[0]})";
}

[TestClass]
public class PricingValidatorTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(
        dynamicDataSourceName:    nameof(CommonTestData.BoundaryCurrencyAmounts),
        dynamicDataSourceType:    DynamicDataSourceType.Method,
        dynamicDataDeclaringType: typeof(CommonTestData),
        DynamicDataDisplayName:   nameof(CommonTestData.FormatRowDisplayName))]
    public void Validate_BoundaryAmount_IsHandledGracefully(decimal amount, string label)
    {
        var validator = new PricingValidator();
        var isValid = validator.IsValidAmount(amount);
        Assert.IsInstanceOfType<bool>(isValid, $"Expected bool result for '{label}' ({amount})");
    }
}

[TestClass]
public class InvoiceCalculatorTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(
        dynamicDataSourceName:    nameof(CommonTestData.BoundaryCurrencyAmounts),
        dynamicDataSourceType:    DynamicDataSourceType.Method,
        dynamicDataDeclaringType: typeof(CommonTestData))]
    public void Calculate_WithBoundaryAmount_DoesNotOverflow(decimal amount, string _)
    {
        var calc = new InvoiceCalculator(taxRate: 0.1m);
        // No OverflowException for boundary inputs
        var total = calc.ComputeTotal(amount);
        Assert.IsTrue(total >= 0 || amount < 0,
            "Total must be non-negative for non-negative input");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Centralise shared test data in a static helper class and reference it via `dynamicDataDeclaringType` to avoid duplication across test classes. The tradeoff is a slightly more verbose attribute declaration; use `DynamicDataDisplayName` to keep test explorer names readable so the added ceremony pays off in discoverability. [official]
