### Community Gotchas — Cycle 35

**xUnit v3 `TestContext.Current` is `null` when accessed outside the test execution thread — any background `Task` that logs via `TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage(...)` after the test method returns will `NullReferenceException` silently [community]** — `TestContext.Current` is a thread-static context that is set by xUnit v3 on the thread that executes the test body. If a `Task` is created inside the test but awaited with `ConfigureAwait(false)`, the continuation may run on a different thread where `TestContext.Current` is `null`. WHY it causes problems: telemetry middleware or logging helpers that capture the context in a closure and use it after the test returns will silently swallow a `NullReferenceException`, producing no diagnostic output and no test failure — the evidence developers most need when debugging a flaky integration test is simply absent. Fix: capture the context in a local variable at the start of the test (`var ctx = TestContext.Current`) and pass it as a parameter to background work, or avoid accessing `TestContext` in fire-and-forget tasks entirely.

**Moq `SetupSequence` does not throw `MockException` by default when the call count exceeds the configured sequence — after exhausting all configured returns, the mock reverts to default-value behavior (returns `default(T)`) silently [community]** — `SetupSequence` is designed to return different values on successive calls, but once all configured returns are consumed, Moq does not fail the test. Instead, it falls back to `MockBehavior.Loose` defaults (`null` for reference types, `0` for numerics). WHY it causes problems: a service that retries a failing API call three times will correctly get three configured failures, but a fourth unexpected retry receives `null` instead of the configured exception — the test passes even though the retry count contract was violated. Fix: add a final `.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("too many calls")` to the sequence, or switch to `MockBehavior.Strict` so any call beyond the sequence length throws immediately.

**NUnit 4 `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` does not re-run `[OneTimeSetUp]` for each instance — only `[SetUp]` and the constructor are called per instance, while `[OneTimeSetUp]` still runs once per fixture class [community]** — Teams switching from `LifeCycle.SingleInstance` to `InstancePerTestCase` sometimes assume that all lifecycle methods now run per-test. `[OneTimeSetUp]` is designed for class-level initialization that runs once regardless of instance count; it is unaffected by `InstancePerTestCase` and runs only once per test class assembly load. WHY it causes problems: if `[OneTimeSetUp]` configures a shared resource that `InstancePerTestCase` was supposed to isolate (e.g., a static database seed), each new instance reads stale state from the single `[OneTimeSetUp]` invocation, negating the isolation intent. Fix: move all instance-specific state into the constructor or field initializers; reserve `[OneTimeSetUp]` for truly class-scoped resources like database migrations that run once regardless.

**FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` with `WithStrictOrdering()` uses index-based comparison — inserting an element at the beginning of the expected list causes every subsequent element to fail the assertion, making the failure message misleading when only one element was actually wrong [community]** — With `WithStrictOrdering()`, FluentAssertions compares elements at the same index position. If the expected list is `[A, B, C]` and the actual list is `[X, A, B, C]`, the assertion reports four mismatches (every element is at a different index) instead of one (X was unexpectedly present). WHY it causes problems: developers spend time chasing the four individual item failures shown in the output when the real bug is a single spurious prepended element; the failure message names each item mismatch individually, not the structural insertion. Fix: use `BeEquivalentTo` without `WithStrictOrdering` and then assert `Equal(expected.Count, actual.Count)` separately; or use `.ContainInOrder(...)` which asserts subsequence without strict index alignment; or use `Shouldly`'s `ShouldBe` which provides a diff view for sequences.

**Testcontainers.NET `WithReuse(true)` containers are not automatically stopped between test runs in CI — running two parallel CI jobs on the same agent with the same container reuse label causes the second job to pick up a container left in a partially-migrated state by the first job [community]** — `WithReuse(true)` instructs Testcontainers to reuse a running container that matches the hash of the configuration, which is designed for fast developer inner-loop iteration. In CI, multiple jobs on the same agent share the Docker daemon, and a reuse-enabled container from job A is indistinguishable from one from job B by hash alone. WHY it causes problems: job B may connect to a container whose database schema was migrated to version N by job A, while job B's code under test expects version N-1, causing cascade migration failures with confusing error messages. Fix: disable `WithReuse` in CI explicitly via an environment variable check (`builder.WithReuse(!IsCiEnvironment())`), or use the container label pattern combined with a pre-job cleanup step.

**MSTest v3 `[Retry]` attribute silently suppresses non-transient exceptions — a bug that always throws `NullReferenceException` will run three times, log two warnings, and then report the failure, making the test suite three times slower for that test and masking the fact that the failure is deterministic [community]** — The `[Retry]` attribute does not distinguish between transient infrastructure errors (network timeout) and deterministic bugs (null reference, assertion failure). WHY it causes problems: a flaky-looking test reported by a developer is added to the `[Retry]` list, and later a regression introduces a deterministic failure in the same test; the team sees "test passed after 2 retries" in CI output and does not notice that the test is now always failing on the first attempt. Fix: implement a retry predicate filter (if the `[Retry]` extension supports it) that only retries on specific exception types like `HttpRequestException` or `TimeoutException`; otherwise, keep a retry registry with a documented expiry date and review it in each sprint retrospective.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 35 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Accessing `TestContext.Current` in a `ConfigureAwait(false)` continuation | Thread-static context is null on the continuation thread; diagnostic messages silently disappear | Capture `TestContext.Current` in a local before awaiting; pass explicitly to background work |
| `MockBehavior.Loose` on boundary service mocks with no `Verify` call | Unexercised interactions pass silently; retries and unexpected calls invisible | Use `MockBehavior.Strict` on critical collaborators; call `VerifyNoOtherCalls()` |
| `[Retry]` on deterministic (always-failing) tests | Masks permanent regressions; triples run time for each always-failing test | Audit retry list each sprint; filter by exception type; fix the root cause |
| `WithReuse(true)` enabled in CI without per-job label cleanup | Second CI job on same agent picks up partially-migrated container state | Disable `WithReuse` in CI; use `WithLabel` + pre-job `docker prune --filter label=` |
| `[OneTimeSetUp]` used for per-instance state under `InstancePerTestCase` | `[OneTimeSetUp]` still runs once; isolation intent is nullified | Move per-instance init to constructor / field initializers; use `[OneTimeSetUp]` only for class-scoped resources |
| `SetupSequence` without a terminal `.Throws` call | Calls beyond the sequence silently return `default(T)`, hiding excess retry calls | Always end a `SetupSequence` with `.Throws<Exception>("sequence exhausted")` |

## Cycle 36 — 2026-05-14

### xUnit v3 — `ITestOutputHelperAccessor` vs `ITestContextAccessor` for Library Authors

xUnit v3 introduced two distinct interfaces for capturing test output inside shared infrastructure code: `ITestOutputHelperAccessor` (familiar from v2 but evolved) and the new `ITestContextAccessor`. Library authors building test extensions, logging adapters, or shared fixture helpers should prefer `ITestContextAccessor` because it exposes the full `ITestContext` including the current test's metadata, cancellation token, and diagnostic message sink, whereas `ITestOutputHelperAccessor` only surfaces the output helper. Injecting `ITestContextAccessor` into a helper class via constructor DI ensures the helper works regardless of whether the calling test is xUnit v2 or v3 migration-compatible. The key change in v3 is that `ITestContextAccessor.Current` is populated on all threads within the test execution scope, including thread-pool continuations that do not use `ConfigureAwait(false)` — this is a deliberate improvement over the v2 thread-static model but only holds within the test runner's execution context. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;
using Xunit.v3;

// Infrastructure helper used inside IClassFixture<T> and standalone service tests
public sealed class AuditLogCapture(ITestContextAccessor contextAccessor)
{
    private readonly List<string> _entries = [];

    public void Record(string message)
    {
        var ctx = contextAccessor.Current;
        var testName = ctx?.Test?.TestDisplayName ?? "<no-test>";
        _entries.Add($"[{testName}] {message}");
        ctx?.SendDiagnosticMessage($"AuditLog: {message}");
    }

    public IReadOnlyList<string> Entries => _entries;
}

public class AuditLogCaptureTests(ITestContextAccessor accessor) : IClassFixture<AuditLogCapture>
{
    private readonly AuditLogCapture _log = new(accessor);

    [Fact]
    public void Record_StoresEntryWithTestName()
    {
        _log.Record("payment processed");

        Assert.Single(_log.Entries);
        Assert.Contains("payment processed", _log.Entries[0]);
        Assert.Contains("Record_StoresEntryWithTestName", _log.Entries[0]);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `ITestContextAccessor` in library/infrastructure code that needs test-metadata richness (test name, cancellation, diagnostics). Use `ITestOutputHelper` injection directly in test classes that only need to write readable log lines. Avoid using `TestContext.Current` static accessor in shared libraries — prefer injecting `ITestContextAccessor` explicitly so the dependency is visible and testable. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `[NonParallelizable]` and `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.None)]` for State-Sensitive Tests

NUnit 4's parallelism model defaults to running test fixtures concurrently within an assembly. The `[Parallelizable]` attribute family controls scope: `ParallelScope.All` allows both fixtures and cases to run in parallel, `ParallelScope.Fixtures` limits parallelism to the fixture level, and `ParallelScope.None` serializes execution for that fixture. Teams that introduce shared process-level state (static registries, environment variable mutation, singleton databases seeded with unique names) frequently encounter flaky tests only in CI where the CPU count allows true parallel execution. NUnit 4 also added `[NonParallelizable]` as a shorthand alias for `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.None)]` that reads more clearly in test code. Applying `[NonParallelizable]` at the assembly level to a subset of fixtures is the recommended pattern when migrating a legacy suite: most fixtures run in parallel and only the state-sensitive ones are serialized. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

// Assembly-level default: run all fixtures in parallel
[assembly: Parallelizable(ParallelScope.Fixtures)]

namespace IntegrationTests;

// This fixture mutates a shared static registry — must not run concurrently
[NonParallelizable]
[TestFixture]
public class PluginRegistryTests
{
    [SetUp]
    public void SetUp() => PluginRegistry.Clear();

    [TearDown]
    public void TearDown() => PluginRegistry.Clear();

    [Test]
    public void Register_Plugin_AppearsInRegistry()
    {
        PluginRegistry.Register("audit-log");
        Assert.That(PluginRegistry.Count, Is.EqualTo(1));
    }

    [Test]
    public void Register_DuplicatePlugin_Throws()
    {
        PluginRegistry.Register("audit-log");
        Assert.That(() => PluginRegistry.Register("audit-log"),
            Throws.InstanceOf<InvalidOperationException>());
    }
}

// Other fixtures continue running in parallel
[TestFixture]
public class OrderCalculatorTests
{
    [Test]
    public void Calculate_Discount_ReturnsExpected()
    {
        var calc = new OrderCalculator();
        Assert.That(calc.ApplyDiscount(100m, 0.1m), Is.EqualTo(90m));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[NonParallelizable]` adds a serialization bottleneck — the whole test runner thread pool waits for the serialized fixture to finish before picking up the next one from the same assembly. Use it sparingly on genuinely stateful fixtures; prefer fixing the underlying shared state instead. In large suites, more than ~5% of fixtures marked `[NonParallelizable]` will noticeably degrade CI throughput. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `Assert.AreEqual` With `double`/`float` and the `delta` Parameter

MSTest's `Assert.AreEqual(double expected, double actual, double delta)` overload is the correct way to compare floating-point values in unit tests, yet many teams use the two-argument form and then wonder why `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` causes intermittent failures. The `delta` parameter specifies the maximum allowed absolute difference — the assertion passes when `|expected - actual| <= delta`. In MSTest v3, the message format for a failed delta assertion now includes both the computed difference and the configured delta in the failure string, making CI log analysis faster. For `float` comparisons, the separate `Assert.AreEqual(float, float, float)` overload should be used rather than casting to `double`, since casting changes the bit pattern. Teams testing numerical algorithms, physics simulations, pricing engines, or ML model outputs should establish a project-wide delta constant stored in a `TestConstants` file so that tolerance decisions are centralised and reviewable. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class PricingEngineFloatTests
{
    // Centralised tolerance — reviewable in one place
    private const double PricingDelta = 1e-9;
    private const float TaxRateDelta = 1e-6f;

    [TestMethod]
    public void ComputeTotal_WithTaxRate_IsWithinDoublePrecision()
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();
        double total = engine.ComputeTotal(basePrice: 99.99, taxRate: 0.07);
        // 99.99 * 1.07 = 106.9893 exactly in decimal, but may drift in double
        Assert.AreEqual(expected: 106.9893, actual: total, delta: PricingDelta,
            message: $"Total {total} deviates from 106.9893 by more than {PricingDelta}");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public void ApplyDiscount_Float_StaysWithinFloatPrecision()
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();
        float discounted = engine.ApplyDiscountFloat(basePrice: 100f, discount: 0.1f);
        Assert.AreEqual(expected: 90f, actual: discounted, delta: TaxRateDelta,
            message: "Float discount result exceeds acceptable tolerance");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow(0.1,  0.2,  0.3,  1e-10)]
    [DataRow(1.0 / 3.0, 0.333333333, 0.0, 1e-8)]
    public void FractionalArithmetic_IsWithinTolerance(double a, double b,
        double addend, double tol)
    {
        Assert.AreEqual(expected: a + b + addend,
                        actual:   a + b + addend,
                        delta:    tol);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The delta approach is mandatory for any floating-point assertion. Use `decimal` in the production code when exact decimal arithmetic is required (financial totals) and `Assert.AreEqual` without delta for `decimal`. Reserve the delta overload for `double`/`float` computations where IEEE 754 rounding is expected and acceptable. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions 7 — `BeApproximately` and `BeCloseTo` for Numeric Tolerances

FluentAssertions provides two numeric proximity assertions: `BeApproximately(expected, precision)` for `double`/`float`/`decimal` which checks `|actual - expected| <= precision`, and `BeCloseTo(expected, delta)` for integer types and `TimeSpan` which asserts the value falls within an inclusive range. The decimal overload of `BeApproximately` avoids the IEEE 754 precision loss that occurs when casting to `double` for comparison, making it suitable for financial assertion chains. In FluentAssertions 7, `BeCloseTo` for `TimeSpan` accepts a `TimeSpan` delta instead of ticks, making test code more readable when verifying timing constraints. These methods chain naturally with `.And`, allowing a single assertion expression to verify multiple tolerances in a batch without the ceremony of separate `Assert.AreEqual` calls. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class NumericToleranceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Invoice_Total_IsApproximatelyCorrect()
    {
        var invoice = new Invoice(baseAmount: 99.99m, taxRate: 0.075m);

        invoice.Total
            .Should().BeApproximately(expected: 107.489m, precision: 0.001m,
                because: "rounding policy applies banker's rounding to cent level");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Elapsed_IsWithinExpectedWindow()
    {
        var stopwatch = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.StartNew();
        Thread.Sleep(50);
        stopwatch.Stop();

        stopwatch.Elapsed
            .Should().BeCloseTo(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(50),
                delta: TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(30),
                because: "OS scheduling variance up to 30ms is expected in CI");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void BatchItems_EachTotal_IsApproximate()
    {
        var results = new[] { 10.001m, 20.002m, 30.003m };
        var expected = new[] { 10.0m,   20.0m,   30.0m   };

        results.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected,
            options => options.Using<decimal>(ctx =>
                ctx.Subject.Should().BeApproximately(ctx.Expectation, 0.01m))
                .WhenTypeIs<decimal>());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `BeApproximately` reads better in chain assertions than `Assert.AreEqual` with a delta and integrates naturally with `BeEquivalentTo` via the `Using<T>` override hook. The main risk is choosing too large a precision that hides genuine rounding errors. Document the `precision` choice with a `because` clause to make the tolerance decision explicit and auditable. [official]

---

### Moq — `It.Is<T>` With Expression-Based Argument Matching for Complex Request Validation

Moq's `It.Is<T>(Expression<Func<T, bool>>)` overload allows matching mock arguments via an expression tree, and when a setup fails, Moq v4.20+ serializes the expression back to a readable string for the failure message. This is the preferred alternative to `It.IsAny<T>()` in cases where the test cares about the shape or values of the argument passed to a mock but does not want to capture it via `Capture.In<T>`. Using `It.Is<T>` with a lambda that validates a complex DTO verifies the collaboration contract at the point of invocation: if the system under test calls the mock with an incorrectly constructed request, the mock setup will not match, causing an unexpectedly-unmatched invocation that fails the test with a useful diagnostic. For `MockBehavior.Strict` mocks this causes an immediate `MockException`; for `MockBehavior.Loose` mocks, calling `VerifyAll()` at the end surfaces the mismatch. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public class OrderServiceTests
{
    private readonly Mock<IPaymentGateway> _gateway = new(MockBehavior.Strict);
    private readonly OrderService _sut;

    public OrderServiceTests()
    {
        _sut = new OrderService(_gateway.Object);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_SendsCorrectPaymentRequest()
    {
        var orderId = Guid.NewGuid();

        _gateway
            .Setup(g => g.ChargeAsync(It.Is<PaymentRequest>(r =>
                r.OrderId    == orderId       &&
                r.Amount     == 149.99m       &&
                r.Currency   == "USD"         &&
                r.Idempotency != null),
                It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(new PaymentResult { Success = true })
            .Verifiable("ChargeAsync must be called with correct request");

        await _sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new Order(orderId, 149.99m, "USD"));

        _gateway.Verify();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_WithZeroAmount_DoesNotCallGateway()
    {
        // Strict mock will throw if ChargeAsync is called unexpectedly
        await _sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new Order(Guid.NewGuid(), 0m, "USD"));

        _gateway.VerifyNoOtherCalls();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `It.Is<T>` with a predicate catches collaboration errors at call time rather than after the fact; the failure message in Moq v4.20+ shows the expression text. The downside is that complex predicates in the expression tree can be hard to read in diffs. For very complex matching logic, extract the predicate to a named static method (`It.Is<PaymentRequest>(PaymentRequest.IsValid)`) so the intent is clear. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET 4 — `ResourceReaper` Session-Scoped Cleanup for CI Agent Safety

Testcontainers.NET uses a `ResourceReaper` (formerly Ryuk) sidecar container to garbage-collect test containers that are left behind when the test process exits abnormally (killed by OOM, signal, or assertion failure). In v4, the `ResourceReaper` is started per test session and is configured via `ResourceReaperBuilder`. Teams running containers in Docker-in-Docker CI pipelines sometimes disable the reaper via `TestcontainersSettings.ResourceReaperEnabled = false` for performance, but this creates a cleanup debt: any test run that crashes leaves orphaned containers consuming port and memory resources on the CI agent. The correct pattern is to leave the reaper enabled and configure its startup with `TestcontainersSettings.ResourceReaperImage` to point to a registry-local mirror when the public `ghcr.io/testcontainers/ryuk` image is blocked. When running multiple parallel CI jobs, each job's reaper session is isolated by session ID label, preventing cross-job cleanup collisions. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Configurations;
using Xunit;

// Global test setup — configure once per test session in AssemblyInitializer or
// xUnit IAsyncLifetime assembly fixture
public static class TestContainerSessionSetup
{
    public static void Configure(bool isCi)
    {
        // Point to internal mirror when ghcr.io is blocked
        if (isCi && !string.IsNullOrEmpty(Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR")))
        {
            var mirror = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR")!;
            TestcontainersSettings.ResourceReaperImage =
                new DockerImage($"{mirror}/testcontainers/ryuk:0.7.0");
        }

        // Always keep reaper enabled — never disable in CI
        TestcontainersSettings.ResourceReaperEnabled = true;
    }
}

public class PostgresReaperTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _db = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
        .Build();  // no WithReuse — session reaper handles cleanup

    public async Task InitializeAsync() => await _db.StartAsync();

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _db.StopAsync();

    [Fact]
    public async Task Database_IsAvailable()
    {
        await using var conn = new Npgsql.NpgsqlConnection(_db.GetConnectionString());
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        Assert.Equal(System.Data.ConnectionState.Open, conn.State);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Never disable `ResourceReaperEnabled` in CI. The reaper adds ~1 second of startup latency per session but prevents hours of CI agent cleanup work after crashes. In Docker-in-Docker pipelines, the `--privileged` flag or a Docker socket mount is required for the reaper container to access the host Docker daemon — verify this in the CI job configuration, not just locally. [official]

---

### C# 13 — `allows ref struct` Anti-Constraint for High-Performance Test Helpers

C# 13 introduced the `allows ref struct` anti-constraint on generic type parameters, allowing `ref struct` types like `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and `ValueStringBuilder` to be used as type arguments in generic test helpers that previously required boxing to `object`. This is particularly useful in performance-critical unit tests that verify buffer-manipulation APIs: a generic assertion helper can now accept `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` without pinning or converting to an array. The anti-constraint must be declared on both the type parameter and any interfaces or base class constraints. When combined with `scoped` parameters, test helpers can verify span-returning methods without allocating an intermediate array solely to call the assertion API. This feature is purely additive — existing tests without the anti-constraint continue to work as before. [official]

```csharp
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;
using Xunit;

// Generic assertion helper that accepts ref structs — C# 13 allows ref struct
public static class SpanAssert
{
    public static void Equal<T>(
        ReadOnlySpan<T> expected,
        ReadOnlySpan<T> actual,
        [CallerArgumentExpression(nameof(actual))] string? expression = null)
        where T : IEquatable<T>, allows ref struct
    {
        if (!expected.SequenceEqual(actual))
        {
            throw new Xunit.Sdk.EqualException(
                expected: $"[{string.Join(", ", expected.ToArray())}]",
                actual:   $"[{string.Join(", ", actual.ToArray())}]");
        }
    }
}

public class BufferEncoderTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Encode_AsciiString_ProducesExpectedBytes()
    {
        Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[32];
        int written = BufferEncoder.EncodeAscii("hello", buffer);

        // No array allocation — asserts directly on the span slice
        SpanAssert.Equal(
            expected: "hello"u8,
            actual:   buffer[..written]);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Encode_EmptyString_WritesZeroBytes()
    {
        Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[8];
        int written = BufferEncoder.EncodeAscii(string.Empty, buffer);

        Assert.Equal(0, written);
        SpanAssert.Equal(expected: ReadOnlySpan<byte>.Empty, actual: buffer[..written]);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `allows ref struct` unlocks zero-allocation test paths for buffer APIs but adds constraint syntax that newer team members may not recognize. Document the intent with a comment and only add the anti-constraint where the performance benefit is measurable (use BenchmarkDotNet to confirm). For typical business-logic tests, `ToArray()` is fine and produces simpler code. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `[MemberData]` With `TheoryData<T>` Static Properties for IDE-Navigable Theory Data

In xUnit v3, `[MemberData(nameof(...))]` can reference any public static property, field, or method that returns `TheoryData<T>` (or its multi-generic variants). Using a static property returning `TheoryData<T>` rather than `IEnumerable<object[]>` gives the compiler type-safety over theory arguments, makes the data source IDE-navigable (F12/Go-to-Definition works), and produces readable xUnit test runner display names from the strongly-typed values rather than the generic `Object[]` label. In v3, `TheoryData<T>` is directly constructible with collection expressions (`new TheoryData<string, int> { { "a", 1 }, { "b", 2 } }`) using C# 12 collection initializer syntax. This is the recommended upgrade path from `[InlineData]` when the number of cases grows beyond 3-4 or when the test data values are complex objects like records or DTOs. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class CouponValidatorTests
{
    // Strongly-typed theory data — IDE-navigable, compile-time checked
    public static TheoryData<string, decimal, bool> CouponTestCases => new()
    {
        { "SAVE10",   10m, true  },
        { "EXPIRED",   0m, false },
        { "",          0m, false },
        { "MAXDISCOUNT", 50m, true },
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(CouponTestCases))]
    public void Validate_Coupon_ReturnsExpectedResult(
        string code, decimal discount, bool isValid)
    {
        var validator = new CouponValidator();
        var result = validator.Validate(code);

        Assert.Equal(isValid, result.IsValid);
        if (isValid)
            Assert.Equal(discount, result.DiscountPercent);
    }

    // Reusable theory data shared across multiple test classes
    public static TheoryData<string> InvalidCouponCodes => new()
    {
        { null! },
        { string.Empty },
        { "   " },
        { new string('X', 201) }, // exceeds max length
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(InvalidCouponCodes))]
    public void Validate_InvalidCode_ReturnsInvalid(string code)
    {
        var result = new CouponValidator().Validate(code);
        Assert.False(result.IsValid);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TheoryData<T>` over `IEnumerable<object[]>` is a strict upgrade — it is type-safe, IDE-friendly, and produces better failure messages. The only reason to stay with `IEnumerable<object[]>` is backward compatibility with xUnit v1/v2 fixtures that have not yet been migrated. For new tests always use `TheoryData<T>`. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `TestContext.Progress` vs `TestContext.Out` for Real-Time Test Output

NUnit 4 provides two test output channels: `TestContext.Out` (buffered, shown in test report after the test completes) and `TestContext.Progress` (unbuffered, written to the console in real time during test execution). Teams debugging flaky integration tests often use `TestContext.Out.WriteLine(...)` and are confused when the output appears grouped at the end of the run rather than interleaved with container logs. Using `TestContext.Progress.WriteLine(...)` writes immediately to the underlying stream, which is essential when watching a long-running container setup or polling a health-check endpoint. Both channels accept format strings and are thread-safe. In xUnit v3 the equivalent is `TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage`; in MSTest it is `TestContext.WriteLine`. Using the wrong channel in NUnit leads to the classic "output appeared after the test failed, not during it" debugging experience that wastes hours. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Net.Http;

[TestFixture]
public class DatabaseMigrationTests
{
    [Test]
    [Timeout(60_000)]
    public async Task ApplyMigrations_CompletesWithinTimeout()
    {
        var migrator = new DatabaseMigrator(connectionString: "Host=localhost;Database=test");
        int attempt = 0;

        // Progress writes immediately — visible in terminal during the test run
        TestContext.Progress.WriteLine($"[{DateTime.UtcNow:HH:mm:ss}] Starting migration polling...");

        while (attempt < 10)
        {
            attempt++;
            TestContext.Progress.WriteLine($"[{DateTime.UtcNow:HH:mm:ss}] Attempt {attempt}/10");
            try
            {
                await migrator.ApplyPendingAsync(TestContext.CurrentContext.CancellationToken);
                TestContext.Progress.WriteLine($"[{DateTime.UtcNow:HH:mm:ss}] Migration complete");
                break;
            }
            catch (Npgsql.NpgsqlException ex) when (attempt < 10)
            {
                // Out is buffered — diagnostic summary appears in report
                TestContext.Out.WriteLine($"Attempt {attempt} failed: {ex.Message}");
                await Task.Delay(500, TestContext.CurrentContext.CancellationToken);
            }
        }

        Assert.That(attempt, Is.LessThan(10), "Migration did not complete within 10 attempts");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Use `TestContext.Progress` for any output you want to see in real time (polling loops, container health checks, timing checkpoints). Use `TestContext.Out` for diagnostic summaries that only matter on failure. The difference matters most in CI where log streams are line-buffered and progress output is consumed by separate log aggregation tools. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions 7 — `HaveAccessModifier` and `NotBeAbstract` for Architectural Assertion Chains

FluentAssertions 7 includes a rich set of reflection-based assertions under the `Types()` and `AllTypes()` builder that let teams encode architectural constraints as executable tests. `HaveAccessModifier(CSharpAccessModifier.Public)`, `NotBeAbstract()`, `BeDecoratedWith<TAttribute>()`, and `Implement<TInterface>()` can be chained to express rules like "all public service implementations must implement `IDisposable`" or "no controller should be marked `internal`". These assertions are different from NetArchTest in that they use FluentAssertions' standard chain syntax and produce the familiar FA failure messages, making them easy to adopt in a codebase that already uses FA. The `AllTypes().That().AreInNamespace(...)` filter is applied before the assertion chain, allowing namespace-scoped architectural rules without loading the entire assembly graph. [official]

```csharp
using System.Reflection;
using FluentAssertions;
using FluentAssertions.Common;
using Xunit;

public class ArchitectureTests
{
    private static readonly Assembly AppAssembly =
        typeof(PaymentService).Assembly;

    [Fact]
    public void AllRepositories_MustImplementIRepository_AndBeSealed()
    {
        AppAssembly.GetTypes()
            .Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Repository") && t.IsClass)
            .Should()
            .BeDecoratedWith<RegisteredServiceAttribute>(
                because: "repositories must be registered via attribute for source-gen DI")
            .And.NotBeAbstract(
                because: "abstract repositories cannot be registered directly");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void AllControllers_MustNotHavePublicFieldMembers()
    {
        var controllerTypes = AppAssembly.GetTypes()
            .Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Controller"));

        foreach (var controller in controllerTypes)
        {
            controller.GetFields(BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.Instance)
                .Should().BeEmpty(
                    because: $"{controller.Name} exposes public instance fields which break encapsulation");
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void CommandHandlers_MustImplementICommandHandler()
    {
        AppAssembly.GetTypes()
            .Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Handler") && t.IsClass && !t.IsAbstract)
            .Should().OnlyContain(t =>
                t.GetInterfaces().Any(i =>
                    i.IsGenericType &&
                    i.GetGenericTypeDefinition() == typeof(ICommandHandler<,>)),
                because: "all handlers must implement ICommandHandler<TCommand, TResult>");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** FA reflection assertions are well-suited to small-to-medium codebases that already use FA extensively. For large codebases with hundreds of types, prefer NetArchTest or Roslyn-based analyzers which cache the type graph and avoid re-scanning on every test run. FA reflection assertions run in O(n) over loaded types, which adds 100-500ms per test class — acceptable in a dedicated ArchTests project but not mixed into fast unit test suites. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[TestProperty]` and `TestContext.Properties` for Test Metadata Tagging

MSTest v3 supports arbitrary key-value metadata on test methods via the `[TestProperty(name, value)]` attribute. The property values are accessible at runtime through `TestContext.Properties[name]` and are exposed in TRX test result files under `<Properties>`, making them queryable in Azure DevOps test result views and CI pipeline analytics. Teams can use this pattern to tag tests with feature flags (`[TestProperty("FeatureArea", "Billing")]`), work-item IDs (`[TestProperty("WorkItem", "AB#1234")]`), or environment requirements (`[TestProperty("RequiresDocker", "true")]`). A setup method can read `TestContext.Properties["RequiresDocker"]` and call `Assert.Inconclusive("Docker not available")` to skip infrastructure tests on machines without Docker, avoiding false failures without permanently skipping the test. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class BillingIntegrationTests
{
    public TestContext TestContext { get; set; } = null!;

    [TestInitialize]
    public void SkipIfDockerUnavailable()
    {
        if (TestContext.Properties.Contains("RequiresDocker") &&
            TestContext.Properties["RequiresDocker"]?.ToString() == "true")
        {
            // Check Docker availability
            bool dockerAvailable = IsDockerRunning();
            if (!dockerAvailable)
            {
                Assert.Inconclusive("Docker is not available on this machine; skipping infrastructure test.");
            }
        }
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [TestProperty("FeatureArea", "Billing")]
    [TestProperty("WorkItem",    "AB#4523")]
    [TestProperty("RequiresDocker", "true")]
    public async Task ProcessInvoice_WithRealDatabase_PersistsRecord()
    {
        // Integration test using a Testcontainers database
        await using var db = new PostgreSqlContainer(new PostgreSqlConfiguration());
        await db.StartAsync();

        var service = new InvoiceService(db.GetConnectionString());
        var invoiceId = await service.CreateInvoiceAsync(amount: 99.99m, currency: "EUR");

        var loaded = await service.GetInvoiceAsync(invoiceId);
        Assert.IsNotNull(loaded);
        Assert.AreEqual(99.99m, loaded.Amount, delta: 0.001);
    }

    private static bool IsDockerRunning()
    {
        try
        {
            var info = new System.Diagnostics.ProcessStartInfo("docker", "info")
                { RedirectStandardOutput = true, UseShellExecute = false };
            using var proc = System.Diagnostics.Process.Start(info);
            proc?.WaitForExit(3000);
            return proc?.ExitCode == 0;
        }
        catch { return false; }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[TestProperty]` metadata survives the full MSTest pipeline into TRX and Azure DevOps, making it useful for test analytics and dashboards. The runtime `TestContext.Properties` access pattern for conditional skips is more explicit than build-time `[Ignore]` because the test appears as `Inconclusive` in results (visible to the team) rather than silently absent. Use it for infrastructure-dependent integration tests; avoid it for pure unit tests where the overhead of reading properties adds noise. [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `JsonElement.ParseValue` and `JsonDocument.ParseAsync` for Streaming JSON Assertion

.NET 10 added `JsonElement.ParseValue(ref Utf8JsonReader reader)` as a low-allocation way to parse a sub-element from an already-positioned reader, enabling test helpers that verify only a slice of a large JSON payload without deserializing the entire document. Combined with `JsonDocument.ParseAsync(Stream, ...)`, which was improved in .NET 10 to support cancellation-aware cooperative reading from async streams, test helpers can assert on the shape of streaming API responses without buffering the complete response body. For integration tests that call endpoints returning large JSON arrays, the pattern of parsing a `JsonDocument` from the response stream, asserting on the first few elements, and then disposing is more memory-efficient than `ReadAsStringAsync()` followed by `JsonSerializer.Deserialize`. [official]

```csharp
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using System.Text.Json;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using Xunit;

public class ProductCatalogApiTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProducts_ReturnsPagedArray_WithCorrectShape()
    {
        using var response = await _client.GetAsync("/api/products?page=1&pageSize=5");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        // Parse from stream — no string allocation
        await using var stream = await response.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync();
        using var doc = await JsonDocument.ParseAsync(stream);

        var root = doc.RootElement;

        root.TryGetProperty("items", out var items)
            .Should().BeTrue(because: "'items' array must be present");

        items.GetArrayLength().Should().BeGreaterThan(0)
            .And.BeLessOrEqualTo(5, because: "pageSize=5 was requested");

        // Verify first element shape without deserializing the whole array
        var first = items.EnumerateArray().First();
        first.TryGetProperty("id",    out _).Should().BeTrue();
        first.TryGetProperty("name",  out _).Should().BeTrue();
        first.TryGetProperty("price", out _).Should().BeTrue();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProducts_EachItem_HasPositivePrice()
    {
        using var response = await _client.GetAsync("/api/products?page=1&pageSize=20");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        await using var stream = await response.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync();
        using var doc = await JsonDocument.ParseAsync(stream);

        foreach (var item in doc.RootElement.GetProperty("items").EnumerateArray())
        {
            var price = item.GetProperty("price").GetDecimal();
            price.Should().BePositive(because: $"product {item.GetProperty("id").GetString()} must have positive price");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `JsonDocument.ParseAsync` from a stream is substantially more memory-efficient than `ReadAsStringAsync()` for large payloads, but `JsonDocument` is `IDisposable` and must be disposed before the response stream is closed. The pattern is most valuable in integration tests that call endpoints returning large datasets (>10 KB). For small response bodies, `ReadFromJsonAsync<T>()` with a concrete type is simpler and preferred. [official]

---

### C# 14 — `partial` Constructors in Source-Generated Test Fixture Factories

C# 14 stable release includes `partial` constructors, which allow source generators to emit partial constructor bodies that are merged with manually written code. In testing, this pattern is valuable for test fixture factories where a source generator emits DI wiring, container startup, or connection string injection into the partial constructor while the human-written partial handles test-specific configuration overrides. The `partial` constructor must be declared in a `partial class` and both halves must agree on the parameter list. This avoids the previous workaround of using a separate `Initialize()` method that had to be called by each test's `SetUp`, which was fragile because forgetting to call `Initialize()` caused subtle NullReferenceExceptions at runtime rather than a compile error. [official]

```csharp
// In: TestFixtures.Generated.cs (emitted by source generator)
// Generator reads [IntegrationFixture] attribute and emits the wiring half
public partial class BillingServiceFixture
{
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _db;
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;

    // Generator-emitted partial constructor half
    partial void InitializeInfrastructure()
    {
        _db = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
            .Build();
        _httpClient = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:5001") };
    }
}

// In: BillingServiceFixture.cs (human-written)
[IntegrationFixture]
public partial class BillingServiceFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private BillingService? _service;

    // Human-written constructor calls generated half
    public BillingServiceFixture()
    {
        InitializeInfrastructure();
    }

    partial void InitializeInfrastructure();  // forward declaration

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _db!.StartAsync();
        _service = new BillingService(_db.GetConnectionString(), _httpClient!);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        _service?.Dispose();
        await _db!.StopAsync();
    }

    public BillingService Service => _service
        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Fixture not initialized");
}

// In: BillingServiceTests.cs
public class BillingServiceTests(BillingServiceFixture fixture)
    : IClassFixture<BillingServiceFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task CreateInvoice_PersistsToDatabase()
    {
        var id = await fixture.Service.CreateInvoiceAsync(99.99m, "USD");
        var invoice = await fixture.Service.GetInvoiceAsync(id);
        Assert.NotNull(invoice);
        Assert.Equal(99.99m, invoice.Amount);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Partial constructors eliminate the "forgot to call Initialize()" fragility of two-phase construction in test fixtures. The tradeoff is IDE support for partial constructors in test explorer tooling is still maturing in Visual Studio 17.12 and Rider 2024.3. For teams not yet using source generation in tests, the simpler `IAsyncLifetime` pattern with explicit field assignments is still the pragmatic choice. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET 4 — `WithEnvironment(IDictionary<string,string>)` for Config-Driven Container Setup

Testcontainers.NET 4 accepts `WithEnvironment(IDictionary<string, string>)` as an overload alongside the single key-value `WithEnvironment(string, string)`, enabling a clean pattern where test configuration is built from a dictionary that can be composed, overridden, and inspected before the container starts. This is particularly useful in fixture base classes where subclasses extend the base environment with scenario-specific overrides: the base class builds the default environment dictionary, the subclass calls `Merge()` or index-sets additional keys, and the final dictionary is passed to `WithEnvironment`. The overload also accepts environment variable expansion (`${HOST_NAME}`) via Docker's env-substitution when the host environment is configured to pass it through. For cross-platform CI where environment variable names differ (e.g., `RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER` vs `RABBITMQ_USERNAME` between image versions), centralising the mapping in a dictionary constant prevents copy-paste drift across test fixtures. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using Xunit;

public abstract class RabbitMqFixtureBase : IAsyncLifetime
{
    protected virtual IDictionary<string, string> DefaultEnvironment => new Dictionary<string, string>
    {
        ["RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER"]  = "test",
        ["RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS"]  = "test",
        ["RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_VHOST"] = "/",
    };

    private RabbitMqContainer? _container;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        var env = new Dictionary<string, string>(DefaultEnvironment);
        ApplyEnvironmentOverrides(env);

        _container = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("rabbitmq:3-management-alpine")
            .WithPortBinding(5672, true)
            .WithEnvironment(env)   // IDictionary<string,string> overload
            .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilPortIsAvailable(5672))
            .Build() as RabbitMqContainer;

        await _container!.StartAsync();
    }

    protected virtual void ApplyEnvironmentOverrides(IDictionary<string, string> env) { }
    public string ConnectionString => _container!.GetConnectionString();
    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _container!.StopAsync();
}

// Subclass adds management plugin port and user config
public class RabbitMqManagementFixture : RabbitMqFixtureBase
{
    protected override void ApplyEnvironmentOverrides(IDictionary<string, string> env)
    {
        env["RABBITMQ_PLUGINS_DIR"] = "/usr/lib/rabbitmq/plugins";
        env["RABBITMQ_ENABLED_PLUGINS_FILE"] = "/etc/rabbitmq/enabled_plugins";
    }
}

public class RabbitMqBasicTests(RabbitMqFixtureBase fixture)
    : IClassFixture<RabbitMqFixtureBase>
{
    [Fact]
    public void ConnectionString_IsNonEmpty()
    {
        fixture.ConnectionString.Should().NotBeNullOrWhiteSpace();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The dictionary overload avoids calling `WithEnvironment(k, v)` ten times in a row and makes the full environment inspectable in a debugger. The tradeoff is that dictionary keys must exactly match the expected Docker environment variable names — a typo is silently ignored by the container unless you add a post-start healthcheck that verifies the configured value. Always pair environment-driven containers with `WaitStrategy` checks that confirm the service started correctly, not just that the port is open. [official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 36

**xUnit v3 `[MemberData]` pointing to a `static` method that `throws` during data construction causes the entire test class to fail with a cryptic "Test discovery failed" error, not a per-theory failure [community]** — When xUnit v3 discovers theories, it eagerly evaluates `[MemberData]` methods at discovery time (before any test runs) to generate individual test cases. If the data method throws — e.g., a file it reads is missing, a database query fails, or a misconfigured service throws during static constructor evaluation — xUnit reports the entire test class as "Failed to enumerate test cases" with a discovery-phase exception, not as individual test failures. WHY it causes problems: CI reports show a class-level failure with no individual test names, which breaks trend charts and flaky-test detectors that track per-test pass rates; the error message points to xUnit internals, not the data method, making the root cause non-obvious. Fix: wrap `[MemberData]` data method bodies in a `try`/`catch` that returns a single theory row with a sentinel value indicating the error, or use `[ClassData]` with a class that surfaces the error as an `Assert.Skip` case; never perform I/O or service calls in data enumeration methods.

**NUnit `Assert.Multiple` does not prevent the `[TearDown]` from running when an inner assertion throws an exception type that is not caught by the multiple-assertion collector [community]** — `Assert.Multiple` collects `AssertionException` failures internally and continues execution. However, if test code inside `Assert.Multiple` throws any other exception type — e.g., `NullReferenceException`, `OperationCanceledException`, or a custom domain exception — the `Assert.Multiple` block does not catch it; the exception propagates immediately, and `Assert.Multiple` exits without reporting the failures it had already collected. WHY it causes problems: the developer sees only the last thrown non-assertion exception in the test result and not the collection of assertion failures that preceded it, making it appear that all earlier assertions passed. Fix: wrap infrastructure calls inside `Assert.Multiple` in `try`/`catch` blocks that rethrow as `AssertionException` (using `Assert.Fail`) so the collector can absorb them; or use FA's `AssertionScope` instead, which provides the same batch semantics with more consistent exception handling.

**MSTest `[DataRow]` with a `null` argument for a non-nullable reference-typed parameter emits a C# compiler warning (CS8625) but the test still runs at runtime — teams that treat warnings-as-errors will find that adding `null` test cases breaks the build [community]** — MSTest v3 supports `[DataRow(null, "expected")]` to test null-input paths, but since `[DataRow]` values are `object?` at the attribute API level, the compiler may warn that `null` is being passed where a non-nullable string is expected when the attribute is analysed via NRT flow analysis. WHY it causes problems: a team that adds `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` and `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>` to a test project will find that existing tests with null `[DataRow]` arguments no longer compile; removing them masks important null-input edge cases. Fix: use `[DataRow((string?)null, "expected")]` with an explicit nullable cast, or suppress the specific warning with `#pragma warning disable CS8625` scoped tightly around the `[DataRow]` lines; do not remove null test cases.

**FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` with records compares positional constructor parameters by name, not by position — renaming a constructor parameter on a record breaks `BeEquivalentTo` comparisons that relied on name matching, even if the values are identical [community]** — Records use positional constructor parameter names as the property names for the compiler-generated `EqualityContract` and `Deconstruct` methods. FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` compares object graphs by member name by default. If a record `record Point(double X, double Y)` is refactored to `record Point(double Horizontal, double Vertical)`, any `BeEquivalentTo` assertion against an anonymous object `new { X = 1.0, Y = 2.0 }` will fail because the member names no longer match. WHY it causes problems: the rename is a safe refactor in production code (no callers break if they use positional syntax), but it silently breaks test assertions in a way that looks like a value failure rather than a structural mismatch; the FA failure message shows "Expected member Horizontal to be 0, but found no member with that name on the expected object" which is confusing. Fix: assert records using `Should().Be(expected)` for structural equality (which uses the record's generated `Equals`) or create a strongly-typed expected record instead of anonymous objects.

**Testcontainers.NET `PostgreSqlBuilder.WithDatabase()` does not create the named database if it already exists in a `WithReuse(true)` container — subsequent test runs against a reused container use the database created in the first run, potentially with stale schema [community]** — `WithDatabase("mydb")` sets the `POSTGRES_DB` environment variable, which instructs the PostgreSQL Docker entrypoint to create the database on first container start. In reused containers (`WithReuse(true)`), the entrypoint script is not re-run because the container is already running; `POSTGRES_DB` has no effect on a live PostgreSQL process. WHY it causes problems: a test run that migrates the schema to version 3 leaves the database at version 3; the next test run on the same machine reuses the container, runs migrations from the last applied version, and may apply duplicate migrations or skip version-check assertions. Fix: do not rely on `WithDatabase` for schema setup in reused containers; instead, apply migrations explicitly in `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` using `Respawn` to reset data between runs and EF Core `MigrateAsync()` to apply any pending schema changes.

**Moq `Verify(Times.Once())` passes if the method was called once during `Setup` (e.g., in a lazy initializer) and once during the actual test action — the two calls add up to `Times.Exactly(2)` but developers expecting `Times.Once()` to fail are surprised it passes when the setup path triggers a call [community]** — `Verify(Times.Once())` counts all invocations of the mock method across the entire test lifetime, including calls made during fixture setup, constructor, or `[TestInitialize]` methods. If a lazy property initializer on the system under test calls the mock as part of first-access initialization, the call count is 1 before the test action runs. After the test action calls it again, the count reaches 2, and `Verify(Times.Once())` correctly fails. BUT if the SUT caches the result and the test verifies before the cache is populated, the count may be 1 from the setup path alone, causing `Times.Once()` to pass even though the test action never invoked the mock. WHY it causes problems: false-green verifications pass in unit tests but fail in integration tests where the caching behavior differs, and vice versa. Fix: call `mock.Invocations.Clear()` after setup to reset the invocation log to zero before the system under test is exercised; or restructure the SUT to avoid lazy initialization that touches external collaborators.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 36 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Throwing in `[MemberData]` enumeration methods | Causes entire test class "discovery failure", not per-theory failure; breaks trend charts | Wrap in `try/catch`; return sentinel row with `Assert.Skip` or `Assert.Fail` on error |
| `Assert.Multiple` mixing assertion exceptions with domain exceptions | Non-`AssertionException` escapes the collector; preceding failures are swallowed | Wrap infrastructure calls in `try/catch` → `Assert.Fail`; or use FA `AssertionScope` |
| `[DataRow(null)]` on non-nullable parameter in NRT-enabled projects | `CS8625` breaks build under `TreatWarningsAsErrors` | Cast explicitly: `[DataRow((string?)null)]` |
| `BeEquivalentTo` against anonymous objects when the compared type is a record | Record parameter renames silently break name-matching assertions | Use `Should().Be(expected)` for records, or create a typed expected value |
| `WithDatabase("x")` for schema setup in `WithReuse(true)` containers | Entrypoint not re-run on reuse; database exists but schema may be stale | Apply migrations explicitly in `InitializeAsync`; use Respawn for data reset |
| `Verify(Times.Once())` without clearing invocations after setup | Setup-path calls count toward the total; false greens when SUT lazily calls the mock in setup | Call `mock.Invocations.Clear()` before the test action; or assert on `Times.Exactly(N)` |
