## Cycle 37 — 2026-05-14

### xUnit v3 — `IMessageSink` in `IAssemblyFixture<T>` for Assembly-Level Diagnostic Output

xUnit v3 exposes `IMessageSink` as the low-level channel for assembly-level diagnostic output, distinct from the per-test `ITestOutputHelper`. When building a shared infrastructure library — such as an OpenTelemetry span collector or a timing profiler — that needs to emit diagnostics regardless of which test is currently running, inject `IMessageSink` from the constructor of an `IAssemblyFixture<T>`. The sink receives `IDiagnosticMessage` objects that appear in the xUnit runner output under the "Diagnostics" stream, surviving test-method boundaries. Unlike `ITestContextAccessor.Current?.SendDiagnosticMessage(...)`, which silently no-ops when called outside a test execution context, `IMessageSink` is always live for the lifetime of the assembly fixture. This pattern is the canonical replacement for static logger singletons in xUnit-based test infrastructure. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Sdk;

// Assembly-scoped fixture — receives IMessageSink via xUnit DI
public sealed class InfrastructureProbe : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly IMessageSink _sink;
    private int _containerStartMs;

    public InfrastructureProbe(IMessageSink sink) => _sink = sink;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        var sw = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.StartNew();
        await Task.Delay(10); // simulate container warm-up
        _containerStartMs = (int)sw.ElapsedMilliseconds;

        _sink.OnMessage(new DiagnosticMessage(
            $"[InfrastructureProbe] container ready in {_containerStartMs} ms"));
    }

    public int ContainerStartMs => _containerStartMs;
    public Task DisposeAsync() => Task.CompletedTask;
}

[assembly: AssemblyFixture(typeof(InfrastructureProbe))]

public class WarmUpTests(InfrastructureProbe probe)
{
    [Fact]
    public void Container_StartedWithinBudget()
        => Assert.True(probe.ContainerStartMs < 5_000,
            $"Container took {probe.ContainerStartMs} ms — budget is 5 000 ms");
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `IMessageSink` is ideal for assembly-level infrastructure diagnostics that should appear even when no test is executing. The tradeoff is that `IDiagnosticMessage` text appears in the diagnostics stream (visible with `--diagnostics` flag or `<DiagnosticMessages>true</DiagnosticMessages>` in `xunit.runner.json`), not in per-test output — so individual test failure reports will not include infrastructure timing lines. For test-scoped messages that should appear alongside `FAILED` output, continue using `ITestOutputHelper` injected per test class. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `TestContext.Out` and `TestContext.Error` Streams for Portable Diagnostic Output

NUnit 4 provides `TestContext.Out` (a `TextWriter` wrapping the test's output stream) and `TestContext.Error` (wrapping the error stream) as portable ways to emit diagnostic lines from shared helper code without needing a direct reference to the test runner. The key difference: `TestContext.Out` output appears in the test result alongside `PASSED`/`FAILED`/`INCONCLUSIVE`, while `TestContext.Error` appears under a separate error-output section. Libraries that previously wrote to `Console.Out` in NUnit tests may intercept the wrong stream if the test runner has redirected `Console.Out` away from NUnit's capture buffer — always prefer `TestContext.Out` in NUnit-aware code. `TestContext.CurrentContext.Test.FullName` gives the fully qualified test name usable as a correlation key in log aggregation. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

public static class NUnitDiagnostics
{
    // Call from shared helpers — works in [SetUp], [Test], and [TearDown]
    public static void Log(string message)
        => TestContext.Out.WriteLine(
            $"[{DateTime.UtcNow:HH:mm:ss.fff}] [{TestContext.CurrentContext.Test.FullName}] {message}");

    public static void Error(string message)
        => TestContext.Error.WriteLine(
            $"[ERROR] [{TestContext.CurrentContext.Test.FullName}] {message}");
}

[TestFixture]
public class PaymentServiceTests
{
    private PaymentService _sut = null!;

    [SetUp]
    public void SetUp()
    {
        NUnitDiagnostics.Log("Creating PaymentService");
        _sut = new PaymentService(new FakeGateway());
    }

    [Test]
    public void ProcessPayment_ValidCard_ReturnsApproved()
    {
        NUnitDiagnostics.Log("Processing payment with card 4111...");
        var result = _sut.Process("4111111111111111", 99.99m);

        Assert.That(result.Status, Is.EqualTo("Approved"));
        NUnitDiagnostics.Log($"Result: {result.Status}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TestContext.Out` is preferable over `Console.WriteLine` in NUnit tests because NUnit captures it correctly even with `--output none` runner flags. The downside: `TestContext.Out` is only valid within a test execution context — calling it from a static constructor or assembly-level code outside a test will throw `NullReferenceException`. For infrastructure that runs outside the test context, use a proper `ILogger<T>` abstraction. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[TestProperty]` + `TestContext.Properties` for Metadata-Driven Test Filtering

MSTest v3 supports `[TestProperty("Category", "Slow")]` to attach arbitrary key-value metadata to test methods, queryable at runtime via `TestContext.Properties["Category"]`. Unlike `[TestCategory]`, `[TestProperty]` is a generic key-value attribute that integrates with the MSTest runner's `/TestCaseFilter` expression: `dotnet test --filter "TestProperty_Category=Slow"` selects only slow tests, enabling tiered CI pipelines where the fast suite runs on every push and the slow suite runs nightly. Inside the test method, `TestContext.Properties` exposes the compiled collection of all `[TestProperty]` values as a read-only dictionary, enabling adaptive test behaviour — for example, a test can use a reduced iteration count when `TestContext.Properties["Tier"]` equals `"Quick"`. Combined with `[Retry]` from MSTest.Sdk, `[TestProperty]` metadata can also drive a custom retry strategy. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class ReportGeneratorTests
{
    public TestContext TestContext { get; set; } = null!;

    [TestMethod]
    [TestProperty("Tier",     "Slow")]
    [TestProperty("Area",     "Reporting")]
    [TestProperty("RunGroup", "Nightly")]
    public async Task GenerateFullReport_WithLargeDataset_CompletesWithinBudget()
    {
        // Adaptive: use smaller dataset on Quick tier
        int rowCount = TestContext.Properties["Tier"]?.ToString() == "Quick" ? 100 : 50_000;
        TestContext.WriteLine($"Running with {rowCount} rows (Tier={TestContext.Properties["Tier"]})");

        var generator = new ReportGenerator();
        var sw = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.StartNew();
        await generator.GenerateAsync(rowCount);
        sw.Stop();

        Assert.IsTrue(sw.Elapsed < TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),
            $"Report generation took {sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds:F1}s — budget is 30s");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [TestProperty("Tier", "Fast")]
    [TestProperty("Area", "Reporting")]
    public void ParseTemplate_NullArgument_ThrowsArgumentNullException()
    {
        var generator = new ReportGenerator();
        Assert.ThrowsException<ArgumentNullException>(
            () => generator.ParseTemplate(null!));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[TestProperty]` is powerful for metadata-driven pipelines but adds cognitive overhead — teams need to agree on a controlled vocabulary for keys and values. Consider defining constants in a shared `TestTiers` static class. The filter syntax (`TestProperty_<Key>=<Value>`) uses underscore as the separator, which means keys with underscores must be handled carefully; prefer PascalCased keys without underscores. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions v8 — `BeEquivalentTo` With `Using<TComparer>` for Custom Type Comparers

FluentAssertions v8 extended `BeEquivalentTo` with the `Using<TComparer>()` fluent option, where `TComparer` implements `IEqualityComparer<T>` for a specific member type within the object graph. Previously, overriding comparison for a specific type required a lambda form; v8 introduced the cleaner generic overload so custom comparers can be registered without ceremony. This is particularly useful when the graph contains `DateTimeOffset` (where UTC vs local comparison matters), `decimal` (where precision tolerance is required), or domain value objects with custom equality semantics. The comparer applies recursively to all occurrences of `T` within the compared graph, so a single `Using<MoneyAmount>(new MoneyAmountApproximateComparer(tolerance: 0.01m))` fixes all `MoneyAmount` comparisons in a deeply nested DTO without touching each field individually. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

// Custom comparer: two DateTimeOffsets are equivalent if within 1 second
public sealed class WithinOneSecondComparer : IEqualityComparer<DateTimeOffset>
{
    public bool Equals(DateTimeOffset x, DateTimeOffset y)
        => Math.Abs((x - y).TotalSeconds) <= 1.0;

    public int GetHashCode(DateTimeOffset obj) => obj.GetHashCode();
}

public record OrderDto(string Id, DateTimeOffset PlacedAt, decimal Total);

public class OrderDtoTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void CreatedOrder_IsEquivalentToExpected_IgnoringSubSecondTimeDrift()
    {
        var expected = new OrderDto("ORD-001", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, 199.99m);

        // Simulate 500 ms processing delay
        var actual = expected with { PlacedAt = expected.PlacedAt.AddMilliseconds(500) };

        actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, opts => opts
            .Using<DateTimeOffset>(new WithinOneSecondComparer())
            .ComparingByValue<DateTimeOffset>());
    }

    [Fact]
    public void OrderList_IsEquivalentToExpected_WithCustomDateComparison()
    {
        var expected = new[] { new OrderDto("A", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, 50m) };
        var actual   = new[] { new OrderDto("A", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddMilliseconds(200), 50m) };

        actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, opts => opts
            .Using<DateTimeOffset>(new WithinOneSecondComparer())
            .ComparingByValue<DateTimeOffset>());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Using<TComparer>` is more readable and maintainable than the lambda form when the same comparer applies across multiple test classes — register it once via `AssertionOptions.AssertEquivalencyUsing` in an assembly-level fixture to avoid repeating the option in every test. The risk is that globally registered comparers alter default `BeEquivalentTo` behaviour, potentially hiding real bugs if tolerance is too wide; prefer per-test registration for non-trivial tolerances. [official]

---

### Moq — `Capture.In<T>` With `IReadOnlyList<T>` for Multi-Call Argument Inspection

Moq's `Capture.In<T>(collection)` appended to a `Setup` call captures every argument passed to a mocked method across all invocations into a `List<T>`, enabling post-hoc assertion on the full sequence of arguments rather than only the last call. This is essential when testing components that batch operations — e.g., a repository that calls `SaveAsync(entity)` multiple times in a loop, or an event bus that publishes a sequence of domain events. Unlike `Verify(m => m.Publish(It.IsAny<DomainEvent>()), Times.Exactly(3))`, which only confirms count, `Capture.In` lets you assert order, content, and relationships between successive calls using the full FluentAssertions vocabulary. In Moq 4.20+, `Capture.In<T>` works on both synchronous and `ValueTask`/`Task`-returning methods. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public interface IEventBus
{
    Task PublishAsync(DomainEvent evt);
}

public record DomainEvent(string Name, string AggregateId);

public class OrderFulfillmentService(IEventBus bus)
{
    public async Task FulfillOrderAsync(string orderId, string[] lineItemIds)
    {
        await bus.PublishAsync(new DomainEvent("OrderFulfillmentStarted", orderId));
        foreach (var id in lineItemIds)
            await bus.PublishAsync(new DomainEvent("LineItemPicked", id));
        await bus.PublishAsync(new DomainEvent("OrderFulfillmentCompleted", orderId));
    }
}

public class OrderFulfillmentServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FulfillOrder_PublishesEventsInCorrectOrder()
    {
        var publishedEvents = new List<DomainEvent>();
        var mockBus = new Mock<IEventBus>();
        mockBus.Setup(b => b.PublishAsync(Capture.In(publishedEvents)))
               .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

        var sut = new OrderFulfillmentService(mockBus.Object);
        await sut.FulfillOrderAsync("ORD-42", ["LI-1", "LI-2"]);

        publishedEvents.Should().HaveCount(4);
        publishedEvents[0].Name.Should().Be("OrderFulfillmentStarted");
        publishedEvents[3].Name.Should().Be("OrderFulfillmentCompleted");
        publishedEvents.Select(e => e.Name)
            .Should().ContainInOrder(
                "OrderFulfillmentStarted", "LineItemPicked",
                "LineItemPicked", "OrderFulfillmentCompleted");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Capture.In` is the right tool when both count and content/order matter. For simple "was it called?" checks, `Verify` is cleaner. The captured list persists for the lifetime of the test, so if setup is shared across multiple test methods, reset the capture list between tests by creating a fresh `List<T>` per test or pairing with `mock.Invocations.Clear()`. Note: `Capture.In` stores references — mutations to mutable arguments after the call are reflected in the captured list (see Community Gotchas). [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET — `NetworkBuilder` for Multi-Container Communication in Integration Tests

Testcontainers.NET 3.x+ provides `NetworkBuilder` to create isolated Docker networks shared across multiple containers in the same test session. Without an explicit network, containers must expose ports to the Docker host, causing flakiness under parallel test runs when port conflicts occur. With a named network, containers reference each other by alias (e.g., `db`, `cache`) without exposing ports to the host, mirroring the production Compose configuration. `NetworkBuilder.Build()` returns an `INetwork` that is passed to `ContainerBuilder.WithNetwork(network).WithNetworkAliases("alias")` for each container. The `INetwork` implements `IAsyncDisposable` and should be owned by the outermost fixture to ensure the network is removed after all containers stop. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Networks;
using Xunit;

public sealed class AppStackFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private INetwork?   _network;
    private IContainer? _db;
    private IContainer? _app;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _network = new NetworkBuilder()
            .WithName($"test-net-{Guid.NewGuid():N}")
            .Build();
        await _network.CreateAsync();

        _db = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithNetworkAliases("db")
            .WithEnvironment("POSTGRES_PASSWORD", "test")
            .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilPortIsAvailable(5432))
            .Build();
        await _db.StartAsync();

        // App references 'db' by alias — no host-port exposure needed for the DB
        _app = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("myapp:latest")
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithNetworkAliases("app")
            .WithEnvironment("DB_HOST", "db")
            .WithEnvironment("DB_PORT", "5432")
            .WithPortBinding(8080, true)  // expose only the app port for test assertions
            .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilPortIsAvailable(8080))
            .Build();
        await _app.StartAsync();
    }

    public string AppBaseUrl => $"http://localhost:{_app!.GetMappedPublicPort(8080)}";

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_app     is not null) await _app.DisposeAsync();
        if (_db      is not null) await _db.DisposeAsync();
        if (_network is not null) await _network.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

public class AppHealthTests(AppStackFixture fixture) : IClassFixture<AppStackFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task HealthEndpoint_ReturnsOk()
    {
        using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(fixture.AppBaseUrl) };
        var resp = await http.GetAsync("/health");
        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, resp.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Docker networking adds a layer of complexity and slightly increases container startup time. The payoff is realistic inter-service communication without host-port conflicts, making parallel test suites stable on shared CI agents. Always create a dedicated network per test session with a unique name — never reuse the default bridge network, as containers from concurrent test runs can interfere with each other. [official]

---

### C# 13 — `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` Overloads for Zero-Allocation Test Helpers

C# 13 allows `params` parameters to be `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, enabling test helper methods that accept variable arguments without allocating an array on the heap for each call. The compiler emits a `stackalloc`-based span at the call site when the argument count is statically known and the size fits on the stack. For test helpers called inside a tight loop — benchmark setup methods, property-based test generators, or assertion helpers run thousands of times — this reduces GC pressure that would otherwise cause JIT-induced timing variance making micro-benchmark baseline measurements unstable. This is a C# 13 language feature; the runtime support (`RuntimeHelpers.CreateSpan<T>`) exists from .NET 5 but the `params` syntax only became available in C# 13. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

// Zero-allocation assertion helper — params ReadOnlySpan<T> (C# 13)
public static class AllOf
{
    public static void AreTrue(params ReadOnlySpan<bool> conditions)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < conditions.Length; i++)
        {
            if (!conditions[i])
                throw new Xunit.Sdk.TrueException(
                    $"Condition at index {i} was false", false);
        }
    }
}

// Zero-allocation sum helper for decimal test arithmetic
public static class TestMath
{
    public static decimal Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<decimal> values)
    {
        decimal total = 0;
        foreach (var v in values) total += v;
        return total;
    }
}

public class AllOfTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void MultipleConditions_AllTrue_DoesNotThrow()
    {
        var order = new { Total = 150m, HasItems = true, IsConfirmed = true };

        // No array heap allocation — stackalloc span at call site
        AllOf.AreTrue(
            order.Total > 0,
            order.HasItems,
            order.IsConfirmed);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Sum_MultipleDecimals_ReturnsCorrectTotal()
    {
        var total = TestMath.Sum(10m, 20m, 30m, 40m); // no heap alloc
        Assert.Equal(100m, total);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The zero-allocation benefit only materialises when the argument list is statically known at compile time; passing a variable `IEnumerable<T>` at runtime falls back to an array. Do not mix `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` overloads with `params T[]` overloads for the same method — the compiler prefers the span overload on C# 13+ but the behaviour is surprising to developers on older toolchains. Use this pattern selectively in hot-path test infrastructure; for ordinary test assertion helpers, `params T[]` is simpler and more widely understood. [official]

---

### .NET 9 — `FakeTimeProvider` With `PeriodicTimer` for Deterministic Background-Task Testing

The `TimeProvider` abstraction reached ecosystem maturity in .NET 9, with first-class support in `PeriodicTimer`, Polly v8 resilience pipelines, and ASP.NET Core 9 middleware. The core pattern is: production code depends on `TimeProvider` (injected via DI), test code injects `FakeTimeProvider` and calls `Advance(TimeSpan)` to control time deterministically. In .NET 9, `PeriodicTimer` accepts a `TimeProvider` constructor parameter, enabling tests to fire periodic timers on demand without `Task.Delay` or `Thread.Sleep`. `FakeTimeProvider` also supports `CreateTimer` (equivalent to `System.Threading.Timer`) which advances with `Advance()` — critical for testing debounce, rate-limiting, and retry-delay logic without real wall-clock waits. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using Xunit;

public class InvoiceReminderService(TimeProvider clock)
{
    private readonly List<string> _sentReminders = [];

    public void CheckAndSendReminders(IEnumerable<Invoice> invoices)
    {
        var now = clock.GetUtcNow();
        foreach (var inv in invoices)
        {
            if (inv.DueDate <= now && !inv.ReminderSent)
            {
                _sentReminders.Add(inv.Id);
                inv.ReminderSent = true;
            }
        }
    }

    public IReadOnlyList<string> SentReminders => _sentReminders;
}

public record Invoice(string Id, DateTimeOffset DueDate)
{
    public bool ReminderSent { get; set; }
}

public class InvoiceReminderServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void CheckAndSend_OverdueInvoice_SendsReminder()
    {
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider(
            startDateTime: new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
        var sut = new InvoiceReminderService(fakeTime);
        var invoices = new[] { new Invoice("INV-001", fakeTime.GetUtcNow().AddDays(-1)) };

        sut.CheckAndSendReminders(invoices);

        Assert.Contains("INV-001", sut.SentReminders);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void CheckAndSend_AfterTimeAdvanced_PreviouslyFutureInvoiceBecomesOverdue()
    {
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider(
            startDateTime: new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
        var sut = new InvoiceReminderService(fakeTime);
        var invoices = new[] { new Invoice("INV-002", fakeTime.GetUtcNow().AddDays(3)) };

        sut.CheckAndSendReminders(invoices); // not yet overdue
        Assert.Empty(sut.SentReminders);

        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(4)); // advance past due date
        sut.CheckAndSendReminders(invoices);
        Assert.Contains("INV-002", sut.SentReminders);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `FakeTimeProvider` eliminates all `Thread.Sleep`/`Task.Delay` in time-dependent tests and makes them deterministic. The prerequisite is that production code must use `TimeProvider` rather than `DateTime.UtcNow` directly — retrofitting legacy code can require touching many call sites. Use an architecture test (`NetArchTest`) to enforce that `DateTime.UtcNow` is banned in production assemblies once the `TimeProvider` abstraction is adopted. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions v8 — `AllSatisfy` and `SatisfyRespectively` for Composable Collection Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 improved `AllSatisfy` and `SatisfyRespectively` for multi-element collections. `AllSatisfy` accepts an `Action<T>` inspector that runs assertions against every element, allowing the full FA fluency inside the inspector. Unlike `Contain(x => x.Prop > 0)` (which only checks existence and provides a weak failure message), `AllSatisfy` reports exactly which sub-assertion failed and on which element, producing diagnostics like `"Expected items[1].Name to start with 'INV' but found 'ORD'."` `SatisfyRespectively` applies a distinct inspector per element (positional), combining count assertion with per-element content assertion in a single call. Both methods use soft-assertion semantics internally — all element failures are collected and reported together rather than stopping at the first failure. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public record LineItem(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);

public class LineItemCollectionTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void AllLineItems_HaveValidSkuAndPositiveValues()
    {
        var items = new[]
        {
            new LineItem("SKU-001", 2, 9.99m),
            new LineItem("SKU-002", 1, 49.95m),
            new LineItem("SKU-003", 5, 1.49m),
        };

        // AllSatisfy: every element must pass all assertions
        items.Should().AllSatisfy(item =>
        {
            item.Sku.Should().MatchRegex(@"^SKU-\d{3}$");
            item.Quantity.Should().BePositive();
            item.UnitPrice.Should().BeGreaterThan(0m);
        });
    }

    [Fact]
    public void LineItems_SatisfyPositionalExpectations()
    {
        var items = new[]
        {
            new LineItem("SKU-001", 2, 9.99m),
            new LineItem("SKU-002", 1, 49.95m),
        };

        // SatisfyRespectively: different assertion per position
        items.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
            first  => first.Quantity.Should().Be(2),
            second => second.UnitPrice.Should().Be(49.95m));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `AllSatisfy` produces significantly better failure messages than `ForEach` + manual `Assert`, but does not short-circuit — all inspectors are run even after the first failure (soft-assertion semantics). For very large collections (10 000+ elements), this can make test failures slow to report; consider asserting on a representative sample with `.Where(predicate).Should().AllSatisfy(...)`. Note that FA counts all element failures as a single `AssertionFailedException`, so CI failure-count metrics will show one failure per test, not per element (see Community Gotchas). [official]

---

### C# 14 — `extension` Blocks as Strongly-Typed Domain Assertion Builders in Test Projects

C# 14 `extension` blocks allow adding instance methods and computed properties to any type without a wrapper class. In test code, this enables a fluent assertion builder pattern directly on domain objects: `order.ShouldBeApproved()` reads as a domain assertion without polluting the production `Order` type with test concerns or creating a separate `OrderAssertions` wrapper class. Because extension block members appear in IntelliSense on the target type, test authors discover them naturally. Combining `extension` blocks with `internal` visibility and `[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("MyApp.Tests")]` keeps the assertion builder entirely within the test assembly while maintaining the fluent call syntax. Extension properties (computed, no backing store) are useful for exposing computed assertion state like `order.IsOverdue`. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

// Production type — no test code here
public class Order
{
    public string        Id       { get; init; } = "";
    public string        Status   { get; set;  } = "Pending";
    public decimal       Total    { get; init; }
    public DateTimeOffset PlacedAt { get; init; } = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;
}

// Test project only — C# 14 extension block
// (file: OrderTestExtensions.cs in the test project, namespace must be imported)
internal static extension OrderAssertionExtensions for Order
{
    // Extension method — fluent assertion, returns this for chaining
    public Order ShouldBeApproved()
    {
        this.Status.Should().BeOneOf("Approved", "Completed",
            because: $"Order {this.Id} was expected to be in an approved state");
        this.Total.Should().BeGreaterThan(0m,
            because: "an approved order must have a positive total");
        return this;
    }

    // Extension property — computed assertion-friendly state
    public bool HasPositiveTotal => this.Total > 0m;
}

public class OrderExtensionTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void ApprovedOrder_PassesDomainAssertion()
    {
        var order = new Order { Id = "ORD-001", Status = "Approved", Total = 99.99m };

        // Reads like a spec, not a framework call
        order.ShouldBeApproved();
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Order_HasPositiveTotal_ExtensionProperty()
    {
        var order = new Order { Total = 50m };
        Assert.True(order.HasPositiveTotal);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Extension blocks in test code are powerful for DDD-style "ubiquitous language" assertions but require `<LangVersion>14</LangVersion>` (or later) in the test project. Teams on older LTS targets must continue using FluentAssertions' `ReferenceTypeAssertions<T>` wrapper pattern. Extension blocks are not discoverable by reflection-based assertion frameworks, so you cannot use them as custom FluentAssertions matchers directly; combine with FA's `Satisfy` for element-level inspection. The namespace import gotcha (see Community Gotchas) is the most common first-time stumbling block. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `Assert.Fail` With Raw String Literals for Rich Conditional Early-Exit Diagnostics

xUnit v3 added `Assert.Fail(string message)` as a first-class method (previously teams wrote `Assert.True(false, message)` as a workaround). `Assert.Fail` throws `XunitException` immediately with the provided message and is intended for conditional early-exit inside tests with branching logic — for example, aborting after a required precondition check fails without using a thrown exception that the SUT might catch. Combined with C# 11+ raw string literals (`""" ... """`), the message can contain rich context (JSON payloads, SQL query plans, stack traces) that aids debugging. A common pattern is using `Assert.Fail` in the `default` case of a switch expression inside a test, or in a `catch (Exception ex)` block where an unexpected exception should stop the test with full diagnostic context. [official]

```csharp
using System.Text.Json;
using Xunit;

public class CheckoutWorkflowTests
{
    private readonly ICheckoutService _sut = new CheckoutService(new InMemoryInventory());

    [Theory]
    [InlineData("standard", true,  "Confirmed")]
    [InlineData("express",  true,  "Confirmed")]
    [InlineData("standard", false, "OutOfStock")]
    public async Task Checkout_ReturnsExpectedStatus(
        string shippingTier, bool hasStock, string expectedStatus)
    {
        if (!Enum.TryParse<ShippingTier>(shippingTier, true, out var tier))
            Assert.Fail($"Unknown shipping tier '{shippingTier}' — update test data");

        ((InMemoryInventory)_sut.Inventory).SetStockAvailable(hasStock);

        CheckoutResult result;
        try
        {
            result = await _sut.CheckoutAsync(new Cart(["SKU-001"]), tier);
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            // Rich diagnostic failure with raw string literal
            Assert.Fail($"""
                Checkout threw unexpectedly.
                  Tier:    {shippingTier}
                  HasStock:{hasStock}
                  Ex type: {ex.GetType().Name}
                  Message: {ex.Message}
                  Stack:
                {ex.StackTrace}
                """);
            return; // unreachable — compiler doesn't know Assert.Fail throws
        }

        Assert.Equal(expectedStatus, result.Status);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Assert.Fail` is appropriate for guarding preconditions within a test body, not for replacing `[Fact]`-level skips — use `Assert.Skip` for that. Overusing `Assert.Fail` inside complex test branches is a smell that the test is doing too much; prefer splitting into distinct `[Fact]` methods. The `return` after `Assert.Fail` in `catch` blocks is required to satisfy the compiler's flow analysis but is logically unreachable — always add a comment. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[DynamicData(DynamicDataSourceType.AutoDetect)]` for Convention-Based Test Data Discovery

MSTest v3.3+ introduced `DynamicDataSourceType.AutoDetect` as an enhancement to `[DynamicData]`, allowing the framework to infer the source member type (method, property, or field) automatically by name rather than requiring an explicit enum value. When `AutoDetect` is used, MSTest scans the test class for a member matching the given name in priority order: property, method, field. This reduces boilerplate and makes it easier to refactor a data source from a property to a method without updating every `[DynamicData]` attribute that references it. Combine with `DynamicDataDisplayName` to produce human-readable test names from the first string element of each data row. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Reflection;

[TestClass]
public class CurrencyConverterTests
{
    // MSTest AutoDetect finds this as a property named 'ConversionTestCases'
    public static IEnumerable<object[]> ConversionTestCases
    {
        get
        {
            yield return ["USD", "EUR", 1.00m, 0.92m];
            yield return ["USD", "GBP", 1.00m, 0.79m];
            yield return ["EUR", "USD", 1.00m, 1.09m];
        }
    }

    public static string GetDisplayName(MethodInfo _, object[] data)
        => $"Convert {data[2]} {data[0]} to {data[1]} = {data[3]}";

    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(
        nameof(ConversionTestCases),
        DynamicDataSourceType.AutoDetect,
        DynamicDataDisplayName = nameof(GetDisplayName))]
    public void Convert_GivenKnownRate_ReturnsExpectedAmount(
        string from, string to, decimal amount, decimal expected)
    {
        var converter = new CurrencyConverter(new FixedRateProvider());
        var result = converter.Convert(from, to, amount);

        Assert.AreEqual(expected, result, delta: 0.01m,
            message: $"Converting {amount} {from}→{to}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `AutoDetect` is a convenience for codebases with consistent naming conventions. The risk is implicit coupling: renaming the data source member without updating the `[DynamicData]` attribute causes a runtime failure rather than a compile-time error. For maximum refactor safety, use the explicit `DynamicDataSourceType.Property` or `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` overload and rely on `nameof()` to catch renames — but accept that changing from property to method requires updating the enum value. [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` With `ConfigureAwait(false)` for Streaming Integration Test Assertions

.NET 10 extended `ConfigureAwait` support to `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` through `ConfigureAwait(bool)` on async enumerables, allowing integration tests consuming streaming HTTP endpoints to suppress `SynchronizationContext` capture correctly. In test code mixing `HttpClient` streaming reads with xUnit's `AsyncTestSyncContext`, omitting `ConfigureAwait(false)` on the `await foreach` caused deadlocks in .NET 8/9 when the continuation attempted to re-enter the synchronization context from a thread-pool thread. .NET 10 makes the fix explicit: `await foreach (var item in stream.ConfigureAwait(false))`. This also applies to EF Core's `ToAsyncEnumerable()` in integration tests using a real database where the test runner has a custom synchronization context. [official]

```csharp
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using Xunit;

public record StockTick(string Symbol, decimal Price, DateTimeOffset At);

public class StreamingEndpointTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task StockTicker_StreamsAtLeastFiveTicks_WithinBudget()
    {
        using var client = factory.CreateClient();
        using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));

        // .NET 10: ConfigureAwait(false) on IAsyncEnumerable<T>
        var ticks = client
            .GetFromJsonAsAsyncEnumerable<StockTick>("/api/stocks/stream", cts.Token)
            .ConfigureAwait(false);

        var collected = new List<StockTick>();

        await foreach (var tick in ticks)
        {
            collected.Add(tick);
            if (collected.Count >= 5) break;
        }

        Assert.True(collected.Count >= 5,
            $"Expected ≥5 ticks, received {collected.Count}");
        Assert.All(collected, t =>
        {
            Assert.False(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(t.Symbol));
            Assert.True(t.Price > 0m);
        });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Always use `ConfigureAwait(false)` on `await foreach` in test code targeting `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` streams to avoid deadlocks on runners with a custom `SynchronizationContext`. The gotcha is that `.ConfigureAwait(false)` changes the return type to `ConfiguredCancelableAsyncEnumerable<T>`, which is not directly assignable to `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` — use `var` for the variable type to avoid the type-assignment restriction. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET — `WithOutputConsumer` for Container Log Capture on Test Failure

Testcontainers.NET 3.5+ provides `WithOutputConsumer(IOutputConsumer)` to capture stdout/stderr from a container during the test run. `Consume.RedirectStdoutAndStderrToStream(stdout, stderr)` writes container output to `Stream` instances readable in `TearDown` or after a test failure. This is critical for debugging: when a container starts but the application inside crashes immediately after the wait strategy completes, the failure manifests as a `TimeoutException` from the wait strategy rather than the actual container error — typically a misconfigured environment variable or a missing dependency. Capturing container logs in the failure path and writing them to `ITestOutputHelper` (xUnit) or `TestContext.Out` (NUnit/MSTest) surfaces the true root cause in the test run output without requiring developers to re-run with Docker CLI tools. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Consumers;
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Abstractions;

public class DatabaseContainerTests(ITestOutputHelper output) : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private IContainer?   _container;
    private MemoryStream  _stdout = new();
    private MemoryStream  _stderr = new();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        var consumer = Consume.RedirectStdoutAndStderrToStream(_stdout, _stderr);

        _container = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
            .WithEnvironment("POSTGRES_PASSWORD", "test")
            .WithPortBinding(5432, true)
            .WithOutputConsumer(consumer)
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                    .UntilCommandIsCompleted("pg_isready", "-U", "postgres")
                    .WithTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60)))
            .Build();

        try
        {
            await _container.StartAsync();
        }
        catch
        {
            // Seek to start before reading (see Community Gotchas)
            _stdout.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin);
            _stderr.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin);
            output.WriteLine("=== Container STDOUT ===");
            output.WriteLine(new StreamReader(_stdout).ReadToEnd());
            output.WriteLine("=== Container STDERR ===");
            output.WriteLine(new StreamReader(_stderr).ReadToEnd());
            throw;
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Container_Started_PortIsMapped()
        => Assert.True(_container!.GetMappedPublicPort(5432) > 0);

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        _stdout.Dispose();
        _stderr.Dispose();
        if (_container is not null) await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `WithOutputConsumer` adds memory overhead proportional to container output volume — a chatty container can fill the `MemoryStream` quickly. Use it unconditionally only in developer workstation fixture configurations; in CI, limit container verbosity via environment variables (`POSTGRES_LOG_MIN_MESSAGES=fatal`) and only dump logs in the catch path. Never forget `Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin)` before reading the stream (see Community Gotchas). [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 37

**xUnit v3 `IMessageSink.OnMessage(new DiagnosticMessage(...))` called from an `IAssemblyFixture<T>` is silently dropped unless the runner is started with `--diagnostics` — teams expecting assembly-level log output in standard test runs will see nothing [community]** — When `IMessageSink.OnMessage` is called with a `DiagnosticMessage`, xUnit v3 routes it through the diagnostic channel which is only active when `--diagnostics` is passed (CLI) or `<DiagnosticMessages>true</DiagnosticMessages>` is set in `xunit.runner.json`. WHY it causes problems: developers add `IMessageSink` logging to debug a flaky container startup issue, run `dotnet test`, see no output, conclude the logging is broken, and spend time troubleshooting what is actually a runner configuration issue. Fix: document in the fixture class that `--diagnostics` is required, or use `TestContext.Current?.SendDiagnosticMessage(...)` inside individual tests where output appears per-test regardless of the diagnostics flag.

**NUnit 4 `TestContext.Out.WriteLine` called from a thread-pool continuation (e.g., inside `Task.Run` without `await`) throws `NullReferenceException` because the execution context has been lost [community]** — NUnit's `TestContext.Out` resolves the current test context from `ExecutionContext`; thread-pool threads spawned from test code share the execution context only if the `Task` was awaited without suppressing it. When `Task.Run` is called without being awaited from within the test (fire-and-forget), the continuation runs on a thread-pool thread that may not have the test's `ExecutionContext` bound, causing `TestContext.CurrentContext` to be `null` and `TestContext.Out` to throw. WHY it causes problems: the failure is non-deterministic depending on the thread-pool scheduler's scheduling order, making it difficult to reproduce in local development. Fix: capture `TestContext.Out` into a local variable before entering the `Task.Run` lambda, or avoid `Task.Run` in test code entirely in favour of `await`-ed async methods.

**FluentAssertions `AllSatisfy` reports all element failures but counts them all as a single assertion failure in the xUnit test run summary — `dotnet test` reports one failed test, not N failed assertions, misleading quality metrics dashboards [community]** — `AllSatisfy` uses FA's internal soft-assertion collector (`AssertionScope`) which batches all element failures into a single `AssertionFailedException` with a multi-line message. xUnit counts one exception per test method, so ten element failures inside `AllSatisfy` appear as one failing test. WHY it causes problems: quality-metrics dashboards that track "number of assertion failures over time" see an apparent improvement when a team migrates from individual `Assert.Equal` calls to `AllSatisfy`, creating misleading improvement signals. Fix: be aware of this counting difference; document in team norms that `AllSatisfy` is preferred for readability but failure counts are not directly comparable with previous per-assertion counts.

**Moq `Capture.In<T>` stores references to passed objects — mutations to mutable arguments after the mock call are reflected in the captured list, so post-call assertions see the mutated state rather than the state at call time [community]** — `Capture.In<T>` stores the exact reference. If the SUT passes a mutable object and then modifies it after calling the dependency, the captured item reflects the post-mutation state at assertion time. WHY it causes problems: a service that calls `repo.SaveAsync(entity)` and then sets `entity.Status = "Saved"` will cause the captured entity to show `Status = "Saved"` even though the assertion intended to verify the pre-save state; `captured[0].Status.Should().Be("Pending")` unexpectedly fails. Fix: use `Callback<T>(e => captured.Add(e.Clone()))` instead of `Capture.In` when the argument is mutable, so a snapshot is captured rather than the live reference.

**Testcontainers.NET `WithOutputConsumer` with `MemoryStream` does not reset the stream position after `StartAsync` — reading immediately after `StartAsync` returns 0 bytes because the stream position is at the written end [community]** — `IOutputConsumer` writes sequentially; after `StartAsync` completes, the stream's `Position` is at the end. Calling `new StreamReader(_stdout).ReadToEnd()` returns an empty string. WHY it causes problems: developers conclude the container produced no output, check the consumer setup, and waste debugging time — when the fix is `_stdout.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin)` before reading. Fix: always call `Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin)` before reading output streams; wrap in a helper `static string ReadCapturedOutput(MemoryStream s) { s.Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin); return new StreamReader(s).ReadToEnd(); }`.

**C# 14 `extension` blocks in test projects produce `CS9307` ("Static extension member is not accessible on the extended type") when the block is declared in a different namespace from the test class that is not imported [community]** — C# 14 extension blocks are namespace-scoped; the block must be in a namespace that is in-scope at the test call site. If the extensions file uses `namespace MyApp.Tests.Extensions` but the test class file does not `using MyApp.Tests.Extensions`, the extension methods are invisible and `CS9307` is reported. WHY it causes problems: unlike classic `static class` extension methods where the error message suggests "using directive", the `CS9307` message is non-obvious and does not suggest adding a `using` statement. Fix: co-locate extension blocks in the same namespace as the tests that use them, or add `using MyApp.Tests.Extensions` to `GlobalUsings.cs` in the test project.

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 37 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Using `IMessageSink` without enabling `--diagnostics` and expecting console output | Messages silently dropped in standard runs; debugging time wasted | Add `--diagnostics` flag or `<DiagnosticMessages>true</DiagnosticMessages>` in `xunit.runner.json` |
| `TestContext.Out.WriteLine` inside `Task.Run` fire-and-forget | `ExecutionContext` not flowed; `NullReferenceException` thrown non-deterministically | Capture `TestContext.Out` to a local variable before entering `Task.Run` |
| `params T[]` for hot-path test helpers on C# 13+ | Unnecessary heap allocation per call; GC pressure distorts timing | Use `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` for fixed-count call sites; document TFM constraint |
| `Capture.In<T>` with mutable SUT arguments | Post-mutation state pollutes captured list; assertions see wrong state | Use `Callback<T>` with `.Clone()` to capture a snapshot |
| Reading `MemoryStream` from `WithOutputConsumer` without `Seek(0, SeekOrigin.Begin)` | Stream at end after write; `ReadToEnd()` returns empty string | Always seek to 0 before reading; wrap in a helper |
| C# 14 `extension` blocks without a matching `using` import in the consuming file | Extension members invisible; non-obvious `CS9307` error | Add namespace to `GlobalUsings.cs` in the test project |

## Cycle 38 — 2026-05-14

### xUnit v3 — `Assert.Fail(string)` and `Assert.Skip(string)` as Conditional Escape Hatches

xUnit v3 formalised `Assert.Fail(string)` and `Assert.Skip(string)` as first-class static methods on the `Assert` class, replacing the older pattern of throwing `XunitException` directly or using `Skip` on the `[Fact]` attribute to skip programmatically. `Assert.Fail` is useful for guard clauses in parameterised tests where a specific parameter combination is invalid and should be a hard failure rather than a skipped row. `Assert.Skip` allows runtime-detected conditions — such as a missing external service or an OS platform constraint — to mark the test as skipped rather than failed, preventing false failures in CI environments where the precondition cannot be met. Both methods are annotated with `[DoesNotReturn]` so the compiler and static analysers understand control flow terminates at the call site. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class PaymentProcessorTests
{
    [Theory]
    [InlineData("VISA", 100, true)]
    [InlineData("AMEX", 0,   false)]
    [InlineData("UNKNOWN", -1, false)]
    public void ProcessPayment_ValidatesAmountAndProvider(
        string provider, decimal amount, bool expectSuccess)
    {
        if (amount < 0)
            Assert.Fail($"Test data error: amount {amount} is invalid for provider '{provider}'.");

        if (!OperatingSystem.IsWindows() && provider == "AMEX")
            Assert.Skip("AMEX gateway simulation requires Windows crypto stack; skipping on non-Windows.");

        var processor = new PaymentProcessor();
        var result    = processor.Process(provider, amount);

        Assert.Equal(expectSuccess, result.IsSuccess);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Prefer `Assert.Fail` over throwing exceptions so that the runner correctly categorises the outcome as a test failure (not an unhandled exception), and prefer `Assert.Skip` over removing tests so that skipped counts are visible in CI dashboards and regressions are catchable once the environment condition is met. Do not abuse `Assert.Skip` as a way to silence temporarily broken tests; document the skip condition explicitly so it can be reviewed and removed. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `ClassicAssert` Migration Bridge for Incremental NUnit 3 to NUnit 4 Upgrades

NUnit 4 moved all `Assert.AreEqual`, `Assert.IsNotNull`, and similar classic-style assertion methods to `NUnit.Framework.Legacy.ClassicAssert`. Teams with large NUnit 3 test suites can add a `using static NUnit.Framework.Legacy.ClassicAssert;` statement to a `GlobalUsings.cs` file to restore the classic API project-wide without touching individual test files, enabling an incremental migration where test files are rewritten to the constraint-model API one at a time. The alternative — a project-wide find-and-replace from `Assert.AreEqual` to `Assert.That` — creates a massive, unreviewed diff that is risky to merge on a live codebase. Using the bridge buys time for teams to schedule deliberate refactoring without blocking the NUnit 4 upgrade entirely. [official]

```csharp
// GlobalUsings.cs — added once to the test project
global using static NUnit.Framework.Legacy.ClassicAssert;

// ExistingTest.cs — zero changes required; still compiles under NUnit 4
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
public class OrderServiceTests
{
    [Test]
    public void PlaceOrder_ValidOrder_ReturnsOrderId()
    {
        var service = new OrderService();
        var orderId = service.PlaceOrder(new Order { ProductId = 1, Quantity = 2 });

        AreNotEqual(0, orderId);           // classic-style via ClassicAssert bridge
        IsNotNull(orderId.ToString());     // classic-style
    }

    // New tests: use constraint model directly
    [Test]
    public void PlaceOrder_ZeroQuantity_ThrowsArgumentException()
        => Assert.That(
               () => new OrderService().PlaceOrder(new Order { ProductId = 1, Quantity = 0 }),
               Throws.TypeOf<ArgumentException>());
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The bridge eliminates the upgrade blocker but leaves technical debt. Set a team norm (or a Roslyn analyser rule) that new tests MUST use `Assert.That` so the legacy count only decreases. Remove the `global using` once all usages are migrated to confirm zero regressions. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[TestCategory]` + `dotnet test --filter` for Tiered Test Execution in CI

MSTest v3 preserves the `[TestCategory("Integration")]` / `[TestCategory("Unit")]` attribute model and aligns it with the `dotnet test --filter` filter expression syntax, which also works for xUnit's `[Trait]` and NUnit's `[Category]`. Organising tests into categories enables CI pipelines to run a fast unit-test gate on every commit and reserve long-running integration tests for a separate scheduled or merge-gated job. The filter expression `TestCategory=Unit` selects only unit tests; `TestCategory!=Integration` excludes them. On GitHub Actions, separate jobs with different filter expressions allow test parallelism across runners while keeping per-PR feedback times under 60 seconds. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class InvoiceCalculatorTests
{
    [TestMethod, TestCategory("Unit")]
    public void Calculate_SingleLineItem_ReturnsCorrectTotal()
    {
        var calc  = new InvoiceCalculator();
        var total = calc.Calculate([new LineItem { UnitPrice = 10m, Qty = 3 }]);
        Assert.AreEqual(30m, total);
    }

    [TestMethod, TestCategory("Integration"), TestCategory("SlowCI")]
    public async Task Calculate_DatabaseRoundTrip_PreservesDecimalPrecision()
    {
        await using var db = await TestDatabase.OpenAsync();
        var calc  = new InvoiceCalculator(db);
        var total = calc.Calculate([new LineItem { UnitPrice = 9.99m, Qty = 100 }]);
        Assert.AreEqual(999m, total);
    }
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (excerpt)
- name: Unit tests
  run: dotnet test --filter "TestCategory=Unit" --no-build

- name: Integration tests (merge gate only)
  if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  run: dotnet test --filter "TestCategory=Integration" --no-build
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Category-based filtering is opt-in discipline — it only works if every test is tagged. Use a Roslyn analyser (`MSTest.Analyzers`) or a custom rule to enforce that every `[TestMethod]` has a `[TestCategory]`. Avoid very fine-grained categories that create a combinatorial maintenance burden; two to four categories (Unit, Integration, SlowCI, Contract) is the practical ceiling. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions v8 — `HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo` for Defensive Collection Size Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 provides `HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(n)` and `HaveCountLessThanOrEqualTo(n)` as named aliases on `GenericCollectionAssertions<T>`, eliminating the verbose pattern of `.Count().Should().BeGreaterThanOrEqualTo(n)` which accessed the underlying integer and lost the semantic subject in failure messages. The aliased overloads produce failure messages that read "Expected collection to have at least 3 items, but found 1", including the collection contents in the "and" clause when `Because` is provided, which is substantially more diagnostic than the integer assertion that only reports "Expected 1 to be greater than or equal to 3". Defensive size assertions are particularly important in snapshot test gates that verify paginated API responses contain at least one page of data before asserting individual field values. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class ProductCatalogTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProducts_DefaultPage_ReturnsAtLeastOneProduct()
    {
        var client   = factory.CreateClient();
        var products = await client
            .GetFromJsonAsync<List<ProductDto>>("/api/products")
            ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Null response");

        products.Should()
            .HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(1,
                because: "the seed data loader populates at least one product on startup")
            .And.AllSatisfy(p =>
            {
                p.Id.Should().BePositive();
                p.Name.Should().NotBeNullOrWhiteSpace();
                p.Price.Should().BeGreaterThan(0m);
            });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo` and `HaveCountLessThanOrEqualTo` require FluentAssertions 7.0+. Do not use these as a substitute for exact-count assertions in unit tests where the full output is deterministic; reserve size-range assertions for integration test responses where seeded data volume is environment-dependent. [official]

---

### Moq — `MockRepository.Create<T>()` With `VerifyAll()` for Cohesive Fixture Teardown

`MockRepository` is a Moq factory that groups multiple `Mock<T>` instances under a single lifecycle. Calling `_repo.VerifyAll()` in `Dispose` or `[TestCleanup]` verifies that every setup on every mock created by the repository was actually called, catching the common bug where a test only partially exercises a code path because a second downstream call was never set up and never reached. This is strictly stronger than calling `mock.VerifyAll()` per-mock individually because the `MockRepository` call also enforces that no mock in the group was left un-verified due to a missed `VerifyAll` call on a specific mock. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public class OrderDispatcherTests : IDisposable
{
    private readonly MockRepository _repo = new(MockBehavior.Strict);
    private readonly Mock<IInventoryService>    _inventory;
    private readonly Mock<IShippingGateway>     _shipping;
    private readonly Mock<INotificationService> _notifications;
    private readonly OrderDispatcher            _sut;

    public OrderDispatcherTests()
    {
        _inventory     = _repo.Create<IInventoryService>();
        _shipping      = _repo.Create<IShippingGateway>();
        _notifications = _repo.Create<INotificationService>();
        _sut           = new OrderDispatcher(
            _inventory.Object, _shipping.Object, _notifications.Object);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task DispatchOrder_AllCallsCompleted_Succeeds()
    {
        _inventory.Setup(i => i.ReserveAsync(42, 1)).ReturnsAsync(true);
        _shipping.Setup(s  => s.CreateShipmentAsync(It.IsAny<Order>())).ReturnsAsync("TRACK-001");
        _notifications.Setup(n =>
            n.SendConfirmationAsync("user@example.com", "TRACK-001")).Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

        await _sut.DispatchAsync(
            new Order { ProductId = 42, Qty = 1, Email = "user@example.com" });
    }

    public void Dispose() => _repo.VerifyAll(); // catches any un-called setup
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `MockBehavior.Strict` on the `MockRepository` causes tests to fail if any call is made that has no corresponding setup, which is noisy during early development but invaluable in mature test suites as a regression guard. When onboarding a new integration, temporarily create a `Loose`-mode mock directly (`new Mock<T>(MockBehavior.Loose)`) outside the repo so strict verification does not interfere with exploratory work. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET — `ImageFromDockerfileBuilder` for Custom Image Construction in Integration Tests

Testcontainers.NET 3.6+ exposes `ImageFromDockerfileBuilder` so integration tests can build a custom Docker image from a `Dockerfile` in the source tree and run it as a test container, without pre-building and pushing the image to a registry. This is particularly useful for testing database migrations against the exact schema your application deploys — you build an image that copies the migration scripts and runs them at container start, ensuring the test database matches production intent rather than a development `EnsureCreatedAsync` shortcut. The image is cached by the Docker daemon; Testcontainers hashes the Dockerfile and build context, rebuilding only when either changes. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Images;
using Xunit;

public class MigrationIntegrationTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private IFutureDockerImage? _image;
    private IContainer?         _db;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _image = new ImageFromDockerfileBuilder()
            .WithDockerfileDirectory(
                CommonDirectoryPath.GetSolutionDirectory(), "db/migrations-runner")
            .WithDockerfile("Dockerfile")
            .WithName("test-migrations-runner:local")
            .WithDeleteIfExists(true)
            .Build();

        await _image.CreateAsync();

        _db = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage(_image)
            .WithEnvironment("DB_CONNECTION",
                "Host=postgres;Database=testdb;Username=sa;Password=pass")
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                    .UntilMessageIsLogged("Migrations complete"))
            .Build();

        await _db.StartAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public void MigrationsContainer_StartedSuccessfully_IsRunning()
        => Assert.NotNull(_db);

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_db is not null)    await _db.DisposeAsync();
        if (_image is not null) await _image.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Building images during test runs adds first-run latency (10–120 seconds depending on base image and layer caching). In CI, warm the Docker cache in a dedicated step before running tests. Use `WithDeleteIfExists(true)` during development to ensure stale cached layers are removed when the `Dockerfile` changes; remove it in CI to maximise layer reuse. [official]

---

### C# 13 — `System.Threading.Lock` and `Lock.EnterScope()` for Deterministic Lock Release in Tests

C# 13 introduced `System.Threading.Lock` as a dedicated lock primitive with a `Lock.Scope EnterScope()` method that returns a `ref struct` disposable, enabling idiomatic `using` block syntax. In test code, this replaces the error-prone `lock (object) { ... }` pattern around shared state in `IClassFixture<T>` or `IAssemblyFixture<T>` implementations where multiple parallel test threads access a mutable counter, connection pool token, or port allocation table. The `ref struct` scope ensures the lock is released even if an exception is thrown, and the compiler enforces that `Lock.Scope` cannot be stored on the heap, preventing accidental lock retention across async continuations. [official]

```csharp
using System.Threading;

// Shared fixture that allocates ports for parallel integration tests
public sealed class PortAllocatorFixture : IDisposable
{
    private readonly Lock _lock     = new();
    private          int  _nextPort = 5100;

    public int AllocatePort()
    {
        using (_lock.EnterScope())   // ref struct — released deterministically
        {
            return _nextPort++;
        }
    }

    public void Dispose() { }
}

// xUnit test using the shared fixture
public class ListenerTests(PortAllocatorFixture ports)
    : IClassFixture<PortAllocatorFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task StartListener_AllocatedPort_AcceptsConnection()
    {
        var port     = ports.AllocatePort();
        var listener = new System.Net.Sockets.TcpListener(
            System.Net.IPAddress.Loopback, port);
        listener.Start();
        try
        {
            using var client = new System.Net.Sockets.TcpClient();
            await client.ConnectAsync("127.0.0.1", port);
            Assert.True(client.Connected);
        }
        finally { listener.Stop(); }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `System.Threading.Lock` requires .NET 9+ / C# 13+. The key restriction is that `Lock.Scope` is a `ref struct` and therefore CANNOT be used across `await` boundaries — attempt to do so and the compiler raises `CS4012`. For locks held across `await`, continue to use `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` which is `await`-compatible. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions v8 — `Satisfy` With Inline Predicate for Single-Object Contract Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 added `Satisfy(Func<T, bool> predicate, string because, params object[] becauseArgs)` as a single-object alternative to `Match`, providing a richer failure message than `Be(true)` on a boolean expression. Where `Match` requires an `Expression<Func<T,bool>>` (which FA uses for the failure message), `Satisfy` accepts a plain `Func<T, bool>` and requires an explicit `because` string that serves as the assertion description in failures. This is useful when the condition itself is non-trivial to express as a readable expression tree — for example, when the predicate calls extension methods or complex delegates that the expression-tree formatter cannot serialise cleanly. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public record ApiResponse(int StatusCode, string Body, DateTimeOffset Timestamp);

public class ApiClientTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetUser_ReturnsSuccess_WithRecentTimestamp()
    {
        var client   = new ApiClient(baseUrl: "https://api.example.com");
        var response = await client.GetUserAsync(userId: 42);

        response.Should()
            .NotBeNull()
            .And.Satisfy(
                r => r.StatusCode is >= 200 and < 300
                     && !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(r.Body)
                     && r.Timestamp >= DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddMinutes(-1),
                because: "a successful user fetch returns 2xx with a body "
                       + "timestamped within the last minute");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Satisfy` is best for complex multi-field predicates where decomposing into individual `And.` chains would create ten lines of assertions. For simple single-field checks, prefer named assertions (`HaveStatusCode`, `NotBeNullOrWhiteSpace`) because their failure messages are more specific. When the predicate needs to be reused across tests, extract it as a named extension method using the FluentAssertions extensibility API. [official]

---

### xUnit v3 — `IAsyncLifetime` With `ValueTask` Overloads for Zero-Allocation Fixture Setup

xUnit v3 updated `IAsyncLifetime` to accept `ValueTask` returns from `InitializeAsync` and `DisposeAsync`, replacing the previous `Task`-only interface. This allows shared fixture classes to avoid unnecessary `Task` heap allocations in the common case where initialisation completes synchronously. When the fixture must perform real async work (like starting a container), it returns a real `ValueTask` wrapping the async operation; when it is a no-op, `return ValueTask.CompletedTask` avoids any allocation. The change is source-compatible with previous `Task`-returning implementations since `Task` is implicitly convertible to `ValueTask`. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public sealed class SharedHttpClientFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public HttpClient Client { get; private set; } = null!;
    private HttpClientHandler? _handler;

    public ValueTask InitializeAsync()
    {
        // Synchronous setup — zero allocation path
        _handler = new HttpClientHandler { AllowAutoRedirect = false };
        Client   = new HttpClient(_handler)
        {
            BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com"),
            Timeout     = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)
        };
        return ValueTask.CompletedTask;
    }

    public ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        Client.Dispose();
        _handler?.Dispose();
        return ValueTask.CompletedTask;
    }
}

public class ApiSmokeTests(SharedHttpClientFixture fixture)
    : IClassFixture<SharedHttpClientFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task HealthEndpoint_Returns200()
    {
        var response = await fixture.Client.GetAsync("/health");
        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The `ValueTask` overload is a micro-optimisation that matters only when the fixture is created and destroyed at high frequency. For fixtures that perform genuine async setup (database connections, container starts), the overhead of `Task` vs `ValueTask` is negligible compared to the I/O cost. Adopt `ValueTask` for newly-written fixtures for correctness and forward compatibility. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `[RetryAttribute(n)]` With Quarantine Tagging for Flakiness Isolation

NUnit 4 retains the `[Retry(n)]` attribute that re-runs a failing test up to `n` times before marking it as failed. This is intended strictly as a temporary quarantine mechanism for tests with known external flakiness, not as a licence to leave inherently non-deterministic tests in the suite. In NUnit 4, `[Retry]` interacts with `[MaxTime]` — if a test exceeds the max time on one attempt, the retry is still attempted, meaning a timeout-prone test can consume up to `n * MaxTime` milliseconds. Pair `[Retry]` with a tracking comment referencing a GitHub issue so the quarantine is visible and has an owner who can remove it once the root cause is resolved. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
public class ExternalPaymentGatewayTests
{
    // TODO: Remove [Retry] once payment-gateway flakiness is resolved (see: GH #2847)
    [Test, Retry(3)]
    [Category("Integration"), Category("FlakeyQuarantine")]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_StripeTestMode_ReturnsChargeId()
    {
        var gateway = new StripeGateway(apiKey: TestSecrets.StripeTestKey);

        var result = await gateway.ChargeAsync(
            amount: 100_00, currency: "USD", token: "tok_visa");

        Assert.That(result.ChargeId,   Is.Not.Null.And.Not.Empty);
        Assert.That(result.Status,     Is.EqualTo("succeeded"));
        Assert.That(result.AmountPaid, Is.EqualTo(100_00));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[Retry]` hides genuine test reliability problems when overused. Enforce a team policy of allowing a maximum of 2 retries and requiring a linked issue before merging a `[Retry]`-decorated test. Set up a CI report that surfaces `[Category("FlakeyQuarantine")]` tests separately so they do not normalise into the baseline pass rate. Never use `[Retry]` in unit tests — flakiness in unit tests indicates non-deterministic test data or hidden shared state that needs to be fixed, not retried. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[DeploymentItem]` and `TestContext.DeploymentDirectory` for File-Based Test Data

MSTest v3 retains `[DeploymentItem("testdata/sample.json")]` and `TestContext.DeploymentDirectory` for copying files from the project directory to the test run output directory, making them available via relative paths during test execution. This solves the common problem of fragile relative paths (`../../testdata/sample.json`) that break when tests are run from different working directories (IDE run vs `dotnet test` vs CI agent). `[DeploymentItem]` decorates the class or method and is processed by the MSTest runner before any test method executes; the copied file is available at `Path.Combine(TestContext.DeploymentDirectory, "sample.json")`. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.IO;
using System.Text.Json;

[TestClass]
[DeploymentItem("testdata/products.json")]
[DeploymentItem("testdata/invalid-products.json")]
public class ProductImporterTests
{
    public TestContext TestContext { get; set; } = null!;

    [TestMethod]
    public void ImportProducts_ValidJson_ImportsAllRecords()
    {
        var filePath = Path.Combine(TestContext.DeploymentDirectory!, "products.json");
        var json     = File.ReadAllText(filePath);
        var products = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<ProductDto>>(json)!;

        var importer = new ProductImporter();
        var result   = importer.Import(products);

        Assert.AreEqual(products.Count, result.ImportedCount);
        Assert.AreEqual(0,              result.ErrorCount);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public void ImportProducts_InvalidJson_ReportsErrors()
    {
        var filePath = Path.Combine(TestContext.DeploymentDirectory!, "invalid-products.json");
        var json     = File.ReadAllText(filePath);
        var products = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<ProductDto>>(json)!;

        var importer = new ProductImporter();
        var result   = importer.Import(products);

        Assert.IsTrue(result.ErrorCount > 0);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[DeploymentItem]` requires that test data files are included in the project with `Build Action: Content` and `Copy to Output Directory: Copy if newer`. Ensure the `.csproj` includes `<Content Include="testdata/**" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />`. For xUnit and NUnit, the equivalent is configuring `testdata` as a project content item and using `AppContext.BaseDirectory` to resolve paths, since those frameworks do not have a `DeploymentItem` equivalent. [official]

### .NET 10 — `FakeTimeProvider.SetLocalTimeZone` for Time-Zone-Sensitive Assertion Chains

.NET 9 introduced `TimeProvider` as an injectable abstraction over `DateTime.UtcNow` and `DateTime.Now`. .NET 10 extended `FakeTimeProvider` in `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` with improved `SetLocalTimeZone(TimeZoneInfo)` support, allowing tests to verify time-zone-sensitive logic — such as business-hours checks, daylight-saving-time boundary behaviour, and locale-specific date formatting — without manipulating system time. A `FakeTimeProvider` with a fixed `UtcNow` and a configured `LocalTimeZone` provides a deterministic `GetLocalNow()` return value, enabling assertions that verify both the UTC storage path and the local display path through the same test. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using Xunit;

public class BusinessHoursServiceTests
{
    [Theory]
    [InlineData("Eastern Standard Time",  14, 0,  true)]   // 2pm EST -> business hours
    [InlineData("Eastern Standard Time",  19, 0, false)]   // 7pm EST -> after hours
    [InlineData("Pacific Standard Time",  14, 0,  true)]   // 2pm PST -> business hours
    [InlineData("UTC",                     0, 30, false)]  // 12:30am UTC -> after hours
    public void IsOpenForBusiness_RespectsLocalTimeZone(
        string tzId, int hour, int minute, bool expected)
    {
        var tz   = TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById(tzId);
        var fake = new FakeTimeProvider();
        fake.SetUtcNow(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 3, 15, hour, minute, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
        fake.SetLocalTimeZone(tz);

        var service = new BusinessHoursService(fake);
        var result  = service.IsOpenForBusiness();

        Assert.Equal(expected, result);
    }
}

public class BusinessHoursService(TimeProvider time)
{
    public bool IsOpenForBusiness()
    {
        var local = time.GetLocalNow();
        return local.DayOfWeek is not DayOfWeek.Saturday and not DayOfWeek.Sunday
               && local.Hour is >= 9 and < 17;
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById` uses OS-specific zone IDs on Windows ("Eastern Standard Time") and IANA IDs on Linux/macOS ("America/New_York"). In cross-platform CI, use `TimeZoneInfo.TryConvertIanaIdToWindowsId` (.NET 6+) or the `TimeZoneConverter` NuGet package to normalise IDs. Hard-coding Windows zone IDs in tests causes failures on Linux CI agents without extra configuration. [official]

### Polly v8 — `ResiliencePipeline.ExecuteAsync` With `CancellationToken` Propagation in Integration Tests

Polly v8's `ResiliencePipeline` accepts a `CancellationToken` in `ExecuteAsync`, and tests must propagate the test's own `CancellationToken` (from xUnit v3's injected method parameter or the test's explicit `CancellationTokenSource`) into Polly executions. Failure to propagate the token means a test's timeout does not abort a hanging Polly retry loop — the test runner kills the thread but Polly's inner retry may continue running on a background thread, causing port leaks, connection pool exhaustion, or interference with subsequent tests. In xUnit v3, inject the cancellation token directly into the test method signature; the runner provides a token that is cancelled when the test's allocated time expires. [official]

```csharp
using Polly;
using Polly.Retry;
using Xunit;

public class ResilientHttpClientTests
{
    private static readonly ResiliencePipeline<HttpResponseMessage> _pipeline =
        new ResiliencePipelineBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>()
            .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions<HttpResponseMessage>
            {
                MaxRetryAttempts = 3,
                Delay            = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(50),
                ShouldHandle     = new PredicateBuilder<HttpResponseMessage>()
                    .HandleResult(r => (int)r.StatusCode >= 500)
            })
            .AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))
            .Build();

    [Fact]
    public async Task Execute_TransientFailureThenSuccess_ReturnsOk(
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)   // xUnit v3 injects test-scoped CT
    {
        var attempts    = 0;
        var fakeHandler = new FakeDelegatingHandler(_ =>
        {
            attempts++;
            return attempts < 3
                ? new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable)
                : new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK);
        });
        using var client = new HttpClient(fakeHandler);

        var response = await _pipeline.ExecuteAsync(
            async ct => await client.GetAsync("https://api.example.com/data", ct),
            cancellationToken);   // propagate test token into Polly

        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
        Assert.Equal(3, attempts);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Propagating the test's `CancellationToken` into Polly is correct but means that a token cancelled mid-retry (e.g., test timeout) will surface as `OperationCanceledException` rather than the last HTTP error. In tests specifically asserting Polly's retry behaviour, use a `CancellationTokenSource` with a generous explicit timeout rather than the test runner's token, so assertions about retry counts are not defeated by runner-level cancellation. [official]
