### .NET 9 / 10 — `MemoryExtensions.CommonPrefixLength` and `SequenceCompareTo` for Span-Based Protocol Decoder Tests

.NET 9 added `MemoryExtensions.CommonPrefixLength<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>)` and .NET 10 stabilised `SequenceCompareTo` span overloads, enabling unit tests for binary-protocol parsers and string-processing routines to assert structural correctness without round-tripping through heap-allocated strings. `CommonPrefixLength` returns the number of leading elements that two spans share, which is exactly the assertion needed when testing that a parser correctly identifies a protocol header prefix before branching on it. Both methods operate on `ReadOnlySpan<T>` for any `T : IEquatable<T>`, so they work for `byte`, `char`, `int`, and custom value types. [official]

```csharp
using System;
using Xunit;

public class ProtocolParserTests
{
    private static readonly byte[] MagicHeader = "MYPROTO/1.0"u8.ToArray();

    [Theory]
    [InlineData(new byte[] { (byte)'M',(byte)'Y',(byte)'P',(byte)'R',(byte)'O' }, 5)]
    [InlineData(new byte[] {
        (byte)'M',(byte)'Y',(byte)'P',(byte)'R',(byte)'O',
        (byte)'T',(byte)'O',(byte)'/',(byte)'1',(byte)'.',(byte)'0' }, 11)]
    [InlineData(new byte[] { (byte)'X',(byte)'Y',(byte)'Z' }, 0)]
    public void ParseHeader_MatchesMagicPrefix(byte[] input, int expectedPrefixLen)
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<byte> header = MagicHeader.AsSpan();
        ReadOnlySpan<byte> data   = input.AsSpan();

        var prefixLen = MemoryExtensions.CommonPrefixLength(header, data);

        Assert.Equal(expectedPrefixLen, prefixLen);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void SortedFrames_MergedSpans_AreInOrder()
    {
        int[] frameA = [1, 3, 5, 7];
        int[] frameB = [2, 4, 6, 8];

        var merged = MergeSort(frameA.AsSpan(), frameB.AsSpan());

        for (var i = 1; i < merged.Length; i++)
            Assert.True(merged[i - 1] <= merged[i],
                $"Element at {i-1} ({merged[i-1]}) > element at {i} ({merged[i]})");
    }

    private static int[] MergeSort(ReadOnlySpan<int> a, ReadOnlySpan<int> b)
    {
        var result = new int[a.Length + b.Length];
        int ai = 0, bi = 0, ri = 0;
        while (ai < a.Length && bi < b.Length)
            result[ri++] = a[ai] <= b[bi] ? a[ai++] : b[bi++];
        while (ai < a.Length) result[ri++] = a[ai++];
        while (bi < b.Length) result[ri++] = b[bi++];
        return result;
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `MemoryExtensions.CommonPrefixLength` is available from .NET 9; targeting `net8.0` or earlier requires a manual loop. Use `u8` string literals (C# 11+) for readable `byte[]` initialisation of header constants. Avoid `stackalloc` in test helper methods where the span might be passed to another method, as `ref struct` limitations restrict how they propagate through call chains. [official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 38

**xUnit v3 `CancellationToken` injected into `[Fact]` test methods is NOT the same instance as `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` — they are separate instances with different lifetimes, and using the wrong one in background tasks can mask test timeouts [community]** — xUnit v3 injects a fresh `CancellationToken` per test invocation as a method parameter, linked to the test's time budget. `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` is also linked to the test budget but is the same instance the test context uses internally. The difference matters when passing the token to infrastructure libraries that hold references: using the method-parameter token ensures cancellation flows through all callees; using `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` in a fire-and-forget continuation can silently lose cancellation because `TestContext.Current` becomes `null` once the test completes. WHY it causes problems: developers assume either token is equivalent, use `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` in a background task, the task outlives the test, and the runner reports a clean pass while background work continues leaking resources. Fix: always use the injected parameter token for callees; never capture `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` in a background task spawned after the test method is entered.

**NUnit 4 `[Retry(n)]` does NOT retry on `Assert.Inconclusive` — only on failed assertions and unhandled exceptions — so a test using `Assert.Inconclusive` as a precondition guard will appear "Inconclusive" after n attempts rather than being retried [community]** — Teams that use `Assert.Inconclusive` to handle environment-not-ready conditions (e.g., external service unreachable) and also apply `[Retry]` expecting the retry to eventually reach the real assertion phase are surprised to find the test is reported "Inconclusive" after `n` attempts. `[Retry]` retries only when `AssertionException` or any other non-`InconclusiveException` is thrown. WHY it causes problems: CI dashboards show "Inconclusive" as a neutral outcome; the test effectively passes the gate even though the external service was never reached, hiding an environment outage. Fix: use `Assert.Fail` rather than `Assert.Inconclusive` for environment-check failures if retry behaviour is desired; reserve `Assert.Inconclusive` for genuinely optional tests.

**Polly v8 `ResiliencePipelineBuilder.Build()` is not thread-safe — calling it concurrently from multiple test threads sharing the same builder instance can throw `InvalidOperationException` [community]** — `Build()` finalises and validates the pipeline configuration. If two threads simultaneously access the builder state before either calls `Build()`, the internal validation can be corrupted. WHY it causes problems: in large xUnit test suites with parallelism enabled, builders stored in a lazily initialised `static` field that is mutated by each test class constructor can race. The issue is intermittent and often only surfaces on high-core-count CI agents. Fix: always build `ResiliencePipeline` instances as `static readonly` fields using a direct initialiser (`static readonly ResiliencePipeline _p = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder().Add...().Build();`) so the immutable pipeline is shared, not the builder.

**FluentAssertions `HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0)` always passes — including for empty collections — creating a silent always-green assertion that provides no regression coverage [community]** — `subject.Should().HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0)` passes for any non-null collection regardless of contents, and FA will throw `NullReferenceException` (not a clean assertion failure) if `subject` is `null` and the `NotBeNull()` guard is omitted. Teams copy-paste the `HaveCount` pattern from documentation and accidentally set the bound to 0, making the assertion trivially true. WHY it causes problems: the assertion appears to be testing something meaningful but provides zero regression coverage; a code change that introduces an empty-collection bug passes the test without protest. Fix: always use a bound of at least 1 (`HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(1)`) for "not empty" intent; use `NotBeEmpty()` for the zero-tolerance variant which has a clear semantic name.

**`MockRepository.VerifyAll()` called in `IDisposable.Dispose` runs AFTER `IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync` in xUnit's teardown order — if `DisposeAsync` disposes a fixture-owned resource captured in a mock setup, `ObjectDisposedException` surfaces instead of the expected `MockException` [community]** — `IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync` runs before the test class's `Dispose()` in xUnit's teardown sequence. If a mock setup captures a fixture-owned resource (like a `DbConnection`) and `VerifyAll` triggers Moq's internal verification that references the captured resource, the disposed object throws `ObjectDisposedException` before `MockException` can surface the actual "setup was not called" failure. WHY it causes problems: developers see `ObjectDisposedException` in teardown, conclude there is a disposal ordering bug, and spend hours debugging what is actually an un-called mock setup masked by the disposal sequence. Fix: call `_repo.VerifyAll()` at the START of `IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync` (before any infrastructure teardown) rather than in `IDisposable.Dispose`, or explicitly call `VerifyAll()` at the end of each test method body so it runs before any teardown.

**`FakeTimeProvider.SetLocalTimeZone` in the `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` 9.x package does NOT update `GetLocalNow()` until a subsequent `SetUtcNow` call — the 10.x package fixed this, creating a cross-version behaviour difference that causes test failures on agents still targeting `net9.0` [community]** — In the 9.x package version, `GetLocalNow()` caches the zone conversion until `UtcNow` changes. Calling `SetLocalTimeZone(newZone)` without a follow-up `SetUtcNow(sameValue)` leaves `GetLocalNow()` returning a value converted with the old zone. Tests written on a .NET 10 development machine work correctly; running on CI targeting `net9.0` produces different assertion outcomes. WHY it causes problems: the failure is silent — the test passes on the developer's machine and fails in CI with a puzzling time-zone mismatch that does not mention package versions. Fix: always call `SetUtcNow` immediately after `SetLocalTimeZone`; add a code comment explaining the 9.x ordering requirement so future maintainers do not remove what looks like a redundant call.

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 38 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Capturing `TestContext.Current.CancellationToken` in a background task after the test body starts | `TestContext.Current` is null post-test; background task leaks resources without cancellation | Always capture the method-parameter `CancellationToken` before spawning background work |
| `Assert.Inconclusive` in tests decorated with `[Retry(n)]` expecting retries | `[Retry]` does not retry on `InconclusiveException`; gate silently passes without reaching assertions | Use `Assert.Fail` for environment-check failures that should be retried |
| Mutable `ResiliencePipelineBuilder` shared across parallel test class constructors | `Build()` not thread-safe; intermittent `InvalidOperationException` on high-core-count agents | Store the built `ResiliencePipeline` in a `static readonly` field, not the builder |
| `HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0)` as a "not empty" check | Always passes for any non-null collection; zero regression coverage | Use `NotBeEmpty()` or `HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(1)` depending on intent |
| `MockRepository.VerifyAll()` in `Dispose()` when fixture uses `IAsyncLifetime` | Fixture resources disposed before `VerifyAll` runs; `ObjectDisposedException` masks `MockException` | Call `VerifyAll()` at the START of `DisposeAsync` before any infrastructure teardown |
| `SetLocalTimeZone` without a follow-up `SetUtcNow` on `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` 9.x | Zone cache stale in 9.x package; silently wrong `GetLocalNow()` assertions on `net9.0` CI | Pair every `SetLocalTimeZone` call with an immediate `SetUtcNow`; document the ordering requirement |

## Cycle 39 — 2026-05-14

### xUnit v3 — `ITestOutputHelper` Structured Logging With `TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage` for CI-Friendly Diagnostics

xUnit v3 introduces `TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage(string)` as a companion to the classic `ITestOutputHelper.WriteLine` approach. While `ITestOutputHelper` routes to the test runner's output panel, `SendDiagnosticMessage` writes to xUnit's internal diagnostic sink — visible in verbose runner output and captured by CI systems that consume xUnit's XML report extensions. Using both together gives maximum observability: `ITestOutputHelper` for human-readable per-test logs, and `SendDiagnosticMessage` for structured diagnostic data that build tooling can parse. This is especially useful for flaky-test investigations where ambient state (thread pool size, memory pressure) needs to be captured alongside assertion outcomes. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Abstractions;

public class OrderPipelineTests(ITestOutputHelper output)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrder_UnderLoad_CompletesWithin200ms()
    {
        var sw = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.StartNew();
        var service = new OrderPipeline();

        await service.ProcessAsync(new Order { Id = 42, Quantity = 5 });
        sw.Stop();

        // Human-readable output for the test runner panel
        output.WriteLine($"Pipeline elapsed: {sw.ElapsedMilliseconds}ms");
        output.WriteLine($"ThreadPool threads available: {GetThreadPoolInfo()}");

        // Structured diagnostic data for CI tooling / xUnit diagnostic sink
        TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage(
            "PERF order_pipeline elapsed_ms={0} threadpool_available={1}",
            sw.ElapsedMilliseconds, GetThreadPoolInfo());

        Assert.True(sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < 200,
            $"Pipeline too slow: {sw.ElapsedMilliseconds}ms > 200ms threshold");
    }

    private static string GetThreadPoolInfo()
    {
        System.Threading.ThreadPool.GetAvailableThreads(out var wt, out var ct);
        return $"w:{wt},c:{ct}";
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `SendDiagnosticMessage` output is only visible when the xUnit runner is invoked with `--diagnostics` or in verbose mode; it is not shown by default. Teams that use Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions test summary pages will not see diagnostic messages unless they configure the runner flags. Use `ITestOutputHelper` for any message that must be readable without special flags, and `SendDiagnosticMessage` for machine-parseable telemetry that should not clutter the default output. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `Assert.That` With `Is.EqualTo(...).Within(tolerance)` for Floating-Point and DateTime Comparisons

NUnit 4's constraint model provides `Is.EqualTo(expected).Within(tolerance)` for comparing floating-point numbers and `DateTime`/`DateTimeOffset` values with a specified tolerance, replacing ad-hoc `Math.Abs(a - b) < epsilon` guards that are easy to get wrong and produce opaque failure messages. For `DateTime`, the tolerance can be expressed as a `TimeSpan` using the `.Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1))` fluent form, making assertions like "the record was created within one second of now" readable and robust. NUnit 4 extended this to `DateTimeOffset` natively, so tests no longer need to normalise offsets before asserting. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
public class PricingEngineTests
{
    [Test]
    public void CalculateDiscount_10PercentOff_ReturnsCorrectPrice()
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();
        double result = engine.ApplyDiscount(99.99, discountPercent: 10.0);

        // Tolerance for floating-point rounding — 0.001 is the epsilon
        Assert.That(result, Is.EqualTo(89.991).Within(0.001));
    }

    [Test]
    public void CreateOrder_Timestamp_IsRecentWithinOneSecond()
    {
        var service = new OrderService();
        DateTimeOffset before = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow;

        var order = service.CreateOrder(productId: 1, quantity: 2);

        // DateTimeOffset tolerance — handles sub-second clock drift
        Assert.That(order.CreatedAt,
            Is.EqualTo(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)));
        Assert.That(order.CreatedAt,
            Is.GreaterThanOrEqualTo(before));
    }

    [Test]
    public void ComputeScore_FuzzyMatch_ScoresAbove90Percent()
    {
        var matcher = new FuzzyMatcher();
        double score = matcher.Score("colour", "color");

        Assert.That(score, Is.InRange(0.90, 1.00));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Within` tolerance is semantically precise but requires the test author to choose a meaningful epsilon. Too tight a tolerance introduces brittleness (CI agents with different FPU modes may fail); too loose a tolerance masks real bugs. Document the chosen tolerance and its rationale in a comment. For currency calculations, avoid `double` entirely and use `decimal` with `Assert.That(result, Is.EqualTo(89.99m))` — exact decimal equality is correct for financial arithmetic. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[AssemblyInitialize]` / `[AssemblyCleanup]` With `async` for Shared Infrastructure Lifetime Management

MSTest v3 supports `async` on `[AssemblyInitialize]` and `[AssemblyCleanup]` methods, enabling shared async infrastructure (database containers, HTTP servers, message brokers) to be started once per test assembly and torn down cleanly. The pattern pairs an `AssemblyInitialize` method that starts and stores an infrastructure handle in a `static` field with an `AssemblyCleanup` that awaits disposal, mirroring xUnit's `IAssemblyFixture<T>` pattern but without requiring a separate fixture class. MSTest v3 also allows the `AssemblyInitialize` method to receive a `TestContext` argument for logging startup diagnostics. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using Testcontainers.PostgreSql;

[TestClass]
public sealed class AssemblyInfrastructure
{
    public static PostgreSqlContainer DbContainer { get; private set; } = null!;
    public static string ConnectionString          { get; private set; } = null!;

    [AssemblyInitialize]
    public static async Task InitAsync(TestContext context)
    {
        context.WriteLine("Starting PostgreSQL container...");
        DbContainer = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
            .WithDatabase("testdb")
            .Build();

        await DbContainer.StartAsync();
        ConnectionString = DbContainer.GetConnectionString();
        context.WriteLine($"Container ready: {ConnectionString}");

        // Run migrations once for the whole assembly
        await MigrationRunner.ApplyAsync(ConnectionString);
    }

    [AssemblyCleanup]
    public static async Task CleanupAsync()
    {
        if (DbContainer is not null)
            await DbContainer.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

[TestClass]
public class OrderRepositoryTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    public async Task SaveOrder_NewOrder_CanBeRetrieved()
    {
        var repo  = new OrderRepository(AssemblyInfrastructure.ConnectionString);
        var order = new Order { ProductId = 7, Quantity = 3 };

        var id = await repo.SaveAsync(order);
        var loaded = await repo.GetByIdAsync(id);

        Assert.IsNotNull(loaded);
        Assert.AreEqual(7, loaded.ProductId);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Assembly-scoped infrastructure dramatically reduces integration test suite runtime (one container start instead of one per class), but creates a shared-state risk: tests that mutate the database can interfere with each other unless each test either uses a transaction that rolls back or operates on isolated data (unique IDs per test run). Use `[AssemblyInitialize]` for read-heavy or schema-stable scenarios; use per-class `IAsyncLifetime` (xUnit) or per-test `[TestInitialize]` (MSTest) for mutation-heavy tests. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions v8 — `WithStrictOrdering()` Modifier on `BeEquivalentTo` for Ordered-Sequence Contracts

FluentAssertions v8's `BeEquivalentTo` compares collections by value equivalence but ignores element order by default. Calling `.WithStrictOrdering()` on the options lambda enforces that the actual and expected sequences match in exact positional order, converting a set-equality assertion into a sequence-equality assertion. This is critical for testing ordered outputs such as audit logs, event streams, sorted query results, and pipeline stage sequences where position carries meaning. The modifier is composable with other options like `Excluding(x => x.Timestamp)` so that order is enforced across all fields except ignored ones. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class EventStreamProcessorTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void ProcessEvents_MultipleTypes_OutputOrderMatchesInput()
    {
        var processor = new EventStreamProcessor();
        var input = new[]
        {
            new DomainEvent { Type = "OrderPlaced",   Seq = 1 },
            new DomainEvent { Type = "PaymentTaken",  Seq = 2 },
            new DomainEvent { Type = "OrderShipped",  Seq = 3 },
        };

        var result = processor.Process(input).ToList();

        result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
            new[]
            {
                new { Type = "OrderPlaced",  Seq = 1 },
                new { Type = "PaymentTaken", Seq = 2 },
                new { Type = "OrderShipped", Seq = 3 },
            },
            opts => opts
                .WithStrictOrdering()
                .Excluding(x => x.ProcessedAt)   // timestamp is non-deterministic
                .ExcludingMissingMembers());       // anonymous type only has Type + Seq
    }

    [Fact]
    public void SortedLeaderboard_ScoresAreDescending()
    {
        var board = new Leaderboard();
        board.AddEntry("Alice", 95);
        board.AddEntry("Bob",   88);
        board.AddEntry("Carol", 92);

        var entries = board.GetTopEntries(3);

        entries.Select(e => e.Score).Should()
            .BeInDescendingOrder("leaderboard must sort highest score first");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `WithStrictOrdering()` makes tests fragile if the underlying implementation changes ordering as a valid optimisation. Reserve it for cases where ordering is part of the public contract (e.g., `IOrderedQueryable`, sorted audit logs, FIFO queues). For unordered sets, the default behaviour of `BeEquivalentTo` is correct and more resilient to refactoring. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET — `WithWaitStrategy` Custom Health Checks for Non-Standard Container Readiness

Testcontainers.NET's default readiness detection (waiting for the exposed port to accept TCP connections) is insufficient for containers that accept connections before the application inside is fully initialised — a common issue with databases running post-start migrations, message brokers performing cluster formation, and HTTP services that return 503 during startup. `Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPath("/health").ForStatusCode(200))` waits for an HTTP health endpoint, while `UntilCommandIsCompleted("pg_isready", "-U", "postgres")` runs a shell probe inside the container. Combining multiple conditions with `.AddCustomWaitStrategy` provides a composable health check that survives slow-start containers in CI environments. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Containers;
using Xunit;

public class RabbitMqIntegrationTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly IContainer _rabbit;
    private const int ManagementPort = 15672;
    private const int AmqpPort       = 5672;

    public RabbitMqIntegrationTests()
    {
        _rabbit = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("rabbitmq:3.13-management-alpine")
            .WithPortBinding(AmqpPort,       AmqpPort)
            .WithPortBinding(ManagementPort, ManagementPort)
            .WithEnvironment("RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER", "guest")
            .WithEnvironment("RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS", "guest")
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                    .UntilPortIsAvailable(AmqpPort)
                    .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(req =>
                        req.ForPort(ManagementPort)
                           .ForPath("/api/healthchecks/node")
                           .ForStatusCode(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK)))
            .Build();
    }

    public async Task InitializeAsync() => await _rabbit.StartAsync();
    public async Task DisposeAsync()    => await _rabbit.DisposeAsync();

    [Fact]
    public async Task PublishAndConsume_SingleMessage_DeliveredWithCorrectBody()
    {
        var amqpUri = $"amqp://guest:guest@localhost:{_rabbit.GetMappedPublicPort(AmqpPort)}";
        var broker  = new MessageBroker(amqpUri);

        await broker.PublishAsync("test-queue", "hello-world");
        var received = await broker.ConsumeNextAsync("test-queue",
            timeout: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));

        Assert.Equal("hello-world", received);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded` is only appropriate when the container exposes an HTTP health endpoint. For containers without one, use `UntilCommandIsCompleted` to run a native readiness probe. Both strategies add seconds to test startup; measure the overhead and prefer `WithReuse(true)` in local developer inner loops (without health-check re-evaluation) while retaining full wait strategies in CI where containers start cold. [official]

---

### C# 13 — `allows ref struct` Generic Constraint for Zero-Allocation Test Helpers

C# 13 introduced the `allows ref struct` generic anti-constraint, enabling generic methods and types to accept `ref struct` type arguments (like `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and custom `ref struct` types) that were previously blocked from generics entirely. In test helpers, this unlocks zero-allocation assertion utilities that operate on spans without boxing or intermediate array allocations. A generic `AssertSpanEqual<T>` helper using `allows ref struct` can replace per-type overloads for `byte`, `char`, and `int` span comparisons, reducing test helper boilerplate while maintaining maximum performance. [official]

```csharp
using System;
using Xunit;

// Generic zero-allocation span assertion helper — requires C# 13 / .NET 9+
public static class SpanAssert
{
    public static void Equal<T>(
        ReadOnlySpan<T> expected,
        ReadOnlySpan<T> actual,
        string? message = null)
        where T : IEquatable<T>
    {
        if (!expected.SequenceEqual(actual))
        {
            var msg = message
                ?? $"Spans differ. Expected length={expected.Length}, actual length={actual.Length}.";
            throw new Xunit.Sdk.XunitException(msg);
        }
    }
}

// Test using the helper — no heap allocations for the span slices
public class FrameSerialiserTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Serialise_KnownFrame_ProducesExpectedBytes()
    {
        Span<byte> output = stackalloc byte[16];
        var serialiser    = new FrameSerialiser();

        serialiser.Serialise(new Frame { Id = 1, Payload = 0xCAFE }, output);

        ReadOnlySpan<byte> expected = [0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0xFE, 0xCA, 0x00, 0x00];
        SpanAssert.Equal(expected, output[..8], "Frame header bytes mismatch");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void RoundTrip_CharSpan_PreservesContent()
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<char> original = "hello world".AsSpan();
        Span<char> buffer           = stackalloc char[original.Length];

        original.CopyTo(buffer);
        var reversed = new string(buffer.ToArray().Reverse().ToArray());

        SpanAssert.Equal<char>("dlrow olleh".AsSpan(), reversed.AsSpan());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `allows ref struct` is available only from C# 13 (shipped with .NET 9). Projects targeting `net8.0` or earlier cannot use it. When cross-targeting, define the `allows ref struct` overload in a `#if NET9_0_OR_GREATER` block and provide a fallback that accepts `T[]` for older targets. The primary benefit is eliminating `ToArray()` calls in hot-path assertion helpers; for most test helpers the allocation is negligible and the portability cost is not worth it. [official]

---

### FluentAssertions v8 — `MatchRegex` and `NotMatchRegex` for Pattern-Based String Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 provides `MatchRegex(string pattern)` and `NotMatchRegex(string pattern)` for asserting that strings conform to or violate a regular expression pattern, replacing manual `Regex.IsMatch` calls in `Assert.True` which produce opaque failure messages. The methods support both .NET `Regex` patterns (string overload) and pre-compiled `Regex` objects (for performance-sensitive assertion helpers called thousands of times across a test suite). Combining `MatchRegex` with `And` chaining allows multiple constraints in one readable expression: `.Should().StartWith("ORD-").And.MatchRegex(@"^ORD-\d{6}$")`. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using Xunit;

public partial class OrderIdGeneratorTests
{
    [GeneratedRegex(@"^ORD-\d{6}-[A-Z]{3}$")]
    private static partial Regex OrderIdPattern();

    [Fact]
    public void GenerateOrderId_StandardInput_MatchesExpectedFormat()
    {
        var generator = new OrderIdGenerator();
        string orderId = generator.Generate(region: "EUR");

        orderId.Should()
            .NotBeNullOrEmpty()
            .And.StartWith("ORD-")
            .And.MatchRegex(OrderIdPattern(),
                because: "order IDs must follow the ORD-######-AAA format for downstream routing");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void SanitiseInput_UserSuppliedString_ContainsNoSqlKeywords()
    {
        var sanitiser = new InputSanitiser();
        string result = sanitiser.Sanitise("'; DROP TABLE orders; --");

        result.Should()
            .NotMatchRegex(@"(?i)(DROP|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|TRUNCATE|ALTER)\s+",
                because: "sanitised input must not contain SQL DDL/DML keywords");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void FormatEmail_ValidAddress_PassesRfcPattern()
    {
        var formatter = new EmailFormatter();
        string email  = formatter.Normalise("  User@Example.COM  ");

        email.Should().MatchRegex(
            @"^[a-z0-9._%+\-]+@[a-z0-9.\-]+\.[a-z]{2,}$",
            because: "normalised email must be lowercase with no surrounding whitespace");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Pre-compiled `Regex` objects (via `[GeneratedRegex]` in C# 11+) avoid repeated pattern compilation in test suites with large `[Theory]` datasets. For one-off assertions, the string overload is fine. Overly complex regex patterns in tests are a maintenance liability — if the pattern becomes hard to read, extract it to a named constant with a comment, or replace the regex assertion with a dedicated parsing test that validates individual components. [official]

---

### Moq — `SetupSequence<T>` for Stateful Multi-Call Mock Behaviour

Moq's `SetupSequence<T>` configures a mock to return different values or throw different exceptions on successive calls to the same method, modelling stateful external dependencies such as circuit-breaker state machines, retry-affected APIs, or paginated data sources. Unlike stacking multiple `Setup` calls (which overwrite each other), `SetupSequence` chains behaviours in order: first call returns value A, second returns value B, third throws an exception. This removes the need for stateful counter fields in test classes and makes the call sequence explicitly declarative. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public class RetryableApiClientTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FetchData_TransientFailuresThenSuccess_ReturnsDataAfterRetries()
    {
        var mockApi = new Mock<IExternalApi>();

        // Call 1: transient 503, Call 2: transient 503, Call 3: success
        mockApi.SetupSequence(api => api.GetStatusAsync())
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503 Service Unavailable"))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503 Service Unavailable"))
            .ReturnsAsync(new ApiStatus { IsHealthy = true, Version = "2.1.0" });

        var client = new RetryableApiClient(mockApi.Object, maxRetries: 3);

        var result = await client.FetchStatusWithRetryAsync();

        Assert.True(result.IsHealthy);
        Assert.Equal("2.1.0", result.Version);
        mockApi.Verify(api => api.GetStatusAsync(), Times.Exactly(3));
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PaginatedFetch_MultiplePages_AggregatesTotalResults()
    {
        var mockRepo = new Mock<IPagedRepository>();

        mockRepo.SetupSequence(r => r.GetPageAsync(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<int>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(new Page<Product>
            {
                Items = [new Product { Id = 1 }, new Product { Id = 2 }],
                HasMore = true
            })
            .ReturnsAsync(new Page<Product>
            {
                Items = [new Product { Id = 3 }],
                HasMore = false
            });

        var aggregator = new PagedAggregator(mockRepo.Object);
        var all        = await aggregator.FetchAllAsync(pageSize: 2);

        Assert.Equal(3, all.Count);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `SetupSequence` only tracks call order per-sequence; concurrent calls from multiple threads can interleave responses in non-deterministic order. For async-parallel tests, use a thread-safe counter or a `ConcurrentQueue<T>` in a callback lambda instead. When the sequence grows beyond 4-5 steps, the test becomes hard to follow — extract the setup into a named helper method or consider using a fake object (hand-written stub) that makes the state machine explicit. [official]

---

### .NET 9 — `System.Net.Http.Json` Extensions With `JsonTypeInfo<T>` for Source-Generated Deserialization in Integration Tests

.NET 9 extended `HttpClient.GetFromJsonAsync<T>` and related methods with overloads that accept `JsonTypeInfo<T>` from System.Text.Json's source generation, eliminating reflection-based deserialization in integration tests that use `WebApplicationFactory`. Passing the source-generated type info produces AOT-compatible, trim-safe deserialization that also runs faster in test suites with large response payloads. In combination with `[JsonSerializable]` on a `JsonSerializerContext`, this pattern lets integration tests use the same serializer metadata as the production app, ensuring that tests catch serialization contract mismatches at the type level rather than at runtime. [official]

```csharp
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using Xunit;

// Source-generated serializer context — matches what the API uses in production
[JsonSerializable(typeof(OrderResponse))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(ErrorResponse))]
[JsonSourceGenerationOptions(PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonKnownNamingPolicy.CamelCase)]
internal partial class TestSerializerContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

public class OrdersApiIntegrationTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task PostOrder_ValidPayload_Returns201WithOrderId()
    {
        var client  = factory.CreateClient();
        var payload = new { productId = 7, quantity = 2 };

        var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/api/orders", payload,
            TestSerializerContext.Default.Object);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.Created, response.StatusCode);

        // Deserialize with source-generated type info — no reflection
        var order = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync(
            TestSerializerContext.Default.OrderResponse);

        Assert.NotNull(order);
        Assert.True(order.OrderId > 0);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrder_NonExistent_Returns404WithProblemDetails()
    {
        var client   = factory.CreateClient();
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/orders/99999");

        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.NotFound, response.StatusCode);

        var error = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync(
            TestSerializerContext.Default.ErrorResponse);

        Assert.NotNull(error);
        Assert.Equal("Order not found", error.Message);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Source-generated serialization requires all response types to be declared in the `JsonSerializerContext` at compile time. For exploratory integration tests with ad-hoc response shapes, anonymous types with `JsonDocument.Parse` are more ergonomic. The performance gain matters primarily for property-based or load tests that deserialize thousands of responses; for typical integration test suites the difference is negligible. The main benefit is contract safety: the compiler enforces that the type matches what the generator emits. [official]

---

### NUnit 4 — `TestExecutionContext.CurrentContext.CurrentTest.Properties` for Runtime Test Metadata Access

NUnit 4 exposes `TestExecutionContext.CurrentContext.CurrentTest.Properties` as a dictionary accessible from within a test body, helper utilities, and custom constraints, enabling test-aware logging, conditional skip logic, and tracing without injecting `TestContext` through every helper method call stack. This is useful in shared assertion helpers that need to emit the current test name into a diagnostic log without receiving it as a parameter. The `Properties` dictionary also carries custom values from `[Property("key", "value")]` attributes, letting tests declare metadata (environment tier, feature flag, owner) that infrastructure helpers can read at runtime. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

// Shared helper that reads test metadata without a parameter
public static class DiagnosticLogger
{
    public static void Log(string message)
    {
        var ctx      = TestExecutionContext.CurrentContext;
        var testName = ctx.CurrentTest.FullName;
        var category = ctx.CurrentTest.Properties.ContainsKey("Category")
            ? ctx.CurrentTest.Properties.Get("Category")?.ToString() ?? "uncategorised"
            : "uncategorised";

        Console.WriteLine(
            $"[{DateTime.UtcNow:HH:mm:ss.fff}] [{category}] {testName}: {message}");
    }
}

[TestFixture]
[Property("Owner", "payments-team")]
public class PaymentGatewayTests
{
    [Test]
    [Category("Integration")]
    [Property("Feature", "3DS")]
    public async Task Charge_3DsRequired_RedirectsToChallengePage()
    {
        DiagnosticLogger.Log("Starting 3DS charge test");

        var gateway = new PaymentGateway(new FakeAcquirer(require3ds: true));
        var result  = await gateway.ChargeAsync(new ChargeRequest
        {
            Amount    = 150_00,
            Currency  = "GBP",
            CardToken = "tok_3ds_required"
        });

        DiagnosticLogger.Log($"Charge result: {result.Status}");

        Assert.That(result.Status, Is.EqualTo(ChargeStatus.RedirectRequired));
        Assert.That(result.RedirectUrl, Does.StartWith("https://3ds.bank.example.com/"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TestExecutionContext.CurrentContext` is thread-static and works correctly in single-threaded and async test bodies. Accessing it from a background `Task.Run` or `Thread` that is not the test-owning thread returns `null` or an unrelated context. Do not capture the context at class construction time; access it fresh within the test method or `[SetUp]`. Prefer passing `TestContext` as an explicit parameter to deeply nested helpers in complex async pipelines to avoid the hidden ambient-state dependency. [official]

---

### MSTest v3 — `[Timeout]` Attribute With `CancellationToken` Parameter for Deterministic Test Cancellation

MSTest v3 allows `[Timeout(milliseconds)]` to be combined with test methods that accept a `CancellationToken` parameter. When the timeout elapses the runner cancels the token and the test method can observe the cancellation cooperatively, enabling clean async teardown inside the test body instead of an abrupt thread abort. This is superior to the legacy thread-abort model (MSTest v1/v2) where a timeout caused `ThreadAbortException` that could leave resources in inconsistent states. Explicit `CancellationToken` propagation through the test also ensures that async operations (HTTP calls, database queries) are cancelled promptly rather than waiting for socket timeouts. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Threading;

[TestClass]
public class DataSyncServiceTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(5000)]  // 5-second hard wall clock limit
    public async Task SyncAsync_LargeDataset_CompletesBeforeTimeout(
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var syncService = new DataSyncService(new FakeDataSource(recordCount: 10_000));

        try
        {
            // Token is cancelled by MSTest when the 5s timeout elapses
            await syncService.SyncAsync(cancellationToken);

            // Verify result only if sync completed within budget
            Assert.IsTrue(syncService.SyncedCount > 0,
                "Sync must process at least one record");
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) when (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            // Cooperative cancellation — log diagnostic then fail explicitly
            Assert.Fail(
                $"DataSyncService.SyncAsync timed out after 5000ms. " +
                $"Records synced before cancellation: {syncService.SyncedCount}");
        }
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(2000)]
    public async Task NotifySubscribers_CancellationDuringBroadcast_DisposesCleanly(
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var notifier  = new SubscriberNotifier(new FakeChannel());
        using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(cancellationToken);

        // Cancel after first notification to test mid-operation cleanup
        cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));

        await Assert.ThrowsExceptionAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            () => notifier.BroadcastAsync("test-event", cts.Token));

        Assert.IsTrue(notifier.IsDisposed, "Notifier must self-dispose on cancellation");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[Timeout]` with `CancellationToken` requires the test method to propagate the token to all async callees. Tests that create fire-and-forget tasks without passing the token may still exceed the timeout because the tasks are not cancelled. Always propagate the token; treat it as mandatory for any I/O-bound test. The timeout value should be at least 3-5x the expected execution time to avoid flakiness on loaded CI agents. [official]

---

### Testcontainers.NET — `INetwork` With `WithNetwork` for Service-Discovery Testing in Multi-Container Setups

Testcontainers.NET's `INetwork` API creates a Docker network that multiple containers join, enabling containers to reach each other by service name rather than localhost ports. This mirrors Docker Compose service discovery, allowing integration tests to exercise actual inter-service name resolution (as happens in Kubernetes pods) rather than `localhost`-only connections that hide network-configuration bugs. A test that stands up an API container and a PostgreSQL container on the same `INetwork` can configure the API with `Server=db;Port=5432` — the real hostname the production environment uses — instead of `localhost:54321`. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Containers;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Networks;
using Xunit;

public class ApiWithDatabaseNetworkTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly INetwork   _network;
    private readonly IContainer _apiContainer;
    private readonly IContainer _dbContainer;
    private const    string     DbAlias = "db";
    private const    int        ApiPort = 8080;

    public ApiWithDatabaseNetworkTests()
    {
        _network = new NetworkBuilder()
            .WithName($"test-net-{Guid.NewGuid():N}")
            .Build();

        _dbContainer = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithNetworkAliases(DbAlias)
            .WithDatabase("orders")
            .Build();

        _apiContainer = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("myorg/orders-api:latest")
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithEnvironment("DB_CONNECTION",
                $"Host={DbAlias};Database=orders;Username=postgres;Password=postgres")
            .WithPortBinding(ApiPort, ApiPort)
            .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r =>
                    r.ForPath("/health")
                     .ForStatusCode(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK)))
            .Build();
    }

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _network.CreateAsync();
        await _dbContainer.StartAsync();
        await _apiContainer.StartAsync();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _apiContainer.DisposeAsync();
        await _dbContainer.DisposeAsync();
        await _network.DeleteAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_ApiAndDbOnSameNetwork_PersistsAndReturns201()
    {
        using var client = new System.Net.Http.HttpClient();
        var apiBase      = $"http://localhost:{_apiContainer.GetMappedPublicPort(ApiPort)}";
        var payload      = new StringContent(
            "{\"productId\":1,\"qty\":2}",
            System.Text.Encoding.UTF8,
            "application/json");

        var response = await client.PostAsync($"{apiBase}/api/orders", payload);

        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.Created, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Docker user-defined networks require Docker Engine 1.10+ and are not available in all CI environments (some GitHub Actions runners use Docker-in-Docker with limited network capabilities). Verify that the CI Docker daemon supports user-defined bridge networks before adopting this pattern. The setup cost is higher than single-container tests; use this pattern only when service-discovery behaviour itself is under test. For pure database-backed API tests where port mapping is sufficient, `WebApplicationFactory` with Testcontainers remains simpler. [official]

---

### .NET 10 — `Task.WhenEach` for Ordered Async Result Assertions in Integration Tests

.NET 10 introduces `Task.WhenEach(IEnumerable<Task<T>>)` which returns an `IAsyncEnumerable<Task<T>>` that yields each task as it completes (in completion order, not submission order). Integration tests that launch multiple concurrent async operations and need to assert on each result as it arrives — rather than waiting for all to complete via `WhenAll` — can use `WhenEach` to stream results and apply per-result assertions inline. This is particularly useful for testing pub-sub brokers, streaming APIs, and parallel worker queues where the first-failure signal matters more than a fully-aggregated report. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class ParallelWorkerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessJobs_FiveJobs_AllCompleteWithSuccessStatus()
    {
        var worker = new ParallelJobWorker(concurrency: 3);
        var jobs   = Enumerable.Range(1, 5)
            .Select(id => new Job { Id = id, Payload = $"data-{id}" })
            .ToList();

        // Launch all jobs concurrently
        var tasks = jobs.Select(j => worker.ProcessAsync(j)).ToList();

        var completedCount = 0;
        var failedIds      = new List<int>();

        // WhenEach yields results as they complete — no need to wait for all
        await foreach (var completedTask in Task.WhenEach(tasks))
        {
            var result = await completedTask;  // already completed; await just unwraps
            completedCount++;

            if (result.Status != JobStatus.Success)
                failedIds.Add(result.JobId);

            // Incremental assertion — surfaces first failure immediately
            Assert.Equal(JobStatus.Success, result.Status);
        }

        Assert.Equal(5, completedCount);
        Assert.Empty(failedIds);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task StreamingPipeline_ThreeStages_EachStageProducesOutput()
    {
        var pipeline = new ThreeStageProcessor();
        var stageTasks = new[]
        {
            pipeline.RunStageAsync("input-alpha"),
            pipeline.RunStageAsync("input-beta"),
            pipeline.RunStageAsync("input-gamma"),
        };

        var results = new List<StageResult>();
        await foreach (var t in Task.WhenEach(stageTasks))
        {
            var r = await t;
            results.Add(r);
            Assert.NotEmpty(r.Output);
        }

        Assert.Equal(3, results.Count);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Task.WhenEach` is a .NET 10 API; it is not available on `net9.0` or earlier. For `net8.0` / `net9.0` compatibility, use Stephen Cleary's `TaskExtensions.WhenEach` from `Nito.AsyncEx` or implement the pattern manually with `Task.WhenAny` in a loop. Asserting on results inside the `await foreach` body produces a failure at the first bad result, which is ideal for fast feedback but loses visibility of how many other results were also bad. When all failures matter, collect results first and assert on the collection. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 39

**xUnit v3 `[Theory]` rows that share a mutable reference type as `[MemberData]` can cause cross-row state pollution when the SUT mutates the input object, making later rows fail with corrupted data from earlier rows [community]** — `[MemberData]` returns an `IEnumerable<object[]>` and xUnit materialises the full sequence before dispatching rows. If the sequence yields the SAME object instance across multiple rows (e.g., a shared `List<T>` is yielded directly rather than cloned), and the SUT mutates that list, subsequent rows receive the already-mutated object rather than the original test data. WHY it causes problems: the pattern is common when converting existing `[InlineData]` to `[MemberData]` for complex types; developers copy the `static IEnumerable<object[]>` pattern from documentation that uses value types, which are implicitly copied, and do not add cloning for reference types. Fix: yield `new` instances in `[MemberData]` or use record `with` expressions to snapshot-copy complex test-data objects per row.

**NUnit 4 `OneTimeSetUp` in a base class runs BEFORE the derived class's `OneTimeSetUp`, but `OneTimeTearDown` runs in REVERSE order — derived first, base last — creating an asymmetric lifecycle that causes "use after dispose" bugs when the base class tears down shared infrastructure that the derived class's `OneTimeTearDown` still references [community]** — Teams that store a shared `HttpClient` or database connection in a base class `OneTimeSetUp` and dispose it in the base class `OneTimeTearDown` are surprised when the derived class `OneTimeTearDown` throws `ObjectDisposedException` accessing the base's resource. NUnit's teardown order mirrors the constructor/destructor pattern: last initialised, first torn down. WHY it causes problems: the symmetric mental model (both setUp and tearDown run in the same order) is intuitive but wrong; the NUnit documentation describes the order but it is easy to miss. Fix: dispose resources only in the class that created them; if a derived class needs shared resources from the base, store disposal responsibility in the derived class or use `IDisposable` on the resource itself so it is safe to call `Dispose` multiple times.

**`HttpClient` created via `WebApplicationFactory.CreateClient()` follows redirects by default — meaning tests that assert `301`/`302` responses receive `200 OK` instead, causing a "200 is not 301" failure message that makes developers assume the redirect is broken when in fact the client followed it [community]** — `WebApplicationFactory.CreateClient()` sets `AllowAutoRedirect = true` by default. A test that calls `client.GetAsync("/old-path")` and asserts `StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.MovedPermanently` actually receives the redirected page's `200 OK`. WHY it causes problems: the default value follows redirects, so developers who write "I want to see the redirect response" tests do not realise they need to opt-out. The failure message "Expected 301, got 200" looks like a routing bug, not a client configuration issue. Fix: use `factory.CreateClient(new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions { AllowAutoRedirect = false })` for any test that needs to observe redirect responses before the final destination.

**`Moq` `Setup` calls on a `Mock<T>` where `T` is a class (not an interface) silently succeed even when the target method is NOT virtual, causing the mock to call the real implementation instead of the configured stub — the test passes or fails for the wrong reason [community]** — When mocking a concrete class, Moq can only override `virtual` and `abstract` members. A `Setup` call on a non-virtual method compiles without error and registers the configuration, but at runtime Moq invokes the real method because it cannot intercept the call. The configured return value is never used. WHY it causes problems: the test may pass accidentally (the real method returns the expected value by chance) or fail with an unrelated error from the real implementation, and there is no warning or exception from Moq. Fix: prefer mocking interfaces; when mocking classes is unavoidable, mark all methods under test as `virtual`. Enable `MockBehavior.Strict` to surface un-invoked setups eagerly.

**`FluentAssertions` `BeEquivalentTo` with `IncludingAllRuntimeProperties()` on an EF Core entity proxy includes navigation-property backing fields that are in an uninitialised `null` state, causing the equivalence check to fail even when the logical content matches the expected object [community]** — EF Core creates dynamic proxy subclasses for entities with lazy loading enabled. These proxies add backing fields for virtual navigation properties. When `BeEquivalentTo` uses `IncludingAllRuntimeProperties()` it reflects on the proxy type's fields — including the proxy-injected backing fields — and compares them against the plain entity's fields, which do not exist. WHY it causes problems: the failure message mentions an internal EF Core proxy field name that does not appear in the source entity class; developers spend time investigating a field they never defined. Fix: use `.Excluding(x => x.SomeNavigation)` for navigation properties, or `ExcludingMissingMembers()` to align actual-vs-expected structural comparison without requiring both sides to have identical member sets.

**`Testcontainers.NET` containers using `WithCleanUp(true)` (the Ryuk resource reaper) are NOT cleaned up when the test process is killed with `SIGKILL` because Ryuk depends on an orderly TCP keepalive close that `SIGKILL` bypasses, leaving orphaned containers that block subsequent CI jobs with port-in-use errors [community]** — Ryuk, the resource reaper container spawned by Testcontainers, monitors a TCP keepalive connection to the test process. When the test process exits cleanly the connection closes orderly, triggering Ryuk to remove all labelled containers. `SIGKILL` bypasses orderly close: the kernel reclaims file descriptors, Ryuk's keepalive may remain in `CLOSE_WAIT` for minutes, and labelled containers persist until Ryuk's own timeout fires (default: 60s). WHY it causes problems: flaky port-in-use errors appear on CI jobs that follow OOM-killed test jobs, but the root cause is never the current job. Fix: add explicit container label cleanup in CI post-job scripts (`docker ps -q --filter "label=org.testcontainers" | xargs docker rm -f`), or configure Testcontainers to reuse containers (`WithReuse(true)`) so that leftover containers are reused rather than causing conflicts.

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 39 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Yielding the same mutable reference instance across `[MemberData]` rows | SUT mutations in one row corrupt subsequent rows; non-deterministic failures | Yield `new` instances per row or clone with `record with {}` expressions |
| Base-class `OneTimeTearDown` disposes resource referenced in derived-class `OneTimeTearDown` | NUnit tears down derived before base; derived code accesses already-disposed resource | Dispose only in the class that created the resource; make resources safe for multiple `Dispose` calls |
| `WebApplicationFactory.CreateClient()` for 3xx redirect assertion tests | Default `AllowAutoRedirect = true` follows redirect; test sees `200` not `301`/`302` | Use `new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions { AllowAutoRedirect = false }` |
| `Moq.Setup` on a non-virtual method of a concrete class | Setup silently ignored; real method called instead of stub; no Moq warning | Mock interfaces; mark concrete methods `virtual`; use `MockBehavior.Strict` |
| `BeEquivalentTo(IncludingAllRuntimeProperties())` on EF Core lazy-load proxies | Proxy backing fields not present in expected POCO; assertion fails on phantom members | Use `Excluding(x => x.Nav)` or `ExcludingMissingMembers()` for navigation properties |
| Relying on Ryuk to clean Testcontainers after OOM-killed test runners | `SIGKILL` bypasses orderly TCP close; orphaned containers block next CI jobs | Add Docker label-based cleanup in CI post-job hook; use `WithReuse(true)` on dev machines |
