## Cycle 40 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 1 — xUnit v3 `[ClassData]` With `TheoryDataRow<T>` Skip and Label Metadata for Conditional Theory Rows

xUnit v3 adds `TheoryDataRow<T>` (and its multi-parameter overloads) as a first-class row descriptor that can carry a `Skip` reason string and a `Label` for display purposes. This lets a single `[ClassData]` provider mark individual rows as conditionally skipped (e.g., a row that requires an OS feature) without conditional compilation or runtime `Skip.If` workarounds. The `Label` property sets the display name shown in the test runner and in CI reports, replacing the fragile `ToString()` override previously needed on custom theory data objects. Rows that carry a non-null `Skip` value are reported as skipped with the provided reason rather than as failures, which is important for test-suite health metrics. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public class HashAlgorithmData : TheoryData<string, byte[], string>
{
    public HashAlgorithmData()
    {
        // Normal row — will run always
        Add(new TheoryDataRow<string, byte[], string>("MD5", new byte[] { 0x48, 0x65 }, "b80bb7740288fda1f201890375a60c8f")
        {
            Label = "MD5 basic hash"
        });

        // Row skipped on non-Windows — skip reason surfaces in CI report
        Add(new TheoryDataRow<string, byte[], string>("CNG-SHA256", new byte[] { 0x48, 0x65 }, "expected-hash")
        {
            Label = "CNG-SHA256 (Windows only)",
            Skip = !OperatingSystem.IsWindows() ? "CNG not available on this OS" : null
        });

        // Row with explicit label for readability in test explorer
        Add(new TheoryDataRow<string, byte[], string>("SHA512", new byte[] { 0x48, 0x65 }, "expected-sha512")
        {
            Label = "SHA512 two-byte input"
        });
    }
}

public class HashProviderTests
{
    [Theory]
    [ClassData(typeof(HashAlgorithmData))]
    public void ComputeHash_ReturnsExpectedHex(string algorithm, byte[] input, string expectedHex)
    {
        var provider = new HashProvider();
        string result = provider.ComputeHex(algorithm, input);
        Assert.Equal(expectedHex, result, ignoreCase: true);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TheoryDataRow<T>` with `Skip` is ideal when test data requires runtime capabilities (OS features, hardware instructions, network access) that are not uniformly available across all CI matrix legs. The tradeoff is that the skip logic runs inside the data provider rather than inside the test method, so it cannot access injected services or test fixtures. For skips that need runtime infrastructure checks, use xUnit v3's `[SkipUnless]` attribute instead. The `Label` property has no equivalent in xUnit v2 — migration requires updating the data provider class. [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — NUnit 4 `Assert.Multiple` With `TestDelegate` for Bulk Soft-Assertion Blocks

NUnit 4 `Assert.Multiple` accepts a `TestDelegate` block and defers all assertion failures within it until the block exits, then reports them all together rather than stopping at the first failure. This is NUnit's soft-assertion API and matches the semantics of FluentAssertions `AssertionScope` and xUnit v3 `Assert.Multiple`. Using it eliminates the pattern of using a single large string message to pack multiple assertions into one call. NUnit 4 extended `Assert.Multiple` to support `async` delegates via `Assert.MultipleAsync`, which awaits the `AsyncTestDelegate` before collecting failures — critical for async property assertions. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
public class UserProfileTests
{
    [Test]
    public async Task UpdateProfile_AllFieldsChanged_AllFieldsReflectedInResponse()
    {
        var service = new UserProfileService();
        var request = new UpdateProfileRequest
        {
            DisplayName = "Alice Smith",
            Email       = "alice@example.com",
            Timezone    = "America/New_York",
            AvatarUrl   = "https://example.com/avatars/alice.png"
        };

        var response = await service.UpdateAsync(userId: 42, request);

        // Collect ALL failures — test does not stop at first mismatch
        Assert.Multiple(() =>
        {
            Assert.That(response.DisplayName, Is.EqualTo("Alice Smith"));
            Assert.That(response.Email,       Is.EqualTo("alice@example.com"));
            Assert.That(response.Timezone,    Is.EqualTo("America/New_York"));
            Assert.That(response.AvatarUrl,   Does.StartWith("https://"));
            Assert.That(response.UpdatedAt,   Is.GreaterThan(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddSeconds(-5)));
        });
    }

    [Test]
    public async Task UpdateProfile_InvalidEmail_ValidationErrorsContainEmailField()
    {
        var service = new UserProfileService();

        // Async soft-assertion block — awaits before collecting failures
        await Assert.MultipleAsync(async () =>
        {
            var ex = Assert.ThrowsAsync<ValidationException>(
                () => service.UpdateAsync(1, new UpdateProfileRequest { Email = "not-an-email" }));
            Assert.That(ex, Is.Not.Null);
            Assert.That(ex!.Errors, Does.ContainKey("Email"));
        });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Assert.Multiple` improves failure feedback bandwidth — one test run reveals all mismatches rather than only the first. The cost is test complexity: a long `Multiple` block becomes a wall of assertions that is hard to scan. Keep blocks focused on a single logical concern (e.g., all fields of one response object). Avoid mixing arrange and assert inside the block — failures in setup code inside the delegate produce confusing "assertion in setup" errors. For very large objects, prefer `BeEquivalentTo` (FluentAssertions) or a helper method that builds a descriptive failure string. [official]

---

### Pattern 3 — MSTest v3 `[DynamicData]` With `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` and Custom Display Names for Parameterised Test Readability

MSTest v3 `[DynamicData]` supports `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` to source test rows from a static method rather than a property, which allows the source to accept a `MethodInfo` argument for generic resolution. Pairing this with `DynamicDataDisplayName` points to a static method that receives the current row data and returns a human-readable test name, replacing the default `TestMethod (row 0)` naming that makes CI failure logs unreadable. MSTest v3 also introduced `DynamicDataDisplayNameDeclaringType` to locate the display-name method in a separate class, useful for shared naming utilities across test assemblies. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Reflection;

[TestClass]
public class CurrencyConverterTests
{
    // Data source method — returns IEnumerable<object[]>
    public static IEnumerable<object[]> ConversionScenarios()
    {
        yield return new object[] { "USD", "EUR", 100m, 92.50m, 0.01m };
        yield return new object[] { "GBP", "USD", 50m,  63.25m, 0.01m };
        yield return new object[] { "JPY", "USD", 1000m, 6.72m, 0.01m };
    }

    // Display-name method signature: (MethodInfo, object[]) => string
    public static string GetTestDisplayName(MethodInfo method, object[] row)
        => $"{method.Name}: {row[0]}->{row[1]} {row[2]} units";

    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(
        nameof(ConversionScenarios),
        DynamicDataSourceType.Method,
        DynamicDataDisplayName        = nameof(GetTestDisplayName))]
    public void Convert_KnownRates_ProducesExpectedAmount(
        string from, string to, decimal amount, decimal expected, decimal tolerance)
    {
        var converter = new CurrencyConverter(RateSource.Fixed);
        decimal result = converter.Convert(from, to, amount);

        Assert.AreEqual((double)expected, (double)result,
            delta: (double)tolerance,
            message: $"Convert {from}->{to} {amount}: got {result}, expected {expected}±{tolerance}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` is more flexible than `Property` because methods can compute rows lazily and accept generic type resolution. The `DynamicDataDisplayName` callback dramatically improves test-explorer and CI readability. The cost is verbosity: three attributes and two helper methods for what `[InlineData]` / `[DataRow]` covers in one line. Reserve this pattern for complex scenarios where the inputs are too large for inline literals, or where the data is sourced from an external resource (CSV, JSON, database). When rows exceed ~10 entries, prefer a separate `[ClassData]` class for clear ownership. [official]

---

### Pattern 4 — FluentAssertions v8 `AndConstraint` Chaining With `Which` for Nested Property Assertion Chains

FluentAssertions v8 `Which` accessor exposes the subject after a constraint-narrowing assertion, enabling deep assertion chains without assigning intermediate values. For example, after `.Should().ContainSingle(x => x.Id == 1)` the `.Which` property is the matched element, so further assertions on its properties can be expressed fluently on the same line. This eliminates the pattern of assigning `var item = collection.Single(x => x.Id == 1)` before asserting, keeping the assertion chain semantically connected. The `Which` accessor is lazy — it only materialises the subject when used — so the assertion failure message always references the correct narrowed subject. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class OrderSearchTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Search_ByCustomerId_ReturnsSingleMatchWithCorrectTotals()
    {
        var repo = new OrderRepository(TestDatabase.Seed());

        var results = repo.SearchByCustomer(customerId: 7);

        // ContainSingle narrows to the matched element via .Which
        results.Should().ContainSingle(o => o.CustomerId == 7)
            .Which.Should().BeEquivalentTo(new
            {
                CustomerId    = 7,
                Status        = OrderStatus.Confirmed,
                LineItemCount = 3
            }, opts => opts.ExcludingMissingMembers());
    }

    [Fact]
    public void GetInvoice_ForConfirmedOrder_HasNonNullPdfUrl()
    {
        var service = new InvoiceService();
        var invoice = service.GenerateFor(orderId: 101);

        // Chained: assert non-null, then assert on the unwrapped value via Which
        invoice.Should().NotBeNull()
            .And.Subject.PdfUrl.Should().StartWith("https://")
            .And.EndWith(".pdf");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void GetActiveUsers_ReturnsOnly_ActiveStatusUsers()
    {
        var userService = new UserService();
        var users = userService.GetActive();

        users.Should().AllSatisfy(u =>
            u.Status.Should().Be(UserStatus.Active));
        users.Should().HaveCountGreaterThan(0);
        users.Should().ContainSingle(u => u.IsAdmin)
            .Which.Username.Should().Be("admin@example.com");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Which` chains are concise and expressive when the narrowing step (e.g., `ContainSingle`) is the meaningful assertion. They become unreadable when chains exceed 3 levels — at that depth, extract intermediate variables and assert them separately. The `Which` accessor throws a `NullReferenceException` (not an assertion failure) if the narrowed subject is null unexpectedly, which produces a harder-to-diagnose error message than an explicit `.Should().NotBeNull()` call. Always add an explicit null check before entering a deep chain. [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — Moq `Capture.In<T>()` With Post-Assertion Verification for Multi-Call Argument Recording

Moq `Capture.In<T>(list)` accumulates every argument passed to a mocked method across all calls into a `List<T>`, which can then be asserted after all calls are made. This is the idiomatic Moq approach for "what arguments was the mock called with across multiple invocations?", replacing fragile `CallbackArguments` patterns or maintaining a manual `List<T>` inside a `Callback` lambda. Moq's `Capture` is thread-safe for use in parallel test scenarios where multiple threads call the mock concurrently. Pairing `Capture.In` with `Times.Exactly(n)` on the same Setup makes the Setup both record arguments and enforce call count simultaneously. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class EventDispatcherTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessBatch_FiveEvents_DispatchesAllEventsToSink()
    {
        // Capture all payloads dispatched to the event sink
        var capturedPayloads = new List<EventPayload>();

        var sinkMock = new Mock<IEventSink>();
        sinkMock
            .Setup(s => s.SendAsync(Capture.In(capturedPayloads), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(true);

        var dispatcher = new BatchEventDispatcher(sinkMock.Object);
        var events = Enumerable.Range(1, 5)
            .Select(i => new DomainEvent { Id = i, Type = "order.created" })
            .ToList();

        await dispatcher.ProcessBatchAsync(events);

        // Verify call count and inspect every captured argument
        sinkMock.Verify(
            s => s.SendAsync(It.IsAny<EventPayload>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()),
            Times.Exactly(5));

        capturedPayloads.Should().HaveCount(5);
        capturedPayloads.Should().AllSatisfy(p =>
            p.EventType.Should().Be("order.created"));
        capturedPayloads.Select(p => p.SourceEventId)
            .Should().BeEquivalentTo(new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Capture.In` is the cleanest Moq solution for multi-call argument verification. The captured list reflects insertion order (call order), which is reliable for sequential dispatchers but non-deterministic for parallel ones — sort before asserting if concurrency is involved. Avoid `Capture.In` when you only need to verify the arguments of a single specific call: `It.Is<T>(pred)` inside `Verify` is clearer and does not allocate the capture list. When argument objects are mutable and the SUT modifies them after the call, capture a snapshot copy instead of the original reference. [official]

---

### Pattern 6 — Testcontainers.NET `ContainerBuilder.WithBindMount` for Read-Only Configuration File Injection

Testcontainers.NET `WithBindMount(hostPath, containerPath, AccessMode.ReadOnly)` mounts a local file or directory into the container at startup without copying it into the image. This is the cleanest way to inject test-specific configuration files (TLS certificates, JSON config, SQL seed scripts) that vary per test scenario without building a new Docker image per test. `AccessMode.ReadOnly` prevents the container from modifying the host file, making the mount safe for shared test-data directories used by parallel test runs. Testcontainers resolves host paths relative to the test assembly's output directory when a relative path is supplied, so configuration files checked into the repository next to the test project are automatically found. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Configurations;
using Xunit;

public class NginxConfigurationTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly IContainer _nginx;

    public NginxConfigurationTests()
    {
        // Inject a custom nginx.conf from the test project directory
        string configPath = Path.Combine(
            Directory.GetCurrentDirectory(), "TestData", "nginx-test.conf");

        _nginx = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("nginx:1.27-alpine")
            .WithBindMount(configPath, "/etc/nginx/nginx.conf", AccessMode.ReadOnly)
            .WithPortBinding(8080, 80)
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPort(80)))
            .Build();
    }

    public Task InitializeAsync() => _nginx.StartAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()    => _nginx.DisposeAsync().AsTask();

    [Fact]
    public async Task NginxWithCustomConfig_Starts_AndServesHealthEndpoint()
    {
        using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:8080") };
        var response   = await http.GetAsync("/health");
        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Bind mounts are faster than `WithCopyToContainer` for large files because no data is transferred into the container image layer. The downside is host-path coupling: test runs that move the output directory (e.g., `--output` overrides in CI) break the relative path resolution. Always resolve the host path with `Directory.GetCurrentDirectory()` or `AppContext.BaseDirectory` and assert it exists before starting the container to fail fast with a clear error. On Windows Docker Desktop with WSL2, bind-mount performance is excellent for files under `/mnt/` but degrades for paths outside the WSL2 filesystem — prefer placing test data inside the repository root. [official]

---

### Pattern 7 — .NET 9/10 `TimeProvider.GetUtcNow()` Injection for Deterministic Date-Dependent Business Rule Tests

.NET 8 introduced `System.TimeProvider` as an abstract clock that production code can consume via DI, with `TimeProvider.System` as the real implementation and `FakeTimeProvider` (in `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing`) as the injectable test double. Injecting `TimeProvider` into any class that calls `DateTime.UtcNow` or `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` directly makes those classes fully deterministic under test. The `FakeTimeProvider` allows setting an exact `UtcNow`, advancing time by a `TimeSpan`, and controlling `ITimer` callbacks — essential for testing retry policies, cache expiry, subscription renewal, and billing-cycle logic. .NET 10 added `FakeTimeProvider.SetLocalTimeZone` for time-zone-sensitive assertion chains (covered in Cycle 37). [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using Xunit;

public class SubscriptionRenewalTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void CheckRenewal_OnExpiryDay_ShouldTriggerRenewalNotification()
    {
        // Arrange — fix time to exactly the expiry date
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider(
            startDateTime: new DateTimeOffset(2026, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
        var notifier = new Mock<INotificationService>();
        var service  = new SubscriptionRenewalService(fakeTime, notifier.Object);

        var subscription = new Subscription
        {
            Id         = Guid.NewGuid(),
            ExpiresAt  = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero),
            CustomerId = 99
        };

        // Act — check renewal with time set to the expiry instant
        service.CheckAndNotify(subscription);

        // Assert — notification fired because UtcNow == ExpiresAt
        notifier.Verify(n => n.SendRenewalReminder(subscription.CustomerId), Times.Once);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void CheckRenewal_OneDayBeforeExpiry_ShouldNotTrigger()
    {
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider(
            startDateTime: new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 31, 23, 59, 59, TimeSpan.Zero));
        var notifier = new Mock<INotificationService>();
        var service  = new SubscriptionRenewalService(fakeTime, notifier.Object);
        var subscription = new Subscription
        {
            Id        = Guid.NewGuid(),
            ExpiresAt = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero)
        };

        service.CheckAndNotify(subscription);

        notifier.Verify(n => n.SendRenewalReminder(It.IsAny<int>()), Times.Never);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TimeProvider` injection makes every date-dependent test deterministic at zero runtime cost. The prerequisite is that the production class accepts `TimeProvider` via its constructor or DI — retrofitting existing code that calls `DateTime.UtcNow` directly requires a refactoring pass. For libraries that cannot take a DI dependency, the `IClock` adapter pattern (thin wrapper over `TimeProvider`) provides the same test seam with looser coupling. Avoid setting `FakeTimeProvider` time inside loops to simulate time passing — use `FakeTimeProvider.Advance(TimeSpan)` which also fires registered `ITimer` callbacks correctly. [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — xUnit v3 `ICollectionFixture<T>` With `[CollectionDefinition]` for Cross-Class Shared Container Lifecycle

xUnit v3 `[CollectionDefinition("MyCollection")]` marks a non-test class as the definition point for a named collection, and `ICollectionFixture<T>` on that class wires a shared fixture into every `[Collection("MyCollection")]` test class. This is xUnit's primary mechanism for sharing expensive resources (database containers, HTTP servers, message brokers) across multiple test classes without restarting them per class. xUnit v3 guarantees that fixture `InitializeAsync` runs once before any test in the collection and `DisposeAsync` runs after the last test, even when classes run in parallel. The collection boundary is the parallelism isolation unit: test classes in different collections may run in parallel; classes in the same collection are serialised by default. [official]

```csharp
using Testcontainers.Redis;
using Xunit;

// Fixture — started once for the entire collection
public class RedisFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly RedisContainer _redis = new RedisBuilder()
        .WithImage("redis:7.2-alpine")
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _redis.GetConnectionString();

    public Task InitializeAsync() => _redis.StartAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()    => _redis.DisposeAsync().AsTask();
}

// Collection definition — wires the fixture to the collection name
[CollectionDefinition("Redis")]
public class RedisCollection : ICollectionFixture<RedisFixture> { }

// First test class using the shared Redis instance
[Collection("Redis")]
public class CacheServiceTests(RedisFixture redis)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Set_ThenGet_ReturnsStoredValue()
    {
        var cache = new CacheService(redis.ConnectionString);
        await cache.SetAsync("key1", "value1", TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
        var result = await cache.GetAsync("key1");
        Assert.Equal("value1", result);
    }
}

// Second test class — same Redis instance, no restart overhead
[Collection("Redis")]
public class SessionStoreTests(RedisFixture redis)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task CreateSession_StoresTokenWithExpiry()
    {
        var store = new SessionStore(redis.ConnectionString);
        var token = await store.CreateAsync(userId: 42, expiresIn: TimeSpan.FromHours(1));
        Assert.False(string.IsNullOrEmpty(token));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Collections are essential for integration tests that share costly infrastructure. The primary risk is test-order coupling: if one test class corrupts shared state (e.g., leaving stale Redis keys), later classes in the same collection fail for unrelated reasons. Mitigate with per-test key namespacing (prefix keys with `TestRunId` or `Guid.NewGuid()`) and truncating shared state in `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` of each class. Do not put unit tests (which need no shared state) in the same collection as integration tests — doing so prevents them from running in parallel with other unit test classes. [official]

---

### Pattern 9 — FluentAssertions v8 `BeJsonEquivalentTo` for HTTP Response Body Contract Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 added `BeJsonEquivalentTo(expectedJson)` on `string` subjects, which deserialises both the actual and expected JSON strings and performs a structural equivalence check rather than a character-by-character comparison. This handles whitespace normalisation, property-order differences, and number-representation differences (`1.0` vs `1`) automatically, replacing fragile `Assert.Equal(expected.Trim(), actual.Trim())` patterns that break on any formatting change. The method accepts the same `options` callback as `BeEquivalentTo`, so `ExcludingMissingMembers()`, `Excluding(x => x.Timestamp)`, and `Using<decimal>(ctx => ...)` custom comparers all work on the deserialised graph. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using Xunit;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;

public class ProductApiContractTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProduct_ById_ReturnsExpectedJsonShape()
    {
        var client = factory.CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/products/1");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        string body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        // Structural JSON equivalence — ignores whitespace and property order
        body.Should().BeJsonEquivalentTo("""
            {
              "id": 1,
              "name": "Widget Pro",
              "price": 29.99,
              "category": "Tools"
            }
            """,
            opts => opts.Excluding(x => x.Path.EndsWith("updatedAt")));
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProducts_ReturnsArrayWithMinimumFields()
    {
        var client   = factory.CreateClient();
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/products?pageSize=3");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        string body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        // Assert array shape and minimum element count
        body.Should().BeJsonEquivalentTo("""
            [
              { "id": 1, "name": "Widget Pro" },
              { "id": 2, "name": "Gadget Plus" },
              { "id": 3, "name": "Doohickey" }
            ]
            """,
            opts => opts.ExcludingMissingMembers());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `BeJsonEquivalentTo` is the right tool for API contract tests where the response schema matters but incidental fields (audit timestamps, server-generated IDs) should be excluded. The assertion failure message shows the full deserialized diff, which is far more useful than a raw string mismatch. The tradeoff is that it deserialises using `System.Text.Json` with default options — if the API uses custom converters (e.g., for `DateOnly`, polymorphic types), the deserialized expected string may behave differently. For contracts involving custom serialisation, deserialise manually and use `BeEquivalentTo` on the typed object instead. [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — MSTest v3 `[RetryAttribute]` With `[TestCategory("Flaky")]` Quarantine Strategy

MSTest v3 `[Retry(n)]` retries a failing test up to `n` times before marking it as failed. Pairing this with `[TestCategory("Flaky")]` and a CI pipeline filter creates a structured quarantine workflow: flaky tests are tagged, retried automatically, and tracked separately from stable tests in dashboards. The `[Retry]` attribute is in the `MSTest.Extensions` namespace (added in MSTest v3) and integrates with the Microsoft Testing Platform (MTP) runner, reporting the number of retry attempts and each attempt's exception in the test results. Quarantine via `[TestCategory]` allows CI to run `--filter TestCategory!=Flaky` for blocking builds and a separate job that tolerates flaky retries for diagnostic purposes. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting.Extensions; // RetryAttribute

[TestClass]
[TestCategory("Integration")]
public class ExternalPaymentGatewayTests
{
    private PaymentGatewayClient _client = null!;

    [TestInitialize]
    public void Setup()
    {
        _client = new PaymentGatewayClient(TestConfiguration.SandboxApiKey);
    }

    // [Retry(3)] retries up to 3 times; test passes if any attempt succeeds
    [TestMethod]
    [Retry(3)]
    [TestCategory("Flaky")]             // quarantine tag for CI filter
    public async Task ChargeCard_ValidCard_ReturnsApproved()
    {
        var request = new ChargeRequest
        {
            AmountCents = 1000,
            Currency    = "USD",
            CardToken   = "tok_visa_test"
        };

        var result = await _client.ChargeAsync(request);

        Assert.AreEqual(PaymentStatus.Approved, result.Status,
            $"Attempt failed: {result.DeclineCode ?? "no decline code"}");
    }

    // Stable test — no retry needed; runs in blocking CI check
    [TestMethod]
    public void ChargeCard_NullToken_ThrowsArgumentException()
    {
        Assert.ThrowsException<ArgumentNullException>(
            () => new ChargeRequest { CardToken = null! });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[Retry]` is a pragmatic fix for truly non-deterministic tests (rate-limited external APIs, container startup races) but must not be used to mask deterministic failures caused by real bugs. Establish a review process: any test with `[Retry]` and `[TestCategory("Flaky")]` must have a linked tracking issue describing the root cause and a deadline for resolving it or removing the test. Without this gate, `[Retry]` accumulates silently and degrades CI reliability. Monitor retry rates in test dashboards; a test that consistently requires its maximum retries is a signal that the underlying service SLA is not suitable for test usage. [official]

---

### Pattern 11 — C# 14 `extension` Block Instance Methods as Test Builder DSL

C# 14 stable extension blocks allow defining instance methods, properties, and operators on any type — including sealed third-party types and generated types — in a dedicated `extension` block rather than a static helper class. In tests, this enables building a fluent test-builder DSL on top of POCO request/response types without modifying them. The extension methods live in a `TestBuilders` file that is compiled only in the test project, so they add zero runtime cost to production code. Extension blocks with `this TModel` parameter can chain methods that return the same type (builder pattern) without requiring the target type to implement any interface. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

// Extension block (C# 14) — adds test-only builder methods to CreateOrderRequest
// without modifying the production type
extension(CreateOrderRequest req)
{
    // Instance method returning the same type for fluent chaining
    public CreateOrderRequest WithItems(params OrderItem[] items)
    {
        req.Items = items.ToList();
        return req;
    }

    public CreateOrderRequest ForCustomer(int customerId)
    {
        req.CustomerId = customerId;
        return req;
    }

    public CreateOrderRequest WithShipping(string address, string postcode)
    {
        req.ShippingAddress = address;
        req.ShippingPostcode = postcode;
        return req;
    }

    // Computed property — reads from the type without modifying it
    public bool IsValid => req.CustomerId > 0 && req.Items.Count > 0;
}

public class OrderServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task CreateOrder_ValidRequest_ReturnsPendingStatus()
    {
        var service = new OrderService();

        // Fluent builder via extension block — reads like a DSL, zero production overhead
        var request = new CreateOrderRequest()
            .ForCustomer(42)
            .WithItems(new OrderItem { Sku = "SKU-001", Qty = 2 })
            .WithShipping("123 Main St", "SW1A 1AA");

        Assert.True(request.IsValid);
        var order = await service.CreateAsync(request);
        Assert.Equal(OrderStatus.Pending, order.Status);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** C# 14 extension blocks are the cleanest test-builder mechanism available when the target type is sealed, partially generated, or outside your repository. The tradeoff is the C# 14 language version requirement (`<LangVersion>preview</LangVersion>` or targeting .NET 10). In test projects, this is generally safe — test projects do not ship as NuGet packages and can adopt preview language features freely. For teams on C# 12/13, extension methods on a `TestBuilder<T>` wrapper class achieve the same fluent API at the cost of one extra wrapping step. Ensure extension blocks are in a namespace or file scope that makes them visible only in the test project to prevent accidental usage in production code. [official]

---

### Pattern 12 — Testcontainers.NET `WithEnvironment` and `WithCommand` for Seed-Data Container Variants

Testcontainers.NET `WithEnvironment(key, value)` sets container environment variables that control startup behaviour (e.g., database seed mode, feature flags for the containerised service), and `WithCommand(args)` overrides the container entrypoint command. Combining these creates "variant" containers for specific test scenarios — a "seeded" variant for read-heavy query tests and a "empty" variant for write-path tests — without maintaining separate Docker images. Using environment variables for seeding keeps the image generic: the same `my-api:latest` image can start in `SEED_MODE=true` (loads fixture data) or default mode (empty state). [community]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using Xunit;

public class ProductCatalogFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    // Seeded variant — used by read tests
    public IContainer SeededCatalog { get; } = new ContainerBuilder()
        .WithImage("myapp/catalog-service:test")
        .WithEnvironment("SEED_MODE", "true")
        .WithEnvironment("SEED_DATASET", "catalog-e2e-fixture-v3")
        .WithPortBinding(5001, 8080)
        .WithWaitStrategy(
            Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPort(8080).ForPath("/health")))
        .Build();

    // Empty variant — used by write/mutation tests
    public IContainer EmptyCatalog { get; } = new ContainerBuilder()
        .WithImage("myapp/catalog-service:test")
        .WithEnvironment("SEED_MODE", "false")
        .WithPortBinding(5002, 8080)
        .WithWaitStrategy(
            Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPort(8080).ForPath("/health")))
        .Build();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        // Start both variants in parallel
        await Task.WhenAll(SeededCatalog.StartAsync(), EmptyCatalog.StartAsync());
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await Task.WhenAll(SeededCatalog.DisposeAsync().AsTask(),
                           EmptyCatalog.DisposeAsync().AsTask());
    }
}

public class ProductSearchTests(ProductCatalogFixture fixture)
    : IClassFixture<ProductCatalogFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Search_ByCategory_ReturnsSeededProducts()
    {
        using var http = new HttpClient
            { BaseAddress = new Uri($"http://localhost:{fixture.SeededCatalog.GetMappedPublicPort(8080)}") };
        var response = await http.GetAsync("/api/products?category=tools");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Environment-driven seed variants eliminate the "test data contamination" problem between read and write tests by providing isolated starting states. The cost is increased Docker memory consumption: two containers per test class adds up quickly in resource-constrained CI agents. Use `[Collection]` to share the fixture across multiple test classes and amortise the startup cost. If the API under test does not support an environment-driven seed mode, inject a SQL seed script via `WithBindMount` at startup instead. [community]

---

### Pattern 13 — .NET 9/10 `System.Collections.Frozen.FrozenDictionary` for Read-Only Test Lookup Tables

.NET 8 introduced `FrozenDictionary<TKey, TValue>` and `FrozenSet<T>` in `System.Collections.Frozen`. Once constructed via `ToFrozenDictionary()`, these structures are immutable and optimised for lookup performance (no lock contention, no resize risk). In tests, they are ideal as static lookup tables for test data that should never change between test methods — country codes, SKU maps, feature flag seeds — replacing `static readonly Dictionary<K,V>` which is technically mutable and can be accidentally modified by a test. Using `FrozenDictionary` makes the immutability intent explicit and provides a performance advantage when the lookup table is used thousands of times across test parameterisation. [official]

```csharp
using System.Collections.Frozen;
using Xunit;

public class CurrencyFormatterTests
{
    // FrozenDictionary — immutable after construction, optimised for read performance
    private static readonly FrozenDictionary<string, (string Symbol, int Decimals)> CurrencyMap =
        new Dictionary<string, (string, int)>
        {
            ["USD"] = ("$",  2),
            ["EUR"] = ("€",  2),
            ["JPY"] = ("¥",  0),
            ["KWD"] = ("KD", 3),
            ["BHD"] = ("BD", 3),
        }.ToFrozenDictionary();

    public static IEnumerable<object[]> CurrencyRows()
        => CurrencyMap.Select(kv => new object[]
        {
            kv.Key, kv.Value.Symbol, kv.Value.Decimals
        });

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(CurrencyRows))]
    public void Format_KnownCurrency_UsesCorrectSymbolAndDecimals(
        string code, string expectedSymbol, int expectedDecimals)
    {
        var formatter = new CurrencyFormatter();
        string result = formatter.Format(code, 1234.5678m);

        Assert.StartsWith(expectedSymbol, result);

        // Verify decimal precision from the frozen map
        int decimalPlaces = result.Contains('.')
            ? result.Length - result.IndexOf('.') - 1
            : 0;
        Assert.Equal(expectedDecimals, decimalPlaces);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `FrozenDictionary` construction has a one-time cost higher than `Dictionary` (it analyses the key distribution to select an optimal internal algorithm), so it is worth using only for dictionaries that are constructed once and queried many times — exactly the static test-data pattern. For dictionaries built inside a test method and discarded after a few lookups, a plain `Dictionary` is faster overall. `FrozenDictionary` does not support null keys; verify that test data keys are non-null before calling `ToFrozenDictionary()`. [official]

---

### Pattern 14 — NUnit 4 `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` for Guaranteed Test Isolation Without Manual Reset

NUnit 4 `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` (introduced in NUnit 3.13, promoted as the recommended isolation pattern in NUnit 4) creates a fresh test class instance for every test method, mirroring xUnit's default behaviour. This eliminates the need for `[SetUp]` methods that reset mutable state: each test starts with a clean object graph constructed by the class constructor. Fields that hold mock objects, service instances, or in-memory state are reinitialised automatically on every test, making tests structurally independent without relying on `[SetUp]` execution. NUnit 4 applies `InstancePerTestCase` transitively to nested test fixtures. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using Moq;

// Each test gets a fresh instance — no [SetUp] needed to reset mocks
[TestFixture]
[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]
public class ShoppingCartTests
{
    // These fields are initialised in the constructor — fresh per test
    private readonly Mock<IProductRepository>  _productRepo;
    private readonly Mock<IDiscountCalculator> _discountCalc;
    private readonly ShoppingCart              _cart;

    public ShoppingCartTests()
    {
        _productRepo  = new Mock<IProductRepository>();
        _discountCalc = new Mock<IDiscountCalculator>();
        _cart         = new ShoppingCart(_productRepo.Object, _discountCalc.Object);
    }

    [Test]
    public void AddItem_ValidProduct_IncreasesItemCount()
    {
        _productRepo.Setup(r => r.GetById(1))
            .Returns(new Product { Id = 1, Name = "Widget", Price = 9.99m });

        _cart.Add(productId: 1, quantity: 2);

        Assert.That(_cart.Items, Has.Count.EqualTo(1));
        Assert.That(_cart.Items[0].Quantity, Is.EqualTo(2));
    }

    [Test]
    public void AddItem_Twice_SameProduct_AccumulatesQuantity()
    {
        // Fresh _cart — no leakage from the previous test
        _productRepo.Setup(r => r.GetById(1))
            .Returns(new Product { Id = 1, Name = "Widget", Price = 9.99m });

        _cart.Add(productId: 1, quantity: 1);
        _cart.Add(productId: 1, quantity: 3);

        Assert.That(_cart.Items[0].Quantity, Is.EqualTo(4));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `InstancePerTestCase` is the right default for classes that hold mutable state (mock objects, in-memory collections, service instances). The tradeoff is that `[OneTimeSetUp]` and `[OneTimeTearDown]` in the same class are still only called once — they share state across instances. If those methods write to class fields, the fields are lost on the first instance's GC and the second instance reads the default value, not the setup-written value. Move shared infrastructure into a `[CollectionFixture]` / `IClassFixture<T>` pattern or into static fields when `InstancePerTestCase` is active. [official]

---

### Pattern 15 — `WebApplicationFactory<T>` `WithWebHostBuilder` + `IServiceCollection.RemoveAll<T>` for Service Swap Integration Tests

`WebApplicationFactory<T>.WithWebHostBuilder` provides a hook to modify the host's `IServiceCollection` before the test server starts. Calling `services.RemoveAll<IMyService>()` followed by `services.AddSingleton<IMyService, FakeMyService>()` replaces the production service with a test double for the entire request pipeline — enabling integration-level tests that exercise real HTTP routing, middleware, filters, and model binding while controlling one specific dependency. This is cleaner than overriding `ConfigureServices` in a subclass because `WithWebHostBuilder` creates a derived factory instance that leaves the original factory reusable for other test classes. The `RemoveAll<T>` call (from `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection`) removes all registrations of the service type, preventing duplicate-registration bugs when the test adds its own implementation. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions;
using Xunit;

public class PaymentControllerIntegrationTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_WithFakeGateway_Returns200AndTransactionId()
    {
        // Swap the real payment gateway with a deterministic fake
        var client = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
            builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
            {
                // RemoveAll removes every registration for IPaymentGateway
                services.RemoveAll<IPaymentGateway>();
                services.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway, FakePaymentGateway>();
            }))
            .CreateClient();

        var payload = new StringContent(
            """{"cardToken":"tok_visa","amountCents":500}""",
            System.Text.Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");

        var response = await client.PostAsync("/api/payments", payload);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        var body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
        Assert.Contains("transactionId", body);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_GatewayTimeout_Returns503()
    {
        var client = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
            builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
            {
                services.RemoveAll<IPaymentGateway>();
                // Fake that always throws TimeoutException
                services.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway, TimeoutPaymentGateway>();
            }))
            .CreateClient(new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions
            { AllowAutoRedirect = false });

        var response = await client.PostAsync("/api/payments",
            new StringContent("{}", System.Text.Encoding.UTF8, "application/json"));

        Assert.Equal(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `WithWebHostBuilder` + `RemoveAll<T>` is the gold standard for integration tests that need one dependency swapped without changing the production registration. The cost is per-call: `WithWebHostBuilder` builds a new `TestServer` for each invocation, so tests that call it in every test method have significant startup overhead. Refactor common swap configurations into helper methods or derived factory subclasses (`CustomWebApplicationFactory`) and share them via `IClassFixture<T>` to amortise the cost. Be careful with scoped services: `RemoveAll` followed by `AddScoped` is correct; accidentally registering a stateful service as `Singleton` causes shared state between requests in the same test. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 40

**xUnit v3 `[Theory]` with `TheoryDataRow.Skip` set at class-construction time evaluates skip conditions when the data provider is instantiated, NOT when the test runs — meaning a skip condition that depends on runtime state (environment variable, file existence) checked in the `ClassData` constructor may evaluate before the test host is fully configured, producing always-skip or never-skip results depending on startup order [community]** — `[ClassData]` providers are instantiated during test discovery, which happens before `ITestOutputHelper` injection, `[CollectionFixture]` initialisation, and custom `ITestFramework` startup hooks. A condition like `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("CI") == "true"` evaluates at discovery time, which in some CI systems runs in a different process than execution. WHY it causes problems: the skip condition reads stale environment state from the discovery process rather than the configured execution environment, causing rows that should skip to run and rows that should run to be skipped. Fix: for runtime-conditional skips, use xUnit v3 `[SkipUnless(typeof(CiEnvironmentCheckAttribute))]` custom skip attributes which are evaluated at execution time, not discovery time.

**NUnit 4 `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.All)]` combined with `[NonParallelizable]` on individual tests within the same fixture class does NOT always serialise those tests — parallel execution scope is evaluated at the fixture level first, and individual `[NonParallelizable]` markers only prevent a test from being scheduled alongside tests from OTHER fixtures, not alongside tests in the SAME fixture [community]** — Teams that add `[NonParallelizable]` to tests that mutate shared static state expect those tests to run sequentially. Within a fixture that has `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.All)]`, NUnit still schedules all tests in that fixture in parallel because the fixture-level scope overrides individual test markers. WHY it causes problems: the mental model is "NonParallelizable means this specific test runs alone", but the actual semantics are "this test does not run in parallel with tests from other fixtures." Fix: move tests that must not run concurrently into a separate `[NonParallelizable]` fixture class, or use `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.Self)]` at the fixture level (parallelises fixtures, not tests within a fixture).

**MSTest v3 `Assert.ThrowsException<T>` does NOT unwrap `AggregateException` from `async` lambdas — if the action under test is `async` and throws synchronously inside `Task.Run`, the assertion may receive an `AggregateException` wrapping the expected `T`, causing a "AggregateException is not T" failure even when the expected exception was thrown [community]** — `Assert.ThrowsException<T>(() => { /* sync code */ })` works for synchronous throws. `Assert.ThrowsExceptionAsync<T>(async () => { ... })` unwraps task faults. But code that wraps async work in `Task.Run` and the test does not `await` the outer task may get an `AggregateException` at the test boundary. WHY it causes problems: the behaviour depends on whether the exception originates from a continuation or a synchronous call, which is not visible at the assertion site. Fix: always use `Assert.ThrowsExceptionAsync<T>` with `await` for any code path that involves `Task`; use `Should().ThrowAsync<T>()` (FluentAssertions) which unwraps `AggregateException` automatically.

**FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` with `WithStrictOrdering()` fails when comparing collections that contain `null` elements, throwing a `NullReferenceException` inside the FA comparison engine rather than producing a structured assertion failure — making it appear that FA itself has a bug rather than that the actual collection contains unexpected nulls [community]** — `WithStrictOrdering()` uses index-based comparison. When iterating to compare element at index `i`, if either the actual or expected collection has `null` at that index, the internal ordering comparator dereferences the null element to extract a sort key, producing an unhandled `NullReferenceException`. WHY it causes problems: the stack trace points into FA's internal code, leading developers to check for FA version mismatches or DI issues rather than inspecting their test data for null entries. Fix: add `Assert.DoesNotContain(null, actualCollection)` before the `BeEquivalentTo` call, or use `.NotContainNulls()` as a guard assertion. Alternatively, use `.ComparingByMembers<T>()` with an explicit null-safe comparer.

**`Moq` `Verify` calls made after `VerifyAll()` do NOT throw even if the subsequent `Verify` would fail because `VerifyAll()` marks the mock as "verified" and releases the setup registry — any `Verify` call after `VerifyAll()` against a cleared mock always passes silently [community]** — When `VerifyAll()` is called on a `Mock<T>`, Moq internally checks all setups and clears the "pending verification" state. A subsequent `Verify(x => x.Method(), Times.Once)` on the same mock creates a new verification pass against an empty setup registry, which Moq treats as "zero setups pending" and considers passing. WHY it causes problems: developers who call `VerifyAll()` as a "verify everything" step and then add targeted `Verify` calls for critical methods believe both assertions ran, when only `VerifyAll` actually evaluated. Fix: call specific `Verify` assertions BEFORE `VerifyAll()`, or replace `VerifyAll()` with explicit `Verify` calls for every method that must have been called (which is more readable and avoids the ordering dependency).

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 40 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `TheoryDataRow.Skip` condition that reads runtime state in `ClassData` constructor | Evaluated at discovery time, not execution time; produces wrong skip results | Use xUnit v3 `[SkipUnless(typeof(T))]` for runtime-conditional skips |
| `[NonParallelizable]` on individual tests inside a `[Parallelizable(All)]` fixture | Individual marker only prevents cross-fixture parallelism, not intra-fixture; tests still run concurrently | Move non-parallelisable tests to a dedicated `[NonParallelizable]` fixture class |
| `Assert.ThrowsException<T>` for async lambdas or `Task.Run`-wrapped code | `AggregateException` wrapping causes assertion failure unrelated to the actual exception type | Use `Assert.ThrowsExceptionAsync<T>` with `await`; or FA `Should().ThrowAsync<T>()` |
| `BeEquivalentTo` with `WithStrictOrdering()` on collections that may contain nulls | Null dereference inside FA ordering comparator; opaque stack trace disguises root cause | Add `.NotContainNulls()` guard assertion before `BeEquivalentTo` with strict ordering |
| Calling `Verify(...)` after `VerifyAll()` on the same mock | `VerifyAll()` clears the setup registry; subsequent `Verify` always passes silently | Call targeted `Verify` assertions BEFORE `VerifyAll()`; or avoid mixing both styles |
| Static `FrozenDictionary` initialised in a `[OneTimeSetUp]` method rather than a field initialiser | `InstancePerTestCase` lifecycle creates new instances, losing `[OneTimeSetUp]`-written values | Initialise static test lookup tables in field initialisers or `static` constructors |

### Key Resources — Cycle 40

## Cycle 41 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 16 — xUnit v3 `ITestOutputHelper` Injection via Primary Constructor for Structured Diagnostic Logging

xUnit v3 supports `ITestOutputHelper` injection directly through primary constructors (C# 12+), eliminating the boilerplate field declaration and constructor body required in xUnit v2. The helper writes lines to the xUnit diagnostic sink, which surfaces in the test runner, CI log files, and trx reports — providing contextual trace output attached to each test's result rather than to a shared console stream. When tests run in parallel, each helper instance is bound to its owning test case, so log lines are never interleaved between concurrent tests. Pairing `ITestOutputHelper` with `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILogger<T>` via the `Xunit.Extensions.Logging` package lets production code under test emit structured logs that are visible in xUnit output without modifying production logging configuration. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Extensions.Logging;

// Primary constructor injects ITestOutputHelper — no explicit field or ctor body
public class OrderProcessorTests(ITestOutputHelper output)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrder_ValidRequest_EmitsAuditLog()
    {
        // Wire production ILogger to xUnit output sink
        var loggerFactory = new LoggerFactory()
            .AddXunit(output, LogLevel.Debug);
        var logger = loggerFactory.CreateLogger<OrderProcessor>();

        var processor = new OrderProcessor(logger);
        var order = new Order(Id: Guid.NewGuid(), CustomerId: 42, AmountCents: 999);

        output.WriteLine($"[arrange] order.Id = {order.Id}");

        var result = await processor.ProcessAsync(order);

        output.WriteLine($"[assert] result.Status = {result.Status}");
        Assert.Equal(OrderStatus.Accepted, result.Status);
        // Production ILogger calls are now visible in xUnit output per-test
    }

    [Theory]
    [InlineData(0)]
    [InlineData(-1)]
    public void ProcessOrder_ZeroOrNegativeAmount_Throws(int amountCents)
    {
        output.WriteLine($"[theory row] amountCents = {amountCents}");
        var processor = new OrderProcessor(NullLogger<OrderProcessor>.Instance);
        Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(
            () => processor.Validate(new Order(Guid.NewGuid(), 1, amountCents)));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Primary constructor injection of `ITestOutputHelper` is cleaner than xUnit v2 field + constructor pattern and works with C# 12+ primary constructors. The tradeoff is that `ITestOutputHelper` is not available until after the test class is instantiated — calling `output.WriteLine` from a field initialiser throws `NullReferenceException`. For assembly-level or collection-level logging, use `IMessageSink` injected into `ICollectionFixture<T>` rather than `ITestOutputHelper`. The `Xunit.Extensions.Logging` package is a community package; it adds a dependency that must be kept in sync with xUnit v3. [official]

### Pattern 17 — NUnit 4 `[TestFixtureSource]` With Typed Parameter Classes for Parameterised Fixture Initialisation

NUnit 4 `[TestFixtureSource]` allows an entire fixture class to be instantiated with multiple parameter sets, making each parameterisation a first-class test suite entry in test explorers. Unlike `[TestCase]` which parameterises individual tests, `[TestFixtureSource]` parameterises the entire fixture, enabling scenarios where setup/teardown costs are per-configuration (e.g., different database providers, different locale settings, or different feature flags). The source can be a static property, method, or a type implementing `IEnumerable<object[]>` or `IEnumerable<TestFixtureParameters>`. Using a typed parameter class instead of `object[]` makes the constructor call self-documenting and avoids index-based argument errors. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Collections;

// Typed parameter class — self-documenting, no magic index access
public record DbFixtureParams(string Provider, string ConnectionString, bool UseTransactions);

public class DatabaseFixtureSource : IEnumerable
{
    public IEnumerator GetEnumerator()
    {
        yield return new DbFixtureParams("Sqlite",    "Data Source=:memory:",  true);
        yield return new DbFixtureParams("Postgres",  "Host=localhost;Database=test_db", false);
        yield return new DbFixtureParams("SqlServer", "Server=(localdb)\\MSSQLLocalDB;Database=TestDb", true);
    }
}

[TestFixture]
[TestFixtureSource(typeof(DatabaseFixtureSource))]
public class RepositoryProviderTests
{
    private readonly DbFixtureParams _params;
    private IRepository _repo = null!;

    public RepositoryProviderTests(DbFixtureParams p) => _params = p;

    [OneTimeSetUp]
    public void Setup()
    {
        _repo = RepositoryFactory.Create(_params.Provider, _params.ConnectionString);
    }

    [Test]
    public void Insert_ThenFind_ReturnsEntity()
    {
        var entity = new Entity { Name = $"Test-{_params.Provider}" };
        _repo.Insert(entity);
        var found = _repo.FindByName(entity.Name);
        Assert.That(found, Is.Not.Null);
        Assert.That(found!.Name, Is.EqualTo(entity.Name));
    }

    [OneTimeTearDown]
    public void Teardown() => (_repo as IDisposable)?.Dispose();
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[TestFixtureSource]` is the right choice when a whole test class's setup/teardown needs to vary by configuration — it avoids duplicating fixture classes or using base classes with abstract factory methods. The cost is that NUnit creates a separate fixture instance per parameter set, so the total setup/teardown cost multiplies by the number of parameter sets. For expensive setups (e.g., spinning up a real database), this pattern is correct. For cheap setups where only one or two test methods differ, `[TestCase]` or `[Values]` on individual tests is lower overhead. One gotcha: `TestFixtureSource` types must be in the same assembly as the test fixture or NUnit may not discover them. [official]

---

### Pattern 18 — MSTest v3 `[DataRow]` With `DisplayName` Property for Human-Readable Parameterised Test Names

MSTest v3 added a `DisplayName` property to the `[DataRow]` attribute, allowing each parameterised row to carry a human-readable name that appears in test explorer, the terminal reporter, and trx output instead of the default `TestMethod (row 0)` naming. This eliminates the need for the verbose `[DataRow]` + comment-above pattern that teams used to document what each row tests. The `DisplayName` is also used when referencing individual test cases by name in `--filter` expressions for CI partial-run scenarios. Combining `DisplayName` with nullable reference type-annotated parameters produces self-documenting tests that serve as living specification entries. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class PasswordValidatorTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow("abc",         false, DisplayName = "Too short (3 chars)")]
    [DataRow("abcde",       false, DisplayName = "Too short (5 chars)")]
    [DataRow("Abcde1!",     false, DisplayName = "7 chars — under minimum 8")]
    [DataRow("Abcdefg1!",   true,  DisplayName = "Valid — 9 chars, upper, digit, symbol")]
    [DataRow("",            false, DisplayName = "Empty string")]
    [DataRow(null,          false, DisplayName = "Null input")]
    public void Validate_Password_ReturnsExpected(string? password, bool expectedValid)
    {
        var validator = new PasswordValidator(minLength: 8);
        bool result = validator.IsValid(password);
        Assert.AreEqual(expectedValid, result,
            message: $"Password '{password ?? "(null)"}' should be {(expectedValid ? "valid" : "invalid")}");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow("user@example.com",   true,  DisplayName = "Valid standard email")]
    [DataRow("user+tag@host.org",  true,  DisplayName = "Valid plus-addressing")]
    [DataRow("no-at-sign",         false, DisplayName = "Missing @ — invalid")]
    [DataRow("@nodomain.com",      false, DisplayName = "Missing local part — invalid")]
    public void Validate_Email_ReturnsExpected(string email, bool expected)
    {
        var validator = new PasswordValidator(minLength: 8);
        Assert.AreEqual(expected, validator.IsValidEmail(email));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `DisplayName` on `[DataRow]` is a zero-cost readability improvement — always use it when the parameters alone do not communicate test intent. The tradeoff is that display names must be maintained alongside data: when a row's parameter values change, the `DisplayName` may become stale and misleading. Consider pairing with a review convention: if the `DisplayName` uses the word "Valid" or "Invalid", ensure the `expected` parameter value matches. For very large datasets (>20 rows), consider `[DynamicData]` with a generator method that derives the display name programmatically from the row data, reducing the surface for stale names. [official]

### Pattern 19 — FluentAssertions v8 `SatisfyRespectively` for Per-Element Ordered Assertion Blocks

FluentAssertions v8 `SatisfyRespectively` accepts a list of `Action<T>` delegates, one per expected element, and applies them in order to the actual collection. Each delegate can make arbitrary assertions about its corresponding element, enabling structured per-element validation without needing index-based subscript access. This replaces the common pattern of `collection.Should().HaveCount(n); collection[0].Should()...; collection[1].Should()...` that fails with an index-out-of-range error when count differs. When an element fails its delegate, FluentAssertions includes the element index and all failure messages in the combined error, providing complete feedback in one run. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class InvoiceLineItemTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GenerateInvoice_TwoProducts_LineItemsMatchInOrder()
    {
        var invoiceService = new InvoiceService();
        var order = new Order(new[]
        {
            new OrderLine(ProductId: "SKU-A", Qty: 2, UnitPrice: 10.00m),
            new OrderLine(ProductId: "SKU-B", Qty: 1, UnitPrice: 25.00m),
        });

        var invoice = invoiceService.Generate(order);

        // Assert each element with its own block — index-safe, all failures reported
        invoice.LineItems.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
            first =>
            {
                first.ProductId.Should().Be("SKU-A");
                first.Quantity.Should().Be(2);
                first.Total.Should().BeApproximately(20.00m, precision: 0.01m);
            },
            second =>
            {
                second.ProductId.Should().Be("SKU-B");
                second.Quantity.Should().Be(1);
                second.Total.Should().BeApproximately(25.00m, precision: 0.01m);
            });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `SatisfyRespectively` is ideal for ordered collections where each element has distinct expected content, such as audit log entries, invoice lines, or pipeline stage outputs. The tradeoff is verbosity: the block syntax is longer than a simple `BeEquivalentTo` for collections of simple value objects. For collections of uniform objects where all elements share the same shape, `BeEquivalentTo(expectedCollection)` is more concise. `SatisfyRespectively` is intentionally order-sensitive — the first delegate always maps to element `[0]`. When order is not guaranteed, use `Satisfy(predicates)` without the "Respectively" suffix, which performs order-independent matching. [official]

### Pattern 20 — Moq `SetupSequence` for Multi-Invocation Return-Value Progressions

Moq `SetupSequence` configures a mock method to return different values on successive calls without requiring multiple separate `Setup` calls or state-mutating lambdas. Each `.Returns(value)` or `.Throws<TException>()` appended to the chain is consumed in order; once the sequence is exhausted, subsequent calls return the last configured value (or throw if the last entry was a throw). This is essential for testing retry logic, polling loops, and circuit-breaker implementations where the SUT calls the same dependency multiple times expecting the behaviour to change. Combining `SetupSequence` with `Times.Exactly(n)` verification confirms the SUT made exactly the expected number of retry attempts. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public class RetryPolicyTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Execute_TransientFailures_RetriesAndSucceeds()
    {
        var mockService = new Mock<IExternalService>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        // First two calls fail, third call succeeds
        mockService.SetupSequence(s => s.FetchDataAsync(It.IsAny<string>()))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503 Service Unavailable"))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503 Service Unavailable"))
            .ReturnsAsync(new ExternalData { Value = "ok" });

        var policy = new RetryPolicy(maxAttempts: 3, delayMs: 0);
        var result = await policy.ExecuteAsync(
            () => mockService.Object.FetchDataAsync("resource-id"));

        Assert.Equal("ok", result.Value);
        // Exactly 3 calls were made (2 failed + 1 success)
        mockService.Verify(s => s.FetchDataAsync("resource-id"), Times.Exactly(3));
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Execute_AllAttemptsExhausted_ThrowsAfterMaxRetries()
    {
        var mockService = new Mock<IExternalService>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        mockService.SetupSequence(s => s.FetchDataAsync(It.IsAny<string>()))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503"))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503"))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503"));

        var policy = new RetryPolicy(maxAttempts: 3, delayMs: 0);
        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<RetryExhaustedException>(
            () => policy.ExecuteAsync(() => mockService.Object.FetchDataAsync("x")));
        mockService.Verify(s => s.FetchDataAsync("x"), Times.Exactly(3));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `SetupSequence` is the clearest way to test retry and backoff logic because the progression of responses is visible in one block. The tradeoff is that the sequence is consumed globally — if the SUT calls the method more times than the sequence has entries, the last entry is repeated, which can mask an off-by-one bug (the mock never fails the test for extra calls). Always pair with a `Times.Exactly(n)` verify to confirm call count. For complex stateful behaviour (e.g., a polling loop that succeeds only after a flag is set), a `SetupGet` + `SetupSet` approach or a hand-written test double may be clearer than a long sequence. [official]
