### Pattern 21 — Testcontainers.NET `PostgreSqlContainer` With `RespawnCheckpoint` for Fast Per-Test Database Reset

Testcontainers.NET provides the `PostgreSqlContainer` builder (via `Testcontainers.PostgreSql` NuGet package) which creates a real PostgreSQL container with a known connection string for integration tests. Combining this with Respawn's `RespawnCheckpoint` (which deletes rows by disabling FK constraints and truncating tables in dependency order) enables a pattern where the container is created once per test class, migrations run once at startup, and each test resets only the data — not the schema — in under 10 ms. This is orders of magnitude faster than recreating the container or running a new migration per test. The checkpoint is initialised after migrations and re-invoked in `DisposeAsync` to clean up between tests. [community]

```csharp
using Respawn;
using Testcontainers.PostgreSql;
using Xunit;
using Npgsql;

public class CustomerRepositoryTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _container = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
        .Build();

    private NpgsqlDataSource _dataSource = null!;
    private Respawner _respawner = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _container.StartAsync();
        _dataSource = NpgsqlDataSource.Create(_container.GetConnectionString());

        // Run EF Core or Dapper migrations once
        await MigrationHelper.RunAsync(_dataSource);

        // Snapshot DB state after migrations — before any test data
        await using var conn = await _dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync();
        _respawner = await Respawner.CreateAsync(conn, new RespawnerOptions
        {
            DbAdapter = DbAdapter.Postgres,
            SchemasToInclude = new[] { "public" }
        });
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Insert_Customer_CanBeRetrievedById()
    {
        var repo = new CustomerRepository(_dataSource);
        var id = await repo.InsertAsync(new Customer { Name = "Alice", Email = "alice@example.com" });
        var found = await repo.GetByIdAsync(id);
        Assert.NotNull(found);
        Assert.Equal("Alice", found!.Name);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Insert_DuplicateEmail_ThrowsUniqueViolation()
    {
        var repo = new CustomerRepository(_dataSource);
        await repo.InsertAsync(new Customer { Name = "Bob", Email = "dup@example.com" });
        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<Npgsql.PostgresException>(
            () => repo.InsertAsync(new Customer { Name = "Bob2", Email = "dup@example.com" }));
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        // Reset data between tests — runs in ~5-10 ms
        await using var conn = await _dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync();
        await _respawner.ResetAsync(conn);
        await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The Testcontainers + Respawn pattern is the best balance between isolation and speed for integration tests against a real database. The one-time container startup (~2-5 s) is amortised across all tests in the class. The tradeoff is setup complexity: Respawn requires knowing which schemas to include (`SchemasToInclude`) — omitting a schema means its tables are never truncated, leaving dirty data across tests. Also, Respawn does not reset sequences/identity columns by default; tests that rely on auto-increment IDs starting at 1 will fail on the second test onwards unless Respawn is configured with `WithReseed = true` or tests use queries rather than hardcoded IDs. [community]

---

### Pattern 22 — xUnit v3 `IAsyncLifetime` With Staged Teardown via `DisposeAsync` Exception Wrapping

xUnit v3 `IAsyncLifetime` requires `InitializeAsync` and `DisposeAsync` on test fixtures. A common bug is that an exception thrown from `DisposeAsync` during teardown hides the original test failure — xUnit reports only the teardown exception, making it appear the test passed up to teardown even when the test assertion failed. The mitigation is to wrap teardown operations in a try/catch that collects teardown errors and rethrows them as an `AggregateException`, or to make teardown operations safe to call even after a failed test. Using `await using` for resource disposal within `DisposeAsync` ensures each resource disposes sequentially and individual disposal errors are isolated. [official]

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using Xunit;

public class DatabaseFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly List<Exception> _teardownErrors = new();
    public TestDbContext Db { get; private set; } = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        Db = await TestDbContext.CreateAsync();
        await Db.Database.MigrateAsync();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        // Safe teardown: collect errors rather than throwing immediately
        try
        {
            await Db.Database.ExecuteSqlRawAsync("DELETE FROM Orders");
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            _teardownErrors.Add(new Exception("Failed to clean Orders table", ex));
        }

        try
        {
            await Db.DisposeAsync();
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            _teardownErrors.Add(new Exception("Failed to dispose DbContext", ex));
        }

        if (_teardownErrors.Count > 0)
            throw new AggregateException("Teardown failed; see inner exceptions", _teardownErrors);
    }
}

public class OrderRepositoryTests(DatabaseFixture fixture) : IClassFixture<DatabaseFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task CreateOrder_PersistsToDatabase()
    {
        var repo = new OrderRepository(fixture.Db);
        await repo.CreateAsync(new Order { CustomerId = 1, Total = 99.99m });
        var count = await fixture.Db.Orders.CountAsync();
        Assert.Equal(1, count);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Staged teardown with error collection prevents the frustrating "test passed but teardown failed" scenario that masks the true test result. The tradeoff is verbosity: wrapping every teardown step in try/catch adds noise. For simple cases (one resource to dispose), letting `DisposeAsync` throw naturally is acceptable — xUnit v3 does surface both the test failure and the teardown exception in its output. The `AggregateException` approach is most valuable for fixtures that manage multiple independent resources (containers, sockets, temp files) where any one can fail without preventing others from being cleaned up. [official]

---

### Pattern 23 — FluentAssertions v8 `Invoking` / `Awaiting` for Fluent Exception Contract Testing

FluentAssertions `Invoking` and `Awaiting` wrappers replace `Assert.Throws<T>` with a fluent API that integrates exception assertions into FA's chaining model, enabling the same `.Which` property narrowing on the thrown exception for further assertions. `action.Should().Throw<ArgumentNullException>().WithMessage("*must not be null*").And.ParamName.Should().Be("customerId")` tests both the exception type and its properties in one readable chain. The `NotThrow()` / `NotThrowAsync()` assertion documents that a code path is expected to be side-effect-free, which is more explicit than silently succeeding when no exception occurs. `WithInnerException<T>()` chains assert the wrapped cause in scenarios involving `AggregateException` or custom exception hierarchies. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class AccountServiceExceptionTests
{
    private readonly AccountService _svc = new AccountService(new InMemoryAccountStore());

    [Fact]
    public void Deposit_NegativeAmount_ThrowsArgumentOutOfRange()
    {
        // Fluent — exception type, message, and ParamName all in one chain
        _svc.Invoking(s => s.Deposit(accountId: 1, amount: -50m))
            .Should().Throw<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>()
            .WithMessage("*amount*must be positive*")
            .And.Subject.ParamName.Should().Be("amount");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task WithdrawAsync_InsufficientFunds_ThrowsInsufficientFundsException()
    {
        await _svc.Awaiting(s => s.WithdrawAsync(accountId: 99, amount: 1000m))
            .Should().ThrowAsync<InsufficientFundsException>()
            .WithMessage("*balance*")
            .Where(ex => ex.AccountId == 99);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Deposit_ValidAmount_DoesNotThrow()
    {
        // Explicit: documents that the happy path is side-effect-free
        _svc.Invoking(s => s.Deposit(accountId: 1, amount: 100m))
            .Should().NotThrow();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessBatch_NetworkFault_WrapsInDomainException()
    {
        var svc = new AccountService(new FaultingAccountStore());
        await svc.Awaiting(s => s.ProcessBatchAsync(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }))
            .Should().ThrowAsync<BatchProcessingException>()
            .WithInnerException<HttpRequestException>();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** FA exception assertions are more readable than `Assert.Throws<T>` when you need to assert on exception properties beyond just the type. The `Invoking` wrapper incurs a tiny lambda allocation overhead, which is negligible in tests. The main gotcha is that `Invoking` accepts a synchronous `Action<T>` — using it for async code (forgetting to use `Awaiting`) returns a `Task` which is silently discarded and the exception is never observed. Always use `Awaiting` for async methods. The `.Where(ex => ...)` predicate on `ThrowAsync` is evaluated after all other message/type checks, so it only runs when the exception type matches — avoiding confusing failure messages from predicate evaluation on the wrong exception type. [official]

---

### Pattern 24 — .NET 9/10 `FakeTimeProvider` With `Advance` for Deterministic Timer and Polling Tests

.NET 8 introduced `TimeProvider` (abstract base) and .NET 9+ ships `FakeTimeProvider` (in `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing`) which is a concrete test implementation. `FakeTimeProvider.Advance(TimeSpan)` moves virtual time forward synchronously, triggering any `Task.Delay`, `PeriodicTimer`, or `CancellationToken` timeouts that were created from the same provider — making timer-dependent tests deterministic and near-instant. This replaces `Thread.Sleep` / `Task.Delay` in tests, which is a CI flakiness source because CI machines have variable scheduler resolution. Injecting `TimeProvider` as a constructor parameter in production code is the required enabler; using `FakeTimeProvider` in tests and the real `TimeProvider.System` in production. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using Xunit;

public class SessionExpiryTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Session_ExpiresAfterInactivityPeriod_MarkedExpired()
    {
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider();
        var session = new UserSession(userId: 42, timeoutMinutes: 30, fakeTime);

        Assert.False(session.IsExpired);

        // Advance 29 minutes — session should still be valid
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(29));
        Assert.False(session.IsExpired);

        // Advance one more minute (total 30) — now expired
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
        Assert.True(session.IsExpired);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PollingService_AfterInterval_InvokesCallback()
    {
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider();
        int callbackCount = 0;

        var service = new PollingService(
            intervalSeconds: 60,
            onTick: () => { callbackCount++; return Task.CompletedTask; },
            fakeTime);

        await service.StartAsync(CancellationToken.None);

        // Advance by 3 intervals
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60));
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60));
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60));

        await Task.Yield(); // allow async continuations to run
        Assert.Equal(3, callbackCount);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `FakeTimeProvider` is the authoritative solution for any code that depends on wall-clock time or scheduling. The requirement is that production code accepts a `TimeProvider` parameter or injects it from DI — retrofitting this onto legacy code that calls `DateTime.UtcNow` directly requires an interface-wrapping refactor. The `Advance` method is synchronous and does not pump an event loop; tests that use `async/await` with `PeriodicTimer` or `Task.Delay(fakeTime)` may need `await Task.Yield()` after `Advance` to allow awaited continuations to run before asserting. Do not mix `FakeTimeProvider` with real `Task.Delay(ms)` — mixing the two creates race conditions between virtual and wall-clock time. [official]

---

### Pattern 25 — NUnit 4 `Assume.That` Precondition Guards for Environment-Dependent Tests

NUnit 4 `Assume.That` is the test precondition API: when the assumption fails, the test is reported as `Inconclusive` rather than `Failed`, signalling that the test could not run due to an unmet environment precondition rather than a real product bug. This is the NUnit equivalent of xUnit v3's `Skip.If` / `Skip.Unless`. Common uses include: skipping database tests when no connection string is configured, skipping OS-specific file-system tests on non-matching platforms, and skipping tests that require a GPU or external hardware. Unlike `Assert.That`, a failed `Assume.That` does not count as a test failure in CI health gates — it contributes to the `Inconclusive` count, which teams typically monitor separately. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;

[TestFixture]
public class NetworkDependentTests
{
    [Test]
    public async Task FetchExternalData_ReturnsValidResponse()
    {
        // Skip if no network available — marks as Inconclusive, not Failed
        Assume.That(await NetworkHelper.IsAvailableAsync(),
            Is.True,
            "Network unavailable — test skipped (not a failure)");

        var client = new ExternalApiClient();
        var response = await client.GetStatusAsync();

        Assert.That(response.IsSuccess, Is.True);
        Assert.That(response.Latency, Is.LessThan(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)));
    }

    [Test]
    public void FileWatcher_OnWindowsOnly_FiresChangeEvent()
    {
        Assume.That(RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform(OSPlatform.Windows),
            Is.True,
            "FileSystemWatcher reliable only on Windows — skipped on other platforms");

        using var watcher = new FileSystemWatcher(Path.GetTempPath());
        var eventFired = false;
        watcher.Changed += (_, _) => eventFired = true;
        watcher.EnableRaisingEvents = true;

        var tmpFile = Path.GetTempFileName();
        File.WriteAllText(tmpFile, "trigger");
        Thread.Sleep(100); // Allow FS event propagation

        Assert.That(eventFired, Is.True);
        File.Delete(tmpFile);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Assume.That` is correct for tests that are genuinely environment-dependent and whose failure would be a false positive in certain CI configurations. The tradeoff is that over-use of `Assume.That` erodes test suite confidence: if many tests are routinely `Inconclusive`, the "all tests pass" CI green state becomes misleading because a large portion of the suite never ran. Reserve `Assume.That` for truly optional infrastructure (external APIs, hardware, non-portable OS APIs) and use dependency injection with fakes for infrastructure that should always be available in unit tests. In CI, configure a separate matrix leg for tests requiring real infrastructure where those assumptions will always be met. [official]

---

### Pattern 26 — Moq `Mock.Of<T>()` Inline Initialisation for Read-Only Property Stubs in the Arrange Phase

Moq `Mock.Of<T>()` creates a mock where property stubs are configured using a LINQ-style predicate expression rather than `Setup(...).Returns(...)` calls. This is ideal for read-only data-transfer objects (DTOs), immutable domain value objects, and configuration interfaces where the mock exists only to provide property values — not to verify calls. The result is a single-expression arrange that reads like an object initialiser, making the test intent immediately clear. `Mock.Of<T>()` returns the mocked object directly (not the `Mock<T>` wrapper), so it cannot be used when `Verify` calls are needed later; in that case, construct a `Mock<T>` instance explicitly. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class ShippingRateCalculatorTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Calculate_ExpressShipping_AddsExpressSurcharge()
    {
        // Mock.Of<T>() — property stubs as expressions, no Setup().Returns() boilerplate
        var order = Mock.Of<IOrder>(o =>
            o.WeightKg       == 2.5m &&
            o.DestinationZip == "90210" &&
            o.ShippingMethod == ShippingMethod.Express &&
            o.Items          == new[] { Mock.Of<IOrderItem>(i => i.IsFragile == false) });

        var config = Mock.Of<IShippingConfig>(c =>
            c.ExpressSurchargePercent == 0.15m &&
            c.BaseRatePerKg           == 5.00m);

        var calculator = new ShippingRateCalculator(config);
        var rate = calculator.Calculate(order);

        // 2.5 kg * $5.00 = $12.50 base, + 15% surcharge = $14.375 ~ $14.38
        rate.Should().BeApproximately(14.38m, precision: 0.01m);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Calculate_FragileItem_AddsHandlingFee()
    {
        var order = Mock.Of<IOrder>(o =>
            o.WeightKg       == 1.0m &&
            o.ShippingMethod == ShippingMethod.Standard &&
            o.Items          == new[] { Mock.Of<IOrderItem>(i => i.IsFragile == true) });

        var config = Mock.Of<IShippingConfig>(c =>
            c.ExpressSurchargePercent == 0.00m &&
            c.BaseRatePerKg           == 5.00m &&
            c.FragileHandlingFee      == 3.00m);

        var calculator = new ShippingRateCalculator(config);
        var rate = calculator.Calculate(order);

        rate.Should().BeApproximately(8.00m, precision: 0.01m);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Mock.Of<T>()` produces the most concise arrange code for pure data stubs. The tradeoff is that it returns the proxied object, not the `Mock<T>` wrapper — post-test `Verify` calls require accessing `Mock.Get(obj)` which adds back some verbosity. For test doubles where you need both property values AND call verification, prefer `var mock = new Mock<T>(); mock.SetupGet(x => x.Prop).Returns(value)` so the `Mock<T>` wrapper is available throughout. `Mock.Of<T>()` also does not work with sealed classes or non-virtual members; in those cases use hand-written record types or anonymous objects. [official]

---

### Pattern 27 — Testcontainers.NET `ImageFromDockerfileBuilder` for Container Image Smoke Tests

Testcontainers.NET `ImageFromDockerfileBuilder` builds a Docker image from a `Dockerfile` relative to the test project directory and starts a container from that image, enabling tests against custom application images without requiring a pre-built registry image. This is particularly useful for smoke-testing a service's own Dockerfile as part of the test suite — asserting that the containerised version of the application starts, responds to health-check endpoints, and handles a basic request before the image is pushed to a registry. The `WithBuildArgument` method injects build arguments and `WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForHttp("/health"))` ensures the container is ready before the test runs. [community]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Configurations;
using Xunit;

public class ApplicationDockerImageTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private IContainer _container = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        // Build from the project's own Dockerfile — validates the image is buildable
        var image = await new ImageFromDockerfileBuilder()
            .WithDockerfileDirectory(CommonDirectoryPath.GetSolutionDirectory(), ".")
            .WithDockerfile("Dockerfile")
            .WithBuildArgument("BUILD_ENV", "test")
            .BuildAsync();

        _container = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage(image)
            .WithPortBinding(8080, assignRandomHostPort: true)
            .WithEnvironment("ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT", "IntegrationTest")
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                    .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPath("/health").ForPort(8080)))
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task HealthEndpoint_WhenContainerized_Returns200()
    {
        var hostPort = _container.GetMappedPublicPort(8080);
        using var client = new HttpClient
        {
            BaseAddress = new Uri($"http://localhost:{hostPort}")
        };

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/health");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        var body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
        Assert.Contains("healthy", body, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _container.DisposeAsync();
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Building a Docker image in a test is expensive (30-90 s) and should be reserved for smoke tests and contract tests that specifically validate the container image, not for unit or integration tests that run frequently. Wrap these tests in a separate `[Trait("Category", "ContainerSmoke")]` category and run them only on CI during merge-to-main or nightly builds. The `ImageFromDockerfileBuilder` uses the Docker daemon's build cache, so repeated runs on the same machine are faster — but CI agents that purge Docker cache between jobs will incur the full build time every run. `GetSolutionDirectory()` searches upward for `.sln` files; in mono-repo layouts it may find a parent solution rather than the intended one. [community]

---

### Pattern 28 — xUnit v3 `ITestCaseOrderer` for Deterministic Integration Test Sequencing

xUnit v3 `ITestCaseOrderer` is a hook that sorts test cases within a class before execution, enabling deliberately ordered integration tests where the sequence of operations matters (e.g., CRUD lifecycle tests: Create → Read → Update → Delete). Implementing `ITestCaseOrderer` with an `[Order(n)]` attribute on each test method and registering the orderer via `[TestCaseOrderer]` on the fixture class makes execution order explicit and compiler-visible, rather than relying on file order or method name alphabetical sort which are not guaranteed by the spec. This pattern is an intentional deviation from the "tests must be independent" principle and should be reserved for scenarios where resetting state between each step would be prohibitively expensive. [official]

```csharp
using System.Reflection;
using Xunit;
using Xunit.v3;

// Attribute to carry ordering value
public sealed class OrderAttribute(int value) : Attribute
{
    public int Value { get; } = value;
}

// Orderer implementation
public class OrderAttributeTestCaseOrderer : ITestCaseOrderer
{
    public IReadOnlyCollection<TTestCase> OrderTestCases<TTestCase>(
        IReadOnlyCollection<TTestCase> testCases) where TTestCase : IXunitTestCase
    {
        return testCases
            .OrderBy(tc => tc.TestMethod.Method
                .ToRuntimeMethod()
                ?.GetCustomAttribute<OrderAttribute>()?.Value ?? int.MaxValue)
            .ToList();
    }
}

// Fixture using the custom orderer
[TestCaseOrderer(
    ordererTypeName: "MyApp.Tests.OrderAttributeTestCaseOrderer",
    ordererAssemblyName: "MyApp.Tests")]
public class CustomerLifecycleTests : IClassFixture<DatabaseFixture>
{
    private readonly DatabaseFixture _db;
    public CustomerLifecycleTests(DatabaseFixture db) => _db = db;

    [Fact, Order(1)]
    public async Task Step1_CreateCustomer_PersistsEntity()
    {
        await _db.Repository.CreateAsync(new Customer { Id = 1, Name = "Alice" });
        var found = await _db.Repository.GetAsync(1);
        Assert.NotNull(found);
    }

    [Fact, Order(2)]
    public async Task Step2_UpdateCustomer_ReflectsNewName()
    {
        await _db.Repository.UpdateAsync(1, name: "Alice Smith");
        var found = await _db.Repository.GetAsync(1);
        Assert.Equal("Alice Smith", found!.Name);
    }

    [Fact, Order(3)]
    public async Task Step3_DeleteCustomer_EntityNoLongerFound()
    {
        await _db.Repository.DeleteAsync(1);
        var found = await _db.Repository.GetAsync(1);
        Assert.Null(found);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Ordered tests are an explicit trade against the independence principle. Each test method depends on state left by previous ones, so a failure in `Step1` cascades to `Step2` and `Step3` — making root-cause diagnosis harder. Reserve this pattern for lifecycle tests (CRUD flows, state-machine progressions) where independence would require full setup/teardown per step, or for slow integration tests where the setup cost is prohibitive. Always name steps with `Step1_`, `Step2_` prefixes and document the dependency in a class-level comment. Never use ordered tests for unit tests — the cost-benefit does not justify it there. [official]

---

### Pattern 29 — MSTest v3 Constructor + `IAsyncDisposable` as a Replacement for `[TestInitialize]` / `[TestCleanup]`

MSTest v3 supports constructor-based initialisation and `IDisposable` / `IAsyncDisposable` teardown as alternatives to `[TestInitialize]` and `[TestCleanup]`. The constructor runs before each test (MSTest creates a new instance per test method) and `Dispose` runs after, mirroring xUnit's native pattern. This eliminates null-forgiving field declarations (`!`) required for `[TestInitialize]`-assigned fields, since the constructor can assign them directly. Combining `IAsyncDisposable` with `await using` in the cleanup path enables async teardown (e.g., stopping a background service, flushing buffers) that `[TestCleanup]` could not easily express before MSTest v3 added async support to lifecycle methods. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class EventBusTests : IAsyncDisposable
{
    // Assigned in constructor — no null-forgiving operator needed
    private readonly InMemoryEventBus _bus;
    private readonly List<DomainEvent> _captured;

    // Constructor = TestInitialize — runs before every test
    public EventBusTests()
    {
        _captured = new List<DomainEvent>();
        _bus = new InMemoryEventBus();
        _bus.Subscribe<OrderCreatedEvent>(e => _captured.Add(e));
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public async Task Publish_OrderCreatedEvent_SubscriberReceivesIt()
    {
        await _bus.PublishAsync(new OrderCreatedEvent(OrderId: Guid.NewGuid(), Total: 150m));
        Assert.AreEqual(1, _captured.Count);
        Assert.IsInstanceOfType<OrderCreatedEvent>(_captured[0]);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public async Task Publish_MultipleEvents_AllDeliveredInOrder()
    {
        var ids = Enumerable.Range(1, 5).Select(_ => Guid.NewGuid()).ToArray();
        foreach (var id in ids)
            await _bus.PublishAsync(new OrderCreatedEvent(id, 10m));

        CollectionAssert.AreEqual(
            ids,
            _captured.OfType<OrderCreatedEvent>().Select(e => e.OrderId).ToArray());
    }

    // IAsyncDisposable = async TestCleanup — runs after every test
    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _bus.FlushAsync();
        await _bus.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The constructor + `IDisposable` pattern aligns MSTest with xUnit's mental model and is preferred in MSTest v3 for new test classes. The tradeoff is discoverability: developers unfamiliar with the pattern may not realise MSTest v3 calls `Dispose` automatically and may add redundant `[TestCleanup]` methods. If a test class inherits from a base class, both the base and derived constructors run (base first, derived second) and `Dispose` runs in reverse — the same asymmetric order as NUnit `OneTimeSetUp`/`OneTimeTearDown` but at the instance level. For classes shared across many test assemblies, the `[TestInitialize]`/`[TestCleanup]` pattern is still valid and more explicit about lifecycle semantics. [official]

---

### Pattern 30 — FluentAssertions v8 `ContainSingle(predicate).Which` for Combined Count + Element Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 `ContainSingle(predicate).Which` chains a count assertion (exactly one element matching the predicate) with typed element access for further property assertions. For testing collections that should contain exactly one element matching a predicate, `ContainSingle(predicate).Which.Property.Should().Be(value)` is a single fluent chain that reports a descriptive failure at the collection level (when count is wrong) or at the property level (when the element exists but its value is wrong) — rather than requiring two separate assertions that produce less helpful messages. This eliminates the verbose pattern of `var item = collection.Single(x => ...); item.Property.Should()...` while producing better failure messages when `Single` throws. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class AuditLogTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Login_Success_EmitsSingleAuditEntry_WithCorrectDetails()
    {
        var auditStore = new InMemoryAuditStore();
        var authService = new AuthService(auditStore);

        authService.Login("alice@example.com", "correct-password");

        // ContainSingle — fails with count error if not exactly 1; .Which gives typed element
        auditStore.Entries
            .Should().ContainSingle(e => e.EventType == AuditEventType.LoginSuccess)
            .Which.Should().BeEquivalentTo(new
            {
                UserId    = "alice@example.com",
                Success   = true,
                IpAddress = "127.0.0.1"
            }, opts => opts.ExcludingMissingMembers());
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Login_Failure_EmitsFailureAudit_PasswordNotLeaked()
    {
        var auditStore = new InMemoryAuditStore();
        var authService = new AuthService(auditStore);

        authService.Login("alice@example.com", "wrong-password");

        var entry = auditStore.Entries
            .Should().ContainSingle(e => e.EventType == AuditEventType.LoginFailure)
            .Which;

        // Password must never appear in audit logs
        entry.Details.Should().NotContain("wrong-password",
            because: "credentials must never be persisted to audit logs");
        entry.UserId.Should().Be("alice@example.com");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `ContainSingle(predicate).Which` is the clearest way to combine count assertions with element assertions for collections expected to have exactly one match. The tradeoff is that this pattern is intentionally order-free: `ContainSingle` scans the whole collection, not just `[0]`. When the collection unexpectedly contains two matching elements, the failure message says "expected 1 but found 2" — useful feedback. For collections expected to contain exactly one element total (not one matching a predicate), `ContainSingle()` without a predicate is preferred. Do not chain `.Which` after `.HaveCount(n)` with `n > 1` — `Which` is defined for single-element narrowing; for multi-element chains use `.And.Subject` or `.AllSatisfy(x => ...)`. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 41

**`IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync` on an xUnit `IClassFixture<T>` fixture is called ONCE after the last test in the class completes — NOT after each individual test — so teams that write per-test database cleanup in `DisposeAsync` discover that all tests in the class share dirty state because cleanup never runs between tests [community]** — `IClassFixture<T>` instantiates the fixture once and shares it across all tests in the class. `DisposeAsync` is the one-time teardown hook called after the last test finishes. If test 1 inserts a row and test 2 expects an empty table, test 2 will fail because the row from test 1 was never cleaned up between the two. WHY it causes problems: the naming `DisposeAsync` implies "clean up after each use", but `IClassFixture` semantics mean it is called only at the end of the class. Fix: use `IAsyncLifetime` on the test CLASS itself (not the fixture) for per-test setup/teardown, or use Respawn inside the test-level `DisposeAsync` on the class with the fixture only holding shared infrastructure.

**NUnit 4 `[Retry(n)]` re-runs the ENTIRE test including `[SetUp]` on each attempt — tests whose `[SetUp]` inserts seed data without first deleting it will accumulate duplicate rows on each retry, causing the second and third attempts to fail with constraint violations or incorrect counts unrelated to the original failure [community]** — When NUnit retries a test, it runs `[SetUp]` again before each attempt. If `[SetUp]` inserts seed data without first deleting existing data, the second attempt finds rows from the first attempt already present. A `UNIQUE` constraint violation or incorrect `COUNT` assertion then causes the retry to fail with a different error than the original failure. WHY it causes problems: developers add `[Retry]` as a band-aid for flaky tests without realising `[SetUp]` is part of the re-run; the failure mode on retry is often worse and more confusing than the original flaky failure. Fix: make `[SetUp]` idempotent (delete-then-insert, or upsert); or move cleanup to the START of `[SetUp]` so it runs before every attempt.

**Moq `It.IsAny<string>()` in Moq 4.18+ may NOT match `null` arguments because nullable reference type annotation changes in the expression-tree infrastructure altered null-matching behaviour for reference types — setups that previously matched null inputs now bypass the stub and invoke the mock's `DefaultValue` handler silently [community]** — Before Moq 4.18, `It.IsAny<string>()` matched both non-null strings and `null`. After NRT annotation changes in Moq 4.18+, the generated expression tree parameter type for `string` (non-nullable annotation) may exclude `null` as a valid match, depending on the target framework and compiler NRT context. WHY it causes problems: tests that previously validated null-input handling silently start using the mock's default return value rather than the configured stub; the test still passes but is now testing a different code path. Fix: use `It.IsAny<string?>()` (nullable annotation) to explicitly match both null and non-null, or use `It.Is<string?>(s => s == null)` for a null-specific setup.

**xUnit v3 `Assert.Equal` on `double` or `float` values without a precision argument uses exact binary equality — values that appear equal when printed (e.g., the result of `0.1 + 0.2` shown as `0.3`) are not equal in binary representation, causing intermittent CI failures across platforms or .NET runtime versions where floating-point intermediate precision differs [community]** — IEEE 754 arithmetic produces representation errors: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` in binary. xUnit v3 `Assert.Equal(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2)` fails because the binary result of `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. The same computation may produce slightly different bit patterns on x86 vs arm64 or under different JIT optimisation levels, causing a test that passes on one CI matrix leg to fail on another. WHY it causes problems: the test output shows `Expected: 0.3, Actual: 0.3` (both display identically at 1 d.p. in the default formatter), making the failure appear to be an xUnit bug rather than a precision issue. Fix: always use `Assert.Equal(expected, actual, precision: 5)` for floating-point comparisons; for FluentAssertions use `.BeApproximately(expected, precision: 1e-9)`.

**Testcontainers.NET `WithPortBinding(fixedHostPort, containerPort)` with a hardcoded host port causes `PortAlreadyInUseException` when multiple test projects in the same solution run in parallel — because each test session tries to bind the identical fixed port on the same host machine [community]** — When CI runs multiple test assemblies in parallel (e.g., `dotnet test` at the solution level with `--parallel`), each test project starts its own Testcontainers session. If both projects specify `WithPortBinding(5432, 5432)` for their Postgres containers, the second project to start fails with "bind: address already in use". WHY it causes problems: tests pass when run individually or serially but fail only in the CI parallel run; the port-conflict error message looks like infrastructure failure rather than a test configuration issue, so developers escalate to DevOps before finding the root cause. Fix: always use `assignRandomHostPort: true` and retrieve the mapped port via `container.GetMappedPublicPort(containerPort)` at test startup — this guarantees OS-assigned ports that never conflict across parallel processes.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 41 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Async database cleanup in `IClassFixture<T>.DisposeAsync` expected to run between tests | `IClassFixture` `DisposeAsync` fires only once after the whole class, never between tests | Use `IAsyncLifetime` on the test class itself for per-test teardown; keep fixture for shared infrastructure |
| `[Retry(n)]` on NUnit tests whose `[SetUp]` inserts seed data without first deleting it | Each retry re-runs `[SetUp]`, accumulating duplicate data; retries fail with new unrelated errors | Make `[SetUp]` idempotent (delete-then-insert) or clean up at the start of `[SetUp]` |
| `It.IsAny<string>()` setup expected to match `null` in Moq 4.18+ | NRT annotation changes may exclude `null` from `IsAny<string>()` matches; stub silently bypassed | Use `It.IsAny<string?>()` to explicitly include null; verify behaviour with `MockBehavior.Strict` |
| `Assert.Equal(expected, actualDouble)` without precision for floating-point results | Exact binary equality; fails intermittently across platforms and JIT versions | Use `Assert.Equal(expected, actual, precision: n)` or `BeApproximately(expected, delta)` |
| `WithPortBinding(fixedHostPort, containerPort)` in tests that run in parallel solution builds | Fixed ports conflict across parallel test-session processes; looks like infrastructure failure | Use `assignRandomHostPort: true` and `GetMappedPublicPort(containerPort)` at runtime |
| Calling `output.WriteLine` from a test class field initialiser (before constructor completes) | `ITestOutputHelper` is null during field initialisation; produces silent `NullReferenceException` | Call `output.WriteLine` only from constructor body or test methods, never from field initialisers |
