### Pattern 50 — Moq `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` vs `It.IsNotNull<CancellationToken>()` for Cancellation Propagation Verification

Moq requires explicit matching for `CancellationToken` parameters, and a common audit gap is using `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` in `Verify` calls when the intent is to verify that a real (non-default) token was forwarded. `CancellationToken.None` and `default(CancellationToken)` are the same value (`CancellationToken.None`), so `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` matches both correctly-forwarded tokens AND the default token — meaning the `Verify` passes even when the SUT forgot to forward the token. Using `It.Is<CancellationToken>(ct => ct != CancellationToken.None)` instead ensures the verify only passes when an actual cancellation source token was propagated. [community]

```csharp
using Moq;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;

public class ProductServiceTests
{
    private readonly Mock<IProductRepository> _repoMock = new();

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProductAsync_ForwardsCancellationToken_ToRepository()
    {
        using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
        var token = cts.Token;

        _repoMock
            .Setup(r => r.FindAsync(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(new Product { Id = 1, Name = "Widget" });

        var service = new ProductService(_repoMock.Object);
        await service.GetProductAsync(productId: 1, cancellationToken: token);

        // WRONG: passes even if SUT passes CancellationToken.None
        // _repoMock.Verify(r => r.FindAsync(1, It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()), Times.Once);

        // CORRECT: only passes when a live token was forwarded
        _repoMock.Verify(
            r => r.FindAsync(
                1,
                It.Is<CancellationToken>(ct => ct != CancellationToken.None)),
            Times.Once);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProductAsync_WhenTokenCancelled_DoesNotCallRepository_AfterCancellation()
    {
        using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();

        _repoMock
            .Setup(r => r.FindAsync(It.IsAny<int>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
            .Returns<int, CancellationToken>(async (id, ct) =>
            {
                await Task.Delay(100, ct); // Will throw OperationCanceledException
                return new Product { Id = id };
            });

        cts.Cancel(); // Pre-cancel

        var service = new ProductService(_repoMock.Object);
        await Assert.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>(
            () => service.GetProductAsync(1, cts.Token));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The `It.Is<CancellationToken>(ct => ct != CancellationToken.None)` pattern is the correct audit for cancellation propagation, but it is slightly more verbose and can produce a less readable failure message. An alternative is to use a pre-cancelled token and verify the SUT throws `OperationCanceledException` — this is a stronger behavioural test that also confirms the token is propagated and respected. Reserve the `It.Is<ct =>...>` verify pattern for tests that must check propagation without triggering cancellation, such as timeout tests where you need to verify the token was passed but do not want to fire it. Never use `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` in `Verify` calls when the intent is to audit cancellation propagation. [community]

---

### Pattern 51 — Testcontainers.NET `RabbitMqContainer` for Messaging Integration Tests With Channel Assertions

Testcontainers.NET provides a `RabbitMqContainer` module (via `Testcontainers.RabbitMq`) that starts an isolated RabbitMQ broker in Docker, gives tests a real `ConnectionFactory` connection string, and allows asserting full publish-subscribe pipelines without mocking the message broker. Integration tests using `RabbitMqContainer` can verify routing key matching, dead-letter queue behaviour, message TTL expiry, and consumer acknowledgement semantics that are impossible to validate through mock-based tests. The container exposes the management API port (15672) alongside the AMQP port (5672), enabling tests to use the HTTP management API to inspect queue depth and message state after SUT operations. Combining `RabbitMqContainer` with `IAsyncLifetime` on a class fixture ensures the broker is warm before the first test and destroyed after the last. [official]

```csharp
using RabbitMQ.Client;
using RabbitMQ.Client.Events;
using Testcontainers.RabbitMq;
using Xunit;
using System.Text;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class OrderPublisherTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly RabbitMqContainer _rabbit = new RabbitMqBuilder()
        .WithImage("rabbitmq:3.13-management-alpine")
        .Build();

    private IConnection? _conn;
    private IChannel?    _channel;

    public async ValueTask InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _rabbit.StartAsync();
        var factory = new ConnectionFactory
        {
            Uri = new Uri(_rabbit.GetConnectionString())
        };
        _conn    = await factory.CreateConnectionAsync();
        _channel = await _conn.CreateChannelAsync();
        await _channel.QueueDeclareAsync("orders", durable: false,
            exclusive: false, autoDelete: false);
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_channel is not null) await _channel.CloseAsync();
        if (_conn    is not null) await _conn.CloseAsync();
        await _rabbit.StopAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PublishOrder_MessageAppearsInQueue()
    {
        var publisher = new OrderPublisher(_rabbit.GetConnectionString());
        var received  = new TaskCompletionSource<string>(
            TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);

        var consumer = new AsyncEventingBasicConsumer(_channel!);
        consumer.ReceivedAsync += (_, ea) =>
        {
            received.TrySetResult(Encoding.UTF8.GetString(ea.Body.Span));
            return Task.CompletedTask;
        };
        await _channel!.BasicConsumeAsync("orders", autoAck: true, consumer: consumer);

        await publisher.PublishAsync(new Order { Id = 42, Total = 99.99m });

        var body = await received.Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
        body.Should().Contain("\"Id\":42");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `RabbitMqContainer` provides the most faithful test environment for AMQP messaging, but RabbitMQ containers are heavy (~200 MB image) and add 3-8 seconds to cold startup time. Use a single class fixture shared across all messaging tests rather than starting one per test class, and use `WithReuse(true)` in developer local runs to avoid container startup overhead during rapid iteration. Do not use `RabbitMqContainer` for testing pure message-serialisation logic — that belongs in unit tests. The key value is testing routing topology, DLQ behaviour, and consumer acknowledgement flows that require a real broker. [official]

---

### Pattern 52 — NUnit 4 `[SetUpFixture]` at Namespace Level for Assembly-Wide One-Time Infrastructure

NUnit 4's `[SetUpFixture]` attribute applied to a class outside any `[TestFixture]` (directly in a namespace) runs its `[OneTimeSetUp]` and `[OneTimeTearDown]` methods exactly once for all tests in that namespace — including all nested namespaces. Placing a `[SetUpFixture]` at the root namespace of a test assembly creates true assembly-level setup, equivalent to MSTest's `[AssemblyInitialize]` and xUnit v3's `IAssemblyFixture<T>`, without requiring test classes to opt in. This is useful for starting logging infrastructure, registering global serialiser settings, or initialising a DI container that all tests share. NUnit ensures `[OneTimeSetUp]` completes before any test in the namespace begins and `[OneTimeTearDown]` runs after all tests finish, including on failure. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;

// No [TestFixture] attribute — this runs for ALL tests in the assembly
namespace MyApp.Tests
{
    [SetUpFixture]
    public class AssemblySetup
    {
        private static ServiceProvider? _provider;

        public static IServiceProvider Services =>
            _provider ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("DI not initialised");

        [OneTimeSetUp]
        public async Task GlobalSetup()
        {
            var services = new ServiceCollection();
            services.AddSingleton<IFakeEmailSender, FakeEmailSender>();
            services.AddSingleton<IFakeSmsSender, FakeSmsSender>();
            services.AddLogging(b => b.AddConsole().SetMinimumLevel(LogLevel.Warning));
            _provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();

            // Warm up any expensive singletons eagerly
            _ = _provider.GetRequiredService<IFakeEmailSender>();
            await Task.CompletedTask; // Placeholder for async warm-up
        }

        [OneTimeTearDown]
        public async Task GlobalTeardown()
        {
            if (_provider is not null)
                await _provider.DisposeAsync();
        }
    }
}

namespace MyApp.Tests.Orders
{
    [TestFixture]
    public class OrderEmailTests
    {
        [Test]
        public void SendConfirmation_UsesRegisteredFakeSender()
        {
            var sender  = AssemblySetup.Services.GetRequiredService<IFakeEmailSender>();
            var service = new OrderEmailService(sender);
            service.SendConfirmation(orderId: 1, email: "a@b.com");
            Assert.That(sender.SentMessages, Has.Count.EqualTo(1));
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[SetUpFixture]` at the root namespace is the cleanest NUnit equivalent of assembly-level setup, but it is sensitive to namespace placement: if the class is placed inside a sub-namespace (e.g., `MyApp.Tests.Helpers`), it only runs for tests in that sub-namespace and below. Always place the `[SetUpFixture]` class in the top-level project namespace with no enclosing `[TestFixture]` attribute. The global DI container stored in a static field is a shared mutable state risk — only store services that are truly stateless singletons or explicitly thread-safe. For stateful services, use test-level or class-level fixtures to create per-test or per-class instances. [official]

---

### Pattern 53 — FluentAssertions v8 `HaveAccessModifier` / `NotHaveAccessModifier` for Architectural Assertion in Unit Tests

FluentAssertions v8's type-assertion API includes `HaveAccessModifier(CSharpAccessModifier)` and related reflection-based assertions that verify that types and members expose (or do not expose) intended accessibility without requiring a separate NetArchTest dependency. These assertions work directly on `Type` and `MethodInfo`/`PropertyInfo` objects retrieved via reflection, enabling lightweight architectural tests embedded in existing test projects. Common uses include: verifying that repository implementations are `internal`, that public DTOs have no `private set` properties that would break JSON deserialisation, and that service classes expose only the interface methods as `public`. [official]

```csharp
using System.Reflection;
using FluentAssertions;
using FluentAssertions.Types;
using Xunit;

public class ArchitecturalAccessibilityTests
{
    private static readonly Assembly _appAssembly =
        typeof(MyApp.Domain.Order).Assembly;

    [Fact]
    public void RepositoryImplementations_ShouldBeInternal_NotPublic()
    {
        // All types ending in "Repository" in the Infrastructure layer
        var repoTypes = AllTypes.From(_appAssembly)
            .ThatAreInNamespace("MyApp.Infrastructure.Repositories")
            .ThatAreClasses();

        foreach (var type in repoTypes)
        {
            type.Should().HaveAccessModifier(CSharpAccessModifier.Internal,
                because: "repository implementations must not be directly instantiable by consumers");
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void DomainEvents_ShouldHaveOnlyReadOnlyProperties()
    {
        var eventTypes = AllTypes.From(_appAssembly)
            .ThatAreInNamespace("MyApp.Domain.Events")
            .ThatImplement<IDomainEvent>();

        foreach (var type in eventTypes)
        {
            var settableProps = type.GetProperties(BindingFlags.Public | BindingFlags.Instance)
                .Where(p => p.SetMethod is { IsPublic: true });

            settableProps.Should().BeEmpty(
                because: $"{type.Name} is a domain event and must be immutable");
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void ApplicationServices_ShouldNotDependOnInfrastructureNamespace()
    {
        var appServiceTypes = AllTypes.From(_appAssembly)
            .ThatAreInNamespace("MyApp.Application.Services");

        foreach (var type in appServiceTypes)
        {
            var constructorParams = type
                .GetConstructors()
                .SelectMany(c => c.GetParameters())
                .Select(p => p.ParameterType);

            constructorParams.Should().NotContain(
                t => t.Namespace?.StartsWith("MyApp.Infrastructure") == true,
                because: "application services must depend only on abstractions");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The FA reflection-based approach is lighter than NetArchTest for simple accessibility and namespace boundary checks — no extra dependency, no separate test project required. The tradeoff is that FA does not provide the full rule-DSL that NetArchTest does (e.g., dependency-cycle detection, transitive dependency analysis). For projects where architectural enforcement is a core quality gate with many rules, NetArchTest or NDepend is still the correct tool. Use FA access-modifier assertions as a lightweight addition to existing unit test projects for the most common checks: interface-vs-implementation visibility, DTO mutability, and layer boundary contracts. [official]

---

### Pattern 54 — .NET 9/10 `IDistributedCache` Testing With `MemoryDistributedCache` and `FakeTimeProvider`

`Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Distributed.MemoryDistributedCache` backed by `FakeTimeProvider` provides a fully controllable in-process distributed cache harness for testing components that use `IDistributedCache`. Unlike a mock of `IDistributedCache`, `MemoryDistributedCache` respects `DistributedCacheEntryOptions.AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow` and `SlidingExpiration` — meaning tests can validate that items expire correctly by advancing `FakeTimeProvider` rather than sleeping. This eliminates flaky timing-based tests and produces deterministic cache-eviction test coverage without a Redis container. The `FakeTimeProvider` from `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` integrates with `MemoryDistributedCache` when injected via the options pattern. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Distributed;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Memory;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Options;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;
using System.Text;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class ProductCacheServiceTests
{
    private static (IDistributedCache cache, FakeTimeProvider time) BuildCache()
    {
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider();
        var options  = Options.Create(new MemoryDistributedCacheOptions());
        // MemoryDistributedCache respects TimeProvider via MemoryCacheOptions
        var cache = new MemoryDistributedCache(options);
        return (cache, fakeTime);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrSetAsync_ReturnsStoredValue_BeforeExpiry()
    {
        var (cache, fakeTime) = BuildCache();
        var service = new ProductCacheService(cache, fakeTime);
        var ct      = CancellationToken.None;

        await service.SetAsync("sku-123", "Widget Pro", ttl: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), ct);

        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(4)); // Still within TTL
        var result = await service.GetAsync("sku-123", ct);
        result.Should().Be("Widget Pro");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrSetAsync_ReturnsNull_AfterExpiry()
    {
        var (cache, fakeTime) = BuildCache();
        var service = new ProductCacheService(cache, fakeTime);
        var ct      = CancellationToken.None;

        await service.SetAsync("sku-123", "Widget Pro", ttl: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), ct);

        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(6)); // Past TTL
        var result = await service.GetAsync("sku-123", ct);
        result.Should().BeNull(because: "cache entry should have expired after 5 minutes");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrSetAsync_SlidingExpiry_ResetsOnEachRead()
    {
        var (cache, fakeTime) = BuildCache();
        var entry   = new DistributedCacheEntryOptions
            { SlidingExpiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2) };
        var ct      = CancellationToken.None;

        await cache.SetAsync("key", Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("value"), entry, ct);

        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1)); // Read before sliding window closes
        var mid = await cache.GetAsync("key", ct);
        mid.Should().NotBeNull("sliding window should reset on read");

        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3)); // Now past reset window
        var expired = await cache.GetAsync("key", ct);
        expired.Should().BeNull("sliding expiry should have elapsed after last read");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `MemoryDistributedCache` + `FakeTimeProvider` is the preferred approach for unit-testing cache TTL and eviction logic — no Redis container, no `Thread.Sleep`, fully deterministic. The main limitation is that `MemoryDistributedCache` does not support distributed-specific semantics like keyspace notifications, Lua scripting, or Redis cluster failover. Do not use this pattern to test cache-miss stampede prevention, distributed locking, or pub/sub — those require a real Redis instance via `Testcontainers.Redis`. Use this pattern for: TTL correctness, sliding expiration, cache-aside read-through logic, and serialisation round-trips. [official]

---

### Pattern 55 — xUnit v3 `[MemberData]` With `TheoryDataRow<T>` Typed Overloads and `Label` for IDE Navigation

xUnit v3 extends `[MemberData]` to support strongly-typed `TheoryDataRow<T1, T2, ...>` objects returned from a `static IEnumerable<TheoryDataRow<...>>` property or method. Each `TheoryDataRow` can carry a `Label` property that overrides the display name in test runners and IDEs, providing human-readable names without requiring a separate `ITestCaseDisplayNameFormatter`. Combining `Label` with the `Skip` property on individual rows enables conditionally skipping specific data combinations at discovery time — before the test body is entered — which is faster than `Assert.Skip` inside the test. The `TheoryDataRow` approach is strictly type-safe: mismatched parameter counts or types are caught at compile time rather than at runtime. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class PricingEngineTests
{
    public static IEnumerable<TheoryDataRow<decimal, string, decimal>> PricingCases()
    {
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<decimal, string, decimal>(100m, "NONE", 100m)
            { Label = "No discount — full price" };
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<decimal, string, decimal>(100m, "PROMO10", 90m)
            { Label = "10% promo code applied" };
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<decimal, string, decimal>(100m, "HALF50", 50m)
            { Label = "50% promo code applied" };
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<decimal, string, decimal>(100m, "INVALID", 100m)
            { Label = "Invalid code — falls back to full price" };
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<decimal, string, decimal>(0m, "PROMO10", 0m)
            { Label  = "Zero-value order with discount — still zero",
              Skip   = "Known issue: ZeroValueDiscount — tracked in #4512" };
    }

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(PricingCases))]
    public void Calculate_ReturnsExpectedFinalPrice(
        decimal basePrice, string couponCode, decimal expectedFinalPrice)
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();
        var result = engine.Calculate(basePrice, couponCode);
        result.Should().Be(expectedFinalPrice);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TheoryDataRow<T>` with `Label` and `Skip` is the most ergonomic xUnit v3 theory-data API for complex, named, conditional test cases. The tradeoff compared to `[InlineData]` is that data must be defined in a separate member, which increases code distance between the test and its inputs. For simple parameterised cases with four or fewer arguments and no conditional skipping, `[InlineData]` remains more readable. Use `TheoryDataRow` when: test cases need meaningful display names for CI dashboards, specific rows need conditional skipping, input types are non-primitive (records, collections), or the data set is shared across multiple theory methods via a `static readonly` property. [official]

---

### Pattern 56 — Moq `Protected().Setup<TResult>("MethodName", ...)` for Testing Classes With `protected virtual` Template Methods

Moq's `Protected()` extension allows setting up and verifying calls to `protected` and `protected virtual` methods on partial mock objects, enabling test coverage of template-method-pattern hierarchies without exposing the methods publicly or refactoring to interfaces. This is particularly useful for testing abstract base classes that define a skeleton algorithm with protected abstract steps: create a concrete mock subclass, set up the protected methods via `Protected().Setup<T>("MethodName", exactParameterMatch, args)`, and verify the algorithm calls them in the correct order and with the correct arguments. The `Protected()` API requires the `Moq.Protected` namespace and uses string-based method names, so rename refactorings must be matched manually. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using Moq.Protected;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class ResilientHttpClientTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task SendAsync_RetriesOnTransientFailure_ThreeTimesBeforeSuccess()
    {
        // Arrange: mock HttpMessageHandler (has protected SendAsync)
        var handlerMock = new Mock<HttpMessageHandler>();
        var callCount   = 0;

        handlerMock
            .Protected()
            .SetupSequence<Task<HttpResponseMessage>>(
                "SendAsync",
                ItExpr.IsAny<HttpRequestMessage>(),
                ItExpr.IsAny<CancellationToken>())
            .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable))
            .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable))
            .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK));

        var httpClient = new HttpClient(handlerMock.Object)
        {
            BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com")
        };
        var resilientClient = new ResilientHttpClient(httpClient, maxRetries: 3);

        // Act
        var response = await resilientClient.GetAsync("/resource");

        // Assert
        response.StatusCode.Should().Be(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK);

        handlerMock.Protected().Verify(
            "SendAsync",
            Times.Exactly(3),
            ItExpr.IsAny<HttpRequestMessage>(),
            ItExpr.IsAny<CancellationToken>());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Protected().Setup` with string-based method names is the only way to mock `protected` methods without exposing them as `public virtual` — a meaningful encapsulation benefit. The major tradeoff is that string-based names break silently on rename refactorings (the compiler does not verify the string). Mitigate this by adding `nameof`-style constants or using `[Fact]`-level `CallerMemberName` wrappers, or by using strongly-typed `Protected().Setup<T>(nameof(MyBase.SendAsync), ...)` where `nameof` can at least reference the inherited name. For `HttpMessageHandler` specifically — the most common use of `Protected().Setup` — consider the `MockHttpMessageHandler` helper from the `RichardSzalay.MockHttp` NuGet package, which provides a higher-level API for the common HTTP stubbing case. [official]

---

### Pattern 57 — Testcontainers.NET `WithOutputConsumer` for Container Log Assertions in Failing Tests

Testcontainers.NET's `WithOutputConsumer(IOutputConsumer)` API captures all container stdout/stderr output and makes it available for inspection in test assertions or failure diagnostics. The built-in `Consume.RedirectStdoutAndStderrToStream(stdout, stderr)` implementation redirects output to `MemoryStream` objects that tests can read after exercising the SUT. This enables: asserting that a database container emitted expected startup messages, verifying that a message-broker container processed expected number of messages (via management log lines), and attaching container logs to xUnit/NUnit test output on failure for post-mortem diagnostics without requiring a Docker daemon log-driver change. [official]

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Consumers;
using System.IO;
using System.Text;
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Abstractions;

public class ContainerLogAssertionTests(ITestOutputHelper output) : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MemoryStream _stdout = new();
    private readonly MemoryStream _stderr = new();
    private IContainer? _container;

    public async ValueTask InitializeAsync()
    {
        var consumer = Consume.RedirectStdoutAndStderrToStream(_stdout, _stderr);

        _container = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
            .WithEnvironment("POSTGRES_PASSWORD", "test")
            .WithPortBinding(5432, assignRandomHostPort: true)
            .WithOutputConsumer(consumer)
            .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilPortIsAvailable(5432))
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_container is not null)
            await _container.StopAsync();
        _stdout.Dispose();
        _stderr.Dispose();
    }

    [Fact]
    public void PostgresContainer_EmitsReadyMessage_InStartupLogs()
    {
        _stdout.Position = 0;
        var logs = Encoding.UTF8.GetString(_stdout.ToArray());

        output.WriteLine("=== Container Stdout ===");
        output.WriteLine(logs);

        logs.Should().Contain("database system is ready to accept connections",
            because: "Postgres must emit its ready message before the test proceeds");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void ContainerStartup_ProducesNoErrorLogs_InStderr()
    {
        _stderr.Position = 0;
        var errors = Encoding.UTF8.GetString(_stderr.ToArray());

        errors.Should().NotContain("FATAL",
            because: "a FATAL error in Postgres startup indicates a misconfigured container");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `WithOutputConsumer` is invaluable for diagnosing flaky container startup failures and for asserting infrastructure behaviour observable only through log output (e.g., verifying that a broker applied a configuration change). The tradeoff is memory consumption: redirecting to `MemoryStream` buffers all container output in-process, which can be large for verbose containers (Redis, Elasticsearch). For long-running containers, use `Consume.RedirectStdoutAndStderrToStream` only in debug-mode test runs, or buffer with a size-limited `CircularStream` wrapper to keep only the last N bytes. Always emit captured logs to `ITestOutputHelper` or `TestContext.Current.AddDiagnosticMessage` so they appear in failure output even when the assertion does not fail. [official]

---

### Pattern 58 — MSTest v3 `[DataSource]` With CSV External Test Data for Data-Driven Integration Tests

MSTest v3 supports `[DataSource]` pointing to CSV, XML, or database sources for data-driven tests, enabling large test-case tables to be maintained outside source code by QA teams or product owners. The `[DataSource("Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.DataExtension.CsvDataSource", ...)]` attribute combined with `TestContext.DataRow` access provides a clear contract between test infrastructure and business-owned test data without requiring test recompilation when cases change. In CI pipelines, the CSV file is embedded as a test-project resource (`Build Action: Content, Copy to Output Directory: Always`) so the path is deterministic. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class TaxCalculatorDataDrivenTests
{
    public TestContext TestContext { get; set; } = default!;

    // CSV file: TaxTestCases.csv — columns: Country,Income,ExpectedTax
    // File is in test project root with "Copy to Output Directory: Always"
    [TestMethod]
    [DataSource(
        "Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.DataExtension.CsvDataSource",
        @"|DataDirectory|\TaxTestCases.csv",
        "TaxTestCases#csv",
        DataAccessMethod.Sequential)]
    [DeploymentItem("TaxTestCases.csv")]
    public void Calculate_ReturnsCorrectTax_ForEachCountryAndIncome()
    {
        // Read row data typed from CSV columns
        var country      = TestContext.DataRow["Country"].ToString()!;
        var income       = decimal.Parse(TestContext.DataRow["Income"].ToString()!);
        var expectedTax  = decimal.Parse(TestContext.DataRow["ExpectedTax"].ToString()!);

        var calculator = new TaxCalculator();
        var actualTax  = calculator.Calculate(country, income);

        Assert.AreEqual(expectedTax, actualTax,
            $"Tax mismatch for Country={country}, Income={income}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** CSV-based `[DataSource]` is the only MSTest mechanism that allows non-developer stakeholders to add test cases without touching C# source. The tradeoff is fragility: column name changes in the CSV break the test at runtime (not compile time), the legacy `DataExtension` provider has no NuGet package separate from the full MSTest runner, and `TestContext.DataRow` returns untyped `object` columns requiring explicit parsing. For new projects, prefer `[DynamicData]` reading from a `static IEnumerable<object[]>` method that parses the CSV internally — this provides the same data-externalisation benefit with stronger typing and better error messages. Reserve the `[DataSource]` attribute for projects that already have established CSV-based test data pipelines managed by QA. [official]

---

### Pattern 59 — FluentAssertions v8 `Satisfy` With Predicate Expression for Inline Complex Object Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 adds `Satisfy(Expression<Func<T, bool>> predicate)` on object assertions as a lighter-weight alternative to `BeEquivalentTo` when only one or two properties need validation against computed conditions, but `Match` or `BeEquivalentTo` would be overly broad. `Satisfy` accepts a LINQ expression, extracts the predicate's body as a string for the failure message, and evaluates it — producing a failure message that shows both the actual object and the predicate expression that failed, without requiring the developer to write a custom `because` string. This is particularly useful in collection assertions: `collection.Should().AllSatisfy(x => x.Price > 0 && x.Price < 1000)` produces per-element failure messages with the predicate expression visible. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class InventoryServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GetLowStockItems_ReturnedItems_SatisfyLowStockDefinition()
    {
        var service = new InventoryService(new FakeInventoryRepository());
        var items   = service.GetLowStockItems(threshold: 10);

        // Satisfy: assertion message includes the predicate expression on failure
        items.Should().AllSatisfy(item =>
            item.Quantity >= 0 && item.Quantity < 10,
            because: "low-stock definition is 0 ≤ quantity < 10");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void GetLowStockItems_NeverIncludesDiscontinuedItems()
    {
        var service = new InventoryService(new FakeInventoryRepository());
        var items   = service.GetLowStockItems(threshold: 10);

        items.Should().NotContain(item => item.Status == ProductStatus.Discontinued,
            because: "discontinued items are excluded from low-stock reports");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void CreateOrder_ReturnedOrder_SatisfiesInvariantsInSingleExpression()
    {
        var service = new OrderService(new FakeProductRepository());
        var order   = service.CreateOrder(customerId: 7, skus: new[] { "SKU-1", "SKU-2" });

        // Compact assertion with expression-based failure message
        order.Should().Satisfy(o =>
            o.CustomerId == 7 &&
            o.Lines.Count == 2 &&
            o.Status == OrderStatus.Draft &&
            o.TotalAmount > 0);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Satisfy` with an expression predicate produces better failure messages than `(condition).Should().BeTrue()` because FA can extract the expression body as a string and include it in the failure output alongside the actual value. The tradeoff is that expression compilation has a small overhead on the first call (the expression tree is compiled via `Compile()`) and that complex multi-part predicates produce long, hard-to-read expression strings in failure messages. For assertions with more than three conditions, use `BeEquivalentTo` with `Including` / `Excluding` or `Assert.Multiple` / `AssertionScope` to get per-property failures rather than a single composite expression failure. Reserve `Satisfy` for three-or-fewer condition assertions on single objects, and `AllSatisfy` for homogeneous collection invariants. [official]

---

### Pattern 60 — .NET 10 `Task.WhenEach` + Streaming Assertion Pattern for Concurrent Result Ordering Tests

.NET 9 introduced `Task.WhenEach(IEnumerable<Task<T>>)` returning `IAsyncEnumerable<Task<T>>` that yields each task as it completes — in completion order, not declaration order. This enables testing concurrent result ordering, first-response latency, and early-exit optimisation (returning the first successful result from N parallel calls) without `Task.WhenAll` which forces all tasks to complete before any assertion. The streaming pattern is testable by combining `Task.WhenEach` with `FakeTimeProvider`-controlled `Task.Delay` simulators that allow precise control over which simulated operation "completes first". [official]

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using FluentAssertions;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using Xunit;

public class ParallelSearchServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Search_WhenEach_YieldsResultsInCompletionOrderNotDeclarationOrder()
    {
        // Arrange: three "data sources" with controlled latencies
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider();
        var results  = new List<string>();

        async Task<string> SlowSource()
        {
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3), fakeTime);
            return "slow-result";
        }

        async Task<string> FastSource()
        {
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), fakeTime);
            return "fast-result";
        }

        async Task<string> MediumSource()
        {
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), fakeTime);
            return "medium-result";
        }

        var tasks = new[] { SlowSource(), FastSource(), MediumSource() };

        // Act: collect results via WhenEach as they complete
        var collectTask = Task.Run(async () =>
        {
            await foreach (var completedTask in Task.WhenEach(tasks))
                results.Add(await completedTask);
        });

        // Advance fake time to drive completions in order
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); // FastSource completes
        await Task.Yield();
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); // MediumSource completes
        await Task.Yield();
        fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); // SlowSource completes
        await Task.Yield();
        await collectTask;

        // Assert: completion order, not declaration order
        results.Should().ContainInOrder("fast-result", "medium-result", "slow-result");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Search_ReturnsFirstSuccessfulResult_WithoutWaitingForSlowerSources()
    {
        var service  = new ParallelSearchService(sources: new[] { "slow", "fast", "medium" });
        var ct       = CancellationToken.None;

        var firstResult = await service.FindFirstAsync("query", ct);

        firstResult.Should().NotBeNull(
            because: "service must return as soon as the first source responds");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Task.WhenEach` is ideal for testing "hedged request" patterns, parallel fan-out with early-return, and race-condition-sensitive ordering logic. The tradeoff is that `FakeTimeProvider` does not truly control `Task.Delay` in all runtime environments without injecting the `TimeProvider` into the `Task.Delay` overload — the `Task.Delay(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)` overload (available in .NET 8+) is required. Without explicit `TimeProvider` injection in `Task.Delay`, `FakeTimeProvider.Advance` does not drive the delay tasks forward, and tests must fall back to real `Task.Delay` with short durations. Always inject `TimeProvider` into all delay-using components and use `FakeTimeProvider` in tests. For scenarios where `Task.WhenEach` result ordering under load is what is being tested (not latency simulation), `Channel<T>` with a producer for each task and a consumer ordering assertion is an alternative that avoids time-manipulation complexity altogether. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 43

**FluentAssertions `AllSatisfy` vs `SatisfyRespectively` confusion: `AllSatisfy` applies the SAME predicate to every element, while `SatisfyRespectively` applies a DIFFERENT predicate per element in positional order — mixing them up produces tests that pass trivially or fail on the wrong element [community]** — `AllSatisfy(x => x.Price > 0)` passes if every element satisfies the single predicate. `SatisfyRespectively(x => x.Name == "A", x => x.Name == "B")` passes if the first element satisfies the first predicate AND the second element satisfies the second predicate; it fails if the collection has more or fewer elements than predicates. Teams migrating from `Should().OnlyContain(predicate)` to `AllSatisfy` discover that both share the "same-predicate-for-all" semantics, while `SatisfyRespectively` is for positional heterogeneous assertions. WHY it causes problems: a test using `SatisfyRespectively` with a single predicate that evaluates positional state silently passes when the collection has exactly one element but the developer intended to assert all elements. Fix: always use `AllSatisfy` for uniform invariants and `SatisfyRespectively` only when each position has a distinct expected state; add a `HaveCount(n)` assertion before `SatisfyRespectively` to guard against incorrect element counts.

**Moq `SetupSequence` does NOT reset between test runs when the mock is stored in a static field — subsequent test method invocations consume the remaining sequence items, causing the third-or-later test to receive the last configured return value (which Moq falls through to after exhausting the sequence) rather than the first [community]** — `SetupSequence` maintains an internal counter on the `Mock<T>` instance. If a mock is created once (e.g., in a static field or a shared fixture) and `SetupSequence` is called once, the sequence is consumed across calls spanning multiple test methods. After the sequence is exhausted, Moq returns the last configured return value for all subsequent calls. WHY it causes problems: the first test method that runs behaves correctly (gets the first value), but the second test method gets the second value without its own `SetupSequence` call, and later tests get the last value indefinitely — failure manifests as flaky tests whose outcome depends on execution order. Fix: always create new `Mock<T>` instances per test method, never reuse mocks with sequence setups across tests; or call `_mock.Reset()` at the start of each test to clear all setups and recorded calls.

**xUnit v3 `IClassFixture<T>` and `ICollectionFixture<T>` both call `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` on the SAME thread as test discovery — if `InitializeAsync` throws synchronously (not via async propagation) before the first `await`, xUnit may record the failure against the fixture class rather than the individual test, causing all tests in the collection to appear as skipped/not-run rather than failed [community]** — When `InitializeAsync` throws before hitting its first `await`, the exception is thrown synchronously on the discovery/runner thread rather than being propagated via the returned `Task`/`ValueTask`. xUnit v3's fixture initialisation handler wraps the call in a try/catch that catches `Exception` from the returned task, but a synchronous throw before the first `await` bypasses this wrapper. WHY it causes problems: CI dashboards show 0 failures and N skipped tests — easy to interpret as "no tests ran" rather than "all tests failed" — leading teams to assume the test runner crashed rather than a fixture initialisation error. Fix: always ensure `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` hits an `await` before any code that can throw (e.g., open with `await Task.Yield()` as the first line in complex setup methods, or ensure the first line is an async operation).

**MSTest v3 `[DataRow]` with `null` arguments for reference types works correctly, but `[DataRow]` with `null` for `struct` (non-nullable value-type) parameters causes `ArgumentNullException` at test-method invocation time — not at attribute construction time — producing a confusing runtime error that looks like a test failure rather than a configuration error [community]** — MSTest uses reflection to invoke test methods and passes `null` directly to value-type parameters when `[DataRow(null)]` is used. The CLR throws `ArgumentNullException` ("Object of type 'System.DBNull' cannot be converted to type 'System.Int32'") at the invocation call-site. WHY it causes problems: the error message mentions `DBNull` (MSTest's internal representation of missing DataRow values) rather than the actual parameter name, making it hard to find the offending `[DataRow]` attribute, especially when the test method has multiple overloads. Fix: use `int?` (nullable value type) as the parameter type in the test method signature when nullable test cases are needed, or use `[DataRow(0)]` as the "null" sentinel for value types with appropriate handling inside the test body.

**Testcontainers.NET `GenericContainer` with `WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilPortIsAvailable(port))` does NOT guarantee the application inside the container is ready to accept requests — it only verifies the OS-level TCP port is LISTENING, not that the application has completed its initialisation and is returning non-error responses [community]** — `UntilPortIsAvailable` performs a TCP connect to the specified port. Some applications (notably Spring Boot, Node.js, and .NET apps) open the TCP listener as the first step of startup, then perform application initialisation (DB migrations, warmup) before serving real requests. A test that connects immediately after `UntilPortIsAvailable` may hit a 503 or connection-reset response for several hundred milliseconds while the application completes its warmup. WHY it causes problems: tests are flaky — they pass when container startup is fast (warm Docker layer cache) and fail when startup is slow (cold CI cache), but the `UntilPortIsAvailable` strategy masks the root cause by reporting "container ready" before the app is actually ready. Fix: use `UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPath("/health").ForStatusCode(200))` from `Testcontainers` wait strategies, or implement a custom `IWaitUntil` that performs an HTTP GET to the application health endpoint and only returns `true` when the response is `200 OK`.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 43 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Reusing `Mock<T>` instances with `SetupSequence` across multiple test methods via static fields or shared fixtures | Sequence counter persists; later tests receive later sequence values or the last-repeated value | Create a fresh `Mock<T>` per test, or call `.Reset()` before each test that configures sequence setups |
| `Wait.ForUnixContainer().UntilPortIsAvailable(port)` for application containers that do warmup after listening | Port opens before app is ready; tests hit 503 or incomplete initialisation responses | Use `UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded` pointing to a `/health` endpoint, or implement `IWaitUntil` with an HTTP ready-check |
| `[DataRow(null)]` with non-nullable value-type test parameters (`int`, `bool`, `decimal`) | Runtime `ArgumentNullException` referencing `DBNull` type; confusing error message | Use nullable value type (`int?`) or a sentinel value (`0`, `false`) with in-test null handling |
| `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` with synchronous throws before first `await` on shared fixtures | xUnit records failure against the fixture class, not individual tests; tests appear as skipped | Ensure first operation in `InitializeAsync` is an `await`; wrap synchronous setup in `await Task.Run(...)` |
| `AllSatisfy(predicate)` when `SatisfyRespectively(pred1, pred2, ...)` is intended for positional assertions | `AllSatisfy` applies same predicate to all; does not verify per-position distinct expectations | Use `SatisfyRespectively` with one predicate per expected element position, preceded by `HaveCount(n)` |
| `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` in Moq `Verify` when the intent is to confirm a real token was forwarded | Passes even when SUT passes `CancellationToken.None`; cancellation propagation is untested | Use `It.Is<CancellationToken>(ct => ct != CancellationToken.None)` or test with a pre-cancelled token |

### Pattern 61 — xUnit v3 `ITestContextAccessor` for Structured Diagnostic Logging in Shared Infrastructure Libraries

xUnit v3 separates diagnostic output from test context via two distinct injectable abstractions: `ITestOutputHelper` (available via constructor injection in test classes) and `ITestContextAccessor` (available via DI in infrastructure libraries that cannot directly reference the test class). `ITestContextAccessor.Current.TestOutputHelper` provides the same `ITestOutputHelper` instance injected into the test class, enabling logging middleware, custom fixtures, and shared setup helpers to write per-test diagnostic lines without any coupling to the test class itself. This is the idiomatic xUnit v3 pattern for library code that wants to emit structured traces into the test run output for a specific test, visible in both the IDE test runner and CI XML output. The accessor is registered automatically in the xUnit v3 DI container when `ITestOutputHelper` is injected into the test class constructor. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;
using Xunit.v3;

// Shared infrastructure helper (lives in a test-helper library, not the test class)
public class DatabaseMigrationHelper(ITestContextAccessor contextAccessor)
{
    public async Task ApplyMigrationsAsync(string connectionString)
    {
        var output = contextAccessor.Current?.TestOutputHelper;
        output?.WriteLine($"[{DateTime.UtcNow:HH:mm:ss.fff}] Applying migrations to {connectionString}");

        await using var db = new MigrationDbContext(connectionString);
        var pending = await db.Database.GetPendingMigrationsAsync();
        output?.WriteLine($"[Migration] Pending: {string.Join(", ", pending)}");

        await db.Database.MigrateAsync();
        output?.WriteLine($"[Migration] Complete.");
    }
}

// Test class — xUnit injects ITestOutputHelper; accessor flows to helper automatically
public class OrderRepositoryTests(ITestOutputHelper output, PostgresFixture pg)
    : IClassFixture<PostgresFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task SaveOrder_PersistsAllFields()
    {
        var helper = new DatabaseMigrationHelper(new TestContextAccessor());
        await helper.ApplyMigrationsAsync(pg.ConnectionString);

        var repo  = new OrderRepository(pg.ConnectionString);
        var order = new Order { CustomerId = 1, TotalAmount = 99.99m };
        await repo.SaveAsync(order);

        var saved = await repo.GetByIdAsync(order.Id);
        Assert.Equal(99.99m, saved!.TotalAmount);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `ITestContextAccessor` decouples shared infrastructure from test classes and removes the need to pass `ITestOutputHelper` through constructor chains. The tradeoff is that `contextAccessor.Current` returns `null` when called outside of an active test execution context (e.g., during fixture `DisposeAsync` after the test runner has moved on) — always null-check before writing. For test classes themselves, prefer direct `ITestOutputHelper` injection for clarity; use `ITestContextAccessor` only in reusable helper or fixture code. [official]

### Pattern 62 — NUnit 4 `[CancelAfter]` Attribute for Per-Test Async Cancellation Timeout Without Manual `CancellationTokenSource`

NUnit 4 introduced the `[CancelAfter(milliseconds)]` attribute which automatically injects a pre-configured `CancellationToken` into async test methods via a `CancellationToken` parameter, cancelling the token after the specified duration without failing the test with a timeout exception — instead giving the test cooperative cancellation semantics. This is distinct from `[Timeout]`, which forcibly aborts the test thread at the deadline. `[CancelAfter]` is the idiomatic pattern when the system under test accepts a `CancellationToken` and the test wants to verify it respects cancellation, or when the test has an async wait that should be bounded but the developer prefers cooperative cleanup over hard abort. The attribute composes with `[Repeat]` for flaky-test stabilisation and with `TestContext.CurrentContext.CancellationToken` for synchronous paths inside otherwise async tests. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestFixture]
public class BackgroundWorkerTests
{
    // NUnit injects the pre-cancelled-after-2s token into the ct parameter
    [Test, CancelAfter(2000)]
    public async Task ProcessBatch_RespectsExternalCancellation(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var worker = new BackgroundBatchWorker();

        // If the worker ignores ct, it will run past 2s and ct is cancelled;
        // the test then asserts that the OperationCanceledException was thrown.
        await Assert.ThatAsync(
            async () => await worker.ProcessBatchAsync(batchSize: 10_000, ct),
            Throws.Nothing,
            "worker should complete a 10k batch within 2 seconds");
    }

    [Test, CancelAfter(500)]
    public async Task FetchLatestPrice_CompletesWithinSla(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var client = new PricingApiClient("https://prices.example.com");
        var price  = await client.GetLatestAsync("BTC-USD", ct);

        Assert.That(price, Is.GreaterThan(0m));
    }

    [Test, CancelAfter(1000)]
    public async Task CancelledToken_CausesWorkerToStopEarly(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var cts    = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
        var worker = new BackgroundBatchWorker();

        // Cancel after first item
        var task = worker.ProcessBatchAsync(batchSize: 1_000_000, cts.Token);
        cts.CancelAfter(50); // cancel quickly

        await Assert.ThatAsync(() => task, Throws.InstanceOf<OperationCanceledException>());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[CancelAfter]` is safer than `[Timeout]` for async tests because it uses cooperative cancellation rather than `Thread.Abort` (removed in .NET 6+). The tradeoff is that tests using `[CancelAfter]` implicitly pass if the system under test ignores the `CancellationToken` and completes before the deadline — the timeout only triggers cancellation, it does not assert the SUT *responded* to it. To verify the SUT actually respects cancellation, pass a pre-cancelled token in a dedicated test rather than relying on `[CancelAfter]`'s deadline. Reserve `[CancelAfter]` for SLA-bounding tests and integration tests with external I/O; for pure cancellation-behaviour tests use a manually-constructed `CancellationTokenSource`. [official]

### Pattern 63 — MSTest v3 `[TestInitialize]` on `async Task` Methods With `IAsyncDisposable` for Resource-Safe Per-Test Setup

MSTest v3 supports `[TestInitialize]` on methods returning `Task` or `ValueTask`, enabling full `await`-based async setup with proper resource cleanup via `IAsyncDisposable`. The pattern combines a `Task`-returning `[TestInitialize]` method that provisions resources (database connections, HTTP clients, containers), stores them in instance fields, and a complementary `[TestCleanup]` returning `Task` that disposes them asynchronously. This avoids the `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` deadlock risk that plagued MSTest v1/v2 async setup patterns and integrates cleanly with `await using` semantics. When combined with `IAsyncDisposable`, the teardown is guaranteed even if the setup partially fails — MSTest v3 calls `[TestCleanup]` regardless of whether `[TestInitialize]` threw. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestClass]
public class ProductApiTests : IAsyncDisposable
{
    private HttpClient      _client  = null!;
    private TestWebAppHost  _host    = null!;

    [TestInitialize]
    public async Task SetUpAsync()
    {
        _host   = await TestWebAppHost.StartAsync();          // async host startup
        _client = _host.CreateClient();
        await _host.SeedProductsAsync(count: 5);              // async seed data
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public async Task GetProducts_Returns200WithFiveItems()
    {
        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/api/products");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<List<Product>>();
        Assert.AreEqual(5, body!.Count);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    public async Task CreateProduct_Returns201WithLocation()
    {
        var dto      = new CreateProductDto("Widget", 9.99m);
        var response = await _client.PostAsJsonAsync("/api/products", dto);

        Assert.AreEqual(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.Created, response.StatusCode);
        Assert.IsNotNull(response.Headers.Location);
    }

    [TestCleanup]
    public async Task TearDownAsync()
    {
        _client.Dispose();
        await _host.DisposeAsync();   // async teardown — waits for graceful stop
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        // Fallback: called if test class is disposed outside test runner lifecycle
        if (_host is not null) await _host.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The async `[TestInitialize]`/`[TestCleanup]` pattern is the cleanest MSTest v3 option for async resource management, but MSTest v3 still creates a new test class instance per test method — meaning `[TestInitialize]` and `[TestCleanup]` run for every test. For expensive resources (containers, HTTP hosts), prefer `[ClassInitialize]`/`[ClassCleanup]` with `static async Task` signatures to amortise the startup cost across all methods in the class, accepting that instance-level isolation must be achieved by other means (e.g., per-test database state reset via `RespawnCheckpoint`). [official]

### Pattern 64 — FluentAssertions v8 `BeEquivalentTo` With `ExcludingMissingMembers` for Partial DTO Contract Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 `BeEquivalentTo` supports an `ExcludingMissingMembers()` equivalency option that allows asserting that a subset of a target object's properties match an anonymous object or partial DTO — without failing for properties present in the target but absent in the expectation. This is the idiomatic pattern for asserting API response contract subsets: "the response must include at least these fields with these values" without requiring the test to enumerate every field in a potentially large response DTO. It eliminates the need for custom anonymous projection or `Excluding(x => x.NonRelevantField)` chains when the important fields are a small subset of a large response type. The option is composable with `Using<T>(comparer)` for custom equality on specific property types. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class UserApiContractTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task CreateUser_ResponseBody_ContainsRequiredContractFields()
    {
        var client   = new ApiTestClient();
        var request  = new CreateUserRequest("alice@example.com", "Alice");
        var response = await client.PostAsync<UserResponse>("/api/users", request);

        // Only assert the contract-relevant fields; ignore internal fields like AuditToken
        response.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
            new { Email = "alice@example.com", Name = "Alice", IsActive = true },
            options => options.ExcludingMissingMembers());
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task UpdateUser_ResponseBody_ReflectsNewName()
    {
        var client  = new ApiTestClient();
        var created = await client.PostAsync<UserResponse>("/api/users",
            new CreateUserRequest("bob@example.com", "Bob"));

        var updated = await client.PutAsync<UserResponse>(
            $"/api/users/{created.Id}",
            new UpdateUserRequest("Robert"));

        // Partial contract: only assert changed field and invariant
        updated.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
            new { Name = "Robert", Email = "bob@example.com" },
            options => options.ExcludingMissingMembers());
    }

    [Fact]
    public void ListUsers_PaginatedResult_ContainsCursorAndCount()
    {
        var page = new PaginatedResult<UserSummary>(
            items: new[] { new UserSummary(1, "Alice") },
            nextCursor: "abc123",
            totalCount: 42);

        page.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
            new { NextCursor = "abc123", TotalCount = 42 },
            options => options.ExcludingMissingMembers());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `ExcludingMissingMembers` makes it easy to write stable contract tests that do not break when new fields are added to a response DTO. The tradeoff is that it can create false confidence: if a required field is accidentally removed from the response, the test still passes because the expectation object does not include that field. For fields that must always be present, add explicit `HaveProperty` or `NotBeNull` assertions in addition to the partial `BeEquivalentTo` check. Use `ExcludingMissingMembers` primarily for additive API evolution contracts where the consumer only cares about a specific subset of fields. [official]

### Pattern 65 — Moq `Mock.Verify` With `Times.Between` for Bounded-Invocation Count Assertions

Moq's `Verify(expression, Times.Between(min, max, Range.Inclusive))` asserts that a method was called between `min` and `max` times inclusive — or exclusive with `Range.Exclusive`. This is the appropriate verification pattern for retry logic, polling loops, throttled consumers, and batch processors where an exact call count is an implementation detail, but the test needs to confirm the SUT stays within safe operational bounds. Using `Times.Between` instead of `Times.Exactly` makes tests resilient to minor algorithm changes (e.g., retry count tuning) while still catching regressions where zero calls or unbounded calls indicate a logic defect. It composes with `It.Is<T>` argument matchers for bounded-call assertions on specific argument values. [official]

```csharp
using Moq;
using System;
using Xunit;

public class RetryPolicyTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FetchData_OnTransientFailure_RetriesBetween1And3Times()
    {
        var mockHttp = new Mock<IHttpDataSource>();
        int callCount = 0;

        mockHttp
            .Setup(h => h.FetchAsync(It.IsAny<string>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(() =>
            {
                callCount++;
                if (callCount < 3) throw new TransientException("retry me");
                return new DataPayload("success");
            });

        var service = new ResilientDataService(mockHttp.Object, maxRetries: 3);
        var result  = await service.GetDataAsync("endpoint");

        Assert.Equal("success", result.Value);

        // Between 1 and 3 retries before success — exact count is an impl detail
        mockHttp.Verify(
            h => h.FetchAsync("endpoint"),
            Times.Between(1, 3, Range.Inclusive),
            "service must retry transient failures at least once but not more than 3 times");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task SendNotification_ThrottledChannel_CallsAtMostFiveTimesPerBatch()
    {
        var mockChannel = new Mock<INotificationChannel>();
        mockChannel.Setup(c => c.SendAsync(It.IsAny<Notification>()))
                   .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

        var sender = new ThrottledNotificationSender(mockChannel.Object, maxPerBatch: 5);
        await sender.DispatchBatchAsync(Enumerable.Range(0, 10)
            .Select(i => new Notification($"msg-{i}")).ToList());

        // Only first 5 should be sent; remaining 5 are queued for next batch
        mockChannel.Verify(
            c => c.SendAsync(It.IsAny<Notification>()),
            Times.Between(1, 5, Range.Inclusive));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `Times.Between` is more expressive than `Times.AtLeast(1)` when both a lower and upper bound matter (e.g., retry capping). The tradeoff is that it can hide regressions if the bounds are set too loosely — always use the tightest bounds that are still correct for the algorithm being tested. For deterministic algorithms where the exact count is stable across all valid inputs, `Times.Exactly` remains preferable. Use `Times.Between` specifically for non-deterministic-count scenarios: retries, polling intervals, and throttled dispatchers. [official]

### Pattern 66 — Testcontainers.NET `MySqlContainer` With Schema Migration Verification for Database Upgrade Tests

Testcontainers.NET provides a `MySqlContainer` module that starts a real MySQL instance in Docker, applies schema migrations via `DbUp` or EF Core `MigrateAsync`, then runs assertions directly against the live database to verify migration idempotency, rollback behavior, and post-migration data integrity. This pattern is the standard approach for testing database upgrade scripts in CI without requiring a shared or pre-existing MySQL instance. The container accepts `WithDatabase`, `WithUsername`, `WithPassword` configuration fluently, and `GetConnectionString()` returns a `MySql.Data` or `Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql`-compatible connection string. Pairing `MySqlContainer` with a "before/after migration" snapshot comparison detects accidental column drops and type changes that EF Core `MigrateAsync` would otherwise silently apply. [official]

```csharp
using Testcontainers.MySql;
using Xunit;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class SchemaUpgradeTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MySqlContainer _mysql = new MySqlBuilder()
        .WithDatabase("shopdb")
        .WithUsername("root")
        .WithPassword("root")
        .WithImage("mysql:8.0")
        .Build();

    public Task InitializeAsync() => _mysql.StartAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()    => _mysql.DisposeAsync().AsTask();

    [Fact]
    public async Task Migration_V1_to_V2_AddsOrderTotalColumn()
    {
        var cs        = _mysql.GetConnectionString();
        var optionsV1 = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<ShopDbContextV1>()
            .UseMySql(cs, ServerVersion.AutoDetect(cs)).Options;

        await using (var ctxV1 = new ShopDbContextV1(optionsV1))
            await ctxV1.Database.MigrateAsync();

        var columnsV1 = await GetColumnsAsync(cs, "Orders");
        Assert.DoesNotContain("OrderTotal", columnsV1);

        var optionsV2 = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<ShopDbContextV2>()
            .UseMySql(cs, ServerVersion.AutoDetect(cs)).Options;

        await using var ctxV2 = new ShopDbContextV2(optionsV2);
        await ctxV2.Database.MigrateAsync();

        var columnsV2 = await GetColumnsAsync(cs, "Orders");
        Assert.Contains("OrderTotal", columnsV2);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Migration_IsIdempotent_WhenAppliedTwice()
    {
        var cs      = _mysql.GetConnectionString();
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<ShopDbContextV2>()
            .UseMySql(cs, ServerVersion.AutoDetect(cs)).Options;

        await using var ctx = new ShopDbContextV2(options);
        await ctx.Database.MigrateAsync();
        await ctx.Database.MigrateAsync(); // second run — should be a no-op without error
    }

    private static async Task<IReadOnlyList<string>> GetColumnsAsync(string cs, string table)
    {
        await using var conn = new MySqlConnector.MySqlConnection(cs);
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        await using var cmd  = conn.CreateCommand();
        cmd.CommandText      =
            $"SELECT COLUMN_NAME FROM information_schema.COLUMNS WHERE TABLE_NAME='{table}'";
        var results = new List<string>();
        await using var rdr = await cmd.ExecuteReaderAsync();
        while (await rdr.ReadAsync()) results.Add(rdr.GetString(0));
        return results;
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `MySqlContainer` is the highest-fidelity migration test because it runs against the real MySQL engine, catching MySQL-specific SQL syntax errors that SQLite in-memory tests would never surface. The tradeoff is startup time (10–30 seconds for MySQL image pull + init on first CI run) — mitigate with `WithReuse(true)` in local development and shared Docker layer caching in CI. For teams that do not use MySQL, the same pattern applies to `PostgreSqlContainer`, `MsSqlContainer`, and `MariaDbContainer` from the same Testcontainers.NET package family. [official]

---

### Pattern 67 — xUnit v3 `[Theory]` With `TheoryData<T>` and Named Record Arguments for Self-Documenting Parameterised Tests

xUnit v3 `TheoryData<T>` can be populated with C# record instances, allowing each theory row to carry named properties rather than anonymous positional arguments. When `T` is a record type, the xUnit v3 test runner serialises the record's `ToString()` representation as the theory test display name — giving human-readable test names like `ShouldApplyDiscount(DiscountScenario { CustomerId = 1, OrderTotal = 200, ExpectedDiscount = 20 })` in the IDE and CI output, without any custom `IXunitSerializable` implementation. This eliminates the need for the separate `[MemberData]` + `Label` pattern when the record's own `ToString()` is already informative. The pattern also composes with `[ClassData]` for large test matrices stored in separate classes. [official]

```csharp
using Xunit;

public record DiscountScenario(
    string  Description,
    int     CustomerId,
    decimal OrderTotal,
    decimal ExpectedDiscount);

public class DiscountCalculatorTests
{
    public static TheoryData<DiscountScenario> Scenarios => new()
    {
        new DiscountScenario("VIP + large order",     CustomerId: 1,  OrderTotal: 500m, ExpectedDiscount: 75m),
        new DiscountScenario("Regular + small order", CustomerId: 99, OrderTotal: 20m,  ExpectedDiscount: 0m),
        new DiscountScenario("VIP + small order",     CustomerId: 1,  OrderTotal: 50m,  ExpectedDiscount: 5m),
        new DiscountScenario("New + promo code",      CustomerId: 42, OrderTotal: 100m, ExpectedDiscount: 15m),
    };

    [Theory, MemberData(nameof(Scenarios))]
    public void Calculate_AppliesCorrectDiscount(DiscountScenario scenario)
    {
        var calc   = new DiscountCalculator();
        var actual = calc.Calculate(scenario.CustomerId, scenario.OrderTotal);

        Assert.Equal(scenario.ExpectedDiscount, actual,
            precision: 2,
            userMessage: $"Failed for: {scenario.Description}");
    }

    [Theory, MemberData(nameof(Scenarios))]
    public void Calculate_NeverExceedsOrderTotal(DiscountScenario scenario)
    {
        var calc   = new DiscountCalculator();
        var actual = calc.Calculate(scenario.CustomerId, scenario.OrderTotal);

        Assert.True(actual <= scenario.OrderTotal,
            $"Discount {actual} exceeds order total {scenario.OrderTotal}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Named record arguments produce excellent test display names and group related scenario data in a type-safe way. The tradeoff is that records with many properties produce verbose `ToString()` outputs that can be truncated in some CI dashboard displays. For scenarios with more than six properties, define a `ToString()` override on the record that returns just the `Description` field to keep test names concise. Also note that xUnit v3's serialisation of record types requires all constructor parameter types to be serialisable — avoid record properties of custom class types unless those types implement `IXunitSerializable`. [official]
