### Pattern 68 — NUnit 4 `TestCaseData` With `SetName` and `SetDescription` for Enriched Parameterised Test Metadata

NUnit 4 `TestCaseData` supports `SetName(string)`, `SetDescription(string)`, and `SetCategory(string)` builder methods, allowing test data factories to embed display name, documentation string, and category tag directly on each test case row without polluting the test method with complex `[TestCase]` attribute overloads. This is particularly useful for `[TestCaseSource]` methods that generate test cases from external data (CSV, JSON) where the test row should carry its own human-readable label derived from domain data. `SetDescription` appears in NUnit's XML result output alongside the test name, enabling test report post-processors to link test cases to requirements. The `SetCategory` builder on `TestCaseData` is equivalent to applying `[Category]` to individual data rows, enabling per-row CI filter tags. [official]

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Collections.Generic;

[TestFixture]
public class TaxCalculatorTests
{
    private static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> TaxScenarios()
    {
        yield return new TestCaseData("US", 50_000m, 7_500m)
            .SetName("US | $50k income → $7.5k tax")
            .SetDescription("Standard US federal bracket for $50k income")
            .SetCategory("unit");

        yield return new TestCaseData("DE", 60_000m, 14_000m)
            .SetName("DE | €60k income → €14k tax")
            .SetDescription("German progressive rate for €60k income")
            .SetCategory("unit");

        yield return new TestCaseData("GB", 45_000m, 6_750m)
            .SetName("GB | £45k income → £6.75k tax")
            .SetDescription("UK basic rate above personal allowance for £45k")
            .SetCategory("unit");

        yield return new TestCaseData("AU", 80_000m, 17_547m)
            .SetName("AU | A$80k income → A$17.5k tax")
            .SetDescription("Australian 2024/25 bracket for A$80k")
            .SetCategory("integration")
            .Explicit("Pending ATO rate table update");
    }

    [TestCaseSource(nameof(TaxScenarios))]
    public void Calculate_ReturnsExpectedTax(string country, decimal income, decimal expected)
    {
        var calculator = new TaxCalculator();
        var actual     = calculator.Calculate(country, income);

        Assert.That(actual, Is.EqualTo(expected).Within(0.01m),
            $"Tax mismatch for {country} income={income}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `TestCaseData` with `SetName`/`SetDescription` produces excellent CI report output and supports per-row explicit marking (`.Explicit("reason")`). The tradeoff is verbosity: each row requires more code than a simple `[TestCase(arg1, arg2, ExpectedResult = ...)]` attribute. Reserve `TestCaseData` for complex multi-argument scenarios, externally-sourced data, or rows that need individual category or explicit tags. For simple 2–3 parameter rows with no per-row metadata needs, `[TestCase]` remains more readable. [official]

---

### Pattern 69 — FluentAssertions v8 `ExecutionTimeOf` for Performance Regression Guardrails in Unit Tests

FluentAssertions v8 `ExecutionTimeOf(action)` and `subject.ExecutionTime()` measure the wall-clock time for a delegate to complete and assert it is `BeLessThanOrEqualTo(TimeSpan)` or `BeCloseTo(TimeSpan, precision)`. While not a replacement for `BenchmarkDotNet`, the pattern is appropriate for detecting severe regressions in algorithms that are sensitive to O(n²) growth — a test that seeds 1000 items and asserts completion within 500ms will fail if a quadratic regression is introduced but pass if the algorithm stays linear. Combining `ExecutionTimeOf` with a `[Category("perf-guard")]` attribute allows CI pipelines to run or skip these tests independently from the main unit test suite. The `BeCloseTo` overload is particularly useful for asserting that two implementations have comparable performance (within ±20%) rather than an absolute wall-clock limit. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;
using System;
using System.Linq;

public class SortingPerformanceTests
{
    [Fact]
    [Trait("Category", "perf-guard")]
    public void BucketSort_1000Items_CompletesWithin100ms()
    {
        var rng   = new Random(42);
        var input = Enumerable.Range(0, 1_000)
                              .Select(_ => rng.Next(0, 10_000))
                              .ToArray();
        var sorter = new BucketSorter();

        // Wall-clock assertion — catches O(n²) regression
        Action sort = () => sorter.Sort(input);
        sort.ExecutionTime().Should().BeLessThanOrEqualTo(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100),
            because: "bucket sort of 1000 items must stay under 100ms to meet SLA");
    }

    [Fact]
    [Trait("Category", "perf-guard")]
    public void BatchImport_10kRecords_CompletesWithin5Seconds()
    {
        var records = Enumerable.Range(0, 10_000)
                                .Select(i => new ImportRecord($"SKU-{i}", i * 1.5m))
                                .ToList();
        var importer = new BatchImporter(new InMemoryProductRepository());

        Action importAll = () => importer.Import(records);
        importAll.ExecutionTime().Should().BeLessThanOrEqualTo(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
    }

    [Fact]
    [Trait("Category", "perf-guard")]
    public void NewAlgorithm_IsNotSlowerThan_LegacyAlgorithm_Beyond20Percent()
    {
        var data    = Enumerable.Range(0, 5_000).Select(i => (double)i).ToArray();
        var legacy  = new LegacyStatisticsCalculator();
        var updated = new OptimisedStatisticsCalculator();

        var legacyTime  = FluentActions.Invoking(() => legacy.ComputeMedian(data))
                          .ExecutionTime();
        var updatedTime = FluentActions.Invoking(() => updated.ComputeMedian(data))
                          .ExecutionTime();

        updatedTime.Should().BeLessThanOrEqualTo(
            legacyTime.Multiply(1.2),
            because: "new algorithm must not be more than 20% slower than legacy");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `ExecutionTimeOf` is suitable for coarse-grained regression detection in CI but inherently noisy: a single measurement on a shared CI runner is susceptible to OS scheduling jitter, JIT warm-up variance, and competing processes. Set thresholds at 5–10× the median expected execution time (not the minimum) to avoid spurious failures. For precise micro-benchmarks (nanosecond-level algorithms), use `BenchmarkDotNet` with `[MemoryDiagnoser]` in a dedicated benchmark project. Never run `ExecutionTimeOf` assertions in parallel test runs without `[Collection("sequential")]` isolation, as resource contention inflates measurements. [official]

---

### Pattern 70 — Moq `Callback<T>` With `TaskCompletionSource` for Async Continuation Verification

Moq's `Callback<T>(action)` captures arguments passed to mocked methods during setup — not only for synchronous verification after the fact, but as a hook to drive async test flow by signalling continuations. The `ArgumentCaptor` pattern stores captured values in a `List<T>` field and uses a `TaskCompletionSource` to signal the test when a specific argument arrives, enabling "wait until the SUT calls the dependency with argument X" flows without polling or `Task.Delay` sleeps. This avoids `Thread.Sleep` in async integration test scenarios where the SUT invokes a dependency asynchronously after receiving an event, and the test needs to assert the argument value after the async chain completes. [community]

```csharp
using Moq;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;

public class OrderEventHandlerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task HandleOrderPlaced_PublishesEnrichedEventToOutbox()
    {
        // Arrange
        var capturedMessages = new List<OutboxMessage>();
        var published        = new TaskCompletionSource<OutboxMessage>(
            TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);

        var mockOutbox = new Mock<IOutboxRepository>();
        mockOutbox
            .Setup(o => o.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<OutboxMessage>()))
            .Callback<OutboxMessage>(msg =>
            {
                capturedMessages.Add(msg);
                published.TrySetResult(msg);  // signal arrival
            })
            .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

        var handler = new OrderEventHandler(mockOutbox.Object, new ProductEnricher());

        // Act: fire domain event asynchronously
        await handler.HandleAsync(new OrderPlacedEvent(
            OrderId: 99, CustomerId: 1, Sku: "WIDGET-A", Quantity: 3));

        // Wait for the async chain to publish — timeout guard with cancellation
        var cts     = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
        var message = await published.Task.WaitAsync(cts.Token);

        // Assert enriched values were written to outbox
        Assert.Equal("OrderPlaced", message.EventType);
        Assert.Equal(99, message.AggregateId);
        Assert.NotNull(message.EnrichedPayload);
        mockOutbox.Verify(o => o.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<OutboxMessage>()), Times.Once);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** The `Callback` + `TaskCompletionSource` pattern is the cleanest way to assert async side-effects without sleeping. The tradeoff is complexity: the test has two sources of truth (the `capturedMessages` list and the `published` task), which must both be consulted. If the SUT calls `SaveAsync` multiple times, `TrySetResult` silently ignores subsequent calls — use `SetResult` to throw `InvalidOperationException` on duplicate signals if strict single-call semantics are required. For simpler cases where the SUT's return value carries the evidence (not a side-effecting call to a dependency), prefer direct `Assert` on the return value rather than `Callback` capture. [community]

---

### Pattern 71 — .NET 9/10 `IMemoryOwner<T>` Pooled Buffer Testing With Disposal Spy for Leak Detection

.NET's `System.Buffers.MemoryPool<byte>.Shared` underpins high-performance streaming code. Testing classes that use `IMemoryOwner<T>` or rent buffers from `ArrayPool` requires verifying both correctness of the data written into the rented buffer and that buffers are returned (not leaked). The pattern uses `MemoryPool<T>.Shared.Rent(minimumLength)` in the test to provide the buffer, then asserts `Memory<T>.Span` contents after the SUT writes into it; buffer leaks are detected by wrapping the `IMemoryOwner<T>` in a test-tracking `DisposeSpy`. This avoids allocating test-private byte arrays that do not exercise the pooled code path and catches cases where the SUT forgets to call `owner.Dispose()`. [official]

```csharp
using System;
using System.Buffers;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

// Spy wrapper that tracks disposal
public sealed class DisposeSpy<T>(IMemoryOwner<T> inner) : IMemoryOwner<T>
{
    public bool     IsDisposed { get; private set; }
    public Memory<T> Memory    => inner.Memory;

    public void Dispose()
    {
        IsDisposed = true;
        inner.Dispose();
    }
}

public class ProtocolFramerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void WriteFrame_FillsHeaderBytesCorrectly()
    {
        using var spy = new DisposeSpy<byte>(MemoryPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64));
        var framer    = new ProtocolFramer();

        framer.WriteFrame(spy.Memory, payloadLength: 42, messageType: 0x01);

        var span = spy.Memory.Span;
        span[0].Should().Be(0xFF, because: "magic byte must be 0xFF");
        span[1].Should().Be(0x01, because: "message type must match");
        BitConverter.ToInt32(span[2..6]).Should().Be(42,
            because: "payload length encoded in bytes 2–5");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void WriteFrame_DoesNotLeakBuffer_WhenDisposingOwner()
    {
        var spy    = new DisposeSpy<byte>(MemoryPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(128));
        var framer = new ProtocolFramer();

        framer.WriteFrame(spy.Memory, payloadLength: 10, messageType: 0x02);
        spy.Dispose();

        spy.IsDisposed.Should().BeTrue(
            because: "framer must not prevent buffer disposal");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void RoundTrip_WriteAndRead_PreservesPayloadIntegrity()
    {
        var payload = new byte[] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
        using var writeOwner = MemoryPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64);

        var framer  = new ProtocolFramer();
        framer.WriteFrame(writeOwner.Memory, payload);

        var decoded = framer.ReadFrame(writeOwner.Memory.Slice(0, 9 + payload.Length));
        decoded.Should().BeEquivalentTo(payload);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Testing with `MemoryPool<T>` exercises the same code path as production, catching bugs where the SUT writes beyond the rented buffer length. The tradeoff is that test assertions on `Memory<T>.Span` require careful slicing to avoid reading uninitialised bytes beyond the logical payload — always slice the memory to the known logical size before asserting content with `BeEquivalentTo`. Use `DisposeSpy` to detect buffer leaks in tests that cover resource-constrained producers. [official]

---

### Pattern 72 — xUnit v3 `ICollectionFixture<T>` With `IAsyncLifetime` for Stateful Integration Test Suites Across Multiple Test Classes

xUnit v3's `[Collection("DatabaseSuite")]` combined with `ICollectionFixture<T>` where `T : IAsyncLifetime` enables multiple test classes to share a single expensive fixture (e.g., a seeded database container) that is initialised once before any test in the collection and torn down after all tests complete. The key distinction from `IClassFixture<T>` is that collection fixtures are shared across classes, not just within one class — enabling test suites that split integration tests into `OrderTests`, `CustomerTests`, and `ProductTests` classes while reusing one PostgreSQL container. xUnit v3 calls `InitializeAsync` exactly once per collection, even when tests from multiple classes run in parallel within the collection. [official]

```csharp
using Testcontainers.PostgreSql;
using Xunit;

// The shared fixture — started once for the entire collection
public class DatabaseFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _postgres = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
        .WithDatabase("testdb")
        .WithUsername("tester")
        .WithPassword("secret")
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _postgres.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _postgres.StartAsync();
        await using var ctx = new AppDbContext(ConnectionString);
        await ctx.Database.MigrateAsync();
        await ctx.SeedTestDataAsync();
    }

    public Task DisposeAsync() => _postgres.DisposeAsync().AsTask();
}

[CollectionDefinition("DatabaseSuite")]
public class DatabaseCollection : ICollectionFixture<DatabaseFixture> { }

// Test class 1 — shares the same container via collection
[Collection("DatabaseSuite")]
public class OrderIntegrationTests(DatabaseFixture db)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrder_ReturnsSeededOrder()
    {
        var repo  = new OrderRepository(db.ConnectionString);
        var order = await repo.GetByIdAsync(1);
        Assert.NotNull(order);
    }
}

// Test class 2 — same container, different domain
[Collection("DatabaseSuite")]
public class CustomerIntegrationTests(DatabaseFixture db)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetCustomer_ReturnsSeededCustomer()
    {
        var repo     = new CustomerRepository(db.ConnectionString);
        var customer = await repo.GetByIdAsync(1);
        Assert.NotNull(customer);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** Sharing a single database container across multiple test classes dramatically reduces integration test suite startup time (one container start vs N). The tradeoff is test isolation: tests share the seeded data, so a test that mutates state can corrupt subsequent tests in the same collection. Mitigate with per-test transaction rollback (`DbContext.Database.BeginTransaction()` + rollback in `DisposeAsync`), `RespawnCheckpoint` reset, or by structuring each test to be additive-only. For tests that require pristine state per class, prefer `IClassFixture<T>` with its own container instance. [official]

---

### Pattern 73 — MSTest v3 `[AssemblyInitialize]` With `TestContext.Properties` for Environment-Driven Test Configuration

MSTest v3 `[AssemblyInitialize]` on a `static async Task` method provides a single entry point for assembly-wide one-time setup that reads `TestContext.Properties` (populated from `.runsettings` `<TestRunParameters>`) to configure environment-specific behaviour: connection strings, base URLs, feature flags, and external service endpoints. This is the MSTest equivalent of xUnit's `IAssemblyFixture<T>` and NUnit's `[SetUpFixture]` — and the only MSTest mechanism where `TestContext` is available before any test method runs. Combining `[AssemblyInitialize]` with `TestContext.Properties["EnvironmentName"]` allows a single test assembly to run against dev, staging, and production environments from the same `.runsettings` file without code changes. [official]

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestClass]
public static class TestAssemblySetup
{
    public static string ApiBaseUrl { get; private set; } = "http://localhost:5000";
    public static string DatabaseCs { get; private set; } = "Server=localhost;Database=appdb;";

    [AssemblyInitialize]
    public static async Task InitialiseTestRun(TestContext ctx)
    {
        // Read from .runsettings <TestRunParameters> section
        ApiBaseUrl = ctx.Properties["ApiBaseUrl"]?.ToString() ?? ApiBaseUrl;
        DatabaseCs = ctx.Properties["DatabaseCs"]?.ToString() ?? DatabaseCs;

        var env = ctx.Properties["EnvironmentName"]?.ToString() ?? "local";
        ctx.WriteLine($"[AssemblyInit] Running against environment: {env}");
        ctx.WriteLine($"[AssemblyInit] API base URL: {ApiBaseUrl}");

        // Warm up the API (avoids cold-start penalty on first test)
        using var client   = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(ApiBaseUrl) };
        using var response = await client.GetAsync("/health");
        if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
            throw new InvalidOperationException(
                $"Health check failed with {response.StatusCode} — aborting test run");

        ctx.WriteLine($"[AssemblyInit] Health check passed: {response.StatusCode}");
    }

    [AssemblyCleanup]
    public static async Task CleanUpTestRun()
    {
        await Task.CompletedTask; // async cleanup placeholder
    }
}

[TestClass]
public class OrderApiTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    public async Task GetOrders_Returns200()
    {
        using var client   = new HttpClient
            { BaseAddress = new Uri(TestAssemblySetup.ApiBaseUrl) };
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/orders");
        Assert.AreEqual(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `[AssemblyInitialize]` with `TestRunParameters` is the cleanest way to inject environment configuration into MSTest suites without environment variables or hardcoded strings. The tradeoff is discoverability: `TestContext.Properties` values are stringly-typed and only validated at runtime — a typo in a parameter name silently falls back to the default value. Mitigate by logging all resolved values in `[AssemblyInitialize]` and by writing a separate smoke test that asserts expected keys are present. Also note that `[AssemblyInitialize]` runs exactly once per process — it is not re-run between `dotnet test` invocations in the same CI job unless the assembly is re-loaded. [official]

---

### Pattern 74 — FluentAssertions v8 `NotThrowAsync` + `CompleteWithinAsync` for Async Method SLA Assertions

FluentAssertions v8 provides `Awaiting(func).Should().NotThrowAsync()` for asserting an async method completes without exceptions, and `CompleteWithinAsync(TimeSpan)` for asserting it completes before a wall-clock deadline. Chaining `CompleteWithinAsync` in a single expression — `await subject.Awaiting(s => s.ProcessAsync()).Should().CompleteWithinAsync(2.Seconds())` — gives both a timing SLA and an exception contract in one assertion line. This is cleaner than wrapping the call in `Task.WhenAny` + `Task.Delay` idioms and produces a failure message that distinguishes between "threw an exception" and "timed out" rather than a generic `True` assertion failure. [official]

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;

public class DataIngestionServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task IngestAsync_SmallBatch_CompletesWithin2Seconds()
    {
        var service = new DataIngestionService(new FakeDataStore());
        var records = GenerateRecords(count: 100);

        // Assert: completes within SLA AND does not throw
        await service
            .Awaiting(s => s.IngestAsync(records))
            .Should().CompleteWithinAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2),
                because: "100-record batches must complete under 2s SLA");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task IngestAsync_NullBatch_ThrowsArgumentNullExceptionQuickly()
    {
        var service = new DataIngestionService(new FakeDataStore());

        await service
            .Awaiting(s => s.IngestAsync(null!))
            .Should().ThrowAsync<ArgumentNullException>()
            .WithMessage("*records*");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task CancelledToken_CausesEarlyExit_WithOperationCancelledException()
    {
        var service = new DataIngestionService(new SlowFakeDataStore(delayMs: 5000));
        var cts     = new CancellationTokenSource();
        cts.CancelAfter(100); // cancel quickly

        await service
            .Awaiting(s => s.IngestAsync(GenerateRecords(1000), cts.Token))
            .Should().ThrowAsync<OperationCanceledException>();
    }

    private static List<DataRecord> GenerateRecords(int count) =>
        Enumerable.Range(0, count)
                  .Select(i => new DataRecord($"key-{i}", $"value-{i}"))
                  .ToList();
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `CompleteWithinAsync` is subject to the same CI jitter caveat as `ExecutionTimeOf` — set thresholds generously (5–10× the expected p95 completion time) to avoid flaky failures on slow runners. The key advantage over `Assert.True(await Task.WhenAny(task, Task.Delay(2000)) == task)` is the descriptive failure message that names the timeout as the cause. Do not use `CompleteWithinAsync` as a substitute for proper load tests — it measures wall-clock time on a single test thread. Reserve it for documenting SLA contracts in unit/integration tests and combine with `[Trait("Category", "sla-guard")]` to enable selective CI execution. [official]

---

### Pattern 75 — Testcontainers.NET `RedisContainer` With `StackExchange.Redis` for Distributed Cache Integration Tests

Testcontainers.NET's `RedisContainer` module starts a real Redis instance for integration tests that use `IDistributedCache`, `StackExchange.Redis`, or `IConnectionMultiplexer`-based caching logic. Tests connect via `GetConnectionString()`, create a `ConnectionMultiplexer`, and assert cache reads, writes, TTL expiry, and pub/sub message delivery against a live Redis engine — catching bugs in serialisation, key-naming conventions, and TTL logic that in-memory `IDistributedCache` stubs cannot detect. Combining `RedisContainer` with `FakeTimeProvider` allows testing cache-expiry logic by fast-forwarding time without waiting for real TTL expiry. [official]

```csharp
using Testcontainers.Redis;
using StackExchange.Redis;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.StackExchangeRedis;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using FluentAssertions;
using System;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Xunit;

public class ProductCacheTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly RedisContainer _redis = new RedisBuilder()
        .WithImage("redis:7-alpine")
        .Build();

    private IConnectionMultiplexer _mux = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _redis.StartAsync();
        _mux = await ConnectionMultiplexer.ConnectAsync(_redis.GetConnectionString());
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _mux.DisposeAsync();
        await _redis.DisposeAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task SetAndGet_StringValue_RoundTripsCorrectly()
    {
        var db = _mux.GetDatabase();

        await db.StringSetAsync("product:1:name", "Widget A");
        var value = await db.StringGetAsync("product:1:name");

        value.Should().Be("Widget A");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task SetWithTtl_KeyExpires_AfterDeadline()
    {
        var db = _mux.GetDatabase();

        await db.StringSetAsync("session:abc", "user-123", TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
        var beforeExpiry = await db.StringGetAsync("session:abc");
        beforeExpiry.HasValue.Should().BeTrue();

        await Task.Delay(150); // real TTL wait — Redis enforces actual expiry
        var afterExpiry = await db.StringGetAsync("session:abc");
        afterExpiry.HasValue.Should().BeFalse(
            because: "TTL expired after 100ms");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task ProductCacheService_UsesRedis_WithIDistributedCacheAdapter()
    {
        var services = new ServiceCollection();
        services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(opt =>
            opt.Configuration = _redis.GetConnectionString());

        var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
        var cache    = provider.GetRequiredService<
            Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Distributed.IDistributedCache>();
        var svc = new ProductCacheService(cache);

        await svc.CacheProductAsync(new Product(1, "Gadget", 29.99m));
        var cached = await svc.GetProductAsync(1);

        cached.Should().NotBeNull();
        cached!.Name.Should().Be("Gadget");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff / when to use:** `RedisContainer` provides the highest-fidelity Redis test environment and catches production bugs that `MemoryDistributedCache` silently hides — particularly around TTL semantics (in-memory cache uses sliding vs absolute expiry differently from Redis), key eviction under `maxmemory-policy`, and pub/sub ordering. The tradeoff is startup time (2–5 seconds for Redis alpine) and the need for Docker in CI. Use `WithReuse(true)` in local development to keep the container alive between test runs. For tests that only need to verify serialisation logic, mock `IDistributedCache` directly to avoid the container overhead. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 44

**xUnit v3 `[Collection]` does NOT prevent parallelism between tests WITHIN the same class — it only prevents parallelism between different test classes in the same collection. Two `[Fact]` methods in different classes sharing the same `[Collection]` tag can still run in parallel unless `DisableParallelization = true` is set on the `[CollectionDefinition]` [community]** — Many developers assume that adding `[Collection("DatabaseSuite")]` to a test class serialises ALL tests globally, but xUnit's parallelism model has two levels: collection-level (different collections run in parallel by default) and class-level (classes in the same collection can run in parallel). WHY it causes problems: shared mutable state — a static field, singleton service, or shared container's seeded data — is mutated by two tests in different classes of the same collection simultaneously, producing interference failures that look like data corruption or race conditions. Fix: use `[CollectionDefinition("DatabaseSuite", DisableParallelization = true)]` to force serial execution across all classes in the collection, or implement per-test state isolation (transactions, unique key prefixes) so concurrent test execution is safe.

**FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` with `ExcludingMissingMembers` STILL compares members present in BOTH the expectation and the subject using deep structural equality — it does NOT skip members that are present in the expectation but absent from the subject, and such members throw `MissingMemberException` at assertion time [community]** — Teams using anonymous objects as expectations (e.g., `new { Name = "Alice" }`) sometimes expect that any property present in the expectation but missing from the subject will also be "excluded". In fact, `ExcludingMissingMembers` only excludes members that are in the SUBJECT but not in the EXPECTATION — not the reverse. WHY it causes problems: refactoring the subject DTO to remove a property that was in the test's expectation object causes a `MissingMemberException` at assertion time, not a clear "property was removed" message, and the error mentions the expectation type (anonymous) rather than the subject type — making the root cause hard to identify. Fix: keep expectation objects minimal (only include contractually required properties) and run the test suite after DTO refactors to catch missing-property failures before code review.

**Moq `ReturnsAsync(value)` on an `async Task<T>` setup does NOT call a factory on each invocation — when passed a pre-computed value, the same object reference is returned for every call. Mutating the returned object in the test (or in the SUT) affects all subsequent invocations [community]** — `ReturnsAsync(value)` captures the value at setup time and returns the same reference on every call. If the SUT modifies the returned object (e.g., setting a property, adding to a list), a second test invocation that calls the same mocked method receives the already-mutated object. WHY it causes problems: the second test asserts a state that was established by the first invocation's side effects, not by the test's own arrange phase — a classic order-dependent test failure. Fix: use `ReturnsAsync(() => new MyObject(...))` (lambda overload) to generate a fresh instance on each invocation, or create a new `Mock<T>` per test method.

**NUnit 4 `Assume.That` does NOT produce a "skipped" result in all test runners — when run via `dotnet test` with certain Azure DevOps configurations, a failing `Assume.That` is reported as "Inconclusive" which some CI dashboards count as a failure rather than a skip [community]** — NUnit's `Assume.That` throws `InconclusiveException` when the assumption fails, which NUnit records as "Inconclusive". The NUnit3TestAdapter for VSTest translates "Inconclusive" to `TestOutcome.Skipped` for most CI systems, but certain configurations (Azure DevOps with "Fail on Inconclusive" result mapping, or custom test result parsers) treat `Inconclusive` as a test failure. WHY it causes problems: environment-dependent tests that use `Assume.That` to guard against missing infrastructure show as failures in CI environments without that infrastructure, causing the build to fail instead of skipping gracefully. Fix: document the expected `Inconclusive` outcomes in the CI pipeline configuration, or use `Assert.Ignore("reason")` explicitly combined with a known CI adapter mapping setting.

**MSTest v3 `[AssemblyInitialize]` static fields are silently skipped as uninitialized when running individual test methods via "Run Test" in Visual Studio if the static initialiser class is not discovered in the isolated test execution scope — causing `NullReferenceException` on fields populated by `[AssemblyInitialize]` [community]** — Visual Studio's "Run Test" context menu invokes MSTest's runner with `--filter` scoped to a single method. While `[AssemblyInitialize]` is still technically invoked, static fields populated there may not be visible if the bootstrap class is in a separately-loaded assembly or if test discovery order changes. WHY it causes problems: developers run individual failing tests in isolation and get a `NullReferenceException` (NPE) that does not reflect the actual test failure, wasting debugging time chasing a false root cause. Fix: always null-check static resources populated by `[AssemblyInitialize]` and throw a descriptive `InvalidOperationException("Assembly initialiser did not run — execute the full class or assembly")` rather than NPE; alternatively, move resource resolution into `Lazy<T>` fields that initialise on first access.

**Testcontainers.NET `WithReuse(true)` does NOT reuse containers that were started with a different builder configuration — the container identity is computed from the full builder configuration hash including image tag, environment variables, and port bindings. Upgrading the image version leaves the old container running orphaned [community]** — `WithReuse(true)` attaches a hash label to the container computed from the full `ContainerBuilder` configuration. On subsequent runs, if a running container matches the hash, it is reused. When developers upgrade the image version in the builder but forget that `WithReuse(true)` is active, both the old and new containers are running — consuming memory and port bindings. WHY it causes problems: the test connects to the NEW container (matching its config hash) but the old container remains, accumulating across runs until Docker resources are exhausted, leading to port-binding failures or OOM errors on developer machines. Fix: run `docker container prune --filter "label=org.testcontainers.reuse=true"` periodically in CI setup scripts, and document image version bumps as requiring a container cleanup step.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 44 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `[Collection("X")]` without `DisableParallelization = true` on the `[CollectionDefinition]` when tests share mutable state across classes | Classes in the same collection still run in parallel by default; cross-class state interference causes non-deterministic failures | Add `DisableParallelization = true` to `[CollectionDefinition]` or implement per-test state isolation (transactions, unique key prefixes) |
| `ReturnsAsync(precomputedObject)` in Moq setups on shared mocks when SUT mutates the returned object | Same reference returned on every call; SUT mutation affects subsequent test invocations | Use `ReturnsAsync(() => new MyObject(...))` lambda overload to create a fresh instance per invocation |
| `Assume.That(condition)` in NUnit without checking CI adapter's `Inconclusive` result mapping | Azure DevOps and some adapters treat `Inconclusive` as a failing test, blocking the build | Use `Assert.Ignore("reason")` with documented CI adapter configuration, or extract environment guards into `[OneTimeSetUp]` that skips the fixture entirely |
| `[AssemblyInitialize]` static fields without null-guard or lazy initialisation | NPE when individual tests run in isolation; unhelpful error messages obscure root cause | Wrap static resources in `Lazy<T>` or add null-check that throws `InvalidOperationException` with a descriptive message |
| `WithReuse(true)` in Testcontainers.NET without container cleanup on image version bump | Old containers accumulate; Docker resource exhaustion on developer machines and CI agents | Add container prune step to CI setup; document image bumps as requiring `docker container prune --filter label=org.testcontainers.reuse=true` |
| `ExecutionTimeOf` / `CompleteWithinAsync` thresholds set at expected median execution time | CI runner jitter causes flaky failures; single-sample wall-clock measurement is unreliable | Set thresholds at 5–10x expected p95 time; isolate timing tests with `[Collection("sequential")]` to avoid resource contention inflation |

## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 76 — xUnit v3 `Microsoft.Testing.Platform` Native Runner With `--report-trx` for CI-First Test Reporting [official]

xUnit v3 ships with first-class support for `Microsoft.Testing.Platform` (MTP), Microsoft's unified test runner replacing the VSTest adapter for .NET 9+ projects. When the `<UseMicrosoftTestingPlatformRunner>true</UseMicrosoftTestingPlatformRunner>` property is set in the project file, `dotnet run` executes the test assembly directly as a native executable rather than routing through `dotnet test`'s VSTest shim. This eliminates the `vstest.console.exe` process boundary, reduces startup overhead by 40–60 % on large suites, and unlocks MTP-native extensions (retry, blame, coverage) without VSTest adapter version-pinning. The `--report-trx` flag writes a TRX file compatible with Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions test summaries, and the `Trx2Junit` converter. Pass `--results-directory ./TestResults` to control output location.

```csharp
// Consuming xUnit v3 MTP runner – no VSTest adapter required.
// .csproj:
//   <UseMicrosoftTestingPlatformRunner>true</UseMicrosoftTestingPlatformRunner>
//
// Run: dotnet run --project MyTests -- --report-trx --results-directory ./TestResults
//
// The test binary IS the runner; no vstest shim is involved.
//
// In the test class, xUnit v3 DI works identically to the VSTest path:

using Xunit;
using Xunit.Abstractions;

public class OrderServiceTests(ITestOutputHelper output)
{
    [Fact]
    public void CalculateTotal_AppliesDiscount_WhenOrderExceedsThreshold()
    {
        var svc = new OrderService();
        var total = svc.CalculateTotal(items: 6, unitPrice: 20m, threshold: 5);

        output.WriteLine($"Computed total: {total}");
        Assert.Equal(108m, total); // 6 × 20 × 0.90 discount
    }

    [Theory, InlineData(1, 20m, 20m), InlineData(6, 20m, 108m)]
    public void CalculateTotal_ReturnsExpected(int qty, decimal unit, decimal expected)
    {
        var svc = new OrderService();
        Assert.Equal(expected, svc.CalculateTotal(qty, unit, threshold: 5));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** MTP native runner cannot be used alongside projects that still reference `xunit.runner.visualstudio` (VSTest adapter) in the same build invocation — the two runner modes are mutually exclusive per project. Mixed solutions (some projects MTP, some VSTest) work fine at solution level but require `dotnet test` to target specific projects. The `--results-directory` flag is per-runner-invocation, not per-class, so parallel multi-project runs should use unique subdirectory tokens (`./TestResults/$(ProjectName)`) to prevent TRX file collisions. [official]

### Pattern 77 — NUnit 4 `[ValueSource]` With Static `IEnumerable` for Type-Safe Reusable Parameter Feeds [official]

`[ValueSource(nameof(...))]` lets a single `IEnumerable<T>` property or method power multiple `[Test]` parameters across different test classes without repeating inline `[TestCase]` arrays. The source can live in a shared static class, enabling a single authoritative dataset (e.g., all supported currency codes, all valid ISO-8601 date strings) to drive boundary and contract tests in different fixtures. Unlike `[TestCaseSource]`, `[ValueSource]` feeds a single parameter — compose multiple `[ValueSource]` attributes on one parameter list to build cross-product parameterisation without `[Combinatorial]` explosion. NUnit 4 adds generic `IEnumerable<T>` inference so the test parameter type is checked at compile time when the source is `IEnumerable<T>` rather than `IEnumerable`.

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public static class CurrencyData
{
    public static IEnumerable<string> ValidIsoCodes()
    {
        yield return "USD";
        yield return "EUR";
        yield return "GBP";
        yield return "JPY";
    }

    public static IEnumerable<decimal> PositiveAmounts()
    {
        yield return 0.01m;
        yield return 1_000m;
        yield return 999_999.99m;
    }
}

[TestFixture]
public class MoneyParserTests
{
    [Test]
    public void Parse_ReturnsNonNull_ForAllSupportedCurrencies(
        [ValueSource(typeof(CurrencyData), nameof(CurrencyData.ValidIsoCodes))] string code)
    {
        var result = MoneyParser.Parse($"100 {code}");

        Assert.That(result, Is.Not.Null,
            $"Expected a non-null result for currency '{code}'");
        Assert.That(result!.CurrencyCode, Is.EqualTo(code));
    }

    [Test]
    public void Parse_PreservesAmount_ForAllBoundaryValues(
        [ValueSource(typeof(CurrencyData), nameof(CurrencyData.PositiveAmounts))] decimal amount)
    {
        var result = MoneyParser.Parse($"{amount} USD");

        Assert.That(result!.Amount, Is.EqualTo(amount).Within(0.001m));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[ValueSource]` sources are evaluated at test discovery time, not at execution time. If the source property performs I/O (reads a config file, opens a DB connection) the operation runs in the discovery process — a different process lifetime than the test execution process when using `dotnet test`. Sources must be pure, deterministic, and dependency-free. For dynamic sources that require runtime configuration (environment variable–dependent), use `[TestCaseSource]` with a static factory that falls back to a hardcoded set when the config is absent. [official]

---

### Pattern 78 — MSTest v3 `[TestProperty]` + `TestContext.Properties` for Category-Driven CI Test Filtering [official]

`[TestProperty("Area", "Payments")]` attaches arbitrary key-value metadata to an MSTest test method. At CI time, the metadata surfaces in the TRX file and can be used with `--filter "TestCategory=Smoke&Area=Payments"` (combining `[TestCategory]` for tier and `[TestProperty]` for domain) to precisely scope test execution without maintaining separate project files per domain. MSTest v3 extends `[TestProperty]` to support multiple applications (stack them) and the values are accessible in `[TestCleanup]` via `TestContext.Properties["Area"]` for conditional teardown logging. This pattern scales to large enterprise codebases where a single test assembly contains hundreds of tests across unrelated domains.

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;

[TestClass]
public class PaymentGatewayTests
{
    public TestContext TestContext { get; set; } = null!;

    [TestMethod]
    [TestCategory("Smoke")]
    [TestProperty("Area", "Payments")]
    [TestProperty("Owner", "platform-team")]
    public async Task ChargeCard_ReturnsSuccess_ForValidToken()
    {
        var gateway = new PaymentGateway(new FakeStripeClient());
        var result  = await gateway.ChargeAsync("tok_visa", 50_00);

        Assert.IsNotNull(result);
        Assert.AreEqual("succeeded", result.Status);
    }

    [TestCleanup]
    public void LogTestArea()
    {
        // Accessible after execution for conditional cleanup or telemetry.
        var area  = TestContext.Properties["Area"]  as string ?? "unknown";
        var owner = TestContext.Properties["Owner"] as string ?? "unknown";
        TestContext.WriteLine(
            $"[{area}] owned by [{owner}] — " +
            $"{TestContext.TestName}: {TestContext.CurrentTestOutcome}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[TestProperty]` values must be string literals (no constants or expressions), which means refactoring domain names requires a find-and-replace across all attribute usages — there is no compile-time enforcement of allowed values. For large teams, define a static class of `const string` keys (e.g., `TestAreas.Payments`) but note that the attribute still requires a literal; use a custom Roslyn analyser to enforce the allowed-value contract if consistency is critical. [official]

### Pattern 79 — FluentAssertions v8 `HaveAccessModifier` for Architecture-Level API Surface Tests [official]

FluentAssertions v8's `HaveAccessModifier(CSharpAccessModifier.Public)` and `NotHaveAccessModifier` assertions on `TypeAssertions` and `MethodInfoAssertions` enable lightweight architecture tests without pulling in a full architecture-testing library (ArchUnitNET, NetArchTest). The assertions resolve at runtime via reflection and integrate naturally into existing FluentAssertions chains, making them useful for "no internal type should escape the assembly boundary" or "all repository implementations must be internal" rules enforced as xUnit/NUnit/MSTest facts. When combined with `GetExportedTypes()` and `Where(t => t.Namespace.StartsWith("MyApp.Infra"))`, they form a simple but effective public-API guard.

```csharp
using System;
using System.Linq;
using System.Reflection;
using FluentAssertions;
using FluentAssertions.Common;
using Xunit;

public class ArchitectureTests
{
    private static readonly Assembly AppAssembly =
        typeof(MyApp.Domain.Order).Assembly;

    [Fact]
    public void RepositoryImplementations_MustBeInternal()
    {
        var repoImpls = AppAssembly.GetTypes()
            .Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Repository") &&
                        !t.IsInterface)
            .ToList();

        repoImpls.Should().NotBeEmpty(
            because: "the assembly must contain at least one repository implementation");

        foreach (var type in repoImpls)
        {
            type.Should()
                .NotHaveAccessModifier(CSharpAccessModifier.Public,
                    because: $"{type.Name} must not be part of the public API");
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void DomainEntities_MustBePublic()
    {
        var entities = AppAssembly.GetTypes()
            .Where(t => t.Namespace == "MyApp.Domain" && !t.IsInterface)
            .ToList();

        foreach (var type in entities)
        {
            type.Should()
                .HaveAccessModifier(CSharpAccessModifier.Public,
                    because: $"domain entities in MyApp.Domain must be visible to consumers");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `HaveAccessModifier` uses reflection to read `TypeAttributes` flags, which means it evaluates the compiled assembly — not the source-level `internal` keyword. Nested types with `private protected` or `protected internal` modifiers map to `CSharpAccessModifier.ProtectedInternal` and `CSharpAccessModifier.PrivateProtected` respectively; ensure the correct enum value is used or the assertion silently passes for the wrong modifier. For assemblies with `[InternalsVisibleTo]` in tests, `internal` types are still classified as `CSharpAccessModifier.Internal` — the attribute does not promote them to `Public` in the reflection metadata. [official]

### Pattern 80 — Moq `SetupProperty` for Observable Property-Change Tracking in Domain Event Tests [community]

`mock.SetupProperty(m => m.Status)` configures a property on a mock so that it stores and tracks values assigned to it during the test, enabling both get and set assertions without manually backing each property with a field. When a domain service sets `order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped` through an interface, `SetupProperty` allows the test to later assert `mock.Object.Status.Should().Be(OrderStatus.Shipped)` without intercepting the set via `SetupSet`. Chaining `SetupAllProperties()` auto-configures every property on the mock for tracking, which is useful for data-transfer-object interfaces where all properties must survive a round-trip through a mapper.

```csharp
using Moq;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public interface IOrderEntity
{
    OrderStatus Status     { get; set; }
    DateTime?   ShippedAt  { get; set; }
    string?     TrackingCode { get; set; }
}

public class ShipmentServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Ship_SetsStatusAndShippedAt_WhenOrderIsConfirmed()
    {
        var mockOrder = new Mock<IOrderEntity>();
        mockOrder.SetupProperty(o => o.Status,       OrderStatus.Confirmed);
        mockOrder.SetupProperty(o => o.ShippedAt,    null);
        mockOrder.SetupProperty(o => o.TrackingCode, null);

        var svc = new ShipmentService(fakeCarrier: new FakeCarrierClient("TRK-001"));
        svc.Ship(mockOrder.Object);

        mockOrder.Object.Status.Should().Be(OrderStatus.Shipped);
        mockOrder.Object.ShippedAt.Should().NotBeNull();
        mockOrder.Object.TrackingCode.Should().Be("TRK-001");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Ship_AllProperties_SurvivedRoundTripThroughMapper()
    {
        var mockOrder = new Mock<IOrderEntity>();
        mockOrder.SetupAllProperties();  // track every property
        mockOrder.Object.Status = OrderStatus.Confirmed;

        var svc    = new ShipmentService(new FakeCarrierClient("TRK-999"));
        var mapped = OrderMapper.ToDto(mockOrder.Object);

        mapped.Status.Should().Be(mockOrder.Object.Status.ToString());
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SetupProperty` and `SetupAllProperties` only work on properties defined in the mocked interface or virtual in the mocked class — concrete non-virtual properties on a class cannot be intercepted. `SetupAllProperties` sets the initial value of all properties to `default(T)` (null for reference types, 0 for value types); if a property must start with a non-default value, call `SetupProperty` with an explicit initial value after `SetupAllProperties`. Be aware that `SetupAllProperties` silently ignores read-only properties (no setter) rather than throwing — a property you expected to be tracked may not be. [community]

### Pattern 81 — Testcontainers.NET `AzuriteContainer` for Azure Blob/Queue/Table Storage Integration Tests [official]

`AzuriteContainer` (from `Testcontainers.Azurite`) spins up Microsoft's local Azure Storage emulator and exposes connection strings for Blob, Queue, and Table services. Tests using `Azure.Storage.Blobs.BlobServiceClient` or `Azure.Storage.Queues.QueueServiceClient` pointed at the Azurite endpoints run the real SDK client-side retry, SAS token validation, and metadata round-trip logic without needing an Azure subscription. The container exposes the standard Azurite ports (10000/10001/10002) and supports `WithPersistData(path)` for seeding blobs from a local directory before tests run, enabling upload-then-download contract verification in CI.

```csharp
using Azure.Storage.Blobs;
using Azure.Storage.Blobs.Models;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using FluentAssertions;
using Testcontainers.Azurite;
using Xunit;

public class BlobStorageServiceTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly AzuriteContainer _azurite = new AzuriteBuilder()
        .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/azure-storage/azurite:latest")
        .Build();

    public Task InitializeAsync() => _azurite.StartAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()     => _azurite.StopAsync();

    [Fact]
    public async Task UploadAsync_ThenDownload_RoundTripsContent()
    {
        var client    = new BlobServiceClient(_azurite.GetConnectionString());
        var container = client.GetBlobContainerClient("test-uploads");
        await container.CreateIfNotExistsAsync();

        var blobClient = container.GetBlobClient("hello.txt");
        await blobClient.UploadAsync(
            BinaryData.FromString("Hello, Azurite!"),
            overwrite: true);

        var downloaded = await blobClient.DownloadContentAsync();
        downloaded.Value.Content.ToString()
            .Should().Be("Hello, Azurite!");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetBlobProperties_ReturnsCorrectContentType_WhenExplicitlySet()
    {
        var client    = new BlobServiceClient(_azurite.GetConnectionString());
        var container = client.GetBlobContainerClient("typed-blobs");
        await container.CreateIfNotExistsAsync();

        var blobClient = container.GetBlobClient("report.json");
        await blobClient.UploadAsync(
            BinaryData.FromString("{\"key\":\"value\"}"),
            new BlobUploadOptions
            {
                HttpHeaders = new BlobHttpHeaders { ContentType = "application/json" }
            });

        var props = await blobClient.GetPropertiesAsync();
        props.Value.ContentType.Should().Be("application/json");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Azurite does not implement 100 % of the Azure Storage REST API — features like soft delete, versioning, object replication, and immutability policies are absent or partially implemented; tests relying on these features must target a real Azure storage account. The `GetConnectionString()` helper returns the standard Azurite default-account connection string (`UseDevelopmentStorage=true`), which works for SDK clients but is not accepted by certain Azure SDK helpers that parse the storage account name from the connection string and expect a non-emulator FQDN. Use the `BlobServiceClient(Uri, TokenCredential)` overload with Azurite's well-known dev endpoint (`http://127.0.0.1:10000/devstoreaccount1`) to avoid connection string parsing issues in those helpers. [official]

### Pattern 82 — xUnit v3 `BeforeAfterTestAttribute` Custom Attribute for Cross-Cutting Test Infrastructure [official]

xUnit v3 restores and enhances the `BeforeAfterTestAttribute` extensibility hook. Subclassing it and overriding `Before(MethodInfo)` / `After(MethodInfo)` allows cross-cutting concerns — ambient tracing context, database ambient transaction scope, culture override for locale-sensitive tests — to be applied declaratively per test method without fixture inheritance. Unlike `ITestOutputHelper` injection, `BeforeAfterTestAttribute` runs in the test execution pipeline before `[Fact]`/`[Theory]` body execution and after teardown, making it appropriate for infrastructure that must bracket the entire test body rather than just the arrange phase.

```csharp
using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.Reflection;
using System.Threading;
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Sdk;

/// <summary>
/// Overrides thread culture for the duration of a test, then restores it.
/// Useful for locale-sensitive formatting and parsing assertions.
/// </summary>
[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method, AllowMultiple = false)]
public sealed class UsingCultureAttribute(string cultureName) : BeforeAfterTestAttribute
{
    private CultureInfo? _savedCulture;
    private CultureInfo? _savedUiCulture;

    public override void Before(MethodInfo methodUnderTest)
    {
        _savedCulture   = Thread.CurrentThread.CurrentCulture;
        _savedUiCulture = Thread.CurrentThread.CurrentUICulture;
        var culture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo(cultureName);
        Thread.CurrentThread.CurrentCulture   = culture;
        Thread.CurrentThread.CurrentUICulture = culture;
    }

    public override void After(MethodInfo methodUnderTest)
    {
        Thread.CurrentThread.CurrentCulture   = _savedCulture!;
        Thread.CurrentThread.CurrentUICulture = _savedUiCulture!;
    }
}

public class InvoiceFormatterTests
{
    [Fact]
    [UsingCulture("de-DE")]
    public void FormatAmount_UsesPeriodAsThousandsSeparator_InGerman()
    {
        var formatted = InvoiceFormatter.FormatAmount(1_234.56m);
        Assert.Equal("1.234,56 €", formatted);
    }

    [Fact]
    [UsingCulture("en-US")]
    public void FormatAmount_UsesCommaAsThousandsSeparator_InEnglish()
    {
        var formatted = InvoiceFormatter.FormatAmount(1_234.56m);
        Assert.Equal("$1,234.56", formatted);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `BeforeAfterTestAttribute.After` is called even when `Before` throws, but if `After` itself throws, xUnit wraps the exception rather than propagating the original test failure — the test is reported as errored with the teardown exception masking the real failure. Always guard `After` with a null check on state captured in `Before` and suppress or log secondary teardown failures rather than letting them propagate. Note that `BeforeAfterTestAttribute` does not compose with `IClassFixture` teardown order — fixture `DisposeAsync` runs after all test methods (including their `After` hooks), so infrastructure torn down in a fixture's `Dispose` is still available when `After` runs. [official]

---

### Pattern 83 — NUnit 4 `[Combinatorial]` With `[Values]` for Exhaustive Input-Space Coverage on Small Parameter Sets [official]

`[Combinatorial]` combined with `[Values(...)]` attributes on each parameter generates the full Cartesian product of all parameter combinations without manually listing each `[TestCase]`. For a method with 3 parameters of 3 values each, NUnit generates 27 test cases automatically. This is ideal for stateless pure-function boundary tests (string sanitisers, enum converters, bitfield validators) where exhaustive coverage is tractable and desirable. NUnit 4 improves combinatorial test naming so each generated case receives a unique, readable display name derived from the parameter values — visible in VS Test Explorer and TRX output.

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;

[TestFixture]
public class StatusTransitionValidatorTests
{
    [Test, Combinatorial]
    public void IsValidTransition_ReturnsExpected(
        [Values(OrderStatus.Draft, OrderStatus.Confirmed, OrderStatus.Shipped)] OrderStatus from,
        [Values(OrderStatus.Draft, OrderStatus.Confirmed, OrderStatus.Shipped)] OrderStatus to)
    {
        // 9 combinations generated; each tested independently.
        var result = StatusTransitionValidator.IsValidTransition(from, to);

        // Self-transitions are always invalid:
        if (from == to)
        {
            Assert.That(result, Is.False,
                $"Self-transition {from} -> {to} must be rejected");
            return;
        }

        // Only forward transitions are legal in this domain:
        var expected = (int)from < (int)to;
        Assert.That(result, Is.EqualTo(expected),
            $"Transition {from} -> {to}: expected {expected} but got {result}");
    }

    [Test, Combinatorial]
    public void FormatStatusLabel_NeverReturnsNullOrEmpty(
        [Values(OrderStatus.Draft, OrderStatus.Confirmed, OrderStatus.Shipped)] OrderStatus status,
        [Values("en-US", "de-DE", "ja-JP")] string culture)
    {
        var label = StatusLabelFormatter.Format(status, culture);
        Assert.That(label, Is.Not.Null.And.Not.Empty,
            $"Expected non-empty label for {status} in {culture}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[Combinatorial]` scales as the product of all value set sizes — 5 parameters with 4 values each generates 1,024 test cases. Discovery and reporting of 1,000+ cases noticeably slows VS Test Explorer and bloats TRX files. For large parameter spaces, prefer `[Pairwise]` (generates the minimum set of pairs covering all 2-way combinations) which reduces case count by 60–90 % while catching most interaction bugs. Reserve `[Combinatorial]` for parameter sets where 3-way or higher interactions are known domain concerns (e.g., security policy evaluation with 3 independent flags). [official]

---

### Pattern 84 — MSTest v3 `[Timeout]` Attribute With `TestContext.CancellationTokenSource` for Cooperative Async Test Cancellation [official]

MSTest v3 honours `[Timeout(milliseconds)]` on async test methods and wires the timeout to a `CancellationToken` accessible via `TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Token`. Passing this token into async SUT methods (HTTP clients, DB commands, message consumers) achieves cooperative cancellation rather than forcible thread-abort — the test infrastructure signals cancellation and the SUT's async plumbing propagates it cleanly through `await`, resulting in a `TaskCanceledException` that MSTest records as a timed-out test rather than an unhandled exception. This eliminates the common pattern of manually constructing a `CancellationTokenSource` with `CancelAfter` in `[TestInitialize]`.

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestClass]
public class ReportExportServiceTests
{
    public TestContext TestContext { get; set; } = null!;

    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(5_000)] // 5-second wall-clock limit
    public async Task ExportReport_CompletesWithinSla_ForStandardSizedReport()
    {
        // TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Token is pre-wired to [Timeout].
        var ct  = TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Token;
        var svc = new ReportExportService(new FakeReportRepository());

        var result = await svc.ExportAsync(
            reportId: "RPT-001",
            format: ExportFormat.Pdf,
            cancellationToken: ct);

        Assert.IsNotNull(result);
        Assert.IsTrue(result.ContentLength > 0,
            "Expected non-empty PDF output");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(2_000)]
    public async Task ExportReport_ThrowsOperationCanceled_WhenCancelled()
    {
        // Manually cancel before calling, to verify the SUT respects the token.
        TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Cancel();
        var ct  = TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Token;
        var svc = new ReportExportService(new FakeReportRepository());

        await Assert.ThrowsExceptionAsync<TaskCanceledException>(
            () => svc.ExportAsync("RPT-001", ExportFormat.Pdf, ct));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[Timeout]` in MSTest v3 operates at wall-clock time and fires on a background thread managed by the test runner — if the SUT ignores the `CancellationToken` (e.g., blocking synchronous I/O), MSTest v3 will record the test as timed out but cannot forcibly terminate the blocked thread, meaning the test process may hang waiting for the unresponsive code to unblock. Always verify the SUT's async path threads through the `CancellationToken` to every I/O boundary. For tests that cannot be made cooperative (third-party sync calls), wrap them in a `Task.Run` with an `await Task.WhenAny(workTask, Task.Delay(timeout, ct))` guard pattern and call `Assert.Inconclusive` if the guard fires. [official]

---

### Pattern 85 — FluentAssertions v8 `SatisfyRespectively` With Named Action Lambdas for Ordered Collection Element Assertions [official]

`SatisfyRespectively` applies a separate assertion lambda to each element of a collection in order, providing per-element customised assertions with independent failure messages — a significant improvement over `BeEquivalentTo` when elements differ structurally or when per-element context matters for failure readability. In FluentAssertions v8, lambdas passed to `SatisfyRespectively` can be assigned to local `Action<T>` variables with descriptive names which causes the failure message to include useful context — giving a precise per-element message rather than a generic "element at index 2 failed". This pattern is ideal for asserting that a pipeline produced an ordered sequence of domain events or HTTP responses.

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using Xunit;

public class OrderPipelineTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Process_ProducesExpectedEventSequence_ForNewOrder()
    {
        var pipeline = new OrderProcessingPipeline();
        var events   = pipeline.Process(new NewOrderCommand(
            CustomerId: "CUST-1",
            Items: [new OrderItem("SKU-A", Quantity: 2)]));

        Action<DomainEvent> beOrderCreated = e =>
        {
            e.Should().BeOfType<OrderCreatedEvent>();
            ((OrderCreatedEvent)e).CustomerId.Should().Be("CUST-1");
        };

        Action<DomainEvent> beInventoryReserved = e =>
        {
            e.Should().BeOfType<InventoryReservedEvent>();
            ((InventoryReservedEvent)e).Sku.Should().Be("SKU-A");
        };

        Action<DomainEvent> bePaymentInitiated = e =>
        {
            e.Should().BeOfType<PaymentInitiatedEvent>();
            ((PaymentInitiatedEvent)e).Amount.Should().BeGreaterThan(0m);
        };

        events.Should()
              .HaveCount(3)
              .And.SatisfyRespectively(
                  beOrderCreated,
                  beInventoryReserved,
                  bePaymentInitiated);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SatisfyRespectively` is strictly positional — the number of lambdas must exactly match the number of elements in the collection, otherwise the assertion fails with a count mismatch rather than evaluating any elements. If the pipeline can produce variable-length event sequences (e.g., with optional compensation events), use `Satisfy` (which applies one predicate to all elements) for the variable portion and `SatisfyRespectively` only for a known-fixed prefix. For unordered collections where only membership matters, `ContainSingle(e => e is OrderCreatedEvent)` is more resilient. [official]

### Pattern 86 — Moq `InSequence` With `MockSequence` for Strict Call-Order Verification [community]

`MockSequence` combined with `mock.InSequence(sequence).Setup(...)` enforces that mock setups are invoked in a specific declared order — any out-of-order call throws `MockException` immediately rather than silently returning a default value. This is essential for verifying protocols where the SUT must call dependencies in a legally mandated sequence (e.g., `BeginTransaction` before `ExecuteCommand` before `Commit`, or `AcquireLock` before `ReadData` before `ReleaseLock`). Without `MockSequence`, Moq allows setups to be called in any order by default — a SUT that calls `Commit` before `BeginTransaction` passes the test silently.

```csharp
using Moq;
using Xunit;

public interface IUnitOfWork
{
    void Begin();
    void SaveChanges();
    void Commit();
    void Rollback();
}

public class TransactionalOrderServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void PlaceOrder_CallsUnitOfWorkInCorrectSequence()
    {
        var sequence = new MockSequence();
        var uow      = new Mock<IUnitOfWork>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        // Declare expected call order:
        uow.InSequence(sequence).Setup(u => u.Begin());
        uow.InSequence(sequence).Setup(u => u.SaveChanges());
        uow.InSequence(sequence).Setup(u => u.Commit());

        var svc = new TransactionalOrderService(uow.Object);
        svc.PlaceOrder(new OrderRequest("CUST-1", "SKU-A", Qty: 1));

        // MockSequence enforces order; out-of-sequence calls throw MockException.
        uow.Verify(u => u.Begin(),       Times.Once);
        uow.Verify(u => u.SaveChanges(), Times.Once);
        uow.Verify(u => u.Commit(),      Times.Once);
        uow.Verify(u => u.Rollback(),    Times.Never);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void PlaceOrder_CallsRollback_WhenSaveChangesFails()
    {
        var sequence = new MockSequence();
        var uow      = new Mock<IUnitOfWork>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        uow.InSequence(sequence).Setup(u => u.Begin());
        uow.InSequence(sequence)
           .Setup(u => u.SaveChanges())
           .Throws<InvalidOperationException>();
        uow.InSequence(sequence).Setup(u => u.Rollback());

        var svc = new TransactionalOrderService(uow.Object);
        Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(
            () => svc.PlaceOrder(new OrderRequest("CUST-1", "SKU-A", Qty: 1)));

        uow.Verify(u => u.Rollback(), Times.Once);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockSequence` requires `MockBehavior.Strict` — without it the sequence constraint is not enforced and the test gives a false green. `MockBehavior.Strict` means every call on the mock must be explicitly set up; unexpected calls (like property getters used for logging) throw `MockException` and require additional `Setup` entries. For complex mocks with many incidental calls, `MockBehavior.Strict` + `MockSequence` can produce brittle tests — scope the strict mock to a narrow wrapper interface covering only the sequence-critical calls and use a separate `MockBehavior.Loose` mock for auxiliary dependencies. [community]

### Pattern 87 — Testcontainers.NET `MongoDbContainer` for Document Store Integration Tests With BsonDocument Assertion [official]

`MongoDbContainer` (from `Testcontainers.MongoDb`) provides a real MongoDB instance for integration tests that exercise aggregation pipelines, indexing strategies, and the .NET MongoDB driver's serialisation attributes (`[BsonId]`, `[BsonElement]`). Unlike an in-memory mock, the container validates BSON-level concerns: null handling in `[BsonIgnoreIfNull]`, `ObjectId` vs `string` `_id` field mapping, and `$lookup` pipeline correctness. Tests can use `IMongoDatabase.RunCommandAsync<BsonDocument>` to assert collection metadata (index existence, document count) without going through the application's repository layer.

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using MongoDB.Bson;
using MongoDB.Bson.Serialization.Attributes;
using MongoDB.Driver;
using Testcontainers.MongoDb;
using Xunit;

public record ProductDocument(
    [property: BsonElement("sku")]  string  Sku,
    [property: BsonElement("name")] string  Name,
    [property: BsonElement("price")] decimal Price);

public class ProductRepositoryTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MongoDbContainer _mongo = new MongoDbBuilder()
        .WithImage("mongo:7.0")
        .Build();

    private IMongoDatabase _db = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _mongo.StartAsync();
        var client = new MongoClient(_mongo.GetConnectionString());
        _db = client.GetDatabase("testdb");

        var collection = _db.GetCollection<BsonDocument>("products");
        await collection.Indexes.CreateOneAsync(
            new CreateIndexModel<BsonDocument>(
                Builders<BsonDocument>.IndexKeys.Ascending("sku"),
                new CreateIndexOptions { Unique = true }));
    }

    public Task DisposeAsync() => _mongo.StopAsync();

    [Fact]
    public async Task InsertProduct_RetrievesWithCorrectFields_RoundTrip()
    {
        var col  = _db.GetCollection<ProductDocument>("products");
        var doc  = new ProductDocument(Sku: "SKU-X1", Name: "Widget", Price: 9.99m);
        await col.InsertOneAsync(doc);

        var found = await col.Find(p => p.Sku == "SKU-X1").FirstOrDefaultAsync();

        found.Should().NotBeNull();
        found!.Name.Should().Be("Widget");
        found.Price.Should().Be(9.99m);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task InsertDuplicate_Throws_WhenUniqueIndexViolated()
    {
        var col = _db.GetCollection<ProductDocument>("products");
        await col.InsertOneAsync(new ProductDocument("SKU-DUP", "A", 1m));

        var act = async () =>
            await col.InsertOneAsync(new ProductDocument("SKU-DUP", "B", 2m));

        await act.Should().ThrowAsync<MongoWriteException>()
            .WithMessage("*E11000*",
                because: "duplicate key violation must be a MongoDB E11000 error");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** MongoDB containers use port 27017 by default; when running multiple test classes in parallel with separate `MongoDbContainer` instances, Docker must bind each container to a random host port (`WithPortBinding(27017, assignRandomHostPort: true)` is the default for Testcontainers.NET). Verify that `GetConnectionString()` returns the correct mapped host port before constructing `MongoClient` — using a hardcoded `localhost:27017` string bypasses the dynamic port mapping and silently connects to the wrong container or fails if port 27017 is already occupied. [official]

### Pattern 88 — .NET 9/10 `System.Threading.Lock` Testing With Contention Simulation [official]

.NET 9 introduces `System.Threading.Lock`, a purpose-built lock type that replaces `lock (object)` statements for better performance and richer diagnostics. Testing code that uses `Lock` requires verifying mutual exclusion under contention — a naive single-threaded test cannot exercise the locking path. The pattern uses `Task.WhenAll` with a `SemaphoreSlim` rendezvous to synchronize multiple threads at the contention point, then asserts that shared state was mutated exactly once (no lost updates) and that no `LockRecursionException` was thrown (the new `Lock` throws on recursive acquisition by default, unlike `Monitor`).

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class ThreadSafeCounterTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Increment_IsAtomicUnderHighContention()
    {
        const int threadCount    = 50;
        const int incrementsEach = 1_000;
        var counter = new ThreadSafeCounter();          // uses new Lock internally
        var barrier = new SemaphoreSlim(0, threadCount); // rendezvous gate
        var ready   = new SemaphoreSlim(0, threadCount);

        var tasks = Enumerable.Range(0, threadCount).Select(_ => Task.Run(async () =>
        {
            ready.Release();           // signal: this thread is ready
            await barrier.WaitAsync(); // wait for all threads to be ready
            for (int i = 0; i < incrementsEach; i++)
                counter.Increment();
        })).ToArray();

        // Wait for all tasks to signal ready, then release the barrier at once.
        for (int i = 0; i < threadCount; i++)
            await ready.WaitAsync();
        barrier.Release(threadCount);

        await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

        counter.Value.Should().Be(threadCount * incrementsEach,
            because: $"each of {threadCount} threads incremented {incrementsEach} times");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Lock_ThrowsLockRecursionException_OnRecursiveAcquisition()
    {
        // System.Threading.Lock (not Monitor) throws on same-thread recursion.
        var counter = new ThreadSafeCounter();

        var act = () => counter.SimulateRecursiveAcquisition();

        act.Should().Throw<LockRecursionException>(
            because: "System.Threading.Lock does not support reentrancy");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The `SemaphoreSlim` rendezvous pattern provides a best-effort contention scenario — on a single-core CI runner the OS scheduler may not interleave threads at the critical section, so the test does not guarantee observed contention but still validates the correctness invariant (final count). For strict contention observation, use `Interlocked.CompareExchange` to detect whether two threads truly overlapped. Note that `System.Threading.Lock` is a value type introduced in .NET 9 and is not the same as `object` — code using `lock(this)` or `lock(staticObject)` still uses `Monitor` internally and will not benefit from the diagnostics improvements; a separate migration step is needed. [official]

### Pattern 89 — xUnit v3 `[Collection(DisableParallelization = true)]` Without a Named Collection for Lightweight Global Serialisation [official]

xUnit v3 adds an overload of `[Collection]` that accepts `DisableParallelization = true` without requiring a named collection and a matching `[CollectionDefinition]` class. This inline form serialises the decorated test class relative to all other test classes with the same flag, without needing a shared string key. It is the lightest-weight way to mark a single test class as "must not run in parallel with anything" — useful for tests that manipulate global process state (environment variables, static fields, GDI+ font caches, culture) where adding a named collection would introduce cross-cutting concerns. Compared to putting every such class in a named collection, the nameless form is more discoverable: a developer reading the class immediately understands the parallelism intent without hunting for a `[CollectionDefinition]` in another file.

```csharp
using System;
using Xunit;

// Serialise this class against ALL other test classes — no [CollectionDefinition] needed.
[Collection(DisableParallelization = true)]
public class EnvironmentVariableTests
{
    // These tests mutate process-level environment variables —
    // they MUST NOT run alongside any test that reads the same variables.

    [Fact]
    public void ReadConfig_UsesEnvVar_WhenSet()
    {
        Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable("APP_ENV", "staging");
        try
        {
            var config = AppConfig.Load();
            Assert.Equal("staging", config.Environment);
        }
        finally
        {
            Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable("APP_ENV", null); // restore
        }
    }

    [Fact]
    public void ReadConfig_FallsBackToDefault_WhenEnvVarAbsent()
    {
        Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable("APP_ENV", null);
        try
        {
            var config = AppConfig.Load();
            Assert.Equal("production", config.Environment);
        }
        finally
        {
            Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable("APP_ENV", null);
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[Collection(DisableParallelization = true)]` serialises the class against ALL other test classes, not just other classes with the same attribute — this can cause a significant throughput reduction if used broadly, because a single "disabled" class stalls the entire test assembly's parallel pipeline while it executes. If you only need to serialise two specific classes against each other (not the whole assembly), use a shared named `[Collection("EnvVarTests")]` with `[CollectionDefinition("EnvVarTests", DisableParallelization = true)]` so the serialisation scope is limited to those specific classes. Reserve the nameless `DisableParallelization = true` form for truly global-state mutations (static application state, OS-level resources) where broader isolation is genuinely required. [official]
