## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 106 — xUnit v3 `TheoryData<T1, T2>` Strongly-Typed Inline Data for Compile-Time Theory Safety [official]

xUnit v3 introduced `TheoryData<T1, T2, …>` (up to eight generic type parameters) as a type-safe alternative to `[InlineData]` and `MemberData` that returns `IEnumerable<object[]>`. Declaring data via `TheoryData` prevents the most common theory bug — a mismatch between the number or types of columns in the data source and the method signature — from reaching runtime. The IDE understands the generic parameter types and offers completion and refactoring support that object arrays do not. `TheoryData` can be exposed as a static property, a static field, or a `ClassData` subclass, giving teams full flexibility over data locality.

```csharp
public class PricingCalculatorTests
{
    public static TheoryData<decimal, int, decimal> DiscountCases => new()
    {
        { 100m, 0,  100m },
        { 100m, 10,  90m },
        { 200m, 25, 150m },
        { 0m,   50,   0m },
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(DiscountCases))]
    public void ApplyDiscount_ReturnsCorrectTotal(
        decimal price, int discountPct, decimal expected)
    {
        var result = PricingCalculator.ApplyDiscount(price, discountPct);
        Assert.Equal(expected, result);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `TheoryData<T>` requires the generic arity to match the method parameter count exactly at compile time — a strength in large codebases but a friction point when rapidly prototyping tests that add or drop columns. For data sourced from external files (CSV, JSON), object arrays produced by a custom `IEnumerable<object[]>` remain more flexible, at the cost of losing compile-time column validation. [official]

---

### Pattern 107 — NUnit 4 `[ValueSource]` With Static `IEnumerable<T>` Property for Reusable Per-Parameter Data [official]

NUnit 4's `[ValueSource]` attribute populates a single test parameter from a named static property or method returning `IEnumerable<T>`, allowing the same data source to be shared across multiple tests or composed with other `[Values]` / `[ValueSource]` parameters via the Cartesian product. Unlike `[TestCaseSource]`, which provides full rows, `[ValueSource]` targets individual parameters — making it ideal for boundary-value testing where each dimension varies independently. The named source can live in the test class or in a dedicated static helper class for project-wide reuse.

```csharp
public class EmailValidatorTests
{
    private static IEnumerable<string> ValidEmails()
    {
        yield return "user@example.com";
        yield return "first.last+tag@sub.domain.org";
        yield return "x@y.io";
    }

    private static IEnumerable<string> InvalidEmails()
    {
        yield return "not-an-email";
        yield return "@nodomain.com";
        yield return "missing@.tld";
        yield return "";
    }

    [Test]
    public void IsValid_ReturnsTrueForValidEmail(
        [ValueSource(nameof(ValidEmails))] string email)
    {
        Assert.That(EmailValidator.IsValid(email), Is.True, $"Expected valid: {email}");
    }

    [Test]
    public void IsValid_ReturnsFalseForInvalidEmail(
        [ValueSource(nameof(InvalidEmails))] string email)
    {
        Assert.That(EmailValidator.IsValid(email), Is.False, $"Expected invalid: {email}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[ValueSource]` with a generator method produces one NUnit test case per yielded value (visible as separate rows in the test runner), which aids diagnosis but increases test count — a `[ValueSource]` with 50 emails combined with a second `[ValueSource]` with 3 encodings produces 150 test cases via Cartesian product, which can be unexpectedly expensive in CI parallelism configuration. Use `[TestCaseSource]` instead when you need to specify the full row (all parameters together) and want to keep case counts controlled. [official]

---

### Pattern 108 — MSTest v3 `[DynamicData]` With `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` for Computed Test Data [official]

MSTest v3's `[DynamicData]` attribute accepts a static method name (via `DynamicDataSourceType.Method`) or static property name (via `DynamicDataSourceType.Property`) on the test class or a separate type. Each overload returns `IEnumerable<object[]>`. Unlike `[DataRow]`, `[DynamicData]` supports complex objects, collections, and computed values that cannot be expressed as attribute constructor arguments. The optional `DynamicDataDisplayName` property on the attribute names a second static method that formats the display name for each test case — eliminating the generic "Test (row 0)" labels that make failure triage slower.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class OrderProcessorTests
{
    private static IEnumerable<object[]> GetProcessingScenarios()
    {
        yield return new object[]
        {
            new Order { Id = 1, Items = 3, TotalAmount = 150m },
            OrderStatus.Confirmed,
            true,
        };
        yield return new object[]
        {
            new Order { Id = 2, Items = 0, TotalAmount = 0m },
            OrderStatus.Rejected,
            false,
        };
    }

    public static string GetDisplayName(MethodInfo _, object[] data)
    {
        var order = (Order)data[0];
        var expected = (OrderStatus)data[1];
        return $"Order {order.Id} ({order.Items} items) → {expected}";
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(nameof(GetProcessingScenarios),
        DynamicDataSourceType.Method,
        DynamicDataDisplayName = nameof(GetDisplayName))]
    public void Process_SetsCorrectStatus(Order order, OrderStatus expectedStatus, bool shouldSucceed)
    {
        var result = OrderProcessor.Process(order);
        Assert.AreEqual(expectedStatus, result.Status);
        Assert.AreEqual(shouldSucceed, result.IsSuccess);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `DynamicDataDisplayName` must return a unique string per case — if two cases share the same display name, MSTest silently de-duplicates them by appending a numeric suffix, making the runner output harder to read and breaking test name filters that rely on exact matching. The `DynamicDataDisplayName` method signature is `static string Method(MethodInfo methodInfo, object[] data)` — accepting a `MethodInfo` first argument is mandatory even if unused; omitting or changing the signature causes a silent fallback to the generic display name. [official]

---

### Pattern 109 — FluentAssertions v8 `SatisfyRespectively` for Per-Element Assertions on Ordered Collections [official]

FluentAssertions v8's `SatisfyRespectively` allows a collection to be asserted element-by-element with a separate lambda per element, executed in order. This is the correct tool when each element in a result set has distinct expected values and you want independent, well-described failures rather than a single aggregate message. It is especially useful for validating ordered projection results — for example, a paged query result where each row has a different expected ID, name, and computed field. Failure messages include the element index and the assertion that failed, making it immediately obvious which row broke and why.

```csharp
[Fact]
public void GetTopSellers_ReturnsCorrectlyRankedProducts()
{
    var sut = new SalesReportService(_repositoryMock.Object);

    var results = sut.GetTopSellers(month: 3, year: 2026, limit: 3).ToList();

    results.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
        first =>
        {
            first.ProductId.Should().Be(42);
            first.Rank.Should().Be(1);
            first.Revenue.Should().BeGreaterThan(10_000m);
        },
        second =>
        {
            second.ProductId.Should().Be(17);
            second.Rank.Should().Be(2);
            second.Revenue.Should().BeInRange(5_000m, 10_000m);
        },
        third =>
        {
            third.ProductId.Should().Be(99);
            third.Rank.Should().Be(3);
            third.Revenue.Should().BePositive();
        });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SatisfyRespectively` asserts an exact element count — if the collection has more or fewer elements than the number of lambdas provided, the assertion fails with a count mismatch before any per-element assertion runs. This is usually desirable but means you cannot use `SatisfyRespectively` to assert "the first three elements satisfy these predicates without caring about the rest" — use `.Take(3).Should().SatisfyRespectively(…)` for that. It also does not compose with `.Because(…)` at the collection level; add `.Because(…)` to individual inner assertions instead. [official]

---

### Pattern 110 — Moq `SetupSequence` for Multi-Call Return Value Progression [official]

`SetupSequence` configures a single mock method to return different values (or throw different exceptions) on successive calls. This is the correct approach when the SUT calls the same dependency multiple times within a single operation and the responses must vary — for example, a retry loop that reads a status endpoint until it transitions from `Pending` to `Complete`. Using a queue-based `SetupSequence` keeps the test body clean and avoids fragile side-effect counters in `Returns` lambdas.

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task PollUntilComplete_SucceedsAfterThreeAttempts()
{
    var clientMock = new Mock<IStatusClient>();
    clientMock
        .SetupSequence(c => c.GetStatusAsync(It.IsAny<string>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(JobStatus.Pending)
        .ReturnsAsync(JobStatus.Pending)
        .ReturnsAsync(JobStatus.Complete);

    var poller = new JobPoller(clientMock.Object, maxAttempts: 5);

    var finalStatus = await poller.PollAsync("job-123");

    finalStatus.Should().Be(JobStatus.Complete);
    clientMock.Verify(c => c.GetStatusAsync("job-123"), Times.Exactly(3));
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Once a `SetupSequence` exhausts all configured return values, subsequent calls fall through to the default mock behaviour (returning `default(T)` for value types, `null` for reference types, or throwing `InvalidOperationException` if strict mode is used). If the SUT calls the method more times than the sequence configures, the fallthrough can produce subtle assertion failures that look like SUT bugs. Always pair `SetupSequence` with a `Verify(…, Times.Exactly(n))` assertion to confirm the exact call count so unexpected extra calls surface immediately. [official]

---

### Pattern 111 — Testcontainers.NET `RedisContainer` With `StackExchange.Redis` for Cache Integration Testing [official]

Testcontainers.NET's `RedisContainer` spins up a real Redis instance in Docker and exposes the connection string via `GetConnectionString()`. Integration tests using `StackExchange.Redis` connect to this container and exercise actual Redis serialization, TTL expiry, and key-space behavior rather than relying on `IDistributedCache` in-memory stubs that do not honor TTLs or data encoding. Container startup is encapsulated in an `IAsyncLifetime` fixture, keeping test methods free of infrastructure setup code.

```csharp
public class RedisCacheServiceTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly RedisContainer _redis = new RedisBuilder()
        .WithImage("redis:7-alpine")
        .Build();

    private IConnectionMultiplexer _mux = null!;
    private RedisCacheService _sut = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _redis.StartAsync();
        _mux = await ConnectionMultiplexer.ConnectAsync(_redis.GetConnectionString());
        _sut = new RedisCacheService(_mux);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _mux.CloseAsync();
        await _redis.DisposeAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Set_ThenGet_ReturnsValueBeforeTtlExpiry()
    {
        await _sut.SetAsync("session:abc", "user-42", ttl: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
        var value = await _sut.GetAsync("session:abc");
        value.Should().Be("user-42");
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Get_AfterKeyDeletion_ReturnsNull()
    {
        await _sut.SetAsync("temp:key", "data", ttl: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
        await _mux.GetDatabase().KeyDeleteAsync("temp:key");
        var value = await _sut.GetAsync("temp:key");
        value.Should().BeNull();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** A real Redis container enforces encoding fidelity (e.g., `byte[]` vs `string` serialisation, JSON escaping) and TTL resolution at the millisecond level, catching bugs invisible to `IDistributedCache` stubs. The tradeoff is 1–3 seconds of container startup overhead per test class using a private fixture; share a single container across tests using `ICollectionFixture<RedisFixture>` in xUnit or `[OneTimeSetUp]` in NUnit to amortize this cost when you have many Redis-dependent tests. [official]

---

### Pattern 112 — xUnit v3 `IClassFixture<T>` Shared Fixture With `ITestOutputHelper` Bridged via Constructor Injection [official]

xUnit v3 allows a test class to receive both a typed fixture and an `ITestOutputHelper` via constructor injection simultaneously. A common pattern for integration test suites is to have the fixture manage expensive infrastructure (database, HTTP server) while the `ITestOutputHelper` routes per-test diagnostic output without coupling the fixture to logging concerns. Bridging the helper into the fixture via a method call at test-class construction time lets the fixture emit diagnostics attributed to the currently running test.

```csharp
public class ApiFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory = null!;
    public HttpClient Client { get; private set; } = null!;
    private Action<string>? _log;

    public void AttachLogger(Action<string> log) => _log = log;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _factory = new WebApplicationFactory<Program>()
            .WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.UseEnvironment("Testing"));
        Client = _factory.CreateClient();
        _log?.Invoke("WebApplicationFactory started.");
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        Client.Dispose();
        await _factory.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

public class OrdersEndpointTests : IClassFixture<ApiFixture>
{
    private readonly ApiFixture _fixture;
    private readonly ITestOutputHelper _output;

    public OrdersEndpointTests(ApiFixture fixture, ITestOutputHelper output)
    {
        _fixture = fixture;
        _output = output;
        _fixture.AttachLogger(output.WriteLine);
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrders_Returns200WithContent()
    {
        var response = await _fixture.Client.GetAsync("/api/orders");
        _output.WriteLine($"Status: {response.StatusCode}");
        response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.OK);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `AttachLogger` replaces the previous test's output bridge at construction time, so the fixture log is always attributed to the most recently constructed test instance. In parallel test runs within the same class, two test instances may overwrite each other's `_log` reference, causing log lines from one test to appear in another test's output. Guard against this by capturing the logger in a local `Action<string>` before each test method body executes, or use a `ConcurrentQueue<string>` per-instance. [official]

---

### Pattern 113 — NUnit 4 `Assert.Multiple` With `Assume.That` Guard for Conditional Block Assertions [official]

NUnit 4's `Assume.That` acts as a precondition check — it throws `InconclusiveException` rather than `AssertionException`, marking the test as inconclusive rather than failed. Combining `Assume.That` as a guard before an `Assert.Multiple` block prevents the multi-assertion block from running when the SUT's output is in a state that makes the assertions meaningless — for example, when a nullable navigation property is `null` because an earlier database step was skipped. The test result is flagged as inconclusive (yellow in most runners) rather than producing a cascade of `NullReferenceException` failures from the assertion block.

```csharp
[Test]
public void InvoiceDto_HasCorrectLineItems_WhenOrderExists()
{
    var dto = _invoiceService.BuildDto(orderId: 101);

    Assume.That(dto, Is.Not.Null,
        "InvoiceDto was null — SUT returned no invoice for orderId 101");
    Assume.That(dto!.LineItems, Is.Not.Null.And.Not.Empty,
        "LineItems collection was null or empty — cannot assert item-level details");

    Assert.Multiple(() =>
    {
        Assert.That(dto.LineItems[0].Sku, Is.EqualTo("SKU-001"));
        Assert.That(dto.LineItems[0].Quantity, Is.EqualTo(2));
        Assert.That(dto.LineItems[0].UnitPrice, Is.EqualTo(49.99m).Within(0.01m));
        Assert.That(dto.TotalAmount, Is.EqualTo(99.98m).Within(0.01m));
    });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Tests marked inconclusive by `Assume.That` can mask genuine bugs if the guard condition is too permissive — a test that is always inconclusive never actually validates the assertion block. CI pipelines should treat a rising count of inconclusive tests as a health signal, not as "not failed". Configure your CI dashboard to alert on a threshold of inconclusive test counts, and periodically audit `Assume.That` guards to ensure they only fire for genuinely environmental preconditions (shared fixture not set up) rather than SUT behavioral gaps. [official]

---

### Pattern 114 — MSTest v3 `[TestInitialize]` / `[TestCleanup]` With `TestContext.CancellationTokenSource` for Timeout-Scoped Setup [official]

MSTest v3 injects a `TestContext` into test classes via a property setter. `TestContext.CancellationTokenSource` provides a pre-configured `CancellationToken` that is cancelled when the test's configured timeout expires — using this token in `[TestInitialize]` and the test body ensures that expensive async setup (HTTP requests, database seeding) respects the test-level timeout and produces a clean cancellation rather than hanging indefinitely.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class UserServiceIntegrationTests
{
    public TestContext TestContext { get; set; } = null!;

    private UserServiceClient _client = null!;
    private string _testUserId = string.Empty;

    [TestInitialize]
    public async Task SetUpAsync()
    {
        var ct = TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Token;
        _client = new UserServiceClient(TestSettings.BaseUrl);
        _testUserId = await _client.CreateTestUserAsync(
            new CreateUserRequest { Name = $"Test-{Guid.NewGuid():N}" },
            ct);
        TestContext.WriteLine($"Created test user: {_testUserId}");
    }

    [TestCleanup]
    public async Task TearDownAsync()
    {
        if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(_testUserId))
            await _client.DeleteUserAsync(_testUserId, CancellationToken.None);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(10_000)]
    public async Task GetUser_ReturnsCreatedUser()
    {
        var ct = TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Token;
        var user = await _client.GetUserAsync(_testUserId, ct);
        Assert.IsNotNull(user);
        Assert.IsTrue(user.Name.StartsWith("Test-"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `TestContext.CancellationTokenSource` is cancelled when the `[Timeout]` attribute fires, but `[TestCleanup]` runs unconditionally after the timeout regardless of whether the test was cancelled. This means `[TestCleanup]` may attempt to delete the test user even if `[TestInitialize]` never completed (and `_testUserId` is empty), which is why the `!string.IsNullOrEmpty(_testUserId)` guard is essential. If `[TestCleanup]` itself needs cancellation semantics, pass `CancellationToken.None` with an explicit short timeout wrapping the cleanup HTTP call, not `TestContext.CancellationTokenSource.Token` which may already be in the cancelled state. [official]

---

### Pattern 115 — FluentAssertions v8 `ContainSingle` With Lambda for One-And-Only-One Element Assertion [official]

FluentAssertions v8's `ContainSingle(predicate)` asserts that a collection contains exactly one element matching the predicate and returns that element (as a `AndWhichConstraint`) for chained property assertions. This is the canonical pattern for asserting both uniqueness and correctness of a single expected item — it replaces the common fragile pattern of `.Where(predicate).Should().HaveCount(1)` followed by `.First()`, which produces two separate failure messages and obscures intent.

```csharp
[Fact]
public void ProcessRequests_EmitsExactlyOneAuditLogForEachUser()
{
    var processor = new RequestProcessor(_auditLogger);
    processor.HandleAll(new[]
    {
        new Request { UserId = "u1", Action = "Login" },
        new Request { UserId = "u2", Action = "Login" },
        new Request { UserId = "u1", Action = "ViewDashboard" },
    });

    var logs = _auditLogger.CapturedLogs;

    var u1Login = logs.Should()
        .ContainSingle(l => l.UserId == "u1" && l.Action == "Login")
        .Which;

    u1Login.Timestamp.Should().BeCloseTo(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, precision: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
    u1Login.Severity.Should().Be(AuditSeverity.Info);
    u1Login.CorrelationId.Should().NotBeNullOrEmpty();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `ContainSingle` fails immediately if zero or two-or-more elements match — it does not give you the matching elements when it fails with "found 2". If your test discovers an unexpected duplicate, you need to add a separate `Where(predicate).Should().BeEquivalentTo(…)` assertion to inspect what the duplicates actually are. For collections that legitimately can have zero or one matching elements, use `.Where(predicate).Should().HaveCountLessOrEqualTo(1)` followed by a conditional single-element assertion rather than `ContainSingle`. [official]

---

### Pattern 116 — Moq `Mock.Of<T>(predicate)` Declarative Mock Inline Factory for Value-Object Stubs [community]

`Mock.Of<T>(predicate)` creates a pre-configured mock where `It.IsAny<…>()` is not needed — the predicate sets up property getters via expression syntax in a single line. This is the idiomatic way to create lightweight stubs for interfaces with simple property contracts (e.g., `ICurrentUser`, `IClock`, `IFeatureFlags`) that are injected into many SUT constructors. It eliminates the two-step `new Mock<T>()` / `.Setup(…).Returns(…)` boilerplate for read-only stubs.

```csharp
[Fact]
public void CreateOrder_StampsWithCurrentUserAndTime()
{
    var currentUser = Mock.Of<ICurrentUser>(u =>
        u.Id == "user-99" &&
        u.Name == "Alice" &&
        u.IsAuthenticated == true);

    var clock = Mock.Of<IClock>(c =>
        c.UtcNow == new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 14, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));

    var sut = new OrderFactory(currentUser, clock);
    var order = sut.Create(productId: 7, quantity: 2);

    order.CreatedBy.Should().Be("user-99");
    order.CreatedAt.Should().Be(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 14, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Mock.Of<T>` returns the mocked object directly (not the `Mock<T>` wrapper), so you cannot call `.Verify(…)` on it after the test. If you need to verify that a method was called on the stub, use `Mock.Get(stub).Verify(…)` to retrieve the underlying `Mock<T>`. For purely return-value stubs with no interaction verification, `Mock.Of<T>` is cleaner; for spies and interaction-verified mocks, use the explicit `new Mock<T>()` approach so the `Mock<T>` instance is available without `Mock.Get`. [community]

---

### Pattern 117 — xUnit v3 `[MemberData]` With `TheoryData` From an External Static Class for Cross-Test-Class Data Sharing [official]

When multiple test classes need the same data set — for example, a set of invalid currency codes tested by both a parser test class and a formatter test class — extracting `TheoryData` into a dedicated static class prevents duplication and creates a single source of truth. xUnit's `[MemberData(nameof(X), MemberType = typeof(SharedData))]` overload points to a property or method on any accessible type, not just the current class.

```csharp
// Shared data in TestData/CurrencyTestData.cs
public static class CurrencyTestData
{
    public static TheoryData<string, string> InvalidCodes => new()
    {
        { "XX",   "Unknown ISO-4217 code" },
        { "123",  "Numeric code not supported" },
        { "",     "Empty string" },
        { "USDX", "Code too long" },
        { null!,  "Null input" },
    };

    public static TheoryData<string, decimal, string> FormattingCases => new()
    {
        { "USD", 1_234.56m, "$1,234.56" },
        { "EUR",   999.00m, "€999.00"   },
        { "JPY", 10_000m,   "¥10,000"   },
    };
}

// Used in two separate test classes:
public class CurrencyParserTests
{
    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(CurrencyTestData.InvalidCodes),
        MemberType = typeof(CurrencyTestData))]
    public void Parse_ThrowsForInvalidCode(string code, string reason)
    {
        var act = () => CurrencyParser.Parse(code);
        act.Should().Throw<FormatException>(because: reason);
    }
}

public class CurrencyFormatterTests
{
    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(CurrencyTestData.FormattingCases),
        MemberType = typeof(CurrencyTestData))]
    public void Format_ProducesCorrectString(string code, decimal amount, string expected)
    {
        CurrencyFormatter.Format(code, amount).Should().Be(expected);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Centralising test data in an external class makes data changes affect every consumer at once — a valuable single source of truth when the domain rule is stable, but fragile when different test classes need subtly different edge cases. Avoid evolving a shared `TheoryData` class by adding rows that are only relevant to one consumer; instead, subclass or compose data sets. Also, the external class must be in the same assembly as the tests (or a referenced test-helper assembly) because xUnit reflects on it at test discovery time and will throw `MissingMethodException` if the type is not accessible. [official]

---

### Pattern 118 — NUnit 4 `[Order]` Attribute With `[Dependency]` for Explicit Sequential Integration Test Chains [official]

NUnit 4's `[Order(n)]` attribute on test methods within a fixture (not across fixtures) guarantees a specific execution sequence when the fixture is run without parallelism. Combined with the `Assert.That(result, Is.Not.Null)` precondition check and `Assume.That` guards, this pattern is appropriate for integration tests that model a stateful workflow — for example, an API test suite where order creation must precede order approval, which must precede shipment dispatch. The `[Order]` attribute does not imply data sharing; use instance fields updated by each step to propagate state.

```csharp
[TestFixture]
[NonParallelizable]
public class OrderLifecycleIntegrationTests
{
    private static string _orderId = string.Empty;
    private static string _shipmentId = string.Empty;
    private readonly OrderApiClient _api = new(TestSettings.BaseUrl);

    [Test, Order(1)]
    public async Task Step1_CreateOrder_ReturnsOrderId()
    {
        var result = await _api.CreateOrderAsync(new CreateOrderRequest
        {
            ProductId = 42,
            Quantity  = 3,
        });
        Assert.That(result.OrderId, Is.Not.Null.And.Not.Empty);
        _orderId = result.OrderId;
    }

    [Test, Order(2)]
    public async Task Step2_ApproveOrder_SetsStatusApproved()
    {
        Assume.That(_orderId, Is.Not.Empty, "Step 1 did not produce an order ID");
        var result = await _api.ApproveOrderAsync(_orderId);
        Assert.That(result.Status, Is.EqualTo(OrderStatus.Approved));
    }

    [Test, Order(3)]
    public async Task Step3_DispatchShipment_ReturnsTrackingNumber()
    {
        Assume.That(_orderId, Is.Not.Empty, "Step 1 did not produce an order ID");
        var result = await _api.DispatchAsync(_orderId);
        Assert.That(result.TrackingNumber, Does.StartWith("TRK-"));
        _shipmentId = result.TrackingNumber;
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[Order]` guarantees sequence within a single fixture instance, but does not guarantee sequence across fixtures or across parallel workers. State stored in `static` fields (as shown above) is the only way to propagate values between `[Order]`-tagged tests because NUnit creates a fresh instance of the fixture per test by default — unless the fixture is marked `[Fixture(LifeCycle = LifeCycle.SingleInstance)]`. Using `static` fields creates a global state pollution risk if the fixture is ever run in parallel with other instances of the same class; always pair `[Order]` usage with `[NonParallelizable]`. [official]

---

### Pattern 119 — FluentAssertions v8 `AndAlso` Chained on `Throw` for Exception Property Assertions [official]

When testing that a method throws a specific exception with both a predictable message and a meaningful inner state, FluentAssertions v8's `AndAlso()` connector chains additional assertions on the same caught exception after the initial `Throw<TException>()` assertion. `.Which` exposes the caught exception; `AndAlso()` continues the fluent chain without re-executing the action or catching a second exception. This is the idiomatic way to assert multiple exception properties in a single readable pipeline.

```csharp
[Fact]
public void ProcessPayment_ThrowsDomainExceptionWithCorrectCodeAndMessage()
{
    var request = new PaymentRequest
    {
        Amount       = -50m,
        CurrencyCode = "USD",
        AccountId    = "acc-007",
    };

    Action act = () => _paymentService.Process(request);

    act.Should()
        .Throw<DomainException>()
        .WithMessage("*negative amount*")
        .And.Which.ErrorCode.Should().Be("PAYMENT_NEGATIVE_AMOUNT");

    // Alternative chained form when asserting multiple exception properties:
    act.Should()
        .Throw<DomainException>()
        .Where(ex => ex.ErrorCode == "PAYMENT_NEGATIVE_AMOUNT"
                  && ex.HttpStatusCode == 422);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `.And.Which` re-evaluates the exception caught by the preceding `.Throw<T>()` assertion — it does not re-execute `act`. However, if the action has side effects that should not be repeated (e.g., a database insert attempted before the exception is thrown), note that `act` is invoked once for each `.Should().Throw<T>()` call. Splitting into two separate `act.Should().Throw<T>()` chains calls the action twice. Use the single-chain `.And.Which` pattern to assert all exception properties in one invocation to avoid double-triggering side effects. [official]

---

### Pattern 120 — Testcontainers.NET `PostgreSqlContainer` With Respawn for Fast Database Reset Between Tests [official]

Combining Testcontainers.NET's `PostgreSqlContainer` with the Respawn library (by Jimmy Bogard) provides the fastest database reset strategy for integration test suites: the container starts once per test class (or collection), and Respawn issues targeted `DELETE` or `TRUNCATE` statements against only the tables that were modified — far faster than dropping and re-creating the schema on every test. The `Respawner` is configured with the connection string once in `[OneTimeSetUp]` or `InitializeAsync`; each test's cleanup calls `ResetAsync` in a `[TearDown]` or equivalent.

```csharp
public class OrderRepositoryTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _postgres = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
        .WithDatabase("orders_test")
        .Build();

    private NpgsqlConnection _connection = null!;
    private Respawner _respawner = null!;
    private OrderRepository _sut = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _postgres.StartAsync();
        _connection = new NpgsqlConnection(_postgres.GetConnectionString());
        await _connection.OpenAsync();

        await ApplySchemaAsync(_connection);

        _respawner = await Respawner.CreateAsync(_connection, new RespawnerOptions
        {
            DbAdapter = DbAdapter.Postgres,
            SchemasToInclude = new[] { "public" },
        });

        _sut = new OrderRepository(_postgres.GetConnectionString());
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _connection.DisposeAsync();
        await _postgres.DisposeAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Insert_ThenFind_ReturnsMatchingOrder()
    {
        var id = await _sut.InsertAsync(new Order { ProductId = 7, Quantity = 2 });
        var found = await _sut.FindAsync(id);
        found.Should().NotBeNull();
        found!.ProductId.Should().Be(7);
    }

    // Called in a per-test cleanup fixture wrapper omitted for brevity:
    private async Task ResetDatabaseAsync() => await _respawner.ResetAsync(_connection);

    private static async Task ApplySchemaAsync(NpgsqlConnection conn)
    {
        await using var cmd = conn.CreateCommand();
        cmd.CommandText = """
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (
                id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
                product_id INT NOT NULL,
                quantity INT NOT NULL
            );
        """;
        await cmd.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Respawn discovers tables to reset by querying the database schema at `CreateAsync` time — if your test suite dynamically creates tables (e.g., EF Core migrations run per-test), Respawn's table list is stale and newly created tables are not reset. Re-create the `Respawner` instance after any migration that changes the schema. Also, `Respawner.ResetAsync` must be awaited in a per-test cleanup hook — placing it in the test body's `finally` block is not sufficient if the test is cancelled. Use xUnit's `IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync` or NUnit's `[TearDown]` to guarantee cleanup execution even on test timeout. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 47

**xUnit v3 `[MemberData]` pointing to a `TheoryData` property on an external class throws `ArgumentException: Object of type 'System.Object[]' cannot be converted to type 'System.String'` at runtime when the property returns `TheoryData<string, int>` but the test method has parameters in the wrong order [community]** — `TheoryData<string, int>` produces columns `[string, int]` but if the test method signature is `(int n, string label)` the types are swapped and xUnit throws an argument conversion exception. The xUnit v3 runner reports this as a test failure rather than a discovery error, so all theory cases fail with the same misleading exception rather than a parameter-order warning. WHY it causes problems: developers reading the failure assume their test data contains invalid values and spend time debugging the data source rather than the method signature; the fix is trivial (swap the parameter order) but the error message `ArgumentException: Object of type 'System.Object[]' cannot be converted to type 'System.String'` does not mention the parameter mismatch. Fix: always declare `TheoryData<T1, T2>` type arguments in the same order as the method parameters, and add a compile-time comment noting the expected column order when the data is in a shared external class.

**NUnit 4 `[Order]` attribute does not affect execution order when `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.Children)]` is set at the fixture level — the order is advisory only within a single-threaded fixture [community]** — Developers who rely on `[Order]` to sequence integration test steps and also inherit a `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.Children)]` assembly-level attribute find that ordered tests run in unpredictable sequences on machines with sufficient CPU cores. NUnit 4 explicitly documents that `[Order]` only guarantees sequencing within a non-parallel context. WHY it causes problems: tests that pass locally (often on a developer's laptop where parallelism is lower) fail on CI build agents with 8+ cores, and the failure looks like a race condition in the SUT rather than a test ordering problem. Fix: always annotate `[Order]`-dependent fixtures with `[NonParallelizable]` and verify the attribute is not being overridden by an assembly-level parallel scope attribute in `GlobalSetup.cs`.

**MSTest v3 `[TestInitialize]` does not run if the test class inherits from a base class that also has a `[TestInitialize]` method without calling `base.SetUpAsync()` — MSTest calls only the most-derived `[TestInitialize]` method in the inheritance chain [community]** — Unlike some frameworks, MSTest does not automatically chain `[TestInitialize]` up the inheritance hierarchy. A test class that overrides `SetUpAsync` without calling `await base.SetUpAsync()` silently skips the base class setup, leaving shared fixtures (e.g., database connections, mock registrations) in an uninitialised state. WHY it causes problems: the test runs but operates against null or default-valued dependencies, producing `NullReferenceException` in the test body rather than a setup failure — the stack trace points to the test body line, not the missing base initialisation. Fix: document the `base` call requirement in a `CLAUDE.md` or `README` note in the test infrastructure folder, and use a `[TestCleanup]` base method pattern that asserts `_sut is not null` as an invariant check.

**FluentAssertions v8 `ContainSingle` fails with an unhelpful message when the collection contains zero elements — the message says "Expected collection to contain a single item matching the predicate, but 0 items were found" without showing any of the actual items in the collection [community]** — When `ContainSingle(predicate)` fails because no items match, the failure message does not dump the collection contents, making it hard to diagnose whether the collection is empty or contains items that almost-but-not-quite match the predicate. WHY it causes problems: a filter bug in the SUT that returns a non-empty collection where all items fail the predicate produces the same "0 items found" message as an empty collection, so the developer cannot distinguish between "the query returned nothing" and "the query returned items but with wrong values". Fix: add `.And.Subject.Should().NotBeEmpty("the processor should have emitted at least one log entry")` as a preceding assertion to separate the "collection is empty" case from the "no matching item" case, and log the actual collection to `ITestOutputHelper` on assertion failure using a custom assertion extension.

**Moq `SetupSequence` does not reset between test runs when the `Mock<T>` is declared as a `static` or `[ClassFixture]`-shared field — the sequence position persists across tests in the same fixture, causing later tests in the class to consume residual return values from earlier tests' sequences [community]** — `SetupSequence` internally maintains a queue of configured responses. If a `Mock<T>` instance is shared across tests (via a static field or fixture property) without calling `.Reset()`, the queue from one test's `SetupSequence` is partially consumed, and the next test's `SetupSequence` call adds to the existing queue rather than replacing it. WHY it causes problems: a test calling a method three times consumes the first three responses; the next test expecting its own first response actually receives whatever was left in the queue, producing an assertion failure that appears to be caused by wrong SUT behavior. Fix: create fresh `Mock<T>` instances per test (declare them in the test class field initialiser), or call `mock.Reset()` in `[TestInitialize]` / `[SetUp]` to clear all setups and sequences before each test.

**Testcontainers.NET `PostgreSqlContainer` `GetConnectionString()` returns a connection string using `localhost` as the hostname, which fails inside GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps pipeline agents that run Docker-in-Docker — the test host is inside a container itself and `localhost` does not resolve to the Docker host [community]** — In standard CI environments, `GetConnectionString()` works because the test runner is on the Docker host. In DinD (Docker-in-Docker) environments, the test runner is itself a container, and `localhost` inside that container refers to the test-runner container, not the Postgres container's host. WHY it causes problems: the test suite passes locally and on standard CI agents but fails only on DinD-based self-hosted runners, producing `Connection refused` on `localhost:5432`, which is indistinguishable from the container not starting. Fix: set the `TESTCONTAINERS_HOST_OVERRIDE` environment variable to the Docker host IP in DinD environments, or configure the Testcontainers `TestcontainersSettings.DockerEndpointAuthConfig` via a `testcontainers.properties` file to use the bridge network gateway address.

**xUnit v3 `Assert.ThrowsAsync<TException>` does not unwrap `AggregateException` from `Task.WhenAll` — if the SUT awaits multiple tasks and one throws, the `AggregateException` wrapping it is rethrown, not the inner exception, and the assertion fails with "Expected ArgumentException but got AggregateException" [community]** — When a SUT calls `await Task.WhenAll(tasks)` and one task throws `ArgumentException`, C# unwraps the first inner exception on `await` in most cases. However, certain async state machine configurations retain the `AggregateException` wrapper. `Assert.ThrowsAsync<ArgumentException>` does not unwrap `AggregateException` and fails. WHY it causes problems: the test error message shows `AggregateException` with the correct `ArgumentException` as its inner exception, confusing developers who believe the SUT is throwing the wrong type when in fact the framework wrapping is the issue. Fix: use `await act.Should().ThrowAsync<ArgumentException>()` from FluentAssertions, which correctly unwraps `AggregateException` inner exceptions, or catch and unwrap manually with `ex.InnerException.Should().BeOfType<ArgumentException>()`.

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 47 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `[MemberData]` with `TheoryData<T1, T2>` where method parameters are in a different order | xUnit throws `ArgumentException` at runtime with misleading conversion error | Declare `TheoryData` generic args in the same left-to-right order as method parameters |
| `[Order]` in NUnit 4 without `[NonParallelizable]` | Assembly-level parallelism overrides `[Order]`; tests run in unpredictable sequence on multi-core CI | Always annotate ordered fixtures with `[NonParallelizable]` and verify no parent attribute overrides it |
| Overriding `[TestInitialize]` in MSTest v3 without calling `base.SetUpAsync()` | Base class setup skipped silently; test runs with null dependencies; error reported in test body, not setup | Always call `await base.SetUpAsync()` and assert non-null invariants in base cleanup method |
| `ContainSingle(predicate)` as sole assertion when collection may be non-empty with wrong values | Failure message shows "0 matched" but cannot distinguish empty vs. all-items-wrong-values | Precede with `.NotBeEmpty()` and log actual collection contents on failure |
| Shared `Mock<T>` across tests without `.Reset()` when using `SetupSequence` | Sequence queue persists between tests; later tests consume stale residual responses | Create fresh `Mock<T>` per test, or call `mock.Reset()` in `[SetUp]` / `[TestInitialize]` |
| `GetConnectionString()` used without `TESTCONTAINERS_HOST_OVERRIDE` in Docker-in-Docker CI | `localhost` resolves to test-runner container, not Postgres container; `Connection refused` in DinD | Set `TESTCONTAINERS_HOST_OVERRIDE` env var or configure bridge network gateway address |
| `Assert.ThrowsAsync<T>` on a method that uses `Task.WhenAll` internally | `AggregateException` wrapper not unwrapped; assertion fails with wrong exception type message | Use FluentAssertions `ThrowAsync<T>()` which unwraps `AggregateException`, or assert `.InnerException` |

## Cycle 48 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 121 — xUnit v3 `ICollectionFixture<T>` With Cross-Class Shared Database Seeding [official]

`ICollectionFixture<T>` combined with `[Collection("DbSeed")]` allows multiple test classes to share a single expensive database seed operation. Declare a `[CollectionDefinition]` marker and implement the fixture with `IAsyncLifetime` so seed data is inserted once per collection and torn down after all classes have run.

```csharp
[CollectionDefinition("DbSeed")]
public class DbSeedCollection : ICollectionFixture<DbSeedFixture> { }

public class DbSeedFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public SqlConnection Connection { get; private set; } = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        Connection = new SqlConnection("Server=localhost;Database=TestDb;Integrated Security=true");
        await Connection.OpenAsync();
        await SeedAsync(Connection);
    }

    private static async Task SeedAsync(SqlConnection conn)
    {
        await using var cmd = conn.CreateCommand();
        cmd.CommandText = "INSERT INTO Products (Name) VALUES ('Widget'), ('Gadget')";
        await cmd.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await using var cmd = Connection.CreateCommand();
        cmd.CommandText = "DELETE FROM Products";
        await cmd.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
        await Connection.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

[Collection("DbSeed")]
public class ProductQueryTests(DbSeedFixture db, ITestOutputHelper output)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetAll_ReturnsSeededProducts()
    {
        await using var cmd = db.Connection.CreateCommand();
        cmd.CommandText = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Products";
        var count = (int)(await cmd.ExecuteScalarAsync())!;
        output.WriteLine($"Product count: {count}");
        Assert.Equal(2, count);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** All test classes sharing the collection run serially by default within that collection — the collection mutex is exclusive. If you have many test classes in the same collection and want to parallelise across them, you cannot: `ICollectionFixture<T>` enforces serial collection execution. Prefer coarse-grained seeding (one fixture seeds everything) and keep collection scope as narrow as possible — one collection per database, not one per test file — to minimise the serial execution blast radius. [official]
