### Pattern 122 — NUnit 4 `TestCaseData.SetName` With Tokens for Human-Readable Parameterised Test Names [official]

NUnit 4 supports `{0}`, `{1}`, and `{m}` tokens in `SetName` for substituting method name and argument values into the displayed test name, giving parameterised tests descriptive names in test runners without hard-coding the full string.

```csharp
public class PricingCalculatorTests
{
    private static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> DiscountCases()
    {
        yield return new TestCaseData(100m, 0.1m, 90m)
            .SetName("{m}_GivenPrice{0}_Discount{1}_Expects{2}");
        yield return new TestCaseData(200m, 0.25m, 150m)
            .SetName("{m}_GivenPrice{0}_Discount{1}_Expects{2}");
        yield return new TestCaseData(50m, 0m, 50m)
            .SetName("{m}_GivenPrice{0}_NoDiscount_ExpectsFull");
        yield return new TestCaseData(0m, 0.5m, 0m)
            .SetName("{m}_ZeroPrice_AnyDiscount_ExpectsZero");
    }

    [TestCaseSource(nameof(DiscountCases))]
    public void ApplyDiscount_ReturnsExpected(
        decimal basePrice, decimal discountRate, decimal expected)
    {
        var sut = new PricingCalculator();
        var result = sut.ApplyDiscount(basePrice, discountRate);
        Assert.That(result, Is.EqualTo(expected));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `{m}` inserts the test method name, so renaming the method silently updates all test names — useful for refactoring but can break any test-name-based dashboards or filter expressions that rely on the old string. Token substitution only applies when `SetName` is called; if any `TestCaseData` in the source omits `SetName`, NUnit falls back to the positional argument display `(100, 0.1, 90)`. Maintain consistency by always calling `SetName` or never calling it within a given source method to avoid a mixed-display result in test explorers. [official]

---

### Pattern 123 — MSTest v3 `[DataRow]` With `DisplayName` for Named Parameterised Test Cases [official]

MSTest v3 supports a `DisplayName` property on `[DataRow]` to provide human-readable names in Visual Studio's Test Explorer and in CI test result XML, replacing the default `(param1, param2, ...)` representation.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class PasswordValidatorTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow("", false, DisplayName = "EmptyPassword_IsInvalid")]
    [DataRow("abc", false, DisplayName = "TooShortPassword_IsInvalid")]
    [DataRow("Abcdefg1!", true, DisplayName = "StrongPassword_IsValid")]
    [DataRow("ALLUPPERCASE1!", false, DisplayName = "NoLowercase_IsInvalid")]
    [DataRow("alllowercase1!", false, DisplayName = "NoUppercase_IsInvalid")]
    [DataRow("NoSpecialChar1", false, DisplayName = "NoSpecialChar_IsInvalid")]
    [DataRow("ValidPass1!", true, DisplayName = "ValidPassword_IsValid")]
    [DataRow("12345678!", false, DisplayName = "NoLetters_IsInvalid")]
    public void Validate_ReturnsExpected(string password, bool expectedValid)
    {
        var sut = new PasswordValidator();
        var result = sut.Validate(password);
        Assert.AreEqual(expectedValid, result.IsValid,
            $"Password '{password}' validity should be {expectedValid}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `DisplayName` is a compile-time string literal on `[DataRow]` — it cannot include runtime values or interpolated expressions. For cases where the display name must include the parameter value itself (e.g., for long or structured values), it must be duplicated manually in the attribute, creating a maintenance burden if the data value changes. In such cases, `[DynamicData]` with a `DynamicDataDisplayName` method delegate is more maintainable because the display name is generated from the same data row at runtime. [official]

---

### Pattern 124 — FluentAssertions v8 `BeEquivalentTo` With `Using(comparer)` for Custom Equality in Object Graph Comparison [official]

FluentAssertions v8 `BeEquivalentTo` accepts an options lambda that allows injecting a custom `IEqualityComparer<T>` for specific types within the object graph, enabling decimal precision tolerance, case-insensitive string matching, or domain-specific equality rules without implementing `Equals` on the SUT classes.

```csharp
public class InvoiceComparisonTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void ProcessInvoice_ProducesExpectedLineItems()
    {
        var sut = new InvoiceProcessor();
        var result = sut.Process(BuildRawInvoice());

        var expected = new Invoice
        {
            Number = "INV-001",
            Lines = new[]
            {
                new InvoiceLine { Description = "Widget", UnitPrice = 9.999m, Quantity = 3 },
                new InvoiceLine { Description = "Gadget", UnitPrice = 14.995m, Quantity = 1 },
            }
        };

        result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, opts => opts
            .Using<decimal>(ctx =>
                ctx.Subject.Should().BeApproximately(ctx.Expectation, precision: 0.01m))
            .WhenTypeIs<decimal>()
            .Excluding(l => l.Path.Contains("CreatedAt")));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Using<T>(comparer).WhenTypeIs<T>()` applies the custom equality to ALL properties of that type in the entire graph — if the graph has `decimal` fields where you want exact equality (e.g., a tax ID stored as decimal), you cannot selectively exclude them without restructuring the options lambda. Prefer using a dedicated value object or strongly-typed wrapper (`Money`, `Quantity`) so the custom comparer targets only the types that need tolerance, rather than all `decimal` properties in the graph. [official]

---

### Pattern 125 — Moq `MockSequence` With `InSequence` for Ordered Multi-Mock Interaction Verification [community]

When testing workflows where two mocks must be called in a specific order (e.g., a repository `Save` before a notification `Send`), Moq's `MockSequence` with `InSequence` enforces strict call ordering and fails the test immediately if a mock is called out of sequence.

```csharp
public class OrderWorkflowTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void PlaceOrder_SavesThenNotifies_InCorrectOrder()
    {
        var sequence = new MockSequence();
        var repoMock = new Mock<IOrderRepository>(MockBehavior.Strict);
        var notifierMock = new Mock<IOrderNotifier>(MockBehavior.Strict);

        repoMock.InSequence(sequence)
            .Setup(r => r.Save(It.IsAny<Order>()))
            .Returns(true);

        notifierMock.InSequence(sequence)
            .Setup(n => n.Notify(It.IsAny<string>()))
            .Verifiable();

        var sut = new OrderWorkflow(repoMock.Object, notifierMock.Object);
        var order = new Order { Id = Guid.NewGuid(), Total = 99.99m };

        sut.PlaceOrder(order);

        repoMock.Verify(r => r.Save(order), Times.Once);
        notifierMock.Verify(n => n.Notify(It.IsAny<string>()), Times.Once);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockSequence` requires `MockBehavior.Strict` on all participating mocks, which means every call to any method on those mocks must be set up — forgetting a secondary method called internally by the SUT will throw `MockException` rather than giving a sequencing-specific error. In practice, teams find `MockBehavior.Strict` too brittle for deep integration slices; reserve `MockSequence` + `Strict` for pure unit tests where the exact interaction surface is fully controlled and documented. [community]

---

### Pattern 126 — xUnit v3 `[assembly: AssemblyFixture]` for True Assembly-Scoped One-Time Initialisation [official]

xUnit v3 introduces `IAssemblyFixture<T>` (via `[assembly: AssemblyFixture(typeof(T))]`) for resources that are expensive to spin up and should be shared across all test classes in the assembly — such as a single `WebApplicationFactory` instance or a container cluster.

```csharp
// AssemblySetup.cs — not a test class, just the fixture
public class AppFactoryFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public WebApplicationFactory<Program> Factory { get; private set; } = default!;
    public HttpClient Client { get; private set; } = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        Factory = new WebApplicationFactory<Program>()
            .WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.UseEnvironment("Testing"));
        Client = Factory.CreateClient();
        // warm up
        await Client.GetAsync("/healthz");
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        Client.Dispose();
        await Factory.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

// In any test class in the assembly:
[assembly: AssemblyFixture(typeof(AppFactoryFixture))]

public class ProductEndpointTests(AppFactoryFixture app)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProducts_Returns200()
    {
        var response = await app.Client.GetAsync("/api/products");
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Assembly fixtures are torn down after all tests in the assembly complete, so they outlive individual collection or class fixtures — any mutation of the shared resource (e.g., inserting test data) by one test class persists for all subsequent test classes unless explicitly cleaned up. This makes assembly fixtures appropriate only for truly read-only or stateless infrastructure (a factory, a container, a read-only cache). For writable state, prefer `IClassFixture<T>` with per-class seeding and cleanup. [official]

---

### Pattern 127 — NUnit 4 `[SetUpFixture]` With `[OneTimeTearDown]` for Assembly-Level Resource Management [official]

NUnit 4's `[SetUpFixture]` with `[OneTimeSetUp]` and `[OneTimeTearDown]` provides assembly-scoped (or namespace-scoped) lifecycle control for resources that must be initialised before any test in the namespace runs — useful for starting a mock HTTP server, seeding a shared SQLite file, or pre-compiling templates.

```csharp
[SetUpFixture]
public class AssemblySetup
{
    private static WireMockServer? _wireMock;
    public static string WireMockBaseUrl { get; private set; } = string.Empty;

    [OneTimeSetUp]
    public void GlobalSetup()
    {
        _wireMock = WireMockServer.Start();
        WireMockBaseUrl = _wireMock.Url!;

        _wireMock.Given(Request.Create().WithPath("/api/rates").UsingGet())
            .RespondWith(Response.Create()
                .WithStatusCode(200)
                .WithBodyAsJson(new { usd = 1.0, eur = 0.92 }));
    }

    [OneTimeTearDown]
    public void GlobalTeardown()
    {
        _wireMock?.Stop();
        _wireMock?.Dispose();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[SetUpFixture]` without a namespace is global to the entire assembly. Adding a namespace restricts the scope to all tests under that namespace, which is more precise but can confuse newcomers who expect `[OneTimeSetUp]` on a regular fixture class to have the same scope. NUnit executes `[SetUpFixture]` teardown after all tests in scope complete — if a test run is aborted early (e.g., CI timeout kill), `[OneTimeTearDown]` may not run. Pair with a `ProcessExit` fallback handler for resources that must not leak (e.g., network ports). [official]

---

### Pattern 128 — FluentAssertions v8 `HaveCount` With `because` for Contextual Collection-Size Assertions [official]

Using `HaveCount` with a `because` argument produces failure messages that include domain context, making it immediately clear why the count matters rather than just reporting a numeric mismatch.

```csharp
public class ShoppingCartTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Checkout_RemovesAllItems_WhenPaymentSucceeds()
    {
        var cart = new ShoppingCart();
        cart.Add(new CartItem("Widget", 2));
        cart.Add(new CartItem("Gadget", 1));
        cart.Add(new CartItem("Donut", 5));

        var paymentResult = new PaymentResult { Success = true, TransactionId = "TXN-42" };
        cart.Checkout(paymentResult);

        cart.Items.Should().HaveCount(0,
            because: "successful checkout should clear all items from the cart, " +
                     "transaction {0} completed", paymentResult.TransactionId);

        cart.CompletedTransactions.Should().HaveCount(1,
            because: "one completed transaction record should be created per checkout");

        cart.CompletedTransactions.Single().TransactionId
            .Should().Be("TXN-42",
            because: "the transaction ID from the payment gateway must be preserved");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The `because` string supports `{0}`, `{1}`, etc. format arguments — however, the formatter uses FluentAssertions' own `Formatter.ToString()`, not `string.Format`, so complex objects are rendered using FA's pretty-printer. This is generally desirable but can produce very long failure messages for large object arguments. Keep `because` arguments concise and use them for domain reason rather than data dumps; use `ITestOutputHelper` / `TestContext.Out` for full object dumps. [official]

---

### Pattern 129 — Moq `SetupProperty` for Auto-Stubbing Gettable/Settable Properties With Change Tracking [official]

`Mock<T>.SetupProperty(x => x.Prop)` auto-configures a property to behave like a normal auto-property — storing the last set value and returning it on get — without requiring explicit `Setup(x => x.Prop).Returns(...)` for every initial value.

```csharp
public class UserSessionManagerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void UpdateDisplayName_SetsPropertyAndRaisesEvent()
    {
        var sessionMock = new Mock<IUserSession>();
        sessionMock.SetupProperty(s => s.DisplayName, "Initial Name");
        sessionMock.SetupProperty(s => s.LastModifiedUtc, DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-1));

        var raisedEvents = new List<string>();
        sessionMock.Object.DisplayNameChanged += (_, name) => raisedEvents.Add(name);

        var sut = new UserSessionManager(sessionMock.Object);
        sut.UpdateDisplayName("Alice");

        sessionMock.Object.DisplayName.Should().Be("Alice",
            because: "UpdateDisplayName should persist the new name on the session");
        sessionMock.Object.LastModifiedUtc.Should()
            .BeCloseTo(DateTime.UtcNow, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5),
            because: "UpdateDisplayName should update the modification timestamp");
        raisedEvents.Should().ContainSingle()
            .Which.Should().Be("Alice");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SetupProperty` only works on properties declared on an interface or virtual properties on a class — it cannot track non-virtual concrete properties. The initial value passed to `SetupProperty` is set once at setup time; if the SUT reads the property before modifying it, it will see the seed value, which is useful for state-dependent logic but can be confusing when the seed value is stale (e.g., `LastModifiedUtc` seeded to `DateTime.UtcNow` at setup time may drift relative to the assertion). Use `SetupAllProperties()` to configure all settable properties in one call when you do not need per-property seed values. [official]

---

### Pattern 130 — Testcontainers.NET `MsSqlContainer` With EF Core Migrations for Schema-Up Integration Tests [official]

`MsSqlContainer` (SQL Server image) combined with EF Core's `Database.MigrateAsync()` creates a fresh migrated database per test class, ensuring integration tests always run against the current schema without manual script management.

```csharp
public class EfCoreOrderRepositoryTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MsSqlContainer _sqlContainer = new MsSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
        .WithPassword("Strong@Passw0rd!")
        .Build();

    private OrderDbContext _db = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _sqlContainer.StartAsync();
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<OrderDbContext>()
            .UseSqlServer(_sqlContainer.GetConnectionString())
            .Options;
        _db = new OrderDbContext(options);
        await _db.Database.MigrateAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task SaveOrder_PersistsAllFields()
    {
        var order = new Order
        {
            Id = Guid.NewGuid(),
            CustomerName = "Alice",
            TotalAmount = 199.99m,
            PlacedAt = DateTime.UtcNow
        };
        _db.Orders.Add(order);
        await _db.SaveChangesAsync();

        var loaded = await _db.Orders.FindAsync(order.Id);
        loaded.Should().BeEquivalentTo(order,
            opts => opts.Excluding(o => o.PlacedAt));
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _db.DisposeAsync();
        await _sqlContainer.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Running `MigrateAsync()` per test class means every migration in your history is applied on each test class initialisation. On a project with many migrations, this adds seconds of overhead per class. Mitigate by using a `IClassFixture<T>` that runs migration once and shares the container across multiple test classes, accepting that tests must not mutate schema state. Alternatively, use `EnsureCreatedAsync()` (bypasses migration history) when you only need schema correctness and do not test migration logic itself. [official]

---

### Pattern 131 — xUnit v3 `Assert.Multiple` (Soft Assertions) for Accumulating All Failures in One Pass [official]

xUnit v3 introduces `Assert.Multiple(Action[])` allowing multiple independent assertions to run even after earlier ones fail, so all failures are reported in one test run rather than stopping at the first.

```csharp
public class InvoiceValidationTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void ValidateInvoice_AllFieldsPopulated_PassesAllRules()
    {
        var sut = new InvoiceValidator();
        var invoice = BuildTestInvoice();

        var result = sut.Validate(invoice);

        Assert.Multiple(
            () => Assert.True(result.IsValid,
                    $"Invoice should be valid but has errors: {string.Join(", ", result.Errors)}"),
            () => Assert.NotEmpty(result.InvoiceNumber),
            () => Assert.NotNull(result.CustomerReference),
            () => Assert.True(result.TotalAmount > 0,
                    $"Total amount must be positive, got {result.TotalAmount}"),
            () => Assert.NotEmpty(result.LineItems),
            () => Assert.All(result.LineItems,
                    li => Assert.True(li.UnitPrice > 0,
                        $"Line item '{li.Description}' has non-positive unit price")),
            () => Assert.True(result.DueDate > result.IssuedDate,
                    "Due date must be after issued date")
        );
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Assert.Multiple` in xUnit v3 reports all failures as a single `AggregateException` with inner `XunitException`s. Some CI reporters count this as one test failure regardless of how many inner assertions failed, which can mask the true failure breadth. FluentAssertions' `AssertionScope` is an alternative that produces similarly soft assertions with better diagnostic formatting. Do not nest `Assert.Multiple` inside another `Assert.Multiple` — the inner failures are silently swallowed in xUnit v3 beta versions; always keep assertion groups flat. [official]

---

### Pattern 132 — NUnit 4 `Warn.Unless` for Advisory Assertions That Don't Fail Tests [official]

NUnit 4's `Warn.Unless` (and `Warn.If`) records a warning in the test output and marks the test as "Warning" rather than "Failed" when a condition that is important but not strictly required is violated — useful for performance budget checks or deprecated-API usage alerts.

```csharp
[TestFixture]
public class PerformanceBudgetTests
{
    [Test]
    public async Task GetDashboardData_CompletesWithinBudget()
    {
        var sut = new DashboardService(BuildRealDependencies());
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();

        var result = await sut.GetDashboardDataAsync(userId: 42);

        sw.Stop();

        // Hard fail: must return a result
        Assert.That(result, Is.Not.Null);
        Assert.That(result.Widgets, Is.Not.Empty);

        // Soft warning: should be fast, but a slow CI machine shouldn't block the build
        Warn.Unless(sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < 2000,
            $"Dashboard load took {sw.ElapsedMilliseconds}ms — budget is 2000ms. " +
            "Consider profiling if this regresses further.");

        // Hard fail: must not take absurdly long (indicates a deadlock or hang)
        Assert.That(sw.ElapsedMilliseconds, Is.LessThan(30_000),
            "Dashboard load exceeded 30s timeout — likely a deadlock or blocking query");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Tests in "Warning" state are shown as passed (green) in most CI dashboards that do not distinguish NUnit's `ResultState.Warning` — the warning is visible only in the detailed XML report or the console log. Teams relying on automated pass/fail gates will not be alerted to warning regressions unless CI is configured to parse and escalate `<warning>` elements in the NUnit XML output. Use `Warn.Unless` for metrics and budget checks; never for correctness assertions where a silent pass would be harmful. [official]

---

### Pattern 133 — MSTest v3 `[TestProperty]` With Custom Trait Filtering for CI Stage Routing [official]

MSTest v3 `[TestProperty]` (the MSTest equivalent of xUnit `[Trait]`) allows attaching arbitrary key-value metadata to tests. Combined with `dotnet test --filter "TestCategory=Smoke"` or `--filter "TestProperty[Priority]=1"`, test properties enable fine-grained routing of tests to different CI stages.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class ApiSmokeSuiteTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [TestProperty("TestCategory", "Smoke")]
    [TestProperty("Priority", "1")]
    [TestProperty("Owner", "platform-team")]
    public async Task HealthEndpoint_Returns200()
    {
        using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com") };
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/health");
        Assert.AreEqual(HttpStatusCode.OK, response.StatusCode);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [TestProperty("TestCategory", "Integration")]
    [TestProperty("Priority", "2")]
    [TestProperty("Owner", "checkout-team")]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_PersistsToDatabase()
    {
        // full integration test body
        await Task.CompletedTask;
        Assert.IsTrue(true);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [TestProperty("TestCategory", "Smoke")]
    [TestProperty("Priority", "1")]
    [TestProperty("RequiresNetwork", "true")]
    public void Configuration_AllRequiredSettingsPresent()
    {
        var config = ConfigurationFactory.Build();
        Assert.IsNotNull(config["ConnectionStrings:Primary"]);
        Assert.IsNotNull(config["Auth:JwtSecret"]);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[TestProperty]` values are strings and are not validated at compile time — a typo like `"Smok"` instead of `"Smoke"` will cause the test to be silently excluded from all smoke runs with no error. Centralise property key constants in a `static class TestCategories` with `public const string Smoke = "Smoke"` fields, and reference them in all `[TestProperty]` attributes to catch typos at compile time. Additionally, only the `"TestCategory"` key supports the shorthand filter `TestCategory=Value`; all other property keys require the full expression `TestProperty[Key]=Value`. [official]

---

### Pattern 134 — FluentAssertions v8 `Invoking(...).Should().NotThrow` for Asserting Side-Effect-Free Calls [official]

`subject.Invoking(x => x.Method()).Should().NotThrow()` provides a clean way to assert that a method executes without throwing while also capturing context for follow-up assertions, as an alternative to wrapping in a try/catch or using `Record.Exception`.

```csharp
public class ConfigurationLoaderTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Load_WithValidFile_DoesNotThrowAndReturnsConfig()
    {
        var loader = new ConfigurationLoader();
        var filePath = Path.GetTempFileName();
        File.WriteAllText(filePath, """
            {
              "ConnectionString": "Server=localhost;Database=App",
              "MaxRetries": 3,
              "TimeoutSeconds": 30
            }
            """);

        try
        {
            loader.Invoking(l => l.Load(filePath))
                .Should().NotThrow(
                    because: "a well-formed configuration file should load without errors");

            var config = loader.Load(filePath);
            config.ConnectionString.Should()
                .Contain("Server=localhost",
                because: "connection string should preserve the server setting");
            config.MaxRetries.Should().Be(3);
            config.TimeoutSeconds.Should().Be(30);
        }
        finally
        {
            File.Delete(filePath);
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Invoking(...).Should().NotThrow()` executes the delegate once for the "no throw" assertion; any follow-up call to the same method calls it a second time, which doubles the execution cost and can be incorrect if the method is not idempotent (e.g., a file-move operation). For non-idempotent methods, use `xUnit.Record.Exception(act)` and assert the result is `null`, or capture the return value via `Invoking(...).Should().NotThrow().Which` when the FluentAssertions version supports `.Which` on `NotThrow`. [official]

---

### Pattern 135 — Testcontainers.NET `MongoDbContainer` With `MongoDB.Driver` for NoSQL Repository Integration Tests [official]

`MongoDbContainer` provides a lightweight MongoDB instance for integration tests against document repositories, enabling full CRUD lifecycle testing without an external MongoDB installation.

```csharp
public class MongoProductRepositoryTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MongoDbContainer _mongoContainer = new MongoDbBuilder()
        .WithImage("mongo:7.0")
        .Build();

    private IMongoCollection<ProductDocument> _collection = default!;
    private MongoClient _client = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _mongoContainer.StartAsync();
        _client = new MongoClient(_mongoContainer.GetConnectionString());
        var db = _client.GetDatabase("TestDb");
        _collection = db.GetCollection<ProductDocument>("products");
        await _collection.Indexes.CreateOneAsync(
            new CreateIndexModel<ProductDocument>(
                Builders<ProductDocument>.IndexKeys.Ascending(p => p.Sku),
                new CreateIndexOptions { Unique = true }));
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task InsertProduct_CanBeRetrievedBySku()
    {
        var product = new ProductDocument
        {
            Id = ObjectId.GenerateNewId(),
            Sku = "WGT-001",
            Name = "Widget",
            PriceUsd = 9.99m
        };

        await _collection.InsertOneAsync(product);

        var found = await _collection
            .Find(p => p.Sku == "WGT-001")
            .FirstOrDefaultAsync();

        found.Should().NotBeNull();
        found!.Name.Should().Be("Widget");
        found.PriceUsd.Should().Be(9.99m);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        _client.Dispose();
        await _mongoContainer.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** MongoDB Testcontainers images pull 600+ MB for the full `mongo:7.0` image. On CI agents with limited disk or cold-start pulls, this can add 2–5 minutes to the first run. Mitigate with a pre-pulled image layer cache in CI (Docker layer caching in GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines cache step) or by using a dedicated Atlas Free Tier cluster in CI. Also note that `MongoDbContainer` does not configure authentication by default — add `.WithUsername` and `.WithPassword` for tests that validate auth-related repository behaviour. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 48

**xUnit v3 `Assert.Multiple` nested inside another `Assert.Multiple` silently swallows inner failures — the outer `Assert.Multiple` catches all exceptions from its delegates, including the `AggregateException` produced by the inner `Assert.Multiple`, and treats the inner failure as a single outer failure entry, losing individual inner assertion details [community]** — Developers who refactor a large flat `Assert.Multiple` into a two-level hierarchy (outer for logical sections, inner per-section) discover that the inner failures are collapsed into a single generic entry in the failure report, making it impossible to tell which inner assertion failed. WHY it causes problems: the test output shows "Multiple assertions failed (1)" for the outer delegate rather than the specific inner assertion text, so the developer must un-nest the multiple block to identify the failure, negating the refactoring benefit. Fix: keep all assertions in a single flat `Assert.Multiple` block, and use comments to group them logically rather than nesting `Assert.Multiple` calls.

**NUnit 4 `[SetUpFixture]` `[OneTimeTearDown]` does NOT run when the test run is cancelled via Ctrl+C or a CI timeout SIGTERM — the NUnit runner exits without invoking teardown, leaking external resources such as WireMock servers, Docker containers, or temp files [community]** — `[OneTimeTearDown]` is registered as a normal teardown step that runs after test completion. When the process receives SIGTERM (common in Azure DevOps when the job timeout expires), the CLR runtime terminates without calling NUnit's post-run hooks. WHY it causes problems: a WireMock server or custom socket listener started in `[OneTimeSetUp]` continues holding its port after the CI agent exits the test run, causing the next run to fail with "Address already in use" — an error that points to port binding rather than the missed teardown. Fix: register a `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.ProcessExit` handler or a `CancellationToken`-linked `IHostedService` to stop external resources on process exit, independently of NUnit's teardown machinery.

**MSTest v3 `[TestProperty]` with the key `"TestCategory"` is the only property key that MSTest's `--filter` expression parser supports natively with the shorthand `TestCategory=Value` — other property keys require the full syntax `TestProperty[Key]=Value`, which many developers do not know, causing custom filter keys like `"Priority"` to silently match nothing [community]** — A team that adds `[TestProperty("Priority", "1")]` and runs `dotnet test --filter Priority=1` gets zero tests rather than a filter error, because `Priority` is not a first-class filter dimension. The runner silently reports "no tests matched the filter" rather than "unknown filter key". WHY it causes problems: developers conclude their test properties are misconfigured or that MSTest does not support custom traits, when the actual fix is using the full expression `TestProperty[Priority]=1`. Fix: document the correct filter syntax in `CLAUDE.md` and provide a `Makefile`/`justfile` target with the correct filter expression so developers copy-paste rather than re-discover the syntax.

**FluentAssertions v8 `BeEquivalentTo` with `ExcludingMissingMembers()` combined with `Using<T>(comparer).WhenTypeIs<T>()` — the custom comparer is not applied to members that exist only on the subject side; `ExcludingMissingMembers` suppresses the "member not found" error but also prevents the custom comparer from running on those members, silently bypassing precision-tolerance checks [community]** — A team comparing a DTO to an anonymous expected object uses `ExcludingMissingMembers()` to ignore extra DTO properties and `Using<decimal>(...).WhenTypeIs<decimal>()` for decimal tolerance. When a new `decimal` property is added to the DTO but not to the anonymous expected object, `ExcludingMissingMembers` treats it as missing and skips it entirely — including the decimal comparer — so a newly introduced `decimal` field with a wrong value is never asserted. WHY it causes problems: the regression (wrong decimal value in new field) is not caught because the equivalency check does not know it should be asserting that field at all. Fix: explicitly list expected properties in the anonymous expected object rather than relying on `ExcludingMissingMembers`; create a helper method that builds the expected anonymous object from the same DTO to keep them in sync.

**Moq `MockBehavior.Strict` throws `MockException` for any interface member that is not explicitly set up — including `IDisposable.Dispose()`, `IAsyncDisposable.DisposeAsync()`, and `IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` when the SUT calls `foreach` on a mocked collection property — causing test failures that appear to be in the SUT when they are actually caused by missing mock setups for boilerplate members [community]** — A team mocking `IOrderRepository` which implements `IDisposable` (via the underlying `DbContext`) uses `MockBehavior.Strict` and discovers that the SUT's `using (var repo = _factory.Create())` causes a `MockException: Invocation of Dispose() was not set up` rather than the expected assertion failure. WHY it causes problems: the error message names the interface member (`Dispose`) and the developer assumes the SUT has a bug in its disposal logic rather than recognising that `Strict` mode requires explicit setup of every called member. Fix: add `repoMock.Setup(r => r.Dispose())` in the fixture base, or use `MockBehavior.Default` and verify only the specific interactions that matter for the test.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 48 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Nesting `Assert.Multiple` inside `Assert.Multiple` in xUnit v3 | Inner failure details are collapsed; individual assertions indistinguishable in failure report | Keep all assertions in a single flat `Assert.Multiple` block; use comments for logical grouping |
| `[SetUpFixture]` `[OneTimeTearDown]` without a `ProcessExit` fallback | SIGTERM from CI timeout kills process before teardown runs, leaking ports and resources | Register `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.ProcessExit` handler for external resource cleanup |
| `[TestProperty("Priority", "1")]` with `--filter Priority=1` in MSTest v3 | Non-`TestCategory` properties require `TestProperty[Key]=Value` syntax; wrong syntax matches nothing silently | Use `TestProperty[Priority]=1` syntax or provide pre-built filter targets in a `Makefile` |
| `BeEquivalentTo` with `ExcludingMissingMembers()` + `Using<decimal>` type comparer | Missing members bypass the custom comparer entirely; new decimal fields with wrong values go unasserted | Explicitly include all expected properties in the expected object; never rely solely on `ExcludingMissingMembers` for precision-sensitive comparisons |
| `MockBehavior.Strict` without setup for `IDisposable.Dispose` on mocked interfaces | SUT disposal triggers `MockException` that looks like a SUT bug rather than a missing setup | Add `mock.Setup(x => x.Dispose())` in base fixture, or use `MockBehavior.Default` with explicit `Verify` calls |
| `[TestCaseSource]` without `SetName` on any case in a mixed-named source method | Test explorer shows `(arg1, arg2)` for unnamed cases alongside descriptive names; inconsistent display | Always call `SetName` on every `TestCaseData` within a source method, or call it on none |
| `IAssemblyFixture<T>` used for writable/mutable shared state | State mutated by one test class persists for all subsequent classes; tests become order-dependent | Use assembly fixtures only for read-only infrastructure; use `IClassFixture<T>` for mutable state |

## Cycle 49 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 136 — xUnit v3 `TheoryData<T1, T2>` Strongly-Typed Theory Dataset for Compile-Time Row Safety [official]

`TheoryData<T1, T2>` replaces `IEnumerable<object[]>` as the data source for `[Theory]` tests, giving compile-time type checking on every row so that a row with the wrong column count or type fails at build time rather than at runtime.

```csharp
public class PricingEngineTests
{
    public static TheoryData<decimal, int, decimal> DiscountCases => new()
    {
        { 100m, 0,  100m },   // no discount
        { 100m, 10,  90m },   // 10 % discount
        { 200m, 25, 150m },   // 25 % discount
        { 50m,  50,  25m },   // 50 % discount
        { 0m,   99,   0m },   // zero base price
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(DiscountCases))]
    public void ApplyDiscount_ReturnsExpectedFinalPrice(
        decimal basePrice,
        int discountPct,
        decimal expectedFinal)
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();

        var actual = engine.ApplyDiscount(basePrice, discountPct);

        actual.Should().Be(expectedFinal,
            because: $"a {discountPct}% discount on {basePrice} should yield {expectedFinal}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `TheoryData<T1, T2>` is only available from xUnit v2 2.4.2+ and native in v3; adding new columns requires changing the generic arity, which forces updates to every `[Theory]` method consuming the dataset. For datasets that evolve frequently, consider a dedicated record type and use `IEnumerable<object[]>` with a factory method so that column additions don't cascade. Also note that `TheoryData` enumerates eagerly at class construction — avoid putting I/O or expensive computation inside the static property initialiser. [official]

---

### Pattern 137 — NUnit 4 `[Values]` Attribute With `[Combinatorial]` for Exhaustive Parameter-Grid Testing [official]

`[Values(...)]` applied to individual parameters combined with `[Combinatorial]` generates every possible parameter combination automatically, eliminating manual `[TestCase]` rows for small enumerations and ensuring full Cartesian coverage.

```csharp
[TestFixture]
public class ShippingRateCalculatorTests
{
    [Test, Combinatorial]
    public void Calculate_AllCarrierRegionPairs_ReturnsPositiveRate(
        [Values("UPS", "FedEx", "USPS")] string carrier,
        [Values("Domestic", "International")]  string region,
        [Values(1, 5, 25)]                    int weightKg)
    {
        var calculator = new ShippingRateCalculator();

        var rate = calculator.Calculate(carrier, region, weightKg);

        Assert.That(rate, Is.GreaterThan(0m),
            $"Expected positive rate for {carrier}/{region}/{weightKg}kg");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Combinatorial explosion is the primary risk: 3 carriers x 2 regions x 3 weights = 18 tests; adding a 4th dimension with 4 values produces 216 tests, each with its own test-runner overhead. If the full grid runs in under 2 seconds it is fine; if it approaches 10 seconds, switch to `[Pairwise]` (also an NUnit attribute) which covers all two-way combinations in far fewer test cases while still catching most real-world interaction bugs. Never use `[Combinatorial]` with enum-backed `[Values]` parameters that have 10+ members without explicitly profiling the runtime impact. [official]

---

### Pattern 138 — MSTest v3 `[DynamicData]` With `DynamicDataSourceType.Method` for Computed Test Rows [official]

`[DynamicData(nameof(Method), DynamicDataSourceType.Method)]` lets MSTest pull test rows from a static factory method rather than a property, which enables conditional row generation, environment-driven exclusions, and reuse of row data across multiple `[TestMethod]`s by returning `IEnumerable<object[]>`.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class EmailValidatorTests
{
    private static IEnumerable<object[]> ValidEmailRows()
    {
        yield return new object[] { "user@example.com",         true  };
        yield return new object[] { "user+tag@sub.domain.io",   true  };
        yield return new object[] { "user@[IPv6:2001:db8::1]",  true  };
        yield return new object[] { "plainaddress",             false };
        yield return new object[] { "@missinguser.com",         false };
        yield return new object[] { "user@",                    false };
        yield return new object[] { string.Empty,               false };
        yield return new object[] { "  user@example.com  ",    false };
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(nameof(ValidEmailRows), DynamicDataSourceType.Method)]
    public void IsValid_ReturnsExpectedResult(string email, bool expectedValid)
    {
        var validator = new EmailValidator();

        var result = validator.IsValid(email);

        Assert.AreEqual(expectedValid, result,
            $"IsValid(\"{email}\") should be {expectedValid}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The method must be `static` and must return `IEnumerable<object[]>`; a non-static method compiles but throws `System.InvalidOperationException: Method must be static` at runtime with an error that mentions the attribute rather than the method, confusing developers. For display-name customisation use the `DynamicDataDisplayName` property on the attribute pointing to a `static string FormatRow(MethodInfo method, object[] data)` method; without it, MSTest shows the raw array index as the test name, making test-explorer navigation difficult. [official]

---

### Pattern 139 — FluentAssertions v8 `BeOfType<T>().Which` Chain for Post-Cast Assertions [official]

`.Should().BeOfType<T>().Which` performs a type assertion and returns the subject cast to `T` in a single fluent chain, eliminating the need for a separate explicit cast variable and keeping related assertions co-located without intermediate local variables.

```csharp
public class EventDispatcherTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Dispatch_OrderPlaced_PublishesCorrectEventType()
    {
        var capturedEvents = new List<IDomainEvent>();
        var dispatcher = new EventDispatcher(e => capturedEvents.Add(e));
        var order = Order.Create("cust-001", new[] { new OrderLine("SKU-A", 2) });

        dispatcher.Dispatch(order);

        capturedEvents.Should().ContainSingle(
            because: "a single OrderPlaced event should be raised");

        capturedEvents.Single()
            .Should().BeOfType<OrderPlacedEvent>()
            .Which.Should().Match<OrderPlacedEvent>(e =>
                e.CustomerId == "cust-001" &&
                e.LineCount  == 1          &&
                e.OccurredAt <= DateTime.UtcNow,
                because: "OrderPlacedEvent should carry the correct order metadata");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `.BeOfType<T>().Which` returns the concrete `T` but does **not** assert that the original subject is **only** of type `T` — a derived class passes `BeOfType<T>()` only if the runtime type is exactly `T`, not a subtype. If polymorphism is intentional (the event is a `SpecialOrderPlacedEvent : OrderPlacedEvent`), use `.BeAssignableTo<T>().Which` instead. Mixing up the two assertions is a common source of false-negative test failures when inheritance hierarchies are refactored. [official]

---

### Pattern 140 — Moq `SetupSequence` for Multi-Call Responses on the Same Method [official]

`mock.SetupSequence(x => x.Method())` configures different return values (or exceptions) for successive calls to the same method, enabling tests for retry logic, polling loops, and idempotency checks without introducing stateful test doubles.

```csharp
public class RetryServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ExecuteWithRetry_RetriesOnTransientFailure_SucceedsOnThirdAttempt()
    {
        var httpClientMock = new Mock<IHttpService>();

        httpClientMock
            .SetupSequence(s => s.GetAsync("/api/status"))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503 Service Unavailable"))
            .ThrowsAsync(new HttpRequestException("503 Service Unavailable"))
            .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponse { StatusCode = 200, Body = "OK" });

        var retryService = new RetryService(
            httpClientMock.Object,
            maxAttempts: 3,
            delayMs: 0);

        var result = await retryService.ExecuteWithRetry("/api/status");

        result.StatusCode.Should().Be(200);
        httpClientMock.Verify(
            s => s.GetAsync("/api/status"),
            Times.Exactly(3),
            because: "two transient failures should trigger exactly two retries");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Once a `SetupSequence` exhausts all configured responses (all `Returns`/`Throws` entries have been consumed), subsequent calls fall back to the mock's default behaviour for that method — for `MockBehavior.Loose`, this means returning the default value of the return type rather than throwing; for `MockBehavior.Strict`, a `MockException` is thrown. This silent fallback is frequently mistaken for a test bug when in fact the SUT is calling the method more times than expected. Add an explicit `Times` verification with the exact expected call count to catch over-call regressions. [official]

---

### Pattern 141 — Testcontainers.NET `NetworkBuilder` for Multi-Container Communication [official]

`NetworkBuilder` creates an isolated Docker network shared by multiple Testcontainers so that containers can resolve each other by alias name, enabling realistic service-to-service integration tests without port-forwarding hacks.

```csharp
public class OrderServiceIntegrationTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly INetwork _network = new NetworkBuilder()
        .WithName($"test-net-{Guid.NewGuid():N}")
        .Build();

    private IContainer _dbContainer    = default!;
    private IContainer _cacheContainer = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _network.CreateAsync();

        _dbContainer = new MsSqlBuilder()
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithNetworkAliases("db")
            .Build();

        _cacheContainer = new GenericContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("redis:7-alpine")
            .WithNetwork(_network)
            .WithNetworkAliases("cache")
            .WithPortBinding(6379, true)
            .Build();

        await Task.WhenAll(
            _dbContainer.StartAsync(),
            _cacheContainer.StartAsync());
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_PersistsToDbAndInvalidatesCache()
    {
        var connStr = _dbContainer.GetConnectionString();
        // test body using "db" and "cache" hostnames
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await Task.WhenAll(
            _dbContainer.DisposeAsync().AsTask(),
            _cacheContainer.DisposeAsync().AsTask());
        await _network.DeleteAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `NetworkBuilder` names must be unique per run to avoid collisions when tests run in parallel across multiple agents; appending `Guid.NewGuid():N` to the network name solves this but means network names in Docker logs are not human-readable. Alternatively, use Testcontainers' automatic resource-reaper (Ryuk) which cleans up named resources after the test process exits, but note that Ryuk is disabled in some locked-down enterprise CI environments, requiring explicit `DeleteAsync` in `DisposeAsync`. [official]

---

### Pattern 142 — xUnit v3 `IAsyncLifetime` + `CancellationToken` Parameter for Timeout-Bounded Fixture Initialisation [official]

xUnit v3 overloads of `IAsyncLifetime` accept a `CancellationToken` in `InitializeAsync` and `DisposeAsync`, letting fixtures honour the test runner's timeout and produce a clear `OperationCanceledException` instead of hanging indefinitely when infrastructure startup stalls.

```csharp
public class RedisFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly RedisContainer _container = new RedisBuilder()
        .WithImage("redis:7-alpine")
        .Build();

    public IConnectionMultiplexer Connection { get; private set; } = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        await _container.StartAsync(cancellationToken);

        Connection = await ConnectionMultiplexer.ConnectAsync(
            _container.GetConnectionString(),
            options =>
            {
                options.AbortOnConnectFail = true;
                options.ConnectTimeout     = 5_000;
            });

        // warm-up ping with timeout propagation
        var db = Connection.GetDatabase();
        await db.PingAsync().WaitAsync(cancellationToken);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        Connection.Dispose();
        await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

[Collection("Redis")]
public class CacheRepositoryTests(RedisFixture redis) : IClassFixture<RedisFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Set_ThenGet_ReturnsStoredValue()
    {
        var repo = new CacheRepository(redis.Connection);
        await repo.SetAsync("key1", "hello");
        var value = await repo.GetAsync("key1");
        value.Should().Be("hello");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The `CancellationToken`-accepting overloads of `IAsyncLifetime` are xUnit v3-only and do not exist in v2; upgrading to v3 is required to use them. When `InitializeAsync(CancellationToken)` is cancelled mid-way (e.g., container pulled but `PingAsync` times out), the partially initialised fixture is still handed to the test class constructor — so all test methods in the fixture class will NullReferenceException on `redis.Connection`. Add a null guard or an `_initialised` flag and skip test body execution with `Skip.When(!_initialised, "fixture failed to initialise")`. [official]

### Pattern 143 — NUnit 4 `Assert.That` With `Is.EqualTo(...).Within(...)` for Floating-Point and DateTime Tolerance [official]

`Is.EqualTo(expected).Within(tolerance)` performs a tolerance-bounded equality assertion directly in the NUnit constraint expression, avoiding manual `Math.Abs` comparisons and ensuring the tolerance is explicitly documented at the assertion site.

```csharp
[TestFixture]
public class TelemetryProcessorTests
{
    [TestCase(100.0,  0.001)]
    [TestCase(0.0,    0.001)]
    [TestCase(-273.15, 0.001)]
    public void ConvertCelsiusToFahrenheit_ReturnsTolerantResult(
        double celsius, double toleranceDegF)
    {
        var processor = new TelemetryProcessor();

        double fahrenheit = processor.ConvertCelsiusToFahrenheit(celsius);
        double expected   = celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;

        Assert.That(fahrenheit, Is.EqualTo(expected).Within(toleranceDegF),
            $"Conversion of {celsius}°C should be within {toleranceDegF}°F of {expected}°F");
    }

    [Test]
    public void RecordTimestamp_IsWithinOneSecondOfUtcNow()
    {
        var processor = new TelemetryProcessor();
        var before = DateTime.UtcNow;

        processor.RecordTimestamp();

        Assert.That(processor.LastTimestamp,
            Is.EqualTo(DateTime.UtcNow).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)),
            "Recorded timestamp should be within 1 second of UtcNow");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Within(tolerance)` works for `double`, `float`, `decimal`, `DateTime`, and `TimeSpan`, but the tolerance type must be compatible with the value type — passing a `double` tolerance for a `DateTime` assertion compiles but interprets the value as ticks rather than a `TimeSpan`, producing an assertion that is either always-pass (tolerance of `0.001` ticks rounds to zero) or nonsensical. Always use `TimeSpan.FromSeconds(n)` for `DateTime` tolerances and verify the unit by checking a clearly-wrong expected value fails the assertion during test authoring. [official]

### Pattern 144 — MSTest v3 `[AssemblyInitialize]` With `TestContext.WriteLine` for CI-Visible Startup Logging [official]

`[AssemblyInitialize]` combined with `TestContext.WriteLine` logs infrastructure setup details (connection strings, image tags, environment) into the MSTest result XML, making them visible in Azure Pipelines test result tabs without requiring a separate logging sink.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public static class TestAssemblyBootstrap
{
    private static IContainer? _dbContainer;
    public  static string       DbConnectionString { get; private set; } = string.Empty;

    [AssemblyInitialize]
    public static async Task InitialiseAsync(TestContext context)
    {
        context.WriteLine("[Bootstrap] Starting SQL Server container...");

        _dbContainer = new MsSqlBuilder()
            .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
            .WithPassword("Str0ngP@ssw0rd!")
            .Build();

        await _dbContainer.StartAsync();

        DbConnectionString = _dbContainer.GetConnectionString();

        context.WriteLine($"[Bootstrap] Container started. Port: " +
            $"{_dbContainer.GetMappedPublicPort(1433)}");
        context.WriteLine($"[Bootstrap] Connection string: " +
            $"{DbConnectionString[..Math.Min(60, DbConnectionString.Length)]}...");

        await ApplyMigrationsAsync(DbConnectionString, context);
    }

    private static async Task ApplyMigrationsAsync(string cs, TestContext ctx)
    {
        var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<AppDbContext>()
            .UseSqlServer(cs).Options;
        await using var db = new AppDbContext(options);
        await db.Database.MigrateAsync();
        ctx.WriteLine("[Bootstrap] Migrations applied successfully.");
    }

    [AssemblyCleanup]
    public static async Task CleanupAsync()
    {
        if (_dbContainer is not null)
            await _dbContainer.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `TestContext.WriteLine` output is captured per-test, not per-assembly: text written in `[AssemblyInitialize]` appears in the very first test's output attachment in the TRX file, not in a dedicated bootstrap section. On Azure Pipelines, this means the startup log is buried in the result of whatever test executes first alphabetically. A more visible alternative is to write to `Console.Out` (which MSTest also captures) or use a lightweight structured logger writing to a temp file that is then attached to the `TestContext` as a result file via `context.AddResultFile(path)`. [official]

### Pattern 145 — FluentAssertions v8 `SatisfyRespectively` for Ordered Per-Element Assertions on Collections [official]

`collection.Should().SatisfyRespectively(elem => {...}, elem => {...})` asserts a distinct constraint lambda for each element at its specific position, replacing a manual loop or index-based array access that obscures which position failed.

```csharp
public class AuditLogServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void GetRecentEntries_ReturnsEntriesInDescendingChronologicalOrder()
    {
        var store   = new InMemoryAuditStore();
        var service = new AuditLogService(store);

        store.Append(new AuditEntry("login",  DateTime.UtcNow.AddMinutes(-10), "alice"));
        store.Append(new AuditEntry("update", DateTime.UtcNow.AddMinutes(-5),  "bob"));
        store.Append(new AuditEntry("logout", DateTime.UtcNow.AddMinutes(-1),  "alice"));

        var entries = service.GetRecentEntries(limit: 3);

        entries.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
            first =>
            {
                first.Action.Should().Be("logout");
                first.Actor.Should().Be("alice");
            },
            second =>
            {
                second.Action.Should().Be("update");
                second.Actor.Should().Be("bob");
            },
            third =>
            {
                third.Action.Should().Be("login");
                third.Actor.Should().Be("alice");
            });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SatisfyRespectively` requires knowing the exact element count at compile time; if the collection size is dynamic or can vary by environment (e.g., a repository returning results that depend on seeded data), a count mismatch produces a failure message that lists both the expected lambda count and actual element count, which is clear but means the test itself becomes a count assertion. For dynamic-length collections where only some positions matter, prefer `Contain(x => ...)` with `Which` chains or `ContainSingle`, and add a separate explicit count assertion with `HaveCount`. [official]

### Pattern 146 — Moq `Callback` for Asserting Complex Arguments Passed to Dependencies [official]

Using `mock.Setup(x => x.Method(It.IsAny<T>())).Callback<T>(arg => captured.Add(arg))` captures all arguments passed to a mock method during the test, enabling rich post-execution assertions on the captured values without embedding complex predicates inside `It.Is<T>`.

```csharp
public class NotificationDispatcherTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task SendWelcomeEmail_PassesCorrectPayloadToEmailGateway()
    {
        var sentMessages = new List<EmailMessage>();
        var gatewayMock  = new Mock<IEmailGateway>();

        gatewayMock
            .Setup(g => g.SendAsync(It.IsAny<EmailMessage>()))
            .Callback<EmailMessage>(msg => sentMessages.Add(msg))
            .ReturnsAsync(true);

        var dispatcher = new NotificationDispatcher(gatewayMock.Object);

        await dispatcher.SendWelcomeEmail(
            userId:   "u-42",
            userName: "Alice",
            email:    "alice@example.com");

        sentMessages.Should().ContainSingle(
            because: "exactly one email should be sent per welcome dispatch");

        var payload = sentMessages.Single();
        payload.To.Should().Be("alice@example.com");
        payload.Subject.Should().Contain("Welcome");
        payload.Body.Should().Contain("Alice",    because: "body should address the user by name");
        payload.Body.Should().Contain("u-42",     because: "body should embed the user ID for tracking");
        payload.Headers.Should().ContainKey("X-Source")
            .WhoseValue.Should().Be("welcome-flow");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Callback` captures a reference to the argument object. If the SUT mutates the argument after passing it to the mock (e.g., reusing a builder instance and clearing fields), the captured reference reflects the post-mutation state, making assertions on captured values unreliable. Fix: clone or deep-copy complex argument objects inside the `Callback` lambda (`sentMessages.Add(msg with {})` for records, or `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<EmailMessage>(JsonSerializer.Serialize(msg))` for other types). This is particularly important for `byte[]` and `Memory<T>` arguments where the underlying buffer is pooled and returned after the call. [official]

---

### Pattern 147 — NUnit 4 `[Retry]` Attribute for Flaky Network-Dependent Tests With Explicit Flakiness Documentation [community]

`[Retry(n)]` re-executes a test up to `n` times before recording a failure, providing a controlled safety-net for tests that interact with real external services under unreliable network conditions — provided the retry usage is accompanied by an issue tracker reference so it is not silently left in place indefinitely.

```csharp
[TestFixture]
[Category("ExternalNetwork")]
public class WeatherApiClientTests
{
    private readonly WeatherApiClient _client =
        new(apiKey: TestEnvironment.WeatherApiKey,
            baseUrl: "https://api.weatherapi.com/v1");

    // KNOWN FLAKY: external API throttles under CI load.
    // Tracked: https://github.com/example/repo/issues/882
    // Remove [Retry] once we have a WireMock stub for this endpoint.
    [Test, Retry(3)]
    [Category("ExternalNetwork")]
    public async Task GetCurrentWeather_ValidCity_ReturnsTemperature()
    {
        var result = await _client.GetCurrentWeatherAsync("London");

        Assert.That(result,          Is.Not.Null);
        Assert.That(result.CityName, Is.EqualTo("London"));
        Assert.That(result.TempC,    Is.InRange(-30.0, 60.0),
            "Temperature should be within plausible Earth range");
        Assert.That(result.ConditionText, Is.Not.Empty);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[Retry]` masks genuine intermittent failures by recording a pass on the second or third attempt; the CI pipeline shows green even though the SUT may have a real race condition or the external service is degraded. NUnit does not emit a warning-level result for "passed on retry 2 of 3" in the standard TRX format — the pass is indistinguishable from a first-attempt pass. Implement a custom `EventListener` or post-process the TRX with a CI step that flags any `passed` result with a `retryCount > 0` attribute, and treat those as amber (investigation required) rather than green (ship). [community]

### Pattern 148 — xUnit v3 `[MemberData]` With `Skip` Property for Environment-Conditional Row Skipping [official]

xUnit v3 allows individual `[MemberData]` rows to carry a `Skip` reason via `TheoryDataRow.Skip`, causing specific rows to be skipped without skipping the entire `[Theory]`, which is useful when certain parameter combinations require unavailable infrastructure in the current environment.

```csharp
public class DatabaseProviderTests
{
    public static IEnumerable<TheoryDataRow<string, string>> ProviderRows()
    {
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<string, string>("sqlite", ":memory:");
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<string, string>("postgres", "Host=localhost;Database=test")
        {
            Skip = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("POSTGRES_AVAILABLE") != "true"
                ? "POSTGRES_AVAILABLE env var not set; skipping Postgres row"
                : null
        };
        yield return new TheoryDataRow<string, string>("mssql", "Server=.;Database=TestDb;Trusted_Connection=True")
        {
            Skip = !OperatingSystem.IsWindows()
                ? "MSSQL Windows auth row skipped on non-Windows"
                : null
        };
    }

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(ProviderRows))]
    public async Task Migrate_AllProviders_AppliesSchemaWithoutError(
        string providerName,
        string connectionString)
    {
        var options = DbContextOptionsBuilderFactory
            .Create(providerName, connectionString);
        await using var ctx = new AppDbContext(options);
        await ctx.Database.MigrateAsync();
        var tables = await ctx.Database.GetAppliedMigrationsAsync();
        tables.Should().NotBeEmpty(
            because: $"{providerName} should have at least one applied migration");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `TheoryDataRow.Skip` is a null-or-string field; setting it to an empty string `""` is treated as "no skip" (not skipped), while `null` is also "no skip". Only a non-null, non-empty string triggers the skip. A common mistake is setting `Skip = condition ? "reason" : ""` — the empty-string branch does not skip the row. Always use the ternary `condition ? "reason" : null` pattern, and add a static analysis rule or Roslyn analyser to flag `Skip = ""`. [official]

---

### Pattern 149 — FluentAssertions v8 `HaveAccessModifier` for Structural Architecture Tests on Public API Surface [community]

FluentAssertions' `HaveAccessModifier` combined with type reflection lets architecture-level tests assert that only intended types are `public`, catching accidental API surface expansions during code review before they reach consumers.

```csharp
public class ApiSurfaceTests
{
    private readonly Assembly _assembly =
        typeof(OrderService).Assembly;

    [Fact]
    public void AllPublicTypes_AreInPublicApiNamespace()
    {
        var publicTypes = _assembly.GetExportedTypes()
            .Where(t => !t.Namespace!.StartsWith("MyApp.Public"))
            .ToList();

        publicTypes.Should().BeEmpty(
            because: "types outside MyApp.Public namespace must not be public; " +
                     "move them to an internal namespace or add the `internal` modifier");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void RepositoryImplementations_AreInternal()
    {
        var repoImpls = _assembly.GetTypes()
            .Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Repository") &&
                        !t.IsInterface                &&
                        !t.IsAbstract)
            .ToList();

        foreach (var type in repoImpls)
        {
            type.Should()
                .HaveAccessModifier(CSharpAccessModifier.Internal,
                    because: $"{type.Name} is an implementation detail and " +
                             "must not be visible outside the assembly");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `HaveAccessModifier` is part of the `FluentAssertions.Types` extension namespace and requires the `FluentAssertions` package version 6+; in v8 the API is stable but the `CSharpAccessModifier` enum members differ from earlier versions (`ProtectedInternal` vs `ProtectedOrInternal`). Additionally, `Assembly.GetExportedTypes()` throws `ReflectionTypeLoadException` if any referenced assembly in the dependency chain is missing — common in test projects that reference infrastructure assemblies with optional NuGet dependencies. Wrap in a try/catch or use `GetTypes()` with a filter for `t != null && t.IsPublic` to avoid false positives from load failures. [community]

### Pattern 150 — MSTest v3 `[Timeout]` Attribute With `TestTimeout` Class Constant for Uniform Async Test Deadlines [official]

`[Timeout(milliseconds)]` on `[TestMethod]` causes MSTest to fail the test if it does not complete within the given duration, preventing hung async tests from blocking the entire test run indefinitely. Defining a shared constant ensures all tests in a fixture use a consistent deadline.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class PaymentGatewayTests
{
    private const int DefaultTimeoutMs  = 10_000;  // 10 s per test
    private const int SlowTestTimeoutMs = 30_000;  // 30 s for integration tests

    private Mock<IPaymentProvider>   _providerMock    = default!;
    private Mock<IIdempotencyStore>  _idempotencyMock = default!;
    private PaymentGatewayService    _gateway         = default!;

    [TestInitialize]
    public void SetUp()
    {
        _providerMock    = new Mock<IPaymentProvider>();
        _idempotencyMock = new Mock<IIdempotencyStore>();
        _gateway         = new PaymentGatewayService(
            _providerMock.Object,
            _idempotencyMock.Object);
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(DefaultTimeoutMs)]
    public async Task Charge_WhenProviderResponds_ReturnsSuccess()
    {
        _providerMock
            .Setup(p => p.ChargeAsync(It.IsAny<ChargeRequest>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(new ChargeResult { Success = true, TransactionId = "txn-001" });

        var result = await _gateway.ChargeAsync(
            amount:   49.99m,
            currency: "USD",
            token:    "tok_test_visa");

        result.Success.Should().BeTrue();
        result.TransactionId.Should().StartWith("txn-");
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [Timeout(SlowTestTimeoutMs)]
    public async Task Charge_WhenProviderIsThrottled_WaitsAndRetries()
    {
        _providerMock
            .SetupSequence(p => p.ChargeAsync(It.IsAny<ChargeRequest>()))
            .ThrowsAsync(new ProviderThrottledException(retryAfterMs: 100))
            .ReturnsAsync(new ChargeResult { Success = true, TransactionId = "txn-002" });

        var result = await _gateway.ChargeAsync(49.99m, "USD", "tok_test_visa");

        result.Success.Should().BeTrue();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** MSTest's `[Timeout]` attribute cancels the test thread by calling `Thread.Abort` on .NET Framework but uses `Task.WhenAny` with a `CancellationToken` on .NET 5+. On .NET 5+ the timeout causes the test to be marked `Failed` with a `TestTimeoutException` message but does **not** kill any background tasks the SUT spawned — those continue running after the test method returns. If the SUT starts long-running `Task.Run` operations, add a `CancellationTokenSource` that is cancelled in `[TestCleanup]` and pass the token into the SUT so background tasks terminate cleanly. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 49

**xUnit v3 `[MemberData]` methods that return `IEnumerable<TheoryDataRow<T>>` are not interchangeable with methods returning `IEnumerable<object[]>` — the test runner serialises the row differently for each, and switching types without updating the method signature causes a `System.InvalidCastException` at discovery time rather than at execution time [community]** — Teams that migrate from `object[]` row methods to `TheoryDataRow<T>` often change only the method body and forget to update the return type annotation. The xUnit v3 discovery process attempts to cast each yielded element to `ITheoryDataRow`; the old `object[]` elements implement no such interface and cause a cast exception during test collection, which masquerades as a discovery failure and hides the actual method. WHY it causes problems: the failure is reported as "0 tests found in assembly" rather than a useful error message pointing to the offending `[MemberData]` source, so developers spend time checking assembly references and project SDK versions before finding the real issue. Fix: change the return type to `IEnumerable<TheoryDataRow<T>>` (or `IEnumerable<ITheoryDataRow>` for heterogeneous rows) and re-run discovery.

**NUnit 4 `[Combinatorial]` silently treats `null` entries inside `[Values]` as valid test-case inputs — `[Values("a", null, "c")]` generates tests where the parameter is `null`, which passes type-checking at compile time but causes `NullReferenceException` inside the SUT if the implementation does not guard against `null`, producing a test failure whose error points to the SUT rather than to the test fixture [community]** — A developer adds `null` to a `[Values]` list to check null-guard behaviour but forgets that `null` entries bypass FluentAssertions' `.NotBeNull()` on the parameter because the assertion is inside the SUT, not the test. WHY it causes problems: the stack trace names a line deep inside `OrderService.Process()` rather than the test method, making it appear as a SUT bug investigation rather than a deliberate test input. Fix: separate null-guard tests into their own `[TestCase(null)]` with `[Test]` and an explicit `Assert.Throws<ArgumentNullException>` wrapper, keeping `[Values]` lists for non-null valid inputs.

**Moq v4 `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` matches even a cancelled token — a mock set up with `Setup(x => x.GetAsync(It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))` will return its configured value regardless of whether the token is already cancelled when passed, so tests that intend to verify cancellation-cooperative behaviour pass even when the SUT ignores the token entirely [community]** — A developer writes a test that pre-cancels a `CancellationTokenSource` and expects the mock to surface a `TaskCanceledException`, but the mock's `ReturnsAsync` always returns the configured result because `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` does not inspect token state. WHY it causes problems: the test asserts `Should().ThrowAsync<OperationCanceledException>()` but the act never throws — it returns the mock response — so the assertion fails with "no exception was thrown" and the developer assumes the `[Fact]` itself is wrong rather than recognising the mock bypasses cancellation entirely. Fix: use `It.Is<CancellationToken>(t => !t.IsCancellationRequested)` for the non-cancelled call path, and test cancellation propagation by calling the real collaborator or using a `TaskCompletionSource` that honours the token.

**FluentAssertions v8 `.And` continuation after `.Throw<T>()` does not re-execute the `Action` — `.Should().Throw<ArgumentException>().And.Message.Should().Contain("value")` calls the action once to capture the exception, then all `.And` chains operate on the same captured exception object, but calling `.And.Should().Throw<T>()` a second time in the chain attempts to re-evaluate the subject (the already-evaluated `Action`) and finds no exception because the action has already been called [community]** — A developer building a multi-step exception chain tries to assert both the exception type and a nested inner exception using `action.Should().Throw<X>().And.InnerException.Should().BeOfType<Y>().And.Should().Throw<Z>()`, expecting each `.Should().Throw` to call the action. Instead, the second `.Throw` is evaluated against the already-invoked `Action` object (not re-invoked), returning no exception and failing. WHY it causes problems: the failure message is "Expected action to throw Z, but no exception was thrown" which implies the SUT is broken, when the issue is the test-chain structure. Fix: use `.WithInnerException<Y>()` on the first `.Throw<X>()` result to assert nested exception type, staying within a single fluent chain rooted at the initial `Throw`.

**MSTest v3 `[AssemblyInitialize]` and `[AssemblyCleanup]` methods must be `static async Task` (not `static void` or `static Task`) when performing async operations — a `static async void` signature compiles with no warning but causes `AssemblyInitialize` to complete before the awaited async work finishes, starting test execution against partially-initialised infrastructure [community]** — A team migrates their `[AssemblyInitialize]` from synchronous to async by adding `async` and `await` but leaves the return type as `void`. The method fires and returns immediately after the first `await`, so the test runner proceeds to collect and execute tests while the database container is still starting. WHY it causes problems: the first 2-3 tests fail with `SqlException: A network-related or instance-specific error` even though the same setup code worked in isolation, because the container was not ready. The async void issue is particularly insidious because the MSTest runner swallows unhandled exceptions from async void, meaning a failure inside `InitialiseAsync` does not abort the run. Fix: change the signature to `public static async Task InitialiseAsync(TestContext context)` and verify the MSTest NuGet package version is 3.x where the `async Task` overload is supported.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 49 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `TheoryData` with I/O in the static property initialiser | Runs at test discovery, not at test execution; exceptions during discovery hide all tests in the class | Move I/O to `[ClassFixture]` or a `Lazy<T>` and keep `TheoryData` properties pure value construction |
| `[Combinatorial]` on parameters with 5+ values each | Cartesian explosion produces hundreds of test cases with significant runner overhead | Use `[Pairwise]` for coverage of all two-way interactions with far fewer cases |
| `DynamicData` source method that is not `static` | Compiles; throws `InvalidOperationException` at runtime naming the attribute, not the method | Always mark `DynamicData` source methods `static`; add a Roslyn analyser or code comment |
| `.BeOfType<T>()` when derived types should also pass | Fails for subclasses even when polymorphism is intentional | Use `.BeAssignableTo<T>()` for inheritance-compatible type checks |
| `SetupSequence` without `Times.Exactly` verification | Excess calls silently fall through to default mock behaviour; over-calling SUT goes undetected | Always pair `SetupSequence` with `mock.Verify(..., Times.Exactly(n))` for the sequenced method |
| `[Timeout]` without CancellationToken propagation into the SUT | Background tasks spawned by the SUT survive the test timeout and pollute subsequent tests | Pass a `CancellationToken` from `[TestInitialize]` into the SUT and cancel it in `[TestCleanup]` |
| `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` when testing cancellation paths | Mock returns configured value regardless of cancellation state; cooperative cancellation is never exercised | Use `It.Is<CancellationToken>(t => !t.IsCancellationRequested)` for normal path; verify cancellation with `TaskCompletionSource` |
