### Pattern 151 — xUnit v3 `ITestOutputHelper` Structured Log Capture With JSON Serialisation [official]

xUnit v3's `ITestOutputHelper` is thread-safe and supports structured JSON line emissions when the test helper is combined with `System.Text.Json`. This enables CI log parsers to index test-phase events without scraping unstructured strings, and lets infrastructure libraries correlate test output with distributed traces.

```csharp
using Xunit;
using Xunit.Abstractions;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class OrderServiceTests(ITestOutputHelper output)
{
    private readonly ITestOutputHelper _output = output;

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_PublishesEvent_ToOutbox()
    {
        // Arrange
        var orderId  = Guid.NewGuid();
        var service  = new OrderService(new InMemoryOutbox());
        var request  = new PlaceOrderRequest(orderId, "SKU-99", qty: 2);

        // Act
        await service.PlaceAsync(request);

        // Emit a structured JSON line that CI tooling can parse
        _output.WriteLine(JsonSerializer.Serialize(new
        {
            test    = nameof(PlaceOrder_PublishesEvent_ToOutbox),
            orderId = orderId.ToString(),
            phase   = "assert",
            result  = "ok"
        }));

        // Assert
        var outbox = (InMemoryOutbox)service.Outbox;
        outbox.Messages.Should().ContainSingle(m =>
            m.AggregateId == orderId.ToString() &&
            m.EventType   == nameof(OrderPlaced));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `ITestOutputHelper.WriteLine` in xUnit v3 is thread-safe (unlike v2 where concurrent calls from `Task.Run` could throw), but output written after the test method returns is silently dropped. Async `Task.Run` continuations that outlive the test method lose their output. Always `await` all work before the test method exits to guarantee output capture. [official]

---

### Pattern 152 — NUnit 4 Custom `RetryWithBackoff` Attribute Using `DelegatingTestCommand` [official]

NUnit 4 exposes `TestExecutionContext.CurrentContext.CurrentResult` inside a custom attribute that implements `IWrapSetUpTearDown`, enabling delay-between-retries logic with exponential back-off without depending on Polly. This replaces fragile `Thread.Sleep` polls in flaky integration tests.

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using NUnit.Framework.Internal;
using NUnit.Framework.Internal.Commands;
using System;
using System.Threading;

[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method, AllowMultiple = false)]
public sealed class RetryWithBackoffAttribute : PropertyAttribute, IWrapSetUpTearDown
{
    private readonly int _maxAttempts;
    public RetryWithBackoffAttribute(int maxAttempts) : base(maxAttempts)
        => _maxAttempts = maxAttempts;

    public TestCommand Wrap(TestCommand command)
        => new BackoffRetryCommand(command, _maxAttempts);

    private sealed class BackoffRetryCommand(TestCommand inner, int max)
        : DelegatingTestCommand(inner)
    {
        public override TestResult Execute(TestExecutionContext ctx)
        {
            int attempt = 0;
            while (true)
            {
                ctx.CurrentResult = ctx.CurrentTest.MakeTestResult();
                innerCommand.Execute(ctx);
                if (ctx.CurrentResult.ResultState.Status != TestStatus.Failed
                    || ++attempt >= max)
                    return ctx.CurrentResult;
                Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(Math.Pow(2, attempt)));
            }
        }
    }
}

[TestFixture]
public class ExternalApiTests
{
    [Test, RetryWithBackoff(3)]
    public async Task GetQuote_ReturnsValidPrice()
    {
        var client   = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com") };
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/quote/BTC-USD");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        var body     = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
        body.Should().NotBeNullOrEmpty();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `DelegatingTestCommand` lives in `NUnit.Framework.Internal.Commands`, an internal namespace that is stable across NUnit 4.x but carries no public API guarantee. Inspect `ctx.CurrentResult.Message` to distinguish infrastructure failures from assertion failures if you want to retry only on transient errors, not on logic bugs. [official]

---

### Pattern 153 — MSTest v3 `[ClassInitialize(InheritanceBehavior.BeforeEachDerivedClass)]` for Shared Base-Class Setup [official]

MSTest v3 supports `InheritanceBehavior.BeforeEachDerivedClass` on `[ClassInitialize]`, ensuring each derived test class runs the base initializer independently without requiring `base.Initialize()` calls. The complementary `[ClassCleanup(InheritanceBehavior.BeforeEachDerivedClass)]` handles teardown symmetrically.

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;

[TestClass]
public abstract class IntegrationTestBase
{
    protected static SqlConnection DbConnection { get; private set; } = default!;

    [ClassInitialize(InheritanceBehavior.BeforeEachDerivedClass)]
    public static async Task BaseClassInitialize(TestContext ctx)
    {
        var connString = ctx.Properties["IntegrationDbConnectionString"] as string
                         ?? "Server=localhost;Database=TestDb;Integrated Security=true";
        DbConnection   = new SqlConnection(connString);
        await DbConnection.OpenAsync();
        await DbConnection.ExecuteAsync("DELETE FROM Orders WHERE IsTestData = 1");
    }

    [ClassCleanup(InheritanceBehavior.BeforeEachDerivedClass)]
    public static async Task BaseClassCleanup()
    {
        if (DbConnection is not null)
            await DbConnection.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

[TestClass]
public class OrderQueryTests : IntegrationTestBase
{
    [TestMethod]
    public async Task GetAll_ReturnsOnlyActiveOrders()
    {
        var repo   = new OrderRepository(DbConnection);
        var orders = await repo.GetAllActiveAsync();
        orders.Should().OnlyContain(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Active);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `InheritanceBehavior.BeforeEachDerivedClass` invokes the static initializer once per concrete derived class, not once per assembly. For expensive setup (containers, schema migrations), prefer `[AssemblyInitialize]` + a shared static field; use `InheritanceBehavior` only for lightweight per-fixture initialisation. [official]

---

### Pattern 154 — FluentAssertions v8 `BeEquivalentTo` With `Using<T>(Func<IAssertionContext<T>>)` Custom Rule [official]

FluentAssertions v8 allows per-type custom comparison rules via `.Using<T>(ctx => ...)` + `.WhenTypeIs<T>()`, enabling domain-aware equality (e.g., monetary amounts within a tolerance) without implementing `IEquatable<T>` on production types.

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);
public record InvoiceLine(string Sku, int Qty, Money UnitPrice);

[Fact]
public void CreateInvoice_CalculatesLineTotals_WithMoneyTolerance()
{
    var expected = new List<InvoiceLine>
    {
        new("SKU-A", 3, new Money(9.99m,  "USD")),
        new("SKU-B", 1, new Money(49.95m, "USD"))
    };

    var actual = InvoiceFactory.CreateLines(
        new[] { ("SKU-A", 3, 9.990001m), ("SKU-B", 1, 49.950001m) },
        "USD");

    actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, opts => opts
        .Using<Money>(ctx =>
        {
            ctx.Subject.Currency.Should().Be(ctx.Expectation.Currency);
            Math.Abs(ctx.Subject.Amount - ctx.Expectation.Amount)
                .Should().BeLessThan(0.01m,
                    because: "float rounding within 1 cent is acceptable");
        })
        .WhenTypeIs<Money>());
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `.Using<T>()` + `.WhenTypeIs<T>()` applies globally to all occurrences of `T` in the object graph; different rules for the same type in different properties are not supported. For mixed-precision requirements, use a custom `IEquivalencyStep` registered via `AssertionOptions.AssertEquivalencyUsing`. [official]

---

### Pattern 155 — Moq `Mock.Of<T>()` Inline Specification for Concise Read-Only Property Stubs [community]

`Mock.Of<T>(x => x.Property == value)` creates a fully configured mock inline, reducing `Mock<T>` variable boilerplate for simple read-only dependencies where no verification is needed after the test.

```csharp
using Moq;
using FluentAssertions;
using System;

public interface IUserContext
{
    string UserId   { get; }
    string TenantId { get; }
    bool   IsAdmin  { get; }
}

[Fact]
public void AuditService_CreateEntry_StampsCurrentUser()
{
    // Arrange — inline property specification without a Mock<T> variable
    var userCtx = Mock.Of<IUserContext>(u =>
        u.UserId   == "user-42"  &&
        u.TenantId == "tenant-7" &&
        u.IsAdmin  == false);

    var clock = Mock.Of<ISystemClock>(c =>
        c.UtcNow == new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 14, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));

    var service = new AuditService(userCtx, clock);

    // Act
    var entry = service.CreateEntry("ORDER_PLACED", entityId: "ord-99");

    // Assert
    entry.UserId.Should().Be("user-42");
    entry.TenantId.Should().Be("tenant-7");
    entry.Timestamp.Should().Be(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 14, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
    entry.EventType.Should().Be("ORDER_PLACED");
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Mock.Of<T>` uses `MockBehavior.Loose` by default; unspecified member calls silently return `default(TReturn)`. For dependencies where unexpected calls should fail immediately, use `new Mock<T>(MockBehavior.Strict)`. Reserve `Mock.Of<T>` for data-carrier or read-only configuration interfaces. [community]

---

### Pattern 156 — xUnit v3 `Assert.Equal` With `IEqualityComparer<T>` Overload for Reusable Domain Comparers [official]

xUnit v3 exposes `Assert.Equal<T>(T expected, T actual, IEqualityComparer<T> comparer)` natively, enabling shared comparison strategies across multiple `[Fact]` and `[Theory]` tests without wrapper helper methods or custom `IEquatable<T>` implementations.

```csharp
using Xunit;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public sealed class CaseInsensitiveStringComparer : IEqualityComparer<string>
{
    public static readonly CaseInsensitiveStringComparer Instance = new();
    public bool Equals(string? x, string? y)
        => string.Equals(x, y, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    public int GetHashCode(string obj)
        => obj.ToUpperInvariant().GetHashCode();
}

public class SlugGeneratorTests
{
    [Theory]
    [InlineData("Hello World",  "hello-world")]
    [InlineData("C# Patterns",  "c-patterns")]
    [InlineData("  Trim Me  ",  "trim-me")]
    public void Generate_ProducesExpectedSlug(string input, string expected)
    {
        var slug = SlugGenerator.Generate(input);

        // Platform-independent comparison — ignores case variations in CI vs developer
        Assert.Equal(expected, slug, CaseInsensitiveStringComparer.Instance);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Generate_EmptyInput_ReturnsEmptySlug()
    {
        Assert.Equal(string.Empty, SlugGenerator.Generate(string.Empty),
            CaseInsensitiveStringComparer.Instance);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The comparer overload produces a minimal failure message ("Expected: X, Actual: Y") with no property-level diff. For complex objects, FluentAssertions `.BeEquivalentTo` with custom options gives more actionable failure messages. Reserve this overload for leaf types (strings, value types) where the comparison rule is the entire concern. [official]

---

### Pattern 157 — Testcontainers.NET `UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded` Wait Strategy for Health-Check Gating [official]

Testcontainers.NET wait strategies allow containers to be considered ready only after a specific HTTP endpoint returns a success status, preventing tests from hitting a service that is up but whose application is still initialising.

```csharp
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Builders;
using DotNet.Testcontainers.Containers;
using Xunit;
using System;
using System.Net.Http;

public class PaymentServiceContainerTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private IContainer _container = default!;
    private HttpClient _client    = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _container = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("example/payment-service:latest")
            .WithPortBinding(8080, assignRandomHostPort: true)
            .WithEnvironment("ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT", "IntegrationTest")
            .WithStartupTimeout(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3))
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                    .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r
                        .ForPath("/health/ready")
                        .ForPort(8080)
                        .ForStatusCode(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK)))
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();

        var port = _container.GetMappedPublicPort(8080);
        _client  = new HttpClient
        {
            BaseAddress = new Uri($"http://{_container.Hostname}:{port}")
        };
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PostCharge_ValidCard_Returns200()
    {
        var payload  = new StringContent(
            """{"card":"tok_visa","amount":100}""",
            System.Text.Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");
        var response = await _client.PostAsync("/charges", payload);
        response.StatusCode.Should().Be(System.Net.HttpStatusCode.OK);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        _client.Dispose();
        await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The strategy polls on a 100 ms interval with a default 60-second timeout; containers running database migrations need `.WithStartupTimeout(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3))` or more. Do not use against containers that rate-limit health probes — the frequent polling may trigger back-off responses. [official]

---

### Pattern 158 — `FakeTimeProvider` With `IHostedService` Background Timer for Deterministic Tick Tests [official]

.NET 8+ `FakeTimeProvider` from `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` allows hosted-service timers to be advanced deterministically in unit tests, removing real-time delays from tick-based logic tests.

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions;
using Xunit;
using System;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class MetricsFlushServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FlushTimer_AfterInterval_CallsFlushOnce()
    {
        var fake  = new FakeTimeProvider();
        var store = new InMemoryMetricsStore();
        var svc   = new MetricsFlushService(
            store, fake,
            NullLogger<MetricsFlushService>.Instance,
            flushInterval: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));

        using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
        await svc.StartAsync(cts.Token);

        // Advance past the flush interval
        fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5).Add(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1)));
        await Task.Delay(50); // yield so the ThreadPool callback fires

        store.FlushCallCount.Should().Be(1);
        await cts.CancelAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task FlushTimer_AdvancedTwoPeriods_CallsFlushTwice()
    {
        var fake  = new FakeTimeProvider();
        var store = new InMemoryMetricsStore();
        var svc   = new MetricsFlushService(
            store, fake,
            NullLogger<MetricsFlushService>.Instance,
            flushInterval: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));

        using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
        await svc.StartAsync(cts.Token);

        fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10).Add(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(1)));
        await Task.Delay(100);

        store.FlushCallCount.Should().Be(2);
        await cts.CancelAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `FakeTimeProvider.Advance` is synchronous but timer callbacks run on `ThreadPool` threads. The `await Task.Delay(50)` is a pragmatic yield; for fully deterministic synchronisation, use a `SemaphoreSlim` or `TaskCompletionSource` inside the service that the test can `await`. [official]

---

### Pattern 159 — NUnit 4 `TestCaseData` With `SetName` and `SetCategory` for Rich Theory Metadata [official]

`TestCaseData` in NUnit 4 supports chaining `.SetName(string)` for readable test names in CI reports and `.SetCategory(string)` to allow targeted filtering, keeping all metadata co-located with test inputs.

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class PricingEngineTests
{
    public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> DiscountCases()
    {
        yield return new TestCaseData("PREMIUM", 1000m, 0.15m)
            .SetName("Premium tier gets 15% discount on orders over 500")
            .SetCategory("Pricing")
            .SetCategory("Regression");

        yield return new TestCaseData("STANDARD", 500m, 0.05m)
            .SetName("Standard tier gets 5% discount on orders over 200")
            .SetCategory("Pricing");

        yield return new TestCaseData("GUEST", 100m, 0m)
            .SetName("Guest tier gets no discount")
            .SetCategory("Pricing")
            .SetCategory("Smoke");
    }

    [TestCaseSource(nameof(DiscountCases))]
    public void CalculateDiscount_AppliesCorrectRate(
        string tier, decimal amount, decimal expectedRate)
    {
        var engine   = new PricingEngine();
        var discount = engine.CalculateDiscount(tier, amount);

        Assert.That(discount,
            Is.EqualTo(amount * expectedRate).Within(0.001m),
            $"Expected {expectedRate:P0} discount for tier '{tier}'");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SetName` replaces the auto-generated name entirely; non-unique names across cases cause NUnit to append a numeric suffix silently. Always include the distinguishing parameter values in the name string. `.SetCategory` is additive — a single `TestCaseData` can belong to multiple categories. [official]

---

### Pattern 160 — FluentAssertions v8 `ContainEquivalentOf` for Partial-Match Collection Membership [official]

`ContainEquivalentOf` checks that at least one collection element is equivalent to a given expectation using the deep-equivalence engine, enabling "contains" assertions on complex object collections without full equality or `IEquatable<T>`.

```csharp
using FluentAssertions;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public record Notification(string RecipientId, string Channel, string Subject, bool Sent);

[Fact]
public void SendOrderConfirmation_EmitsEmailAndSmsNotifications()
{
    var store   = new InMemoryNotificationStore();
    var service = new OrderNotificationService(store);

    service.NotifyOrderPlaced(orderId: "ORD-55", recipientId: "user-9");

    var notifications = store.GetAll();

    // Assert email notification exists — ignore Sent flag and Subject wording
    notifications.Should().ContainEquivalentOf(
        new { RecipientId = "user-9", Channel = "email" },
        opts => opts.ExcludingMissingMembers());

    // Assert SMS notification exists
    notifications.Should().ContainEquivalentOf(
        new { RecipientId = "user-9", Channel = "sms" },
        opts => opts.ExcludingMissingMembers());

    // Assert no push notification was sent
    notifications.Should().NotContainEquivalentOf(
        new { Channel = "push" },
        opts => opts.ExcludingMissingMembers());
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `ContainEquivalentOf` with `ExcludingMissingMembers()` performs a one-sided structural match — extra properties on actual elements are ignored. This is intentional for partial-match scenarios but can allow tests to pass when unexpected extra data is present. Use `BeEquivalentTo` with `Including(x => ...)` when precise field selection is required. [official]

---

### Pattern 161 — MSTest v3 `[DynamicData]` With Async Enumerable Source Method [official]

MSTest v3 supports `IAsyncEnumerable<object[]>` from a `[DynamicData]` source method with `DynamicDataSourceType.Method`, enabling test data loaded from async I/O (JSON files, database snapshots) at data-population time.

```csharp
using Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.IO;
using System.Reflection;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

[TestClass]
public class ContractValidatorTests
{
    public static async IAsyncEnumerable<object[]> LoadContractCases()
    {
        var json  = await File.ReadAllTextAsync("testdata/contracts.json");
        var cases = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<ContractTestCase>>(json)!;
        foreach (var c in cases)
            yield return new object[] { c.Input, c.ExpectedValid, c.ExpectedErrorCode };
    }

    [DataTestMethod]
    [DynamicData(nameof(LoadContractCases),
                 DynamicDataSourceType.Method,
                 DynamicDataDisplayName = nameof(GetDisplayName))]
    public void Validate_Contract_MatchesExpected(
        string input, bool expectedValid, string? expectedErrorCode)
    {
        var result = ContractValidator.Validate(input);

        result.IsValid.Should().Be(expectedValid);
        if (!expectedValid)
            result.ErrorCode.Should().Be(expectedErrorCode);
    }

    public static string GetDisplayName(MethodInfo method, object[] data)
        => $"Contract '{data[0]}' valid={data[1]}";
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Async enumerable sources are enumerated at discovery time via `GetAwaiter().GetResult()`. Sources that depend on a DI container or network will throw during discovery, resulting in zero collected test cases with no clear error. Limit async sources to file I/O or embedded resources. [official]

---

### Pattern 162 — Moq `MockSequence` + `InSequence` for Strict Call-Order Verification [community]

Moq's `MockSequence` + `InSequence` API enforces that mock calls occur in a specified order, throwing `MockException` immediately at the call site when a call is made out of sequence.

```csharp
using Moq;
using FluentAssertions;

[Fact]
public void ProcessPayment_QueriesRiskBeforeCharging()
{
    var sequence = new MockSequence();
    var risk     = new Mock<IRiskService>(MockBehavior.Strict);
    var gateway  = new Mock<IPaymentGateway>(MockBehavior.Strict);

    // Risk check MUST precede gateway charge
    risk.InSequence(sequence)
        .Setup(r => r.EvaluateAsync(It.IsAny<PaymentRequest>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(RiskLevel.Low);

    gateway.InSequence(sequence)
        .Setup(g => g.ChargeAsync(It.IsAny<PaymentRequest>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(new ChargeResult { Success = true, TransactionId = "txn-77" });

    var processor = new PaymentProcessor(risk.Object, gateway.Object);

    var act = () => processor.ProcessAsync(new PaymentRequest
    {
        Amount   = 150m,
        Currency = "EUR",
        Token    = "tok_mastercard"
    });

    act.Should().NotThrowAsync();
    risk.Verify(r => r.EvaluateAsync(It.IsAny<PaymentRequest>()), Times.Once);
    gateway.Verify(g => g.ChargeAsync(It.IsAny<PaymentRequest>()), Times.Once);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockSequence` requires all sequence-registered calls to be set up before any are made. Mocks with `MockBehavior.Strict` and `InSequence` cannot receive unregistered calls. Use `MockBehavior.Loose` if some calls on the mock are intentionally unordered and should not fault. [community]

---

### Pattern 163 — `WebApplicationFactory<T>` With `RemoveAll<T>` + `AddSingleton<T>` for Full-Stack Stub Injection [official]

`WebApplicationFactory.WithWebHostBuilder` replaces production service registrations with test doubles via `RemoveAll<T>`, enabling full HTTP stack tests against a real ASP.NET Core pipeline with controlled dependencies.

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions;
using Xunit;
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Text;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class OrdersApiTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public OrdersApiTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    {
        _client = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
        {
            builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
            {
                services.RemoveAll<IPaymentGateway>();
                services.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway>(new StubPaymentGateway(
                    alwaysSucceed: true, fixedTransactionId: "TEST-TXN-001"));

                services.RemoveAll<IEmailSender>();
                services.AddSingleton<IEmailSender>(new SpyEmailSender());
            });
        }).CreateClient();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Post_Order_ReturnsCreatedWithTransactionId()
    {
        var body = new StringContent(
            """{"sku":"WIDGET-5","qty":1,"cardToken":"tok_visa"}""",
            Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");

        var response = await _client.PostAsync("/api/orders", body);

        response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.Created);
        var json = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
        json.Should().Contain("TEST-TXN-001");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `RemoveAll<T>` removes all registrations for the service type including scoped and transient registrations. `WithWebHostBuilder` creates a new factory instance (new host) — expensive in large suites. Prefer a single shared factory in `IClassFixture<T>` and call `CreateClient()` per test rather than `WithWebHostBuilder` per test. [official]

---

### Pattern 164 — AutoFixture `[InlineAutoData]` + `[Frozen]` for Minimalist Dependency-Wired Unit Tests [community]

Combining `[Theory]`, `[InlineAutoData]`, and `[Frozen]` from AutoFixture.Xunit2 lets tests receive explicit inline values alongside auto-wired dependencies in a single parameter list. `[Frozen]` ensures the same mock instance is injected everywhere in the object graph.

```csharp
using AutoFixture.Xunit2;
using Moq;
using FluentAssertions;
using Xunit;

public class InvoiceServiceTests
{
    [Theory]
    [InlineAutoData("CORP-001", 5000m)]
    [InlineAutoData("RETAIL-007", 199.99m)]
    public void CreateInvoice_ForKnownCustomer_SetsCorrectTotal(
        string customerId,
        decimal amount,
        [Frozen] Mock<ICustomerRepository> repoMock,   // resolved before sut
        [Frozen] Mock<ITaxService>         taxMock,    // resolved before sut
        InvoiceService                     sut)        // receives frozen mocks
    {
        repoMock.Setup(r => r.GetByIdAsync(customerId))
            .ReturnsAsync(new Customer { Id = customerId, TaxExempt = false });

        taxMock.Setup(t => t.CalculateTaxAsync(amount, It.IsAny<string>()))
            .ReturnsAsync(amount * 0.20m);

        var invoice = sut.Create(customerId, amount);

        invoice.SubTotal.Should().Be(amount);
        invoice.Tax.Should().BeApproximately(amount * 0.20m, precision: 0.001m);
        invoice.Total.Should().BeApproximately(amount * 1.20m, precision: 0.001m);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** AutoFixture resolves parameters left-to-right; `[Frozen]` must appear before any parameter that depends on the frozen type. Placing `[Frozen]` after `sut` causes `sut` to be created with a different (non-frozen) instance and mock setup has no effect. [community]

---

### Pattern 165 — NUnit 4 `Throws.InstanceOf<T>` vs `Throws.TypeOf<T>` for Exception Hierarchy Assertions [official]

NUnit 4's `Throws.InstanceOf<T>` matches any subclass of `T`, while `Throws.TypeOf<T>` requires exact type equality. Choosing the correct constraint prevents tests from breaking when exception hierarchies evolve and makes intent explicit.

```csharp
using NUnit.Framework;
using System;

public class OrderCancellationServiceTests
{
    [Test]
    public void Cancel_AlreadyShippedOrder_ThrowsDomainException()
    {
        var order   = OrderBuilder.Create()
                        .WithStatus(OrderStatus.Shipped)
                        .Build();
        var service = new OrderCancellationService();

        // InstanceOf<T>: passes for OrderAlreadyShippedException
        // which derives from DomainException — subclasses are acceptable
        Assert.That(
            () => service.Cancel(order),
            Throws.InstanceOf<DomainException>()
                  .With.Message.Contains("cannot be cancelled")
                  .And.Property(nameof(DomainException.ErrorCode))
                      .EqualTo("ORDER_ALREADY_SHIPPED"));
    }

    [Test]
    public void Cancel_NullOrder_ThrowsArgumentNullExactly()
    {
        var service = new OrderCancellationService();

        // TypeOf<T>: exact contract — must be ArgumentNullException, not a subclass
        Assert.That(
            () => service.Cancel(null!),
            Throws.TypeOf<ArgumentNullException>()
                  .With.Property("ParamName").EqualTo("order"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Throws.InstanceOf<T>` is intentionally liberal — a completely unrelated exception that shares the same base class will also pass. In exception-hierarchy-rich domain models, use `Throws.InstanceOf<T>` for framework exceptions (subclasses expected) and `Throws.TypeOf<T>` for custom domain exceptions where the concrete type is part of the public contract. [official]

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 50

**xUnit v3 `[ClassData]` types that implement `IEnumerable<TheoryDataRow<T>>` must have a public parameterless constructor — a C# 12 primary constructor with a required parameter prevents xUnit's discovery infrastructure from instantiating the data class, causing the `[Theory]` to be listed with zero test cases and no error message [community]** — A developer moves test data into `public class PricingCases(IConfiguration cfg)` to inject test-environment config. xUnit's `TheoryDiscoverer` calls `Activator.CreateInstance(type)` with no arguments; the instantiation throws `MissingMethodException`, which xUnit swallows during discovery. WHY it causes problems: "0 test cases" is not reported as an error, so developers debug the data-generation logic rather than the constructor signature, spending time auditing assembly references and project SDK versions first. Fix: use a public parameterless constructor for `[ClassData]` types and read config from `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable`; inject context via `IClassFixture<T>`, not data-source constructors.

**NUnit 4 `[assembly: Parallelizable(ParallelScope.All)]` causes `[OneTimeSetUp]` methods to run concurrently across fixture classes — fixtures that share a static resource (e.g., a static `HttpClient`, a shared database table) experience concurrent interleaved setup, causing non-deterministic `IOException` or stale-data failures that only appear on multi-core CI agents [community]** — A team adds `[assembly: Parallelizable(ParallelScope.All)]` to maximise CI throughput without auditing fixtures for shared statics. Two database-seeding `[OneTimeSetUp]` methods each truncate and re-seed the same table concurrently; one seeder deletes rows the other just inserted. WHY it causes problems: failures only appear on multi-core CI, not on developer laptops running tests sequentially, making the root cause appear to be a CI environment configuration issue rather than a parallelism hazard. Fix: apply `[NonParallelizable]` to any fixture touching shared mutable state, or redesign fixtures to use isolated database instances per class.

**Moq `VerifyAll()` succeeds silently when no `Setup` calls were made — a mock with zero setups and a `VerifyAll()` at the end of the test always passes even if the SUT made calls on the dependency, because `VerifyAll` only checks that all registered expectations were called [community]** — A developer writes a test that stubs nothing but ends with `mock.VerifyAll()`, intending to assert that no unexpected interactions occurred. Because `VerifyAll` verifies only `Setup`-decorated expectations, and there are none, it returns immediately without inspecting actual invocations. WHY it causes problems: the test appears to verify mock interactions rigorously but asserts nothing; calls to the dependency go entirely undetected, giving false confidence in the SUT's behaviour. Fix: use `mock.VerifyNoOtherCalls()` after setting up and verifying expected calls, or use `MockBehavior.Strict` so unsetup calls throw immediately.

**FluentAssertions `.Should().NotThrow()` wraps the original exception in `AssertionException`, discarding the original call stack — on failure the message includes the exception type and message but not the stack trace from inside the SUT, making it impossible to determine which SUT line threw without running the test under a debugger [community]** — A developer uses `act.Should().NotThrow()` expecting that a failure will include full stack trace information for diagnosis. The failure message reads "Did not expect any exception, but found System.NullReferenceException with message '...'" with no stack trace. WHY it causes problems: diagnosing which line of the SUT threw requires switching to a bare `act()` call or attaching a debugger, adding unnecessary overhead for what was a routine assertion failure. Fix: call the action directly (`act()`) without `.Should().NotThrow()` for actions you expect to succeed; the test runner captures the full stack trace from any unhandled exception automatically.

**MSTest v3 `--filter TestCategory=Smoke` uses contains semantics in legacy vstest mode and exact-match semantics in MTP mode — tests tagged `[TestCategory("SmokeAndPerf")]` are included by `TestCategory=Smoke` under vstest but excluded under MTP, causing CI pipeline timing to differ dramatically between runner versions [community]** — A team relies on `--filter TestCategory=Smoke` in their fast CI pipeline. Upgrading to MTP mode switches from contains to exact-match; `SmokeAndPerf` tests are excluded and the smoke gate becomes green while important integration tests are no longer exercised. WHY it causes problems: the behaviour difference is not surfaced as an error — both modes succeed, but the coverage scope silently changes. Fix: standardise category names to avoid substring ambiguity (use `smoke` only for pure smoke tests), audit category usage after any runner upgrade, and validate filter results with `--list-tests` before changing runner versions.

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 50 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `Mock.Of<T>` for side-effecting dependencies | Unsetup member calls return `default(T)` silently, masking missing setups | Use `new Mock<T>(MockBehavior.Strict)` for side-effecting dependencies; reserve `Mock.Of<T>` for read-only property stubs |
| `VerifyAll()` on a mock with zero `Setup` calls | Always passes regardless of actual SUT interactions | Pair with `VerifyNoOtherCalls()` or use `MockBehavior.Strict` |
| `[ClassData]` with a C# 12 primary-constructor data class | Discovery fails silently: 0 test cases, no error | Use a parameterless constructor; inject context via `IClassFixture<T>` |
| `FakeTimeProvider.Advance` without a synchronisation point | Timer callback races on `ThreadPool`; assertion may evaluate before callback fires | Use `SemaphoreSlim` or `TaskCompletionSource` inside the service for deterministic timing |
| `ContainEquivalentOf` without `ExcludingMissingMembers` on anonymous expectations | Anonymous type lacks all element properties; throws member-not-found equivalency error | Always pair anonymous-type expectations with `ExcludingMissingMembers()` |
| `WithWebHostBuilder` per test instead of per fixture | Creates a new host per test; expensive startup cost multiplied by test count | Share a single `WebApplicationFactory<T>` via `IClassFixture<T>`; call `CreateClient()` per test |

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 166 — xUnit v3 `Assert.Equivalent` for Deep Structural Equality Without Custom Comparers [official]

`Assert.Equivalent` performs deep structural equivalence checking — it compares public property and field values recursively without requiring the type to implement `IEquatable<T>` or a custom `IEqualityComparer<T>`. The optional `strict` parameter controls whether extra properties on the actual object cause failure: `strict: true` matches the full shape; `strict: false` (default) allows the actual to have more members than the expected. This pattern is ideal for asserting DTO/record shapes returned from commands where reference equality is meaningless.

```csharp
public record CreateOrderResult(Guid OrderId, string Status, int LineCount);

public class OrderCommandHandlerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Handle_ValidCommand_ReturnsExpectedShape()
    {
        var handler = new OrderCommandHandler(new InMemoryOrderRepository());
        var cmd = new CreateOrderCommand(CustomerId: Guid.NewGuid(), Lines: 3);

        var result = await handler.Handle(cmd, CancellationToken.None);

        // strict: false — extra properties on result (e.g. CreatedAt) are ignored
        Assert.Equivalent(
            new { Status = "Pending", LineCount = 3 },
            result,
            strict: false);

        // strict: true — result must have exactly these members and no others
        Assert.Equivalent(
            new CreateOrderResult(result.OrderId, "Pending", 3),
            result,
            strict: true);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Assert.Equivalent` with `strict: false` is intentionally lenient — new properties added to the response type will never break this test, which can mask accidental payload growth. For public API contracts, prefer `strict: true` or a dedicated schema-snapshot tool (e.g., Verify.NET) to lock the full shape. [official]

---

### Pattern 167 — NUnit 4 `Assert.EnterMultipleScope()` Disposable Soft-Assertion Block [official]

NUnit 4.2 introduced `Assert.EnterMultipleScope()`, a disposable alternative to `Assert.Multiple(Action)`. Placing assertions inside a `using` block means the compiler enforces proper scoping, and any exceptions thrown by non-NUnit code inside the scope are re-thrown as `MultipleAssertException` alongside the assertion failures. This pattern is the recommended migration target for teams moving away from the delegate-based `Assert.Multiple`.

```csharp
[Test]
public void Invoice_CalculateTotals_AllFieldsCorrect()
{
    var invoice = new Invoice(
        lines: new[] { new InvoiceLine("Widget", qty: 2, unitPrice: 9.99m) },
        taxRate: 0.20m);

    invoice.Calculate();

    using (Assert.EnterMultipleScope())
    {
        Assert.That(invoice.SubTotal, Is.EqualTo(19.98m));
        Assert.That(invoice.TaxAmount, Is.EqualTo(4.00m).Within(0.01m));
        Assert.That(invoice.GrandTotal, Is.EqualTo(23.98m).Within(0.01m));
        Assert.That(invoice.LineCount, Is.EqualTo(1));
        Assert.That(invoice.IsPaid, Is.False);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The disposable scope model works well with `using` declarations (C# 8+), but wrapping a wide block of assertions can obscure which logical concept is being tested — each scope should correspond to a single observable behaviour. Avoid nesting `Assert.EnterMultipleScope()` blocks; NUnit 4 does not guarantee correct aggregation of inner scope failures in all runner versions. [official]

---

### Pattern 168 — MSTest v3 `[TestProperty]` With Custom Test Explorer Grouping for Large Test Suites [official]

MSTest v3 `[TestProperty("key", "value")]` tags decorate tests with arbitrary key-value metadata that is surfaced in Visual Studio Test Explorer grouping and in TRX report XML. When combined with the `--filter` flag (`dotnet test --filter "TestProperty[Area]=Checkout"`), `[TestProperty]` enables fine-grained pipeline segmentation without creating separate test projects. This is particularly effective in monorepo setups where a single project hosts hundreds of tests across multiple bounded contexts.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class CheckoutServiceTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [TestProperty("Area", "Checkout")]
    [TestProperty("Risk", "High")]
    [TestProperty("Owner", "payments-team")]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_ValidCard_ReturnsConfirmation()
    {
        // Arrange
        var paymentGateway = Substitute.For<IPaymentGateway>();
        paymentGateway.ChargeAsync(Arg.Any<ChargeRequest>())
            .Returns(new ChargeResult(Success: true, TransactionId: "txn_001"));

        var service = new CheckoutService(paymentGateway);

        // Act
        var result = await service.ProcessPaymentAsync(
            new PaymentRequest(Amount: 49.99m, CardToken: "tok_abc"));

        // Assert
        Assert.IsTrue(result.Success);
        Assert.AreEqual("txn_001", result.TransactionId);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[TestProperty]` metadata is only honoured by vstest-based runners; the MTP (Microsoft Testing Platform) runner uses a different property bag API and `--filter` syntax. Always validate filter expressions against both runner modes in CI before relying on `[TestProperty]` for pipeline gating. [official]

---

### Pattern 169 — FluentAssertions v8 `Satisfy` With Inline Predicate for Complex Single-Object Assertions [official]

`Should().Satisfy(Func<T, bool>)` combined with an optional `because` message provides a concise single-expression alternative to manually asserting multiple related properties. The overload accepting an `Expression<Func<T, bool>>` additionally prints the predicate source text in the failure message, eliminating the need to write a custom assertion message that re-states the condition. This is particularly useful for value objects and records where multiple invariants must hold simultaneously.

```csharp
public record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);

public class PricingEngineTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void ApplyDiscount_TenPercent_ProducesCorrectMoneyValue()
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();
        var original = new Money(100.00m, "GBP");

        var discounted = engine.ApplyDiscount(original, discountPct: 10);

        // Expression overload prints the predicate in failure messages
        discounted.Should().Satisfy(
            m => m.Amount == 90.00m && m.Currency == "GBP",
            because: "a 10% discount on £100 should yield £90 in the same currency");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Satisfy` with a multi-condition predicate reports only that "the predicate returned false" — it does not identify which sub-condition failed. For debugging purposes, prefer chained `.And` assertions or `BeEquivalentTo` when the individual condition names matter; reserve `Satisfy` for compact invariant smoke-checks where the predicate body is self-explanatory in the failure output. [official]

---

### Pattern 170 — Moq `SetupSequence` for Multi-Call Return Value Progression [official]

`SetupSequence` configures a mock to return different values on successive calls to the same member. Each `.Returns(...)` call appended to the sequence corresponds to one invocation; once the sequence is exhausted, the final value is repeated indefinitely (or `default(T)` for `Returns`-less terminations). This pattern is essential for testing retry logic, polling loops, and state-machine transitions where the SUT calls the same dependency multiple times with different expected responses.

```csharp
public class InventoryPollerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Poll_UntilStockAvailable_RetriesCorrectly()
    {
        var stockApi = new Mock<IStockApi>();
        stockApi.SetupSequence(a => a.GetStockLevelAsync("SKU-42"))
            .ReturnsAsync(0)   // 1st call: out of stock
            .ReturnsAsync(0)   // 2nd call: still out
            .ReturnsAsync(5);  // 3rd call: back in stock

        var poller = new InventoryPoller(stockApi.Object, maxRetries: 5);
        var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider();

        var result = await poller.WaitForStockAsync("SKU-42", fakeTime);

        Assert.Equal(5, result.StockLevel);
        Assert.Equal(3, result.AttemptsRequired);
        stockApi.Verify(a => a.GetStockLevelAsync("SKU-42"), Times.Exactly(3));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** After the `SetupSequence` is exhausted, Moq repeats the last configured return value — this can mask bugs where the SUT makes more retries than expected because all extra calls quietly succeed. Pair `SetupSequence` with an explicit `Verify(Times.Exactly(n))` call to assert the exact call count, or configure a final `.Throws<Exception>()` at the end of the sequence to fail fast on over-polling. [official]

---

### Pattern 171 — Testcontainers.NET `WithResourceMapping` for Injecting Init SQL Scripts Into Database Containers [official]

`WithResourceMapping(localPath, containerPath)` copies a file or directory from the build output into the container filesystem before startup. For PostgreSQL or SQL Server containers, this enables declarative schema seeding via the database's standard init-script directory (`/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/` for Postgres) rather than running migrations programmatically in test setup. The container executes scripts alphabetically, so naming scripts `001-schema.sql`, `002-seed.sql` controls ordering deterministically.

```csharp
public class PostgresContainerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private PostgreSqlContainer _container = null!;
    public string ConnectionString { get; private set; } = string.Empty;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _container = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
            .WithResourceMapping(
                source: new FileInfo("TestData/001-schema.sql"),
                target: "/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/001-schema.sql")
            .WithResourceMapping(
                source: new FileInfo("TestData/002-seed.sql"),
                target: "/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/002-seed.sql")
            .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                .UntilCommandIsCompleted("pg_isready -U postgres"))
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();
        ConnectionString = _container.GetConnectionString();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _container.DisposeAsync();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `WithResourceMapping` copies files at container-build time, not at test-run time — changes to SQL scripts require a rebuild of the test project to be picked up. In CI, this is expected behaviour; in local development, forgetting to rebuild after editing a seed script causes tests to run against stale schema and produces confusing "table does not exist" failures. Consider symlinking or using `EmbeddedResourceMapping` for scripts that change frequently during development. [official]

---

### Pattern 172 — `IServiceScope` Disposal Testing With `IAsyncDisposable` Mocks to Catch Scope Leaks [community]

Scoped services that hold resources (database connections, file handles) must be disposed when the `IServiceScope` is disposed. Tests that exercise service lifetimes should explicitly assert that `DisposeAsync` was called by the DI container's scope machinery. Using NSubstitute or Moq to implement both `ISomeService` and `IAsyncDisposable` on the same mock object allows tests to assert the teardown contract alongside the functional contract.

```csharp
public class OrderProcessorTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessAsync_ServiceScope_DisposesConnectionOnCompletion()
    {
        var services = new ServiceCollection();

        // A mock that is both a service AND tracks disposal
        var mockConnection = Substitute.For<IDbConnection, IAsyncDisposable>();
        services.AddScoped<IDbConnection>(_ => mockConnection);
        services.AddScoped<OrderProcessor>();

        await using var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();

        await using (var scope = provider.CreateAsyncScope())
        {
            var processor = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<OrderProcessor>();
            await processor.ProcessAsync(new Order(Guid.NewGuid()));
        } // scope disposed here — triggers DisposeAsync on IAsyncDisposable services

        await ((IAsyncDisposable)mockConnection).Received(1).DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** This pattern couples the test to the DI container wiring; if the scope is replaced with a factory or manually-managed lifetime, the test may not exercise real teardown paths. Use integration-level scope-leak tests sparingly alongside a global `ServiceCollection` rule enforced by NetArchTest or custom Roslyn analysers that forbid `new SomeService(...)` instantiation in production code. [community]

---

### Pattern 173 — xUnit v3 `IAsyncLifetime` With `CancellationToken` Support for Timeout-Safe Fixture Initialization [official]

xUnit v3's `IAsyncLifetime` interface exposes `InitializeAsync(CancellationToken)` and `DisposeAsync(CancellationToken)` overloads. Passing the cancellation token to every async operation inside the fixture means that if the xUnit test runner applies a timeout to fixture setup (via `[assembly: TestTimeout]` or CI-level process timeout), the initialisation will be aborted cleanly rather than leaving the container or external resource in a half-started state. This is critical for Testcontainers fixtures on slow CI agents.

```csharp
public class RedisFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private RedisContainer _container = null!;
    public IConnectionMultiplexer Redis { get; private set; } = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        _container = new RedisBuilder()
            .WithImage("redis:7-alpine")
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync(cancellationToken);

        Redis = await ConnectionMultiplexer.ConnectAsync(
            _container.GetConnectionString());
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        Redis.Dispose();
        await _container.StopAsync(cancellationToken);
        await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Not all third-party async initialisation APIs accept `CancellationToken` — if an upstream SDK ignores the token, the fixture will still block. Use `CancellationToken.Register` with a fallback `Task.WhenAny(initTask, Task.Delay(timeout, ct))` for SDKs that lack token support. Always test fixture teardown paths locally by simulating a `CancellationTokenSource.Cancel()` midway through `InitializeAsync`. [official]

---

### Pattern 174 — NUnit 4 `[ValueSource]` With Static Property for Reusable Cross-Fixture Parameter Sets [official]

`[ValueSource(typeof(SharedTestData), nameof(SharedTestData.ValidSkus))]` lets multiple test fixtures share the same parameter enumeration without duplicating data. Unlike `[TestCaseSource]`, `[ValueSource]` annotates individual parameters rather than entire test signatures, making it composable: one parameter can come from a `[ValueSource]` while another uses a literal `[Values(1, 2, 3)]`. The source member must be a public static property or field returning `IEnumerable`.

```csharp
public static class SharedTestData
{
    public static IEnumerable<string> ValidSkus { get; } = new[]
    {
        "SKU-001", "SKU-042", "SKU-999", "BUNDLE-XL"
    };
}

[TestFixture]
public class InventoryValidatorTests
{
    [Test]
    public void IsValid_KnownSku_ReturnsTrue(
        [ValueSource(typeof(SharedTestData), nameof(SharedTestData.ValidSkus))]
        string sku,
        [Values(1, 5, 100)] int quantity)
    {
        var validator = new InventoryValidator();

        var result = validator.IsValid(new StockRequest(sku, quantity));

        Assert.That(result.IsValid, Is.True,
            () => $"Expected valid for SKU={sku}, qty={quantity}");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `[ValueSource]` generates a Cartesian product when multiple parameters use it on the same test — four SKUs × three quantities yields twelve test cases. As the number of parameters and source lengths grow, combinatorial explosion can make the test suite slow and failures hard to triage. Use `[Sequential]` to zip parameters instead of combining them when independence between parameters cannot be assumed. [official]

---

### Pattern 175 — FluentAssertions v8 `HaveCount` With `Which` Continuation for Length-Then-Content Assertions [official]

`collection.Should().HaveCount(n).And.Subject` accesses the collection after the count assertion passes, but the `.And.Subject` property type is `IEnumerable<T>` — losing strongly-typed `Which`. The correct pattern is `HaveCount(n, "...")` followed by a separate assertion, or chaining via `.And.ContainSingle().Which` for single-element collections. For multi-element cases, `SatisfyRespectively` is the idiomatic replacement that combines count and per-element assertions in one statement.

```csharp
public class CartServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void AddItem_TwoDifferentProducts_CartHasExactlyTwoLines()
    {
        var cart = new ShoppingCart();
        cart.AddItem(new Product("P1", 9.99m), qty: 1);
        cart.AddItem(new Product("P2", 4.99m), qty: 2);

        cart.Lines.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
            first =>
            {
                first.ProductId.Should().Be("P1");
                first.Quantity.Should().Be(1);
                first.LineTotal.Should().Be(9.99m);
            },
            second =>
            {
                second.ProductId.Should().Be("P2");
                second.Quantity.Should().Be(2);
                second.LineTotal.Should().Be(9.98m);
            });
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SatisfyRespectively` is order-sensitive — it pairs each inspector with the element at the same index. If the collection is ordered by insertion but the SUT's implementation sorts it, the inspectors will mis-match silently (no count error, just wrong-value failures). Always assert or enforce ordering before using `SatisfyRespectively`, or use `BeEquivalentTo` with `WithoutStrictOrdering` when element order is not a contract requirement. [official]

---

### Pattern 176 — `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing` `FakeLogger` Category Verification [official]

`FakeLogger<T>` from `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing` records log entries and exposes them as `IReadOnlyList<FakeLogRecord>` via `.Collector.GetSnapshot()`. Each `FakeLogRecord` exposes `Category`, `Level`, `Message`, `Exception`, and structured `State` values. Asserting on `Category` confirms that the correct logger was injected into the SUT — a common source of category-mismatch bugs where a base-class logger is injected instead of the derived-class logger.

```csharp
public class PaymentProcessorLogTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_GatewayTimeout_LogsWarningWithTransactionId()
    {
        var fakeLogger = new FakeLogger<PaymentProcessor>();
        var gateway = Substitute.For<IPaymentGateway>();
        gateway.ChargeAsync(Arg.Any<ChargeRequest>())
            .Returns<ChargeResult>(_ => throw new TimeoutException("Gateway timeout"));

        var processor = new PaymentProcessor(gateway, fakeLogger);

        await processor.ProcessPaymentAsync(
            new ChargeRequest(Amount: 50m, CardToken: "tok_xyz"));

        var snapshot = fakeLogger.Collector.GetSnapshot();
        snapshot.Should().ContainSingle(r =>
            r.Level == LogLevel.Warning &&
            r.Category == "MyApp.Payments.PaymentProcessor" &&
            r.Message.Contains("tok_xyz"));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `FakeLogger<T>` only captures log entries for the exact generic type `T` — if the SUT logs via an injected `ILogger<BaseProcessor>` rather than `ILogger<PaymentProcessor>`, the collector will be empty and the test will fail confusingly. Use `FakeLogCollector` with a `LoggerFactory` configured via `AddFakeLogging()` to capture all categories when the SUT uses a non-generic logger or a base-class logger. [official]

---

### Pattern 177 — NSubstitute `Returns` With Multiple Values for Sequential Response Simulation [official]

NSubstitute's `Returns(T first, params T[] others)` overload configures a substitute to return different values on successive calls, paralleling Moq's `SetupSequence`. After the configured values are exhausted, the last value repeats. This pattern integrates naturally with NSubstitute's `Arg.Any<T>()` matching and `Received()` verification, making it the preferred approach when the test uses NSubstitute throughout rather than mixing in Moq just for sequencing.

```csharp
public class CircuitBreakerTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Execute_TransientThenSuccess_ClosesCircuit()
    {
        var inner = Substitute.For<IOrderApi>();
        inner.GetOrderAsync(Arg.Any<Guid>())
            .Returns(
                _ => throw new HttpRequestException("503"),
                _ => throw new HttpRequestException("503"),
                x => Task.FromResult(new Order(x.Arg<Guid>(), "Confirmed")));

        var breaker = new SimpleCircuitBreaker(inner, failureThreshold: 2);
        var orderId = Guid.NewGuid();

        // first two calls raise, third succeeds
        var result = await breaker.GetOrderWithRetryAsync(orderId);

        result.Status.Should().Be("Confirmed");
        await inner.Received(3).GetOrderAsync(orderId);
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** NSubstitute's lambda-based `Returns` overload is more flexible than value-based returns because the lambda can inspect call arguments. However, lambdas that throw exceptions must use `_ => throw new Exception()` syntax — using `x => { throw new Exception(); }` (statement lambda) compiles but may confuse IDE tooling. Document the call sequence with inline comments matching each lambda to its invocation number. [official]

---

### Pattern 178 — `WebApplicationFactory<T>` With `IHostEnvironment` Override for Environment-Specific Behaviour Testing [official]

`WebApplicationFactory<T>` allows overriding the hosting environment via `WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.UseEnvironment("Staging"))`. ASP.NET Core's middleware pipeline, error handling, and feature flags frequently branch on `IHostEnvironment.EnvironmentName`. Testing each environment variant in isolation — `Development`, `Staging`, `Production` — ensures that environment-specific middleware (e.g., developer exception page, HTTPS redirection, security headers) is applied correctly at each tier.

```csharp
public class ErrorHandlingIntegrationTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Theory]
    [InlineData("Development", 200)]   // developer exception page returns 200 with details
    [InlineData("Production", 500)]    // production returns 500 with no stack trace
    public async Task Get_UnhandledExceptionEndpoint_ReturnsEnvironmentAppropriateCode(
        string environment, int expectedStatus)
    {
        var client = factory
            .WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.UseEnvironment(environment))
            .CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/test/throw");

        ((int)response.StatusCode).Should().Be(expectedStatus);
        if (environment == "Production")
        {
            var body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
            body.Should().NotContain("at ", because:
                "stack traces must not leak in production responses");
        }
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Each `factory.WithWebHostBuilder(...)` call creates a new child factory and a new `TestServer` instance. In a theory with many environment variants, this multiplies startup cost. Cache factory instances per environment using `Dictionary<string, WebApplicationFactory<Program>>` in an `IClassFixture` implementation, building each variant lazily on first access and disposing all on `DisposeAsync`. [official]

---

### Pattern 179 — `Verify.NET` Snapshot Testing for Command/Query Response Contracts [community]

`Verify` (the `Verify` NuGet package) serialises an object to a `.verified.txt`/`.verified.json` file on the first run, then on subsequent runs compares the serialised output to the stored snapshot. Unlike `BeEquivalentTo`, snapshot tests catch additive changes (new properties, changed enum labels, reformatted decimals) that would not break a hand-written assertion. This is particularly powerful for API response shapes and domain event payloads that must not change without a deliberate review.

```csharp
public class OrderCreatedEventSnapshotTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Handle_NewOrder_EventPayloadMatchesSnapshot()
    {
        var handler = new OrderCreatedEventHandler();
        var evt = new OrderCreatedEvent(
            OrderId: Guid.Parse("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"),
            CustomerId: Guid.Parse("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002"),
            Lines: new[] { new OrderLine("SKU-1", 2, 9.99m) },
            CreatedAt: new DateTime(2026, 1, 15, 10, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc));

        var enrichedEvent = handler.Enrich(evt);

        // First run: writes OrderCreatedEventSnapshotTests.Handle_NewOrder_EventPayloadMatchesSnapshot.verified.json
        // Subsequent runs: compares to stored file; diff viewer opens on mismatch
        await Verify(enrichedEvent)
            .UseDirectory("Snapshots")
            .UseFileName(nameof(Handle_NewOrder_EventPayloadMatchesSnapshot));
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Snapshot files must be committed to source control and reviewed as part of every PR that changes the serialised output — teams that auto-approve snapshot diffs without review lose the safety guarantee. Set up a CI step that fails if any `.received.*` file exists after the test run (these are uncommitted diffs); use `VerifierSettings.DerivePathInfo` to keep snapshots alongside test files rather than in a centralised directory so reviewers see them in the PR diff. [community]

### Pattern 180 — MSTest v3 `[DataTestMethod]` With `[DataRow]` `DisplayName` for Self-Documenting Parameterised Tests [official]

MSTest v3 `[DataRow]` supports a `DisplayName` named property that overrides the auto-generated test name in Test Explorer and TRX reports. When test names contain machine-generated GUIDs or numeric codes, `DisplayName` replaces them with human-readable scenario labels. Combining `DisplayName` with the `[DataTestMethod]` attribute (which is mandatory for `[DataRow]` in MSTest) makes parameterised test output directly usable as acceptance-test evidence in sprint reviews.

```csharp
[TestClass]
public class DiscountRuleEngineTests
{
    [DataTestMethod]
    [DataRow("SUMMER20", 100.00, 80.00, DisplayName = "Summer20 coupon: £100 → £80")]
    [DataRow("NEWUSER",  50.00, 40.00, DisplayName = "NewUser coupon: £50 → £40")]
    [DataRow("VIP",     200.00, 150.00, DisplayName = "VIP coupon: £200 → £150")]
    [DataRow("EXPIRED",  75.00, 75.00, DisplayName = "Expired coupon: no discount applied")]
    public void Apply_ValidCouponCode_ProducesCorrectDiscountedPrice(
        string couponCode,
        double originalPrice,
        double expectedPrice,
        string? _displayName = null)  // not used in test body; for DataRow metadata only
    {
        var engine = new DiscountRuleEngine(new InMemoryCouponRepository());

        var result = engine.Apply(new CartPrice((decimal)originalPrice), couponCode);

        Assert.AreEqual((decimal)expectedPrice, result.DiscountedPrice, delta: 0.01m,
            message: $"Coupon '{couponCode}' produced unexpected price");
    }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `DisplayName` is a compile-time string literal — dynamic labels (e.g., including runtime-computed values) are not supported. For scenarios where the display name must embed parameter values, use a test naming pattern in the `[DataTestMethod]` method name itself (e.g., `Apply_{coupon}_ProducesDiscount`) and rely on the auto-generated `(couponCode, ...)` suffix in Test Explorer. MSTest v3's auto-generated names already include parameter values, so `DisplayName` adds value only when those values are opaque identifiers. [official]

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 51

**xUnit v3 `Assert.Equivalent` with `strict: false` silently passes when the expected object has a typo in a property name — because the default mode only checks that all expected properties exist on actual, a mistyped expected property name (e.g., `Statuss` instead of `Status`) is simply absent from actual, causing the equivalence check to succeed vacuously [community]** — A developer writes `Assert.Equivalent(new { Statuss = "Pending" }, result, strict: false)`, intending to assert the `Status` property. The typo produces an anonymous type with a property `Statuss` that does not exist on `result`; because `strict: false` allows actual to have more members, there is nothing to compare and the assertion passes. WHY it causes problems: the assertion provides zero coverage — the test could return any value for `Status` and still pass — but appears to be checking a property. Fix: always use `strict: true` when asserting named properties, or use FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` which explicitly fails on unmatched expected members.

**NSubstitute `Returns` lambda that mutates a captured list causes non-deterministic behaviour when tests share a fixture — the lambda captures a reference to the list, not a snapshot, so later tests that clear or replace the list in fixture setup change what earlier-configured substitutes return [community]** — A class fixture pre-configures a substitute with `.Returns(_ => capturedOrders.First())`, where `capturedOrders` is a `List<Order>` on the fixture. A later test calls `capturedOrders.Clear()` in its arrange phase; the substitute's lambda now throws `InvalidOperationException` during a different test's act phase because the list is empty. WHY it causes problems: the failure appears in a different test than the one that cleared the list, making the connection invisible in a standard sequential failure report. Fix: create fresh substitutes per test using `Substitute.For<T>()` in the test constructor, not in fixture initialisation, for any substitute whose return values depend on mutable state.

**Testcontainers.NET `WithResourceMapping` does not watch for file changes — SQL init scripts copied at container-build time are embedded into the Docker image layer cache and are not refreshed even when the source file on disk is modified, because Docker layer caching keyed on the file hash is only invalidated when the container image is explicitly rebuilt [community]** — A developer edits `002-seed.sql` to add a new test row, runs the tests, and sees the old seed data. The `PostgreSqlBuilder` produces the same image hash because the test project DLL (the cache key) has not changed; Docker reuses the cached layer containing the old script. WHY it causes problems: the developer concludes the seed script has a bug and spends time debugging SQL syntax rather than understanding the Docker build cache. Fix: add a `--no-cache` flag to the container build step during local development iteration, or use Testcontainers.NET `WithBindMount` instead of `WithResourceMapping` for init scripts that change frequently, as bind mounts bypass the image layer cache.

**FluentAssertions v8 `SatisfyRespectively` does not report which element's inspector failed when multiple inspectors fail simultaneously — it aggregates all failures into a single `AssertionException` with a message listing offending elements by index, but the index shown corresponds to the inspector position, not the element value, making it difficult to identify the failing domain object in large collections [community]** — A test asserts on a 20-element `IReadOnlyList<OrderLine>` using `SatisfyRespectively`. Three inspectors fail. The failure message reads "Element at index 3 did not satisfy assertion: Expected ProductId to be ...", but the test reader must manually correlate index 3 back to the original domain object to understand context. WHY it causes problems: in collections containing opaque identifiers or large object graphs, index-based failure messages require additional debugging to decode. Fix: include a `because` argument with a human-readable label in every inner assertion (`productId.Should().Be("SKU-1", because: $"element {index} must reference the first product")`), or assert `.ContainEquivalentOf` for non-ordered checks.

**MSTest v3 `[TestInitialize]` in a base class runs after a derived class's constructor — if the derived class constructor establishes state that `[TestInitialize]` in the base class depends on, the base-class init silently sees the pre-constructor state [community]** — A base class `[TestInitialize]` reads `this.ConnectionString` (set in the derived class constructor) to open a database connection. The `[TestInitialize]` runs after the derived constructor, so `ConnectionString` is available, but if the developer moves the assignment into the derived class's own `[TestInitialize]`, the execution order becomes Base-TestInitialize → Derived-TestInitialize, and the base-class init now sees an empty `ConnectionString`. WHY it causes problems: the order of constructor vs `[TestInitialize]` vs base-class `[TestInitialize]` is non-obvious and differs from NUnit and xUnit constructor-based patterns, leading to subtle class-hierarchy bugs that only appear when setup logic is refactored. Fix: document the full MSTest setup chain (ctor → base `[TestInitialize]` → derived `[TestInitialize]`) with a comment in any base test class, and prefer constructor injection over `[TestInitialize]` for state shared across the hierarchy.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 51 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `Assert.Equivalent` with `strict: false` and anonymous expected types | Typos in property names pass silently; assertion provides zero coverage | Use `strict: true` or `BeEquivalentTo` which validates all expected members exist |
| `SetupSequence` without a final `Verify(Times.Exactly(n))` | Extra SUT calls silently return the last configured value; over-polling goes undetected | Always pair `SetupSequence` with an explicit call-count verification |
| Testcontainers `WithResourceMapping` for frequently-edited init scripts | Docker layer cache serves stale scripts; edits appear to have no effect | Use `WithBindMount` during local development iteration to bypass the image cache |
| NSubstitute substitute return lambdas capturing shared mutable fixture state | Fixture teardown or other tests mutate the captured reference, causing cross-test failures | Create fresh substitutes per test; do not capture mutable fixture fields in return lambdas |
| `[TestInitialize]` in a derived MSTest class that depends on base-class `[TestInitialize]` side-effects | Execution order is Base ctor → Base init → Derived ctor → Derived init; assumptions break on refactor | Prefer explicit constructor chaining or document the full init chain with assertions on expected state |
| `SatisfyRespectively` without per-element `because` arguments | Index-only failure messages require manual correlation to identify the domain object | Add `because: $"element {n} (ProductId={x.ProductId})"` to every inner assertion |
