## Cycle 56 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 241: xUnit v3 `TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage` ambient diagnostic logging** [official]
xUnit v3 exposes `TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage` as the preferred replacement for `ITestOutputHelper.WriteLine` in infrastructure code that has no direct reference to the test instance. It outputs to the same console sink but can be called from any thread without injecting the helper through the entire call stack.
```csharp
public class OrderProcessorTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrder_SendsConfirmationEmail()
    {
        // TestContext.Current is ambient — no constructor injection required
        TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage(
            "Starting ProcessOrder test at {0}", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow);

        var sut = new OrderProcessor(
            emailSender: new FakeEmailSender(),
            logger: new FakeLogger<OrderProcessor>());

        var result = await sut.ProcessAsync(new Order { Id = Guid.NewGuid() });

        TestContext.Current.SendDiagnosticMessage("Order result: {0}", result.Status);
        Assert.Equal(OrderStatus.Confirmed, result.Status);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `TestContext.Current` is null outside of a running test — helper/utility classes that may be invoked outside tests (e.g., in production-support scripts) must null-check before calling `SendDiagnosticMessage`, otherwise a `NullReferenceException` is silently swallowed during infrastructure teardown. Wrap calls with `TestContext.Current?.SendDiagnosticMessage(...)` in shared utility code.

**Pattern 242: NUnit 4 `Assert.Multiple` / `Assert.MultipleAsync` for collecting all failures in one pass** [official]
NUnit 4's `Assert.Multiple` block runs all contained assertions even when earlier ones fail, collecting every failure into a single report. This is ideal for complex DTOs or API response validation where you want to see all field errors at once rather than stopping at the first.
```csharp
[Test]
public async Task GetProductDetails_ReturnsAllExpectedFields()
{
    var client = _factory.CreateClient();
    var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/products/42");
    var product = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<ProductDto>();

    Assert.Multiple(() =>
    {
        Assert.That(response.StatusCode, Is.EqualTo(HttpStatusCode.OK));
        Assert.That(product, Is.Not.Null);
        Assert.That(product!.Id, Is.EqualTo(42));
        Assert.That(product.Name, Is.Not.Empty);
        Assert.That(product.Price, Is.GreaterThan(0m));
        Assert.That(product.StockCount, Is.GreaterThanOrEqualTo(0));
        Assert.That(product.Category, Is.Not.Null);
    });
}
```
Tradeoff: `Assert.Multiple` only collects `AssertionException` subclasses. Any non-assertion exception (e.g., `NullReferenceException` from dereferencing the null DTO before the null-check assertion runs) escapes the block immediately. Reorder assertions so null-guard assertions come first, or use `Assume.That(product, Is.Not.Null)` to abort cleanly rather than proceed into a crash.

**Pattern 243: MSTest v3 `[DataRow]` with `DisplayName` for human-readable parameterised test names** [official]
MSTest v3 adds a `DisplayName` property to `[DataRow]` that overrides the default auto-generated test name, making CI failure logs immediately readable without decoding method parameter values.
```csharp
[TestClass]
public class DiscountCalculatorTests
{
    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow(0,    100m, 100m,  DisplayName = "No loyalty — no discount")]
    [DataRow(1,    100m,  95m,  DisplayName = "1 year — 5% loyalty discount")]
    [DataRow(5,    100m,  80m,  DisplayName = "5 years — 20% loyalty discount")]
    [DataRow(10,   100m,  65m,  DisplayName = "10 years — 35% loyalty discount")]
    [DataRow(10,     0m,   0m,  DisplayName = "10 years — zero base price stays zero")]
    public void Calculate_AppliesCorrectDiscount(
        int loyaltyYears, decimal basePrice, decimal expected)
    {
        var sut = new DiscountCalculator();
        var actual = sut.Calculate(basePrice, loyaltyYears);
        Assert.AreEqual(expected, actual,
            $"Expected {expected} for {loyaltyYears} year(s) on {basePrice}");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `DisplayName` is a static string; it cannot interpolate the `DataRow` values at attribute declaration time. For data-driven tests with many rows where the name must reflect the actual value, use `[DynamicData]` with `DynamicDataDisplayName` pointing to a method that computes the name at runtime — this avoids the repetition of encoding values twice (once in the row and once in the display name string).

**Pattern 244: FluentAssertions v8 `Using<T>().WhenTypeIs<T>()` custom equality comparator in `BeEquivalentTo`** [official]
When two object graphs contain a type whose default `Equals` implementation is unsuitable for test comparison (e.g., a third-party `Money` struct using reference equality), FluentAssertions v8 lets you inject a custom `IEqualityComparer<T>` scoped to that specific type within a `BeEquivalentTo` call.
```csharp
public class MoneyComparerTests
{
    private sealed class MoneyComparer : IEqualityComparer<Money>
    {
        public bool Equals(Money x, Money y) =>
            x.Amount == y.Amount && x.Currency == y.Currency;
        public int GetHashCode(Money m) => HashCode.Combine(m.Amount, m.Currency);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Invoice_TotalsMatchExpected()
    {
        var actual = InvoiceBuilder.BuildSample();
        var expected = new Invoice
        {
            LineTotal  = new Money(150.00m, "USD"),
            TaxTotal   = new Money(12.00m,  "USD"),
            GrandTotal = new Money(162.00m, "USD")
        };

        actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, options => options
            .Using(new MoneyComparer())
            .WhenTypeIs<Money>());
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `Using<T>().WhenTypeIs<T>()` replaces the comparer for every occurrence of `Money` anywhere in the object graph, including deeply nested collections. If the graph contains two conceptually different uses of `Money` that require different comparison semantics (e.g., one that should ignore currency for a multi-currency report), you need separate `BeEquivalentTo` calls rather than one combined assertion.

**Pattern 245: `WebApplicationFactory<T>` with `IServiceCollection.RemoveAll<T>()` for targeted service substitution** [official]
Integration tests using `WebApplicationFactory` can replace specific services via `WithWebHostBuilder` without touching the rest of the DI graph. `RemoveAll<T>` removes all registrations of an interface before adding the test double, avoiding duplicate registration errors that silently return the last-registered instance.
```csharp
public class PaymentEndpointTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public PaymentEndpointTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    {
        _client = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
        {
            builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
            {
                services.RemoveAll<IPaymentGateway>();
                services.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway, FakePaymentGateway>();
            });
        }).CreateClient();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_Returns202_WhenGatewayAccepts()
    {
        var payload = new { Amount = 99.99m, Currency = "USD" };
        var response = await _client.PostAsJsonAsync("/api/payments", payload);
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Accepted, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `RemoveAll<T>` removes only registrations keyed to the exact type `T`. If the original registration was added as a concrete type (`services.AddSingleton<PaymentGateway>()`) rather than the interface, `RemoveAll<IPaymentGateway>()` will not remove it. Inspect the real service registrations (via `builder.ConfigureServices(s => { foreach (var d in s) ... })`) when a fake is not being resolved as expected.

**Pattern 246: Testcontainers.NET `WithWaitStrategy` for reliable container readiness in CI** [official]
Testcontainers.NET provides composable wait strategies that prevent test setup from proceeding until the container is actually ready to serve traffic, replacing fragile `Thread.Sleep` or retry loops.
```csharp
public class SqlServerContainerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MsSqlContainer _db = new MsSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
        .WithPassword("StrongPassword!23")
        .WithWaitStrategy(
            Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                .UntilPortIsAvailable(1433)
                .UntilMessageIsLogged(
                    "SQL Server is now ready for client connections"))
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _db.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync() => await _db.StartAsync();
    public async Task DisposeAsync()    => await _db.DisposeAsync();
}

public class ProductRepositoryTests(SqlServerContainerFixture db)
    : IClassFixture<SqlServerContainerFixture>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Save_PersistsProduct()
    {
        await using var ctx = new AppDbContext(db.ConnectionString);
        await ctx.Database.MigrateAsync();
        await ctx.Products.AddAsync(new Product { Name = "Widget" });
        await ctx.SaveChangesAsync();
        Assert.Equal(1, await ctx.Products.CountAsync());
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `UntilMessageIsLogged` matches a fixed substring against the container's stdout. If the image version changes the log message wording (e.g., SQL Server 2025 changes "client connections" to "client requests"), the wait strategy hangs until the configured timeout. Pin the exact image tag in CI (`2022-latest` can drift) and add `WithStartupTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(120))` as a fallback to surface clear timeout errors rather than silent CI hangs.

**Pattern 247: `Moq` `Capture.In<T>` for recording arguments across multiple calls** [official]
When a mock is expected to be called multiple times with different arguments and you need to assert on all captured values after the fact, `Capture.In<T>` stores each invocation argument into a `List<T>` without requiring `Callback` chains.
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task OrderService_SendsNotificationForEachItem()
{
    var sentMessages = new List<NotificationMessage>();
    var notifier = new Mock<INotificationService>();

    notifier
        .Setup(n => n.SendAsync(Capture.In(sentMessages)))
        .ReturnsAsync(true);

    var sut = new OrderService(notifier.Object);
    await sut.FulfillAsync(new Order
    {
        Items = [new("SKU-1"), new("SKU-2"), new("SKU-3")]
    });

    Assert.Equal(3, sentMessages.Count);
    Assert.Contains(sentMessages, m => m.Sku == "SKU-1");
    Assert.Contains(sentMessages, m => m.Sku == "SKU-2");
    Assert.Contains(sentMessages, m => m.Sku == "SKU-3");
}
```
Tradeoff: `Capture.In<T>` captures the argument reference, not a deep copy. If the service reuses a mutable message object and mutates it before each call (e.g., sets fields on a pooled `NotificationMessage` instance), all entries in `sentMessages` will point to the same object with the last-written values. Use `Callback<T>(msg => sentMessages.Add(msg.Clone()))` when the service mutates a shared argument object across calls.

**Pattern 248: `FakeLogger<T>` from `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing` for structured log output assertions** [official]
.NET 8+ ships `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing` with `FakeLogger<T>` and `FakeLogCollector`, enabling assertions on log entries without third-party libraries. You can assert on log level, message template, and structured property values.
```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing;

[Fact]
public async Task Processor_LogsWarning_WhenRetryLimitExceeded()
{
    var collector = new FakeLogCollector();
    var logger = new FakeLogger<RetryProcessor>(collector);
    var sut = new RetryProcessor(logger, maxRetries: 2);

    await sut.ProcessAsync(new FailingJob());

    var warnings = collector.GetSnapshot()
        .Where(e => e.Level == LogLevel.Warning)
        .ToList();

    Assert.Single(warnings);
    Assert.Contains("RetryLimitExceeded", warnings[0].Message);
    Assert.Equal(2, (int)warnings[0].StructuredState!
        .First(kv => kv.Key == "RetryCount").Value!);
}
```
Tradeoff: `FakeLogger<T>` buffers all log entries in memory for the test's lifetime. In long-running integration test scenarios (e.g., a `WebApplicationFactory` shared across a large `[Collection]`), the accumulated log buffer can consume significant memory and make `GetSnapshot()` queries slow. Prefer `FakeLogger<T>` in isolated unit tests; for integration tests, use a scoped `ILoggerFactory` with `AddFakeLogging()` and call `collector.Clear()` between test runs.

**Pattern 249: `AutoFixture` with `[Frozen]` attribute for automatic dependency wiring in `[Theory]` tests** [community]
AutoFixture's `[Frozen]` attribute in combination with `AutoMoqCustomization` injects the same mock instance for every parameter in a `[Theory]` method that shares the same interface type. This eliminates manual mock wiring while keeping the arrange section minimal.
```csharp
public class OrderHandlerTests
{
    [Theory, AutoMoqData]
    public async Task Handle_PublishesEvent_WhenOrderSaved(
        [Frozen] Mock<IOrderRepository> repoMock,
        [Frozen] Mock<IEventBus> busMock,
        Order order,
        OrderHandler sut)
    {
        repoMock.Setup(r => r.SaveAsync(order)).ReturnsAsync(true);

        await sut.HandleAsync(new SaveOrderCommand(order));

        busMock.Verify(b => b.PublishAsync(
            It.Is<OrderSavedEvent>(e => e.OrderId == order.Id)), Times.Once);
    }
}

// Customization wiring
public class AutoMoqDataAttribute : AutoDataAttribute
{
    public AutoMoqDataAttribute()
        : base(() => new Fixture().Customize(new AutoMoqCustomization())) { }
}
```
Tradeoff: Parameter order matters — `[Frozen]` must appear on a parameter that is declared before the SUT (`sut`) parameter, otherwise AutoFixture creates the SUT first (without the frozen mock) and then creates a separate instance for the frozen parameter. Always declare `[Frozen]` dependency mocks before the SUT in the method signature.

**Pattern 250: `WireMock.Net` for HTTP dependency stubbing in integration tests** [community]
WireMock.Net starts an in-process HTTP server that intercepts outbound `HttpClient` calls, letting you define request-response mappings without real external services.
```csharp
public class ExchangeRateServiceTests : IDisposable
{
    private readonly WireMockServer _server = WireMockServer.Start();

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetRate_ReturnsParsedRate_FromExternalApi()
    {
        _server
            .Given(Request.Create()
                .WithPath("/rates/USD/GBP")
                .UsingGet())
            .RespondWith(Response.Create()
                .WithStatusCode(200)
                .WithHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .WithBody("""{"rate": 0.7912, "timestamp": 1715000000}"""));

        var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(_server.Url!) };
        var sut = new ExchangeRateService(client);

        var rate = await sut.GetRateAsync("USD", "GBP");

        Assert.Equal(0.7912m, rate.Value);
    }

    public void Dispose() => _server.Stop();
}
```
Tradeoff: WireMock.Net stubs are matched in registration order — if two `Given` mappings could match the same request, the first one wins and the second is silently ignored. When building complex stub scenarios, register more specific matchers first (e.g., a stub with both path and query-string conditions) before registering broad fallback stubs; otherwise test setup silently produces wrong responses without any error.

**Pattern 251: `Respawn` for fast database reset between integration tests** [community]
Respawn clears only the tables that have changed since the last checkpoint by issuing targeted `DELETE` or `TRUNCATE` statements, making database reset far faster than dropping and recreating the schema for each test.
```csharp
public class DatabaseFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public AppDbContext Db { get; private set; } = null!;
    private Respawner _respawner = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await using var conn = new SqlConnection(TestConnectionString);
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        Db = new AppDbContext(TestConnectionString);
        await Db.Database.MigrateAsync();
        _respawner = await Respawner.CreateAsync(conn, new RespawnerOptions
        {
            DbAdapter = DbAdapter.SqlServer,
            TablesToIgnore = [new Table("__EFMigrationsHistory")]
        });
    }

    public async Task ResetAsync()
    {
        await using var conn = new SqlConnection(TestConnectionString);
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        await _respawner.ResetAsync(conn);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await Db.DisposeAsync();
}
```
Tradeoff: Respawn analyses foreign key relationships to determine delete order. If your schema uses `NOCHECK` constraints or has FK cycles, Respawn may emit incorrect delete order and fail with FK violation errors. Verify constraint health with `DBCC CHECKCONSTRAINTS` before adopting Respawn, and add tables with FK cycles to `TablesToIgnore`, resetting them manually in a `[OneTimeSetUp]` step.

**Pattern 252: `Alba` ASP.NET Core integration testing DSL for concise HTTP scenario setup** [community]
Alba wraps `WebApplicationFactory` with a fluent API that reduces HTTP scenario boilerplate, handling serialisation, status code assertions, and header checks in one chained expression.
```csharp
public class ProductScenarioTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private IAlbaHost _host = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync() =>
        _host = await AlbaHost.For<Program>(x =>
            x.ConfigureServices(s => s.RemoveAll<ICacheService>()));

    [Fact]
    public async Task Post_CreateProduct_Returns201WithLocation()
    {
        await _host.Scenario(scenario =>
        {
            scenario.Post.Json(new { Name = "Gadget", Price = 29.99 })
                    .ToUrl("/api/products");
            scenario.StatusCodeShouldBe(201);
            scenario.Header("Location")
                    .SingleValueShouldStartWith("/api/products/");
        });
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _host.DisposeAsync();
}
```
Tradeoff: Alba's `Scenario` helper buffers the entire response body before returning. For streaming responses (SSE or chunked JSON), or very large paginated payloads, fall back to `_host.Server.CreateClient()` and consume `HttpResponseMessage.Content` via `ReadAsStreamAsync` to avoid silent truncation.

**Pattern 253: `.NET 9` `TimeProvider` + `FakeTimeProvider` for deterministic date-dependent logic** [official]
`System.TimeProvider` (introduced in .NET 8 and expanded in .NET 9) abstracts date/time access. Tests inject `Microsoft.Extensions.Time.Testing.FakeTimeProvider` to control `UtcNow`, advance time deterministically, and test timer callbacks without real waits.
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task SubscriptionService_Expires_AfterTrialPeriod()
{
    var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider(
        startDateTime: new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));

    var sut = new SubscriptionService(fakeTime);
    sut.StartTrial(userId: "u1", trialDays: 14);

    // Advance to day 13 — still active
    fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(13));
    Assert.True(await sut.IsActiveAsync("u1"));

    // Advance one more day past expiry
    fakeTime.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(2));
    Assert.False(await sut.IsActiveAsync("u1"));
}
```
Tradeoff: `FakeTimeProvider` does not auto-advance during `Task.Delay` — code under test that calls `await Task.Delay(timeout, timeProvider.CreateCancellationToken(...))` will hang unless you explicitly advance the `FakeTimeProvider` from a concurrent task. Use `Task.Run(() => fakeTime.Advance(...))` in a separate thread or restructure delay-dependent logic to accept an `ITimer` so you can trigger the callback directly.

**Pattern 254: `Stryker.NET` mutation testing to validate test suite kill rate** [community]
Stryker.NET introduces source-level mutations (negating conditions, removing statements, substituting literals) and runs the test suite against each mutant. Tests that do not catch mutations indicate coverage gaps even where line coverage is 100%.
```csharp
// stryker-config.json — recommended minimal configuration
// {
//   "stryker-config": {
//     "project": "src/MyApp/MyApp.csproj",
//     "test-projects": ["tests/MyApp.Tests/MyApp.Tests.csproj"],
//     "reporters": ["html", "cleartext"],
//     "threshold-high": 80,
//     "threshold-low": 60,
//     "threshold-break": 50
//   }
// }

// Example: a boundary mutation Stryker catches when test data is precise
public decimal CalculateDiscount(int years)
{
    // Mutant: years >= 5  →  years > 5  (boundary shift)
    if (years >= 5) return 0.20m;
    return years >= 1 ? 0.05m : 0m;
}

// Test that kills the boundary mutant — both sides of the boundary are exercised:
[Theory]
[InlineData(4, 0.05m)]  // just below boundary
[InlineData(5, 0.20m)]  // at boundary — essential to kill >= vs > mutant
public void CalculateDiscount_BoundaryValues(int years, decimal expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, new DiscountCalculator().CalculateDiscount(years));
```
Tradeoff: Stryker.NET can take 10–30x longer than a normal test run on large projects because it compiles and runs the suite per mutant. Limit scope to changed files in CI using `--since git-diff-target`, or run Stryker only in nightly/weekly pipelines, treating mutation score as a quality-gate dashboard metric rather than a per-PR blocker.

**Pattern 255: `OpenTelemetry` `InMemoryExporter` for span and metric assertions in unit tests** [community]
The `OpenTelemetry.Exporter.InMemory` package routes spans and metrics to in-memory collections during tests, enabling assertions on telemetry without a real collector or Jaeger instance.
```csharp
public class TelemetryAssertionTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrder_EmitsOrderProcessedSpan()
    {
        var exportedActivities = new List<Activity>();
        using var tracerProvider = Sdk.CreateTracerProviderBuilder()
            .AddSource("MyApp.OrderProcessor")
            .AddInMemoryExporter(exportedActivities)
            .Build();

        var sut = new OrderProcessor(
            tracer: new ActivitySource("MyApp.OrderProcessor"),
            repository: new InMemoryOrderRepository());

        await sut.ProcessAsync(new Order { Id = Guid.NewGuid(), Amount = 50m });

        // Assert BEFORE disposing tracerProvider
        var span = exportedActivities.SingleOrDefault(
            a => a.DisplayName == "ProcessOrder");
        Assert.NotNull(span);
        Assert.Equal(ActivityStatusCode.Ok, span.Status);
        Assert.Equal("50", span.GetTagItem("order.amount")?.ToString());
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `InMemoryExporter` receives activities only after they are ended (activity `Stop()` / `Dispose()`). If code under test starts an activity but does not properly dispose it (e.g., an exception swallowed before the `using` block closes), the exported list will be empty. Add `Assert.All(exportedActivities, a => Assert.NotEqual(default, a.Duration))` to verify all captured spans were properly completed. Also assert before disposing the `TracerProvider` — the buffer may be cleared on `ForceFlush` in some SDK versions.

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 56

**Gotcha G16: `AutoFixture` `[Frozen]` parameter ordering bug — declaring the SUT parameter before a `[Frozen]` dependency injects a different mock instance into the SUT than the one captured for verification**
A developer writes a `[Theory, AutoMoqData]` test with `OrderHandler sut` declared before `[Frozen] Mock<IEventBus> busMock`. AutoFixture resolves parameters left-to-right: it creates `OrderHandler` first (satisfying its `IEventBus` dependency with a fresh anonymous mock), then creates the `[Frozen]` mock — but this second mock is not the same instance the SUT holds. WHY: `[Frozen]` pins a single instance for all subsequent resolutions in the parameter list, but "subsequent" means parameters declared after the `[Frozen]` one. Parameters already resolved before `[Frozen]` are not retroactively rewired. Fix: always declare all `[Frozen]` mock parameters before the SUT parameter in the method signature.

**Gotcha G17: WireMock.Net stub registration order shadowing — a broad path-only `Given` registered before a specific path+query `Given` silently absorbs requests intended for the specific stub**
A team registers a general fallback stub for `/api/rates` first (to return a 404 for unmapped currencies) and then a specific stub for `/api/rates?from=USD&to=GBP`. All requests for the specific pair still match the general fallback because WireMock.Net evaluates stubs in insertion order, and the broad stub matches first. WHY: WireMock.Net uses a "first match wins" strategy rather than "most specific match wins". Fix: always register the most specific stubs first and add the broad fallback stub last; or use `.AtPriority(int)` to assign explicit matching priorities so specific mappings always win regardless of registration order.

**Gotcha G18: `Respawn` with SQL Server `NOCHECK` constraints produces FK violation errors during reset — disabled FK constraints are invisible to Respawn's dependency sort, causing parent-row deletions before child rows**
A team has a legacy table pair where the FK was disabled with `ALTER TABLE child NOCHECK CONSTRAINT fk_parent`. Respawn reads the `sys.foreign_keys` catalog but filters by `is_disabled = 0`, so the disabled FK is invisible to its dependency sort. Respawn deletes the parent table before the child table, producing `The DELETE statement conflicted with the REFERENCE constraint` errors. WHY: Respawn's delete-order algorithm is correct for enabled FKs but cannot account for unenforced relationships. Fix: add the child table to `TablesToIgnore` and truncate it manually in a `[OneTimeSetUp]` step, or re-enable the FK so Respawn can detect the dependency correctly.

**Gotcha G19: `OpenTelemetry` `InMemoryExporter` returns zero activities when the `TracerProvider` is disposed before the test assertion — the exporter buffer may be cleared on `ForceFlush` during dispose**
A developer wraps `Sdk.CreateTracerProviderBuilder()...Build()` in a `using` block and calls `ProcessAsync` inside the block, but places the assertion after the closing brace. By the time the assertion runs, the `TracerProvider` has flushed and the exporter's internal `List<Activity>` is empty in some SDK versions. WHY: the `InMemoryExporter` does not use a persistent external store — its buffer can be cleared on `ForceFlush`/dispose cycles. Fix: keep the `using var tracerProvider` scope open until after all assertions have completed, ensuring the buffer is still live when assertions run.

**Gotcha G20: `Alba` `Scenario` helper silently truncates large response bodies — paginated endpoints returning thousands of items appear to have fewer rows without any exception**
A team uses Alba's `Scenario` to test a paginated product list endpoint that returns 5,000 items. The deserialized response object has fewer rows than expected, and the test's row count assertion fails intermittently depending on average item JSON size. WHY: Alba's default in-memory response stream inherits the `MaxResponseBodySize` from the `WebApplicationFactory` Kestrel configuration, which caps the buffered body. There is no exception — the stream simply closes at the limit. Fix: for large-payload endpoints, call `_host.Server.CreateClient()` directly and use `ReadAsStreamAsync` + `JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsyncEnumerable` rather than Alba's buffered `Scenario` helper.

---

### Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — Cycle 56 Additions

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|---|---|---|
| `[Frozen]` mock declared after SUT in AutoFixture theory | SUT gets a different mock instance than the one verified against | Always declare `[Frozen]` dependencies before the SUT parameter |
| WireMock broad stub registered before specific stub | First-match-wins silently absorbs specific requests | Register specific stubs first; use `.AtPriority` for explicit ordering |
| `Respawn` with `NOCHECK` FK constraints | Delete order ignores disabled FKs, causing constraint violations | Add affected child tables to `TablesToIgnore`; truncate manually |
| `InMemoryExporter` asserted after `TracerProvider` dispose | Exporter buffer cleared on dispose; assertions see empty activity list | Keep `TracerProvider` scope open until all assertions complete |
| Alba `Scenario` for large paginated response bodies | Silent truncation produces intermittent count failures | Use `CreateClient()` + `ReadAsStreamAsync` for large payloads |
| `Assert.Multiple` with nullable dereference before null-guard assertion | `NullReferenceException` escapes the multiple block immediately | Order null-guard assertions first inside every `Assert.Multiple` block |

## Cycle 57 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 256** — `IClassFixture<CustomWebApplicationFactory<T>>` with `ConfigureTestServices` for per-test service override [official]
```csharp
public class OrdersControllerTests : IClassFixture<CustomWebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public OrdersControllerTests(CustomWebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    {
        _client = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
        {
            builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
            {
                // Replace the real payment gateway with a test double
                services.AddScoped<IPaymentGateway, StubPaymentGateway>();
            });
        }).CreateClient();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Post_PlaceOrder_Returns201_WithConfirmationId()
    {
        var payload = new StringContent(
            """{"productId": "abc-123", "quantity": 2}""",
            Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");

        var response = await _client.PostAsync("/orders", payload);

        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Created, response.StatusCode);
        var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<OrderConfirmation>();
        Assert.NotNull(body?.ConfirmationId);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `WithWebHostBuilder` creates a new `WebApplicationFactory` child per call, which re-boots the whole `TestServer`. For tests that share identical service overrides, inject the factory once via `IClassFixture` and call `CreateClient()` directly, reserving `WithWebHostBuilder` for the rare tests that genuinely need a different service graph. Paying the server-startup cost on every test doubles or triples total suite time in large endpoint suites.

**Pattern 257** — `WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions.AllowAutoRedirect = false` for redirect assertion [official]
```csharp
public class AuthRedirectTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;

    public AuthRedirectTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _factory = factory;

    [Fact]
    public async Task Get_ProtectedRoute_RedirectsToLogin_WhenUnauthenticated()
    {
        // Arrange — disable auto-redirect so we can inspect the 302 directly
        var client = _factory.CreateClient(new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions
        {
            AllowAutoRedirect = false
        });

        // Act
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/dashboard");

        // Assert
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.Redirect, response.StatusCode);
        Assert.StartsWith(
            "http://localhost/Identity/Account/Login",
            response.Headers.Location!.OriginalString);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: With `AllowAutoRedirect = true` (the default), the client follows redirects and the final status code is `200 OK`, hiding the redirect chain entirely. Always disable auto-redirect when the test purpose is to verify the redirect target URL, status code, or cookie behavior; re-enable it only when you want to exercise the full round-trip through the redirect destination page.

**Pattern 258** — `TestAuthHandler` with `AuthenticationHeaderValue` for protected endpoint integration tests [official]
```csharp
public class TestAuthHandler : AuthenticationHandler<AuthenticationSchemeOptions>
{
    public const string SchemeName = "TestScheme";

    public TestAuthHandler(IOptionsMonitor<AuthenticationSchemeOptions> options,
        ILoggerFactory logger, UrlEncoder encoder)
        : base(options, logger, encoder) { }

    protected override Task<AuthenticateResult> HandleAuthenticateAsync()
    {
        var claims = new[]
        {
            new Claim(ClaimTypes.Name, "integration-test-user"),
            new Claim(ClaimTypes.Role, "Admin"),
            new Claim("tenant", "acme-corp")
        };
        var identity  = new ClaimsIdentity(claims, SchemeName);
        var principal = new ClaimsPrincipal(identity);
        var ticket    = new AuthenticationTicket(principal, SchemeName);
        return Task.FromResult(AuthenticateResult.Success(ticket));
    }
}

// In custom factory:
builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
{
    services.AddAuthentication(o =>
    {
        o.DefaultAuthenticateScheme = TestAuthHandler.SchemeName;
        o.DefaultChallengeScheme    = TestAuthHandler.SchemeName;
    })
    .AddScheme<AuthenticationSchemeOptions, TestAuthHandler>(
        TestAuthHandler.SchemeName, _ => { });
});

// In test:
client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
    new AuthenticationHeaderValue(TestAuthHandler.SchemeName);
```
Tradeoff: The handler injects a static claim set, which is sufficient for most RBAC scenarios. When tests need distinct user identities or tenant values per test case, pass a claim bag via `IOptionsMonitor<T>` or a shared `ConcurrentDictionary<string, ClaimsPrincipal>` keyed by a test-scoped header value rather than hard-coding claims in the handler, or the handler becomes a global mutable fixture that causes cross-test interference.

**Pattern 259** — `Moq` `mock.Object` vs `mock` confusion — always use `.Object` when passing to production code [community]
```csharp
public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Task<Order?> GetByIdAsync(Guid id);
    Task SaveAsync(Order order);
}

[Fact]
public async Task ProcessOrder_CallsSave_WhenOrderIsValid()
{
    // Arrange
    var repoMock = new Mock<IOrderRepository>();
    repoMock
        .Setup(r => r.GetByIdAsync(It.IsAny<Guid>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(new Order { Id = Guid.NewGuid(), Status = OrderStatus.Pending });

    // CORRECT: pass mock.Object, not mock
    var sut = new OrderService(repoMock.Object);

    // Act
    await sut.ProcessAsync(Guid.NewGuid());

    // Assert — verify the mock was called
    repoMock.Verify(r => r.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<Order>()), Times.Once);
}
```
Tradeoff: `mock` itself is the `Mock<T>` proxy wrapper — passing it to a constructor expecting `IOrderRepository` will cause a compile error or runtime `InvalidCastException`. `mock.Object` is the actual proxied implementation instance. This is one of the most common Moq beginner errors; consider enforcing it via a custom Roslyn analyzer rule or team code review checklist item.

---

**Pattern 260** — `Mock<T>` Strict vs Loose behavior and `MockBehavior.Strict` for fail-fast verification [community]
```csharp
[Fact]
public void StrictMock_ThrowsOnUnexpectedCall()
{
    // Strict mode: any call not explicitly set up throws MockException immediately
    var strictMock = new Mock<IEmailSender>(MockBehavior.Strict);

    // Only set up the one method we expect to be called
    strictMock
        .Setup(s => s.SendAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<string>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(true);

    var sut = new NotificationService(strictMock.Object);

    // This call matches the setup — passes
    sut.NotifyAsync("user@example.com", "Welcome!").GetAwaiter().GetResult();

    // If NotificationService unexpectedly calls s.LogAsync(...)
    // MockException fires immediately instead of silently swallowing the call.
    strictMock.VerifyAll();
}
```
Tradeoff: `MockBehavior.Strict` makes tests brittle to internal implementation changes — adding a benign logging call to the SUT breaks every strict test that didn't set it up. Prefer `MockBehavior.Loose` (default) for the majority of tests and reserve `Strict` for security-critical or billing-critical paths where any unexpected external call is a defect. Document the choice with a comment so reviewers understand the intent.

**Pattern 261** — `[Theory]` with `[MemberData]` using `TheoryData<T1, T2>` for strongly-typed parameterised tests [official]
```csharp
public class PricingCalculatorTests
{
    public static TheoryData<decimal, int, decimal> DiscountTestCases => new()
    {
        { 100m, 0,  100m },   // no discount tier
        { 100m, 10,  90m },   // 10% applied
        { 200m, 25, 150m },   // 25% applied
        { 50m,  50,  25m },   // 50% edge case
    };

    [Theory]
    [MemberData(nameof(DiscountTestCases))]
    public void Calculate_AppliesDiscount_Correctly(
        decimal basePrice, int discountPct, decimal expected)
    {
        var sut = new PricingCalculator();

        var actual = sut.Calculate(basePrice, discountPct);

        Assert.Equal(expected, actual);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `TheoryData<T1, T2>` provides compile-time type safety and IDE refactoring support that `IEnumerable<object[]>` lacks. The downside is that `TheoryData` is xUnit-specific; for cross-framework portability use the `object[]` overload. Also be aware that the static property is evaluated once at test-discovery time — if the data source depends on DI or runtime configuration, use a custom `DataAttribute` subclass instead.

---

**Pattern 262** — `FakeLogger<T>` + `FakeLogCollector` for structured log assertion without third-party libraries (.NET 8+) [official]
```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing;

[Fact]
public void ProcessPayment_LogsWarning_WhenAmountExceedsLimit()
{
    // Arrange
    var collector = new FakeLogCollector();
    var logger    = new FakeLogger<PaymentProcessor>(collector);
    var sut       = new PaymentProcessor(logger, maxAmount: 1000m);

    // Act
    sut.Process(amount: 1500m, currency: "USD");

    // Assert
    var warnings = collector.GetSnapshot()
        .Where(e => e.Level == LogLevel.Warning)
        .ToList();

    Assert.Single(warnings);
    Assert.Contains("exceeds limit", warnings[0].Message);
    Assert.Equal(1500m, warnings[0].State!
        .FirstOrDefault(kvp => kvp.Key == "amount").Value);
}
```
Tradeoff: `FakeLogger<T>` and `FakeLogCollector` are included in `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing` (shipped in .NET 8+) and require zero third-party dependencies. The limitation is that `FakeLogCollector` only captures in-process, synchronous log records — it cannot assert logs emitted from background threads after `GetSnapshot()` is called. For background-service tests, call `GetSnapshot()` only after `await Task.Delay(...)` or after awaiting a `TaskCompletionSource` signaled by the log event.

---

**Pattern 263** — `Microsoft.Testing.Platform` (MTP) mode in `.NET 10` `global.json` for native `dotnet test` integration [official]
```json
// global.json — root of the repository
{
  "sdk": { "version": "10.0.100" },
  "test": { "runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform" }
}
```
```xml
<!-- In each test .csproj -->
<PropertyGroup>
  <EnableMSTestRunner>true</EnableMSTestRunner>
  <!-- or for xUnit.net v3: <UseXunitRunner>true</UseXunitRunner> -->
  <TestingPlatformDotnetTestSupport>true</TestingPlatformDotnetTestSupport>
</PropertyGroup>
```
```bash
# Run all tests — MTP mode handles multi-framework solutions natively
dotnet test --report-trx
```
Tradeoff: MTP mode in .NET 10 eliminates the legacy VSTest bridge overhead and supports per-project argument routing via `TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments`. The catch is that VSTest-specific `--logger` options are silently ignored; replace them with MTP equivalents like `--report-trx`. Mixed solutions containing both VSTest and MTP projects are unsupported — migrate all test projects to MTP before enabling `global.json` mode, or CI pipelines may produce misleading exit codes.

---

**Pattern 264** — `Directory.Build.props` `TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments` condition routing for multi-framework solutions [official]
```xml
<!-- Directory.Build.props at solution root -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <!-- Apply MSTest-specific filter only to MSTest.Sdk projects -->
    <TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments
      Condition="'$(UsingMSTestSdk)' == 'true'"
      >$(TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments) $(MSTestArgs)</TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments>

    <!-- Apply xUnit-specific filter to all other test projects -->
    <TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments
      Condition="'$(UsingMSTestSdk)' != 'true'"
      >$(TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments) $(XUnitArgs)</TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments>

    <!-- Arguments valid across ALL frameworks — no condition needed -->
    <TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments
      >$(TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments) --ignore-exit-code 8</TestingPlatformCommandLineArguments>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```
```bash
# Pass framework-specific filter from CI command line
dotnet test \
  -p:MSTestArgs="--filter FullyQualifiedName~Integration" \
  -p:XUnitArgs="--filter-trait Category=Integration"
```
Tradeoff: Centralising argument routing in `Directory.Build.props` keeps per-project `.csproj` files clean and prevents copy-paste drift. The risk is that the `UsingMSTestSdk` property is defined by `MSTest.Sdk` — if a project uses plain `MSTest` without `MSTest.Sdk`, the condition evaluates to `false` and xUnit arguments are routed to it, producing exit code 5. Audit all test project styles before adopting this pattern and add a CI check that validates the condition property is present.

---

**Pattern 265** — `Moq` `Capture.In<T>` with `IList<T>` for multi-call argument recording and post-call assertion [community]
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task BulkImport_SendsOneEmailPerRecord()
{
    // Arrange
    var capturedAddresses = new List<string>();
    var emailMock = new Mock<IEmailSender>();
    emailMock
        .Setup(s => s.SendAsync(Capture.In(capturedAddresses), It.IsAny<string>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(true);

    var sut = new BulkImportService(emailMock.Object);
    var records = new[] { "alice@example.com", "bob@example.com", "carol@example.com" };

    // Act
    await sut.ImportAsync(records);

    // Assert — verify each address was targeted exactly once
    Assert.Equal(3, capturedAddresses.Count);
    Assert.Contains("alice@example.com", capturedAddresses);
    Assert.Contains("bob@example.com",   capturedAddresses);
    Assert.Contains("carol@example.com", capturedAddresses);
}
```
Tradeoff: `Capture.In<T>` appends every matched argument to the provided `IList<T>`, enabling rich post-call assertions across multiple invocations without writing a custom callback. The list is shared across all setups that reference it — if the mock is configured in a fixture shared across tests (e.g., `IClassFixture`), the list accumulates entries across test cases, producing false positives. Always use a fresh `List<T>` per test.

---

**Pattern 266** — `IDateTimeProvider` / `TimeProvider` seam pattern for deterministic date-dependent logic [official]
```csharp
// Production code uses the injected TimeProvider abstraction
public class SubscriptionService
{
    private readonly TimeProvider _clock;
    private readonly ISubscriptionRepository _repo;

    public SubscriptionService(TimeProvider clock, ISubscriptionRepository repo)
    {
        _clock = clock;
        _repo  = repo;
    }

    public bool IsExpired(Subscription sub)
        => sub.ExpiresAt < _clock.GetUtcNow();
}

// Test — use .NET 8+ FakeTimeProvider
[Fact]
public void IsExpired_ReturnsTrue_WhenCurrentTimeIsAfterExpiry()
{
    var fakeTime = new FakeTimeProvider();
    fakeTime.SetUtcNow(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 6, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));

    var sub = new Subscription
    {
        ExpiresAt = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 31, 23, 59, 0, TimeSpan.Zero)
    };

    var sut = new SubscriptionService(fakeTime, Mock.Of<ISubscriptionRepository>());

    Assert.True(sut.IsExpired(sub));
}
```
Tradeoff: The `TimeProvider` abstract class (introduced in .NET 8) is the official Microsoft-blessed seam for time — prefer it over home-grown `IDateTimeProvider` interfaces in new code. `FakeTimeProvider` from `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` supports `Advance(TimeSpan)` for timer-driven tests. The only gotcha is that `TimeProvider.System` uses `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` internally, so tests that forget to inject the fake and rely on the default `TimeProvider.System` will be non-deterministic on CI runners in different time zones.

---

**Pattern 267** — `ArchUnitNET` `Types().That().ResideInNamespace()` for enforcing Clean Architecture dependency rules [community]
```csharp
using ArchUnitNET.Domain;
using ArchUnitNET.Loader;
using ArchUnitNET.xUnit;
using static ArchUnitNET.Fluent.ArchRuleDefinition;

public class ArchitectureTests
{
    private static readonly Architecture Architecture =
        new ArchLoader()
            .LoadAssemblies(
                typeof(Domain.Order).Assembly,
                typeof(Application.OrderService).Assembly,
                typeof(Infrastructure.OrderRepository).Assembly)
            .Build();

    [Fact]
    public void Domain_MustNotDependOn_Infrastructure()
    {
        var rule = Types().That()
            .ResideInNamespace("MyApp.Domain", useRegularExpressions: false)
            .Should().NotDependOnAny(
                Types().That()
                    .ResideInNamespace("MyApp.Infrastructure",
                        useRegularExpressions: false));

        rule.Check(Architecture);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Application_MustNotDependOn_Infrastructure()
    {
        var rule = Types().That()
            .ResideInNamespace("MyApp.Application", useRegularExpressions: false)
            .Should().NotDependOnAny(
                Types().That()
                    .ResideInNamespace("MyApp.Infrastructure",
                        useRegularExpressions: false));

        rule.Check(Architecture);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ArchUnitNET` catches accidental cross-layer dependencies at build time, providing a safer net than code reviews. The cost is test-suite startup time — loading and analysing all assemblies adds 1–3 seconds per test class. Put all architecture tests in a single `ArchitectureTests` class sharing one static `Architecture` instance to amortise the load cost. Also note that the `useRegularExpressions: false` overload performs exact prefix matching; omitting it causes the namespace string to be interpreted as a regex, which can silently widen the scope.

---

**Pattern 268** — `Bogus` `Faker<T>.StrictMode(true)` for exhaustive test data generation [community]
```csharp
using Bogus;

public class CustomerFakerTests
{
    private static readonly Faker<Customer> CustomerFaker =
        new Faker<Customer>()
            .StrictMode(true)          // Every property must be configured
            .RuleFor(c => c.Id,        f => f.Random.Guid())
            .RuleFor(c => c.FirstName, f => f.Name.FirstName())
            .RuleFor(c => c.LastName,  f => f.Name.LastName())
            .RuleFor(c => c.Email,     f => f.Internet.Email())
            .RuleFor(c => c.CreatedAt, f => f.Date.RecentOffset(days: 30));

    [Fact]
    public void Generate_ReturnsValidCustomer_WithAllFieldsPopulated()
    {
        var customer = CustomerFaker.Generate();

        Assert.NotEqual(Guid.Empty, customer.Id);
        Assert.False(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(customer.FirstName));
        Assert.Contains("@", customer.Email);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Generate_HundredCustomers_AreAllDistinct()
    {
        var customers = CustomerFaker.Generate(100);
        var uniqueEmails = customers.Select(c => c.Email).Distinct().Count();
        Assert.Equal(100, uniqueEmails);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `StrictMode(true)` throws `FakerException` at test-discovery time if any public property lacks a `RuleFor` — this is a forcing function that prevents stale fakers after model changes add new properties. The tradeoff is that every model change requires updating the faker, which adds friction. For DTOs with many optional fields, use `StrictMode(false)` and add explicit `RuleFor` only for fields that must be non-null in tests. Store fakers as `static readonly` fields shared across the fixture class — `Faker` is thread-safe for `Generate()` calls but not for `RuleFor` configuration.

**Pattern 269** — `Verify` snapshot testing with `DerivePathInfo` for organised snapshot storage [community]
```csharp
using VerifyXunit;

[UsesVerify]
public class InvoiceRendererTests
{
    static InvoiceRendererTests()
    {
        // Store snapshots alongside the test class file in a _snapshots sub-folder
        VerifierSettings.DerivePathInfo((sourceFile, projectDir, type, method) =>
            new PathInfo(
                directory: Path.Combine(Path.GetDirectoryName(sourceFile)!, "_snapshots"),
                typeName:  type.Name,
                methodName: method.Name));
    }

    [Fact]
    public Task RenderInvoice_MatchesApprovedSnapshot()
    {
        var renderer = new InvoiceRenderer();
        var invoice  = new Invoice
        {
            Number     = "INV-0042",
            CustomerName = "Acme Corp",
            Lines      = new[] { new InvoiceLine("Widget", 3, 9.99m) },
            IssuedAt   = new DateOnly(2026, 5, 14)
        };

        var html = renderer.Render(invoice);

        return Verify(html).UseExtension("html");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `Verify` snapshot tests catch unintended rendering regressions without writing brittle string-comparison assertions. The first run creates the snapshot file (marked `.verified`), and subsequent runs diff the output. The operational cost is that all approved snapshots must be committed to source control — `*.verified.*` should be explicitly tracked in `.gitignore`'s negation rules. Also, `DerivePathInfo` must be set before any test runs in the class; the static constructor is the correct location, but ensure only one `DerivePathInfo` call exists globally (it cannot be reset between test classes in the same process).

**Pattern 270** — `WebApplicationFactory` database seeding with `IServiceScopeFactory` and `ReinitializeDbForTests` per-test reset [official]
```csharp
public class CustomWebApplicationFactory<TProgram>
    : WebApplicationFactory<TProgram> where TProgram : class
{
    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
        {
            // Replace production DB with SQLite in-memory for speed + isolation
            var descriptor = services.SingleOrDefault(
                d => d.ServiceType == typeof(DbContextOptions<AppDbContext>));
            if (descriptor is not null) services.Remove(descriptor);

            services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(options =>
                options.UseSqlite("DataSource=:memory:"));
        });
    }

    public void SeedDatabase(Action<AppDbContext> seedAction)
    {
        using var scope = Services.CreateScope();
        var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
        db.Database.EnsureCreated();
        seedAction(db);
        db.SaveChanges();
    }
}

// In test class:
public class ProductsEndpointTests
    : IClassFixture<CustomWebApplicationFactory<Program>>, IDisposable
{
    private readonly CustomWebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public ProductsEndpointTests(CustomWebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    {
        _factory = factory;
        factory.SeedDatabase(db =>
        {
            db.Products.RemoveRange(db.Products);  // reset
            db.Products.Add(new Product { Id = 1, Name = "Widget", Price = 9.99m });
        });
        _client = factory.CreateClient();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Get_Products_ReturnsSeededProduct()
    {
        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/products");
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        var products = await response.Content
            .ReadFromJsonAsync<List<ProductDto>>();
        Assert.Single(products!);
        Assert.Equal("Widget", products![0].Name);
    }

    public void Dispose() => _client.Dispose();
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `IServiceScopeFactory` to access the `DbContext` outside the request pipeline is the correct pattern for seeding — accessing `AppDbContext` directly from `Services` without a scope throws `InvalidOperationException` on scoped services. The per-test reset via `RemoveRange` + re-seed is simple but incurs EF change-tracking overhead; for large datasets prefer `Respawn` or raw `DELETE FROM` SQL via `db.Database.ExecuteSqlRaw(...)` to reset faster.

### Community Gotchas

**G21** — `Moq` Strict mock throws `MockException` on unmatched calls in async disposal paths — a `Strict` mock used inside a service with `IAsyncDisposable` fires `MockException` on the implicit `DisposeAsync()` call that was never set up, crashing the test after the assertion passes
Why this matters: `MockBehavior.Strict` raises on every unmatched invocation including framework-level lifecycle calls. When the SUT implements `IAsyncDisposable` and the test disposes it via `await using var sut = ...`, the runtime calls `DisposeAsync()` which is not in the test setup. The test body passes, then the `await using` teardown throws `MockException`, which xUnit reports as a test failure with a confusing stack trace pointing to the `}` of the test method.
Fix: Add `.Setup(s => s.DisposeAsync()).Returns(ValueTask.CompletedTask)` to every strict mock whose concrete type implements `IAsyncDisposable`, or switch to `MockBehavior.Loose` for mocks that are only used structurally (not verified against). Alternatively, never use `await using` with `Strict` mocks — call `sut.Dispose()` explicitly after assertions.

**G22** — `WebApplicationFactory<T>` `ConfigureServices` vs `ConfigureTestServices` ordering — services registered in `ConfigureServices` run before `Startup.ConfigureServices`, so production registrations added after the override win; use `ConfigureTestServices` instead
Why this matters: A developer overrides the DI container in `ConfigureWebHost` using `builder.ConfigureServices(...)` to replace a real external service. At runtime the real service still wins because ASP.NET Core processes `ConfigureServices` callbacks in order, and the app's own `Startup.ConfigureServices` runs afterward, re-registering the production implementation. Only the last `TryAdd*` or the last `AddScoped*` for a given interface wins, so the stub is silently shadowed.
Fix: Always use `builder.ConfigureTestServices(services => { ... })` instead of `builder.ConfigureServices(...)`. `ConfigureTestServices` hooks into the `IStartupFilter` pipeline and runs after `Startup.ConfigureServices`, guaranteeing the test override is the final registration. The distinction is documented in the ASP.NET Core integration test docs but frequently confused by developers who have used the `ConfigureServices` overload in non-test `WebHost` configuration.

**G23** — `TheoryData<T>` property evaluated at test-discovery time — constructors, DI containers, and `IConfiguration` are unavailable when `MemberData` is resolved
Why this matters: A developer creates a `static TheoryData<string>` property that reads connection strings from `IConfiguration` or environment variables via `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable`. On local machines the variables are set; on CI they are absent. The data source returns an empty `TheoryData`, and xUnit silently skips all theory cases rather than failing, yielding a deceptively green CI run with zero test executions.
Fix: Never read environment-dependent values inside `TheoryData` or `MemberData` source properties. Use `[InlineData]` for constants, or implement a custom `DataAttribute` subclass that defers resolution to test-method invocation time (after the DI scope is active). For truly configuration-driven test cases, generate them in a `[Theory]` using `IEnumerable<object[]>` populated from a JSON fixture file committed to source control.

**G24** — `FakeTimeProvider.Advance()` does not trigger timer callbacks synchronously — background `ITimer` callbacks fire on the thread pool after an indeterminate delay, causing `Assert` to run before the callback executes
Why this matters: A developer uses `FakeTimeProvider.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))` expecting that any `ITimer` registered with a 30-second interval fires immediately and synchronously before the next line. In reality, `FakeTimeProvider` signals timer callbacks on the thread pool via `Task.Run`, so the callback may execute after the assertion line, producing intermittent false failures that only appear under load on CI agents.
Fix: After calling `Advance(...)`, await a `Task.Delay(1)` or poll a `TaskCompletionSource` that the timer callback signals upon completion. Alternatively, use `FakeTimeProvider.Advance` together with `await Task.Yield()` to hand control back to the thread pool before asserting. The `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` NuGet package documentation notes this async dispatch behaviour explicitly in the remarks section of `ITimer`.

**G25** — `xUnit` `IClassFixture<T>` constructor is called once per test class but `T` constructor exceptions are swallowed as `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` failures, reporting every test in the class as failed with a generic `XunitException` rather than the actual exception message
Why this matters: A developer puts Testcontainers startup logic or database schema migration in the `IClassFixture` constructor. When Docker is unavailable on the CI agent, the constructor throws `DockerApiException`. xUnit catches this internally during fixture construction and wraps it as a generic fixture-initialization failure. Each test in the class reports `"Class fixture type 'DatabaseFixture' had one or more errors during construction"` without the original exception message, making CI failures extremely hard to diagnose without enabling verbose test output.
Fix: Move async infrastructure startup (Docker, migrations, HTTP clients) from the constructor into `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync()`. When `InitializeAsync` throws, xUnit propagates the original exception type and message directly into each test's failure output. For synchronous failures that cannot be async, wrap the constructor body in `try/catch` and store the exception, then rethrow it from `InitializeAsync()` with `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Throw(storedEx)` to preserve the original stack trace.

## Cycle 58 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 271** — xUnit v3 `ITestOutputHelper` + `ILogger<T>` bridge for structured diagnostic capture
```csharp
// XunitLoggerProvider bridges ILogger to ITestOutputHelper so all
// structured log lines appear inline in the test output window.
public class OrderServiceTests : IClassFixture<ServiceFixture>
{
    private readonly OrderService _sut;
    private readonly ITestOutputHelper _out;

    public OrderServiceTests(ServiceFixture fix, ITestOutputHelper output)
    {
        _out = output;
        var loggerFactory = LoggerFactory.Create(b =>
            b.AddProvider(new XunitLoggerProvider(output))
             .SetMinimumLevel(LogLevel.Debug));
        _sut = new OrderService(fix.Repository, loggerFactory.CreateLogger<OrderService>());
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_EmitsAuditLog()
    {
        await _sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new OrderRequest { Sku = "ABC", Qty = 2 });
        // Any Debug/Info/Warning lines from OrderService are now visible
        // in the test runner output — no separate log sink needed.
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `XunitLoggerProvider` (from the `Xunit.Extensions.Logging` NuGet) is zero-config but adds a package dependency. For projects already using `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions`, inline `FakeLogger<T>` is lighter weight and lets you assert on specific log entries programmatically; `ITestOutputHelper` bridging is better for diagnostic visibility without assertion coupling.

**Pattern 272** — NUnit 4 `Assert.That` with `Is.EqualTo(...).Using(IEqualityComparer<T>)` for custom domain equality
```csharp
// Supply a custom IEqualityComparer<T> directly inside the constraint
// rather than overriding Equals/GetHashCode on production DTOs.
public class MoneyAmountComparer : IEqualityComparer<Money>
{
    public bool Equals(Money? x, Money? y) =>
        x?.Amount == y?.Amount && x?.Currency == y?.Currency;
    public int GetHashCode(Money obj) =>
        HashCode.Combine(obj.Amount, obj.Currency);
}

[Test]
public void Refund_Returns_CorrectAmount()
{
    var invoice = new Invoice(100m, "USD");
    Money result = invoice.CalculateRefund(0.10m);

    Assert.That(result,
        Is.EqualTo(new Money(10m, "USD"))
          .Using(new MoneyAmountComparer()));
}
```
Tradeoff: Keeping equality logic in a dedicated comparer avoids polluting value types with test-only `Equals` overrides. The downside is that `GetHashCode` must be consistent with `Equals` even for test-only comparers — a mismatch causes `HashSet<T>`/`Dictionary<T>` lookups to silently fail in tests that combine comparison and collection membership checks.

**Pattern 273** — MSTest v3 `[DataTestMethod]` + `[DynamicData]` with `IEnumerable<object[]>` sourced from JSON fixture file
```csharp
// Load test cases from a checked-in JSON file to keep test code clean
// and allow non-developers to add cases without touching C#.
[TestClass]
public class TaxCalculatorTests
{
    public static IEnumerable<object[]> TaxCases =>
        JsonSerializer
            .Deserialize<TaxCase[]>(File.ReadAllText("TestData/tax-cases.json"))!
            .Select(c => new object[] { c.Income, c.FilingStatus, c.ExpectedTax });

    [DataTestMethod]
    [DynamicData(nameof(TaxCases), DynamicDataSourceType.Property)]
    public void Calculate_Tax_MatchesExpected(
        decimal income, string filing, decimal expected)
    {
        var calc = new TaxCalculator();
        decimal actual = calc.Compute(income, filing);
        Assert.AreEqual(expected, actual, delta: 0.01m);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: JSON-driven test data separates concerns cleanly and enables domain experts to curate cases. The risk is test-discovery failures at CI time when the JSON file path is relative and the working directory differs — always embed the file as `CopyToOutputDirectory = Always` in the `.csproj` and prefer `Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "TestData/tax-cases.json")` over bare relative paths.

**Pattern 274** — FluentAssertions v8 `BeEquivalentTo` with `options.Excluding(m => m.CreatedAt)` for volatile timestamp fields
```csharp
// Exclude non-deterministic fields from equivalence checks without
// touching production model equality logic.
[Fact]
public async Task CreateUser_Returns_ExpectedProfile()
{
    var sut = new UserService(_repo);
    UserProfile result = await sut.CreateAsync("alice@example.com");

    result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
        new UserProfile
        {
            Email    = "alice@example.com",
            IsActive = true,
            Role     = "Member",
        },
        opts => opts
            .Excluding(p => p.Id)
            .Excluding(p => p.CreatedAt)
            .Excluding(p => p.UpdatedAt));
}
```
Tradeoff: `Excluding(...)` keeps tests focused on business-meaningful properties without requiring clock injection. The danger is over-exclusion — accidentally excluding a field that should be validated. Prefer an explicit allowlist via `Including(...)` when the DTO is small; use `Excluding` only when the excluded set is clearly volatile (timestamps, auto-generated IDs).

**Pattern 275** — Moq `SetupSequence` for stateful multi-call repository stubs
```csharp
// Simulate a repository that returns "not found" on the first call
// then the entity on the subsequent call (e.g., after a create).
[Fact]
public async Task EnsureExists_CreatesOnFirstMiss_ReturnsOnSecond()
{
    var repo = new Mock<IProductRepository>();
    repo.SetupSequence(r => r.FindBySkuAsync("XYZ"))
        .ReturnsAsync((Product?)null)          // first call: miss
        .ReturnsAsync(new Product { Sku = "XYZ", Name = "Widget" }); // second call: hit

    var svc = new ProductEnsureService(repo.Object);
    var result = await svc.EnsureExistsAsync("XYZ", "Widget");

    result.Sku.Should().Be("XYZ");
    repo.Verify(r => r.CreateAsync(It.Is<Product>(p => p.Sku == "XYZ")), Times.Once);
}
```
Tradeoff: `SetupSequence` is ideal for testing retry or create-then-read patterns but the sequence is consumed destructively — if the SUT makes more calls than sequences configured, the mock falls back to its default `Loose` return value (`null`/`default`), which may silently pass instead of failing loudly. Add a `repo.VerifyAll()` or an explicit call-count `Verify` to guard against under-call scenarios.

**Pattern 276** — `Testcontainers.NET` `PostgreSqlContainer` with `WithImage` pinned digest for reproducible CI builds
```csharp
// Pin the container image by digest rather than tag to guarantee
// the exact same database binary on every developer machine and CI run.
public class DatabaseFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly PostgreSqlContainer _db = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage(
            "postgres@sha256:3d722d4e17f91c1d1f1f2b07a9c0c1b7d3456ef123abcd1234567890abcdef12")
        .WithDatabase("testdb")
        .WithUsername("test")
        .WithPassword("test")
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => _db.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _db.StartAsync();
        await MigrateAsync(ConnectionString);
    }

    public Task DisposeAsync() => _db.DisposeAsync().AsTask();

    private static async Task MigrateAsync(string cs)
    {
        await using var conn = new NpgsqlConnection(cs);
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        // apply Flyway/EF migrations here
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Digest pinning eliminates silent breakage caused by tag mutation (e.g., `postgres:16` being silently updated upstream). The operational cost is periodic manual digest updates when the team intentionally upgrades the DB engine — automate via Renovate or Dependabot with a `docker-digest` update type to keep this from becoming stale.

**Pattern 277** — `FluentAssertions` `BeJsonEquivalentTo` for HTTP response contract assertions without deserialization
```csharp
// Assert JSON responses structurally without deserializing to a
// concrete type — useful for polymorphic or schema-unstable payloads.
[Fact]
public async Task GetSummary_ReturnsExpectedJson()
{
    var client = _factory.CreateClient();
    var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/summary/42");

    response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.OK);

    string body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
    body.Should().BeJsonEquivalentTo("""
        {
            "id": 42,
            "status": "active",
            "itemCount": 3
        }
        """,
        options => options.Excluding("$.updatedAt"));
}
```
Tradeoff: `BeJsonEquivalentTo` (FluentAssertions v8+) avoids tight coupling to a specific DTO shape and is resilient to additive API changes (new fields are ignored by default). The tradeoff is that failures report JSON path diffs rather than property names, making them slightly harder to read for developers unfamiliar with JSONPath notation.

**Pattern 278** — `AutoFixture` `Build<T>().With(...)` + `OmitAutoProperties` for focused SUT construction
```csharp
// Construct only the properties relevant to the test; let AutoFixture
// skip properties that would trigger complex sub-graph generation.
[Fact]
public void Discount_AppliedCorrectly_ForPremiumCustomer()
{
    var fixture = new Fixture();

    var customer = fixture.Build<Customer>()
        .With(c => c.Tier, CustomerTier.Premium)
        .With(c => c.LoyaltyPoints, 500)
        .OmitAutoProperties()   // skip Address, Orders, etc.
        .Create();

    // Manually supply the navigation property the SUT actually uses
    customer.Address = new Address { Country = "US" };

    var svc = new PricingService();
    decimal discount = svc.GetDiscount(customer);

    discount.Should().Be(0.15m);
}
```
Tradeoff: `OmitAutoProperties` keeps tests readable and fast by skipping expensive recursive object graphs. However, it requires manually setting every property the SUT touches — missed properties remain `null`/`default`, which can cause `NullReferenceException` during the act phase rather than a clear assertion failure. Keep `OmitAutoProperties` tests co-located with a comment listing which properties the SUT actually reads.

**Pattern 279** — `IHostedService` integration test via `IHost` + `BackgroundService` extraction pattern with `CancellationTokenSource`
```csharp
// Test a BackgroundService in a real IHost without the full
// WebApplicationFactory overhead, using a cooperative cancellation.
[Fact]
public async Task PriceRefreshService_PublishesUpdate_WhenTriggered()
{
    var published = new List<string>();
    using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));

    using IHost host = Host.CreateDefaultBuilder()
        .ConfigureServices(s =>
        {
            s.AddSingleton<IEventBus>(new CapturingEventBus(published));
            s.AddHostedService<PriceRefreshService>();
        })
        .Build();

    await host.StartAsync(cts.Token);

    // Trigger the service logic (e.g., via internal channel or direct call)
    var svc = host.Services.GetRequiredService<PriceRefreshService>();
    await svc.TriggerRefreshAsync(cts.Token);

    await host.StopAsync(cts.Token);

    published.Should().ContainSingle()
        .Which.Should().StartWith("price-updated:");
}
```
Tradeoff: A real `IHost` exercises the actual `IHostedService` lifecycle (`StartAsync`/`StopAsync`) and DI wiring, which unit tests on the extracted worker method cannot catch. The cost is test duration — `IHost.StartAsync` spins up the full service graph. Limit this pattern to smoke/integration tests; unit-test the extracted core logic method separately for fast feedback.

**Pattern 280** — NSubstitute `Arg.Do<T>` side-effect capture for argument inspection without a dedicated capturer
```csharp
// Capture the exact argument passed to a void/async dependency
// for detailed assertion without a separate Capture.In<T> setup.
[Fact]
public async Task NotifyUser_SendsEmailWithCorrectSubject()
{
    var emailClient = Substitute.For<IEmailClient>();
    EmailMessage? captured = null;

    emailClient
        .When(c => c.SendAsync(Arg.Do<EmailMessage>(m => captured = m)))
        .Do(_ => { });  // no-op return, just capture

    var svc = new NotificationService(emailClient);
    await svc.NotifyAsync(userId: 7, event: "OrderShipped");

    captured.Should().NotBeNull();
    captured!.Subject.Should().Be("Your order has shipped");
    captured.To.Should().Be("user7@example.com");
}
```
Tradeoff: `Arg.Do<T>` is concise and avoids the `ReceivedCalls()` LINQ traversal. The limitation is that it only captures the last invocation when the method is called multiple times. For multi-call capture use `NSubstitute`'s `ReceivedCalls()` API or maintain an explicit `List<T>` inside the `Arg.Do` lambda.

**Pattern 281** — `Verify` snapshot library with `VerifyJson` for API response regression testing
```csharp
// Store and diff JSON API responses as checked-in snapshots.
// On first run, the snapshot is created; on subsequent runs, diffs
// are shown as test failures with contextual JSON path output.
public class ProductApiSnapshotTests : IClassFixture<ApiFactory>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public ProductApiSnapshotTests(ApiFactory factory)
        => _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProduct_MatchesSnapshot()
    {
        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/api/products/1");
        string json = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        await VerifyJson(json)
            .ScrubMember("createdAt")
            .ScrubMember("updatedAt");
    }
}
// Snapshot stored at: ProductApiSnapshotTests.GetProduct_MatchesSnapshot.verified.txt
```
Tradeoff: `Verify` snapshots catch unintentional API contract changes (added/removed fields, renamed properties) that typed deserialization silently swallows. The maintenance cost is that intentional changes require an explicit snapshot-approval step (`dotnet verify accept` or `--accept` CLI flag), which adds a step to the PR workflow. Mitigate by enforcing snapshot reviews in the PR checklist.

**Pattern 282** — `Microsoft.Extensions.Http` `AddHttpClient` + `MockHttpMessageHandler` for named-client unit testing
```csharp
// Replace the real HTTP transport with a MockHttpMessageHandler so
// the production IHttpClientFactory wiring is exercised in unit tests.
[Fact]
public async Task GetWeather_ParsesSuccessResponse()
{
    var handler = new MockHttpMessageHandler();
    handler
        .When("/weather/London")
        .Respond(HttpStatusCode.OK,
                 new StringContent("""{"temp":15,"unit":"C"}""",
                                   Encoding.UTF8, "application/json"));

    var services = new ServiceCollection();
    services.AddHttpClient<WeatherClient>()
            .ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler(() => handler);
    services.AddScoped<WeatherService>();

    await using var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
    var svc = provider.GetRequiredService<WeatherService>();

    var result = await svc.GetCurrentAsync("London");

    result.Temp.Should().Be(15);
    handler.VerifyNoOutstandingExpectation();
}
```
Tradeoff: Wiring through `AddHttpClient` + `ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler` exercises the actual `IHttpClientFactory` pipeline (base address, Polly retry policies, delegating handlers). This is heavier than newing up the client directly but prevents regressions where the real factory config differs from the test config. For purely unit-level tests with no retry policies, mocking `IWeatherClient` directly is faster.

**Pattern 283** — `BenchmarkDotNet` `[GlobalSetup]` + `Params` attribute for parameterised micro-benchmark suites
```csharp
// Combine [Params] with [GlobalSetup] to benchmark the same operation
// across different input sizes in a single benchmark class.
[MemoryDiagnoser]
[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net90)]
public class SerializerBenchmarks
{
    [Params(10, 100, 1_000)]
    public int Count { get; set; }

    private List<Product> _products = null!;
    private JsonSerializerOptions _opts = null!;

    [GlobalSetup]
    public void Setup()
    {
        _products = Enumerable.Range(1, Count)
            .Select(i => new Product { Id = i, Name = $"P{i}", Price = i * 1.5m })
            .ToList();
        _opts = new JsonSerializerOptions(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);
    }

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public string SystemTextJson() =>
        JsonSerializer.Serialize(_products, _opts);

    [Benchmark]
    public string NewtonsoftJson() =>
        Newtonsoft.Json.JsonConvert.SerializeObject(_products);
}
```
Tradeoff: `[Params]` multiplies benchmark variants automatically, providing a scaling curve with a single `[GlobalSetup]`. The risk is that `[GlobalSetup]` runs once per `[Params]` value combination — if setup is expensive (DB seed, network call) and there are many param combinations, total benchmark runtime grows quickly. Use `[IterationSetup]` for per-iteration fresh state only when the benchmark itself mutates the input; `[GlobalSetup]` should be idempotent for all `[Params]` values.

**Pattern 284** — Polly v8 `ResiliencePipeline` unit test with `FakeTimeProvider` + `ResilienceContextPool` for retry delay verification
```csharp
// Test that a Polly retry policy delays by the configured backoff
// using FakeTimeProvider so the test completes instantly.
[Fact]
public async Task RetryPipeline_BacksOff_BeforeSecondAttempt()
{
    var timeProvider = new FakeTimeProvider();
    int callCount = 0;
    var delays = new List<TimeSpan>();

    var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder()
        .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions
        {
            MaxRetryAttempts = 2,
            BackoffType = DelayBackoffType.Exponential,
            Delay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2),
            UseJitter = false,
            OnRetry = args =>
            {
                delays.Add(args.RetryDelay);
                timeProvider.Advance(args.RetryDelay);
                return default;
            }
        })
        .Build();

    await pipeline.ExecuteAsync(async ct =>
    {
        callCount++;
        if (callCount < 3) throw new HttpRequestException("transient");
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    });

    callCount.Should().Be(3);
    delays.Should().HaveCount(2);
    delays[0].Should().Be(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
    delays[1].Should().Be(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(4));
}
```
Tradeoff: Advancing `FakeTimeProvider` inside `OnRetry` keeps the test synchronous and CI-safe. The caveat is that `UseJitter = false` must be set explicitly — jitter randomises delays and makes `delays[n]` assertions non-deterministic. In production, always enable jitter to avoid thundering-herd scenarios; only disable it in unit tests where exact delay values need to be verified.

**Pattern 285** — `WebApplicationFactory` `HttpClient` + `IDistributedCache` stub for session-dependent endpoint testing
```csharp
// Swap out IDistributedCache with an in-memory implementation to test
// session-dependent endpoints without a real Redis dependency.
public class CachedProfileFactory : WebApplicationFactory<Program>
{
    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
        {
            services.RemoveAll<IDistributedCache>();
            services.AddDistributedMemoryCache();  // in-process, no Redis
        });
    }
}

public class UserProfileCacheTests : IClassFixture<CachedProfileFactory>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public UserProfileCacheTests(CachedProfileFactory factory)
        => _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProfile_Twice_HitsCache_OnSecondCall()
    {
        // First call populates cache; second call reads from in-memory cache
        var r1 = await _client.GetAsync("/api/profile/42");
        var r2 = await _client.GetAsync("/api/profile/42");

        r1.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.OK);
        r2.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.OK);
        // Assert identical ETag / body to confirm cache hit
        r1.Headers.ETag.Should().Be(r2.Headers.ETag);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `AddDistributedMemoryCache` faithfully exercises the cache read/write code paths in the controller without a network dependency. The limitation is that in-memory cache does not enforce TTL expiry as accurately as Redis — tests for cache expiration logic must advance a `FakeTimeProvider` or manually call `cache.Remove(key)` to simulate expiry rather than relying on wall-clock timeout.
