### Community Gotchas

**G26** — `FluentAssertions` `BeEquivalentTo` on `IEnumerable<T>` ignores collection ordering by default — tests pass even when element order is wrong
Why this matters: A developer uses `result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected)` to assert that a sorted query returns items in a specific order. `BeEquivalentTo` performs set-like comparison by default: it checks that every element in `expected` exists in `result` with matching properties regardless of position. The sorted order is never validated, so a bug in the `ORDER BY` clause or `LINQ .OrderBy()` produces a green test.
Fix: Append `.WithStrictOrdering()` to the options lambda: `result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, o => o.WithStrictOrdering())`. When order is only relevant for a subset of properties, use `.WithStrictOrderingFor(x => x.Price)`. Document the intent with a comment so future maintainers understand why strict ordering was chosen.

**G27** — `Moq` `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` in `Setup` masks real cancellation propagation bugs
Why this matters: A developer writes `mock.Setup(r => r.FetchAsync(It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))` to avoid setup failures when a `CancellationToken` is passed. The setup works but the real SUT code may never forward the token to the dependency — it may pass `CancellationToken.None` instead. Because `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` matches any token including `None`, the test never catches the missing forwarding, and the application silently ignores cancellation in production.
Fix: Capture the token with `Arg.Do<CancellationToken>` or `Capture.In<CancellationToken>` and assert it is not `CancellationToken.None` when the test is specifically validating cancellation propagation. For most tests, accept `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` as a pragmatic convenience but add a dedicated cancellation test that passes a pre-cancelled token and asserts the SUT throws `OperationCanceledException`.

**G28** — xUnit `[Collection]` attribute on a test class disables `IClassFixture<T>` — both cannot be used simultaneously for the same fixture instance
Why this matters: A developer marks a test class with both `[Collection("IntegrationTests")]` and `IClassFixture<DatabaseFixture>`. The intent is to share the database fixture across the class and also serialise tests globally. xUnit ignores `IClassFixture<T>` on a class that belongs to a `[Collection]` — the fixture registered with `[CollectionDefinition]` is used instead. If `DatabaseFixture` is not listed in the `CollectionDefinition`, a new instance is created per test invocation (or none at all), and the test may fail with `NullReferenceException` on the fixture reference.
Fix: Register all shared fixtures in the `[CollectionDefinition]` class using `ICollectionFixture<T>` rather than `IClassFixture<T>` on individual test classes. Inject the fixture as a constructor parameter — xUnit resolves it from the collection. Remove any stray `IClassFixture<T>` implementations from classes that already belong to a collection.

**G29** — `ConfigureAwait(false)` in test code causes `SynchronizationContext`-dependent assertions (e.g., `Dispatcher.Invoke`) to run on the wrong context
Why this matters: A developer copies `ConfigureAwait(false)` from production code into integration tests. In xUnit, the test runner supplies a custom `SynchronizationContext` (`AsyncTestSyncContext`) that marshals continuation exceptions back to the test thread. When `ConfigureAwait(false)` is used, the continuation resumes on a thread-pool thread outside `AsyncTestSyncContext`. Exceptions thrown after `ConfigureAwait(false)` are captured on the pool thread and may not be observed by xUnit, causing the test to report as passed despite an unhandled exception in the continuation.
Fix: Never use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in test method bodies or test helper methods. Reserve it for production library code where avoiding deadlocks on `SynchronizationContext` matters. In test projects, `ConfigureAwait(false)` provides no benefit (no UI thread deadlock risk) and introduces subtle failure-masking. Add a Roslyn analyzer rule or `.editorconfig` warning to flag `ConfigureAwait(false)` in `*.Tests` projects.

**G30** — `Testcontainers.NET` `WithReuse(true)` + EF Core migrations leave the database in a stale schema state across test sessions
Why this matters: `WithReuse(true)` keeps the container alive between `dotnet test` invocations to save startup time. If an EF Core migration adds a column between runs but the reused container still holds the old schema, the next test run applies migrations on top of a partially-migrated state. EF Core's `MigrationsHistory` table may already contain the migration row (from a previous run where the migration was applied to an in-memory or fresh container), causing EF to skip the column-add migration. Tests that depend on the new column then fail with `PostgresException: column does not exist`.
Fix: Call `await context.Database.MigrateAsync()` unconditionally at the start of each test session — EF Core's idempotent migration runner is safe to call repeatedly and applies only unapplied migrations. Alternatively, skip `WithReuse` in CI where a fresh container per-run is cheap, and reserve `WithReuse` for local development only using a `[assembly: CollectionBehavior(MaxParallelThreads = 1)]` guard to prevent concurrent migration races.

## Cycle 59 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 286** — xUnit v3 `ITestOutputHelper` + `ActivityListener` for distributed-trace assertion in unit tests
```csharp
// Register an ActivityListener in the fixture to capture OpenTelemetry spans
// produced by the SUT, then assert on them in individual tests.
public class ActivityCapture : IDisposable
{
    private readonly List<Activity> _activities = new();
    private readonly ActivityListener _listener;

    public IReadOnlyList<Activity> Activities => _activities;

    public ActivityCapture(string sourceName)
    {
        _listener = new ActivityListener
        {
            ShouldListenTo = src => src.Name == sourceName,
            Sample = (ref ActivityCreationOptions<ActivityContext> _) =>
                ActivitySamplingResult.AllDataAndRecorded,
            ActivityStopped = a => _activities.Add(a)
        };
        ActivitySource.AddActivityListener(_listener);
    }

    public void Dispose() => _listener.Dispose();
}

public class OrderServiceTracingTests
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_EmitsSpan_WithOrderId()
    {
        using var capture = new ActivityCapture("OrderService");
        var sut = new OrderService();

        await sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new Order { Id = Guid.NewGuid() });

        capture.Activities.Should().ContainSingle(a =>
            a.OperationName == "order.place" &&
            a.GetTagItem("order.id") != null);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ActivityListener` is synchronous and lives in-process, so no collector/exporter dependency is required. The limitation is that `ActivityStopped` fires on the thread that calls `Activity.Stop()` — if the SUT disposes the activity on a background thread, the assertion must account for async ordering (use `await Task.Yield()` or a brief `SpinWait` before asserting). Do not use this approach for cross-process trace correlation; use a real OTLP exporter to an in-process collector (e.g. `InMemoryExporter`) for those scenarios.

**Pattern 287** — NUnit 4 `ClassicAssert.AreEqual` → `Assert.That` migration shim using `.editorconfig` diagnostic suppression
```csharp
// When migrating a large NUnit 3 suite to NUnit 4, suppress the ClassicAssert
// obsoletion warning per file rather than doing a big-bang rewrite.
// In .editorconfig:
// [*.Tests/**/*.cs]
// dotnet_diagnostic.NUnit2005.severity = none   # AreEqual → Assert.That migration

// Migrate incrementally: new tests use Assert.That; touched legacy tests get
// upgraded as a pre-commit habit. Example of the target form:
[Test]
public void Invoice_Total_IsCalculatedCorrectly()
{
    var invoice = new Invoice(lines: new[] { 10m, 20m, 30m });

    // Modern NUnit 4 constraint model — preferred
    Assert.That(invoice.Total, Is.EqualTo(60m),
        "Total must be the sum of all line amounts");

    // Equivalent FluentAssertions form if FA is also in the project
    invoice.Total.Should().Be(60m);
}

// If multiple asserts are logically independent, wrap in Assert.Multiple
// to collect all failures in one run:
[Test]
public void Invoice_Fields_AreAllSet()
{
    var invoice = Invoice.CreateDraft(customerId: 7);

    Assert.Multiple(() =>
    {
        Assert.That(invoice.CustomerId, Is.EqualTo(7));
        Assert.That(invoice.Status, Is.EqualTo(InvoiceStatus.Draft));
        Assert.That(invoice.CreatedAt, Is.Not.EqualTo(default(DateTime)));
    });
}
```
Tradeoff: Suppressing the diagnostic per-directory allows a gradual migration without blocking CI during the transition. The risk is that suppressed warnings get forgotten — schedule removal of the suppression rule in the backlog once the migration is complete, and add a CI check (`grep -r "ClassicAssert" tests/` → fail if count > 0) to enforce the end state.

**Pattern 288** — MSTest v3 `[DataSource]` replacement: `[DynamicData]` reading from embedded JSON resource
```csharp
// Embed a JSON array as a test resource and supply it via DynamicData
// to drive parameterised tests without a database or external file.
public class PricingCalculatorTests
{
    public static IEnumerable<object[]> PricingCases =>
        JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<PricingCase>>(
            ReadEmbeddedResource("PricingCases.json"))!
        .Select(c => new object[] { c.Input, c.Vat, c.Expected });

    [DataTestMethod]
    [DynamicData(nameof(PricingCases),
        DynamicDataSourceType.Property,
        DynamicDataDisplayName = nameof(GetDisplayName))]
    public void Calculate_ReturnsExpectedTotal(
        decimal net, decimal vatRate, decimal expected)
    {
        var result = PricingCalculator.Calculate(net, vatRate);
        Assert.AreEqual(expected, result, $"Net={net} VAT={vatRate}");
    }

    public static string GetDisplayName(MethodInfo _, object[] args)
        => $"Net={args[0]}, VAT={args[1]} => {args[2]}";

    private static string ReadEmbeddedResource(string name)
    {
        var asm = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();
        using var stream = asm.GetManifestResourceStream(
            $"{asm.GetName().Name}.{name}")!;
        using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
        return reader.ReadToEnd();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Embedding the JSON as an assembly resource eliminates file-path resolution issues in CI artefact directories. The `DynamicDataDisplayName` delegate keeps Test Explorer output human-readable. Downside: the resource is compiled into the assembly, so changes require a rebuild — for large or frequently-edited datasets, prefer an external file via `[DataSource]` (MSTest v3 still supports it) or a shared `TestDataDirectory` constant pointing to a versioned folder.

**Pattern 289** — FluentAssertions `Using<T>` custom equality comparer inside `BeEquivalentTo` for value-type wrappers
```csharp
// When a domain type wraps a primitive but does not override Equals,
// supply a custom IEqualityComparer<T> inline via Using<T>.
public record MoneyAmount(decimal Value, string Currency);

public class MoneyAmountComparer : IEqualityComparer<MoneyAmount>
{
    public bool Equals(MoneyAmount? x, MoneyAmount? y)
        => x?.Currency == y?.Currency
           && Math.Abs((x?.Value ?? 0) - (y?.Value ?? 0)) < 0.005m;

    public int GetHashCode(MoneyAmount obj)
        => HashCode.Combine(obj.Currency, Math.Round(obj.Value, 2));
}

[Fact]
public void Order_LineAmounts_MatchInvoice_WithRounding()
{
    var order = new Order(lines: new[] { 10.004m, 20.006m });
    var invoice = Invoice.From(order);

    invoice.Lines.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
        new[]
        {
            new MoneyAmount(10.00m, "EUR"),
            new MoneyAmount(20.01m, "EUR")
        },
        opts => opts.Using(new MoneyAmountComparer())
                    .WhenTypeIs<MoneyAmount>());
}
```
Tradeoff: `Using<T>(...).WhenTypeIs<T>()` scopes the custom comparer only to `MoneyAmount` instances in the object graph, leaving other property comparisons at default FA equivalency semantics. This avoids blunt global comparer overrides. The tradeoff is readability — the options lambda grows long when multiple custom comparers are chained. Extract them into a `static EquivalencyOptions Monetary => ...` helper method for reuse.

**Pattern 290** — Moq `InSequence` global ordering across multiple mocks for strict workflow testing
```csharp
// Enforce that two separate mocks are called in a specific order
// using MockSequence — useful for validating multi-step workflows.
[Fact]
public async Task Checkout_CallsPayment_ThenFulfillment_InOrder()
{
    var seq = new MockSequence();
    var paymentMock = new Mock<IPaymentGateway>(MockBehavior.Strict);
    var fulfillMock = new Mock<IFulfillmentService>(MockBehavior.Strict);

    paymentMock.InSequence(seq)
        .Setup(p => p.ChargeAsync(It.IsAny<decimal>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(PaymentResult.Success);

    fulfillMock.InSequence(seq)
        .Setup(f => f.DispatchAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
        .ReturnsAsync(DispatchResult.Queued);

    var sut = new CheckoutService(paymentMock.Object, fulfillMock.Object);
    await sut.ExecuteAsync(new Order { Total = 99.95m });

    paymentMock.Verify(p =>
        p.ChargeAsync(99.95m, It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()), Times.Once);
    fulfillMock.Verify(f =>
        f.DispatchAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()), Times.Once);
}
```
Tradeoff: `MockSequence` enforces call ordering at invocation time and throws immediately on an out-of-order call, giving precise failure messages. The cost is that `MockBehavior.Strict` must be set on participating mocks, making the setup verbose. When the exact ordering between two independent services is an implementation detail rather than a contract, prefer `Verify(Times.Once)` without a sequence constraint to avoid over-specifying behaviour.

**Pattern 291** — `Verify` library snapshot testing with `VerifySettings` scrubbing for volatile fields
```csharp
// Use Verify to snapshot-test API responses, scrubbing timestamps and IDs
// that change between runs to avoid false failures.
[UsesVerify]
public class ProductApiSnapshotTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public ProductApiSnapshotTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
        => _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProducts_MatchesApprovedSnapshot()
    {
        var settings = new VerifySettings();
        settings.ScrubMember("createdAt");
        settings.ScrubMember("id");
        // Use deterministic GUIDs for repeated runs
        settings.AddExtraSettings(s =>
            s.Converters.Add(new GuidScrubber()));

        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/api/products");
        var json = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        await Verify(json, settings);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Snapshot tests catch unintended serialisation changes (added/removed fields, renamed properties, format regressions) with zero assertion code. The operational cost is managing `.verified.txt` files in source control — every intentional API change requires running `dotnet test` with `VERIFY_ACCEPT=true` to re-approve the snapshot. For high-churn early development, defer snapshot tests until the API shape stabilises.

**Pattern 292** — `WebApplicationFactory` + `IHostEnvironment` override for environment-conditional middleware testing
```csharp
// Test middleware that behaves differently in Staging vs Production
// by overriding IHostEnvironment inside the factory.
public class StagingFactory : WebApplicationFactory<Program>
{
    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.UseEnvironment("Staging");
        builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
        {
            // Remove production-only middleware side-effects
            services.RemoveAll<ICorrelationIdMiddleware>();
        });
    }
}

public class HealthCheckStagingTests : IClassFixture<StagingFactory>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public HealthCheckStagingTests(StagingFactory factory)
        => _client = factory.CreateClient();

    [Fact]
    public async Task HealthCheck_InStaging_ReturnsDetailedReport()
    {
        var response = await _client.GetAsync("/healthz");
        var body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.OK);
        // Staging health endpoint returns full component breakdown
        body.Should().Contain("\"status\":\"Healthy\"")
            .And.Contain("\"db\"");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `builder.UseEnvironment(...)` overrides the `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` variable for the in-process test host without polluting the CI environment. The caveat is that `Program.cs` startup code that branches on `IHostEnvironment.IsProduction()` / `.IsStaging()` runs its real branch, so the test exercises the real startup path for that environment — both an advantage (authentic) and a risk (Staging startup may attempt to reach real external endpoints if not stubbed out with `ConfigureTestServices`).

**Pattern 293** — `FakeTimeProvider` + `ITimer` for `PeriodicTimer`-based background-service unit tests
```csharp
// .NET 8+ PeriodicTimer does not accept an IClock abstraction directly,
// but TimeProvider.CreateTimer can stand in for interval-triggered logic.
public class MetricsFlushService : BackgroundService
{
    private readonly IMetricsSink _sink;
    private readonly TimeProvider _time;

    public MetricsFlushService(IMetricsSink sink, TimeProvider time)
        => (_sink, _time) = (sink, time);

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var timer = _time.CreateTimer(
            _ => _sink.FlushAsync(),
            null, TimeSpan.Zero, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));

        await Task.Delay(Timeout.Infinite, ct).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
}

[Fact]
public async Task MetricsFlush_FiresOnInterval_VisFakeTimeProvider()
{
    var fake = new FakeTimeProvider();
    var sink = Substitute.For<IMetricsSink>();
    sink.FlushAsync().Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

    var svc = new MetricsFlushService(sink, fake);
    using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
    _ = svc.StartAsync(cts.Token);

    // Advance time twice to trigger two timer firings
    fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
    await Task.Yield();
    fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
    await Task.Yield();

    await cts.CancelAsync();
    await sink.Received(2).FlushAsync();
}
```
Tradeoff: `FakeTimeProvider.Advance` fires `ITimer` callbacks synchronously in the calling thread, making interval logic fully deterministic and CI-safe. The gotcha is that the callback fires on the test thread — if `FlushAsync` itself does async work that captures `SynchronizationContext`, use `await Task.Yield()` after each advance to flush the continuation queue before asserting call counts.

**Pattern 294** — `AutoFixture` `Customize<T>` with `Without` + `With` chain for domain-invariant-respecting fixture generation
```csharp
// Teach AutoFixture to generate valid domain objects that satisfy
// business invariants (non-negative price, non-empty name) without
// wrapping every test in manual object construction.
public class ValidProductCustomization : ICustomization
{
    public void Customize(IFixture fixture)
    {
        fixture.Customize<Product>(c => c
            .Without(p => p.Id)              // auto-assigned by domain
            .With(p => p.Name,
                fixture.Create<string>()[..10])  // max 10 chars
            .With(p => p.Price,
                Math.Abs(fixture.Create<decimal>()) + 0.01m) // always positive
            .With(p => p.Stock,
                Math.Abs(fixture.Create<int>()))             // non-negative
        );
    }
}

public class ProductServiceTests
{
    private readonly IFixture _fixture =
        new Fixture().Customize(new ValidProductCustomization());

    [Fact]
    public void AddProduct_WithValidProduct_SucceedsWithoutThrow()
    {
        var product = _fixture.Create<Product>();
        var svc = new ProductService();

        var act = () => svc.Add(product);

        act.Should().NotThrow();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Domain-aware customizations prevent tests from randomly failing on invariant violations (negative stock, empty name) without needing per-test manual setup. The maintenance cost is keeping `ICustomization` classes in sync as domain invariants evolve — a customization that no longer reflects current rules silently generates invalid objects. Add a self-test: a unit test that asserts `_fixture.Create<Product>()` passes domain validation logic, acting as a canary for stale customizations.

**Pattern 295** — `Respawn` + `IAsyncLifetime` for fast per-test SQL Server database reset
```csharp
// Use Respawn to delete only test-inserted rows (respecting FK order)
// rather than rebuilding the schema between tests — orders of magnitude faster.
public class SqlResetFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public SqlConnection Connection { get; private set; } = null!;
    private Respawner _respawner = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        Connection = new SqlConnection(
            "Server=localhost;Database=TestDb;Trusted_Connection=true;");
        await Connection.OpenAsync();

        _respawner = await Respawner.CreateAsync(Connection,
            new RespawnerOptions
            {
                TablesToIgnore = new Table[] { "MigrationHistory" },
                DbAdapter = DbAdapter.SqlServer,
                SchemasToInclude = new[] { "dbo" }
            });
    }

    public async Task ResetAsync() => await _respawner.ResetAsync(Connection);

    public Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        Connection.Dispose();
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

public class OrderRepositoryTests : IClassFixture<SqlResetFixture>, IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly SqlResetFixture _db;

    public OrderRepositoryTests(SqlResetFixture db) => _db = db;

    public Task InitializeAsync() => _db.ResetAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync() => Task.CompletedTask;

    [Fact]
    public async Task Insert_ThenQuery_ReturnsSameOrder()
    {
        var repo = new OrderRepository(_db.Connection);
        var id = await repo.InsertAsync(new Order { Total = 55m });
        var loaded = await repo.GetAsync(id);
        loaded!.Total.Should().Be(55m);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Respawn issues a single `DELETE` statement per table in FK-safe order and completes in milliseconds even for schemas with 50+ tables — far faster than `DROP/CREATE` or `TRUNCATE`. The limitation is that it does not reset identity seeds by default; if test assertions depend on specific auto-increment IDs (e.g. `id == 1`), configure `WithReseed = true` in `RespawnerOptions` or avoid asserting on generated IDs.

**Pattern 296** — NSubstitute `Configure` + `Returns` chaining for fluent stub setup in test builders
```csharp
// Use NSubstitute's Configure extension method to set up multiple
// returns in a readable builder-style chain without separate lines per member.
public static class MockRepositoryBuilder
{
    public static IProductRepository WithProducts(
        this IProductRepository repo, params Product[] products)
    {
        repo.GetAllAsync(Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
            .Returns(products.ToList());
        return repo;
    }

    public static IProductRepository WithNotFound(
        this IProductRepository repo, Guid id)
    {
        repo.GetByIdAsync(id, Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
            .Returns((Product?)null);
        return repo;
    }
}

[Fact]
public async Task GetProducts_ReturnsMappedDtos()
{
    var repo = Substitute.For<IProductRepository>()
        .WithProducts(
            new Product { Id = Guid.NewGuid(), Name = "Widget", Price = 9.99m },
            new Product { Id = Guid.NewGuid(), Name = "Gadget", Price = 19.99m });

    var sut = new ProductQueryService(repo);
    var dtos = await sut.GetAllAsync();

    dtos.Should().HaveCount(2)
        .And.AllSatisfy(d => d.Price.Should().BePositive());
}
```
Tradeoff: Extension method builders eliminate repetitive `Substitute.For<T>()` + multiple `.Returns()` boilerplate and make test intent explicit at the call site. The risk is over-abstraction — if the builder hides setups that are material to understanding a specific test, inline the setup for that test and keep the builder for the common case. Treat test builders as production code: version them, test them with their own canary tests.

**Pattern 297** — `HttpClient` `DelegatingHandler` test double for unit-testing `HttpClient`-consuming services
```csharp
// Inject a DelegatingHandler test double directly into HttpClient
// to unit-test service logic without spinning up a real server.
public class FakeHttpHandler : DelegatingHandler
{
    private readonly Func<HttpRequestMessage, HttpResponseMessage> _responder;

    public FakeHttpHandler(
        Func<HttpRequestMessage, HttpResponseMessage> responder)
        => _responder = responder;

    protected override Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(
        HttpRequestMessage request,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
        => Task.FromResult(_responder(request));
}

[Fact]
public async Task FetchProduct_DeserializesResponse_Correctly()
{
    var expected = new ProductDto { Id = 1, Name = "Widget" };
    var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(expected);

    var handler = new FakeHttpHandler(_ =>
        new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)
        {
            Content = new StringContent(json,
                Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")
        });

    var client = new HttpClient(handler)
        { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com") };

    var sut = new ProductApiClient(client);
    var result = await sut.GetProductAsync(1);

    result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected);
}
```
Tradeoff: A `DelegatingHandler` test double is the simplest possible HTTP seam — no third-party library required, fully controlled per test. The limitation is that it bypasses all real `HttpClient` pipeline handlers (retry, auth, logging) added via `AddHttpClient(...)` in production. For testing the full pipeline stack, prefer `WebApplicationFactory` + a real `HttpClient`, or `MockHttpMessageHandler` (from `RichardSzalay.MockHttp`) which also validates request content and method.

**Pattern 298** — `ILogger<T>` assertion using `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing` `FakeLogger`
```csharp
// Capture structured log output in unit tests using FakeLogger<T>
// from the Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing package.
[Fact]
public async Task ProcessOrder_LogsWarning_WhenStockLow()
{
    var fakeLogger = new FakeLogger<OrderProcessor>();
    var sut = new OrderProcessor(fakeLogger, stock: 1);

    await sut.ProcessAsync(new Order { Quantity = 1 });

    var warningEntry = fakeLogger.Collector.GetSnapshot()
        .FirstOrDefault(e => e.Level == LogLevel.Warning);

    warningEntry.Should().NotBeNull();
    warningEntry!.Message.Should().Contain("low stock");
    warningEntry.StructuredState
        .Should().ContainKey("remainingStock")
        .WhoseValue.Should().Be("0");
}
```
Tradeoff: `FakeLogger<T>` captures the exact structured key-value pairs emitted via `LogInformation(...)`, making it possible to assert on semantic log data (not just formatted strings). The key gotcha is that `FakeLogger` only captures logs for the exact `T` category — logs emitted by injected services inside the SUT use a different category and appear in a separate `FakeLogger` instance (or are silently dropped if that logger is not injected). For SUT-wide log capture, use `FakeLogCollector` registered in a `ServiceCollection`.

**Pattern 299** — `NetArchTest` namespace dependency rule enforcement as a CI gate
```csharp
// Enforce clean-architecture dependency rules as failing unit tests
// so that architecture violations are caught in CI before merge.
public class ArchitectureTests
{
    private const string DomainNs   = "MyApp.Domain";
    private const string AppNs      = "MyApp.Application";
    private const string InfraRaNs  = "MyApp.Infrastructure";
    private const string WebNs      = "MyApp.Web";

    [Fact]
    public void Domain_MustNotDependOn_Application()
    {
        var result = Types.InCurrentDomain()
            .That().ResideInNamespace(DomainNs)
            .ShouldNot().HaveDependencyOn(AppNs)
            .GetResult();

        result.IsSuccessful.Should().BeTrue(
            because: $"Domain layer must not reference {AppNs}; " +
                     $"failing types: {string.Join(", ", result.FailingTypeNames ?? [])}");
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Infrastructure_MustNotDependOn_Web()
    {
        var result = Types.InCurrentDomain()
            .That().ResideInNamespace(InfraRaNs)
            .ShouldNot().HaveDependencyOn(WebNs)
            .GetResult();

        result.IsSuccessful.Should().BeTrue(
            because: $"Infrastructure must not reference Web layer; " +
                     $"failing types: {string.Join(", ", result.FailingTypeNames ?? [])}");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `NetArchTest` operates on IL reflection via `Types.InCurrentDomain()` — it catches real compiled dependencies, not just `using` directives that might be left over after dead-code removal. The critical gotcha is that `InCurrentDomain()` loads all assemblies currently in the AppDomain, which in a unit-test host includes test assemblies and test frameworks themselves. Always scope with `.ResideInNamespace(...)` to avoid false positives from test infrastructure types appearing in the scan.

**Pattern 300** — `xUnit v3` `[MemberData]` with `TheoryDataRow<T>` `Label` and `Skip` metadata for self-documenting parameterised tests
```csharp
// xUnit v3 TheoryDataRow<T> supports Label (displayed in Test Explorer)
// and Skip (skips individual rows without skipping the whole theory).
public static TheoryData<TheoryDataRow<string, int, string>> ParseCases =>
    new()
    {
        new TheoryDataRow<string, int, string>("42",   42,  "simple integer")
            { Label = "simple integer" },
        new TheoryDataRow<string, int, string>("-1",  -1,  "negative value")
            { Label = "negative value" },
        new TheoryDataRow<string, int, string>("2147483648", 0, "overflow case")
            { Label = "int overflow → 0 fallback",
              Skip = "Overflow behaviour not yet specified — see issue #412" },
    };

[Theory]
[MemberData(nameof(ParseCases))]
public void TryParseInt_MatchesExpected(
    string input, int expected, string _description)
{
    var ok = IntParser.TryParse(input, out var result);

    ok.Should().Be(expected != 0 || input == "0");
    result.Should().Be(expected);
}
```
Tradeoff: `Label` makes Test Explorer output self-documenting without needing a `[DisplayName]` attribute or custom display name delegate. `Skip` on individual rows prevents a not-yet-implemented edge case from blocking the suite while keeping the intent visible in the test file. The risk is normalising `Skip` as a permanent state — enforce a policy (e.g., Roslyn analyser or CI grep) that flags `Skip =` entries older than 30 days without an associated issue reference.

### Community Gotchas

**G31** — `FluentAssertions` `Should().Throw<T>()` does not work with `async void` methods — the exception is never captured
Why this matters: A developer writes `action.Should().ThrowAsync<InvalidOperationException>()` for an `async void` event handler or fire-and-forget method. `async void` methods do not return a `Task`, so FluentAssertions cannot await them — the exception propagates onto the `SynchronizationContext` and is either swallowed or crashes the test runner with an unhandled exception, depending on the xUnit / NUnit context. The test may green when it should red.
Fix: Refactor `async void` methods to `async Task` wherever the method is under test. For event handlers that must remain `async void`, extract the implementation into an `async Task` method and test that instead. If refactoring is not immediately possible, wrap the invocation in a `TaskCompletionSource` and subscribe to `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException` in a test-scoped handler — but treat this as a temporary workaround, not a pattern.

**G32** — `Moq` `SetupSequence` does not throw on unexpected extra calls beyond the configured sequence — it falls through to the last configured return
Why this matters: A developer configures `mock.SetupSequence(x => x.Get()).Returns(1).Returns(2)` expecting that a third call throws `MockException`. Instead, Moq silently returns the last configured value (`2`) for all subsequent calls. If the SUT calls `Get()` three times due to a retry bug, the test still passes because the mock returns `2` rather than throwing, masking the extra call.
Fix: After `SetupSequence(...)`, append `.Throws<InvalidOperationException>()` as the final entry in the chain to assert that no calls occur beyond the expected sequence: `mock.SetupSequence(x => x.Get()).Returns(1).Returns(2).Throws<InvalidOperationException>()`. Then `Verify(x => x.Get(), Times.Exactly(2))` to make the intent explicit.

**G33** — `WebApplicationFactory` `CreateClient()` follows redirects by default — `3xx` responses are never asserted
Why this matters: A developer tests that a controller action returns `302 Found` to redirect authenticated users. `factory.CreateClient()` returns an `HttpClient` with `AllowAutoRedirect = true` (the default). The client silently follows the redirect and returns the final destination's `200 OK` response. The test asserts `response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.Found)` and fails — or worse, the developer sees `200 OK` and incorrectly concludes the redirect is not happening.
Fix: Create the client with `factory.CreateClient(new WebApplicationFactoryClientOptions { AllowAutoRedirect = false })` when testing redirect responses. This is almost always the correct setting for integration tests that assert on HTTP semantics — let the test assert the exact status code the SUT emits rather than the final resolved destination.

**G34** — `FakeTimeProvider` `SetUtcNow` does not fire previously registered `ITimer` callbacks retroactively — only `Advance` triggers them
Why this matters: A developer calls `fakeTimeProvider.SetUtcNow(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddMinutes(5))` expecting that any `ITimer` created before the time jump fires its callback. `SetUtcNow` sets the clock but does not invoke timer callbacks — it is equivalent to editing the clock face without winding the mechanism. Callbacks only fire when `Advance(TimeSpan)` is called, which steps the clock forward and fires all timers whose next scheduled firing falls within the advanced interval.
Fix: Always use `fakeTimeProvider.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5))` (not `SetUtcNow`) when the test needs timer callbacks to fire. Use `SetUtcNow` only to establish the initial clock value at test start (before any timers are registered) or to set a known wall-clock reference for `DateTime.UtcNow` readings that do not involve timers.

**G35** — NUnit `[OneTimeSetUp]` failures silently mark all tests in the fixture as `Ignored` rather than `Failed` — CI pass rate is misleadingly green
Why this matters: A `[OneTimeSetUp]` method throws an exception (e.g., a database migration fails). NUnit marks every test in the fixture as `Ignored` with a message referencing the setup failure. Most CI pipelines count `Ignored` separately from `Failed` and do not fail the build on ignored tests. The pipeline reports green; the team does not notice that an entire fixture was skipped.
Fix: Configure the CI pipeline's NUnit results parser to treat `Ignored` tests that have a `SetUpError` reason as failures. In Azure DevOps, set `failTaskOnRunningFail: true` and add a `publishTestResults` threshold for maximum allowed ignored tests. In GitHub Actions, use `dorny/test-reporter` with `fail-on-error: true`. Additionally, write a `[OneTimeSetUp]` self-check: wrap the setup body in a `try/catch`, log the exception, and call `Assert.Fail(ex.Message)` explicitly — NUnit then records a genuine test failure rather than an ignored fixture.

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 301** — FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` with `WithStrictOrdering` for position-sensitive collection assertions
```csharp
// Asserting that a sorted result matches the expected order exactly.
// Without WithStrictOrdering, BeEquivalentTo treats order as irrelevant.
var actual = service.GetRankedItems();

actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
    new[]
    {
        new RankedItem(id: 1, score: 0.98),
        new RankedItem(id: 5, score: 0.87),
        new RankedItem(id: 3, score: 0.74),
    },
    options => options
        .WithStrictOrdering()
        .ComparingByMembers<RankedItem>());
```
Tradeoff: `WithStrictOrdering` catches ranking regressions that the default unordered comparison misses entirely, but it makes the test fragile when two items have equal scores and the tiebreak order is implementation-defined — add a secondary sort key to the SUT's contract or scope `WithStrictOrdering` to only the first N elements via `o.Including(x => x[0..2])` to avoid false failures on equal-score ties.

**Pattern 302** — NSubstitute `Arg.Is<T>` predicate for partial-match argument capture in async method stubs
```csharp
// Stub only calls where the request meets a domain constraint;
// let all other overloads fall through to NSubstitute's default (null/Task.CompletedTask).
var emailClient = Substitute.For<IEmailClient>();

emailClient
    .SendAsync(
        Arg.Is<EmailMessage>(m =>
            m.To.EndsWith("@internal.example.com", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
            && m.Priority == Priority.High),
        Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
    .Returns(Task.FromResult(SendResult.Queued));

var result = await sut.NotifyAsync(internalHighPriorityMessage, CancellationToken.None);

result.Should().Be(NotifyOutcome.Queued);
await emailClient.Received(1).SendAsync(
    Arg.Is<EmailMessage>(m => m.Priority == Priority.High),
    Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
```
Tradeoff: `Arg.Is<T>` predicate stubs are precise but the predicate lambda is not type-checked at compile time — a typo in a property name compiles fine and silently falls through to the default return value, making the test pass when it should fail. Prefer named helper methods (`IsInternalHighPriority()`) returning `Arg.Is<T>` to keep predicates readable and testable in isolation.

**Pattern 303** — xUnit `IAsyncLifetime` `InitializeAsync` / `DisposeAsync` for per-test async resource setup without `Task.Run` hacks
```csharp
public class OrderRepositoryTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private SqliteConnection _connection = null!;
    private OrderRepository _repo = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _connection = new SqliteConnection("Data Source=:memory:");
        await _connection.OpenAsync();
        await DbMigrations.ApplyAsync(_connection);
        _repo = new OrderRepository(_connection);
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _connection.DisposeAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_PersistsLineItems()
    {
        var order = OrderFaker.Generate();
        await _repo.SaveAsync(order);
        var loaded = await _repo.GetByIdAsync(order.Id);
        loaded.LineItems.Should().BeEquivalentTo(order.LineItems);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `IAsyncLifetime` gives each test a clean in-memory database without the constructor/finalizer async anti-pattern (`Task.Run(...).Wait()`), but because xUnit constructs and disposes one class instance per test method, a 200-test fixture opens and migrates 200 in-memory connections. Use `IClassFixture<T>` for the connection and `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` for per-test data seeding only to keep suite-level setup cost bounded.

**Pattern 304** — Moq `Capture<T>` via `Callback` to assert on complex argument values after the call
```csharp
// Capture the exact command sent to the downstream service for post-call assertion.
AuditCommand? captured = null;

auditServiceMock
    .Setup(s => s.RecordAsync(It.IsAny<AuditCommand>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
    .Callback<AuditCommand, CancellationToken>((cmd, _) => captured = cmd)
    .ReturnsAsync(true);

await sut.ProcessPaymentAsync(payment, CancellationToken.None);

captured.Should().NotBeNull();
captured!.EntityId.Should().Be(payment.Id);
captured.Actor.Should().Be("system");
captured.EventType.Should().Be(AuditEventType.PaymentProcessed);
```
Tradeoff: `Callback` capture is the only Moq-native way to inspect complex argument values without resorting to a custom `It.Is<T>` predicate, and it enables full FluentAssertions chains on the captured value. The risk is that `captured` is null if the method was never called — always assert `captured.Should().NotBeNull()` first so failures produce a clear "method was not called" message rather than a `NullReferenceException` inside a subsequent assertion.

**Pattern 305** — FluentAssertions `Monitor()` + `Should().Raise()` for strongly typed event assertion in domain models
```csharp
// Assert that a domain aggregate raises the correct integration event.
var order = new Order(Guid.NewGuid());

using var monitor = order.Monitor();

order.Ship(trackingNumber: "TRACK-001");

monitor.Should()
    .Raise(nameof(Order.OrderShipped))
    .WithArgs<OrderShippedEventArgs>(args =>
        args.TrackingNumber == "TRACK-001"
        && args.ShippedAt <= DateTimeOffset.UtcNow);
```
Tradeoff: `Monitor()` uses reflection to subscribe to all events on the target object at the point the `using` block opens — events raised before `Monitor()` is called are invisible. Place the `using` declaration as close as possible to the act step, and be aware that `Monitor()` on a sealed or non-public event-accessor class may throw `InvalidOperationException` at runtime rather than compile time.

**Pattern 306** — NUnit `Assert.MultipleAsync` for collecting all async assertion failures in a single test run
```csharp
[Test]
public async Task CreateUser_SetsAllRequiredFields()
{
    var command = new CreateUserCommand("alice", "alice@example.com");
    var user = await _handler.HandleAsync(command);

    await Assert.MultipleAsync(async () =>
    {
        Assert.That(user.UserName, Is.EqualTo("alice"));
        Assert.That(user.Email, Is.EqualTo("alice@example.com"));
        Assert.That(user.CreatedAt, Is.GreaterThan(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddSeconds(-5)));
        var dbUser = await _repo.FindByIdAsync(user.Id);
        Assert.That(dbUser, Is.Not.Null);
        Assert.That(dbUser!.IsActive, Is.True);
    });
}
```
Tradeoff: `Assert.MultipleAsync` collects all failures and reports them together, eliminating the "fix one failure, re-run, find the next" loop for multi-field creation tests. The tradeoff is that later assertions inside the block can throw `NullReferenceException` (e.g., `dbUser!.IsActive`) when an earlier assertion would have short-circuited the block — guard nullable values explicitly or split structurally dependent assertions into a separate `Assert.Multiple` block that only runs after null checks pass.

**Pattern 307** — `Bogus` `Faker<T>` with `RuleForType` seed-based deterministic generation for reproducible property-based tests
```csharp
// Using Bogus with a fixed seed produces identical data on every run —
// making CI failures 100% reproducible from the seed printed in the test output.
const int Seed = 42;

var faker = new Faker<Customer>()
    .UseSeed(Seed)
    .RuleFor(c => c.Id,       f => f.Random.Guid())
    .RuleFor(c => c.FullName, f => f.Name.FullName())
    .RuleFor(c => c.Email,    f => f.Internet.Email())
    .RuleFor(c => c.Age,      f => f.Random.Int(18, 99));

var customers = faker.Generate(20);

customers.Should().AllSatisfy(c =>
{
    c.Age.Should().BeInRange(18, 99);
    c.Email.Should().Contain("@");
});

TestContext.WriteLine($"Seed: {Seed}"); // always log the seed
```
Tradeoff: A fixed seed makes test output deterministic, but using the same seed across all test classes means every faker instance in the suite generates the same sequence of names and emails, masking bugs that only appear with specific values. Prefer a per-test-run seed derived from `Environment.TickCount` stored in a static field, logged at suite startup, so any failure is reproducible by passing the seed as an environment variable.

**Pattern 308** — `TestServer` + `HttpMessageHandler` for in-process integration tests without opening a TCP port
```csharp
// TestServer eliminates port binding entirely — faster and avoids port exhaustion in CI.
await using var application = new WebApplicationFactory<Program>()
    .WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
        builder.UseEnvironment("IntegrationTest"));

var client = application.CreateClient(); // uses in-process TestServer handler

var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/health");

response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.OK);
var body = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<HealthResponse>();
body!.Status.Should().Be("Healthy");
```
Tradeoff: In-process `TestServer` tests are 10–50x faster than real TCP-bound servers and survive in CI environments where random port binding is restricted by firewall rules. However, `TestServer` shares the same process memory as the test — a test that exhausts memory or corrupts static state will affect sibling tests in the same `WebApplicationFactory` instance. Use `IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>` to share one factory instance across the fixture class, and isolate test data with per-test database scopes rather than per-test factory instances.

**Pattern 309** — NSubstitute `Returns(x, y, z)` multi-value sequence for paginated API stub responses
```csharp
// Simulate a paginated API that returns data across multiple calls.
var apiClient = Substitute.For<IProductApiClient>();

apiClient
    .GetPageAsync(Arg.Any<int>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
    .Returns(
        Task.FromResult(new Page<Product>(items: PageOneItems,   hasMore: true,  nextCursor: "cur1")),
        Task.FromResult(new Page<Product>(items: PageTwoItems,   hasMore: true,  nextCursor: "cur2")),
        Task.FromResult(new Page<Product>(items: PageThreeItems, hasMore: false, nextCursor: null)));

var allProducts = await sut.FetchAllProductsAsync(CancellationToken.None);

allProducts.Should().HaveCount(
    PageOneItems.Length + PageTwoItems.Length + PageThreeItems.Length);
await apiClient.Received(3).GetPageAsync(Arg.Any<int>(), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
```
Tradeoff: NSubstitute's multi-value `Returns(x, y, z)` repeats the final value for all calls beyond the configured count — the same caveat as Moq's `SetupSequence`. If the SUT's pagination loop has a boundary bug and calls `GetPageAsync` a fourth time, the stub returns the last page again (with `hasMore: false`), which may prevent an infinite loop but also masks the extra call. Always pair with `Received(3)` to assert the call count is exactly correct.

**Pattern 310** — FluentAssertions `AndConstraint` custom extension for domain-specific readable assertion chains
```csharp
// Extend FluentAssertions to add domain vocabulary to test assertions.
public static class OrderAssertionExtensions
{
    public static AndConstraint<ObjectAssertions> BeFulfillable(
        this ObjectAssertions assertions)
    {
        var order = assertions.Subject as Order
            ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Subject must be an Order");

        order.LineItems.Should().NotBeEmpty("a fulfillable order must have line items");
        order.ShippingAddress.Should().NotBeNull("fulfillable orders require a shipping address");
        order.Status.Should().BeOneOf(OrderStatus.Confirmed, OrderStatus.PartiallyShipped);

        return new AndConstraint<ObjectAssertions>(assertions);
    }
}

// Usage in tests:
order.Should().BeFulfillable().And.Subject.As<Order>()
    .LineItems.Should().HaveCountGreaterThan(0);
```
Tradeoff: Custom `AndConstraint` extensions make test intent readable at a glance ("this order should be fulfillable") and encapsulate multi-field domain rules in one place — when the fulfillability definition changes, only the extension method needs updating. The risk is that extension methods in a shared test helper assembly grow into a parallel domain model: keep them thin (delegating to existing assertions rather than using raw `if`/`throw`), and validate the extension library is itself tested by its own unit tests.

**Pattern 311** — `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing` `FakeLogger<T>` log-level and structured-property assertion
```csharp
// Assert that a service logs a warning with specific structured properties
// when a dependency is slow — without writing to a real sink.
var logger = new FakeLogger<OrderProcessor>();
var sut = new OrderProcessor(logger, _repo, _clock);

await sut.ProcessAsync(slowOrder, CancellationToken.None);

var warningLogs = logger.Collector.GetSnapshot()
    .Where(e => e.Level == LogLevel.Warning)
    .ToList();

warningLogs.Should().ContainSingle();
warningLogs[0].Message.Should().Contain("slow dependency detected");
warningLogs[0].StructuredState
    .Should().ContainKey("ElapsedMs")
    .WhoseValue.Should().BeGreaterThan("500");
```
Tradeoff: `FakeLogger<T>` captures log entries in-process with zero I/O overhead, making structured-log assertions faster and more reliable than sinks like `Serilog.Sinks.TestCorrelator` that require static state. The limitation is that `FakeLogger` is Microsoft-runtime-only — third-party libraries that log through `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging` abstractions are captured correctly, but libraries that use `Serilog` or `NLog` directly bypass `FakeLogger` entirely. For those, configure a Serilog `TestSink` or assert via `ILogEventSink` instead.

**Pattern 312** — Moq `Protected().Setup()` for testing `HttpMessageHandler`-derived `SendAsync` override directly
```csharp
// Unit-test a custom DelegatingHandler without needing a live HTTP server.
var innerHandlerMock = new Mock<HttpMessageHandler>();

innerHandlerMock
    .Protected()
    .Setup<Task<HttpResponseMessage>>(
        "SendAsync",
        ItExpr.IsAny<HttpRequestMessage>(),
        ItExpr.IsAny<CancellationToken>())
    .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests)
    {
        Headers = { RetryAfter = new RetryConditionHeaderValue(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)) }
    });

var handler = new RetryDelegatingHandler(retryCount: 3)
{
    InnerHandler = innerHandlerMock.Object
};
var client = new HttpClient(handler) { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com") };

var response = await client.GetAsync("/resource");
response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests);
innerHandlerMock.Protected().Verify(
    "SendAsync",
    Times.Exactly(3),
    ItExpr.IsAny<HttpRequestMessage>(),
    ItExpr.IsAny<CancellationToken>());
```
Tradeoff: `Protected().Setup()` uses string-based method names rather than compile-safe lambda expressions — a rename of `SendAsync` (impossible for framework types but possible for custom handlers) will compile and silently produce no setups. Always pair with a corresponding `Protected().Verify()` call to catch the "setup was never matched" case, and prefer `DelegatingHandler` test doubles (Pattern 297) over `Protected()` mock setups for truly custom handlers.

**Pattern 313** — xUnit `ICollectionFixture<T>` for sharing expensive database containers across multiple test collection classes
```csharp
// Share a single Testcontainers SQL Server instance across all fixtures
// in the "Database" collection — avoiding N container start/stop cycles.
[CollectionDefinition("Database")]
public class DatabaseCollection : ICollectionFixture<SqlServerContainerFixture> { }

public class SqlServerContainerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public MsSqlContainer Container { get; } = new MsSqlBuilder()
        .WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest")
        .Build();

    public string ConnectionString => Container.GetConnectionString();

    public Task InitializeAsync() => Container.StartAsync();
    public Task DisposeAsync()    => Container.StopAsync();
}

[Collection("Database")]
public class CustomerRepositoryTests(SqlServerContainerFixture db)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task FindById_ReturnsCustomer()
    {
        var repo = new CustomerRepository(db.ConnectionString);
        // ... test body
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ICollectionFixture<T>` with Testcontainers reduces container start-up from O(N fixtures) to O(1) per collection, cutting integration suite cold-start time from minutes to seconds. The cost is that all tests in the collection share mutable database state — always use unique identifiers (GUID primary keys generated in `Arrange`) and never rely on row counts or absence of data left by other tests; structure cleanup as `DELETE WHERE Id = @testId` in `IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync`.

**Pattern 314** — FluentAssertions `SatisfyRespectively` for asserting ordered heterogeneous collections element-by-element
```csharp
// Assert each element in a result list independently with different rules per position.
var events = await eventStore.LoadEventsAsync(orderId);

events.Should().SatisfyRespectively(
    first =>
    {
        first.Should().BeOfType<OrderCreatedEvent>();
        first.As<OrderCreatedEvent>().CustomerId.Should().Be(customerId);
    },
    second =>
    {
        second.Should().BeOfType<OrderLineAddedEvent>();
        second.As<OrderLineAddedEvent>().ProductId.Should().Be(productId);
    },
    third =>
    {
        third.Should().BeOfType<OrderSubmittedEvent>();
        third.As<OrderSubmittedEvent>().SubmittedAt.Should().BeCloseTo(
            DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, precision: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
    });
```
Tradeoff: `SatisfyRespectively` reads like a specification of the exact event stream and fails with per-element diff messages that pinpoint exactly which element violated which assertion. It couples the test tightly to element count and order — adding a new domain event between `OrderCreated` and `OrderLineAdded` requires updating the test. For event-sourced aggregates this tight coupling is usually desirable (event sequence is the contract), but for result lists where ordering is incidental, prefer `Satisfy(collection => ...)` or individual `ContainSingle(x => ...)` calls.

**Pattern 315** — NSubstitute `WhenForAnyArgs` for callback side-effects that apply regardless of argument values
```csharp
// Track all invocations of a void/async-void-equivalent method for side-effect assertion,
// regardless of what arguments are passed.
var auditLog = new List<string>();
var cache = Substitute.For<IDistributedCache>();

cache
    .WhenForAnyArgs(c => c.SetAsync(default!, default!, default, default))
    .Do(ci => auditLog.Add(ci.ArgAt<string>(0))); // capture the cache key (index 0)

await sut.RefreshProductCatalogAsync(CancellationToken.None);

auditLog.Should().Contain(key => key.StartsWith("product:"));
auditLog.Should().HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(3,
    because: "catalog refresh must warm at least 3 product keys");
```
Tradeoff: `WhenForAnyArgs` is the correct NSubstitute idiom when argument values vary and you cannot enumerate them in advance, but it bypasses NSubstitute's argument matching entirely — if the method signature changes (e.g., a new parameter is added), `ci.ArgAt<string>(0)` silently shifts to the wrong argument. Always document the parameter index with a comment (`// 0 = key`), and re-validate parameter positions whenever the interface is updated.

### Community Gotchas

**G36** — FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` recursively compares all public properties by default — including navigation properties that trigger lazy loading
Why this matters: A developer calls `actualUser.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expectedUser)` on an EF Core entity. FluentAssertions traverses all public properties and, if `actualUser.Orders` is a lazy-load proxy, accessing it outside a DbContext scope throws `ObjectDisposedException`. Even inside an active context, the comparison recursively walks all `Order.OrderLines`, `OrderLine.Product`, and so on — causing N+1 queries and test timeouts that only appear when the entity graph is large.
Fix: Scope `BeEquivalentTo` explicitly: `options => options.ExcludingMissingMembers().Excluding(u => u.Orders)` for navigation-property exclusion, or project the entity to a DTO before asserting. Alternatively, call `options => options.IncludingAllDeclaredProperties()` to limit traversal to only declared (non-inherited) properties and avoid proxy navigation.

**G37** — xUnit `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` cannot pass `null` for a non-nullable value type parameter — the attribute silently coerces to default
Why this matters: A developer writes `[InlineData(null, "expected")]` for a theory parameter typed as `int`. The C# compiler does not reject this — attribute constructor parameters are `object?`, so `null` is accepted. At runtime, xUnit converts `null` to `0` (the default for `int`) silently. If the test is specifically designed to assert boundary behaviour at zero vs. null, the test passes with `0` input but the developer believes they tested `null`, creating a false sense of coverage.
Fix: Change the parameter type to `int?` (nullable) if null is a valid input domain value, or use `[MemberData]` with a `TheoryData<int?>` source that explicitly expresses nullability. The xUnit analyzer `xUnit1012` flags `null` literals in `[InlineData]` for non-nullable parameter types — enable it in the project's `.editorconfig`.

**G38** — Moq `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` in setup does not verify that the caller propagates a non-default token — masks cancellation propagation bugs
Why this matters: A developer stubs `repo.FindAsync(id, It.IsAny<CancellationToken>())` and verifies with `Received(1)`. The SUT passes `CancellationToken.None` (hardcoded) instead of forwarding the caller's token. The test passes because `It.IsAny` matches any token including `CancellationToken.None`. In production, a cancelled outer operation cannot propagate its cancellation into the repository call, causing hung requests under load.
Fix: Use `It.Is<CancellationToken>(ct => ct != CancellationToken.None)` in the `Verify` call — not the `Setup` call — to assert propagation without blocking the call when the token is default. Alternatively, use a `CancellationTokenSource` in `Arrange`, pass its token to the SUT, and verify `It.Is<CancellationToken>(ct => ct == cts.Token)` to prove the exact token flowed through.

**G39** — NUnit `[TestCase]` string comparisons are culture-sensitive by default on non-English CI runners
Why this matters: A developer writes `Assert.That(result, Is.EqualTo("Straße"))` (German street name). On a CI runner with a Turkish or Azeri locale, `String.Equals` with the default `CurrentCulture` comparison may return `false` for casing differences involving locale-specific rules (the infamous Turkish I/i case). Tests that pass on an English developer laptop fail on international CI infrastructure, producing intermittent build failures that are extremely hard to diagnose.
Fix: Always use `Is.EqualTo(...).Using(StringComparer.Ordinal)` or `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` in NUnit constraints, or wrap string values with `StringAssert` overloads that accept an explicit `StringComparison`. Add `<InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>` to the test project's `.csproj` to lock the culture to invariant in all test runs.

**G40** — `WebApplicationFactory` service re-registration order matters — `ConfigureTestServices` runs after `ConfigureServices` but before `Configure` middleware, so `IStartupFilter` registrations are not replaced
Why this matters: A developer calls `builder.ConfigureTestServices(s => s.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway, FakePaymentGateway>())` expecting the fake to override the real gateway everywhere including inside startup filters. An `IStartupFilter` registered in `Program.cs` that resolves `IPaymentGateway` from the DI container during `Configure()` still receives the real registration because `IStartupFilter.Configure` is invoked during `WebHost.Build()`, which happens before `ConfigureTestServices` overrides are applied in some hosting configurations.
Fix: Move the override into a custom `IWebHostBuilder.ConfigureServices` delegate registered via `WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.ConfigureServices(...))`, which is applied earlier in the pipeline. Alternatively, remove startup-filter DI resolution and pass dependencies as constructor arguments to the filter (constructor injection is resolved after all `ConfigureServices` calls complete, respecting test overrides).
