## Cycle 64 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 361** — xUnit v3 `ITestContextAccessor` to access current test metadata inside production logging middleware during integration tests
```csharp
public class ContextAwareLoggingTests : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly WebApplicationFactory<Program> _factory;
    private readonly ITestContextAccessor _contextAccessor;

    public ContextAwareLoggingTests(
        WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory,
        ITestContextAccessor contextAccessor)
    {
        _contextAccessor = contextAccessor;
        _factory = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder =>
        {
            builder.ConfigureLogging(logging =>
            {
                logging.AddFilter(
                    (category, level) =>
                        level >= LogLevel.Warning ||
                        category.StartsWith("MyApp", StringComparison.Ordinal));
            });
        });
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task Get_Products_Returns200_AndLogsRequestId()
    {
        var testName = _contextAccessor.Current?.Test.TestCase.TestMethod.MethodName
                       ?? "unknown";
        var client = _factory.CreateClient();
        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("X-Test-Name", testName);

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/products");

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        response.Headers.Should().ContainKey("X-Correlation-Id");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ITestContextAccessor` (xUnit v3) is constructor-injected by the runner and exposes the live `TestContext` — test name, display name, and cancellation token — without any static ambient state, enabling correlation headers that tie HTTP logs back to the specific test method in structured log sinks. The limitation is that `ITestContextAccessor` is only available in xUnit v3; projects on xUnit v2 must replicate this via a custom `ITestOutputHelper`-backed adapter, and the accessor is `null` when accessed outside a running test (e.g., in a `Task.Run` that outlives the test), so it must not be cached in long-lived service singletons.

**Pattern 362** — NUnit `[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]` to eliminate shared-state contamination without per-test constructor overhead
```csharp
[TestFixture]
[FixtureLifeCycle(LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase)]
public class ShoppingCartTests
{
    // Each test gets its own fresh instance; no [SetUp] boilerplate required
    private readonly ShoppingCart _cart = new();
    private readonly FakeInventoryService _inventory = new();

    // Arrange is expressed as field initialisers; no shared mutation risk
    [Test]
    public void AddItem_IncreasesItemCount()
    {
        _cart.Add(new CartItem("sku-1", quantity: 2));

        Assert.That(_cart.ItemCount, Is.EqualTo(2));
    }

    [Test]
    public void RemoveItem_DecreasesItemCount_WhenItemPresent()
    {
        _cart.Add(new CartItem("sku-1", quantity: 3));
        _cart.Remove("sku-1", quantity: 1);

        Assert.That(_cart.ItemCount, Is.EqualTo(2));
    }

    [Test]
    public void Checkout_ReservesInventory_ForEachItem()
    {
        _cart.Add(new CartItem("sku-2", quantity: 5));
        _cart.Checkout(_inventory);

        Assert.That(_inventory.Reservations, Has.One.Matches<Reservation>(
            r => r.Sku == "sku-2" && r.Quantity == 5));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `LifeCycle.InstancePerTestCase` causes NUnit to construct a fresh fixture object for every test case, eliminating shared mutable state and the need for `[SetUp]` / `[TearDown]` in the common case where all arrange state is field-initialised. The cost is that object construction time is multiplied by the number of tests in the fixture; if the constructor performs expensive I/O (e.g., opens a database connection), this lifecycle becomes a significant bottleneck and `IClassFixture`-style shared setup should be preferred instead.

**Pattern 363** — FluentAssertions `.Which` chained property accessor for deep navigation assertions without intermediate variables
```csharp
[Fact]
public void ProcessOrder_ShouldEmitDomainEvent_WithCorrectOrderId()
{
    var sut = new OrderProcessor(new FakeEventBus());
    var order = new Order(id: Guid.NewGuid(), customerId: "cust-42");

    sut.Process(order);

    sut.EventBus.PublishedEvents
       .Should().ContainSingle()
       .Which.Should().BeOfType<OrderPlacedEvent>()
       .Which.OrderId.Should().Be(order.Id);
}
```
Tradeoff: FluentAssertions' `.Which` accessor returns the typed subject after a `ContainSingle()` or `BeOfType<T>()` constraint, enabling a fluent continuation onto the matched element's properties without introducing intermediate `var domainEvent = ...` assignments that break the assertion chain's readability. The precision risk is that `.Which` silently propagates the first match from `ContainSingle`; if the collection later has more than one element the `ContainSingle` assertion fails first with a count mismatch rather than a type-mismatch, which can obscure which assertion caused the regression when multiple failures accumulate inside an `AssertionScope`.

**Pattern 364** — Moq `InSequence` with `MockSequence` to enforce strict inter-mock call ordering
```csharp
[Fact]
public void PaymentFlow_MustAuthoriseBeforeCapture()
{
    var sequence    = new MockSequence();
    var authMock    = new Mock<IPaymentAuthoriser>(MockBehavior.Strict);
    var captureMock = new Mock<IPaymentCapturer>(MockBehavior.Strict);

    authMock.InSequence(sequence)
            .Setup(a => a.Authorise(It.IsAny<PaymentRequest>()))
            .Returns(new AuthResult { Token = "tok_123" });

    captureMock.InSequence(sequence)
               .Setup(c => c.Capture(It.Is<string>(t => t == "tok_123")))
               .Returns(new CaptureResult { ChargeId = "ch_456" });

    var sut    = new PaymentService(authMock.Object, captureMock.Object);
    var result = sut.Execute(new PaymentRequest { Amount = 99.00m });

    result.ChargeId.Should().Be("ch_456");
    authMock.Verify(a => a.Authorise(It.IsAny<PaymentRequest>()), Times.Once);
    captureMock.Verify(c => c.Capture("tok_123"), Times.Once);
}
```
Tradeoff: `MockSequence` enforces that setups across multiple mocks are satisfied in declaration order — if `Capture` is called before `Authorise`, Moq throws `MockException` immediately rather than deferring to `VerifyAll`, providing a precise point of failure that names the wrong-order call. The limitation is that `MockSequence` only works with `MockBehavior.Strict` mocks; using it with loose mocks causes the sequence check to be silently ignored, and mixing strict-sequenced mocks with loose mocks in the same test requires careful documentation so future maintainers do not inadvertently switch `MockBehavior` and lose the ordering guarantee.

**Pattern 365** — NSubstitute `Returns` with `callInfo` lambda for stateful response building based on call count
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task RetryPolicy_RetriesOnTransientFailure_ThenSucceeds()
{
    var callCount = 0;
    var service   = Substitute.For<IRemoteService>();

    service.FetchDataAsync(Arg.Any<string>())
           .Returns(callInfo =>
           {
               callCount++;
               if (callCount < 3)
                   throw new HttpRequestException("Transient error");
               return Task.FromResult(new ServiceResponse { Data = "ok" });
           });

    var policy = Policy
        .Handle<HttpRequestException>()
        .RetryAsync(3);

    var result = await policy.ExecuteAsync(
        () => service.FetchDataAsync("resource-id"));

    result.Data.Should().Be("ok");
    await service.Received(3).FetchDataAsync("resource-id");
}
```
Tradeoff: Passing a lambda to `Returns(callInfo => ...)` allows a single substitute setup to produce different outcomes on successive calls by closing over a local counter variable, which is more readable than chaining multiple `Returns(...).AndDoes(...)` setups when the control logic is non-trivial. The risk is that the lambda captures mutable state; if the test is inadvertently run in parallel or the substitute is shared between tests (e.g., injected via a shared fixture), the counter is not reset between invocations, causing the third-call success path to be reached prematurely and hiding failures in the retry policy's handling of the first two transient errors.

**Pattern 366** — Testcontainers.NET `ResourceReaper` session label override to prevent orphan containers on CI agent recycling
```csharp
public class PostgresFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private PostgreSqlContainer? _container;

    public string ConnectionString => _container!.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _container = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithDatabase("testdb")
            .WithUsername("testuser")
            .WithPassword("testpass")
            // Tie container lifecycle to this process via Ryuk session label
            .WithLabel("com.testcontainers.session-id",
                       ResourceReaper.DefaultSessionId.ToString("D"))
            // Explicit cleanup label for CI debugging
            .WithLabel("ci.build-id",
                       Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("BUILD_ID") ?? "local")
            .WithCleanUp(true)
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();

        await using var conn = new NpgsqlConnection(ConnectionString);
        await conn.OpenAsync();
        await conn.ExecuteAsync(
            "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (id UUID PRIMARY KEY, total NUMERIC)");
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_container is not null)
            await _container.StopAsync();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Attaching the `ResourceReaper.DefaultSessionId` label ties the container to the Testcontainers.NET Ryuk session, so Ryuk terminates the container even when the test process is killed (e.g., OOM kill in CI) rather than allowing orphan containers to accumulate and exhaust Docker host resources. The operational caveat is that `WithCleanUp(true)` and Ryuk-based reaping are mutually redundant; enabling both causes Ryuk to attempt deletion first and `DisposeAsync` to receive a "container not found" error on `StopAsync`, so the fixture should swallow `DockerContainerNotFoundException` in `DisposeAsync` or use `WithReuse(false)` rather than `WithCleanUp(true)` when Ryuk is active.

**Pattern 367** — WireMock.NET `WithBodyAsJson` request matcher combined with `LogEntries` post-call body inspection
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task CreateOrder_PostsCorrectJsonPayload_ToDownstreamApi()
{
    using var server = WireMockServer.Start();

    server
        .Given(Request.Create()
            .WithPath("/api/orders")
            .UsingPost()
            .WithHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .WithBodyAsJson(new
            {
                customerId = WireMock.Matchers.WildcardMatcher.MatchAny,
                items      = WireMock.Matchers.WildcardMatcher.MatchAny,
                total      = WireMock.Matchers.WildcardMatcher.MatchAny
            }))
        .RespondWith(Response.Create()
            .WithStatusCode(201)
            .WithBodyAsJson(new { orderId = "ord-generated-001" }));

    var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(server.Url!) };
    var sut    = new OrderApiClient(client);

    var result = await sut.CreateOrderAsync(new CreateOrderRequest
    {
        CustomerId = "cust-99",
        Items      = new[] { new OrderItem("sku-A", 2) },
        Total      = 49.98m
    });

    result.OrderId.Should().Be("ord-generated-001");

    var logEntry = server.LogEntries.Single();
    var body     = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<JsonElement>(
                       logEntry.RequestMessage.BodyAsJson!.ToString()!);
    body.GetProperty("customerId").GetString().Should().Be("cust-99");
    body.GetProperty("total").GetDecimal().Should().Be(49.98m);
}
```
Tradeoff: `WithBodyAsJson` in WireMock.NET matches requests by deserialising the incoming body and comparing it structurally against the provided anonymous object, allowing the test to assert both that the stub was reached (via `LogEntries`) and that the serialised payload is semantically correct without hard-coding a raw JSON string. The trade-off is that anonymous-object matching uses WireMock's internal `JObjectMatcher`, which performs a deep equality check against all provided fields; if the SUT adds an unspecified field (e.g., a new optional `notes` property), the match fails and the test breaks even though the client's handling of the new field is correct, so fields that are intentionally optional should be asserted only via `LogEntries` post-call inspection rather than in the stub matcher itself.

**Pattern 368** — AutoFixture `Customize<T>` with `OmitAutoProperties` for aggregate-root entities with mandatory factory constructors
```csharp
public class OrderCustomization : ICustomization
{
    public void Customize(IFixture fixture)
    {
        fixture.Customize<Order>(c => c
            .FromFactory(() => Order.Create(
                id: fixture.Create<Guid>(),
                customerId: fixture.Create<string>().Substring(0, 12),
                placedAt: fixture.Create<DateTimeOffset>()))
            .OmitAutoProperties());   // prevent reflection-based property setting
                                      // that bypasses domain invariants

        fixture.Customize<OrderLine>(c => c
            .FromFactory(() => new OrderLine(
                sku: fixture.Create<string>().Substring(0, 8),
                unitPrice: fixture.Create<decimal>() % 1000 + 0.01m,
                quantity: fixture.Create<int>() % 10 + 1))
            .OmitAutoProperties());
    }
}

public class OrderTests
{
    [Theory, AutoData]
    public void AddLine_IncreasesTotalCorrectly([Frozen] Order order, OrderLine line)
    {
        var expectedTotal = order.Lines.Sum(l => l.LineTotal) + line.LineTotal;

        order.AddLine(line);

        order.TotalAmount.Should().Be(expectedTotal);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `OmitAutoProperties()` prevents AutoFixture from setting properties via reflection after the factory method runs, ensuring that entities whose invariants are enforced in factory or constructor methods are never left in an invalid state (e.g., a `null` `CustomerId` that was overwritten by AutoFixture's auto-property setters). The necessary coupling is that the `ICustomization` implementation must be kept in sync with the entity's factory method signature; if the factory gains a new required parameter, the customization silently constructs the entity with the old signature and the test may compile against a stale constructor overload, so the customization class should be co-located in the same assembly as the domain entity and updated as part of the same commit.

**Pattern 369** — xUnit v3 `IAssemblyFixture<T>` for one-per-process expensive resource shared across all test classes
```csharp
// Assembly-wide fixture — created once per test run, not per class
public class OidcServerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public WireMockServer? Server { get; private set; }
    public string Authority => Server!.Url!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        Server = WireMockServer.Start();
        Server
            .Given(Request.Create().WithPath("/connect/token").UsingPost())
            .RespondWith(Response.Create()
                .WithStatusCode(200)
                .WithBodyAsJson(new
                {
                    access_token = "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.stub",
                    token_type   = "Bearer",
                    expires_in   = 3600
                }));
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    public Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        Server?.Dispose();
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

// Register at assembly level (typically in AssemblyInfo.cs — xUnit v3 only)
[assembly: AssemblyFixture(typeof(OidcServerFixture))]

public class AuthenticatedApiTests(OidcServerFixture oidc)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task CallProtectedEndpoint_WithBearerToken_Returns200()
    {
        var tokenResponse = await new HttpClient()
            .PostAsync($"{oidc.Authority}/connect/token",
                new FormUrlEncodedContent(new[]
                {
                    new KeyValuePair<string, string>("grant_type", "client_credentials")
                }));
        var token = (await tokenResponse.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<JsonElement>())
            .GetProperty("access_token").GetString();
        token.Should().NotBeNullOrWhiteSpace();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `IAssemblyFixture<T>` (xUnit v3) initialises the fixture exactly once per assembly process and injects it into any test class that declares it as a constructor parameter, making it ideal for heavy OIDC servers, Docker containers, or in-process gRPC hosts that take multiple seconds to start. The architectural risk is that shared assembly fixtures introduce implicit ordering dependency — tests that mutate the fixture's state (e.g., registering new OIDC clients dynamically) affect all subsequent tests in the run; fixture state should therefore be read-only after `InitializeAsync`, and any per-test variation should be injected via `IClassFixture`-scoped child fixtures rather than modifying the assembly-level instance.

**Pattern 370** — NUnit `Assert.Multiple` with `Assert.That` lambdas for atomic multi-property validation without early bailout
```csharp
[Test]
public void CreateInvoice_ShouldPopulateAllRequiredFields()
{
    var sut     = new InvoiceFactory(new FakeTaxCalculator());
    var order   = OrderFixtures.StandardOrder();

    var invoice = sut.Create(order);

    // Guard: null-check before entering Assert.Multiple to avoid NullReferenceException
    Assert.That(invoice, Is.Not.Null, "InvoiceFactory must not return null");

    Assert.Multiple(() =>
    {
        Assert.That(invoice.InvoiceNumber, Does.StartWith("INV-"),
            "InvoiceNumber must start with INV-");

        Assert.That(invoice.IssuedAt.Date, Is.EqualTo(DateTime.UtcNow.Date),
            "IssuedAt date should be today");

        Assert.That(invoice.LineItems, Has.Count.EqualTo(order.Lines.Count),
            "LineItems count must match order lines");

        Assert.That(invoice.SubTotal,
            Is.EqualTo(order.Lines.Sum(l => l.Amount)).Within(0.01m),
            "SubTotal should be sum of line amounts");

        Assert.That(invoice.TaxAmount, Is.GreaterThan(0m),
            "TaxAmount must be positive");

        Assert.That(invoice.DueDate, Is.GreaterThan(invoice.IssuedAt),
            "DueDate must be after IssuedAt");
    });
}
```
Tradeoff: `Assert.Multiple` collects all failures from its delegate and reports them as a single aggregated failure rather than stopping at the first failing assertion, which is especially valuable when validating multi-field domain objects because a single test run reveals all missing fields simultaneously and prevents the fix-one-reveal-next cycle. The cost is that assertions inside `Assert.Multiple` that throw non-`AssertionException` exceptions (e.g., `NullReferenceException` from accessing a property on a `null` `invoice`) immediately abort the lambda, so the remaining assertions after the throw are never reached; the `invoice` object should be null-checked with a separate early `Assert.That(invoice, Is.Not.Null)` before entering the `Assert.Multiple` block.

**Pattern 371** — FluentAssertions `BeJsonSerializable` combined with round-trip `BeEquivalentTo` for DTO stability verification
```csharp
[Fact]
public void OrderDto_MustRoundTripThroughSystemTextJson_WithoutDataLoss()
{
    var original = new OrderDto
    {
        OrderId    = Guid.NewGuid(),
        CustomerId = "cust-567",
        PlacedAt   = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow,
        Lines      = new[]
        {
            new OrderLineDto { Sku = "sku-A", Quantity = 3, UnitPrice = 14.99m }
        },
        Status     = OrderStatus.Pending
    };

    // Phase 1 — assert no serialisation exception
    original.Should().BeJsonSerializable<OrderDto>();

    // Phase 2 — assert round-trip fidelity
    var json         = JsonSerializer.Serialize(original);
    var deserialized = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<OrderDto>(json);

    deserialized.Should().BeEquivalentTo(original,
        opts => opts
            .Using<DateTimeOffset>(ctx =>
                ctx.Subject.Should().BeCloseTo(
                    ctx.Expectation, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)))
            .WhenTypeIs<DateTimeOffset>());
}
```
Tradeoff: Combining `BeJsonSerializable<T>` (which invokes `JsonSerializer.Serialize` and asserts no exception is thrown) with a full `BeEquivalentTo` round-trip assertion catches two distinct failure modes: serialisation exceptions (e.g., circular references, non-serialisable types) and silent data loss (e.g., `[JsonIgnore]` accidentally placed on a required field). The important nuance is that `BeEquivalentTo` uses structural equivalence by default, so `DateTimeOffset` values with different UTC offset representations (e.g., `+00:00` vs `Z`) compare as unequal unless a custom `Using<DateTimeOffset>` comparer with `BeCloseTo` is applied, making the `WhenTypeIs<DateTimeOffset>()` clause load-bearing for any DTO carrying timestamps.

**Pattern 372** — Moq `.Callback(...)` chained before `.ReturnsAsync(...)` for argument capture with a configured async response
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task SendNotification_PassesCorrectPayload_ToEmailService()
{
    NotificationPayload? captured = null;

    var emailMock = new Mock<IEmailService>();
    emailMock
        .Setup(e => e.SendAsync(
            It.Is<NotificationPayload>(p => p.RecipientId != Guid.Empty),
            It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
        .Callback<NotificationPayload, CancellationToken>(
            (payload, _) => captured = payload)
        .ReturnsAsync(new SendResult { MessageId = "msg-001", Success = true });

    var sut = new NotificationService(emailMock.Object);
    await sut.NotifyAsync(userId: Guid.NewGuid(), message: "Your order shipped.");

    captured.Should().NotBeNull();
    captured!.Subject.Should().Contain("order");
    captured.Body.Should().Contain("shipped");
    captured.RecipientId.Should().NotBeEmpty();
}
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `.Callback(...)` before `.ReturnsAsync(...)` in Moq captures the exact argument instance passed to the mock without requiring a separate `Capture.In<T>` list — a single variable holds the last-captured value, which is sufficient when the SUT calls the dependency exactly once. The limitation is that `.Callback` fires only when the `It.Is<T>` predicate on the same `Setup` matches; if the SUT passes a payload with `RecipientId == Guid.Empty` the setup does not match, the callback never fires, `captured` remains `null`, and the assertion `captured.Should().NotBeNull()` produces a misleading "was null" failure rather than exposing the root cause that the predicate guard rejected the call.

**Pattern 373** — Testcontainers.NET layered `UntilPortIsAvailable` + `UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded` wait strategy for Elasticsearch
```csharp
public class ElasticSearchFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private ElasticsearchContainer? _container;
    public string Url => _container!.GetConnectionString();

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _container = new ElasticsearchBuilder()
            .WithImage("docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.13.0")
            .WithEnvironment("discovery.type", "single-node")
            .WithEnvironment("xpack.security.enabled", "false")
            .WithPortBinding(9200, assignRandomHostPort: true)
            .WithWaitStrategy(
                Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                    .UntilPortIsAvailable(9200)
                    .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r
                        .ForPath("/_cluster/health")
                        .ForStatusCode(HttpStatusCode.OK)
                        .ForResponseMessageMatching(msg =>
                            msg.Content.ReadAsStringAsync()
                               .GetAwaiter().GetResult()
                               .Contains("\"status\":\"green\""))))
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        if (_container is not null)
            await _container.DisposeAsync();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Layering `UntilPortIsAvailable` with `UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded` creates a two-phase wait strategy — the first phase ensures the TCP socket is listening (fast), the second phase polls the application-level health endpoint until the cluster reports `green` — so tests never begin before Elasticsearch has fully initialised its index engine. The operational cost is that `ForResponseMessageMatching` calls `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` synchronously inside the polling lambda because Testcontainers.NET's wait predicate API is synchronous; this is safe inside the polling loop but blocks a thread pool thread on each poll iteration, so `UntilMessageIsLogged` (which uses Docker log streaming) is a lower-overhead alternative when the container emits a distinct ready-signal log line.

**Pattern 374** — NSubstitute `ReceivedWithAnyArgs` vs `Received(1)` two-phase verification to distinguish missing calls from wrong arguments
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task AuditLogger_IsCalledOnce_WithCorrectEventType_WhenOrderCancelled()
{
    var auditLogger = Substitute.For<IAuditLogger>();
    var sut         = new OrderService(auditLogger);
    var orderId     = Guid.NewGuid();

    await sut.CancelOrderAsync(orderId);

    // Phase 1 — verify the method was invoked at all (argument-agnostic)
    auditLogger.ReceivedWithAnyArgs(1).LogEventAsync(default!, default);

    // Phase 2 — verify the arguments are semantically correct
    await auditLogger.Received(1).LogEventAsync(
        Arg.Is<AuditEvent>(e =>
            e.EventType == AuditEventType.OrderCancelled &&
            e.ResourceId == orderId.ToString()),
        Arg.Any<CancellationToken>());
}
```
Tradeoff: Splitting verification into a `ReceivedWithAnyArgs` phase followed by an argument-specific `Received` phase produces two distinct failure messages: the first pinpoints "method was never called" (indicating a missing code path) while the second pinpoints "method was called but with wrong arguments" (indicating incorrect argument construction), making CI failure diagnosis faster than a single combined assertion that reports only an argument mismatch when the real bug is actually a missing invocation. The readability cost is that two consecutive received-checks on the same method appear redundant to reviewers unfamiliar with the pattern, so a comment explaining the two-failure-mode rationale should accompany any use in a shared test suite.

**Pattern 375** — WireMock.NET `IRequestMatcher` custom implementation for business-rule validation inside stub matchers
```csharp
public class NonEmptyLineItemsMatcher : IRequestMatcher
{
    public double GetMatchingScore(IRequestMessage requestMessage,
                                   IRequestMatchResult matchResult)
    {
        try
        {
            var body      = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<JsonElement>(
                                requestMessage.BodyAsJson!.ToString()!);
            var lineCount = body.GetProperty("lineItems").GetArrayLength();
            var score     = lineCount > 0 ? 1.0 : 0.0;
            matchResult.AddScore(GetType(), score);
            return score;
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            Console.Error.WriteLine(
                $"[NonEmptyLineItemsMatcher] body parse failed: {ex.Message}");
            matchResult.AddScore(GetType(), 0.0);
            return 0.0;
        }
    }
}

[Fact]
public async Task CreateOrder_WithEmptyLineItems_Returns404_NotRoutedToStub()
{
    using var server = WireMockServer.Start();

    server
        .Given(Request.Create()
            .WithPath("/api/orders")
            .UsingPost()
            .WithMatcher(new NonEmptyLineItemsMatcher()))
        .RespondWith(Response.Create().WithStatusCode(201));

    var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(server.Url!) };
    var empty  = await client.PostAsJsonAsync(
        "/api/orders", new { lineItems = Array.Empty<object>() });
    var valid  = await client.PostAsJsonAsync(
        "/api/orders", new { lineItems = new[] { new { sku = "A", qty = 1 } } });

    empty.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.NotFound);
    valid.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.Created);
}
```
Tradeoff: Implementing `IRequestMatcher` directly allows the stub to encode business rules (e.g., "only match requests with at least one line item") that cannot be expressed via WireMock.NET's built-in body matchers, making the test both a functional assertion and a documentation artefact of the downstream service's contract. The maintenance risk is that `IRequestMatcher` implementations live in the test project and diverge from the actual downstream service's validation logic over time; to prevent drift the matcher's rule should be derived from a shared contract interface or JSON Schema rather than hard-coded, and the matcher class itself should have its own unit test to verify it scores requests correctly.

### Community Gotchas

**G56** — NUnit `Assert.Multiple` silently aborts on `NullReferenceException` inside the delegate — remaining assertions are never evaluated, producing a partial failure report that appears to be a single-field problem
Why this matters: A developer uses `Assert.Multiple` to validate all fields on a response object. The SUT returns `null` for the `Address` property. An assertion inside the lambda calls `invoice.Address.City.Should().Be("London")`, which throws `NullReferenceException`. NUnit's `Assert.Multiple` catches `AssertionException` to collect failures but does not catch `NullReferenceException`, so the delegate terminates immediately. The test reports a single `NullReferenceException` failure rather than collecting the other failing assertions below it, giving the developer the impression that `Address.City` is the only problem.
Fix: Always null-guard nested navigation before entering `Assert.Multiple`: `Assert.That(invoice.Address, Is.Not.Null, "Address must not be null")` before the `Assert.Multiple` block. Inside the block use null-conditional navigation (`invoice.Address?.City`) and assert `Is.Not.Null.And.EqualTo("London")` so a `null` dereference becomes a collectable assertion failure rather than an uncaught exception that aborts the entire block.

**G57** — FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` includes `internal` members when the test assembly has `[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo]` — refactoring internal fields breaks equivalence assertions that were intended to verify only the public contract
Why this matters: A developer adds `[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("MyApp.Tests")]` to allow the test project to access `internal` domain helpers. FluentAssertions uses reflection to enumerate properties and, because the test assembly can now see `internal` members, it includes them in the default `BeEquivalentTo` comparison. A refactoring renames an `internal` tracking property (`_internalVersion`), causing `BeEquivalentTo` to report a mismatch even though no public API changed. The test was intended only to verify the public contract, but the developer does not realise internal properties are included, leading to a confusing test failure with no visible change to the public surface.
Fix: Explicitly scope `BeEquivalentTo` to public members: `opts => opts.ExcludingNonBrowsableMembers()` or filter with `opts => opts.Including(m => m.IsPublic())`. For value-object comparisons where only specific fields matter, prefer `opts => opts.Including(o => o.PublicProp1).Including(o => o.PublicProp2)` to make the comparison contract explicit and immune to additions of new internal members.

**G58** — xUnit v3 `IAssemblyFixture<T>` is silently ignored on xUnit v2 runners — the constructor parameter receives `null` or causes the test class to be skipped without any error
Why this matters: A developer reads xUnit v3 documentation and adds `[assembly: AssemblyFixture(typeof(DatabaseFixture))]` along with `DatabaseFixture db` as a constructor parameter. The project's test runner is still targeting xUnit v2 (the NuGet package reference was not updated). xUnit v2 does not understand `IAssemblyFixture` or the `AssemblyFixture` attribute; it attempts to resolve the constructor but cannot supply a `DatabaseFixture` argument, so it skips the test class silently (or instantiates it with `null` depending on the runner version). Tests pass against an uninitialised state that happens to be valid, hiding that the shared resource was never set up.
Fix: Verify the xUnit runner version in `xunit.runner.json` and confirm the NuGet package is `xunit` v3 (distinct package ID from v2). Add a loud guard in `InitializeAsync`: `if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(ConnectionString)) throw new InvalidOperationException("AssemblyFixture was not initialised — verify xUnit v3 package version.")` so any misconfigured environment fails fast with a clear message rather than silently running tests against an empty fixture.

**G59** — Testcontainers.NET `GetConnectionString()` captured at DI registration time before container start — EF Core `UseNpgsql` caches the stale port, causing all queries to fail with "connection refused"
Why this matters: A developer registers `services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(opts => opts.UseNpgsql(fixture.ConnectionString))` inside `WebApplicationFactory.ConfigureServices`. When the factory's `CreateClient()` is called before the Testcontainers fixture's `InitializeAsync` completes (possible when `IClassFixture` and `IAsyncLifetime` ordering is non-deterministic), `fixture.ConnectionString` returns an empty string or a stale port. EF Core caches this connection string at startup, and all subsequent queries fail with "connection refused on port 0" or the wrong port number. The container starts successfully, so the error appears only in the application layer, making the root cause hard to diagnose.
Fix: Delay `WebApplicationFactory` construction until after `InitializeAsync` completes by constructing the factory inside `InitializeAsync`, or use `IDbContextFactory<T>` with a factory lambda that reads from a live `IConfiguration` key populated after container start, ensuring the connection string is resolved lazily on first use rather than captured eagerly at DI registration time.

**G60** — WireMock.NET custom `IRequestMatcher` returning `0.0` is represented as a near-miss in `LogEntries` — the aggregate match score misleads post-hoc debugging toward the wrong matcher
Why this matters: A developer writes a custom `IRequestMatcher` that returns `0.0` when the business rule is not satisfied. WireMock.NET's routing engine computes a weighted match score across all matchers; because other matchers (path, HTTP method) returned `1.0`, the aggregate score is non-zero (e.g., `0.67`). The `LogEntries` near-miss report shows the stub at `67%` match confidence, suggesting a minor discrepancy. The developer investigates the path or header matchers rather than the custom body matcher, wasting time before realising the custom matcher's `0.0` was the decisive veto that prevented the stub from firing.
Fix: Log a diagnostic message inside the matcher whenever score is `0.0` — `Console.Error.WriteLine($"[{GetType().Name}] rejected: {reason}")` — so the root cause appears in test output before examining `LogEntries`. For mandatory veto matchers, add an integration test that sends a request violating the rule and asserts `server.LogEntries.Should().BeEmpty()` to confirm the stub was not matched, making matcher failures immediately visible rather than inferred from aggregate score breakdowns.

## Cycle 66 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 376** — xUnit v3 `TheoryData<T>` with `ITheoryDataRow` for per-row `Skip`, `Label`, and `Timeout` metadata
```csharp
// ITheoryDataRow lets each row carry metadata independently of the dataset
public static TheoryData<string, int, string> InvalidOrderCases()
{
    var data = new TheoryData<string, int, string>();
    data.Add("", 1, "empty customer name");
    data.Add("Alice", 0, "zero quantity");
    data.Add("Alice", -5, "negative quantity");
    return data;
}

[Theory]
[MemberData(nameof(InvalidOrderCases))]
public void CreateOrder_InvalidInput_ThrowsArgumentException(
    string customer, int quantity, string scenario)
{
    var act = () => new Order(customer, quantity);
    act.Should().Throw<ArgumentException>(because: scenario);
}

// xUnit v3: use TheoryDataRow<T1,T2> to attach Skip per row
public static IEnumerable<ITheoryDataRow> SkippableCases()
{
    yield return new TheoryDataRow<string, int>("Alice", 1);
    yield return new TheoryDataRow<string, int>("", 0)
        { Skip = "Validation rules under revision in sprint-47" };
}
```
Tradeoff: `ITheoryDataRow` per-row `Skip` metadata avoids polluting an entire `[Theory]` with `Skip` when only a subset of cases is blocked by a known issue, but adding per-row metadata requires xUnit v3 and breaks compilation against v2 without a polyfill shim, so gating adoption on a committed v3 migration is essential before spreading this pattern across the test suite.

**Pattern 377** — NUnit 4 `TestCaseData` with `SetDescription` and `SetCategory` for filterable parameterised tests in CI pipelines
```csharp
[TestFixture]
public class PricingEngineTests
{
    public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> DiscountScenarios()
    {
        yield return new TestCaseData("PREMIUM", 100m, 10m)
            .SetName("Premium tier gets 10% discount")
            .SetDescription("Verifies tier-based discount calculation")
            .SetCategory("Pricing");

        yield return new TestCaseData("STANDARD", 100m, 0m)
            .SetName("Standard tier has no discount")
            .SetCategory("Pricing");

        yield return new TestCaseData("TRIAL", 100m, 50m)
            .SetName("Trial tier gets 50% discount")
            .SetCategory("Pricing").SetCategory("Trial");
    }

    [TestCaseSource(nameof(DiscountScenarios))]
    public void CalculateDiscount_ReturnsExpectedAmount(
        string tier, decimal price, decimal expectedDiscount)
    {
        var engine = new PricingEngine();
        var discount = engine.CalculateDiscount(tier, price);
        Assert.That(discount, Is.EqualTo(expectedDiscount));
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `SetCategory` on individual `TestCaseData` rows allows `dotnet test --filter TestCategory=Pricing` to run a meaningful subset in CI without a separate test class, but categories are stringly typed and silently ignored if misspelled, so a project-level `enum` or constant class for category strings prevents drift between the filter command in the pipeline YAML and the test code.

**Pattern 378** — MSTest v3 `[DataTestMethod]` with `[DynamicData]` sourced from an `IAsyncEnumerable` factory for database-driven parameterised tests
```csharp
[TestClass]
public class ProductValidationTests
{
    // MSTest v3: DynamicData supports async IEnumerable<object[]> source
    public static async IAsyncEnumerable<object[]> ProductTestCases()
    {
        await using var db = new TestDbContext();
        await foreach (var product in db.Products
                           .Where(p => p.IsActive)
                           .AsAsyncEnumerable())
        {
            yield return new object[] { product.Sku, product.Price, product.IsValid };
        }
    }

    [TestMethod]
    [DynamicData(
        nameof(ProductTestCases),
        DynamicDataSourceType.Method)]
    public void Validate_ActiveProduct_MatchesExpectedValidity(
        string sku, decimal price, bool expectedValid)
    {
        var result = ProductValidator.Validate(sku, price);
        Assert.AreEqual(expectedValid, result.IsValid,
            $"SKU={sku} price={price}");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Sourcing test cases from an async DB query ensures parameterised tests always reflect the live seed data without maintaining a parallel in-code dataset, but it creates a hard dependency on the test database being available during discovery (not just execution), which breaks test listing on machines without DB access and can cause IDE test explorers to hang; a guard that falls back to an empty sequence when the DB is unavailable preserves discoverability.

**Pattern 379** — FluentAssertions `AndConstraint` with `.Which` for chained deep-object assertion chains on nested aggregates
```csharp
public class OrderDto
{
    public string Id { get; set; } = "";
    public CustomerDto Customer { get; set; } = null!;
    public IReadOnlyList<LineItemDto> LineItems { get; set; } = [];
}

[Fact]
public void PlaceOrder_ValidRequest_ReturnsOrderWithExpectedStructure()
{
    var service = new OrderService(new FakeInventory());
    var order = service.PlaceOrder("CUST-1", [("SKU-A", 2), ("SKU-B", 1)]);

    order.Should().NotBeNull();

    order.Customer.Should().NotBeNull()
        .And.Subject.Name.Should().Be("Alice");

    order.LineItems.Should().HaveCount(2)
        .And.ContainSingle(li => li.Sku == "SKU-A" && li.Quantity == 2)
        .Which.UnitPrice.Should().BePositive();

    order.LineItems
        .Should().OnlyContain(li => li.UnitPrice > 0,
            because: "all line items must have a resolved price");
}
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `.And.Subject` combined with `.Which` allows a single assertion expression to drill into nested objects without introducing intermediate local variables that obscure the logical assertion flow, but deeply chained `.Which` calls fail with a `NullReferenceException` when any intermediate node is `null` rather than emitting a descriptive "was null at depth N" message, so a null guard `Should().NotBeNull()` must be inserted at each navigation boundary before chaining further assertions.

**Pattern 380** — Moq `SetupSequence` for simulating retry-eligible transient failures before a successful response
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task SendMessage_TransientFailureThenSuccess_RetriesAndSucceeds()
{
    var mockClient = new Mock<IMessageBrokerClient>(MockBehavior.Strict);

    mockClient
        .SetupSequence(c => c.SendAsync(
            It.IsAny<Message>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
        .ThrowsAsync(new TransientBrokerException("timeout"))    // attempt 1
        .ThrowsAsync(new TransientBrokerException("timeout"))    // attempt 2
        .ReturnsAsync(new SendReceipt { MessageId = "MSG-001" }); // attempt 3

    var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder<SendReceipt>()
        .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions<SendReceipt>
        {
            MaxRetryAttempts = 3,
            Delay = TimeSpan.Zero,
            ShouldHandle = new PredicateBuilder<SendReceipt>()
                .Handle<TransientBrokerException>()
        })
        .Build();

    var receipt = await pipeline.ExecuteAsync(
        async ct => await mockClient.Object.SendAsync(new Message("hello"), ct),
        CancellationToken.None);

    receipt.MessageId.Should().Be("MSG-001");
    mockClient.Verify(
        c => c.SendAsync(It.IsAny<Message>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()),
        Times.Exactly(3));
}
```
Tradeoff: `SetupSequence` exhausts its entries in declaration order and throws `MockException` on any call beyond the last entry when using `MockBehavior.Strict`, which gives precise failure attribution; however `SetupSequence` cannot be extended after construction, so a test that needs to vary the failure count across parameterised cases must recreate the mock entirely, favouring a factory helper over a shared mock field.

**Pattern 381** — NSubstitute `When...Do` for void methods with side effects that must be verified without return values
```csharp
[Fact]
public void AuditService_OnOrderPlaced_WritesAuditEntryWithCorrectFields()
{
    var captured = new List<AuditEntry>();
    var auditStore = Substitute.For<IAuditStore>();

    auditStore
        .When(s => s.Write(Arg.Any<AuditEntry>()))
        .Do(callInfo => captured.Add(callInfo.Arg<AuditEntry>()));

    var service = new OrderService(auditStore);
    service.PlaceOrder("CUST-1", "SKU-A", 2);

    captured.Should().ContainSingle()
        .Which.Should().BeEquivalentTo(new AuditEntry
        {
            EntityType = "Order",
            Action = "Placed",
            ActorId = "CUST-1"
        }, opts => opts.Excluding(e => e.Timestamp).Excluding(e => e.Id));

    auditStore.Received(1).Write(Arg.Any<AuditEntry>());
}
```
Tradeoff: `When...Do` captures arguments for full structural assertion beyond what `Received(1).Write(Arg.Is<AuditEntry>(...))` can concisely express, but `When...Do` runs synchronously even for async substitute methods; for `Task`-returning methods the `.Do` callback is invoked before the awaited continuation, so side effects that depend on the awaited result will silently not execute if the production call path uses `await` on the substitute return value.

**Pattern 382** — `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing` `FakeLogCollector` for structured log assertion without custom `ILoggerFactory` boilerplate
```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing;

[Fact]
public async Task ProcessOrder_WhenInventoryInsufficient_LogsWarningWithOrderId()
{
    using var collector = new FakeLogCollector();
    var logger = new FakeLogger<OrderProcessor>(collector);

    var inventory = Substitute.For<IInventoryService>();
    inventory.CheckStock(Arg.Any<string>(), Arg.Any<int>())
             .Returns(false);

    var processor = new OrderProcessor(logger, inventory);
    await processor.ProcessAsync(
        new Order { Id = "ORD-99", Sku = "SKU-A", Qty = 5 });

    var warnings = collector.GetSnapshot()
        .Where(e => e.Level == LogLevel.Warning)
        .ToList();

    warnings.Should().ContainSingle()
        .Which.Message.Should().Contain("ORD-99")
        .And.Subject.Should().Contain("insufficient stock");

    warnings.Single().StructuredState
        .Should().ContainSingle(
            kv => kv.Key == "OrderId" && kv.Value == "ORD-99");
}
```
Tradeoff: `FakeLogCollector` captures both rendered message strings and the raw structured state key-value pairs, enabling assertion on structured logging properties without parsing the formatted string, but it is part of `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing` which ships separately from the main logging packages and requires an explicit NuGet reference; teams that already use a third-party logging assertion library (e.g., `Serilog.Sinks.InMemory`) should not add both to avoid duplicating configuration surfaces.

**Pattern 383** — `WebApplicationFactory` with `IServiceCollection.RemoveAll<T>` + `AddSingleton` service-swap exposing fakes as factory properties for side-effect assertion
```csharp
public class OrderApiFactory : WebApplicationFactory<Program>
{
    public FakeEmailSender EmailSender { get; } = new FakeEmailSender();
    public FakePaymentGateway PaymentGateway { get; } = new FakePaymentGateway();

    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.ConfigureServices(services =>
        {
            services.RemoveAll<IEmailSender>();
            services.RemoveAll<IPaymentGateway>();
            services.AddSingleton<IEmailSender>(EmailSender);
            services.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway>(PaymentGateway);
        });
    }
}

[Fact]
public async Task PlaceOrder_ValidCard_SendsConfirmationEmail()
{
    await using var factory = new OrderApiFactory();
    var client = factory.CreateClient();

    var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/api/orders",
        new { customerId = "CUST-1", sku = "SKU-A", quantity = 1,
              cardToken = "tok_visa" });

    response.Should().HaveStatusCode(HttpStatusCode.Created);
    factory.EmailSender.SentEmails
        .Should().ContainSingle(
            e => e.To == "alice@example.com"
              && e.Subject.Contains("confirmation"));
    factory.PaymentGateway.Charges
        .Should().ContainSingle(
            c => c.Amount > 0 && c.CardToken == "tok_visa");
}
```
Tradeoff: Exposing fake collaborators as public properties on the factory allows the test to assert on side effects (emails sent, payments charged) without an additional messaging bus or event sink, but registering fakes as `AddSingleton` means the same fake instance is shared across all requests in a single factory lifetime; parallelised tests that mutate the fake's captured state list must either use a fresh factory per test class or synchronise access to the captured-call collections with a thread-safe list.

**Pattern 384** — `BenchmarkDotNet` `[Params]` multi-size sweep with `[SimpleJob]` multi-runtime for allocation-scaling micro-benchmarks
```csharp
using BenchmarkDotNet.Attributes;
using BenchmarkDotNet.Running;

[MemoryDiagnoser]
[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net90)]
[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net80)]
public class JsonSerializationBenchmarks
{
    [Params(1, 10, 100, 1000)]
    public int ItemCount;

    private IReadOnlyList<OrderDto> _orders = null!;
    private string _json = null!;

    [GlobalSetup]
    public void Setup()
    {
        _orders = Enumerable.Range(1, ItemCount)
            .Select(i => new OrderDto { Id = $"ORD-{i}", Total = i * 9.99m })
            .ToList();
        _json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(_orders);
    }

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public string Serialize_SystemTextJson()
        => JsonSerializer.Serialize(_orders);

    [Benchmark]
    public IReadOnlyList<OrderDto>? Deserialize_SystemTextJson()
        => JsonSerializer.Deserialize<IReadOnlyList<OrderDto>>(_json);
}

// In Program.cs: BenchmarkRunner.Run<JsonSerializationBenchmarks>();
```
Tradeoff: `[Params]` sweeps expose how serialisation throughput and allocation scale with collection size within a single benchmark run, revealing O(n) vs O(n²) allocation behaviour that a single fixed-size benchmark would hide; however each unique `[Params]` value multiplies the total benchmark duration, so combining more than four param values with multiple `[SimpleJob]` runtimes can produce runs exceeding an hour, favouring a smaller representative param set for CI and the full sweep for quarterly regression baselines.

**Pattern 385** — Polly v8 `ResiliencePipeline` with custom `DelayGenerator` capturing delays for deterministic backoff-series assertion without real waits
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Pipeline_ExponentialBackoff_WaitsCorrectDelaysBetweenRetries()
{
    var delays = new List<TimeSpan>();

    var pipeline = new ResiliencePipelineBuilder()
        .AddRetry(new RetryStrategyOptions
        {
            MaxRetryAttempts = 3,
            BackoffType = DelayBackoffType.Exponential,
            Delay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1),
            UseJitter = false,
            DelayGenerator = args =>
            {
                var delay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(Math.Pow(2, args.AttemptNumber));
                delays.Add(delay);
                // Return TimeSpan.Zero so the pipeline doesn't actually sleep
                return ValueTask.FromResult<TimeSpan?>(TimeSpan.Zero);
            },
            ShouldHandle = new PredicateBuilder()
                .Handle<HttpRequestException>()
        })
        .Build();

    var callCount = 0;
    await pipeline.ExecuteAsync(async _ =>
    {
        callCount++;
        if (callCount < 4) throw new HttpRequestException("unavailable");
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    });

    delays.Should().BeEquivalentTo(
        new[] { TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(4) },
        opts => opts.WithStrictOrdering());
    callCount.Should().Be(4);
}
```
Tradeoff: Injecting a custom `DelayGenerator` that returns `TimeSpan.Zero` alongside a captured `delays` list allows exact verification of the intended backoff series without sleeping, but `DelayGenerator` receives an `AttemptNumber` that is zero-indexed from the first retry rather than the first attempt, so a developer expecting `delays[0]` to correspond to attempt 1 will miscalculate the expected series; documentation comments on the capture lambda prevent this off-by-one interpretation.

**Pattern 386** — `Alba` `IScenario` DSL for readable ASP.NET Core integration test scenarios without raw `HttpClient` boilerplate
```csharp
// Alba: lightweight integration testing DSL over WebApplicationFactory
// NuGet: Alba

public class AlbaHostFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public IAlbaHost Host { get; private set; } = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
        => Host = await Alba.AlbaHost.For<Program>(builder =>
            builder.ConfigureServices(s =>
                s.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway, StubPaymentGateway>()));

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await Host.DisposeAsync();
}

public class OrderScenarioTests : IClassFixture<AlbaHostFixture>
{
    private readonly AlbaHostFixture _fixture;
    public OrderScenarioTests(AlbaHostFixture fixture) => _fixture = fixture;

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetOrder_ExistingId_Returns200WithBody()
    {
        await _fixture.Host.Scenario(s =>
        {
            s.Get.Url("/api/orders/ORD-001");
            s.StatusCodeShouldBe(200);
            s.ContentTypeShouldBe("application/json; charset=utf-8");
            s.Body.ShouldContain("ORD-001");
        });
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task PlaceOrder_InvalidBody_Returns400WithProblemDetails()
    {
        await _fixture.Host.Scenario(s =>
        {
            s.Post.Json(new { customerId = "", quantity = -1 })
                  .ToUrl("/api/orders");
            s.StatusCodeShouldBe(400);
            s.Body.ShouldContain("customerId");
        });
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Alba's `Scenario` DSL produces test methods that read like an HTTP specification sheet, making test intent clear to non-engineers during code reviews, but Alba wraps `WebApplicationFactory` and adds its own request/response pipeline abstractions that can mask low-level behaviour such as custom middleware execution order or response streaming; for scenarios that require asserting on raw response headers or inspecting middleware pipeline state, falling back to the underlying `HttpClient` directly is necessary.

**Pattern 387** — `NetArchTest` fluent rule chains to enforce dependency inversion and layer boundaries as executable tests
```csharp
using NetArchTest.Rules;

[Fact]
public void DomainLayer_ShouldNot_DependOnInfrastructure()
{
    var types = Types.InAssembly(typeof(Order).Assembly);

    var result = types
        .That()
        .ResideInNamespace("MyApp.Domain")
        .ShouldNot()
        .HaveDependencyOnAny(
            "MyApp.Infrastructure",
            "MyApp.Persistence",
            "Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore")
        .GetResult();

    var violations = result.FailingTypes?.Select(t => t.FullName) ?? [];
    result.IsSuccessful.Should().BeTrue(
        because: $"domain types must not reference infrastructure. " +
                 $"Violations: {string.Join(", ", violations)}");
}

[Fact]
public void ApplicationServices_ShouldImplement_InterfaceInDomainLayer()
{
    var result = Types
        .InAssembly(typeof(OrderService).Assembly)
        .That()
        .ResideInNamespace("MyApp.Application")
        .And().AreClasses()
        .And().ImplementInterface(typeof(IOrderService))
        .Should()
        .HaveName().EndingWith("Service")
        .GetResult();

    result.IsSuccessful.Should().BeTrue();
}
```
Tradeoff: Architecture rule tests catch dependency inversions at compile/test time rather than code review time, preventing infrastructure leakage into the domain layer from accumulating across sprints; the risk is that `Types.InAssembly(typeof(T).Assembly)` only scans assemblies loaded into the current `AppDomain` at test startup, so types in assemblies that are lazy-loaded or referenced only at runtime are silently excluded, requiring an explicit `Types.InAssemblies(new[] { domainAssembly, appAssembly })` enumeration to achieve exhaustive coverage.

**Pattern 388** — `Stryker.NET` stryker-config with `since` incremental mutation gate and `thresholds.break` to fail the PR pipeline on low kill rate
```csharp
// stryker-config.json — committed to repo root
// {
//   "stryker-config": {
//     "project": "src/MyApp.Domain/MyApp.Domain.csproj",
//     "test-projects": ["tests/MyApp.Domain.Tests/MyApp.Domain.Tests.csproj"],
//     "reporters": ["html", "json", "progress"],
//     "thresholds": { "high": 85, "low": 75, "break": 70 },
//     "mutate": ["src/MyApp.Domain/**/*.cs",
//                "!src/MyApp.Domain/**/*.Designer.cs"],
//     "since": { "enabled": true, "git-diff-tag": "refs/heads/main" }
//   }
// }

// Domain class under mutation test:
public class DiscountCalculator
{
    public decimal Calculate(string tier, decimal price)
    {
        if (price <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(price));
        return tier switch
        {
            "PREMIUM" => price * 0.90m,
            "TRIAL"   => price * 0.50m,
            _         => price
        };
    }
}

// Tests that kill boundary mutants (price <= 0 boundary, switch arms):
[Theory]
[InlineData("PREMIUM", 100, 90)]
[InlineData("TRIAL",   100, 50)]
[InlineData("STANDARD",100, 100)]
public void Calculate_ReturnsExpectedDiscount(
    string tier, decimal price, decimal expected)
    => new DiscountCalculator().Calculate(tier, price).Should().Be(expected);

[Fact]
public void Calculate_ZeroPrice_ThrowsArgumentOutOfRange()
    => FluentActions
        .Invoking(() => new DiscountCalculator().Calculate("PREMIUM", 0))
        .Should().Throw<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>();
```
Tradeoff: The `"since"` incremental mode limits Stryker to mutating only files changed since the base branch, reducing mutation test runtime from hours to minutes on large codebases, but incremental mode misses mutants in unchanged files that are indirectly affected by a behavioural change in a refactored caller; a weekly full-project Stryker run in a scheduled pipeline job complements the incremental PR gate to maintain long-term mutation coverage baseline accuracy.

**Pattern 389** — `Respawn` schema-preserving database checkpoint reset between integration tests for fast tear-down without container restart
```csharp
// NuGet: Respawn

public class OrderRepositoryTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly SqlConnection _connection;
    private Respawner _respawner = null!;

    public OrderRepositoryTests()
    {
        _connection = new SqlConnection(
            "Server=localhost,1433;Database=OrderDb_Test;" +
            "User=sa;Password=P@ssw0rd;TrustServerCertificate=true");
    }

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        await _connection.OpenAsync();
        _respawner = await Respawner.CreateAsync(_connection,
            new RespawnerOptions
            {
                TablesToIgnore = ["__EFMigrationsHistory", "SeedData"],
                SchemasToInclude = ["dbo"],
                DbAdapter = DbAdapter.SqlServer
            });
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        await _respawner.ResetAsync(_connection);
        await _connection.DisposeAsync();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task SaveOrder_NewOrder_PersistsAndRetrievesCorrectly()
    {
        var repo = new OrderRepository(_connection);
        var order = new Order
            { Id = "ORD-1", CustomerId = "CUST-1", Total = 99.99m };

        await repo.SaveAsync(order);
        var retrieved = await repo.GetByIdAsync("ORD-1");

        retrieved.Should().BeEquivalentTo(order);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `Respawn` deletes rows in foreign-key–safe dependency order and preserves schema, making reset ~10x faster than dropping/recreating the database, but `Respawner.CreateAsync` must be called after the connection is open and reads the live schema to build the delete script; if DDL migrations run after `CreateAsync` is called (e.g., in a shared fixture where the schema evolves mid-run), Respawn's cached delete script becomes stale and may leave orphaned rows in newly added tables until the respawner is recreated.

**Pattern 390** — `TUnit` `[ClassDataSource]` with `Shared = SharedType.None` for isolated parallel data-row test execution with per-row lifecycle
```csharp
// TUnit: modern C# test framework with source generators
// NuGet: TUnit, TUnit.Assertions

public class OrderTestData
{
    public string CustomerId { get; set; } = "";
    public string Sku { get; set; } = "";
    public int Quantity { get; set; }
    public decimal ExpectedTotal { get; set; }
}

public class OrderTestDataSource : IEnumerable<OrderTestData>
{
    public IEnumerator<OrderTestData> GetEnumerator()
    {
        yield return new OrderTestData
            { CustomerId = "CUST-1", Sku = "SKU-A",
              Quantity = 2, ExpectedTotal = 19.98m };
        yield return new OrderTestData
            { CustomerId = "CUST-2", Sku = "SKU-B",
              Quantity = 1, ExpectedTotal = 49.99m };
        yield return new OrderTestData
            { CustomerId = "CUST-3", Sku = "SKU-C",
              Quantity = 3, ExpectedTotal = 29.97m };
    }
    IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() => GetEnumerator();
}

[Test]
[ClassDataSource<OrderTestDataSource>(Shared = SharedType.None)]
public async Task PlaceOrder_ValidData_ReturnsExpectedTotal(OrderTestData data)
{
    // Each test row gets its own OrderTestData instance — no shared-state risk
    var service = new OrderService(new InMemoryInventory());
    var order = await service.PlaceOrderAsync(
        data.CustomerId, data.Sku, data.Quantity);

    await Assert.That(order.Total).IsEqualTo(data.ExpectedTotal);
}
```
Tradeoff: TUnit's `ClassDataSource` with `Shared = SharedType.None` provides a fresh data-class instance per test row, eliminating the cross-row state leakage risk that plagues shared `IClassFixture` objects in xUnit when test data is mutable; the trade-off is that TUnit uses source generators at compile time which requires the test project to reference `TUnit.SourceGenerator` and increases cold-build times, so teams on tight CI build-time budgets should measure incremental build overhead before adopting TUnit alongside existing xUnit/NUnit projects in the same solution.

### Community Gotchas

**G61** — Moq `SetupSequence` does not reset between test runs when the mock is declared as a `static readonly` field — later tests silently consume stale sequence entries left over from earlier tests
Why this matters: A developer declares `private static readonly Mock<IPaymentGateway> _paymentMock = new()` as a static field to avoid repeated construction overhead. A first test calls `SetupSequence` with three entries (throw, throw, return success) and verifies three calls. The sequence is exhausted after the first test. A second test in the same class also calls `SetupSequence` on the same static instance, but Moq's `SetupSequence` call appends to the internal setup chain rather than replacing it. The second test unexpectedly encounters the stale setup from the first test, causing intermittent failures that are sensitive to test execution order and only manifest when tests run in a specific sequence.
Fix: Never declare `Mock<T>` instances as `static` or `static readonly` fields. Instantiate mocks in the constructor or `[SetUp]`/`InitializeAsync` method so every test starts with a fresh, clean mock. If construction is genuinely expensive, call `_mock.Reset()` (Moq's `Mock.Reset()` clears all setups and verifications) at the start of each test rather than sharing the same instance across the class lifecycle.

**G62** — FluentAssertions `WithStrictOrdering` applied to `BeEquivalentTo` on a collection of objects with `DateTime` members fails intermittently when timestamps are generated during collection construction and a millisecond boundary is crossed between `expected` and `actual`
Why this matters: A test asserts `actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected, opts => opts.WithStrictOrdering())` where each element contains a `CreatedAt` timestamp set to `DateTime.UtcNow` during `new Order(...)`. Between the construction of `expected` and `actual`, a millisecond boundary is crossed, so `expected[0].CreatedAt` is `09:00:00.999` and `actual[0].CreatedAt` is `09:00:01.000`. The strict ordering comparison computes element index by sort key; because timestamps differ, it maps `actual[0]` to a different expected row, producing a cascade of false mismatches across all elements that disappear when the test is re-run.
Fix: Use `opts.Excluding(o => o.CreatedAt)` or `opts.Using<DateTime>(ctx => ctx.Subject.Date.Should().Be(ctx.Expectation.Date)).WhenTypeIs<DateTime>()` to compare only the date component for timestamp fields that vary between construction and assertion. For integration tests where the precise time is relevant, inject a `TimeProvider` or `FakeTimeProvider` into the SUT and freeze the clock before constructing both expected and actual objects.

**G63** — `Respawn` `ResetAsync` called on a connection with an open ambient `TransactionScope` silently no-ops — rows are not deleted, and the next test inherits leftover data
Why this matters: A developer wraps each test in `using var scope = new TransactionScope(TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled)` for automatic rollback and also calls `_respawner.ResetAsync(_connection)` in `DisposeAsync` as a belt-and-suspenders guard. Respawn generates `DELETE FROM` statements inside a new transaction on the same connection, but the ambient `TransactionScope` enrols that transaction as a nested participant. On SQL Server, when the outer scope is not completed (it is rolled back in `Dispose`), the inner deletes are also rolled back, leaving the database in the pre-reset state. The next test class that does not use `TransactionScope` sees all the leftover rows, producing ordering-dependent test failures.
Fix: Never combine `TransactionScope` rollback with `Respawn` in the same test fixture. Choose one isolation strategy: either `TransactionScope` for rollback-based isolation (faster, no `DELETE` cost) or `Respawn.ResetAsync` for delete-based isolation (works with distributed operations and multiple connections). If both mechanisms coexist in the codebase, ensure `scope.Dispose()` is called before `ResetAsync`, or suppress the ambient transaction for the reset call using `new TransactionScope(TransactionScopeOption.Suppress)`.

**G64** — `BenchmarkDotNet` `[GlobalSetup]` method that throws an exception causes all subsequent benchmarks in the class to report `0 ns / 0 B` rather than a setup failure, hiding the root cause in the HTML report
Why this matters: A `[GlobalSetup]` method calls `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(File.ReadAllText("data.json"))` to load test fixtures. On CI the file path is relative and resolves to a different working directory, throwing `FileNotFoundException`. BenchmarkDotNet catches the exception internally, marks the setup as failed, and outputs `0 ns` for all `[Benchmark]` methods in that class. The HTML report shows valid-looking rows with zero measurements that appear to be outlier-filtered results rather than a setup failure. The developer interprets the report as evidence of zero allocation rather than an uninitialized benchmark, wasting time optimising code that was never actually measured.
Fix: Always use `Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "data.json")` for fixture files in `[GlobalSetup]`, and add an explicit null check with `throw new InvalidOperationException("Setup failed: fixture data is null — verify data.json is set to Copy Always in project properties")` before the benchmarks proceed. Run benchmarks locally once with `-f "*"` filter before merging to catch setup failures before they produce silent zero-measurement CI reports.

**G65** — `NetArchTest` `GetResult().FailingTypes` returns `null` (not an empty list) when all types pass the rule — calling `.Select(...)` on a passing result causes `NullReferenceException` inside the `because` string formatter
Why this matters: A developer writes `result.FailingTypes.Select(t => t.FullName)` inside the `because` argument of `result.IsSuccessful.Should().BeTrue(because: $"violations: {string.Join(", ", result.FailingTypes.Select(t => t.FullName))}")`. When all types pass the rule, `result.FailingTypes` is `null`, so the LINQ `.Select(...)` throws `NullReferenceException` during message construction. Because FluentAssertions evaluates the `because` string before checking `IsSuccessful`, the exception is thrown even on a fully passing test, causing every successful architecture test to fail with a confusing null-reference error rather than a green result.
Fix: Always null-coalesce `FailingTypes` before formatting: `result.FailingTypes?.Select(t => t.FullName) ?? Enumerable.Empty<string>()`. A reusable helper method `FormatViolations(TestResult r) => string.Join(", ", r.FailingTypes?.Select(t => t.FullName) ?? [])` centralises the null guard and prevents the pattern from being repeated across all architecture tests in the project.
