## Cycle 68 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 406** — xUnit v3 `IAsyncEnumerable<object[]>` `ClassData` for async-sourced theory rows
```csharp
public class ProductTheoryData : IAsyncEnumerable<object[]>
{
    private readonly IProductRepository _repo;

    public ProductTheoryData(IProductRepository repo) => _repo = repo;

    public async IAsyncEnumerator<object[]> GetAsyncEnumerator(
        CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        await foreach (var p in _repo.GetAllAsync(ct))
        {
            yield return new object[] { p.Id, p.Sku, p.Price };
        }
    }
}

[Theory]
[ClassData(typeof(ProductTheoryData))]
public async Task PriceCalculator_AllProducts_ProducesPositiveTotal(
    int id, string sku, decimal price)
{
    var result = await _calculator.ComputeTaxAsync(id, price);
    result.Total.Should().BeGreaterThan(0m,
        because: $"product {sku} price {price} must yield positive tax-inclusive total");
}
```
Tradeoff: `IAsyncEnumerable<object[]>` theory data integrates naturally with async repositories but requires xUnit v3 (v2 does not support async `IEnumerable` sources natively); wrapping a real repository makes the theory dependent on external state, so prefer an in-memory stub or a local JSON fixture when the dataset must remain deterministic across CI runs.

**Pattern 407** — FluentAssertions `AssertionScope` for batching multiple failures into one report
```csharp
[Fact]
public void OrderDto_MappedFromOrder_AllFieldsCorrect()
{
    var order = OrderFactory.Create(
        id: 42, status: OrderStatus.Shipped, total: 199.99m);
    var dto = _mapper.Map<OrderDto>(order);

    using (new AssertionScope())
    {
        dto.Id.Should().Be(order.Id);
        dto.Status.Should().Be("Shipped");
        dto.Total.Should().Be(order.Total);
        dto.ShippedAt.Should().NotBeNull(
            because: "shipped orders must carry a ShippedAt timestamp");
        dto.CustomerName.Should().NotBeNullOrWhiteSpace();
        dto.LineItems.Should().HaveCount(order.Lines.Count);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `AssertionScope` collects all failures inside the `using` block and reports them together, eliminating the need to re-run the test after fixing each individual assertion in sequence; the downside is that a failure in an early assertion that corrupts the object state (e.g., `NullReferenceException` in a later `dto.LineItems.Count`) will surface as a misleading second failure rather than cleanly indicating the root cause, so guard nullable navigation paths before asserting on their members.

**Pattern 408** — Moq `Capture<T>` for argument capture without `Callback` side effects
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task PlaceOrder_PublishesCorrectEvent()
{
    OrderPlacedEvent? capturedEvent = null;
    var capture = new CaptureMatch<OrderPlacedEvent>(e => capturedEvent = e);
    _busMock
        .Setup(b => b.PublishAsync(Capture.With(capture), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
        .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

    await _sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new PlaceOrderCommand { ProductId = 7, Qty = 3 });

    capturedEvent.Should().NotBeNull();
    capturedEvent!.ProductId.Should().Be(7);
    capturedEvent.Quantity.Should().Be(3);
    capturedEvent.OccurredAt.Should().BeCloseTo(
        DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, precision: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
}
```
Tradeoff: `Capture.With(new CaptureMatch<T>(...))` extracts the argument for post-call assertion without relying on `Callback`, which can silently suppress exceptions if the callback itself throws; the captured value is set synchronously during `Setup` invocation so it is always available after `await`, but the approach requires a field-level or closure variable per captured argument, making tests with multiple distinct captured arguments more verbose than a single `Callback` with a local tuple.

**Pattern 409** — NUnit `[ValueSource]` with a computed Fibonacci boundary sequence
```csharp
public class FibonacciInputs
{
    public static IEnumerable<long> BoundaryValues()
    {
        long a = 0, b = 1;
        while (b <= 1_000_000L)
        {
            yield return b;
            (a, b) = (b, a + b);
        }
        yield return long.MaxValue; // overflow sentinel
    }
}

[TestFixture]
public class FibonacciCalculatorTests
{
    [Test]
    public void Compute_FibonacciBoundaryInputs_NeverOverflows(
        [ValueSource(typeof(FibonacciInputs), nameof(FibonacciInputs.BoundaryValues))] long n)
    {
        Assert.DoesNotThrow(() => FibonacciCalculator.Compute(n),
            message: $"Compute({n}) must not throw on Fibonacci boundary value");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `[ValueSource]` with a generator method keeps boundary definitions co-located with domain knowledge (Fibonacci growth) and avoids duplicating a hardcoded list across multiple test methods; the generator executes at discovery time, so any exception in `BoundaryValues()` causes test discovery to fail entirely rather than marking individual cases, meaning defensive guards inside the generator are mandatory.

**Pattern 410** — Testcontainers.NET custom `IWaitUntil` strategy for Elasticsearch green-cluster health
```csharp
public sealed class ElasticsearchHealthWait : IWaitUntil
{
    public async Task<bool> UntilAsync(IContainer container)
    {
        var (exitCode, stdout, _) = await container.ExecAsync(new[]
        {
            "curl", "-s", "-o", "/dev/null", "-w", "%{http_code}",
            "http://localhost:9200/_cluster/health?wait_for_status=green&timeout=1s"
        });
        return exitCode == 0 && stdout.Trim() == "200";
    }
}

// In test fixture
var esContainer = new ContainerBuilder()
    .WithImage("docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.13.0")
    .WithEnvironment("discovery.type", "single-node")
    .WithEnvironment("xpack.security.enabled", "false")
    .WithPortBinding(9200, true)
    .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer()
        .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPath("/_cluster/health")
            .ForStatusCode(HttpStatusCode.OK))
        .AddCustomWaitStrategy(new ElasticsearchHealthWait()))
    .Build();
```
Tradeoff: A custom `IWaitUntil` using `ExecAsync` to poll Elasticsearch's cluster health endpoint avoids timing-based `Thread.Sleep` waits and correctly handles delayed green state in single-node deployments; the `ExecAsync` approach requires `curl` to be present in the image (true for the official Elasticsearch image) — if the image changes its base layer and removes `curl`, the wait strategy silently times out rather than giving a meaningful diagnostic message, so pair it with `.WithStartupCallback` logging.

**Pattern 411** — AutoFixture `CompositeCustomization` grouping domain-specific customizations
```csharp
public class MoneyCustomization : ICustomization
{
    public void Customize(IFixture fixture)
    {
        fixture.Customize<Money>(c => c.FromFactory(() =>
            new Money(Math.Abs(fixture.Create<decimal>()) % 10000m + 0.01m,
                      fixture.Create<CurrencyCode>())));
    }
}

public class OrderCustomization : ICustomization
{
    public void Customize(IFixture fixture)
    {
        fixture.Customize<Order>(c => c
            .With(o => o.Status, OrderStatus.Pending)
            .Without(o => o.ShippedAt));
    }
}

public class DomainCustomization : CompositeCustomization
{
    public DomainCustomization()
        : base(new MoneyCustomization(), new OrderCustomization()) { }
}

// In test
var fixture = new Fixture().Customize(new DomainCustomization());
var order = fixture.Create<Order>();
```
Tradeoff: `CompositeCustomization` aggregates multiple single-responsibility customizations into one injectable unit, making test setup a one-liner while keeping each customization independently testable; the composite applies customizations in declaration order, so if `OrderCustomization` depends on `Money` being already customized, reversing the order silently produces orders with un-customized `Money` values — document the dependency order in an XML comment or enforce it via an integration test of the customization itself.

**Pattern 412** — xUnit v3 `ITestOutputHelper` structured JSON emission for CI log parsing
```csharp
public class PaymentServiceTests(ITestOutputHelper output)
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessPayment_ValidCard_ReturnsAuthorized()
    {
        var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        var response = await _sut.ProcessAsync(
            new PaymentRequest { Amount = 100m, CardToken = "tok_valid" });
        stopwatch.Stop();

        output.WriteLine(JsonSerializer.Serialize(new
        {
            test    = nameof(ProcessPayment_ValidCard_ReturnsAuthorized),
            elapsed = stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds,
            status  = response.Status.ToString(),
            traceId = response.TraceId
        }));

        response.Status.Should().Be(PaymentStatus.Authorized);
        response.TraceId.Should().NotBeEmpty();
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Emitting structured JSON via `ITestOutputHelper.WriteLine` enables log-parsing pipelines (e.g., Azure DevOps log analytics, Datadog CI Visibility) to extract per-test latency and trace IDs without a separate telemetry SDK; the output is only flushed when the test completes (pass or fail), so an infinite-hang test will produce no log output — add a `[Timeout]` attribute or wrap the await with `Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))` to guarantee output on timeout.

**Pattern 413** — FluentAssertions `BeEquivalentTo` with deep nested `Excluding` path expressions
```csharp
[Fact]
public void GetOrderResponse_MapsCorrectly_ExcludingAuditFields()
{
    var order = OrderBuilder.Build(id: 55);
    var response = _mapper.Map<GetOrderResponse>(order);

    response.Should().BeEquivalentTo(order, opts => opts
        .ExcludingMissingMembers()
        .Excluding(o => o.CreatedAt)
        .Excluding(o => o.UpdatedAt)
        .Excluding(o => o.Lines[0].InternalSku)
        .For(o => o.Lines).Exclude(l => l.AuditHash)
        .WithStrictOrdering());
}
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `.Excluding` with `.For(...).Exclude(...)` precisely scopes exclusions to nested collection elements without blanket exclusion of entire sub-trees, preventing silent regressions where newly added audit fields on `OrderLine` would otherwise slip through unverified; using `[0]` in a path expression (`o.Lines[0].InternalSku`) applies the exclusion to all elements of the collection in FluentAssertions v6+, but this behaviour changed from v5 where only the first element was excluded — confirm the FA version before relying on collection-wide indexed exclusions.

**Pattern 414** — Moq `Protected()` setup for `HttpMessageHandler`-derived base handler
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task GetProduct_Returns404_ThrowsNotFoundException()
{
    var handlerMock = new Mock<HttpMessageHandler>(MockBehavior.Strict);
    handlerMock
        .Protected()
        .Setup<Task<HttpResponseMessage>>(
            "SendAsync",
            ItExpr.IsAny<HttpRequestMessage>(),
            ItExpr.IsAny<CancellationToken>())
        .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.NotFound)
        {
            Content = new StringContent("{\"detail\":\"not found\"}")
        });

    var client = new HttpClient(handlerMock.Object)
        { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com") };
    var sut = new ProductApiClient(client);

    await sut.Invoking(s => s.GetProductAsync(99))
             .Should().ThrowAsync<NotFoundException>()
             .WithMessage("*99*");
}
```
Tradeoff: Mocking `HttpMessageHandler.SendAsync` via `Protected()` lets you unit-test `HttpClient`-consuming services without a live endpoint; using `ItExpr` (not `It`) for protected member matchers is mandatory and easy to forget — `It.IsAny<>` compiles but silently never matches, causing the mock to throw `MockException: unexpected invocation` on the first `SendAsync` call instead of returning the configured response.

**Pattern 415** — NUnit `[TestFixtureSource]` for parameterized database-provider fixtures
```csharp
public class DatabaseFixtureArgs
{
    public static IEnumerable<TestFixtureData> Providers()
    {
        yield return new TestFixtureData("SqlServer",
            "Server=localhost,1433;Database=TestDb;User=sa;Password=Test!1234")
            .SetName("SqlServer");
        yield return new TestFixtureData("PostgreSQL",
            "Host=localhost;Port=5432;Database=testdb;Username=test;Password=test")
            .SetName("PostgreSQL");
    }
}

[TestFixtureSource(typeof(DatabaseFixtureArgs), nameof(DatabaseFixtureArgs.Providers))]
public class RepositoryContractTests(string provider, string connectionString)
{
    private IOrderRepository _repo = null!;

    [OneTimeSetUp]
    public async Task SetUp()
    {
        _repo = RepositoryFactory.Create(provider, connectionString);
        await _repo.MigrateAsync();
    }

    [Test]
    public async Task SaveAndRetrieve_Order_RoundTripsCorrectly()
    {
        var order = OrderFactory.Create();
        await _repo.SaveAsync(order);
        var loaded = await _repo.GetByIdAsync(order.Id);
        loaded.Should().BeEquivalentTo(order);
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: `[TestFixtureSource]` instantiates the entire fixture class once per provider, making provider-level `[OneTimeSetUp]` and `[OneTimeTearDown]` lifecycle hooks run per provider independently; the tradeoff is that NUnit's parallel execution model runs each parameterised fixture as a separate fixture type, so `--workers` counts multiply per provider — for three providers with ten workers each, thirty threads may contend on a shared Docker host, degrading Testcontainers startup performance.

**Pattern 416** — NSubstitute `ForPartsOf<T>` for partial abstract-class substitution in template-method tests
```csharp
public abstract class ReportGeneratorBase
{
    public string Generate(ReportRequest request)
    {
        var data   = LoadData(request);      // abstract — will be substituted
        var header = BuildHeader(request);   // concrete — real implementation
        return $"{header}\n{RenderRows(data)}";
    }

    protected abstract IEnumerable<ReportRow> LoadData(ReportRequest request);

    protected virtual string BuildHeader(ReportRequest req)
        => $"Report: {req.Title} — {DateTime.UtcNow:yyyy-MM-dd}";
}

[Fact]
public void Generate_WithStubbedData_RendersHeaderFromConcreteImpl()
{
    var sub = Substitute.ForPartsOf<ReportGeneratorBase>();
    sub.Configure().LoadData(Arg.Any<ReportRequest>())
       .Returns(new[] { new ReportRow("Row1", 42m) });

    var result = sub.Generate(new ReportRequest { Title = "Q1 Sales" });

    result.Should().Contain("Q1 Sales");
    result.Should().Contain("Row1");
}
```
Tradeoff: `ForPartsOf<T>` allows the concrete `BuildHeader` method to execute normally while stubbing the abstract `LoadData`, enabling contract tests that verify the template-method pattern without a concrete subclass; NSubstitute generates the partial substitute via `Castle.DynamicProxy`, so non-virtual concrete methods cannot be intercepted and will always run — document this to avoid confusion when contributors later make methods non-virtual as a "performance optimization".

**Pattern 417** — Testcontainers.NET `WithEnvironment` and `IConfiguration` secrets injection after container startup
```csharp
public class AppConfigurationFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    public IConfiguration Configuration { get; private set; } = null!;
    private IContainer _vaultContainer = null!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _vaultContainer = new ContainerBuilder()
            .WithImage("hashicorp/vault:1.16")
            .WithEnvironment("VAULT_DEV_ROOT_TOKEN_ID", "test-root-token")
            .WithEnvironment("VAULT_DEV_LISTEN_ADDRESS", "0.0.0.0:8200")
            .WithPortBinding(8200, true)
            .WithWaitStrategy(Wait.ForUnixContainer()
                .UntilHttpRequestIsSucceeded(r => r.ForPath("/v1/sys/health")))
            .Build();

        await _vaultContainer.StartAsync();

        var vaultPort = _vaultContainer.GetMappedPublicPort(8200);
        Configuration = new ConfigurationBuilder()
            .AddInMemoryCollection(new Dictionary<string, string?>
            {
                ["Vault:Address"] = $"http://localhost:{vaultPort}",
                ["Vault:Token"]   = "test-root-token"
            })
            .Build();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync() => await _vaultContainer.DisposeAsync();
}
```
Tradeoff: Injecting runtime container ports into `IConfiguration` via `AddInMemoryCollection` after container startup bridges Testcontainers' dynamic port allocation with the `IOptions<T>` pattern used by production code; the `Configuration` property is only valid after `InitializeAsync` completes, so accessing it in a constructor (before xUnit's `IAsyncLifetime` lifecycle hook fires) returns `null` — validate in `InitializeAsync` with a null-guard and throw a descriptive `InvalidOperationException` rather than relying on NRE stack traces.

**Pattern 418** — AutoFixture `OmitOnRecursionBehavior` vs custom `ISpecimenBuilder` — performance and diagnostic tradeoff
```csharp
// Approach A: OmitOnRecursionBehavior (simple, fast, produces null children)
var fixtureA = new Fixture();
fixtureA.Behaviors.OfType<ThrowingRecursionBehavior>().ToList()
        .ForEach(b => fixtureA.Behaviors.Remove(b));
fixtureA.Behaviors.Add(new OmitOnRecursionBehavior(recursionDepth: 2));
var categoryA = fixtureA.Create<Category>(); // Children null beyond depth 2

// Approach B: Custom ISpecimenBuilder (explicit depth, non-null empty collections)
public class BoundedCategoryBuilder : ISpecimenBuilder
{
    private int _depth;
    private readonly int _max;
    public BoundedCategoryBuilder(int max = 2) => _max = max;

    public object Create(object request, ISpecimenContext ctx)
    {
        if (request is not Type t || t != typeof(Category)) return new NoSpecimen();
        if (++_depth > _max) { _depth--; return new Category { Children = [] }; }
        var result = ctx.Resolve(typeof(Category));
        _depth--;
        return result;
    }
}

var fixtureB = new Fixture();
fixtureB.Customizations.Add(new BoundedCategoryBuilder(max: 3));
var categoryB = fixtureB.Create<Category>(); // Children is [] not null at max depth
```
Tradeoff: `OmitOnRecursionBehavior` is approximately three times faster than a custom `ISpecimenBuilder` for deep recursive graphs because it short-circuits at the behavior pipeline level; the downside is that omitted navigation properties silently produce `null` children rather than empty collections, which can mask `NullReferenceException` bugs in code that expects `ICollection<T>` to always be non-null — use a custom builder when the production invariant requires non-null empty collections.

**Pattern 419** — xUnit v3 `TheoryData<T1, T2, T3>` strongly-typed theory rows replacing `object[]`
```csharp
public class DiscountTheoryData : TheoryData<decimal, string, decimal>
{
    public DiscountTheoryData()
    {
        Add(100m,   "SAVE10",   90m);    // 10% off
        Add(200m,   "SAVE20",  160m);    // 20% off
        Add(50m,    "FREESHIP", 50m);    // free shipping only, price unchanged
        Add(0m,     "SAVE10",    0m);    // zero-price edge case
        Add(1000m,  "BOGO",    500m);    // buy one get one
    }
}

[Theory]
[ClassData(typeof(DiscountTheoryData))]
public void ApplyDiscount_KnownCodes_ProducesCorrectPrice(
    decimal originalPrice, string couponCode, decimal expectedPrice)
{
    var result = _discountEngine.Apply(originalPrice, couponCode);

    result.FinalPrice.Should().Be(expectedPrice,
        because: $"coupon '{couponCode}' on {originalPrice:C} should yield {expectedPrice:C}");
}
```
Tradeoff: `TheoryData<T1, T2, T3>` provides compile-time type safety and IDE autocompletion when adding rows, catching type mismatches at build time rather than at test runtime; it requires the type parameters to match the theory method signature exactly — a mismatch between `TheoryData<decimal, string, decimal>` and a method parameter typed as `double` produces a `System.InvalidCastException` at runtime (not compile time) because xUnit's serialization pipeline boxes values, so explicit `decimal` literals (`100m`) rather than integer literals (`100`) are mandatory.

**Pattern 420** — FluentAssertions `Monitor()` for event-assertion with `Should().Raise()`
```csharp
[Fact]
public void CancelOrder_RaisesOrderCancelledEvent_WithCorrectArgs()
{
    var order = OrderFactory.CreatePending(id: 7);
    using var monitor = order.Monitor();

    order.Cancel(reason: "Customer request");

    monitor.Should()
           .Raise(nameof(Order.OrderCancelled))
           .WithArgs<OrderCancelledEventArgs>(args =>
               args.OrderId == 7 &&
               args.Reason  == "Customer request" &&
               args.CancelledAt <= DateTimeOffset.UtcNow);

    monitor.Should().NotRaise(nameof(Order.OrderShipped));
}
```
Tradeoff: `Monitor()` captures events raised synchronously on the monitored object throughout the `using` block lifetime, enabling post-hoc assertion on both which events were raised and the exact `EventArgs` values; the monitor only captures events raised after `Monitor()` is called — events raised during construction are invisible, and `monitor.Should().NotRaise(...)` passes vacuously for event names that do not match any public event on the type, so confirm the event name string before treating a `NotRaise` assertion as meaningful.

### Community Gotchas

**G71** — xUnit `[Theory]` with `[InlineData(null)]` on a nullable struct parameter causes `ArgumentException` during test discovery rather than a test failure
Why this matters: A developer adds `[InlineData(null)]` to test the null-handling path of a method accepting `int?`. xUnit's default serialization pipeline attempts to deserialise the boxed `null` constant from the attribute metadata into `Nullable<int>` using `Convert.ChangeType`, which does not support null-to-nullable-struct conversion and throws `ArgumentException` during test discovery (not execution). The test runner marks the entire theory as a discovery error, so it vanishes from the test list entirely without a red indicator — the null-path appears "covered" when it is in fact never run.
Fix: Use `[InlineData((int?)null)]` which forces the C# compiler to emit the value as a typed nullable literal rather than a bare `null`, or switch to `[MemberData(nameof(NullIntCases))]` where `NullIntCases` yields `new object?[] { (int?)null }`. For xUnit v3, use `TheoryData<int?>` which handles nullable struct rows correctly without a cast.

**G72** — FluentAssertions v7 `BeEquivalentTo` treats `string` as `IEnumerable<char>` when comparing `object`-typed properties, causing spurious element-by-element character-level failure messages
Why this matters: A developer upgrades from FluentAssertions v6 to v7 and has an assertion like `actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected)` where both objects have an `object`-typed property holding a `string`. In v7, the default equivalency strategy honours the declared type (`object`) and falls through to structural equivalency which, for `string`, applies the `IEnumerable<char>` rule and compares character by character. A string like `"Hello"` against `"Hello "` (trailing space) now reports five char-level differences rather than one string difference, obscuring the actual mismatch in CI output.
Fix: Use `opts => opts.ComparingByValue<string>()` to force `string` comparisons to use value equality rather than enumerable equivalence when properties are typed as `object`. Alternatively, strongly-type DTO properties as `string` rather than `object` so FluentAssertions' type-selection heuristic picks the string comparator directly.

**G73** — Moq `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` is required in setups that must match calls originating from `HttpContext.RequestAborted`; a literal `default(CancellationToken)` in the setup does not match a non-default token and `MockBehavior.Default` silently returns `null`
Why this matters: A developer sets up `.Setup(s => s.GetAsync(id, default(CancellationToken)))` expecting to match calls from the SUT. When the SUT passes `HttpContext.RequestAborted` (a non-default, non-cancelled token), Moq's literal argument matcher for structs fails to match. `MockBehavior.Default` silently returns `default(Task<T>)` (i.e., `null`), causing `NullReferenceException` downstream in the SUT rather than in the test assertion, making the failure appear unrelated to the mock setup.
Fix: Always use `It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()` in mock setups unless the test specifically validates cancellation propagation. When testing cancellation, use a named `CancellationTokenSource` and pass its `.Token` explicitly to both the SUT and the setup matcher via `It.Is<CancellationToken>(ct => ct == cts.Token)`.

**G74** — NUnit `[OneTimeSetUp]` with a static `Lazy<T>` resource caches a faulted exception permanently when initialization fails transiently, causing all subsequent test runs to fail until the process is restarted
Why this matters: A developer uses a static `Lazy<DbConnection>` with the default `LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication` to share an expensive connection across fixture instances in a `[Parallelizable(ParallelScope.All)]` suite. When the factory throws (e.g., connection timeout), the `Lazy<T>` enters a faulted state permanently, re-throwing the cached exception on every subsequent access even after the transient failure has cleared. All remaining tests in the suite fail with the original `TimeoutException` wrapped in a `LazyInitializationException`.
Fix: Use `LazyThreadSafetyMode.PublicationOnly` so that a faulted initialization does not cache the exception — concurrent accessors each retry independently. Better still, replace the static `Lazy<DbConnection>` with a per-class `IAsyncLifetime`-managed connection, eliminating the shared-static race entirely.

**G75** — Testcontainers.NET `IAsyncLifetime.DisposeAsync` ordering: xUnit disposes `IClassFixture<T>` before `ICollectionFixture<T>`, causing `ObjectDisposedException` when the collection fixture's container is accessed during class-fixture teardown SQL
Why this matters: A developer has a collection-scoped `DatabaseCollectionFixture` providing a shared Testcontainers Postgres container, and a class-scoped `SchemaClassFixture` that drops the test schema in `DisposeAsync`. When xUnit tears down the test class, it disposes `IClassFixture<SchemaClassFixture>` first, then disposes `ICollectionFixture<DatabaseCollectionFixture>`. However, if a parallel sibling class' collection fixture `DisposeAsync` has already torn down the container's port mapping, the schema-drop SQL in `SchemaClassFixture.DisposeAsync` throws `ObjectDisposedException` or `SocketException` with a misleading "TCP connection forcibly closed" message.
Fix: Ensure class fixtures performing teardown SQL create a fresh `NpgsqlConnection` from the connection string rather than reusing the collection fixture's long-lived connection, which may already be disposed. Add a defensive try/catch for `OperationCanceledException` and `ObjectDisposedException` in class-fixture `DisposeAsync`, logging a diagnostic warning rather than propagating the exception.

## Cycle 67 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 421** — xUnit `IAsyncLifetime` on a test class with `CancellationTokenSource` for per-test timeout enforcement
```csharp
public class OrderIntegrationTests : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private CancellationTokenSource _cts = default!;
    protected CancellationToken TestTimeout => _cts.Token;

    public Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    public Task DisposeAsync()
    {
        _cts.Dispose();
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task ProcessOrder_CompletesWithinSla()
    {
        Func<Task> act = async () => await _orderService.ProcessAsync(
            new OrderRequest { Sku = "SKU-001", Quantity = 1 },
            TestTimeout);

        await act.Should().CompleteWithinAsync(
            TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),
            because: "order processing must not exceed the 30-second SLA");
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Wiring `CancellationTokenSource` through `IAsyncLifetime.InitializeAsync` gives every test method a per-test deadline without relying on the framework's global test timeout (which aborts the entire run), providing actionable failure messages scoped to the individual test; the limitation is that `CancellationTokenSource` is not reset between `[Theory]` inline data rows — each row reuses the same `CTS` created in `InitializeAsync`, so on slow machines the token may be cancelled mid-run for later rows if an earlier row consumes most of the budget, requiring a longer timeout or a per-invocation `CTS`.

**Pattern 422** — NUnit `[Retry]` paired with `TestContext.CurrentRepeatCount` for structured flakiness logging
```csharp
[Test]
[Retry(3)]
public async Task SendNotification_DeliveredWithinSla()
{
    var attempt = TestContext.CurrentContext.CurrentRepeatCount + 1;
    TestContext.Out.WriteLine($"[Attempt {attempt}/3] started at {DateTime.UtcNow:O}");

    var sw     = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    var result = await _notificationService.SendAsync(
        new Notification { Recipient = "user@example.com", Body = "Test" });
    sw.Stop();

    TestContext.Out.WriteLine($"Elapsed: {sw.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");

    result.Delivered.Should().BeTrue(
        because: "notification service must confirm delivery");
    sw.Elapsed.Should().BeLessThan(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5),
        because: "delivery confirmation must arrive within the 5-second SLA");
}
```
Tradeoff: Logging `TestContext.CurrentContext.CurrentRepeatCount` per attempt makes each retry distinguishable in CI output, allowing a developer to identify which attempt succeeded and how long it took; the risk is that `[Retry]` silently masks real intermittent failures — use `TestContext.Out` timing data in a post-run flakiness dashboard to detect tests that pass only on retry 2 or 3, which is the signal to fix the underlying issue rather than relying on retries indefinitely.

**Pattern 423** — FluentAssertions `ExecutionTime()` and `CompleteWithinAsync` for SLA regression guards
```csharp
// Synchronous SLA assertion
Action computePricing = () =>
    _pricingEngine.ComputeAll(GenerateLineItems(count: 500));

computePricing.ExecutionTime().Should()
    .BeLessThanOrEqualTo(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200),
        because: "pricing computation for 500 items must meet the < 200 ms SLA");

// Async SLA assertion
Func<Task> computeAsync = async () =>
    await _pricingEngine.ComputeAllAsync(GenerateLineItems(count: 500));

await computeAsync.Should().CompleteWithinAsync(
    TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200),
    because: "async variant must also satisfy the 200 ms budget");
```
Tradeoff: `ExecutionTime()` / `CompleteWithinAsync` integrates performance guards directly in the unit test suite without requiring BenchmarkDotNet, making SLA regressions visible in the standard test run; these assertions are sensitive to CI machine load — a runner processing another job concurrently can make a 150 ms operation appear to take 400 ms, producing spurious failures, so use tolerances of 2–5× the target SLA in CI and reserve tight budget assertions for dedicated perf pipelines where CPU affinity is controlled.

**Pattern 424** — Moq `MockSequence` + `InSequence` for strict call-order verification across multiple mocks
```csharp
var sequence      = new MockSequence();
var repoMock      = new Mock<IOrderRepository>(MockBehavior.Strict);
var publisherMock = new Mock<IEventPublisher>(MockBehavior.Strict);

repoMock
    .InSequence(sequence)
    .Setup(r => r.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
    .ReturnsAsync(true);

publisherMock
    .InSequence(sequence)
    .Setup(p => p.PublishAsync(It.IsAny<OrderPlacedEvent>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
    .ReturnsAsync(true);

await _sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new OrderRequest { Sku = "SKU-001", Quantity = 1 });

repoMock.Verify(r =>
    r.SaveAsync(It.IsAny<Order>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()), Times.Once);
publisherMock.Verify(p =>
    p.PublishAsync(It.IsAny<OrderPlacedEvent>(), It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()), Times.Once);
```
Tradeoff: `MockSequence` enforces that `SaveAsync` is called before `PublishAsync` — a critical ordering invariant in event-sourced systems where publishing before persisting can cause phantom events — and throws `MockException` at the point of the out-of-order call rather than at verification; the limitation is that `MockSequence` requires all participating mocks to use `MockBehavior.Strict`, and any additional call to any mock in the sequence (even an unrelated one) may disrupt the sequence counter, so restrict `InSequence` usage to the minimal set of calls that must be ordered.

**Pattern 425** — NSubstitute `Arg.Do<T>` for side-effect capture without interrupting the return-value chain
```csharp
Order? capturedOrder = null;

_orderRepository
    .SaveAsync(Arg.Do<Order>(o => capturedOrder = o), Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
    .Returns(Task.FromResult(true));

await _sut.PlaceOrderAsync(
    new OrderRequest { Sku = "SKU-001", Quantity = 2, Currency = "USD" });

capturedOrder.Should().NotBeNull();
capturedOrder!.LineItems.Should().HaveCount(1);
capturedOrder.LineItems[0].Sku.Should().Be("SKU-001");
capturedOrder.TotalAmount.Should().BeApproximately(19.98m, precision: 0.01m);
```
Tradeoff: `Arg.Do<T>` captures the argument and returns control to the `.Returns(...)` chain in a single fluent expression, unlike Moq's separate `Callback`-then-`Returns`, making the setup declaration self-contained and avoiding the common error of forgetting to add `Returns` after `Callback`; the limitation is that `Arg.Do<T>` captures the reference at call time — if the SUT mutates the same `Order` instance after calling `SaveAsync`, `capturedOrder` reflects the post-mutation state, so clone the captured value immediately in the lambda if pre-mutation state is needed.

**Pattern 426** — Testcontainers.NET `WithReuse(true)` warm-container label for local development cycle acceleration
```csharp
public class ReusablePostgresFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private PostgreSqlContainer _container = default!;
    public string ConnectionString { get; private set; } = default!;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        var isCI = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("CI") == "true";

        _container = new PostgreSqlBuilder()
            .WithImage("postgres:16-alpine")
            .WithDatabase("devtestdb")
            .WithUsername("dev")
            .WithPassword("dev")
            // Reuse locally; always create fresh in CI
            .WithReuse(!isCI)
            .WithLabel("project", "myapp-tests")
            .WithCleanUp(isCI)
            .Build();

        await _container.StartAsync();
        ConnectionString = _container.GetConnectionString();

        await using var ctx = new AppDbContext(
            new DbContextOptionsBuilder<AppDbContext>()
                .UseNpgsql(ConnectionString).Options);
        await ctx.Database.MigrateAsync();
    }

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
        => await _container.StopAsync();
}
```
Tradeoff: `WithReuse(true)` tells Testcontainers to reuse an already-running container with matching labels, cutting local feedback cycles from ~10 s (pull + start) to under 1 s on warm machines; the cost is that the shared container accumulates data across test sessions unless each test explicitly resets state (e.g., via Respawn), and the `CI=true` guard ensures CI always gets a clean container while developers get the speed benefit.

**Pattern 427** — AutoFixture `Fixture.Inject<T>` for pinning specific instances without a full `ICustomization`
```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task GetOrder_ExistingId_ReturnsMatchingOrder()
{
    var fixture = new Fixture()
        .Customize(new AutoNSubstituteCustomization { ConfigureMembers = true });

    // Pin the exact order ID the test depends on
    var knownId = OrderId.From(Guid.Parse("12345678-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"));
    fixture.Inject(knownId);

    // All Create<Order>() and Create<OrderService>() use the pinned OrderId
    var order   = fixture.Create<Order>();
    var repoSub = fixture.Freeze<IOrderRepository>();

    repoSub.GetByIdAsync(knownId, Arg.Any<CancellationToken>())
           .Returns(Task.FromResult<Order?>(order));

    var sut    = fixture.Create<OrderService>();
    var result = await sut.GetOrderAsync(knownId);

    result.Should().BeEquivalentTo(order);
}
```
Tradeoff: `Fixture.Inject<T>` is lighter-weight than `Fixture.Customize<T>` when only one instance of a type needs to be pinned — it registers the exact value as the specimen for that type without requiring a factory lambda; the limitation is that `Inject` replaces all resolution of that type globally within the fixture, so if the SUT has two constructor parameters of the same type (e.g., two `Guid` parameters for `orderId` and `customerId`), both receive the same injected value, producing subtle test bugs that are hard to detect without inspecting the SUT's constructor signature.

**Pattern 428** — WireMock.NET `WithDelay` + `InScenario` state machine for testing HTTP client timeout and retry behaviour
```csharp
var server = WireMockServer.Start();

// First call is delayed beyond the client's configured timeout — triggers retry
server
    .Given(Request.Create().WithPath("/api/payments").UsingPost())
    .InScenario("payment-retry")
    .WhenStateIs("Started")
    .WillSetStateTo("FirstCallDone")
    .RespondWith(Response.Create()
        .WithDelay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10))
        .WithStatusCode(200));

// Retry call responds immediately with success
server
    .Given(Request.Create().WithPath("/api/payments").UsingPost())
    .InScenario("payment-retry")
    .WhenStateIs("FirstCallDone")
    .RespondWith(Response.Create()
        .WithStatusCode(200)
        .WithBodyAsJson(new { transactionId = "TXN-001", success = true }));

var client = BuildClientWithTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), retries: 1);
var result = await client.ChargeAsync(new PaymentRequest { Amount = 50m });

result.Success.Should().BeTrue();
server.LogEntries.Should().HaveCount(2,
    because: "one timeout + one successful retry expected");
```
Tradeoff: `WithDelay` combined with `InScenario` state machine accurately simulates transient timeouts at the HTTP layer without mocking `HttpClient`, testing the full retry policy (Polly, `IHttpClientFactory` resilience pipeline) through a real `HttpClient`; test execution is bounded by the configured client timeout, not WireMock's delay, but a misconfigured timeout value can make the test take the full 10 s if the client does not time out — always assert `server.LogEntries` count to distinguish "retried and succeeded" from "never timed out".

**Pattern 429** — Bogus `Faker<T>` with `f.UniqueIndex` for monotonically unique identifiers in bulk `Generate(n)` calls
```csharp
var productFaker = new Faker<Product>()
    .RuleFor(p => p.Id,          f => f.UniqueIndex + 1)
    .RuleFor(p => p.Sku,         f => $"SKU-{f.UniqueIndex:D4}")
    .RuleFor(p => p.Name,        f => f.Commerce.ProductName())
    .RuleFor(p => p.Price,       f => Math.Round(f.Random.Decimal(1m, 999m), 2))
    .RuleFor(p => p.IsAvailable, f => f.Random.Bool(weight: 0.8f));

var catalog = productFaker.Generate(50);

catalog.Select(p => p.Sku).Should().OnlyHaveUniqueItems(
    because: "each product must have a unique SKU");
catalog.Count(p => p.IsAvailable).Should().BeGreaterThan(30,
    because: "80 % availability weight should produce > 30 available items in 50");
```
Tradeoff: `f.UniqueIndex` increments monotonically within a single `Faker<T>` instance, guaranteeing unique IDs and SKUs without a separate `HashSet` deduplication step; the counter is not reset between successive `Generate(count)` calls on the same instance — useful for building insertion batches with globally unique keys, but counterintuitive if the developer expects each `Generate` call to start from zero, so document the counter-continuation behaviour with a comment when using the same `Faker<T>` across multiple `Generate` calls.

**Pattern 430** — `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing` `FakeLogger<T>` for asserting structured log entries without string parsing
```csharp
// Package: Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Testing (.NET 8+)
var fakeLogger = new FakeLogger<OrderService>();
var sut        = new OrderService(fakeLogger, _repoMock.Object, _publisherMock.Object);

await sut.PlaceOrderAsync(new OrderRequest { Sku = "OUT-OF-STOCK", Quantity = 1 });

var errorLogs = fakeLogger.Collector.GetSnapshot()
    .Where(e => e.Level == LogLevel.Error)
    .ToList();

errorLogs.Should().ContainSingle(
    e => e.Message.Contains("OUT-OF-STOCK"),
    because: "service must log an error for unavailable SKUs");

errorLogs[0].Exception.Should().BeOfType<InventoryException>(
    because: "the logged exception must be the domain type, not a wrapper");
```
Tradeoff: `FakeLogger<T>` records structured log entries with full fidelity (level, message, exception, state dictionary) without any string-parsing fragility, enabling assertions on specific structured properties; the package targets .NET 8+ only, so projects on earlier TFMs must use a third-party logging test adapter (e.g., `Serilog.Sinks.TestCorrelator` or `xunit.extensions.logging`), which have different API shapes and may not expose the raw `Exception` reference.

**Pattern 431** — xUnit `TheoryData<T1, T2>` for type-safe `[MemberData]` that catches row-type mismatches at compile time
```csharp
public static TheoryData<decimal, string, decimal> TaxCalculationCases => new()
{
    { 100m, "US-CA", 108.25m },
    { 100m, "US-TX", 108.00m },
    { 100m, "GB",    120.00m },
    {   0m, "US-CA",   0.00m },
    { 100m, "AE",    100.00m }
};

[Theory]
[MemberData(nameof(TaxCalculationCases))]
public void CalculateTotal_WithRegionalTax_ReturnsExpectedTotal(
    decimal subtotal, string region, decimal expectedTotal)
{
    var result = _taxEngine.CalculateTotal(subtotal, region);

    result.Should().BeApproximately(expectedTotal, precision: 0.01m,
        because: $"region {region} should produce {expectedTotal:F2}");
}
```
Tradeoff: `TheoryData<T1, T2>` (xUnit v2.5+) is a generic, type-safe alternative to `IEnumerable<object[]>` that gives compile-time errors when data rows do not match the theory method's parameter types, eliminating `InvalidCastException` at runtime that is otherwise hard to trace to a specific row; the limitation is that `TheoryData` cannot be built lazily — the entire dataset is constructed when the property is first accessed during test discovery, so very large or externally-sourced datasets should use `ClassData` with `IAsyncEnumerable` (xUnit v3) to avoid blocking test collection.

**Pattern 432** — NUnit `TestCaseSource(typeof(T), nameof(M))` for cross-fixture data sharing via a static `TestDataProvider`
```csharp
public static class OrderTestData
{
    public static IEnumerable<TestCaseData> InvalidOrderRequests()
    {
        yield return new TestCaseData(new OrderRequest { Sku = null, Quantity = 1 })
            .SetName("NullSku_ThrowsArgumentException")
            .Throws(typeof(ArgumentException));

        yield return new TestCaseData(new OrderRequest { Sku = "SKU-001", Quantity = 0 })
            .SetName("ZeroQuantity_ThrowsArgumentOutOfRange")
            .Throws(typeof(ArgumentOutOfRangeException));

        yield return new TestCaseData(new OrderRequest { Sku = "SKU-001", Quantity = -1 })
            .SetName("NegativeQuantity_ThrowsArgumentOutOfRange")
            .Throws(typeof(ArgumentOutOfRangeException));
    }
}

[TestCaseSource(typeof(OrderTestData), nameof(OrderTestData.InvalidOrderRequests))]
public void PlaceOrder_InvalidRequest_ThrowsExpectedException(OrderRequest request)
    => Assert.Throws(
        Is.TypeOf<ArgumentException>().Or.TypeOf<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(),
        () => _sut.PlaceOrder(request));
```
Tradeoff: Placing `TestCaseSource` data on a separate static `TestDataProvider` class allows the same dataset to be consumed by multiple fixtures without copy-pasting, providing a single point of truth for boundary-value scenarios; the downside is that a static class with `IEnumerable` methods accumulates data over time and can become a maintenance burden — enforce that each method is referenced by at least one `[TestCaseSource]` attribute via a Roslyn analyzer or a CI-time reflection test.

**Pattern 433** — FluentAssertions `Using<T>` + `When(info => info.Path...)` for path-scoped custom comparison rules
```csharp
// Apply null/empty normalisation only to "Description" and "Notes" paths
// where the legacy API may return either null or empty string
actual.Should().BeEquivalentTo(expected,
    opts => opts
        .Using<string>(ctx =>
        {
            var a = string.IsNullOrEmpty(ctx.Subject)     ? "" : ctx.Subject;
            var b = string.IsNullOrEmpty(ctx.Expectation) ? "" : ctx.Expectation;
            a.Should().Be(b,
                because: $"{ctx.SelectedMemberPath} treats null and empty as equal");
        })
        .When(info => info.Path.EndsWith("Description",  StringComparison.Ordinal)
                   || info.Path.EndsWith("Notes",        StringComparison.Ordinal)));
```
Tradeoff: Scoping a custom `Using` rule with `.When(info => ...)` to specific property paths applies lenient null/empty normalisation only where the legacy API contract requires it, without polluting the rest of the object graph comparison with the same lax rule; the `.When` predicate runs against the `IObjectInfo.Path` string using dot-notation paths (e.g., `"Address.Line2"`), so if a property is renamed during refactoring, the predicate silently stops applying — add a test that verifies at least one property matches the expected path pattern to catch renames.

**Pattern 434** — `WebApplicationFactory` with two `WireMockServer` stubs for testing OAuth2 client-credentials token acquisition end-to-end
```csharp
public class PaymentApiClientTests : IAsyncDisposable
{
    private readonly WireMockServer _identityServer = WireMockServer.Start();
    private readonly WireMockServer _paymentServer  = WireMockServer.Start();

    [Fact]
    public async Task ChargeAsync_AcquiresTokenThenCallsApi_ForwardsBearer()
    {
        _identityServer
            .Given(Request.Create().WithPath("/connect/token").UsingPost())
            .RespondWith(Response.Create()
                .WithStatusCode(200)
                .WithBodyAsJson(new
                {
                    access_token = "test-bearer-token",
                    token_type   = "Bearer",
                    expires_in   = 3600
                }));

        _paymentServer
            .Given(Request.Create()
                .WithPath("/api/charge")
                .UsingPost()
                .WithHeader("Authorization", "Bearer test-bearer-token"))
            .RespondWith(Response.Create()
                .WithStatusCode(200)
                .WithBodyAsJson(new { transactionId = "TXN-001" }));

        var client = BuildPaymentClient(
            tokenEndpoint:  new Uri(_identityServer.Url! + "/connect/token"),
            paymentBaseUrl: new Uri(_paymentServer.Url!));

        var result = await client.ChargeAsync(new ChargeRequest { Amount = 50m });

        result.TransactionId.Should().Be("TXN-001");
        _paymentServer.LogEntries.Should().ContainSingle(
            e => e.RequestMatchResult.TotalScore == 1.0,
            because: "the payment call must carry the acquired bearer token");
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        _identityServer.Stop();
        _paymentServer.Stop();
        await Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```
Tradeoff: Using two `WireMockServer` instances tests the full OAuth2 client-credentials flow end-to-end through the real `HttpClient` pipeline (including `IHttpClientFactory`, `DelegatingHandler`, and token caching), catching bugs in handler ordering that mock-based tests miss; the test is tightly coupled to the exact token endpoint path and response shape, so changes to the OAuth2 configuration require updating both the SUT's settings and the stub simultaneously — use strongly-typed constants shared between the SUT configuration and the test to prevent silent mismatches.

**Pattern 435** — Respawn `Respawner.CreateAsync` with an open `SqlConnection` for faster reset by reusing the connection
```csharp
public class TransactionalResetFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private SqlConnection _connection = default!;
    private Respawner     _respawner  = default!;

    public SqlConnection Connection => _connection;

    public async Task InitializeAsync()
    {
        _connection = new SqlConnection(
            "Server=localhost;Database=testdb;User=sa;Password=Test@1234;TrustServerCertificate=true");
        await _connection.OpenAsync();

        _respawner = await Respawner.CreateAsync(_connection, new RespawnerOptions
        {
            DbAdapter = DbAdapter.SqlServer,
            TablesToIgnore = new Table[]
            {
                new("__EFMigrationsHistory"),
                new("dbo", "ReferenceData")
            },
            CommandTimeout = 30
        });
    }

    public async Task ResetDatabaseAsync()
        => await _respawner.ResetAsync(_connection);

    public async Task DisposeAsync()
        => await _connection.DisposeAsync();
}
```
Tradeoff: Passing an open `SqlConnection` to `Respawner.ResetAsync` (rather than a connection string) allows Respawn to reuse the same connection for all its internal DELETE statements, avoiding the overhead of opening a new connection per reset call and preserving any session-level settings (e.g., `SET NOCOUNT ON`); the limitation is that this connection must not be enlisted in an ambient `TransactionScope` during reset — Respawn's internal statements would participate in the transaction and be rolled back, leaving data in place — so always call `ResetDatabaseAsync` outside any `TransactionScope` or use `TransactionScopeOption.Suppress`.

### Community Gotchas

**G76** — xUnit `[ClassData]` whose constructor throws silently marks all theory cases as "not found" rather than reporting a test-collection error, causing a spurious green CI run
Why this matters: A developer creates a `ClassData` class whose constructor connects to a database to load test cases. If the connection string is misconfigured in CI, the constructor throws `SqlException`. xUnit catches exceptions thrown during test discovery and marks all theory methods sourced from that class as "not runnable" — the runner output shows zero tests for those methods with no error. The developer sees a green CI run with suspiciously fewer tests than expected, which may be dismissed as a test filter artifact. The root cause is logged only to the xUnit diagnostic sink, which is not shown in standard CI log output unless `--diagnostics` is passed to the runner.
Fix: Make `ClassData` constructors infallible — defer all I/O to `GetAsyncEnumerator` (xUnit v3 `IAsyncEnumerable`) or `GetEnumerator`. If synchronous `IEnumerable<object[]>` is required, catch all exceptions in the enumerator body and yield a sentinel `new object[] { null, "ERROR: " + ex.Message }` that causes the theory method to fail with a descriptive message, turning a silent discovery failure into a visible test failure.

**G77** — NUnit `[TearDown]` throwing an exception when the test itself has already failed replaces the original failure with the teardown exception in the result, hiding the real bug
Why this matters: A developer writes a `[TearDown]` method that calls `_dbContext.SaveChangesAsync()` to flush test-scoped audit records. When a test fails (e.g., due to a constraint violation), the `DbContext` is in a faulted state and `SaveChangesAsync()` throws `InvalidOperationException`. NUnit replaces the original test failure with this teardown exception, so the CI report shows "teardown failed" with a `DbContext` error rather than the actual assertion failure. Developers diagnose the `DbContext` error, find nothing wrong with the teardown logic, and miss the real bug.
Fix: Wrap all stateful teardown operations in a `try/catch` and log failures to `TestContext.Out` rather than re-throwing: `try { await _dbContext.SaveChangesAsync(); } catch (Exception ex) { TestContext.Out.WriteLine($"TearDown warning: {ex.Message}"); }`. Alternatively, call `_dbContext.ChangeTracker.Clear()` before teardown to detach all entities and ensure `SaveChangesAsync` is a no-op when the context is in an error state.

**G78** — Moq `Returns(Task.FromResult(value))` wraps the same object reference — mutations to the object after setup are reflected in all subsequent mock calls, not just future ones
Why this matters: A developer sets up `repoMock.Setup(r => r.GetUserAsync(1)).Returns(Task.FromResult(user))` and then writes `user.IsActive = false` later in the same test method. Because `Task.FromResult(user)` wraps the same reference, any code that deferred reading `user.IsActive` sees `false` regardless of when the mock was configured. In the reverse antipattern, a developer expects value-copy semantics by writing `Returns(Task.FromResult(new User { IsActive = true }))` in `[SetUp]`, then is surprised when mutations made to the returned object in a prior test (via a shared static mock) persist across test runs.
Fix: Use `ReturnsAsync(() => user with { })` with a factory lambda and a record `with` expression (or a manual clone) so each invocation returns a fresh copy. For tests that need to observe a state transition, use `SetupSequence` to return different objects on successive calls, documenting the expected call order explicitly.

**G79** — AutoFixture `Freeze<T>` only registers the shared instance for the exact type `T` — the concrete type and derived types receive fresh instances, causing hidden coupling when the SUT depends on both the interface and the implementation
Why this matters: A developer freezes `IOrderRepository` to get a shared NSubstitute double: `var repo = fixture.Freeze<IOrderRepository>()`. The first SUT's constructor takes `IOrderRepository` — this works correctly. A second SUT class in the same test takes `OrderRepository` (the concrete type) as a constructor dependency. `fixture.Create<SecondService>()` creates a new `OrderRepository` instance (not the frozen interface substitute) because AutoFixture resolves `OrderRepository` independently of the frozen `IOrderRepository`. The developer sets up behaviour on `repo` expecting both services to use it, but `SecondService` calls the concrete type with no setup, hitting the real database or throwing `NullReferenceException`.
Fix: Freeze both the interface and the concrete type: `fixture.Freeze<IOrderRepository>(); fixture.Inject<OrderRepository>((OrderRepository)repo)`. Alternatively, refactor all SUTs to depend on the interface only (the correct architectural pattern), eliminating the need to freeze both. Use `fixture.Customize<OrderRepository>(c => c.FromFactory(() => (OrderRepository)repo))` as a last resort when the concrete type cannot be replaced.

**G80** — WireMock.NET `WithBodyAsJson(obj)` serialises the object eagerly at registration time — mutations to the object after `RespondWith` are not reflected in stub responses
Why this matters: A developer builds stubs in a loop reusing an anonymous object: `var body = new { orderId = 0, status = "pending" }; foreach (var id in orderIds) { body = body with { orderId = id }; server.Given(...).RespondWith(Response.Create().WithBodyAsJson(body)); }`. Because `WithBodyAsJson` serialises `body` to JSON at registration time, each stub's JSON captures the state of `body` at the moment `RespondWith` is called — which, due to the `body = body with { ... }` reassignment before `RespondWith`, is actually the current iteration's value. However, if the developer mistakenly places `RespondWith` before `body = body with { ... }`, all stubs receive the same initial `orderId = 0` JSON. The bug is invisible at compilation and only surfaces as assertion failures for all stubs except the first.
Fix: Construct a distinct object literal inside the loop body rather than mutating and reassigning a shared variable: `server.Given(...).RespondWith(Response.Create().WithBodyAsJson(new { orderId = id, status = "pending" }))`. This ensures each stub's JSON is serialised from a fresh, correctly-valued anonymous object at registration time, eliminating order-of-operations bugs caused by shared mutable state.

## C# 14 — Instance Increment and Decrement Operators

### Instance `operator ++()` and `operator --()` — In-Place Mutation Without Allocation

C# 14 introduces instance forms of increment and decrement operators: `void operator ++()` and `void operator --()`. Unlike the static form (`static T operator ++(T x) => new T(...)`), the instance form mutates the current object in place and returns nothing. The compiler prefers the instance form over the static form when the expression result is discarded (e.g., `counter++;` as a statement), enabling zero-allocation mutation of large mutable value containers such as `BigInteger`-style types, tensors, or pooled buffers.

```csharp
// In-place counter — avoids allocating a new instance on every increment
public class LargeCounter
{
    private long[] _digits;

    public LargeCounter(long initial) => _digits = [initial];

    // Instance form: void return, no parameters — mutates this instance in-place
    public void operator ++()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < _digits.Length; i++)
        {
            if (_digits[i] < long.MaxValue) { _digits[i]++; return; }
            _digits[i] = 0;
        }
        Array.Resize(ref _digits, _digits.Length + 1);
        _digits[^1] = 1;
    }

    // checked variant required when unchecked instance operator is declared
    public void operator checked ++()
    {
        checked { operator++(); }
    }

    // Static form still available when result is captured (var x = counter++)
    public static LargeCounter operator ++(LargeCounter x)
    {
        var copy = new LargeCounter(0) { _digits = (long[])x._digits.Clone() };
        copy.operator++();
        return copy;
    }

    public override string ToString() => string.Join("_", _digits.Reverse());
}

// Usage — statement form uses void instance operator (no allocation)
var counter = new LargeCounter(long.MaxValue - 1);
counter++;        // calls void operator ++() — no allocation, in-place
counter++;        // rolls over first digit
Console.WriteLine(counter); // "0_1"
```

Key rules:
- Instance operator must not be `static`; must have `void` return; takes no parameters.
- The `checked` instance variant is required whenever the unchecked instance variant is declared.
- If the expression result is _used_ (e.g., `var x = counter++`), the compiler falls back to the static form (copy-modify-assign semantics), because the pre-mutation value must be captured.
- Instance operators can `override` a base-class operator — unique among C# operator types.

```csharp
// Instance compound assignment operator — in-place +=
public class Vector2D
{
    public double X, Y;

    // void return, one parameter — mutates this in place
    public void operator +=(Vector2D other)
    {
        X += other.X;
        Y += other.Y;
    }
    // Without instance +=, v1 += v2 would allocate via static +; now zero allocation
}

var v1 = new Vector2D { X = 1.0, Y = 2.0 };
var v2 = new Vector2D { X = 3.0, Y = 4.0 };
v1 += v2;  // calls void operator +=(v2) — no new Vector2D allocated
Console.WriteLine($"({v1.X}, {v1.Y})"); // (4, 6)
```

Tradeoff: Instance compound-assignment and increment operators are a library author pattern — they provide allocation savings for frequently mutated objects but add cognitive overhead because `x += y` no longer implies `x = f(x, y)`; it now means `x.mutate(y)`. Always document the in-place mutation semantics and provide the static binary operator form so callers who need `var result = a + b` without modifying `a` can still do so.

## async/await vs ContinueWith — Why async/await Is Always Preferred

### Compiler State Machine vs Manual Continuation Chains

`async`/`await` compiles to an optimized state machine; `ContinueWith` requires manual `.Unwrap()` calls for nested `Task<Task>` results and each continuation must explicitly handle faulted tasks. The official docs (updated March 2025) now include a direct comparison showing the readability and correctness advantages.

```csharp
// ContinueWith — 4 sequential operations, deeply nested, error handling manual
static Task ProcessOrderContinueWithAsync(int orderId)
{
    return ValidateOrderAsync(orderId)
        .ContinueWith(t =>
        {
            if (t.IsFaulted) throw t.Exception!.InnerException!;
            return ReserveInventoryAsync(t.Result);
        })
        .Unwrap()   // required: ContinueWith returns Task<Task> — must unwrap
        .ContinueWith(t =>
        {
            if (t.IsFaulted) throw t.Exception!.InnerException!;
            return ChargePaymentAsync(t.Result);
        })
        .Unwrap()
        .ContinueWith(t =>
        {
            if (t.IsFaulted) throw t.Exception!.InnerException!;
            return SendConfirmationAsync(t.Result);
        })
        .Unwrap();
}

// async/await — same 4 operations, linear, exceptions propagate naturally
static async Task ProcessOrderAsync(int orderId)
{
    var order       = await ValidateOrderAsync(orderId);
    var reservation = await ReserveInventoryAsync(order);
    var payment     = await ChargePaymentAsync(reservation);
    await SendConfirmationAsync(payment);
}
```

**Comparison of the two approaches:**

| Dimension | ContinueWith | async/await |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| Exception propagation | Manual `IsFaulted` + `InnerException` unwrap required | Natural — `await` re-throws the first inner exception |
| Debugger call stack | Flat — only continuation lambda shows up | Full async call stack preserved |
| Cancellation | `CancellationToken` must be threaded into each `ContinueWith` call | Single `CancellationToken` parameter flows through all `await` expressions |
| Adding/removing a step | Restructure entire chain, re-add `.Unwrap()` | Add/remove one `await` line |
| `Task<Task>` unwrap bugs | Easy to forget `.Unwrap()` — outer task succeeds while inner task faults silently | Compiler handles unwrapping automatically |

```csharp
// Natural exception handling with async/await
static async Task SafeProcessOrderAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct)
{
    try
    {
        var order       = await ValidateOrderAsync(orderId, ct);
        var reservation = await ReserveInventoryAsync(order, ct);
        var payment     = await ChargePaymentAsync(reservation, ct);
        await SendConfirmationAsync(payment, ct);
    }
    catch (ValidationException ex)
    {
        _logger.LogWarning(ex, "Order {OrderId} validation failed", orderId);
    }
    catch (InventoryException ex)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Inventory reservation failed for {OrderId}", orderId);
        throw;
    }
}
```

Use `ContinueWith` only in these two narrow scenarios: (1) `TaskContinuationOptions.ExecuteSynchronously` in extremely hot, benchmarked code paths where scheduler overhead is measured to be significant; (2) attaching a continuation to a `Task` returned by a library that predates `async`/`await` and cannot be `await`ed directly. In all other cases prefer `async`/`await`.

## ASP.NET Core 10 — Passkey / WebAuthn Support for ASP.NET Core Identity

### Phishing-Resistant Passwordless Authentication with FIDO2

ASP.NET Core Identity 10 ships built-in passkey (WebAuthn / FIDO2) support. Passkeys are device-bound credentials using public-key cryptography — the private key never leaves the device. The Blazor Web App template now includes passkey management and login pages.

```csharp
// Program.cs — enable passkeys via AddPasskeys() on the Identity builder
builder.Services
    .AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(opt => opt.UseSqlite("Data Source=app.db"))
    .AddDefaultIdentity<IdentityUser>(options =>
    {
        options.SignIn.RequireConfirmedAccount = false;
    })
    .AddEntityFrameworkStores<AppDbContext>()
    .AddPasskeys();  // ASP.NET Core 10 — registers passkey services and endpoints

// EF Core migration needed:
// dotnet ef migrations add AddPasskeys
// dotnet ef database update
```

```csharp
// Custom IUserPasskeyStore<T> for non-EF stores
public class CustomPasskeyStore : IUserStore<IdentityUser>, IUserPasskeyStore<IdentityUser>
{
    // Must implement: CreatePasskeyAsync, FindPasskeyAsync, GetPasskeysAsync,
    // RemovePasskeyAsync, plus all IUserStore<T> members

    public async Task CreatePasskeyAsync(
        IdentityUser user,
        UserPasskeyInfo passkey,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // Store all passkey fields: CredentialId (byte[]), PublicKey (byte[]),
        // SignCount (ulong), Transports (string?), CreatedAt, Name
        await _db.Passkeys.AddAsync(new PasskeyEntity
        {
            UserId       = user.Id,
            CredentialId = Convert.ToBase64String(passkey.CredentialId),
            PublicKey    = Convert.ToBase64String(passkey.PublicKey),
            SignCount    = passkey.SignCount,
            CreatedAt    = passkey.CreatedAt,
            Name         = passkey.Name
        }, cancellationToken);
        // IMPORTANT: must also call UpdateAsync(user) to update ConcurrencyStamp
        await _db.SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken);
    }

    public async Task<UserPasskeyInfo?> FindPasskeyAsync(
        ReadOnlyMemory<byte> credentialId,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var id = Convert.ToBase64String(credentialId.Span);
        var entity = await _db.Passkeys
            .AsNoTracking()
            .FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.CredentialId == id, cancellationToken);

        return entity is null ? null : new UserPasskeyInfo(
            Convert.FromBase64String(entity.CredentialId),
            Convert.FromBase64String(entity.PublicKey),
            entity.SignCount,
            transports: entity.Transports,
            createdAt: entity.CreatedAt,
            name: entity.Name);
    }
}
```

Tradeoff: Passkeys eliminate password-related attack vectors (phishing, credential stuffing, brute force) but require WebAuthn-capable browsers and authenticators — iOS 16+, Android 9+, Chrome 109+, Safari 16+. Always provide a fallback authentication method (email OTP, TOTP) for devices that cannot use passkeys; never make passkeys the sole authentication path without an explicit user opt-in.

## ASP.NET Core 10 — Blazor WebAssembly Static Asset Preloading

### `OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders` and HTTP Link Header Preloads

ASP.NET Core 10 enables automatic high-priority preloading of Blazor WebAssembly framework assets (blazor.webassembly.js, dotnet.wasm) via HTTP `Link` headers, reducing Time-to-Interactive on cold loads. Opt-in via an MSBuild property plus two placeholders in `index.html`.

```xml
<!-- *.csproj — opt-in to HTML asset placeholder substitution at publish time -->
<PropertyGroup>
  <OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders>true</OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders>
</PropertyGroup>
```

```html
<!-- wwwroot/index.html — required placeholders (exact id and type attributes) -->
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <title>My Blazor App</title>

    <!-- Preload placeholder — SDK replaces with fingerprinted <link rel="modulepreload"> -->
    <link rel="preload" id="webassembly" />

    <!-- Import map placeholder — SDK injects module fingerprint mappings -->
    <script type="importmap"></script>
</head>
<body>
    <div id="app">Loading...</div>
    <!-- #[.{fingerprint}] token is replaced by SDK with content-hash suffix at publish -->
    <script src="_framework/blazor.webassembly#[.{fingerprint}].js"></script>
</body>
```

```csharp
// Program.cs for a hosted Blazor WASM server — no code changes needed
// MapStaticAssets() middleware handles fingerprinted URL resolution
app.UseStaticFiles();
app.MapRazorComponents<App>().AddInteractiveWebAssemblyRenderMode();
```

Tradeoff: The `Link` preload header is injected by the hosting middleware; if the app is served from a CDN that strips custom response headers, preloading will not trigger — verify the `Link` header is present in DevTools → Network → Response Headers on the initial HTML request. The `id="webassembly"` attribute on the preload `<link>` is an exact string match required by the SDK; a typo silently disables preloading with no build warning.

## ASP.NET Core 10 — Automatic Memory Pool Eviction via `IMemoryPoolFactory<T>`

### Idle-Time Pool Block Release and Built-In Telemetry

`IMemoryPoolFactory<T>` (introduced in .NET 10 libraries, surfaced in ASP.NET Core 10) creates `MemoryPool<T>` instances that automatically evict unreturned blocks when the application is idle, reducing memory footprint for services with bursty request patterns without manual `Trim()` calls.

```csharp
// Service using DI-injected pool with auto-eviction
public sealed class StreamProcessor(IMemoryPoolFactory<byte> poolFactory) : IDisposable
{
    private readonly MemoryPool<byte> _pool = poolFactory.Create();

    public async Task<int> ProcessChunkAsync(Stream stream, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Rent a 4 KB block — returned to pool on Dispose
        // Pool evicts blocks automatically when app is idle
        using IMemoryOwner<byte> buffer = _pool.Rent(4096);
        int bytesRead = await stream.ReadAsync(buffer.Memory, ct);
        return ProcessBytes(buffer.Memory[..bytesRead]);
    }

    private static int ProcessBytes(ReadOnlyMemory<byte> data) => data.Length;

    public void Dispose() => _pool.Dispose();
}

// Program.cs — IMemoryPoolFactory<T> is registered automatically by AddAspNetCore services
builder.Services.AddControllers();
// IMemoryPoolFactory<byte> is available for injection without manual registration
```

```csharp
// Monitoring evictions via built-in OpenTelemetry metrics
// Meter name: "Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool"  (exact casing required)
// Instrument: "memory-pool.evictions" (count of evicted blocks)

// Command-line monitoring:
// dotnet-counters monitor --name MyApp --counters "Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool"
```

Tradeoff: Auto-eviction benefits services with bursty request patterns (high load followed by idle) but adds a one-time re-allocation cost when the next burst arrives after an idle period; for services under continuous load, `ArrayPool<T>.Shared` (no eviction overhead) may give marginally better throughput. Prefer `IMemoryPoolFactory<T>` when pool lifetime is scoped to a component's DI lifetime and load is non-uniform; prefer `ArrayPool<T>.Shared` for tight hot-path loops where allocation latency matters.

## Real-World Gotchas — C# 14 Instance Operators and ASP.NET Core 10 [community]

**G81** — C# 14 instance `operator ++()` on a type constrained as a generic type parameter silently falls back to the static operator form, causing an unexpected heap allocation
Why this matters: A developer declares `void operator ++()` on struct `S` and writes a generic helper `void Increment<T>(ref T val) where T : ICounter`. At the call site `Increment(ref myS)`, the developer expects the in-place mutation. Because the constraint `where T : ICounter` does not include `allows ref struct`, the compiler cannot verify that `T` is mutable through the type parameter, so it falls back to static unary operator overload resolution. If a static `operator ++(S x)` is also declared, it creates a new value and assigns it back through the `ref` parameter — correct but allocating. If no static form exists, the call fails to compile with a misleading "operator not found" error despite the instance operator being present on `S`.
Fix: Add `allows ref struct` to the generic constraint when using instance increment/decrement through a generic type parameter: `void Increment<T>(ref T val) where T : ICounter, allows ref struct`. When writing both instance and static forms on the same type, document which form is chosen in which context to avoid reader confusion.

**G82** — `ContinueWith` without `.Unwrap()` returns `Task<Task>` — the outer task succeeds immediately even when the inner task faults, silently swallowing exceptions
Why this matters: A developer rewrites an `async` method using `ContinueWith` for an experiment: `return fetchTask.ContinueWith(t => ParseAsync(t.Result))`. `ContinueWith` returns `Task<Task<ParsedResult>>`, not `Task<ParsedResult>`. The developer awaits the outer task: it resolves as soon as the continuation *starts* `ParseAsync`, regardless of whether `ParseAsync` later faults or is cancelled. The exception is stored in the inner orphaned task and silently discarded because nothing awaits it. The bug surfaces only when users report incorrect data or missing records — no exception, no log entry.
Fix: Always add `.Unwrap()` after any `ContinueWith` that returns a `Task` or `Task<T>`: `return fetchTask.ContinueWith(t => ParseAsync(t.Result)).Unwrap()`. Even better: replace `ContinueWith` chains entirely with `async`/`await`, which handles unwrapping automatically through the compiler-generated state machine.

**G83** — Blazor WASM `OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders=true` with a missing `<link rel="preload" id="webassembly" />` in `index.html` produces a blank white page in Release builds with no browser error
Why this matters: A developer enables `<OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders>true</OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders>` in `.csproj` but doesn't update `index.html`. During `dotnet publish`, the SDK removes the unfingerpinted `<script src="_framework/blazor.webassembly.js">` reference and attempts to replace the `id="webassembly"` placeholder with a fingerprinted version. Since the placeholder is absent, the SDK writes no script tag at all. The deployed `index.html` has no Blazor bootstrap script — the app loads a blank white page, no JS error, no console warning, because there is literally no script to fail.
Fix: Always add `<link rel="preload" id="webassembly" />` and `<script type="importmap"></script>` to `wwwroot/index.html` before enabling the flag. After `dotnet publish -c Release`, inspect `publish/wwwroot/index.html` and verify it contains both a fingerprinted `<script src="_framework/blazor.webassembly.<hash>.js">` tag and `<link rel="modulepreload">` entries for the framework DLLs.

**G84** — Custom `IUserPasskeyStore<T>` that omits calling `UpdateAsync(user)` after `CreatePasskeyAsync` leaves the user's `ConcurrencyStamp` stale, causing passkey sign-in to fail with a concurrency conflict on first use
Why this matters: A developer implements `IUserPasskeyStore<IdentityUser>` and correctly calls `_db.Passkeys.AddAsync(...)` followed by `_db.SaveChangesAsync()`. The passkey row is created. On the next login, `SignInManager` calls `UserManager.UpdateSecurityStampAsync(user)` which internally calls `UpdateAsync(user)` to refresh the `ConcurrencyStamp`. If the stamp in the database was not updated during `CreatePasskeyAsync` (because the developer's `UpdateAsync` implementation is a no-op for the stamp field), the optimistic concurrency check fails with a `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`. The sign-in manager catches this as a general sign-in failure and redirects the user to the login page with "Invalid login attempt" — the passkey appears registered but can never be used.
Fix: After calling `CreatePasskeyAsync`, always call `await _userManager.UpdateAsync(user)` through the `UserManager`, not directly through the store, so the concurrency stamp is refreshed correctly. For custom EF-backed stores, ensure `UpdateAsync` calls `_db.SaveChangesAsync()` after updating the user entity's `ConcurrencyStamp` field. Use `AddEntityFrameworkStores<TContext>()` to avoid implementing this plumbing manually.

**G85** — `IMemoryPoolFactory<T>` eviction metrics counter category uses exact casing `Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool` — lowercase filter in Prometheus/OTLP dashboards silently produces no data
Why this matters: A developer configures a Grafana panel to track pool evictions using the metric filter `microsoft.aspnetcore.memorypool` (lowercase). Some OTLP exporters normalise metric names to lowercase for Prometheus compatibility, but the .NET SDK emits the meter under the exact name `Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool` (PascalCase). A Prometheus scrape that preserves the original casing will not match a lowercase panel filter. The panel shows a flat zero line even during load tests that trigger significant pool churn. The developer misdiagnoses this as "no evictions occurring" and disables auto-eviction monitoring, losing visibility into memory behaviour.
Fix: Use the exact SDK casing `Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool` in all metric filters and dashboards. When using `dotnet-counters monitor`, always quote the provider name: `dotnet-counters monitor --name MyApp --counters "Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool"`. Add a smoke test that calls `IMeterFactory.Create("Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool")` and asserts at least one instrument is registered to catch meter-name regressions across SDK upgrades.

## Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — C# 14 Instance Operators and ASP.NET Core 10

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|-------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Using `void operator ++()` through an unconstrained generic type parameter | Instance increment is not invokable through an unconstrained type parameter — silently falls back to static operator or compile error | Add `allows ref struct` constraint and pass `ref T`; document which form is chosen per context |
| Replacing `async`/`await` chains with `ContinueWith` without benchmarking | `ContinueWith` without `.Unwrap()` silently swallows inner task faults; harder to maintain; compiler's state machine is already optimal | Profile first; default to `async`/`await`; use `ContinueWith` only with `ExecuteSynchronously` in proven hot paths |
| Enabling `OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders` without adding `id="webassembly"` placeholder | SDK removes original script tag and inserts nothing — blank white page in production with no console error | Add both `<link rel="preload" id="webassembly" />` and `<script type="importmap"></script>` before enabling the flag; verify publish output |
| Implementing `IUserPasskeyStore<T>` without calling `UpdateAsync(user)` after `CreatePasskeyAsync` | Stale `ConcurrencyStamp` causes first passkey sign-in to fail with concurrency conflict | Call `UserManager.UpdateAsync(user)` after passkey creation; prefer `AddEntityFrameworkStores` to avoid manual stamp management |
| Filtering `IMemoryPoolFactory<T>` eviction metrics with lowercase meter name | Case-sensitive OTLP collectors emit zero data; developer misdiagnoses as no evictions | Use exact casing `Microsoft.AspNetCore.MemoryPool`; add meter registration assertion test |
