## `required` Modifier — Deep-Dive: Initialization Guarantees Without Constructors

### Problem: Constructor Overload Explosion vs. Accidental Under-Initialization

Before `required` (C# 11), a class with many optional-but-important properties was either bloated with constructor overloads or silently under-initialized when callers used object initializer syntax and omitted a property. The `required` modifier (stable in C# 11, widely adopted in .NET 8+) forces callers to supply a value in the object initializer — it is a compile-time guarantee, not a runtime check.

```csharp
// BEFORE: 3-overload constructor or silent null fields
public class EmailMessage
{
    public string To   { get; init; } = null!;  // nullability lie
    public string From { get; init; } = null!;
    public string Body { get; init; } = null!;
}
var msg = new EmailMessage { To = "a@b.com" }; // compiles — From and Body are null

// AFTER: required — compiler enforces all three at construction site
public class EmailMessage
{
    public required string To   { get; init; }
    public required string From { get; init; }
    public required string Body { get; init; }
}
var msg = new EmailMessage { To = "a@b.com" }; // CS9035: required members 'From' and 'Body' must be set
var ok  = new EmailMessage { To = "a@b.com", From = "b@b.com", Body = "Hello" }; // compiles
```

### `SetsRequiredMembers` — Allow Constructor Bypass

When you do want a canonical constructor to set required members (e.g., for JSON deserialization or a factory pattern), decorate it with `[SetsRequiredMembers]` from `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis`. The attribute suppresses the required-member check at the call site of that specific constructor.

```csharp
using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis;

public class Order
{
    public required string OrderId      { get; init; }
    public required string CustomerId   { get; init; }
    public required List<OrderLine> Lines { get; init; }

    // Canonical constructor — sets all required members
    [SetsRequiredMembers]
    public Order(string orderId, string customerId)
    {
        OrderId    = orderId;
        CustomerId = customerId;
        Lines      = [];
    }

    // Parameterless constructor for JSON deserialization — do NOT mark [SetsRequiredMembers]
    // because it does NOT set the members; JSON deserializer will set them via init setters
    public Order() { }
}

// Object initializer path — all required members must be provided
var o1 = new Order { OrderId = "X1", CustomerId = "C1", Lines = [] };

// Constructor path — SetsRequiredMembers suppresses the check
var o2 = new Order("X2", "C2");

// JSON path — System.Text.Json sets required init properties during deserialization
// (requires .NET 7+ with JsonSerializerOptions.RespectRequiredConstructorParameters
// or .NET 8+ which automatically respects required init for deserialization)
var o3 = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Order>("""{"OrderId":"X3","CustomerId":"C3","Lines":[]}""");
```

### `required` in Inheritance

A derived class can add new `required` members. A constructor in the derived class can use `[SetsRequiredMembers]` to bypass both its own and inherited required members — but only if it actually sets all of them.

```csharp
public class NamedOrder : Order
{
    public required string DisplayName { get; init; }

    [SetsRequiredMembers]
    public NamedOrder(string orderId, string customerId, string name)
        : base(orderId, customerId)
    {
        DisplayName = name;
    }
}
```

Tradeoff: `required` with object initializers works well for configuration/DTO types and is enforced at compile time with no runtime overhead. For types that need parameter validation (e.g., throw if `OrderId` is empty), a constructor with `[SetsRequiredMembers]` is better because constructors can execute validation logic before assignment, while `init` setters cannot conditionally reject an empty string without the `field` keyword (C# 14). Use `required` + `init` for pure DTOs and API request/response shapes; use a constructor with `[SetsRequiredMembers]` for domain entities that need invariant validation.

## Official Coding Conventions — `.editorconfig` Enforcement and Key Rules

### Why `.editorconfig` Matters

Coding style discussions in code review are high-friction and low-value. `.editorconfig` files encode conventions as machine-checked rules, letting CI fail on violations instead of human reviewers. The `dotnet/docs` and `dotnet/runtime` repositories ship `.editorconfig` files that are a good baseline for production codebases.

```ini
# .editorconfig — C# style rules (representative subset from dotnet/docs)
root = true

[*.cs]
# Use 4 spaces, not tabs
indent_style             = space
indent_size              = 4

# File-scoped namespace (enforced — CS8955 on violation)
csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped:error

# var usage: only when type is obvious on the right-hand side
csharp_style_var_for_built_in_types    = false:suggestion
csharp_style_var_when_type_is_apparent = true:suggestion
csharp_style_var_elsewhere             = false:suggestion

# Expression-bodied members
csharp_style_expression_bodied_methods     = when_on_single_line:suggestion
csharp_style_expression_bodied_properties  = true:suggestion
csharp_style_expression_bodied_constructors = false:suggestion

# Prefer pattern matching
csharp_style_pattern_matching_over_is_with_cast_check = true:error
csharp_style_pattern_matching_over_as_with_null_check  = true:error

# Prefer braces on all control structures (Allman style)
csharp_prefer_braces = true:error

# Require using directives OUTSIDE of namespace declarations
dotnet_sort_system_directives_first     = true
dotnet_style_require_accessibility_modifiers = for_non_interface_members:warning

# Prefer 'throw' expressions
csharp_style_throw_expression = true:suggestion

# Prefer 'is not null' over '!= null'
dotnet_style_prefer_is_null_check_over_reference_equality_method = true:error

# Prefer null-coalescing assignment (x ??= value over if x is null x = value)
dotnet_style_prefer_compound_assignment = true:suggestion
```

### Key Coding Convention Rules from Microsoft Official Docs

**`var` usage discipline — the three-rule hierarchy:**

```csharp
// Rule 1: var when type is apparent from the right-hand side (new, cast, or literal assignment)
var customer = new Customer();          // obvious — new operator
var list = new List<string>();          // obvious — new operator
var count = (int)someDouble;            // obvious — explicit cast

// Rule 2: var for anonymous types and LINQ projections (required — no alternative)
var projection = users.Select(u => new { u.Id, u.Name });
var grouped = from o in orders group o by o.CustomerId into g select g;

// Rule 3: explicit type when the type is NOT obvious from the right side
int iterations       = Convert.ToInt32(Console.ReadLine()); // not obvious
HttpClient client    = CreateClient();                       // not obvious from name alone
IEnumerable<string> names = GetNames();                     // not obvious — documents the contract
```

**Using directives must be outside namespace declarations:**

```csharp
// CORRECT — using at file top, outside namespace
using Azure;

namespace CoolStuff.AwesomeFeature;

public class Awesome { }

// WRONG — using inside namespace block triggers name-resolution ambiguity
namespace CoolStuff.AwesomeFeature
{
    using Azure;  // resolves as CoolStuff.AwesomeFeature.Azure first if such a namespace is added
    // This compiles today and silently breaks tomorrow when any dependency adds CoolStuff.Azure
}
```

**Collection expressions for all collection initializations (C# 12+):**

```csharp
// Preferred: collection expression syntax — uniform across array, List<T>, ImmutableArray<T>, Span<T>
string[] vowels        = ["a", "e", "i", "o", "u"];
List<int> primes       = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11];
ImmutableArray<string> empty = [];

// Also preferred: spread operator in collection expressions
int[] first  = [1, 2, 3];
int[] second = [4, 5, 6];
int[] all    = [..first, ..second];   // spread — avoids Concat().ToArray() chain

// Avoid: pre-collection-expression syntax when writing new code
string[] oldStyle = new string[] { "a", "e", "i", "o", "u" };  // verbose
```

Tradeoff: `.editorconfig` with `:error` severity on style rules converts style violations into build failures, which CI enforces without human review. The risk is that overly aggressive `:error` settings on large legacy codebases create thousands of pre-existing violations that block merges; audit the codebase with `dotnet format --verify-no-changes --report` before switching any rule to `:error`. Start with `:suggestion`, fix the backlog, then promote to `:warning` and finally `:error` on a rule-by-rule basis. Use `#pragma warning disable` sparingly for auto-generated files and suppress with a justification comment.

## Dapper — Micro-ORM Patterns for High-Performance Data Access

### When to Choose Dapper over EF Core

Use Dapper when: (1) SQL queries are complex, hand-tuned, or dynamically constructed at runtime; (2) the data-access layer is a thin read model for CQRS queries that EF Core's change tracker would overhead for no benefit; (3) the team is SQL-proficient and the ORM abstraction costs more than it saves. Use EF Core when: schema is owned by the application, migrations are needed, domain entities participate in change tracking, and the team prefers LINQ over raw SQL.

```csharp
// Install: dotnet add package Dapper
// Dapper extends IDbConnection with QueryAsync<T>, ExecuteAsync, QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync

using Dapper;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;

public sealed class ProductRepository(string connectionString)
{
    // Query — map result set to strongly-typed POCO
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<Product>> GetByCategoryAsync(
        int categoryId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // CommandDefinition wires up CancellationToken to the Dapper call
        var cmd = new CommandDefinition(
            commandText: "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE CategoryId = @CategoryId",
            parameters:  new { CategoryId = categoryId },
            cancellationToken: ct);

        await using var conn = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
        var results = await conn.QueryAsync<Product>(cmd);
        return results.AsList();
    }

    // Query single — returns null if not found (no exception)
    public async Task<Product?> GetByIdAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var conn = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
        return await conn.QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<Product>(
            "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Id = @Id",
            new { Id = id });
    }

    // Execute — returns rows affected
    public async Task<int> UpdatePriceAsync(int id, decimal newPrice, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using var conn = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
        return await conn.ExecuteAsync(
            "UPDATE Products SET Price = @Price WHERE Id = @Id",
            new { Id = id, Price = newPrice });
    }

    // Multi-mapping — map JOIN result to parent + child with splitOn
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<Order>> GetOrdersWithLinesAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        const string sql = """
            SELECT o.Id, o.CustomerId, ol.ProductId, ol.Quantity
            FROM Orders o
            INNER JOIN OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderId = o.Id
            ORDER BY o.Id
            """;

        var orderMap = new Dictionary<int, Order>();
        await using var conn = new SqlConnection(connectionString);

        await conn.QueryAsync<Order, OrderLine, Order>(
            sql,
            (order, line) =>
            {
                if (!orderMap.TryGetValue(order.Id, out var existing))
                {
                    existing = order with { Lines = [] };
                    orderMap[order.Id] = existing;
                }
                existing.Lines.Add(line);
                return existing;
            },
            splitOn: "ProductId");   // column name where the second type starts

        return [..orderMap.Values];
    }
}

// POCO — plain properties, no EF Core annotations needed
public record Product(int Id, string Name, decimal Price);
public record OrderLine(int ProductId, int Quantity);
public record Order(int Id, string CustomerId) { public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; init; } = []; }
```

### Dapper Transaction Pattern

```csharp
public async Task TransferStockAsync(int fromId, int toId, int qty, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await using var conn = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
    await conn.OpenAsync(ct);
    await using var tx = await conn.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
    try
    {
        await conn.ExecuteAsync(
            "UPDATE Products SET Stock = Stock - @Qty WHERE Id = @Id",
            new { Qty = qty, Id = fromId }, transaction: tx);

        await conn.ExecuteAsync(
            "UPDATE Products SET Stock = Stock + @Qty WHERE Id = @Id",
            new { Qty = qty, Id = toId }, transaction: tx);

        await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
    }
    catch
    {
        await tx.RollbackAsync(ct);
        throw;
    }
}
```

Tradeoff: Dapper does not manage connections for you — you must `open`, `close`, and `dispose` connections explicitly. Failing to `await using` a `SqlConnection` leaks a connection from the pool even though the `using` block runs synchronously. Always prefer `await using` (async dispose) over `using` on `SqlConnection` and `SqlTransaction` in async code. Dapper also has no identity map — if you query the same row twice in the same logical operation, you get two independent object instances; never rely on reference equality between two Dapper query results.

## MediatR — CQRS / Mediator Pattern in ASP.NET Core

### Why MediatR Reduces Controller Fat

Controllers in ASP.NET Core frequently become fat orchestrators: they validate input, call services, handle domain events, and manage cross-cutting concerns. MediatR decouples the HTTP layer from application logic by routing commands and queries through a single in-process mediator. Each use-case is a self-contained `IRequestHandler<TRequest, TResponse>` that can be tested without the HTTP layer.

```csharp
// Install: dotnet add package MediatR
// Program.cs — register MediatR with all handlers in the assembly
builder.Services.AddMediatR(cfg =>
    cfg.RegisterServicesFromAssembly(typeof(Program).Assembly));

// --- Command (write operation, no return value) ---
public sealed record CreateOrderCommand(string CustomerId, List<int> ProductIds)
    : IRequest<Guid>;  // IRequest<TResponse> — expects a response

public sealed class CreateOrderHandler(IOrderRepository repo, IMediator mediator)
    : IRequestHandler<CreateOrderCommand, Guid>
{
    public async Task<Guid> Handle(CreateOrderCommand cmd, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = new Order(Guid.NewGuid(), cmd.CustomerId, cmd.ProductIds);
        await repo.SaveAsync(order, ct);

        // Publish a notification (fire-and-forget in-process event)
        await mediator.Publish(new OrderCreatedEvent(order.Id), ct);

        return order.Id;
    }
}

// --- Query (read operation, no side effects) ---
public sealed record GetOrderQuery(Guid OrderId) : IRequest<OrderDto?>;

public sealed class GetOrderHandler(IOrderRepository repo)
    : IRequestHandler<GetOrderQuery, OrderDto?>
{
    public async Task<OrderDto?> Handle(GetOrderQuery query, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await repo.FindAsync(query.OrderId, ct);
        return order is null ? null : new OrderDto(order.Id, order.CustomerId);
    }
}

// --- Notification (event broadcast to multiple handlers) ---
public sealed record OrderCreatedEvent(Guid OrderId) : INotification;

public sealed class OrderCreatedEmailHandler(IEmailService email)
    : INotificationHandler<OrderCreatedEvent>
{
    public async Task Handle(OrderCreatedEvent evt, CancellationToken ct)
        => await email.SendOrderConfirmationAsync(evt.OrderId, ct);
}

// --- Minimal API endpoint — controller replaced by one line ---
app.MapPost("/orders", async (CreateOrderCommand cmd, IMediator mediator, CancellationToken ct)
    => Results.Created($"/orders/{await mediator.Send(cmd, ct)}", null));

app.MapGet("/orders/{id:guid}", async (Guid id, IMediator mediator, CancellationToken ct)
    => await mediator.Send(new GetOrderQuery(id), ct) is { } dto
        ? Results.Ok(dto)
        : Results.NotFound());
```

### MediatR Pipeline Behaviours — Cross-Cutting Concerns

```csharp
// IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse> — wraps every handler call
// Use for: logging, validation (FluentValidation), performance timing, transactions

public sealed class LoggingBehaviour<TRequest, TResponse>(ILogger<LoggingBehaviour<TRequest, TResponse>> logger)
    : IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>
    where TRequest : IRequest<TResponse>
{
    public async Task<TResponse> Handle(
        TRequest request, RequestHandlerDelegate<TResponse> next, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var name = typeof(TRequest).Name;
        logger.LogInformation("Handling {Request}", name);
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        try
        {
            return await next();
        }
        finally
        {
            logger.LogInformation("Handled {Request} in {ElapsedMs}ms", name, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
        }
    }
}

// Register behaviours — ORDER MATTERS: first registered wraps outermost
builder.Services.AddTransient(typeof(IPipelineBehavior<,>), typeof(LoggingBehaviour<,>));
```

Tradeoff: MediatR adds one layer of indirection for every request, making stack traces slightly longer and IDE "go to definition" navigation requires knowing whether a class implements `IRequestHandler` or `INotificationHandler`. The benefit is that each use-case is independently testable — `new CreateOrderHandler(mockRepo, mockMediator).Handle(cmd, ct)` requires no HTTP context or controller lifecycle. The main risk is accidental notification fan-out: if two `INotificationHandler<OrderCreatedEvent>` implementations are registered and one throws, MediatR v12+ (Publish behavior: `AllHandlers`) does not stop others from executing — exceptions are aggregated into an `AggregateException`. Use `MediatR.Contracts` `INotificationHandler` for truly independent handlers; use a typed `IRequestHandler` pipeline for handlers where ordering and failure propagation matter.

## Real-World Gotchas — `required`, EditorConfig, Dapper, MediatR [community]

**G86** — A class with `required` properties fails JSON deserialization with `System.Text.Json` on .NET 7 because the deserializer does not know about `required` init members and does not call a constructor
Why this matters: A developer adds `required` to a DTO used for `HttpClient` response deserialization. On .NET 7, `System.Text.Json` attempts to use the parameterless constructor and then set properties. Because `required` init-only properties can only be set during object initialization (the object initializer phase, which the deserializer cannot reproduce), the deserializer throws `InvalidOperationException: The required members list changed between initialization`. The fix on .NET 7 is to add `[SetsRequiredMembers]` to the parameterless constructor AND mark the properties as `set` instead of `init`. On .NET 8+, `System.Text.Json` respects `required init` automatically — no workaround needed; the exact .NET version is the decisive factor.
Fix: Use `init` + `required` freely in .NET 8+ projects. For .NET 7 projects, either use `[SetsRequiredMembers]` on the parameterless constructor or switch to `set` instead of `init`. Add a comment in the constructor marking the .NET version restriction so future maintainers know when to clean it up.

**G87** — `.editorconfig` rule `csharp_style_var_for_built_in_types = false:error` breaks generated code files that use `var int` / `var string` constructs emitted by source generators, because generated files inherit the editorconfig rules unless explicitly excluded
Why this matters: A developer enforces the `var` convention as `:error` severity. Roslyn source generators emit files into the `obj/` folder during build. If the `.editorconfig` does not exclude `*.g.cs` files, the code analysis treats generated file violations as build errors. The build fails on first `dotnet build` after enabling the rule, even though the generated code is not editable by the developer.
Fix: Add a dedicated `[*.g.cs]` section at the bottom of `.editorconfig` with `generated_code = true` and disable all style rules: `dotnet_analyzer_diagnostic.category-Style.severity = none`. Alternatively, use the `<GeneratedCodeAnalysis>` MSBuild property in the project file: `<AnalysisMode>AllEnabledByDefault</AnalysisMode>` combined with a suppressor attribute.

**G88** — Dapper's `QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<T>` returns `default(T)` when the record is not found — for value types like `int` or `Guid`, this is indistinguishable from a valid zero-value result, silently returning wrong data
Why this matters: A developer queries `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = @Id` using `QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<int>`. When the CustomerId does not exist, Dapper returns `0` — which is the correct count AND the `default(int)` fallback. For a COUNT query this is harmless. But for an `Id` query — `SELECT Id FROM Orders WHERE Code = @Code` — returning `0` as the "not found" sentinel is wrong; an integer primary key of `0` might be a valid row in some schemas, causing silent data corruption. The developer confuses the `default(T)` sentinel with a real result.
Fix: Use `QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<T?>` (nullable value type) for queries that can legitimately return no rows: `QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<int?>` returns `null` for no-result and the actual count for a match. Alternatively, use `QuerySingleAsync<T>` which throws `InvalidOperationException` when zero rows are returned, making the "not found" case an exception that must be explicitly handled.

**G89** — MediatR `INotificationHandler` implementations registered in the DI container are invoked in registration order during `Publish`, but this order is non-deterministic across builds when using `RegisterServicesFromAssembly` because it scans types using reflection in CLR-defined order
Why this matters: A developer writes two handlers for `OrderCreatedEvent`: one sends a confirmation email and one updates an analytics counter. In local development, the email handler always runs first (alphabetical scanning order happens to match registration order). After a refactor that renames the analytics handler, CLR type reflection returns it first, and the analytics update now runs before the email. This reveals a hidden ordering dependency: the analytics handler was accidentally depending on a side effect produced by the email handler (a cache entry). The bug only manifests in staging, not locally.
Fix: Never write `INotificationHandler` implementations that depend on the order of sibling handlers. If ordering matters, use the pipeline behaviour pattern (`IPipelineBehavior`) or explicit orchestration inside a single handler. Use MediatR's `PublishStrategy` (`Async` vs `SyncContinueOnException`) to make concurrency semantics explicit rather than relying on registration order.

**G90** — `csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped:error` in `.editorconfig` does not apply retroactively to existing files until `dotnet format` is explicitly run — a developer who only runs `dotnet build` sees no violations, then CI fails on a fresh checkout
Why this matters: A developer adds the rule to `.editorconfig` and runs `dotnet build` locally — it passes because existing files already violate the rule and the build does not run `dotnet format`. The developer pushes. CI runs `dotnet build` and also passes. A second CI step runs `dotnet format --verify-no-changes`, which fails with hundreds of violations in existing files. The first developer is blamed for introducing the violations even though the existing files were always non-compliant.
Fix: Always run `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` as a pre-commit hook or CI gate when adding new `:error` editorconfig rules. Before adding the rule, run `dotnet format` to fix all pre-existing violations in a dedicated "style cleanup" commit, so future CI failures only relate to new code. Document the cleanup commit in the PR so reviewers do not mistake it for a semantic change.

## Anti-Patterns Quick Reference — `required`, EditorConfig, Dapper, MediatR

| Anti-Pattern | Why It's Harmful | What to Do Instead |
|-------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Using `required` init properties in a DTO on .NET 7 with `System.Text.Json` | Deserializer cannot set required init members on .NET 7; throws at runtime | Use `[SetsRequiredMembers]` + set (not init) on .NET 7; use required init freely on .NET 8+ |
| Setting `.editorconfig` style rules to `:error` without excluding generated `*.g.cs` files | Source-generator output inherits rules and fails the build even though the files are not editable | Add `[*.g.cs]` section with `generated_code = true` and suppress all style diagnostics |
| `QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<int>` for queries that can return no rows | Returns `0` (default) which is indistinguishable from a valid zero result | Use nullable type `QueryFirstOrDefaultAsync<int?>` or `QuerySingleAsync<T>` to force explicit not-found handling |
| Writing `INotificationHandler` implementations with hidden ordering dependencies | Handler execution order is non-deterministic across builds with assembly scanning | Use `IPipelineBehavior` for ordered cross-cutting concerns; never depend on sibling handler side effects |
| Adding `.editorconfig` `:error` rules without running `dotnet format` to fix pre-existing violations | CI fails on existing code, not new violations; misleads blame and blocks all merges | Run `dotnet format` cleanup commit first; use `--verify-no-changes` in CI after the cleanup baseline is established |
